artigo.texto: What to know: - The proposed data center in Inkster will not move forward. The City Council took no action to approve the project after a packed meeting filled with residents opposing the proposal. - The project would have converted a vacant warehouse. Developer Robert Kato of Klever Technology Center LLC sought a special land use permit to turn a 40,000-square-foot building on Southern Street, near Michigan Avenue, into a data center. - Residents turned out in force to oppose the plan. Inkster City Hall reached capacity, forcing some residents to wait outside as the council meeting continued. - Environmental concerns were a major issue. Residents raised concerns about potential environmental impacts, noise pollution and light pollution associated with the proposed facility. - Some residents wanted different businesses at the site. Community members argued that Inkster would be better served by attracting other types of businesses to the vacant property. INKSTER, Mich. — A proposed data center in Inkster will not move forward after a standing-room-only crowd of residents packed city hall to oppose the project — and the city council declined to act on it. The developer, Robert Kato of Klever Technology Center LLC, had applied for a special land use permit to convert a vacant 40,000-square-foot warehouse on Southern Street off Michigan Avenue into a data center. No council member made a motion to approve the request, effectively halting the project. Kato told Local 4 after the meeting that he does not plan to appeal the decision and does not plan to move forward with the data center at that location. Inkster City Hall was filled to capacity, with residents forced to wait outside as the council debated inside. A line of residents stretched out the door throughout the meeting. For hours, community members spoke out against the project, raising concerns about environmental impact, noise, and light pollution. While Kato responded to questions from the crowd, many residents said they believed the city would be better served by attracting different types of businesses to the location. Kato told Local 4 he has the building under contract and formed an LLC to pursue the data center project. The city’s Planning Commission had recommended the council grant conditional approval of the project following a public hearing Oct. 12. Despite that recommendation, no council member moved to approve the special land use.

artigo.texto: Jeep Avenger X BYD Dolphin Mini: qual é o melhor carro por R$ 120 mil? Recém-chegado a combustão encarou o primeiro carro elétrico a figurar no top três dos mais vendidos do Brasil. A BYD lançou oficialmente nesta terça-feira (20) a segunda geração do Dolphin Mini na China — conhecido no mercado asiático como Seagull. O pequeno hatch elétrico passou por uma reformulação profunda: cresceu em dimensões, ganhou um pacote tecnológico muito mais sofisticado com sensor LiDAR e estreou preços altamente competitivos, partindo de menos de R$ 50 mil na conversão direta — conforme o Jornal do Carro já havia adiantado. Com o salto geracional, o compacto assume um posicionamento mais refinado na linha de veículos elétricos da marca chinesa, ficando muito mais próximo do irmão maior Dolphin, mas mantendo a proposta de valor acessível. Leia também - Como o ‘cheiro de carro novo’ mexe com o seu cérebro - ADAS no carro: quatro perguntas antes de confiar ou de comprar - Cadillac Escalade pode fazer o motorista ‘enxergar’ na escuridão da estrada ou na neblina densa A mudança mais perceptível do novo BYD Dolphin Mini está no seu porte. O hatch cresceu 42 cm em relação à primeira geração, alcançando 4,20 metros de comprimento, 1,81 m de largura, 1,57 m de altura e generosos 2,65 m de entre-eixos. Para se ter uma ideia, ele ficou apenas 6 cm mais curto que o Dolphin tradicional. Por fora, o modelo mantém linhas futuristas e aerodinâmicas, mas agora calça rodas de 16 polegadas com desenho de oito raios e adota um conjunto óptico mais agressivo. A transição para um motor elétrico posicionado no eixo traseiro também abriu espaço sob o capô, criando um compartimento dianteiro (frunk) de 94 litros. Já o porta-malas principal pode chegar a 1.380 litros com os bancos traseiros rebatidos. Interior tecnológico traz bancos com massagem Por dentro, a cabine foi totalmente redesenhada. O tradicional quadro de instrumentos atrás do volante foi eliminado — uma mudança ousada que concentra todas as informações vitais em uma grande tela central flutuante de 12,8″, que exibe velocidade, autonomia, modos de condução e entretenimento em alta resolução. O hatch elétrico também traz console central ampliado, volante de dois raios, iluminação ambiente e saídas de ar dedicadas aos ocupantes do banco traseiro. Porém, o principal destaque são os novos equipamentos sofisticados que normalmente vemos apenas em carros mais caros, como ajustes elétricos para os bancos dianteiros e função de massagem para o motorista, além de compartimentos inteligentes sob os assentos traseiros — resta saber se todos esses equipamentos também estarão disponíveis para o mercado brasileiro quando (e se) o carro vier. Motor de 127 cv e recarga ultrarrápida O conjunto mecânico acompanhou o crescimento do carro. O novo Dolphin Mini abandona a motorização básica anterior e passa a contar com um propulsor elétrico traseiro de 127 cv de potência. Há também outra versão mais simples, que desenvolve 114 cv. O torque é sempre de 13,2 kgfm. Em termos de energia, a marca oferece duas opções de baterias de LFP (fosfato de ferro-lítio): 30 kWh e 39,2 kWh. A autonomia declarada varia de 320 km a 420 km no ciclo chinês (CLTC). Uma das grandes inovações técnicas reveladas no lançamento é a tecnologia de carregamento ultrarrápido nas versões topo de linha, capaz de repor a carga de 10% a 70% em apenas 5 minutos. Esse carregador de alta potência, aliás, já foi confirmado pela BYD para o Brasil, com previsão de até mil unidades instaladas por aqui. Outra atualização importante na linha do compacto está na tecnologia de assistência autônoma. O modelo passa a contar com o sistema avançado à condução God’s Eye B (DiPilot 300) integrado ao teto. O sensor LiDAR permite que o veículo escaneie o trânsito em 3D e em tempo real. Com isso, o carro ganha capacidades de navegação assistida em vias urbanas e rodovias, estacionamento automatizado e mudanças de faixa autônomas. artigo.texto: Amazon is backing out of planned data center project at former GW campus ARLINGTON, Va. (7News) — Amazon has backed off of plans to develop a massive data center complex on the former site of George Washington University's Ashburn, Virginia, campus, according to the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors. During Tuesday's general meeting, Board Supervisors said it will work with the company to use the land for mixed-use projects including housing, and that it could be the site of an indoor sports arena and community arts center. PREVIOUS | George Washington University sells Ashburn campus to Amazon Board chair Phyllis Randall said the company also provided $5 million to the county's housing trust fund and funding to support scholarships. "We knew we don't want the data centers on that campus. There's a lot of places we don't want to see data centers, but definitely on that campus," Randall said. "And the fact that we won't see data centers, and we will see so many of the needs that we have to see in Loudoun County and that we wanted to see in Loudoun County for a long time is just tremendous." “Our team moved to seize this opportunity when approached by the University about a sale – but as we heard the community’s pointed concerns about data center development at this particular site, we took them seriously," Amazon Vice President for Data Center Delivery, Josh Weissman said in a statement. "While we see the property’s legal development potential differently than the County does, we concluded that the best outcome for all is to come together on a shared vision for this campus rather than engage in costly litigation. Project Potomac Promise reflects that choice, and we look forward to working with Chair Randall, the County staff, and development partners to move this plan forward." Amazon initially purchased 122-acre GW's Science and Technology Campus in February to develop four data centers with a total of 800,000 square feet in use. Some pushed back on the decision, including Loudoun County Supervisor Juli Briskman, who represents the district the campus is located in and who claimed the company hadn't consulted her office before the purchase. Board Supervisor Kristen Umstattd provided some pushback to the plan, voicing concerns of the cost of the houses and roads. The board moved to direct the County administrator to rezone the land to include residential use and remove zoning for data centers.

artigo.texto: Communities across the U.S. are fighting back against data center developments — and winning. According to a recent report, at least $260 billion in data center projects were cancelled so far this year thanks to the efforts of local organizers. While Donald Trump has thrown his support and funding behind expanding AI infrastructure, opposition remains strong: an NBC News poll found that nearly 70% of participants do not support AI data center construction. That is unwelcome news, of course, for those poised to profit from the AI boom. And reports have uncovered campaigns already working to undermine resistance to data centers. Several of these online disinformation campaigns are run by groups overseas and aim to discredit and influence data center protests in the U.S. For instance, in June, OpenAI published a report claiming that its model was used by accounts originating in China to generate content supporting a covert influence operation attempting to manipulate legitimate conversation about data centers. In July, an investigative report by Alethea, a tech company that assesses online threats, found that countries such as Russia and Iran were responsible for spreading data center misinformation. To be fair, as many experts explained, these acts alone are not entirely responsible for the tension between those who embrace AI development and those fighting against it. As bad actors, both within and outside of the U.S., seek to derail momentum and sideline community voices, those challenging data center development must remain informed and vigilant, taking care not to succumb to disinformation designed to stymie collective action. Here’s how we do it. First, what are data centers? These facilities house the computing infrastructure used to train artificial intelligence models and generate results through a process known as inference, making them essential to the AI industry. According to a Pew Research Center analysis, more than 3,000 data centers are operating in the United States, while more than 1,500 others are in various stages of development. Today, 38% of Americans live within five miles of at least one operational data center, and as their numbers grow, communities are raising concerns about noise, rising electricity bills, heavy water consumption, and air pollution. To maintain resistance to further development, it is imperative to base your opinions on factual information. Community organizers and protesters must seek out and share credible information rather than relying on blogs, essays, and articles that offer speculation or opinion without solid evidence. Independent research organizations increasingly provide publicly available analysis of data centers’ environmental impacts. A recent report from the think tank Next10 and researchers at Santa Clara University, for example, found that data center operators in California often avoid disclosing how much water they use. Such research can give communities a strong evidentiary basis for organizing and holding operators accountable. Fact-checking organizations can also help by publishing explainers and reports that challenge false claims about data centers. Government records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act offer another valuable source of reliable evidence. It goes without saying that protesting AI data centers is a legitimate cause. Communities have the right to protect their lands, health, and access to natural resources, and advancing this cause requires focusing on facts and science to avoid misdirection and keep achieving their goals. Demands for transparency and accountability, hard-won results of organizing, are critical, as questions about the extent of environmental damage remain unanswered. In fact, investigating some of the harm of these centers may require long-term empirical studies. Currently, several pieces of legislation, some at the federal and state levels, request investigations into the environmental impact of AI data centers. A recent survey of Northern Virginia residents found divided “views on living near and among data centers”: half of respondents support data centers in their communities, while the rest are neutral or opposed. Even opponents may disagree over strategy, with some favoring a permanent ban on AI data centers and others supporting a temporary moratorium. Such divisions create openings for disinformation campaigns targeting data center protestors. Sustaining effective resistance will require residents to keep talking, identify their shared concerns, and build consensus around a common position.

artigo.texto: Nebraska data center leaders talk natural resource protection, responsible development By Macy Byars, Reporter Nebraska Public Media News Oct. 22, 2026, 7:50 p.m. · Three Nebraska data center leaders discussed responsible data center development, water and energy usage and community pushback Wednesday at a renewable energy conference panel. Bringing more data centers to Nebraska is a contentious topic. City council and county board meetings discussing data centers have drawn large crowds of opposition across party lines. The panel covered a few of these common concerns, including water consumption, strain on Nebraska’s power system and community impact. Kearney Mayor Jonathan Nikkila said citizen engagement is an involved process, but it is key to creating city regulations. “I'm really thankful for the citizen push, because if they hadn't pushed us at that moment at that time we wouldn't have been ready. Instead, we were able to set the expectations for what we wanted from that kind of development in our town,” Nikkila said at the Nebraska Wind and Solar Conference panel. “Instead of reacting, we were the ones explaining what we expected from them.” More than a dozen Nebraska counties have placed moratoriums on new data centers as a response to the backlash. But other counties are rethinking zoning rules, possibly to allow for data center construction. Responsible resource management Developers are eyeing the Midwest for its wide swaths of land and access to natural resources – like water. Data centers can use anywhere from thousands to millions of gallons of water per day to cool processing chips. Panelist John Winkler is the general manager of the Papio-Missouri Natural Resources District and a Nebraska Data Center Task Force member. He said Nebraska has strong regulatory safeguards to protect groundwater. “There isn't one data center in Nebraska that's using any aquifer water. Every data center that we have is hooked up to a municipal supply,” he said. Those regulations allow Nebraska NRDs to ask industries for analysis on how they would impact the area’s water. Winkler said he is “very comfortable” with the systems Nebraska has to manage data center water usage. “There's a lot of coordination between not only the local jurisdictions but also the state as well,” Winkler said. “There isn't going to be a user that pops up in the middle of the night that throws a bunch of straws into an aquifer and drains it. It's just not going to happen in the state of Nebraska.” The Nebraska Legislature has also tried to safeguard the cost of energy. Passed last session, LB1261 allows private power developers to generate on-site energy for industrial customers – like data center companies – without interference from Nebraska’s public power sector. The bill was supported by Gov. Jim Pillen. Tax incentives for data centers are also restricted following an executive order signed by Pillen in September. He also appointed the Nebraska Data Center Task Force made up of energy, infrastructure and natural resource management leaders. Data center companies developing large facilities must also provide some kind of “community benefit,” like investing in workforce development or road improvements. Chris Matos, energy market development lead for the central U.S. at Google, said the company is doing what it can to protect natural resources when developing data centers. “Google, as a company, has a corporate goal to return 130% of our water usage nationally,” Matos said. “You see that play out here in Nebraska, actually, with our investments in agricultural water initiatives, where we're helping farmers optimize or reduce their water uses using drift lines.” On Monday, Google announced a $6 million contribution to help Omaha Public Power District customers with their bills, install leak detection sensors and invest in clean energy generation. “It works best when we do it with our utility partners because it offers the right mix, I think, of us being the anchor load for those big investments that are needed – particularly as infrastructure is aging and needs to be replaced with newer, more efficient and cheaper resources – where we can.” Matos said Google has made other significant investments in infrastructure that shield ratepayers from increased energy costs. “We did learn that lesson with OPPD and others where we were realizing that our ramp schedules were off due to delays, and we figured out how to make sure that those costs that were being incurred by OPPD were not shared amongst ratepayers,” he said. Water cooling is 30% more efficient than air cooling, said Matos, but Google does switch to air cooling when surface water supply can’t support operations. Matos said Google’s data centers aren’t using less water for cooling, but the computing power they can get from their current water usage is increasing. “Over the last five years, we've reduced our overhead energy demand by 83%. Now, that hasn't slowed down the demand at the data center – we still draw the same amount of power. It increases what we can do with that compute power,” he said. Energy demand is already a top issue in the state – which panelists say data centers are rapidly requiring Nebraska to push forward on. “We're at that point now where we've used up all of our excess generation capacity that was built back in the late '80s and '90s, and so we're at that point where we need to to build more generation,” Winkler said. Managing negative publicity Nebraska could stand to benefit from the industries, jobs and economic boost that data centers bring. artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 19 de outubro de 2026, às 11:05 Um porta-voz da Microsoft afirmou que a empresa mantém seu compromisso com a parceria com a Nscale e que a decisão de desistir do acordo para locar capacidade de um data center da Nscale Global Holdings no Reino Unido refere-se apenas a essa unidade específica. A instalação em Loughton, em Essex, na Inglaterra, deveria entrar em operação até o final deste ano, mas a Nscale informou que isso não será mais possível, devido a desafios relacionados à rede elétrica do Reino Unido. A Nscale também disse estar comprometida tanto com o projeto em Loughton quanto com o Reino Unido. “Estamos explorando fontes de energia alternativas para o local, além de avaliar outras áreas para expansão no país. Nosso relacionamento com a Microsoft permanece sólido e de longo prazo; esse problema na rede elétrica – que afeta toda a região de Londres – não impacta nossos outros contratos”, declarou um porta-voz da empresa. No ano passado, a Nscale informou que havia adquirido um local em Loughton, nos arredores de Londres, para seu primeiro data center no Reino Unido. A Microsoft locaria a instalação de 50 megawatts, equipada com cerca de 23.000 chips Nvidia GB300, para sustentar os serviços do Microsoft Azure. A decisão da Microsoft representa um revés para a Nscale, sediada no Reino Unido, pois demonstra que clientes podem cancelar acordos caso projetos sofram atrasos por circunstâncias imprevistas, o que coloca em risco os fluxos de receita. artigo.texto: Rondo Energy and Rio Tinto Advance Australia's Largest Thermal Energy Storage Project GLADSTONE, Australia, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rondo Energy and Rio Tinto have started front-end engineering and design on the project for a 360 MWh storage / 30 MW discharge Rondo Heat Battery, supported by a grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA). ARENA's funding for the project will be provided in stages, with an initial $3.6 million to complete front-end engineering and design work. Following successful completion of that study, ARENA will provide up to $38 million for deployment. ARENA has also approved up to $33.3 million in conditional contingency support, which would only be made available in defined circumstances to manage specific project risks, including cost overruns and electricity costs. If progressed, the project would be delivered at Rio Tinto's Yarwun alumina refinery near Gladstone, Queensland and would be one of the first large-scale demonstrations of thermal energy storage for industrial process heat globally, and a world-first for the alumina industry. Rondo Heat Batteries use abundant, low-cost midday electricity to charge, storing energy as high-temperature heat in refractory brick, and supplying energy as 24/7 continuous process heat to industry. Typically, the heat is delivered as steam, directly into an industrial facility's steam network. Australia regularly has 4-6 hours of surplus solar-generated renewable electricity in the middle of the day, but industrial facilities need heat 24 hours a day, not just when the sun is shining. By charging when electricity is cheap and abundant and discharging continuously, Rondo Heat Batteries turn short periods of low-cost electricity into 24/7 delivery of low-cost steam. For energy-intensive industries such as alumina refining, Rondo Heat Batteries create a pathway to electrification that addresses both emissions and energy costs. Because the heat battery slots into the existing steam network, the facility's processes run exactly as before — the only thing that changes is the energy for that heat: no longer from fossil fuels, but sourced from low cost electricity instead. The Yarwun study will assess the technical and economic viability of integrating the technology into refinery operations. "This project shows how Australia's abundant energy can become a competitive advantage for industry," said Dr. Kira Rundel, Rondo's Head of Australia. "Heat batteries allow manufacturers to use low-cost electricity to produce the reliable, round-the-clock heat their operations need. Australia's largest heat battery will show how factories can cut emissions without increasing energy costs, helping Australian industry to increase global competitiveness and supporting local manufacturing jobs." Rio Tinto Pacific Operations Managing Director Armando Torres said: "Reducing emissions from alumina refining is complex, particularly when it comes to generating the high-pressure steam needed for our operations. "This study will help us determine whether thermal energy storage can provide a technically and economically viable alternative to fossil fuels for part of Yarwun's steam requirements. "The best way to tackle challenges of this scale is through collaboration between industry, government, and technology partners. We welcome ARENA and Rondo's support as we assess technologies that could help reduce our Scope 1 emissions while maintaining reliable operations at Yarwun." About Rondo Energy Rondo Energy delivers firm heat and power, including combined heat and power (CHP), to heavy industry and provides power solutions and long duration storage to data centers. For industrial heat applications, Rondo Heat Batteries convert 4-6 hours of low-cost electricity into continuous 24-hour, high-temperature heat, delivered as steam or hot air up to 1,000°C. The heat delivered integrates directly with existing industrial equipment and processes, eliminating on-site emissions and running on lower cost energy. Rondo heat storage can integrate with steam turbines to deliver combined heat and power (CHP) for industry, and long duration power-to-power solutions for large energy consumers such as data centers. Built on proven refractory brick as the thermal storage medium, Rondo's platform is engineered for multi-decade operation in the most demanding industrial environments. Rondo Heat Batteries have been delivering firm heat and power at scale since 2023, with operational facilities serving customers in fuels and cement (including steam driving turbines for electricity) in the United States and in Asia. The next unit will come online shortly - a 100 MWh Rondo Heat Battery under construction in Europe for a chemical plant. Rondo is a global company based in California, with teams across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Australia. Providing heat and power solutions to the alumina industry is an area of focus for the company due to the strong fit of Rondo's technology with the heat and power needs of the alumina industry. artigo.texto: Featured Fairfield council calls meeting to discuss data centers Daily Republic Staff Oct 22, 2026 1 hr ago 0 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save FAIRFIELD — The City Council called for a special meeting Nov. 10 to discuss data centers and possible moratorium on them. The suggestion came during council updates. A Facebook post surfaced late last week saying Vice Mayor Pam Bertani would bring up the topic. Appointed Mayor Rick Vaccaro initiated the conversation. Bertani noted she had prepared a motion for a moratorium. The item will be discussed at 5 p.m. in the Harry T. Price Memorial Council Chamber, 1000 Webster St. Several people were in attendance to support the idea. None supported the idea of a data center. A proposed project, to be built between Vanden Road and North Gate Road, includes a data center. "I'm here to speak on the moratorium," Monte Hoover said. "I am not against date centers in general." As a longtime business owner, Hoover said he has dealt with many issues over the years, such as permit issues, etc. "Data centers have no requirements," he said. Two One Lake residents, where the data center would be located, also asked the city to consider a moratorium on data center development in Fairfield. One man said he feels Fairfield mirrors the sentiment of most cities that don't want data centers near their homes. Gail Mahoney said there is not enough information on data centers and was concerned one would "suck our water away," especially since living through the drought. "We should not rush in," Robert Myers said. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- Data from the Tianyancha app shows CATL Chery (Wuhu) New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. has officially registered. Capitalized at 1 billion yuan, the entity is jointly held by CATL and Chery Automobile. Corporate filings indicate this is the second joint venture established by the pair in 2026 focused on battery manufacturing, signaling a deeper integration of their industrial chains. Image Source: Tianyancha App The new company’s business scope spans battery manufacturing, the production and sales of components, and energy storage technical services. It will focus on the R&D and manufacturing of power battery-related products. Back in February 2026, the partners had already registered CATL Chery (Hefei) New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. with a registered capital of 2 billion yuan. CATL holds a 51% stake, while Chery Automobile and Chery Commercial Vehicle collectively hold the remaining 49%. With combined registered capital totaling 3 billion yuan, the Hefei and Wuhu joint ventures appear designed to establish a dual power battery footprint in Anhui province. Image Source: CATL The partnership has deep roots. In 2023, CATL and Chery jointly launched the battery brand ENER-Q, with Chery becoming the first to equip its models with sodium-ion batteries. In April 2026, Chery, CATL, CATL Amperex, and Chery Green Energy signed a strategic cooperation agreement to coordinate on the development of chargeable and swappable models and the rollout of battery swapping networks, aiming to advance a vehicle-energy integration ecosystem. This sustained, multi-tiered collaboration is set to secure a stable supply of core products—including Qilin and sodium-ion batteries—for Chery’s new energy models. The two sides are also jointly pushing the commercial application of frontier technologies like semi-solid-state batteries and battery swapping. Establishing joint ventures between automakers and leading battery makers has become a defining model for deep integration in the new energy supply chain. For Chery, this move locks in battery production capacity and mitigates supply chain volatility, underpinning the sales growth of its new energy lineup. CATL, meanwhile, secures a deeper tie with a key OEM, stabilizing order volume and leveraging Anhui’s industrial cluster advantages to expand its share of the power battery and energy storage markets. As these two major joint venture projects advance, the partners are poised to build synergies in both battery costs and the speed of deploying new technologies.

artigo.texto: As concessionárias de transmissão de energia elétrica podem participar dos leilões de reserva de capacidade com sistemas de armazenamento em baterias (BESS), desde que obtenham autorização prévia da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e cumpram condições previstas nos contratos de concessão. Entre elas está a demonstração de benefícios para os consumidores, com a possibilidade de reversão total ou parcial das receitas obtidas com a nova atividade para a modicidade tarifária. O entendimento é da Procuradoria Federal junto à Aneel, que analisou a possibilidade de atuação das transmissoras no segmento de armazenamento a partir de uma consulta envolvendo a Taesa. A companhia solicitou à agência a ratificação de seu entendimento de que poderia disputar futuros leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) com sistemas de armazenamento autônomos. A Procuradoria concluiu que não há proibição legal para que transmissoras desenvolvam atividades fora do objeto de suas concessões, diferentemente das restrições expressas impostas às distribuidoras. A participação nos certames, contudo, não é automática e depende das condições estabelecidas nos contratos de transmissão. A Taesa discorda de parte desse entendimento. Em posicionamento enviado à MegaWhat, a companhia afirmou que o marco regulatório já dispõe de mecanismos suficientes para permitir a participação dos agentes, sem a necessidade de uma exigência adicional de autorização contratual prévia. A transmissora também contesta a classificação das receitas fixas dos contratos de armazenamento como receitas acessórias da transmissão. Segundo a empresa, os empreendimentos possuem patrimônio, contabilidade, financiamento, obrigações e outorgas próprios, o que justificaria o tratamento independente dessas receitas. Em agosto, a Aneel autorizou a ISA Energia Brasil a explorar atividades atípicas relacionadas à prestação de serviços de eficiência energética e uso racional da energia para clientes B2B, utilizando sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS). O aval contemplo uma atividade econômica diferente daquelas diretamente previstas nos contratos de concessão de transmissão da empresa. Como não havia regulamentação específica da agência sobre a prestação desse tipo de serviço, foi necessário solicitar anuência. Transmissoras poderão atuar por meio de subsidiárias O parecer considera juridicamente admissível que concessionárias de transmissão participem dos leilões de baterias por meio de subsidiárias ou sociedades de propósito específico (SPEs) com objeto social próprio. Essa estrutura, no entanto, não dispensa a autorização regulatória. Segundo a Procuradoria, o exercício de atividades fora do objeto da concessão depende de anuência prévia da Aneel, independentemente de ocorrer diretamente pela transmissora ou por meio de outra empresa controlada. A análise tomou como referência cláusulas do contrato de concessão nº 05/2023 da Taesa, que permitem o desenvolvimento de outras atividades empresariais, desde que observadas as exigências regulatórias. Entre as condições apontadas estão a manutenção de registros contábeis, demonstrações financeiras, fluxos de caixa, contratos e relatórios gerenciais individualizados, de forma a impedir a confusão patrimonial entre a concessão de transmissão e os negócios de armazenamento. A fiscalização dessas condições caberia à Superintendência de Fiscalização Econômica e Financeira (SFF) da Aneel. O parecer também destaca que, em regra, a responsabilidade da transmissora como sócia ou controladora de uma SPE de armazenamento ficaria limitada à sua participação e à integralização do capital social da subsidiária. Receitas de baterias podem ser revertidas O parecer também descreve a necessidade de que a participação das transmissoras em atividades de armazenamento poderá produzir benefícios econômicos para a concessão e, consequentemente, para os usuários do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A Procuradoria aponta que a autorização deverá estar condicionada à preservação da modicidade tarifária, mediante reversão total ou parcial das receitas obtidas com a nova atividade, conforme as disposições do contrato de concessão analisado. Para o órgão, o pedido poderá ser deferido caso fique demonstrado, de maneira objetiva e juridicamente vinculante, que a exploração do armazenamento por meio de uma subsidiária produzirá benefícios econômicos concretos para a concessão. A avaliação caberá à Aneel, que deve considerar as circunstâncias específicas de cada pedido e o interesse público, especialmente a continuidade da prestação do serviço de transmissão e a modicidade tarifária. Taesa contesta exigências para participar dos leilões A Taesa afirmou à MegaWhat que vem desenvolvendo estudos para avaliar oportunidades de negócios relacionadas aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A companhia considera que a tecnologia é necessária para o avanço da transição energética e para aumentar a resiliência e a confiabilidade das redes de transmissão e distribuição. Segundo a empresa, o mercado brasileiro de armazenamento ainda está em desenvolvimento e parte das regras permanece em construção. Nesse contexto, a transmissora entende que o posicionamento sobre a necessidade de anuência prévia e sobre a classificação dos contratos de armazenamento como receitas acessórias ocorreu em caráter preliminar e precisa ser aprofundado à luz do arcabouço regulatório aplicável. Na avaliação da Taesa, os mecanismos de controle e as salvaguardas já existentes são suficientes para assegurar a participação dos agentes, sem a imposição de um requisito adicional de autorização contratual prévia. A companhia também sustenta que as receitas fixas provenientes dos contratos dos leilões de reserva de capacidade são juridicamente independentes das receitas da transmissão. artigo.texto: Gelion shares jump 21% after US laboratory validates battery technology Published: 05:30 19 Oct 2026 EDT Gelion PLC (AIM:GELN, OTC:GELNF, FRA:X0S) shares jumped 21% to 16p on Monday after independent testing by the National Laboratory of the Rockies validated key performance characteristics of its next-generation battery technology. The battery materials developer reported preliminary results showing that its Nano-Encapsulated Sulfur (NES) cells retained 92% of their reference capacity despite a 20-fold increase in cycling rate. The findings strengthen the technical evidence behind Gelion’s efforts to commercialise its sulfur-based cathode material for applications requiring high energy capacity and rapid power delivery. The laboratory independently fabricated electrodes using Gelion’s material, assembled coin cells and reproduced key electrochemical results previously observed in the company’s own facilities. The tests confirmed comparable voltage profiles, sulfur utilisation and capacity retention during cycling, demonstrating that the material’s performance could be replicated outside Gelion’s laboratories. The results also complement earlier testing by QinetiQ, which demonstrated sustained high-power operation in independently assembled battery cells under conditions representative of drone cruising and vertical take-off and landing. Gelion is working with the American laboratory under a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement announced in June, which aims to advance its technology towards commercial qualification. The next stage includes developing and testing larger pouch-cell prototypes, moving beyond initial material-level validation toward batteries suitable for practical applications. The programme also aims to support eventual qualification for American government and defence procurement, alongside the development of domestic battery manufacturing capabilities. The latest results follow two automotive developments in October, when Gelion announced a co-funded evaluation programme with a top-five global carmaker on 13 October and a separate material transfer agreement with a top-15 manufacturer on 6 October. The company has also secured a development and scale-up agreement with the Japanese advanced materials group Mitsui Kinzoku, which includes £2 million in staged payments to advance its sulfur battery technology.

artigo.texto: Aurubis AG Major integrated copper producer and busbar manufacturer According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Silvered Copper Busbars market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The world market for silvered copper busbars is entering a structurally stronger demand phase as electrification, high-frequency power conversion, and renewable energy infrastructure scale through 2035. Silvered copper busbars—copper conductive bars with a silver coating that lowers surface-contact resistance and resists oxidation—are increasingly specified in battery energy storage systems (BESS), electric-vehicle charging infrastructure, semiconductor and RF equipment, and precision industrial automation. IndexBox projects the market to expand at a compound annual growth rate in the range of 5–8% over the 2026–2035 forecast horizon, with the strongest momentum in BESS and EV charging applications, where adoption is accelerating at 12–18% per year. Premium specifications, including controlled silver thickness above 2 µm, ultra-low surface roughness, and tight dimensional tolerances, command a 20–40% price uplift over standard commercial grades and are capturing a growing share of orders from semiconductor and RF equipment sectors. Supply remains concentrated, with roughly 30–40% of global production capacity located in China, while Europe, North America, and parts of Southeast Asia operate smaller but technologically specialized facilities. Import dependence in several large end-use markets exceeds 50%, and qualification bottlenecks for certified suppliers create lead times of 6–14 weeks for qualified material. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, demand architecture, supply structure, trade flows, pricing logic, and competitive positioning, with a transparent analytical definition of product scope and segmentation. The baseline scenario for the world silvered copper busbars market assumes continued electrification of energy and transport systems, steady expansion of renewable generation and storage capacity, and gradual recovery in industrial automation investment through the 2026–2035 forecast period. Under this scenario, global demand is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate in the range of 5–8%, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to a materially higher level by 2035. Growth is front-loaded in BESS and EV charging infrastructure, where adoption rates of 12–18% per year outpace traditional industrial automation and power-distribution applications. Premium specifications—controlled silver thickness above 2 µm, ultra-low surface roughness, and tight dimensional tolerances—are expected to capture a growing share of orders, particularly from semiconductor and RF equipment sectors, supporting value growth ahead of volume growth. Supply-side constraints remain a key variable: copper and silver together represent 60–75% of direct material cost, and silver spot price volatility of 20–35% in recent years creates margin pressure on fixed-price contracts. Qualification bottlenecks for ISO- and UL-registered busbar coaters, with lead times of 6–14 weeks for qualified material, may cap near-term upside in fast-growing segments. Trade and tariff complexity, including multiple HS code headings and sector-specific certifications, adds procedural friction across borders. Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the largest consumption and production center, while North America and Europe show above-average growth in BESS and EV charging applications. The baseline assumes no major demand-destroying recession and a gradual easing of silver price volatility as recycling and thrifting reduce silver usage per part by up to 15–20%. Industrial automation and instrumentation represents a mature but steadily expanding demand base for silvered copper busbars. In this segment, busbars are used in control panels, drive systems, programmable logic controllers, and precision measurement instruments where low contact resistance and oxidation resistance are critical for signal integrity and long service life. Current demand is driven by factory automation upgrades, particularly in Asia-Pacific and Europe, where labor cost pressures and quality requirements favor automated production lines. Through 2035, demand-side indicators to watch include industrial robot installations, PLC and drive shipment volumes, and capital expenditure in process industries such as chemicals, food and beverage, and pharmaceuticals. The segment is gradually shifting toward higher-specification busbars as automation equipment becomes more compact and power-dense, requiring tighter dimensional tolerances and improved surface finish. However, growth in this segment is slower than in BESS and EV charging, and price sensitivity is higher, with buyers often qualifying multiple suppliers to maintain competitive pricing. Replacement demand from aging installed systems provides a stable baseline, while new automation projects in emerging markets offer upside. The segment is expected to maintain its position as the largest single application by share, though its relative weight will decline as BESS and EV charging expand faster. Current trend: Steady growth, with increasing specification of silvered busbars in precision control and measurement equipment. Major trends: Compact, power-dense automation equipment requiring tighter tolerances and improved surface finish, Factory automation upgrades in Asia-Pacific and Europe driven by labor cost pressures, Increasing integration of busbars in modular control panels and drive systems, and Growing replacement demand from aging installed automation systems. Representative participants: Siemens AG, Schneider Electric SE, ABB Ltd, Rockwell Automation, Inc, and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation. artigo.texto: BYD Ties Its European Future to 3,000 Fast Chargers as Deliveries Ease Published on 10/20/2026 at 06:41 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is betting that the infrastructure behind the electric car matters as much as the vehicle itself. At the Paris Motor Show, the Chinese group laid out plans to install 3,000 fast-charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027, a build-out meant to win buyers over to its own rapid-charging technology. The announcement came alongside new metal: the seven-seat ATTO 8 flagship SUV and the second generation of the company's Blade battery, shown together with models from its Denza brand. The ATTO 8 will be the first BYD model in Europe to carry the flash-charging system. Its second-generation Blade pack, rated at 115 kilowatt-hours, is designed for a range of up to 653 kilometers on the WLTP cycle. European launch is slated for the first quarter of 2027. A Wider Push Beyond Passenger Cars The charging pledge is only one strand of a broader international strategy. BYD Energy Storage, the group's battery-storage arm, unveiled a global after-sales network for its storage systems. The structure spans nine operations and maintenance centers and draws on more than 200 field engineers, with additional sites in South Africa and Bulgaria already scheduled for 2027. Over 100 research and development specialists are tied into the network, a move aimed at giving commercial customers technical support well after installation and reinforcing confidence in the reliability of BYD's storage products. Headcount in Europe is climbing in step with the expansion. Stella Li, the group's executive vice chair, told Bloomberg that the European workforce will soon pass 10,000 employees, with roughly 40,000 planned for the region by 2030. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? New Models for China and a Safety Nod At home, BYD introduced the Da Han, an electric flagship sedan built on a 1,000-volt architecture that delivers up to 1,008 kilometers of range on the CLTC cycle. The entry version is priced at 235,900 yuan. The Seagull, meanwhile, entered its second generation on the Chinese market on Tuesday, growing in size and gaining lidar-based driver assistance, according to media reports. On the safety front, the SHARK DMO pickup secured a five-star rating in Euro NCAP crash tests. Software is another front. A strategic partnership with smartphone maker Honor will link the YOYO voice and AI assistant directly to BYD's DiLink system through an agent-to-agent protocol. Media reports suggest the integration is intended for more than 100 of the group's models — a reminder that seamless connection to users' digital lives has become a core selling point in China's fiercely competitive market. Mixed Deliveries, Muted Shares Sales momentum has been uneven. BYD shipped 3,131,576 new-energy vehicles between January and September, down 3.94% from the same period a year earlier. September alone accounted for 463,561 units, of which 180,700 went to export markets. Investors have taken the operational news in stride. The stock slipped 0.1% to EUR 8.33 in today's trading, extending its decline since the turn of the year to 22%. Monday's close of EUR 8.30, a 0.5% daily loss, left the shares just about 3.3% above their 52-week low. A clearer picture may emerge on October 29, 2026, when the board meets to review and approve the unaudited third-quarter figures. artigo.texto: BYD's Overseas Battery Surge Meets a 350,000-Vehicle Ceiling in Europe Published on 10/21/2026 at 05:11 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD's expansion story is running on two tracks that don't move in step. New figures show its battery installations outside China climbing sharply, while at home the volume and market share both slipped. On the vehicle side, a fresh trade understanding between Brussels and Beijing has put a number on how many hybrids can flow into Europe each year. A tale of two battery markets Data from SNE Research cited in an October 15 report put BYD's overseas battery installations at 39.7 GWh for the period covered — a 66.5% jump on the same stretch a year earlier. That growth stands in contrast to a softer home market, though it says nothing about how many cars BYD is shipping abroad. The distinction matters: a strong battery business does not by itself answer questions about vehicle demand. Inside China, installations reached 106.44 GWh, down 4.3% year on year, with a market share of 18.53%. The domestic share fell 4.04 percentage points. So both the installed volume and the relative position weakened at home, even as the overseas picture brightened — the regional split within the battery unit is widening. Europe sets a hard limit The vehicle business faces a different set of constraints. On October 13, BYD shares came under pressure as investors weighed export prospects and margins after the European Union and China agreed to cap Chinese hybrid imports. Reuters reported an annual ceiling of 350,000 vehicles. On top of that, Beijing plans to cut the export tax rebate for alternative-drive vehicles from 13% to 9%. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? The two measures bite in different places. The import cap limits access to the European market by volume; the lower rebate sits behind the margin concerns that were reported. Neither figure, on its own, allows a specific earnings impact for BYD to be calculated. Malaysia: a partner named, a start date missing In Southeast Asia, BYD is pushing local assembly and distribution forward on several fronts. BYD Malaysia named Inokom in Kulim as its assembly partner on Thursday, a deal covering local assembly from shipped vehicle kits — an extension of BYD's Malaysian activities beyond sales, though not evidence that production has begun. No model has been fixed and no start date confirmed, so the economic contribution remains an open question. Distribution is further along. A new outlet opened yesterday in Rawang, Selangor, operated by BE Autohaus — another BYD site for the BE Group after Setia Alam and Kota Kemuning. BYD Sime Motors runs 45 sales and marketing outlets nationwide, 33 service facilities and 16 body-and-paint centres, so the new location slots into a network covering both vehicle sales and after-sales care. An opening promotion in Rawang runs from 19 to 30 October 2026, with test drives and offers on selected models. BYD at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. Philippines: tariff relief, currency drag On the Philippines, BYD is backing an extension of duty-free EV imports through 2040; under the existing rule the exemption ends in 2028. The terms for imported vehicles therefore remain a key variable for regional expansion. AB Capital Securities also flags a weak peso as a possible risk to import costs and margins — growing sales and a broader dealer network don't erase such pressures on their own. Ayala/BYD sales reached 28,399 vehicles through August 2026, already ahead of the full-year 2025 total. The pieces of BYD's Southeast Asian build-out are tangible but unevenly advanced. In the Philippines, sales sit alongside an unresolved tariff question. In Malaysia, the retail network is growing while local assembly waits on specifics about model and production timing. What counts for investors is not the tally of new locations but whether they turn into durable business. Ad BYD Stock: New Analysis - 21 October Fresh BYD information released. artigo.texto: Clifford Chance advises Vattenfall on battery storage tolling agreement with Royal Vopak 21 October 2026 Clifford Chance advises Vattenfall on battery storage tolling agreement with Royal Vopak Global law firm Clifford Chance has advised Vattenfall on a tolling agreement with Royal Vopak (Vopak) for a portion of a planned battery energy storage system near Meeden in the province of Groningen, the Netherlands. Under the agreement, Vattenfall will have access to 100 MW / 400 MWh of battery storage capacity, helping to balance fluctuations in electricity supply and demand. Vopak will develop and operate the battery energy storage system, which will have a total capacity of 150 MW and a storage duration of four hours. Commercial operations are expected to begin in the second quarter of 2028. The agreement supports Vattenfall’s goal of contracting at least 1.5 GW of battery capacity across its core markets and Vopak's expansion into electrical energy storage infrastructure. Read more about the transaction here. The Clifford Chance team consisted of associate Niels Kuil, partner Liesbeth Buiter and senior associate Johanneke Butijn. Press contact: Iva Celic

artigo.texto: BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI’s strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL’s dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI’s standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery’s depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL’s seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - “1+X” Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a “1+X” architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. artigo.texto: O Piauí deu mais um passo para a implantação de sua política de crédito de carbono. Nesta terça-feira (20), foi realizada, no Centro de Educação Ambiental (CEA), em Teresina, a primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor do REDD+(Redução de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa provenientes do Desmatamento e da Degradação Florestal), iniciativa voltada à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa provenientes do desmatamento e da degradação florestal. O conselho reúne representantes do poder público, da sociedade civil, da academia, dos povos indígenas, das comunidades quilombolas e tradicionais, da agricultura familiar e do setor produtivo. A proposta é garantir participação social, transparência e segurança na construção do projeto, que poderá gerar recursos para a conservação ambiental e beneficiar as populações que contribuem para a proteção das florestas. O secretário do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Feliphe Araújo, destacou que a implantação do projeto é uma das prioridades da gestão e ressaltou a importância de construir uma política regulamentada, com participação da sociedade. “Queremos proteger nossas florestas e, ao mesmo tempo, gerar recursos para beneficiar as pessoas que ajudam a preservar o meio ambiente. Por isso, é fundamental que esse processo seja construído com diálogo, transparência e participação de todos os setores”, afirmou. Segundo o secretário, o Estado já avançou na elaboração de normas, na regulamentação da iniciativa e na busca de parceiros para viabilizar o projeto. A experiência de outros estados, como o Tocantins, também serve de referência para acelerar as etapas necessárias à implantação da política no Piauí. Feliphe Araújo ressaltou ainda que a preservação ambiental precisa caminhar junto com o desenvolvimento econômico. Ele citou ações de recuperação de áreas degradadas, educação ambiental, fiscalização e prevenção e combate aos incêndios florestais como medidas complementares para reduzir os impactos ambientais. O modelo de Redução de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa provenientes do Desmatamento e da Degradação Florestal (REDD+) poderá viabilizar mecanismos de pagamento por serviços ambientais, com benefícios para povos indígenas, comunidades quilombolas, populações tradicionais e agricultores familiares, além de contribuir para a conservação dos biomas piauienses. A criação e o funcionamento do conselho representam uma etapa importante para consolidar a governança do projeto, assegurando que as decisões sejam discutidas coletivamente e que a política de crédito de carbono seja construída com responsabilidade ambiental e participação social.

artigo.texto: A inteligência artificial depende de uma infraestrutura física capaz de processar grandes volumes de dados continuamente. Por trás de cada consulta a um chatbot, geração de imagem ou aplicação corporativa de IA, existem servidores executando operações computacionais que consomem energia e geram calor. À medida que essas operações se tornam mais exigentes, a densidade computacional dos Data Centers aumenta. Isso significa que mais capacidade de processamento pode ser concentrada em um mesmo espaço, elevando a carga térmica que precisa ser controlada para manter os equipamentos dentro das condições adequadas de operação. O desafio não se resume a evitar o superaquecimento. A infraestrutura precisa acompanhar a demanda computacional, controlar o consumo de energia e manter condições operacionais estáveis, inclusive em ambientes que funcionam ininterruptamente. Por isso, o resfriamento passou a ocupar uma posição estratégica no planejamento e na expansão dos Data Centers. Fabricantes como a LG Electronics desenvolvem soluções de resfriamento para acompanhar essas novas exigências de eficiência e confiabilidade. O que é um chiller em um Data Center? Um chiller é um equipamento de refrigeração que remove calor de um circuito de água ou de outro fluido utilizado no sistema de climatização. Em instalações de grande porte, ele pode integrar a infraestrutura responsável por retirar o calor dos ambientes e dos equipamentos de TI, conforme a arquitetura de resfriamento adotada. Em um sistema tradicional com água gelada, por exemplo, o chiller resfria a água que circula pelo sistema. Essa água absorve o calor em pontos de troca térmica e retorna ao equipamento para que o ciclo continue. Existem diferentes configurações de chillers, que variam conforme a capacidade, o método de rejeição de calor e as necessidades da instalação. A escolha depende de fatores como densidade computacional, condições climáticas, espaço disponível, demanda energética e requisitos de disponibilidade. Em Data Centers de IA, esse dimensionamento ganha importância porque a infraestrutura de resfriamento precisa responder à carga térmica existente e acompanhar possíveis aumentos na capacidade de processamento. Como chillers ajudam a manter a operação dos Data Centers? O resfriamento integra uma cadeia de sistemas que precisam funcionar de maneira coordenada. Se a capacidade de retirar calor não acompanhar a demanda, a instalação pode precisar limitar o desempenho dos equipamentos ou adotar medidas operacionais para preservar as condições de funcionamento. Por isso, o projeto de cooling considera tanto a capacidade térmica quanto a confiabilidade dos componentes, as estratégias de redundância e a possibilidade de expansão. Em instalações críticas, a continuidade do resfriamento é especialmente relevante: uma interrupção no fornecimento de energia, por exemplo, exige que os sistemas retomem suas funções de acordo com os requisitos operacionais do Data Center. Outro aspecto é o consumo energético. A refrigeração representa uma parcela da energia utilizada por essas instalações, embora seu peso varie conforme o projeto, o clima, a carga de TI e as tecnologias empregadas. Melhorar a eficiência do sistema de resfriamento pode contribuir para reduzir a energia necessária à operação da infraestrutura. Quais tecnologias estão mudando o resfriamento de Data Centers? A evolução dos chillers envolve diferentes frentes tecnológicas. Entre elas estão os compressores mais eficientes, sistemas de controle inteligentes, arquiteturas modulares e recursos que aproveitam as condições ambientais para reduzir o trabalho mecânico de refrigeração. O free-cooling é um exemplo. Dependendo da configuração do sistema e das condições externas, essa estratégia permite utilizar o ambiente para auxiliar na remoção de calor, reduzindo a necessidade de refrigeração mecânica em determinadas situações. O resultado depende de fatores como temperatura ambiente, projeto da instalação e regime de operação. Também há avanços nos sistemas de monitoramento e diagnóstico. Com dados operacionais integrados, equipes de engenharia e facilities podem acompanhar o funcionamento dos equipamentos, identificar desvios e avaliar oportunidades de otimização. A inteligência desses sistemas ajuda a transformar o acompanhamento da infraestrutura em uma atividade mais orientada por dados. A modularidade é outra característica relevante, pois permite planejar a capacidade de acordo com as necessidades da instalação e simplificar etapas de implementação e expansão. Para Data Centers que precisam acompanhar a evolução da IA, essa flexibilidade pode facilitar o planejamento de longo prazo. Como a LG está desenvolvendo soluções para esse cenário? É nesse contexto que a LG Electronics apresenta o LG Air-Cooled Centrifugal Chiller (ACC), desenvolvido para aplicações de grande porte, incluindo a infraestrutura de resfriamento de Data Centers. O equipamento combina compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético e operação oil-free, ou seja, sem óleo no sistema de mancais do compressor. Essa arquitetura dispensa a lubrificação por óleo nesse conjunto, característica que integra a proposta tecnológica do equipamento. O ACC também incorpora a tecnologia refrigerant free-cooling, voltada ao aproveitamento de condições favoráveis para auxiliar o processo de resfriamento. A aplicação desse recurso depende das condições ambientais e operacionais, assim como do projeto da instalação. Outro destaque é a capacidade de recuperação após uma interrupção de energia. Conforme as condições de teste informadas pela fabricante, o equipamento pode restabelecer sua capacidade total de resfriamento em até três minutos após o retorno da energia. Esse intervalo deve ser considerado dentro das condições específicas de operação do sistema, e não como uma garantia de retomada integral de todo o Data Center. artigo.texto: AI's Fragmented Regulatory Landscape Becomes a Data Center Design Challenge Key Highlights - Global AI infrastructure expansion faces mounting challenges from fragmented regulatory requirements, power constraints, and supply chain pressures. - U.S. federal initiatives aim to accelerate data center development, but electricity costs, state regulations, and community opposition remain significant obstacles. - The EU AI Act, UN governance initiatives, and competing U.S.-China approaches are creating different expectations for AI infrastructure and its operation. - Data center operators serving international customers must establish clear contractual responsibilities and verifiable controls for security, workload location, data handling, and access. - Delivering usable AI capacity increasingly requires more than energized infrastructure: developers must demonstrate operational readiness, documented controls, and clear compliance responsibilities. AI infrastructure is expanding across a world increasingly divided over how the technology should be regulated. For data center developers and operators, that fragmentation introduces a challenge beyond securing power, deploying compute, and bringing facilities online: ensuring that the resulting infrastructure can support workloads governed by different legal, security, and contractual requirements. The scale of the buildout makes these distinctions increasingly consequential. According to the International Energy Agency, global data center electricity demand rose 17% in 2025, while consumption at AI-focused facilities increased 50%. The agency projects total data center electricity consumption will reach roughly 950 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2030, nearly double its 2025 level of 485 TWh. Even so, grid constraints, equipment shortages, chip availability, and financing challenges threaten to delay projects, leaving substantial uncertainty over how much announced capacity will actually reach service. At the same time, the regulatory environment is becoming more complex rather than more uniform. The European Union is implementing binding AI rules, the United States is pursuing policies to accelerate domestic infrastructure development, and competing international initiatives are taking shape around AI governance and supply-chain security. Although these measures impose very different obligations, their combined effect is to make verifiable operating controls, clear contractual responsibilities, and jurisdiction-specific requirements increasingly important in delivering AI infrastructure. PBS examines how the rapid expansion of AI data centers is intensifying disputes over electricity, water and the costs borne by host communities. U.S. Policy Meets Local Development Constraints In the United States, the Trump administration has made faster data center development a federal policy goal. Its AI Action Plan calls for accelerated infrastructure permitting, a grid prepared to support AI growth, and more secure facilities for sensitive military, government, and intelligence workloads. A July 2025 executive order, Accelerating Federal Permitting of Data Center Infrastructure, gives federal agencies a more specific assignment: identify ways to expedite reviews and support qualifying data center projects and their supporting infrastructure. Under the order, projects can qualify through several routes, including committed capital expenditures of at least $500 million or an incremental electrical load greater than 100 MW. The order directs agencies to examine environmental review procedures, consider eligible projects for federal permitting schedules, and identify suitable federal land. It also covers supporting infrastructure such as transmission lines, substations, transformers, and switchgear, extending the permitting initiative beyond the data center campus to the electrical systems needed to serve it. These measures create opportunities to accelerate federal reviews, but do not eliminate other applicable approvals or guarantee that a project can proceed. The White House's Ratepayer Protection Pledge, introduced in March 2026, addresses another constraint: who pays for the electricity and grid infrastructure required by large data centers. Participating companies committed to build, bring, or buy the power needed for their facilities, cover required delivery upgrades, and negotiate separate rate structures under which they pay for electricity and infrastructure brought online to serve them, even if actual consumption falls below projections. The pledge remains voluntary, with its practical effect dependent on agreements among developers, utilities, and state authorities. Congress has pursued related legislation. On September 16, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417–3 vote, although the measure subsequently failed to advance in the Senate on September 30. If enacted, the legislation would require state utility regulators to consider standards for assigning the incremental costs of generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades to large-load customers. It would not require states to adopt those standards. The distinction underscores how much responsibility for translating federal energy policy into enforceable arrangements still resides with state regulators and utilities. A separate December 11, 2025 executive order, Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence, targeted the growing patchwork of state AI regulations. It directed the Justice Department to establish an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws the administration considers inconsistent with federal policy, while calling for a legislative proposal establishing a more uniform national framework. Significantly for data center developers, the order specified that such legislation should not preempt otherwise lawful state laws concerning AI compute and data center infrastructure, except for generally applicable permitting reforms. artigo.texto: Doc Brown needed 1.21 gigawatts to send a DeLorean through time in the 1985 movie "Back to the Future." The data-center industry could add about 42 times that next year. Welcome to the Doc Brown Index. Research firm SemiAnalysis expects annual additions to data center IT capacity outside China to more than double next year, to about 51 gigawatts from 25 gigawatts this year. In movie units, that's about 21 Doc Browns ballooning to 42. These are additions in a single year, not the whole fleet or the electricity it uses. By SemiAnalysis's count, that one year would roughly match the world's entire data center build-out through 2024. About three-quarters of next year's projected additions come from projects already operational or under construction. The rest are still planned. SemiAnalysis points to more than 24 gigawatts across 40 campuses in advanced construction for expected delivery next year. Not everyone buys it. At the All-In Summit in September, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner called SemiAnalysis's forecast at the time, 43 gigawatts, too aggressive and guessed the industry would stand up closer to 25 gigawatts. That's only about 21 Doc Browns — no faster than this year. How do you build that much, that quickly? Increasingly, in pieces. Suppliers now build electrical rooms and cooling systems in factories while crews prepare the site. SemiAnalysis calls the results Lego data centers, with bricks that can weigh 50,000 pounds. Amazon (AMZN) is rolling out its own modular design at large scale, and Meta Platforms (META) has put up tent-like halls to enclose buildings faster, according to SemiAnalysis. A SemiAnalysis model of a 50-megawatt AI data hall puts conventional construction at 22 months and a fully modular approach at 14, excluding permitting. The biggest saving comes from electrical and mechanical installation. For the owner of the chips inside, SemiAnalysis values that eight-month head start at about $200 million. That shift puts suppliers in the race alongside chipmakers such as Nvidia (NVDA). SemiAnalysis estimates content per megawatt for Vertiv (VRT) roughly doubles, to as much as $7 million, when it sells the full modular stack. Contractors Comfort Systems USA (FIX) and Sterling Infrastructure (STRL) assemble modules too. But a finished building still needs power. Microsoft (MSFT) confirmed Monday that it pulled out of a lease at a planned 50-megawatt Nscale data center outside London — the same size as the SemiAnalysis model — after grid officials said power might not arrive until the 2030s. Microsoft said the decision involved a single site and that its broader partnership with Nscale continues.
