artigo.texto: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] GM plans lower-cost EVs with new battery chemistry Despite EV sales slump, GM to debut lithium manganese-rich batteries, which will support upcoming SUV Key Takeaways: - General Motors is developing lithium manganese-rich batteries for multiple affordable EVs, including a mainstream battery-powered SUV expected in about three years. - GM's EV sales fell 43% to 82,000 through the third quarter, and GM wrote down more than $11 billion in investments. - GM plans to debut autonomous highway driving on the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028, then expand it to lower-priced models. General Motors Co. is unfazed by the electric vehicle meltdown of the past few years, moving ahead with a new EV program expected to produce a new battery-powered mainstream SUV with about three years. The automaker’s latest effort aims to field multiple affordable EVs in high-volume vehicle segments, GM executives told reporters at an event in New York. At the center of it are batteries leveraging lithium manganese-rich (LMR) chemistry, which offers greater driving range at a lower cost than the technology in GM’s offerings. “Our end goal is profitable EVs,” said Jaclyn McQuaid, GM’s senior vice president for vehicle products. “We see data that says customers who spend time in EVs enjoy the experience.” Staying the course by planning new EV models is a bold move for GM. Under CEO Mary Barra, the company invested $35 billion in electric drive and other technologies to field a lineup that now comprises 12 models. Yet vast majority of car buyers in the U.S. — GM’s biggest source of sales and profit — continue to purchase gasoline-powered models as well as hybrid-electric cars predominantly made by Asian rivals. That dynamic was magnified last year after President Donald Trump and Republican lawmakers slashed federal policies that had pushed carmakers to produce more EVs and incentivized consumers to buy them, including a $7,500 tax credit for EV purchasers. So far this year, GM’s electric vehicle sales have fallen 43% to 82,000 through the third quarter. The company has written down more than $11 billion in EV investments and sold stakes in battery plants to partners LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI. It’s also doubled down on internal combustion with new V-8 engines for its pickup trucks and SUVs. Despite those immediate challenges, the carmaker still sees electric drive as its long-term future that will eventually be embraced by consumers. McQuaid said recent developments with LMR chemistry have made it possible to GM to develop a broad lineup of EV models. Its current EV batteries utilize nickel manganese cobalt chemistry, which offers long driving range but at a high cost. Chinese automakers use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, which are cheaper but don’t go as far on a charge. GM said its LMR batteries are designed to carry 33% more energy density than LFP, and by reducing weight, should be able to deliver 20% longer range on every kilowatt-hour of energy. The company is extracting additional cost savings with new battery packs that are lighter, have less wiring and 40% fewer parts than its current models, said GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson. GM is using more AI tools to coordinate between its design, engineering and manufacturing operations to halve the nearly five-year process of developing new models, Anderson said. EVs also represent GM’s opportunity to introduce GM’s latest autonomous driving capabilities, which will debut on the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028 and then be added to lower-priced models, Anderson said. That system will allow drivers to take their hands off the wheel and eyes off the road on highways. The company is working to eventually have its vehicles capable of off-highway autonomous driving, Anderson said.

artigo.texto: Data Centers: Benefits vs Costs and Risks EconoFact The Issue: The dramatic recent surge in investment in data centers in the United States is boosting the economy but at the same time sparking heated opposition. The stark tensions reflect very different viewpoints on the benefits vs the costs and risks of data centers. For their supporters, data centers are providing the infrastructure backbone for the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with a potentially transformative long-term impact on the US economy, well beyond the already significant short-term stimulus to growth. However, critics have raised a wide range of concerns: that the data center boom and the required massive debt financing needed to sustain it could end in a damaging bust; that the promised local benefits of data centers in terms of jobs and tax revenues are exaggerated while the spending on data centers is crowding out other types of investment; that data centers can impose heavy energy and environmental costs on local communities; and that the Artificial Intelligence that data centers are empowering will destroy jobs and even threaten humanity itself. Data center spending is expected to continue at a high level through the end of the decade, although projections vary widely. The Facts: - Data centers are industrial facilities that house the servers, storage and networking equipment that run digital services provided remotely over the internet. Data centers have been around at a small scale since the late 1990s as the internet and cloud computing developed. However, global data center capacity has taken off over the past decade, growing three times from 2015 to 2024, mainly in the United States (see chart). This boom has intensified since the launch of Chat GPT in late 2023 and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence tools by both businesses and households in the US, which has far outpaced the spread of personal computers and the internet in earlier decades. - The recent surge in capacity has been driven by huge investments by the so-called five hyperscalers: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, Meta and Alphabet [Google]. These companies are spending an estimated $800 billion on data centers in 2026 representing about 9 percent of all U.S. capital expenditures. Modern AI-related data centers are often designed at a massive scale, packing together cutting-edge GPU microprocessors with high-speed interconnects in a single location with large electricity and cooling needs. These mega centers are used to train new AI models such as those offered by Open AI and Anthropic and increasingly to support the use of AI (known as “inference”), which Deloitte estimates at around 2/3 of AI computing needs in 2026, up from one third in 2023. While model training could be accomplished offshore in places with cheap and abundant energy — for instance in the Middle East — inference services need to be near centers of population to minimize delays in real time response by AI applications such as AI agents, fraud detection, and self-driving cars. This means that widespread adoption of artificial intelligence in the United States can't just rely on data centers built in remote locations with abundant cheap energy. - Data center spending is expected to continue at a high level through the end of the decade, although projections vary widely. A report by the International Energy Agency (IEA) provides a baseline scenario with global data center capacity rising from 97 GW in 2025 to 226 GW in 2030, but with three other scenarios ranging from 158 to 305 GW in 2030 (see chart), driven largely by growing AI computing needs. The wide range of uncertainty arises from unresolved questions about the extent to which AI will be widely adopted by businesses and households; whether AI providers can capture monetary returns from the users commensurate with their costs; how quickly the microchips that account for the lion’s share of data center construction costs are replaced by newer, more powerful and more energy efficient chips; and the political resistance to new data center construction. Estimates from a study focusing on the United States, present a central scenario projecting an increase from 57 GW of data center capacity in 2026 to 240 GW by 2032, at a total cost of around $10 trillion. This would represent 3.5 percent of US GDP over 2025-2032, which would be substantially larger than previous surges in infrastructure spending like railroads in the 19th century (2.2 percent of GDP) and the internet in the 20th century (1.1 percent of GDP) (see here). - The recent surge in data center spending has provided a short-term boost to the US economy. A Federal Reserve study used simulations of actual projects to estimate that data center spending on plant and equipment (net of imported components) contributed around 0.20 percentage points to the 2.3 percent US GDP growth in 2025 and is contributing 0.40 percentage points in 2026. (See also these similar estimates based on recent GDP data). The US economy has also benefitted indirectly from the run-up in stock prices of the leading companies providing AI services, which increases investors’ wealth (and therefore spending), partially offset by the crowding out of other types of investment through the competition for funding and the associated increase in long- term interest rates. On the employment front, data center construction boosts US jobs for construction workers and in manufacturing electrical equipment, although the post-construction employment impact is small since running and maintaining data centers requires very few people. There could be a negative impact on jobs displaced by increasing use of AI, although such effects so far seem limited. artigo.texto: [Stay on top of transportation news: Get TTNews in your inbox.] CATL bets big on electric truck market with new upgrades Offerings include battery upgrades and expanded swap stations Key Takeaways: - CATL is betting on the burgeoning electric-truck market to bolster growth, introducing battery upgrades and planning to open more so-called swap stations. - Electric trucks accounted for just over half of China’s vehicle sales last month, according to First Commercial Vehicle Network. - CATL plans to more than double its e-truck battery-swap stations to 2,000 by 2027 and ultimately operate 10,000 facilities. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. is betting on the burgeoning electric-truck market to bolster growth, introducing battery upgrades and planning to open more so-called swap stations. The Chinese battery giant launched a slew of upgrades for the packs used in the cargo-hauling vehicles at an event in Beijing on Oct. 20, and said it has secured orders for swap products covering 13,000 units from major logistics companies including SF Holding Co. and China Postal Express & Logistics Co. The e-truck market is expanding rapidly in China, with vehicle sales accounting for just over half of the total last month, according to First Commercial Vehicle Network. CATL — which has seen its stock price slump this year amid concerns about rising competition — is due to release earnings later Oct. 20. The company plans to more than double its battery-swap stations for e-trucks to 2,000 by 2027, with a goal of running 10,000 facilities in the longer term, according to Yang Jun, CEO of CATL’s e-truck battery-swap business. The sites allow drivers to quickly exchange a depleted battery pack for a charged one, rather than waiting for a recharge of an existing unit. E-truck battery products introduced Oct. 20 included rear-mounted ultra-light and ultra-thin packs that can be suitable for weight- or space-sensitive applications. The company added that it will offer flexible battery leasing options for customers to tailor rental periods to their needs. “This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs,” according to a company statement.

artigo.texto: Near Arlington, Oregon, a 29,950-acre proposal combines 500 MW each of wind and solar with 4,000-MWh battery storage The Columbia River plateau desert of Eastern Washington lying above the Columbia River basin is an expansive area that is mostly windy, where rangeland stretches to the horizon beyond the small city of Arlington, Oregon, which has only 500 people living there. It would be hard for most Americans to locate it on a map. But it has drawn attention of energy experts and planners. An application is under consideration by the state regulators that proposes installing two kinds of renewable energy generation devices, along with a battery system large enough to overturn the assumptions about power grid reliability in the Pacific Northwest region. Remote Oregon plateau at heart of green energy gamble Arlington lies within the rain shadow of the Columbia River Basin – an area defined by high desert, created by the forces of wind, volcanic basalt, and hundreds of years of ranching and wheat farming. Arlington has some of the most consistent winds in the Pacific Northwest, as well as high-intensity summer solar radiation that few coastal areas can equal. The combination of natural features and existing power line routes in the area makes it increasingly attractive for renewable energy development. A developer filed a Notice of Intent with the Oregon Department of Energy on August 4, 2026, to pursue a site certificate for the Big River Renewable Energy Project. For perspective on the size of 29,950 acres, the urban land use in all of Portland occupies about 90,000 acres. This project alone would take up one-third of that space. This is no small project, but an extensive alteration of agricultural land visible from miles away. The Big River Renewable Energy Project proposal A developer filed a Notice of Intent with the Oregon Department of Energy on August 4, 2026, to pursue a site certificate for the Big River Renewable Energy Project. The Notice of Intent is the initial formal step in Oregon’s process of siting a facility and is not an approval in any way. There are four components to this proposal. A 500 MW wind turbine portion will place turbines on the plateau. Another 500 MW solar generation portion will overlay photovoltaic generation on the same footprint — co-location allowing wind and solar generation to share land and other infrastructure. Both will be supported by a 4,000 MWh battery energy storage system, able to store excess generation and dispatch it to the grid during peak times. Public comments can be submitted between August 7, 2026, and September 25, 2026, according to the Oregon Department of Energy – Big River. Why co-location of wind, solar, and storage is significant Wind energy and solar energy have often been referred to as intermittent forms of energy, but the generation patterns for these two in the Columbia Basin region are complementary. While wind blows the hardest at night and during the winter period, solar energy peaks at midday during the summer period. By combining both wind and solar energy together, the generation pattern becomes less intermittent. The addition of a 4,000 MWh battery system makes the entire process even better, as the battery takes care of the surplus generated during peak generation periods. The surplus energy is then used during the evening peak consumption times and when there are periods of cloudy weather without any wind blowing. The total 1,000 MW generating capacity will be enough to power hundreds of thousands of Pacific Northwest households. Grid operators have increasingly favored co-located hybrid projects because they reduce transmission congestion by delivering more usable power through a single interconnection point, improving overall capacity factors. Process review and role of the public in Oregon In Oregon, large energy projects need to get a Site Certificate from the Department of Energy before they can start construction. This process is purposely designed as such. The NOI phase, where Big River finds itself now, sets off environmental scoping, interagency coordination, and public participation. Submitting an NOI does not mean getting approval to build. An informational public hearing was held on August 20, 2026, and was available online and offline. The deadline for comments is set for September 25, 2026. Comments usually revolve around land use compatibility, effects on wildlife and habitats, landscape visual quality, water resources, and transmission corridor issues, given the size of the project. The future of Big River — and the energy situation in Oregon Once the comment period for the NOI is over, the developer will be required to file an application for site cacertificate. This application should respond to any issues identified during the public comment period and must meet all requirements of the Oregon Siting Standards. The project’s trajectory matters well beyond Arlington. Oregon has set ambitious clean energy targets, and the Pacific Northwest grid increasingly needs firm, dispatchable renewable power to replace retiring fossil fuel generation. A hybrid facility of this scale — if approved — would demonstrate that large co-located projects are viable in the American West, potentially accelerating similar proposals elsewhere. If it meets significant opposition or regulatory obstacles, that outcome would be equally instructive. For now, the project’s future remains genuinely open, shaped by the technical record, agency review, and the voices of people who live and work on that high desert plateau. Kelly is an experienced writer with 15 years of experience exploring the big stories that shape our world, from tech breakthroughs and space exploration to climate, energy, and the fascinating quirks of science. She has a talent for turning complex ideas into sharp, memorable insights that stay with readers long after they’ve finished reading.

artigo.texto: Tech CATL Unveils Five-Minute Battery Swapping for Electric Trucks, Targets 2,000 Stations by 2027 CATL introduces new electric-truck batteries and plans thousands of rapid-swapping stations. Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy-duty electric trucks and expanded its battery-swapping technology, offering a system designed to replace depleted truck batteries in approximately five minutes. The announcement marks another step in China’s efforts to electrify freight transportation, an industry traditionally dependent on diesel-powered vehicles. The new Tianxing II battery platform includes different configurations for commercial vehicles, while the company’s Qiji battery-swapping system is designed to reduce the time trucks spend waiting to replenish energy. According to Reuters, CATL is targeting 900 heavy-truck battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026, expanding to 2,000 stations in 2027 and eventually building a network of 10,000. The company’s plans reflect the growing importance of battery replacement technology as manufacturers seek to overcome some of the main obstacles to electric freight transportation, including charging times, battery weight, operating costs and infrastructure availability. How the Five-Minute Battery Swapping System Works Unlike conventional electric trucks that must remain connected to a charger while their batteries recharge, CATL’s system allows a vehicle to enter a specialized station where an automated mechanism removes its depleted battery and installs a charged replacement. The process is designed to take approximately five minutes, allowing drivers to resume operations without waiting for the original battery to recharge. CATL’s Qiji system uses standardized battery modules intended to work across compatible heavy-duty vehicle models. The battery-swapping approach can also separate battery ownership from vehicle ownership. Freight operators may be able to purchase or lease a truck without paying the full upfront cost of its battery, depending on the commercial arrangement. In an earlier company announcement, CATL said its standardized Qiji battery-swapping system could support a wide range of commercial trucks, with compatible designs developed alongside multiple vehicle manufacturers. The company says battery swapping can improve fleet efficiency, particularly for long-distance transportation, ports, mining operations and logistics services where vehicle downtime carries substantial costs. New Batteries Designed for Longer Truck Journeys The Tianxing II platform introduces batteries intended for different heavy-truck operating conditions. Its long-range configuration includes a battery pack with a capacity of 760 kilowatt-hours, which CATL says can support more than 600 kilometres of driving range under specified conditions. The company has also developed lighter battery configurations and chassis-mounted designs aimed at improving vehicle efficiency and preserving cargo capacity. CATL says its new standardized battery-swapping modules contain 52% fewer components and cost approximately 15% less than previous designs. These figures represent company-reported technical improvements. Actual vehicle range, battery performance and operating savings will depend on driving conditions, vehicle weight, climate, electricity prices and the availability of compatible swapping stations. CATL Plans Thousands of Battery-Swapping Stations CATL’s expansion strategy goes beyond developing new batteries. The company plans to establish a nationwide network of heavy-duty truck battery-swapping stations along China’s major freight transportation routes. Its current targets include 900 stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, followed by a longer-term ambition to reach 10,000 locations. The new goals build on earlier infrastructure investments. In May 2025, CATL announced an extensive battery-swapping network intended to connect major freight corridors across China. The company’s strategy includes standardized battery modules, partnerships with commercial vehicle manufacturers and infrastructure development along important highways and industrial routes. CATL has also expanded cooperation with logistics companies. In July 2026, the battery manufacturer announced an agreement with J&T Express to support battery-swapping solutions for more than 5,000 heavy-duty trucks. The collaboration illustrates how the technology could be integrated into large commercial fleets that operate on predictable schedules and transportation routes. China Pushes to Reduce Diesel Dependence The expansion comes as China accelerates efforts to replace diesel-powered heavy trucks with electric alternatives. Heavy commercial vehicles consume substantial amounts of fuel and contribute to transportation-related emissions, making freight electrification an important part of China’s energy transition. A separate Reuters report outlined China’s plans to increase electric vehicles to 40% of new heavy-truck sales by 2030. Battery swapping could help support those ambitions by addressing operational challenges associated with charging large commercial batteries. For freight operators, the potential advantages include shorter stops, more predictable vehicle scheduling and reduced exposure to changes in diesel prices. However, large-scale adoption will require substantial infrastructure investment, reliable electricity supplies, standardized equipment and commercially viable agreements between manufacturers, energy providers and transport companies. Technology Could Influence Global Freight Transportation CATL is also seeking to expand its electric-truck technology beyond China. The company has announced a preliminary collaboration with DHL Group to explore environmentally sustainable freight corridors in Europe using electric trucks. artigo.texto: The Milwaukee Common Council unanimously passed a one-year moratorium last week on new data center projects while officials draft new zoning standards. Mayor Cavalier Johnson signed the ordinance the day after the council’s vote. Data center plans are facing public backlash across the state and the country. Milwaukee joins places like Superior, Madison and Wisconsin Rapids that passed their own data center construction moratoriums. Milwaukee’s moratorium comes in response to public controversy after a proposed project to redevelop a vacant Walmart on the city’s north side. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Debate in the city mirrors what’s happening in other communities. Officials say they need time to write rules for projects that affect neighborhoods, utility costs and other issues. But business leaders say a pause may drive economic investment to other places. There are currently 53 data centers around the state, according to the Data Center Map. And at least 19 of varying sizes are in the Greater Milwaukee area. But while developers are moving quickly to build data centers, Milwaukee Common Council Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic told WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” that local government operates at a slower pace to weigh how major changes could affect residents. Before the moratorium, Dimitrijevic said the city had essentially no zoning rules or regulations regarding data center construction. “Government is not set up to move that fast, which is why we have to pause,” she said. “Zoning code has to account for land use; we have to look at how it would affect neighbors, the noise, the possible pollution; the list goes on and on. And I think there are very few Wisconsinites that want to live right next to one of these (data centers).” Dimitrijevic said she had concerns about how the boom in data centers would affect the region’s energy grid and utility costs for constituents. A Pew Research Center survey released in September found 54 percent of Americans believe that data centers would have a negative impact on the environment, up from 39% in January. The survey found half of Americans believe data centers would negatively affect home energy costs. “No one is asking for this, other than the corporations that are seeking to make money off of us,” Dimitrijevic said. But for the businesses hoping to build in Milwaukee and stimulate its economy, a moratorium like the one the city just passed could scare away potential investment, said Dale Kooyenga, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce. MMAC opposed Milwaukee’s moratorium. Kooyenga said he thought the data center pause could’ve been worse and that businesses still have opportunities to negotiate with the city, but that such a moratorium is essentially putting up a “we’re not open for business” sign on the city’s front door. “We understand that with any economic development, there’s a back-and-forth discussion, but you should have policies that invite a discussion, and then when you have those discussions, then share with the investor what you need to get to a yes,” Kooyenga said. “We just think (the moratorium) sends the wrong message for a city that really needs more economic development.” Building a new data center can take thousands of workers in construction jobs, from electricians to carpenters to engineers. But once built, the centers themselves host relatively few job openings, up to several hundred. Kooyenga said the years of construction jobs shouldn’t be discounted. And he said the jobs the centers host once operational are typically well above the median wage. Kooyenga said such projects raise significant property tax revenue for the area, which local governments could use to bolster schools, fire departments and other public services. Dimitrijevic said she was more skeptical over the long-term payoff of such projects after the construction is done and the builders have moved on to other projects. “I think we want the same (as businesses and developers) when we want investment in the city of Milwaukee, but we’ve got to do it in a way that serves the many, not just the few,” she said.

artigo.texto: Earlier this year, the German government laid out an ambitious plan: By 2030, it would double the scale of the country’s data center fleet, and quadruple the amount of compute available for running artificial intelligence models. The idea was to minimize Germany’s dependence on the United States for access to AI—a point of concern across Europe—and boost its faltering economy. However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy. As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations. “We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED. In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility. Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate. The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment. Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.” In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act. Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says. When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.” Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change. The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten. But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns. As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, an investment company of SKC in the copper foil business for secondary batteries, said Tuesday that it has successfully developed 'high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil' technology, which is considered a core material for next-generation batteries. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil is a product that applies special carbon to the surface of the copper foil to enhance adhesion with the anode material. It is characterized by suppressing the 'delamination phenomenon,' where silicon anode materials expand during charging and discharging processes, causing them to separate from the copper foil, thereby improving the structural stability of the electrode. The company explained that this can also contribute to enhancing battery lifespan and safety. SK Nexilis developed the related technology in line with the trend in the battery industry to increase the silicon content of anode materials to boost energy density. While silicon can store more lithium ions than conventional graphite, its significant volume change during charging and discharging processes is cited as a drawback. This is why adhesion between the anode material and copper foil becomes increasingly important as the silicon content rises. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil can also be applied to dry electrode processes, which are gaining attention as a manufacturing method for next-generation batteries. Unlike conventional wet processes that use liquid solvents, dry electrode processes can reduce steps such as drying, thereby lowering manufacturing costs and energy consumption. However, since it is crucial to stably bond electrode materials with copper foil, the utilization of high-adhesion copper foil is expected to expand. SK Nexilis plans to build a pilot production system for high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil ahead of full-scale Yangsan. The company is currently verifying process stability and aims to commercialize in the second half of next year after securing Yangsan technology. An official from SK Nexilis said, "We will proceed with commercialization optimization work without any issues while strengthening our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technological development."

artigo.texto: Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore. Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy. India is touted as one of the hottest markets for data centers, with several U.S. Big Tech companies investing to set up capacity in the country. But of late, some projects have faced public backlash over the use of water and power resources. Now the Indian government is taking steps to address the situation. Will it work? Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team. The big story Several U.S. Big Tech companies that are spending billions to set up digital infrastructure in India are facing growing public anger over resource sharing and environmental concerns, prompting the government to step in and calm tensions. On Oct. 14, Jitin Prasada, a junior minister for electronics and information technology, announced that India will roll out a policy for data centers, calling the country a "fertile ground for hyperscalers." The minister reportedly said India wants to avoid a situation where consumers have to pay more for power because they have to compete with data centers for supply. Globally, data center companies are facing public backlash as communities raise concerns over electricity, water and land use. India is also grappling with similar issues that pose a threat to its ambitions to host the whole world's data. As per local media reports, Amazon's data center near Mumbai is facing resistance from residents who are worried that the U.S. company's facility would receive priority access to water and electricity during shortages. Meanwhile, environmental activists have been demanding the cancellation of permissions given to AI data centers in Visakhapatnam, where Google is constructing its $15 billion project. Amazon told CNBC that it is committed to being a "good and responsible neighbor," and said it is engaging with the community through educational sessions. They denied using water for cooling and added that their data centers "do not draw electricity from the local distribution network that supplies homes, shops and businesses." The American firm also said it "will be a part of industry consultations with the government to advise on India's data center regulations." Google did not respond to CNBC's request for comments. Experts told CNBC that the government plans to roll out a policy directive to pacify local resistance to some projects across the country. It will also lay down clear approval guidelines that will minimize the risks data center developers face from public pushback and execution challenges, they added. Policy shift The proposed policy indicates a shift in direction from "primarily encouraging the data center investment" to now balancing it with infrastructure readiness and sustainability aspects, Jaspreet Singh, partner at Grant Thornton Bharat, told CNBC. Last week, Niti Aayog, an Indian government think tank, shared a framework for local governments to evaluate data center projects for sustainability and to provide suitable locations, based on grid readiness and water supply availability. It underscored the need to establish guidelines "before constraints emerge," adding that data centers should get faster approvals only in cases where resource readiness, local safeguards and public value are proven. Experts who are part of consultations expect the new policy to lay down clear and consistent rules, which will also help the industry overcome challenges around land acquisition and simplify a fragmented approval process. "India does not have a dedicated national policy for data centers, and it is high time that this gap was addressed," Shobhit Agarwal, chief executive of real estate consultancy ANAROCK Capital, told CNBC. He explained that projects are currently approved under existing environmental and building rules, and every state has its own "variations and incentives." While the Indian government has been enthusiastic in welcoming the hyperscalers to invest in data centers in India, even giving them 20-year tax sops, regional governments are the final decision-makers when it comes to providing land, water and power resources. Nikhil Narendran, a partner for technology at law firm Trilegal, who works with U.S. Big Tech companies, said local governments are proposing data center projects in locations that are already facing constraints in terms of electricity, water and other infrastructure. artigo.texto: - EU lawmakers and member states have reached a provisional agreement on changes to the bloc’s carbon market rules. - The deal raises the Market Stability Reserve’s allowance invalidation threshold from 400 million to 700 million. - Formal approval is still required, with the changes aimed at improving liquidity and predictability for industry. The European Union agreed earlier today to increase the buffer for surplus carbon allowances under its Market Stability Reserve, marking a new step in efforts to balance industrial competitiveness with the bloc’s climate objectives. The provisional compromise increases the threshold above which allowances held in the reserve are invalidated from 400 million to 700 million. The change is intended to improve the availability of permits over time and make the carbon market more predictable for businesses. The agreement follows months of debate over how to maintain the carbon market’s role in reducing emissions while responding to concerns about costs and future supply. It must still be endorsed and formally adopted by both institutions before becoming law. A larger buffer for Europe’s carbon market The Market Stability Reserve was established to address a historical oversupply of emissions permits that had weakened the EU carbon market’s price signal. Under the mechanism, allowances can be withheld from auctions when supply is high, while permits held above a defined threshold have been subject to permanent cancellation since 2023. The European Commission says more than 3 billion allowances have been invalidated since that cancellation mechanism began. Raising the threshold would allow a larger stock of permits to remain available within the reserve, providing more flexibility if market conditions tighten. “In response to European leaders’ call for accelerated action, we reached a balanced outcome on the market stability reserve that provides European industry with immediate flexibility, while ensuring price stability and protecting the integrity of the EU carbon market. The EU is delivering on the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap,” said Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O’Brien. The deal represents a compromise between competing approaches. In its original proposal, the Commission sought to end the invalidation mechanism. The Council’s negotiating position instead envisaged a temporary suspension followed by a higher threshold. The provisional agreement retains the cancellation framework but raises its threshold to 700 million allowances. Industry costs and climate targets remain in focus The changes come amid broader EU efforts to revise emissions trading rules as policymakers weigh high energy costs, industrial competitiveness and emissions-reduction targets. The Commission’s wider ETS review, proposed in July, covers additional elements of the carbon market and industrial decarbonisation policy. The threshold agreement is a targeted adjustment, not a wholesale redesign of emissions trading. Its practical effects will depend on future allowance supply, demand and the implementation of the revised rules. For companies covered by the system, the deal offers a change to the rules governing the reserve, but it does not guarantee lower carbon prices. The EU’s wider challenge remains ensuring that the market supports investment in cleaner production while preserving incentives to cut greenhouse gas emissions. artigo.texto: Chinese EV demand weakens while overseas competition and taxes pressure battery makers while Korean battery firms gain an opening with U.S. ESS orders and automaker diversification The earnings growth of China’s CATL, the world’s number one electric vehicle battery maker, has faltered. The net profit growth rate for the third quarter of this year recorded the lowest in 7 quarters. The slump in the Chinese electric vehicle market and the moves by countries around the world, including the United States and Europe, to keep Chinese electric vehicles in check appear to have had an impact. This is expected to be an opportunity for the domestic battery industry, including LG Energy Solution. While China is being kept in check, domestic companies are continuing a streak of winning orders for energy storage systems (ESS) for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers, utilizing their local production lines in the United States. Domestic battery makers are also a strong alternative for major automakers to execute a ‘break away from Chinese batteries.’ According to Reuters and others on Oct. 21 (local time), CATL, the world’s number one electric vehicle battery maker, announced through its third-quarter earnings report the previous day that its net profit recorded 21.25 billion yuan (about 4.2 trillion won, $3.23 billion), up 14.54% from the same period last year. This figure falls significantly short of the net profit growth rate of the second quarter (36.5%) as well as the market forecast of 41.2% compiled by market research firm London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG). It is also the lowest since the fourth quarter of 2024 (13.6%). Third-quarter sales increased by 58.58% year-on-year to 165.22 billion yuan (about 32.8 trillion won, $25.23 billion). Although the growth rate was higher than the second quarter (56.9%), it fell short of the LSEG compiled market forecast of 60.2%. The South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported that CATL’s stock price has been showing weakness after Chinese electric vehicle makers Xiaomi and Li Auto announced last month that they would collaborate with other battery manufacturers. The Chinese battery industry has grown rapidly for several years, driven by domestic subsidies and price competitiveness. However, as indiscriminate facility expansion and excessive competition continue, even the frontrunner CATL is facing checks from domestic companies in the domestic market. Furthermore, as the Chinese domestic automobile market continued its slump for 12 consecutive months until September, major battery manufacturers are staking their lives on expanding overseas exports. The tax reform by the Chinese authorities has also added to the industry’s burden. In order to curb oversupply and cutthroat competition in the battery industry, the authorities ended the lithium-ion battery consumption tax exemption in July for the first time in 10 years and applied a 2% tax rate starting in September. Following the reduction of the export value-added tax refund rate, a complete abolition was confirmed for next year. Nevertheless, the global electric vehicle battery market share of CATL, which expanded its supply to overseas automakers, rose to 39.4% from January to August this year, up from 37.7% in the same period last year. On the other hand, the market share of the second-place BYD dropped from 17.1% to 15.1%. The market foresaw that the blow could spread not only to the industry leader CATL but also to small and medium-sized battery makers. An official from Citigroup analyzed, “If even CATL cannot completely pass on the consumption tax burden to its customers, second-tier companies will also find it difficult to handle.” The moves by global automakers to ease their dependence on CATL are also a threat factor. As major automakers diversify their orders to stabilize supply chains, they are fueling competition to lower unit prices within the market. Investment bank J.P. Morgan recently downgraded its investment opinion on CATL’s Hong Kong stocks to ‘neutral,’ stating that if the profitability of the Chinese electric vehicle industry deteriorates faster than expected, it could affect the demand for CATL battery products. Analysts say that such moves by global automakers to diversify their supply chains will act as an opportunity for South Korean battery companies. The three major domestic battery makers are rapidly converting their existing lines exclusively for ESS to respond to the slowdown in electric vehicle demand. They are intensively targeting the North American ESS market, which is growing rapidly due to the proliferation of AI data centers. LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On are increasing the production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries locally in the United States while simultaneously preparing for the mass production of next-generation products such as solid-state batteries. CATL also plans to expand the proportion of its ESS business, which currently accounts for about 1/4 of its total sales, to half by 2030. In addition, it recently unveiled a next-generation battery for heavy-duty trucks and announced a plan to expand its battery swap network.

artigo.texto: CATL, BYD, and Gotion Expand Production and Supply Chains in Europe and Southeast Asia Since 2023, Holding 56.2% Share Outside China While South Korean Trio Falls to 26.8% and LFP Battery Share Rises to 27.5% Major Chinese battery companies have invested approximately $90 billion in overseas operations since 2023, expanding their penetration of the global market. While the market share of Chinese companies has increased even in the electric vehicle battery market excluding China, the market share of three domestic battery companies, including LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On, has declined. According to the UK Financial Times (FT) on October 21 (local time), major Chinese battery companies such as CATL, BYD, and Gotion High-tech were found to have invested approximately $90 billion in building overseas battery production and supply chains, including in Europe and Southeast Asia, since 2023. The market share gap in overseas markets is also widening. According to market research firm SNE Research, the combined market share of six Chinese companies, including CATL, BYD, Gotion, CALB, SVOLT, and EVE, in the global electric vehicle battery market excluding China from January to August this year was 56.2%, up 12.6 percentage points compared to the same period last year. On the other hand, the combined market share of the three domestic battery companies was 26.8%, down 11.1 percentage points during the same period. Among Chinese companies, the growth of BYD was prominent. In markets excluding China, the total battery capacity of electric vehicles equipped with BYD batteries was 39.7GWh, an increase of 66.5% compared to the same period last year. Its market share also rose from 8.2% to 11.0%. By region, battery installation volume increased by 65.6% in Europe and 138.5% in South America. Conversely, the combined battery installation volume of the three domestic battery companies, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, and SK On, in markets excluding China was 96.5GWh, a decrease of 12.8% compared to the same period last year. In particular, it dropped by 46.5% from 47.4GWh to 25.3GWh in North America. In Europe, it increased by 5.2% from 49.9GWh to 52.5GWh, but this failed to offset the decline in the North American market. Along with the rising market share of Chinese companies, the proportion of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries is also expanding. According to SNE Research, the proportion of LFP batteries in the global electric vehicle battery market excluding China rose by 11.9 percentage points from 15.6% in January to August last year to 27.5% during the same period this year. LFP batteries have relatively low manufacturing costs and are mainly used in entry-level electric vehicles. As Chinese companies have secured high production competitiveness in this area and overseas automakers increasingly adopt LFP batteries, changes are also appearing in the competitive landscape of the global battery market.

artigo.texto: Energia limpa – O Google planeja construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, Minnesota, nos Estados Unidos, acompanhado de investimentos em energia renovável e armazenamento. O acordo com a Xcel Energy prevê ampliar a capacidade da rede elétrica além da demanda da instalação, mas ainda depende de aprovação da Comissão de Utilidade Pública do estado. Segundo a CNBC, a empresa financiará a adição de 1.400 MW de energia eólica, 200 MW de energia solar e 300 MW de armazenamento em baterias. A capacidade adicional busca compensar a geração intermitente das fontes renováveis. LEIA: Consumo de água por IA varia conforme servidores e geração de energia Proteção contra a saída antecipada O contrato prevê que o Google pague pelo menos 75% da capacidade acordada, mesmo que utilize menos energia. Se encerrar o compromisso antes do prazo, poderá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas. “Ninguém quer ter uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia e ninguém para pagá-la”, diz Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel Energy. “É aí que essas proteções entram.” A iniciativa ocorre em meio à crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados. A Corporação Norte-Americana de Confiabilidade Elétrica (NERC) aponta essas instalações como principal fator de expansão prevista do consumo na América do Norte na próxima década. Nos Estados Unidos, o envelhecimento da infraestrutura também pressiona o setor elétrico. Centros menores como alternativa Para Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, empresas poderiam optar por instalações menores em regiões com capacidade disponível na rede, reduzindo custos para os consumidores. “Se você encaixar o crescimento de carga que os centros de dados querem na rede existente, as tarifas de todo mundo caem muito”, afirma. Segundo ele, construir unidades menores exige mais planejamento, mas pode evitar grandes expansões de infraestrutura. Incentivos das distribuidoras David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, observa que as distribuidoras têm incentivos financeiros para investir em novas estruturas. “Quando [as distribuidoras] constroem algo novo, financiam parte desse investimento com recursos de investidores de Wall Street e desfrutam de retornos incrivelmente altos, exorbitantes sobre esses investimentos, tipicamente em torno de 10%”, afirma. Uma alternativa seria os operadores de data centers financiarem melhorias na rede com capital mais barato. Pomerantz, porém, aponta que essa possibilidade gera conflitos com as distribuidoras. Apesar das ressalvas sobre o modelo, Shah avalia positivamente a proposta do Google, que aguarda autorização regulatória. artigo.texto: Memphis leaders are set to consider a contentious plan Tuesday to pause new data center developments for up to a year — two weeks after a meeting on the issue led to protests, calls to police and a fist fight at City Hall. The moratorium vote comes more than two years after some communities in Memphis got a new life courtesy of trillionaire Elon Musk, as his artificial intelligence company moved in amid a local effort to make the city a hotspot for advanced technology. But the effort ended up angering residents as the company installed dozens of gas-powered turbines, known to produce a cocktail of toxic pollutants. A surge of new data center construction to fuel the booming AI industry is escalating public resentment and fear of both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself in the US, roiling communities from coast to coast and transforming localized energy debates into a high-stakes, multi-million-dollar battleground for the 2026 midterm elections. At an early October council meeting in Memphis — a city used to fighting for clean air as the home to more than a dozen polluting facilities — fierce opposition was on full display. More than 100 people filed into the chamber to hear about the moratorium, bearing witness to clashes between anti-data center protesters and council members, and between the city officials themselves. Two women were also restrained in the lobby as they swung fists at each other. All eyes will be on City Hall as it considers the moratorium, which, if passed, would put a temporary pause on new data centers and on the expansion of existing ones, as well as develop a study committee to establish regulations. It would not shutter data centers already operating legally in Memphis, nor smaller data usages at facilities like hospitals and universities. Here’s what we know: How Memphis got here An abandoned factory in southwest Memphis got a makeover in June 2024, as the AI company owned by the world’s richest man, now called SpaceXAI, worked to turn the building into the “world’s largest supercomputer.” Dubbed “Colossus,” the data center was hailed by Musk at the time as the “most powerful AI training system in the world,” and the company’s website heralded plans for a second facility in the area to quickly follow. For some residents in the southwest Memphis suburb of Boxtown, a historic, majority Black and economically disadvantaged community that has long endured industrial pollution, the new gas-powered turbines represented yet another threat to their health. About 10 miles to the east in Southaven, Mississippi, more SpaceXAI turbines would chug to life at the new site of Colossus 2 — which fuels its Grok AI chatbot. CNN has reached out to SpaceXAI for comment. The NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against SpaceXAI in April of this year under the Clean Air Act, alleging it was operating dozens of unpermitted turbines in Southaven. The Department of Justice has since urged the court to throw out the lawsuit, saying the Grok AI chatbot was “critical” to national security. The case remains active, though tied up in appeals. The data centers have also caused a myriad of disruptions to daily life in Memphis, including relentless noise pollution and physical vibrations from the centers as described in a noise complaint filed by residents; concerns of dangerous emissions from the turbines brought by state officials; and an offer from SpaceXAI to buy Southaven residents’ homes in exchange for not signing onto a class action lawsuit against it. But it was at an August meeting — where the moratorium passed its first reading — that Memphis City Council Member JB Smiley Jr. said he proposed the measure to temporarily halt new data center builds after learning Musk’s company was planning a data center expansion in the city from a post on social media. “Not only did the council not know about the expansion of the data center, the community residents did not know,” Smiley said at the meeting. “I was intentional about bringing this ordinance because I think the people deserve an opportunity to voice their concerns; I think the council deserves to be treated with respect by the folks who are pushing these data centers in our community.” An earlier council meeting on data centers devolved into chaos Members of the Memphis City Council voted on whether to delay making a decision on the moratorium for two weeks at an October 6 meeting. When the effort to delay passed 7-5, the chamber erupted. “Officers, we need to clear it out,” council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington said from the podium as observers began shouting. As people rose from their seats in the chamber and a woman shouted chants into a megaphone speaker, the chairwoman repeatedly slammed her gavel, saying, “Get that f**king bullhorn!” A livestream of the meeting showed dozens of protesters gathering at the front of the room, fists in the air as they chanted above the council members’ shouts to stop, yelling, “Ain’t no power like the power of the people ‘cause the power of the people fight back!” before the livestream went dark. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton clashed with members of the crowd, according to CNN affiliate WMC, as she told one attendee, “You pipe down baby, I clap back.” She also lashed out at Smiley, who voted against postponing the vote on his moratorium, shouting that he “confuse(s) the people over and over,” as she was ushered out of the room by staffers. In the lobby of the building, a fist fight broke out between two women, WMC reported. Memphis police were called to the disturbance at City Hall, but according to WMC, a department spokesperson said no one was harmed or detained. artigo.texto: South Korea's Big 3 Battery Makers Race to Mass-Produce 'Salt Batteries,' Chasing CATL's Head Start South Korea's three major battery makers are accelerating commercialization of sodium-ion batteries, which replace lithium. Using sodium as a raw material, these batteries are seen as a technology that could reshape the next-generation energy storage system (ESS) market thanks to advantages in cost and low-temperature performance. However, China's CATL and BYD have already entered mass production, giving China the early lead. LG Energy Solution has built a sodium-ion battery pilot line at its Ochang Energy Plant in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, and is running sample tests for ESS applications at a scale of 30MWh with North American customers. The company aims for first mass production next year. In the early commercialization phase, it plans to target the vehicle auxiliary battery and ESS markets before expanding into affordable electric vehicles. Samsung SDI is developing sodium-ion batteries for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems at AI data centers and for ESS. It has drawn up mass production plans and will disclose a detailed schedule by the end of this year or during next year. SK On aims to complete prototype development by next year, centered on ESS products, and pursue commercialization in 2028. It is also reviewing the possibility of using the technology in EV batteries. Sodium-ion batteries use sodium, the main component of salt, as a raw material. Unlike lithium, the mining and refining supply chain is not concentrated in a handful of countries, making supply stable and prices cheap. Another highlighted strength is that charge and discharge performance degrades less than lithium-ion batteries in subzero conditions. Energy density, long cited as a weakness, is also improving. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), recently developed products reach energy density of up to 175Wh/kg, approaching lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries at up to 205Wh/kg. Nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries stand at around 255Wh/kg. ESS, where weight and volume constraints are relatively less binding, is the likely first application market. Global sodium-ion battery output last year was less than 1% of lithium-ion battery production, underscoring that the market is still in its early stages. Morgan Stanley expects sodium-ion batteries' share of total battery deployments to rise from 2% in 2027 to 20% in 2030 and 37% in 2035. Annual deployments are projected to reach 830GWh in 2030 and 2.4TWh in 2035, and the analysis estimates that about $800 billion in new investment will be needed by 2035 to achieve this. China is furthest ahead in seizing the market. In April, CATL signed a three-year supply contract for 60GWh with Chinese ESS company HyperStrong and entered a mass production regime. It plans to increase shipments through the end of the year and begin overseas supplies from June next year. BYD is also building a dedicated sodium-ion battery plant. The sense of urgency in South Korea's industry stems from memories of past failures in responding to LFP. The prevailing view is that while Korean companies focused on high-performance NMC batteries, they fell behind in LFP mass production and handed leadership of that market to China. There is a growing sense of crisis that if they are also outrun in sodium-ion batteries, they could lose leadership of the battery industry itself. If sodium-ion batteries are commercialized in earnest, the cost-competition landscape in the ESS market could change. The burden on existing supply chains exposed to lithium price swings would ease, and the economics of long-duration storage facilities could improve. However, a gap with LFP in energy density remains, suggesting it will take considerable time before sodium-ion becomes a mainstream EV battery. Whether South Korea's three companies can move up their mass production timelines is seen as a variable that will determine the supply landscape of the ESS market going forward.

artigo.texto: CATL Tries to Reassure Investors: Next Year's Battery Demand Not as Bleak as Feared, but Shares Still Plunge Nearly 10% CATL (03750.HK), China's battery leader, on the 21st took the rare step of proactively addressing market doubts. Responding to investor concerns about weakening demand in next year's new energy vehicle market and for batteries, the company said "next year's industry demand is still worth looking forward to," emphasizing that the global market size for power batteries and energy storage batteries may not be as bleak as outsiders imagine and still holds solid growth potential. The reassurance, however, failed to reverse the stock's slide. The shares touched an intraday low of HK$371.2 that day and last traded at HK$371.8, down 9.71%, on volume of 5.1631 million shares worth HK$1.964 billion (approximately $250.3 million), extending a run of new lows. CATL's weaker-than-expected third-quarter net profit was the direct trigger for the selloff. Breaking down the fundamentals, the company believes the market's assessment of demand is too conservative. In China, overall passenger vehicle sales have declined this year, but the electrification rate is climbing rapidly, and the battery capacity per vehicle is rising at the same time. Combined, these two forces are keeping shipment growth of power batteries for new energy passenger vehicles in positive territory. The electrification rate for new energy commercial vehicles is also in a rapid ascent. Overseas, the electrification trend in Europe has continuity, with new models continuing to launch and remaining competitive, while electrification potential in other markets may be underestimated. The energy storage business is another bright spot, maintaining solid growth in both China and overseas markets, with demand particularly strong in some overseas markets. Asked about capacity utilization, the company said utilization was at a very saturated level in the first half. In recent years it has accelerated capacity construction in line with market demand, and as new capacity added this year gradually comes on stream, the tightness has eased somewhat. But demand is also continuing to grow, so capacity utilization will remain at a relatively high level going forward and is overall healthy. The change in cash flow that has drawn outside attention is tied to an adjustment in supply chain strategy. The company noted that upstream lithium battery supply chain companies have faced relatively heavy cash flow pressure in recent years, and CATL has proactively adjusted payment arrangements with suppliers since the third quarter, giving priority to supporting partners with R&D capabilities, an innovative spirit and active cooperation in capacity expansion. Measures include shortening payment terms, making prepayments and providing R&D funding support, among others. This approach to supporting the supply chain may continue for some time, with the aim of fostering healthier and more sustainable development across the industry. It will have a phased impact on operating cash flow, but over the long term will not hurt the company's cash profitability, which is expected to return to a relatively healthy level. As for the quarter-on-quarter increase in third-quarter inventory, the company explained that the larger inventory figure is a natural result of business growth. Inventory turnover days have been relatively stable in recent quarters, with no sluggish sales or shipment disruptions, representing normal turnover. By composition, the increase was mainly goods shipped but not yet recognized as revenue, which will gradually be reflected in the company's revenue. In energy storage, the company is shifting from simply selling battery cells and DC-side products to offering AC-side and system-level products. The product mix and formats are richer than before, and the corresponding delivery and revenue recognition cycles have lengthened. In terms of market impact, CATL is a bellwether for the global power and energy storage battery industry, and its read on next year's demand is seen as an important gauge of conditions across the electric vehicle and energy storage sectors. The company's disclosures on capacity, cash flow and inventory in its earnings call and response help investors clarify the line items in its third-quarter report most likely to raise questions. Still, the stock's nearly 10% plunge after the results reflects short-term investors' heightened sensitivity to the profit miss and the phased pressure on cash flow. The strength of the demand recovery and the actual impact of the supply chain payment adjustments will be key focal points as the market re-evaluates the stock.

artigo.texto: Huawei and CATL Partner to Fully Automate EV Battery Swaps, 'Full' in 99 Seconds China's electric vehicle (EV) market has kicked off a race to automate "battery swap" services that replace an entire battery without waiting to charge or discharge. Yinwang (In-One), the automotive technology subsidiary of telecom equipment giant Huawei, CATL, the world's largest automotive battery maker, and Shidai Dianfu, which operates battery-swap services, have formed a partnership aimed at building a system in which vehicles decide on their own whether a swap is needed and complete everything from entering the station to swapping the battery to leaving, unmanned. Huawei disclosed the plan on October 19. At the core of the partnership is connecting Huawei's advanced driver-assistance system "Qiankun" with CATL's battery-swap network "Choco-Swap" at the data level. Information will be exchanged among vehicles, swap stations and the cloud, and the need for a swap will be judged based on remaining battery charge and the user's travel patterns. If a swap is deemed necessary, the vehicle will search on its own for a compatible station, enter it autonomously, adjust its position to align with the swapping equipment, be fitted with a charged battery and then leave autonomously—the envisioned flow. According to CATL, BAIC Group's EV "Arcfox S3 Choco-Swap Edition" can complete the battery swap itself in 99 seconds. However, the total time required, including entering and leaving the station and positioning, has not been disclosed. Huawei plans to make the system available on vehicles that adopt its automotive technology, but it has not touched on which models will be compatible or when the service will launch. Huawei explains that the aim of the collaboration is to realize a power-replenishment experience in which users do not need to think about charging, looking ahead to the era of autonomous driving, and to provide more diverse and convenient swap services. Information on the scale of the battery-swap network is mixed. According to details CATL published in April 2026, it operates more than 1,470 swap stations in 99 cities in China. Meanwhile, according to reports by U.S. EV-specialist media outlet Electrek and others, the network has reached more than 2,520 stations in about 200 cities, with a goal of expanding to more than 30,000 stations in the future. Both sets of figures were provided by CATL, and the differences are believed to stem from different tally dates and definitions. Note: Station counts vary depending on the disclosing party and timing. Total time required, compatible models and service launch timing have not been disclosed. Behind this lies the delay in commercializing all-solid-state batteries, seen as next-generation batteries. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng, speaking at the 2026 Summer Davos (World Economic Forum) in June 2026, rated the technological maturity of all-solid-state batteries on a scale of 1 to 9 and said, "We are currently at stage 4, and mass production will only become possible once we reach stage 9." If the swap network is sufficiently developed, the time spent waiting to charge and the burden of long-distance travel can be reduced without waiting for dramatic improvements in battery performance itself. However, the commercial success of the battery-swap model remains unclear. Tesla began a demonstration project for an automated swap system in 2014 but later withdrew. CEO Elon Musk said at the time that he called on 200 customers to use it, but only about four or five showed interest. He has expressed the view that "charging time" provides users with leisure—time to stretch their legs, go to the restroom or drink coffee during a trip—and takes the position of questioning the superiority of the swap model. Some market participants see the partnership as a move that will shake up the battle for leadership in the battery-swap ecosystem in China's EV market. If Huawei expands the number of vehicles equipped with its driver-assistance technology, CATL's swap network can strengthen its connection with users as a touchpoint that "makes them forget about charging." On the other hand, a design that deeply integrates in-vehicle systems with external infrastructure could become a barrier to entry for other automakers. In the initial phase, when compatible models are limited, investors will likely be watching closely how quickly the partnership is implemented and how utilization rates trend.

artigo.texto: China's CATL Plunges 12% in A-Shares; Management Says 2027 Demand Still Worth Anticipating On Oct. 21, CATL's (300750.SZ) A-shares fell as much as 12% intraday before closing at 227.9 yuan, more than 50% below the all-time high of 460 yuan set on May 6. Its Hong Kong shares fell 11.41% the same day, dragging the combined A+H market capitalization to around 1.1 trillion yuan (approximately $165 billion), with single-day turnover exceeding 16 billion yuan (approximately $2.4 billion). The immediate trigger for the selloff was the third-quarter report released the previous evening: revenue of 165.221 billion yuan, up 58.58% year on year, and net profit attributable to shareholders of 21.246 billion yuan, up just 14.54% year on year and down 5.77% from the prior quarter, with profit growth lagging far behind revenue growth. Facing market doubts, CATL responded intensively on the morning of Oct. 21, with its core message being that "industry demand is not that pessimistic, and capacity utilization will remain at a relatively high level going forward." The company also addressed three focal points one by one: 2027 demand, the cash flow decline and rising inventory. The triple squeeze behind the profit slowdown The third-quarter report showed CATL's revenue for the first nine months at 442.137 billion yuan (approximately $66.3 billion), up 56.19% year on year, with net profit attributable to shareholders of 64.53 billion yuan (approximately $9.7 billion), up 31.60%. But quarterly profit growth slowed steadily, from 48.52% in the first quarter and 36.46% in the second to 14.54% in the third, a pace of margin deterioration that exceeded market expectations. The sources of margin compression are not singular. Management attributed the third-quarter margin decline to an unfavorable product mix, a higher share of low-margin products, and reduced VAT rebates combined with a 2% domestic consumption tax that took effect in September — the two together adding about 1.5 billion yuan (approximately $224.8 million) in costs versus the second quarter. Institutional estimates show per-wh profit on a battery basis fell to about 0.057 yuan in the third quarter, or about 0.081 yuan on a company-wide basis, below the 0.10 yuan of the first half, while gross margin fell 2.5 percentage points quarter on quarter to 20.7%, the lowest since the fourth quarter of 2022. Morgan Stanley analysts Jack Lu and Kaylee Xu noted in a report that unit net margin plunged from 0.10 yuan/Wh in the first half to 0.08 yuan/Wh, a significant drop, and that consensus earnings forecasts are expected to see material downgrades after the results. The bank expects margins to recover somewhat from the trough, but the extent of that recovery increasingly depends on product mix changes and the intensity of competition in the energy storage market. The structural nature of the tax burden deserves more attention. The consumption tax and export rebate adjustments are not one-off shocks: the consumption tax will rise further to 4% in 2027, and the export rebate will be eliminated that year. That means the downward shift in the unit profitability center will not disappear automatically with stabilizing lithium prices or a demand rebound in any single quarter. Company response: demand, capacity and cash flow Addressing investor concerns about new-energy industry demand next year, CATL offered a relatively upbeat assessment. The company said that although overall domestic passenger car sales have declined, the electrification rate is rising rapidly and battery capacity per vehicle is growing quickly, so power battery growth for new-energy passenger cars remains positive; the electrification rate of new-energy commercial vehicles is also climbing fast; Europe's electrification trend is continuous, with competitive new models being launched; and electrification potential in other markets "may be underestimated by the market." In energy storage, growth remains solid both in China and abroad, with demand particularly strong in some overseas markets. The company concluded that global demand for power and energy storage batteries may not be as pessimistic as the market expects. On capacity utilization, the company said the first half was "very saturated," and that tightness has eased somewhat as new capacity came on stream this year, but with demand continuing to grow, utilization will remain at a relatively high level and in healthy shape. A 23.60% year-on-year decline in third-quarter operating cash flow was another core metric that drew attention in the report. The company explained that upstream lithium battery supply chain companies have faced cash flow pressure in recent years, and that from the third quarter it proactively adjusted payment arrangements with suppliers, prioritizing partners with R&D capabilities that actively support capacity expansion — measures including shorter payment terms, prepayments and R&D funding support, which may persist for some time. The company stated clearly that operating cash flow will be affected for a period but that this will not affect cash profitability over the long run, and that it will return to a relatively healthy level. On the quarter-on-quarter inventory increase, the company said it mainly stems from business growth, with inventory turnover days relatively stable in recent quarters and no problems with sales or shipments; the increase is mainly goods shipped, which will gradually be recognized as revenue. The energy storage business's extension from battery cells and DC-side products to AC-side and system products has lengthened delivery and revenue recognition cycles, also contributing to the temporary inventory build. Market share and competitive landscape CATL's global position remains solid for now. According to SNE Research, the company's global market share of power battery usage was 39.4% in January-August 2026, up 1.7 percentage points year on year.
