artigo.texto: Peak Energy Raises $108 Million in Series B Funding Peak Energy, a semiconductor company, has raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B. The round was led by General Motors Ventures, with additional participation from Maverick Silicon, Infinite Capital, Eclipse, Xora Innovation and LG Technology Ventures. The Sacramento-based company develops sodium-ion energy storage systems for grid-scale applications. The new capital will support domestic manufacturing expansion and entry into the data centre market. Peak Energy also plans to fulfil more than $1 billion in existing customer orders. The company was formed in 2023 to provide more affordable and safer large-scale energy storage. It utilises a sodium-ion battery-based technology with an innovative passive cooling system to cut costs without the need for traditional active cooling technology. This investment comes on the back of increased demand for electricity infrastructure. Data centres, for example, consume significant amounts of power in servicing AI applications. Storage solutions can ease grid constraints and bolster electricity grid reliability. Passive Cooling Targets Lower Storage Costs Peak Energy’s system is designed to reduce the costs associated with operating and maintaining conventional energy storage installations. Its passive cooling architecture removes the need for energy-intensive cooling systems. The company says this design can lower energy costs by up to 20%. The platform also aims to reduce maintenance requirements and improve operational reliability. Peak Energy says its systems require no planned maintenance. They also consume no water and produce virtually no noise. Safety remains another central part of the company’s approach. Peak Energy says its design eliminates leading causes of battery fires. These features could make its systems attractive to communities near large storage installations. Sodium-ion technology also offers an alternative to lithium-ion batteries. Sodium is an abundant material that could support domestic supply chains. Peak Energy is developing its platform for utility-scale storage rather than consumer electronics. Sacramento Factory Supports Domestic Manufacturing Peak Energy is expanding its manufacturing operations through a new facility in Sacramento, California. The factory is designed to provide four gigawatt-hours of annual manufacturing capacity. Production is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. The facility will help the company increase output as customer demand grows. Peak Energy has secured commercial agreements with Jupiter Power, RWE and Energy Vault. Its existing commitments exceed $1 billion, according to the company. In June 2026, Peak Energy announced a strategic partnership with General Motors. The companies plan to develop next-generation sodium-ion battery cells for energy storage. GM will contribute its experience in domestic battery manufacturing and industrialisation. More News: Blacksmith Raises $66M for AI Code Testing Infrastructure Data Centre Expansion Creates New Growth Opportunities Peak Energy plans to use its latest financing to enter the data centre market. Artificial intelligence growth has increased pressure on electricity infrastructure. Operators require reliable power solutions that enable growth without incurring the high costs. Energy storage to ease the stress on power systems and meet peak demand Peak Energy says its passive cooling system can bring a “competitive edge” to facilities with space, water and safety concerns. Execution will depend on manufacturing progress and successful commercial deployment. General Motors Ventures sees potential in the company’s approach. Its president, Kevin McCabe, highlighted the technology’s potential as a cost-effective solution using abundant, domestically sourced materials. The planned 2027 production launch will be an important milestone for the company. artigo.texto: Saft, a subsidiary of TotalEnergies, is set to inaugurate new solid-state battery production lines at its site in Bordeaux, marking a significant step towards industrial-scale manufacturing of next-generation energy storage technology. The facility will make Saft the first French manufacturer with the capacity to develop and produce solid-state batteries using both sulphide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. This combination of technologies offers potential applications across several industries, particularly aviation and space. Higher energy density and improved safety Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte found in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid material. According to Saft, this approach offers improved safety and energy density up to 50% higher than that of traditional lithium-ion batteries. The manufacturing process also incorporates dry electrodes, which can reduce carbon dioxide emissions during this stage of production by up to 40%, offering potential environmental benefits alongside improved battery performance. These characteristics make solid-state technology a promising option for applications where safety, compact design and energy density are important requirements. Supporting electrification in aviation and space Saft is targeting the aviation and space sectors, where advances in battery performance could support further electrification. The company has already reached an initial milestone in aviation, delivering semi-solid-state cells for the evaluation of future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. Solid-state batteries have also attracted significant interest from the space industry, highlighting their potential across demanding applications. Turning research into industrial production The new production lines represent the transition from years of research into manufacturing capability, supporting the development of solid-state batteries for future applications. Cedric Duclos, Chief Executive Officer of Saft, said: “Solid-state batteries are among the most promising innovations to meet tomorrow’s electrification needs. These new production lines mark an important milestone for Saft, as we turn several years of research into real industrial capacity, a statement of our ambition to establish France and Europe as leading players in this strategic technology.” The initiative reinforces Saft’s ambition to help establish France and Europe as key participants in the development and production of solid-state battery technology. artigo.texto: Fundos imobiliários de data centers: nova fronteira O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) está abrindo novas possibilidades de investimento no mercado imobiliário. Embora a IA seja frequentemente associada ao desenvolvimento de software, sua operação depende de uma estrutura física robusta, que envolve semicondutores, energia elétrica, redes de transmissão, sistemas de resfriamento e data centers. Para investidores e empresários de Araçatuba e região noroeste paulista, essa tendência pode representar uma nova fronteira de diversificação de portfólio e de negócios. Segundo a XP, os fundos imobiliários podem acessar esse mercado por meio da aquisição de data centers operacionais, do financiamento de projetos em desenvolvimento e do investimento em infraestruturas associadas, como subestações elétricas. Nesse modelo, a exposição do cotista é imobiliária: o fundo adquire o imóvel e recebe os aluguéis pagos pelo operador responsável pelo data center ou pela infraestrutura locada. As receitas provenientes de serviços de computação em nuvem, processamento de dados ou outras atividades tecnológicas permanecem com o operador, e não são diretamente apropriadas pelo fundo. Modelos de investimento em data centers Os fundos imobiliários podem atuar de diferentes formas nesse segmento. A aquisição de data centers operacionais é uma das estratégias: o fundo compra um imóvel já em funcionamento, com contratos de locação vigentes e fluxo de caixa previsível. Outra possibilidade é o financiamento de projetos em desenvolvimento, no qual o fundo fornece capital para a construção ou expansão de um data center, assumindo riscos maiores em troca de retornos potencialmente mais elevados. Há ainda o investimento em infraestruturas associadas, como subestações elétricas, que são essenciais para o fornecimento de energia aos data centers e podem gerar renda estável por meio de contratos de locação de longo prazo. Em todos esses casos, a exposição do cotista é imobiliária. O fundo adquire o imóvel e recebe os aluguéis pagos pelo operador responsável pelo data center ou pela infraestrutura locada. As receitas provenientes de serviços de computação em nuvem, processamento de dados ou outras atividades tecnológicas permanecem com o operador, e não são diretamente apropriadas pelo fundo. Essa separação é fundamental para entender o perfil de risco e retorno do investimento. Perspectivas e riscos do setor A perspectiva de expansão dos serviços digitais pode favorecer a ocupação dos empreendimentos e a capacidade de pagamento dos locatários. Com o crescimento do uso de IA, streaming, comércio eletrônico e outras aplicações, a demanda por processamento e armazenamento de dados tende a aumentar, o que pode elevar a taxa de ocupação dos data centers e a estabilidade dos aluguéis. Para investidores do interior paulista, isso pode significar uma alternativa de renda passiva com lastro em ativos reais. Ainda assim, diz a XP, o resultado depende de como cada ativo foi adquirido, da estrutura de financiamento e das necessidades futuras de investimento para manter a infraestrutura competitiva. Data centers exigem atualizações constantes de equipamentos e sistemas de resfriamento, o que pode demandar novos aportes de capital. Além disso, a localização geográfica e a disponibilidade de energia elétrica são fatores críticos que podem afetar a viabilidade do empreendimento. Built to suit: contratos sob medida Já no modelo built to suit, o imóvel é construído ou adaptado de acordo com as necessidades específicas do futuro ocupante. Em contrapartida, o locatário firma um contrato de longo prazo, que deve remunerar adequadamente o capital investido pelo proprietário. Esse modelo é comum em projetos de data centers, pois as exigências técnicas — como piso elevado, refrigeração redundante e segurança física — são muito específicas e difíceis de encontrar em imóveis prontos. Contratos atípicos podem prever prazos extensos, reajustes periódicos pela inflação e penalidades por rescisão antecipada. Quando essas penalidades são elevadas e vinculadas ao saldo de aluguéis até o vencimento, podem desestimular a saída antecipada do inquilino e favorecer o alinhamento entre o prazo contratual e o horizonte de retorno do investimento. Para o investidor, isso proporciona maior previsibilidade de fluxo de caixa e reduz o risco de vacância. Impacto para o noroeste paulista Embora os grandes data centers estejam concentrados em regiões metropolitanas, a expansão da infraestrutura digital pode gerar efeitos indiretos para cidades como Araçatuba, Birigui, Penápolis e Andradina. A necessidade de energia elétrica confiável, por exemplo, pode impulsionar investimentos em subestações e redes de transmissão na região. Além disso, empresas locais de construção civil, manutenção predial e serviços técnicos podem ser contratadas para obras e operações de data centers de menor porte. Para empresários do comércio e da indústria local, a tendência também pode representar uma oportunidade de diversificação de investimentos. Fundos imobiliários que investem em data centers são negociados na bolsa de valores e podem ser acessados por meio de corretoras, com valores mínimos relativamente baixos. No entanto, é essencial avaliar o perfil de risco e buscar orientação de profissionais especializados antes de investir. A fonte não detalhou valores mínimos de investimento, prazos de retorno ou exemplos específicos de fundos. Ainda assim, a sinalização da XP indica que o setor deve ganhar relevância nos próximos anos, acompanhando o crescimento da economia digital. Para o noroeste paulista, o desafio será criar condições de infraestrutura e mão de obra qualificada para atrair parte desses investimentos. artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, an investment company of SKC in the copper foil business for secondary batteries, said Tuesday that it has successfully developed 'high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil' technology, which is considered a core material for next-generation batteries. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil is a product that applies special carbon to the surface of the copper foil to enhance adhesion with the anode material. It is characterized by suppressing the 'delamination phenomenon,' where silicon anode materials expand during charging and discharging processes, causing them to separate from the copper foil, thereby improving the structural stability of the electrode. The company explained that this can also contribute to enhancing battery lifespan and safety. SK Nexilis developed the related technology in line with the trend in the battery industry to increase the silicon content of anode materials to boost energy density. While silicon can store more lithium ions than conventional graphite, its significant volume change during charging and discharging processes is cited as a drawback. This is why adhesion between the anode material and copper foil becomes increasingly important as the silicon content rises. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil can also be applied to dry electrode processes, which are gaining attention as a manufacturing method for next-generation batteries. Unlike conventional wet processes that use liquid solvents, dry electrode processes can reduce steps such as drying, thereby lowering manufacturing costs and energy consumption. However, since it is crucial to stably bond electrode materials with copper foil, the utilization of high-adhesion copper foil is expected to expand. SK Nexilis plans to build a pilot production system for high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil ahead of full-scale Yangsan. The company is currently verifying process stability and aims to commercialize in the second half of next year after securing Yangsan technology. An official from SK Nexilis said, "We will proceed with commercialization optimization work without any issues while strengthening our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technological development."

artigo.texto: A battle over protecting the electric bills of Xcel Energy residential and small business customers from the costs of burgeoning data centers is set to begin Wednesday before the Colorado Public Utilities Commission. The PUC required Xcel Energy — the state’s largest electricity provider with 1.6 million customers — to develop a “large load tariff,” a set of requirements designed to protect retail customers from the cost of data centers and other high-demand electricity customers. Xcel Energy filed its proposed tariff in April and since then it has been the focus of a debate between environmental and consumer advocates who want even tougher protections and business and data center groups seeking to trim requirements. Hearings on the proposed tariff are scheduled to run for several days beginning Wednesday afternoon. “It’s a big deal,” said Eric Frankowski, executive director of the Western Clean Energy Campaign, a consumer and environment advocacy group. “This determines how data centers are brought into the mix and what it means to every other customer in the Xcel system. “If they get it right then data centers can join the state’s economy and contribute to it and it doesn’t affect customers’ rates,” he added. “If wrong, we are all kind of screwed. Rates will soar; the grid will be stressed.” One controversial element in the proposed tariff is a “speed to market” pathway, which would enable Xcel Energy and a developer to negotiate a confidential contract that would not necessarily have the tariff’s safeguards and would require rapid PUC approval. “The concept is necessary to provide an option for large load customers who require greater commercial flexibility,” Jack Ihle, the company’s vice president for data centers and large loads, said in PUC testimony. But Frankowski said speed to market could “potentially undermine the tariff.” Environmental groups are also worried data centers’ big electricity demands will jeopardize the state’s goal of cutting greenhouse gas emission by 80% over 2005 levels by 2030 and result in data centers relying on natural gas and coal-fired generation. “Load growth stands to raise system costs, increase cumulative greenhouse gas emissions, risk delays of approved retirements of fossil-fuel generation units,” Clare Valentine, a senior policy advisor with environmental law nonprofit Western Resource Advocates, said in a filing. WRA is urging the commission to expand renewable energy options in the tariff. The PUC hearings on data center rates are taking place against the backdrop of a pushback on rapid data center development across Colorado. Eight municipalities and counties have enacted or are considering moratoriums or caps on data centers. Proposed projects have sparked community opposition in Colorado Springs, Brighton and Weld County. A coalition of environmental and community groups delivered a petition with 5,000 signatures to the PUC urging it to protect customers. “On the PUC side, we’re moving full steam ahead to accommodate this,” said Joe Pereira, director of the Colorado Office of the Utility Consumer Advocate. “On the flip side, the general population has not determined what the public interest around these entities looks like.” Still, large-scale data centers and their interconnection to the electric grid “represent a foundational platform for national prosperity,” August Ankum, a consultant for the Data Center Coalition, an industry group, said in PUC testimony. “In the short-run,” Ankum conceded, “the introduction of large load data centers into the system may cause network augmentations that are costly. Ratepayers need to be protected against those costs.” With business groups arguing for the tariff to do less and consumers and environmental advocates calling for it to do more, Xcel Energy says its approach is a compromise. “The company’s proposals reflect a reasonable and balanced middle ground between approaches that would impose commercially impractical obligations and approaches that would reduce customer responsibility in ways that could unreasonably shift costs and risk to existing customers,” Ihle of Xcel said in a filing. As an example of the difference in approach, while Xcel is calling for 15 year contracts the PUC staff recommended 20 years and the Data Center Coalition proposed a 10-year term. The large load tariff would apply to new customers needing 50 megawatts of power or more and each would have to pay a $120,000 application fee to cover Xcel Energy’s costs in handling the request and doing the necessary studies. Xcel Energy would do a study to determine the costs to the grid the project would create and allocate those costs for new generation and transmission to the data center. Xcel Energy estimates it will need 2 gigawatts of generating capacity just for data centers by 2030. Currently total capacity is just over 7 GW. (A gigawatt can power about 700,000 households per year.) A data center would have to sign interconnect and electric service agreements and a 15-year contract for electricity. It would have to commit to paying for at least 80% of the projected electricity. Data centers would be subject to minimum monthly bills. As an example, Xcel Energy said in a filing that the monthly bill from a 500-MW data center could be $22 million. The center would also have to provide a credit guarantee, such as 60 months of minimum bills, and if it wanted to get out of its contract it would have to pay an exit fee equal to the sum of the remaining monthly bills on the contract. A big question is how many of these requirements, and numerous others in the tariff, end up in the confidential speed-to-market agreements. artigo.texto: Support WBUR How some AI researchers skip big data centers by thinking small "Hey, Ava." Ava, a wheeled white pillar with a camera and screen docked in a Tufts University lab hallway, responded with a two-tone bleep. Mattias Scheutz, director of the school's Human-Robot Interaction Lab, continued his request. "I'm wondering if you could take me to the elevators," he said. "Heading there," the robot said from some hidden speaker. And the experimental pylon started to move. Scheutz said he imagines a future where robots like Ava do many things big and small, from search-and-rescue missions to washing dishes. With recent advances in artificial intelligence, he said, that vision feels closer than ever. Scheutz is one player in a cast of Boston-area researchers and engineers using AI to build robots that can adapt to changes in their physical surroundings. And the tech solution they’re harnessing doesn’t rely on data centers. Popular chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT are powered by models trained on enormous amounts of information, which means spending billions on vast data centers that can take more power and water than entire cities. Instead, roboticists like Scheutz are thinking small. They’re designing AI systems compact enough to fit on a single computer chip. Robots powered with these small AI models can make decisions quickly. And because the chips are installed in the robots, there's no need to send signals to and from data centers for processing. That means the robots can run AI without an internet connection. On its journey to the elevators, Ava encountered a student sitting at a desk in its path. The robot stoped and stuttered: It’d never seen this obstacle before. “That's not in its map,” Scheutz explained. “So now it has to plan around it.” Within seconds, Ava skirted around the desk and continued onward. By making that little adjustment, Scheutz said Ava accomplished a key challenge in robotics; it navigated what’s known as a “dynamic obstacle.” The robot tackled this task with a type of AI called a neurosymbolic model. The model allows the robot to execute tasks and recognize patterns in its environment, which allows Ava to move in response to unfamiliar situations. Models like this reduce the most energy-intensive aspect of AI: training. To create the large language model GPT-4, for example, MIT Technology Review cited an estimate that Open AI used as much energy as San Francisco consumes in three days. And small AI models have another energy-saving bonus. Since they don’t need data centers to operate, they bypass the energy costs of running hefty cooling systems and thousands of servers at once. The Tufts team loaded its neurosymbolic model onto a robotic arm and tested it against a larger AI model. The researchers asked both systems to tackle a block stacking puzzle. The results, which they presented at an international robotics conference this year, showed the neurosymbolic model was more accurate and required 100 times less energy to train, compared to the larger AI. “Who doesn't want a model that's more capable given the same data or a model that's as capable but requires less data?” asked Helen Lu, a Ph.D candidate and co-author of the Tufts study. Other companies are working on their own versions of small, energy-efficient AI. “We want to find the most intelligent model per watt,” said Alexander Amini, chief science officer at Liquid AI, an MIT spinoff company. Amini said the startup’s strategy runs counter to most big AI companies, which focus on creating intelligence “at all costs.” By honing in on smallness instead, Liquid AI can run its models on any device with a computer chip. Like the chips in your car. The company has partnered with Mercedes-Benz in North America, and Amini envisions cars that respond to conversational prompts like, “My back hurts.” "And the car is intelligent enough to reason about those statements and start to, let's say, turn on the seat heater, turn on the massager,” he said. A potential downside is that limited training may create AI models with less intelligence, and less usefulness, than large AI. But Liquid AI’s cofounder, Daniela Rus, argues there’s plenty of room for both. “It is important to keep in mind that not all AI problems require cloud-level intelligence,” said Rus, who directs MIT’s Computer Science and AI Laboratory. A lot of what users ask AI chatbots are relatively simple queries that can be answered without “extreme Ph.D-level knowledge,” according to Amini. Big AI — the type of model that can both do astrophysics and write a book report — isn’t going away. But Rus and Amini are betting that not every task, or every robot, needs that. This story is part of Awaiting Data, a special series from the New England News Collaborative.

artigo.texto: Alhambra voters will get a say this November on whether to impose a citywide ban on data centers. Measure DB in Alhambra, which would prohibit data centers in the city, follows on the heels of Monterey Park's Measure NDC, which voters passed earlier this year in June to ban data centers in its city. Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The growth of data centers and artificial intelligence has become a topic of discussion among politicians at a local and federal scale -- from protection against AI in Hollywood to regulating the industry. Now, some local residents will be able to decide whether they should be allowed to be in their communities. What is a data center? A data center houses a network of computer systems that are used for data storage. They require the use of backup diesel generators and freshwater to keep the computers cool. Depending on the size of the center, up to 5 million gallons of freshwater could be used per day, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. Those who oppose data centers have cited environmental concerns as their reasoning, while those who support them say they help the U.S. stay ahead technologically of global competitors. Measure DB in Alhambra The measure allows Alhambra residents to decide whether data centers should be prohibited in the city. The measure reads: “Shall an ordinance be adopted affirming the Council-adopted ban on "Data Centers" by amending the Alhambra Municipal Code to again define "Data Centers" and prohibit them in all zones of the City?” Voting “yes” for the measure would prohibit data centers in the city of Alhambra. Voting “no” against the measure opposes prohibiting data centers in Alhambra, which could pave the way to allow them in the city.

artigo.texto: O cronograma do leilão de espectro, a maturidade do ecossistema de equipamentos, os novos compromissos relacionados aos data centers, o uso e a eficiência do espectro, a limpeza da faixa e o RAN Sharing foram os temas mais debatidos entre a Anatel, representantes de associações e duas das três operadoras nacionais durante a discussão sobre a destinação da faixa de 6 GHz e o futuro leilão, previsto para 2028, cujas propostas estão em consulta pública. Entenda a proposta da Anatel Em evento realizado na unidade da agência em São Paulo (SP) nesta quarta-feira, 21, a Anatel apresentou um cronograma e uma proposta preliminar de leilão da faixa de 6 GHz para o Serviço Móvel Pessoal (SMP), na porção superior da frequência. A porção inferior continuará destinada ao uso não licenciado (Wi-Fi). Confira os detalhes: - Oferta de 700 MHz de espectro contínuo em banda média; - Outorga por 20 anos, com possibilidade de prorrogação; - Divisão técnica em quatro blocos: três de 200 MHz e um de 100 MHz; - Dois lotes nacionais de 200 MHz (A1 e A2) e 14 lotes regionais, distribuídos em sete áreas, seguindo a dinâmica do leilão do 5G; - Modelo financeiro não arrecadatório, com conversão dos valores em compromissos de interesse público; - Disputa vencida pelo proponente que oferecer o maior valor, em uma dinâmica de lances sucessivos; - Limite de 200 MHz por proponente em cada área geográfica; - Exigência de garantias operacionais em até 180 dias e de execução dos compromissos, com renovação a cada 24 meses. De acordo com Nilo Pasquali, superintendente de planejamento e regulamentação da Anatel, o objetivo do leilão é viabilizar a evolução do 5G, do 5,5G e, futuramente, do 6G por meio da faixa de 6 GHz, evitando a concentração de espectro. Assim como ocorreu nos leilões do 5G, em 2021, e da faixa de 700 MHz, a Anatel também propôs uma série de contrapartidas. A principal delas é a criação de uma infraestrutura digital regional, por meio do desenvolvimento do mercado de data centers e de nós de edge computing no Brasil. Segundo Felipe Roberto, gerente de regulamentação da agência, as vencedoras do leilão deverão se associar para realizar os aportes financeiros. A iniciativa será organizada por uma estrutura de governança com participação da Anatel, possivelmente por meio de uma entidade semelhante à Entidade Administradora da Faixa (EAF). O modelo reunirá as empresas e seus aportes, enquanto o Estado ficará responsável por estabelecer a política pública. Os ministérios das Comunicações (MCom) e do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços (MDIC) também deverão participar. Para viabilizar o modelo, será necessário “ter mínimo de viabilidade econômica, pois é um aporte finito”, afirmou Roberto. As regras para as contrapartidas são: - Aporte coletivo para criar infraestrutura regional nas regiões Centro-Oeste, Norte e Nordeste; - Núcleos regionais neutros nas capitais, com capacidade de 1,5 MW a 5 MW, classificação Tier III, hospedagem gratuita no IX.br e três rotas distintas de fibra óptica; - Nós de borda no interior, com capacidade de 100 kW a 500 kW e classificação Tier II; - Garantia de viabilidade, com as vencedoras assegurando demanda mínima equivalente a 30% da capacidade energizada por cinco anos; - Proibição expressa do uso dos recursos para hyperscalers ou para o treinamento de modelos de inteligência artificial; - Liberação dos recursos em três etapas: 40% na implementação, 30% na energização e os 30% restantes após o primeiro ano, conforme o desempenho operacional; - Possibilidade de converter saldos em compromissos de implantação de fibra óptica ou de redes móveis caso não haja projetos elegíveis, conforme uma cláusula de reversão. Com entregas previstas entre 2029 e 2033, os demais compromissos do futuro leilão da faixa de 6 GHz são: - Construção de redes de transporte (backhaul) para localidades sem cobertura, com capacidade de 1 Gbps em cidades com até 20 mil habitantes e de 10 Gbps naquelas com mais de 20 mil habitantes. Também haverá conexão obrigatória a pontos de troca de tráfego e compartilhamento da infraestrutura no atacado; - Cobertura móvel em regiões desassistidas, com tecnologia mínima de LTE Advanced e velocidade mínima a ser definida. O vencedor deverá partir de infraestrutura própria, sendo proibido cumprir essa obrigação por meio de RAN Sharing, MVNO ou roaming; - Regras de ESG, incluindo eficiência energética e consumo de energia proveniente de fontes renováveis. Previsto para ocorrer até 2028, o leilão também terá regras de convivência e uso do espectro. Vinicius Caram, superintendente de outorga e espectro da Anatel, explicou que: - A desocupação da faixa pelos serviços fixos deverá ocorrer em até seis meses após o leilão nas capitais e regiões metropolitanas e em até um ano nos demais municípios; - O modelo será híbrido, com blocos de 10 MHz e agregação mínima de 20 MHz em TDD; - A faixa inferior, de 500 MHz, permanecerá destinada ao uso não licenciado, enquanto a superior, de 700 MHz, será destinada ao IMT (serviços móveis); - Testes realizados pela Anatel no Instituto Eldorado, porém, indicaram a necessidade de filtros físicos para garantir a coexistência entre Wi-Fi e redes móveis na faixa. Após o encerramento da consulta pública e das audiências públicas — a próxima será realizada em Fortaleza (CE) —, o tema será submetido ao Conselho Diretor da Anatel. Se aprovado, o edital do leilão da faixa de 6 GHz seguirá para análise do Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU). Pontos e contrapontos Logo após a apresentação do plano do leilão pelos representantes da Anatel, os participantes da audiência se manifestaram sobre a proposta. O primeiro a falar foi Daniel Azevedo Novais, fundador da Telecom Power Tower, que defendeu que o prazo para desocupação da faixa pelos serviços fixos comece a contar a partir da assinatura do termo de autorização de outorga ou do aviso de ativação. O objetivo, segundo ele, é evitar que os atuais usuários da faixa tenham de deixá-la anos antes da entrada

artigo.texto: Recentemente, foi publicada a revisão do Corporate Net-Zero Standard da Science Based Targets initiative, a SBTi, trazendo uma mudança relevante para empresas que buscam cumprir metas climáticas com maior integridade. A mensagem é clara: a transição para o net zero não será construída apenas com compensações genéricas, mas com ações de mitigação diretamente conectadas às cadeias de valor das empresas. Esse movimento tem implicações profundas para setores intensivos em embalagens, como alimentos e bebidas, cosméticos, higiene, varejo, e-commerce e bens de consumo. Nesses segmentos, parte expressiva das emissões está no Escopo 3, ou seja, fora das operações diretas da empresa. Elas aparecem na produção dos materiais adquiridos, no transporte, no uso e, principalmente, no fim de vida das embalagens colocadas no mercado. Até aqui, muitas empresas trataram essas emissões com uma combinação de redução interna, compromissos de circularidade e compra de créditos de carbono. Mas a nova lógica da SBTi exige uma pergunta mais sofisticada: se a emissão está associada a materiais e embalagens, qual deve ser o instrumento climático mais coerente para mitigá-la? A resposta tende a colocar a reciclagem no centro da estratégia. Redesign, redução de gramatura, substituição de materiais e modelos de refil são fundamentais. Essas ações reduzem o inventário de emissões e devem ser priorizadas. No entanto, elas não eliminam integralmente as emissões associadas à cadeia de materiais. Mesmo após ganhos de eficiência, continuará existindo uma parcela residual ligada à produção, circulação e destinação das embalagens. É nesse espaço que o crédito de carbono da reciclagem ganha relevância estratégica. Ele não deve ser tratado como uma compensação genérica, desconectada da origem da emissão. Ao contrário: seu valor está justamente em financiar e comprovar uma mitigação climática associada à própria cadeia de valor dos materiais. A reciclagem possui uma característica singular nesse debate. Ela atua sobre o fluxo físico da embalagem. O material pode ser coletado, pesado, classificado, rastreado, destinado a um reciclador e reinserido como matéria-prima secundária. Quando esse processo substitui matéria-prima virgem, há redução mensurável de emissões. Quando é feito com tecnologia, documentação e auditoria, passa a existir lastro climático verificável. Essa conexão entre emissão e mitigação é o que diferencia o crédito de carbono da reciclagem de muitos créditos tradicionais. Uma empresa que emite por embalagens plásticas, metálicas, de vidro ou papel não deveria, por coerência climática, tratar essa emissão exclusivamente com créditos desconectados de sua cadeia de materiais. O instrumento mais aderente é aquele que atua sobre o mesmo problema que originou a emissão: o fluxo de materiais pós-consumo. A tese é simples e poderosa: se a emissão vem da embalagem, a mitigação climática mais coerente deve vir da circularidade da própria embalagem. Essa abordagem também responde a uma demanda crescente por integridade no mercado de carbono. Compradores corporativos não buscarão apenas toneladas de CO₂. Buscarão rastreabilidade, adicionalidade, conexão com sua cadeia de valor e benefícios socioambientais comprováveis. Nesse contexto, a reciclagem tem uma vantagem competitiva: é física, mensurável e auditável. No Brasil, essa oportunidade é ainda maior. O país possui uma das cadeias de reciclagem social mais relevantes do mundo, mas ainda recicla muito menos do que poderia. O valor dos materiais, sozinho, muitas vezes não paga a conta da coleta, triagem, tecnologia, transporte, formalização e remuneração adequada dos trabalhadores da cadeia. O crédito de carbono pode ser o mecanismo financeiro capaz de fechar essa equação. Ao financiar operações de reciclagem rastreáveis, empresas não apenas reduzem emissões associadas ao Escopo 3. Elas fortalecem a logística reversa, ampliam a circularidade, geram renda e transformam resíduos em ativos climáticos. O crédito de carbono da reciclagem, portanto, não é apenas mais uma categoria de crédito. Ele representa uma nova infraestrutura de financiamento climático para a economia circular. É um instrumento que conecta metas de net zero, responsabilidade pós-consumo, inovação em rastreabilidade e inclusão produtiva. No novo ambiente regulatório e reputacional da agenda climática, créditos genéricos tendem a perder espaço para ativos com maior conexão material e maior qualidade de evidência. Para empresas que colocam milhões de embalagens no mercado, a reciclagem deixa de ser apenas uma obrigação ambiental ou uma pauta de sustentabilidade. Ela passa a ser uma ferramenta central de mitigação climática. O futuro do carbono será cada vez mais exigente. E, para as embalagens, esse futuro passa necessariamente pela circularidade. Rodrigo Oliveira é CEO da Green Mining e Vice-presidente da ABELORE

artigo.texto: A Anthropic, criadora do assistente Claude, está em tratativas com a Nscale para um acordo de infraestrutura voltado à inteligência artificial que pode chegar a US$ 45 bilhões. A negociação envolveria uma segunda instalação da Nscale no empreendimento Monarch, na Virgínia Ocidental, conforme pessoas com conhecimento das conversas. A Nscale, apoiada pela Nvidia, já tem contratos de infraestrutura com a Anthropic que somam cerca de US$ 44,6 bilhões, conforme documentos regulatórios ligados ao seu IPO. O novo prédio no Monarch poderá ter capacidade computacional de 460 megawatts e usar chips Vera Rubin, da Nvidia. A Anthropic também pode ter preferência para contratar um terceiro edifício planejado no mesmo campus. As empresas podem fechar o acordo nos próximos dias, mas as negociações seguem abertas e ainda podem mudar. Anthropic e Nscale não quiseram se pronunciar. Quando estiver concluído, o complexo Monarch poderá superar 8 gigawatts de capacidade elétrica bruta, de acordo com os documentos do IPO. Num primeiro momento, a Microsoft ficaria com parte do espaço. Em março, a empresa divulgou o interesse em entrar no projeto por meio de uma carta de intenções. Ela desistiu da instalação na temporada de verão do hemisfério norte, o que abriu espaço para a Anthropic ampliar sua presença no complexo. O possível contrato surge enquanto a Nscale prepara sua estreia na Bolsa e busca avaliação próxima de US$ 30 bilhões. A empresa apresentou pedido de listagem em setembro, não começou a divulgar formalmente a oferta e responde a questionamentos da SEC. artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, the copper foil business investment company of SKC for secondary batteries, said on the 20th that it has succeeded in developing "high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil," cited as a key material for next-generation batteries. The technology SK Nexilis developed this time is characterized by coating special carbon on the surface of copper foil to increase adhesion with the anode material. It suppresses "delamination," which can occur due to the volume expansion of silicon anode materials, enhances the structural stability of electrodes, and can help improve battery life and safety. This technology was developed in response to the recent trend in the battery industry of increasing the silicon content in anode materials to boost energy density. In particular, it focused on strengthening the adhesion between the anode material and copper foil, which becomes more important as silicon content rises. The copper foil developed in this way can also be applied to the dry-electrode process, known as a next-generation battery manufacturing process. The dry process is drawing attention as a manufacturing method that can reduce battery manufacturing expense and energy use. Because the dry process also requires stably securing adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil, the technology developed by SK Nexilis is expected to have high applicability. For mass production, SK Nexilis will build a pilot production system for high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil. It is currently verifying process stability and plans to secure technology for mass production and pursue commercialization in the second half of 2027. An SK Nexilis official said, "This development of high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil is a result to respond to technological changes in the next-generation battery market, such as expanding high-content silicon anode materials and introducing the dry-electrode process," adding, "We will proceed with optimization for commercialization without a hitch and strengthen our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technology development."

artigo.texto: Inner Mongolia leads world in energy storage Region forging master key for next industrial revolution, proving that whoever can best store electricity holds future of power For a long time, electricity has been a unique energy commodity, with production and consumption happening almost simultaneously. You use it the moment it is generated. But today, as solar and wind power have become China's largest sources of installed capacity, energy storage is quietly building "warehouses" for the power grid. These massive facilities store surplus green electricity during the day and deliver it to factories, shopping malls and millions of households at night. This time-shifting magic has found its grandest stage in North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Driven by the massive deployment of new-type battery facilities designed to support its vast wind and solar power bases, Inner Mongolia has overtaken California to become the world's largest energy storage region. As of the end of 2025, the region's cumulative installed capacity of new-type energy storage exceeded 25 million kilowatts, ranking first in the nation. Under the blueprint of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), this figure is projected to break the 50 million kW mark, cementing the region's role as the most critical power "reservoir" for the country's renewable mega-bases in the Gobi Desert and other arid areas. The sheer scale of this deployment has triggered a profound industrial metamorphosis. In the past, Inner Mongolia's vast Gobi Desert served merely as an application ground for energy storage, with complete sets of equipment largely purchased from manufacturing clusters in China's eastern provinces. Today, the narrative has shifted from isolated breakthroughs to a multi-city synergy. Hohhot, Baotou and Ordos are firing on all cylinders, forming a differentiated energy storage equipment manufacturing cluster. This has created a new paradigm of "desert application plus multicity collaborative smart manufacturing" — a concentrated reflection of the region's upgrading new energy industry chain. Each city brings a unique strength to the table, but the regional capital, Hohhot, stands out for its specialized focus on system integration and custom solutions engineered for extreme environments. Operating at the forefront of grid resilience, Hohhot's manufacturing sector produces energy storage equipment uniquely designed to withstand the severe cold and punishing sandstorms characteristic of the northern frontiers. While Baotou boasts the most comprehensive industrial chain and Ordos combines equipment manufacturing with ultra-large application scenarios at sites like Envision's zero-carbon industrial park, Hohhot's tailored approach to hostile climate operations ensures these massive systems remain reliable year-round. "Deploying gigawatt-scale battery facilities in the Gobi Desert is fundamentally different from installing systems in temperate coastal plains," said Lin Boqiang, head of the China Institute for Studies in Energy Policy at Xiamen University. "Extreme sub-zero winters can degrade battery performance and discharge efficiency by double digits, while seasonal sandstorms pose severe risks to thermal management and air filtration systems." Hohhot's focus on hostile-climate customization addresses the industry's biggest operational bottleneck — ensuring that massive desert storage parks don't just get built, but actually run safely and reliably 365 days a year, he said. Inner Mongolia's regional triumph mirrors a broader national strategy. Entering 2026, the strategic importance of new-type energy storage has reached unprecedented heights. For the first time, it has been listed among the nation's six emerging pillar industries for the 15th Five-Year Plan. The China New Energy Storage Development Report 2026, released recently by the National Energy Administration, said China's cumulative installed capacity of new-type storage had reached 136 million kW/351 million kilowatt-hours by the end of 2025, representing a year-on-year surge of 84.3 percent. Accounting for roughly 50 percent of the global total, new-type energy storage has surpassed pumped-hydro storage to become China's largest regulating resource, it said. Yet, after years of rapid expansion, the fundamental logic of the industry is evolving. Experts agree that the sector has bid farewell to the era of simple policy-driven scale expansion. "The industry has formally entered a new phase characterized by market-oriented selection, value priority and a focus on quality," said Dai Hongcai, director of the new energy institute at the State Grid Energy Research Institute. While the "forced pairing" of storage with renewable projects drove early growth, future expansion will rely on sustainable business models.

artigo.texto: Huawei’s smart car business is signing on to CATL’s battery swap network, giving the world’s largest battery maker another heavyweight partner for a technology most of the industry wrote off a decade ago. Yinwang, the Huawei-controlled automotive unit also known as Newcool, signed a strategic cooperation framework with CATL and its swap subsidiary CAES on Monday. CATL’s Choco-swap network already counts 2,520 stations across about 200 Chinese cities. What Huawei and CATL agreed to According to Yinwang’s statement, reported by Reuters, the deal covers both swappable battery packs and the station network. CATL says the focus is on vehicles running Huawei’s Qiankun smart driving systems, which would be made compatible with Choco stations. The new partnership is betting heavily on automation. CATL wants to link the car, the station and the cloud so the vehicle works out when it needs energy, based on its battery status and the driver’s habits, then finds a station, drives in on its own and lines itself up for the swap. CATL quotes 99 seconds for the swap itself. CATL chairman Robin Zeng and Jin Yuzhi, Huawei senior vice president and Yinwang CEO, attended the signing. The new partnership looks serious, but the announcement left out a few key details. No vehicle models, launch date or service areas were announced. It’s a framework agreement, and those don’t always turn into products. Who’s behind Yinwang? Huawei owns 80% of it, with Seres and Changan’s Avatr holding 10% each. Seres builds AITO, the premium SUV brand Huawei’s software and retail network helped turn into a hit in China, and plenty of other Chinese automakers buy Huawei’s Qiankun systems. More than 200 new swap stations a month CATL first entered the battery swap market in 2022 with its EVOGO service, then relaunched the effort as Choco-swap around standardized packs at the end of 2024. The growth since has been fast. Choco-swap ended 2025 with 1,020 stations, passed 2,000 at the start of July, and hit 2,520 as of September 29. As we reported this summer, CATL is building more than 200 battery swap stations every month. It’s aiming for more than 3,000 by the end of the year and 30,000 long term. Huawei joins a growing list of Choco partners that includes GAC, BAIC and NIO. CATL is also pushing swapping for heavy trucks, including a joint venture with Octopus Energy for the UK and Europe. For comparison, NIO, which built the first big swap network on its own, hit its 100 millionth swap in February with 3,790 stations. It passed 110 million swaps by June. Electrek’s Take I’ve been skeptical of battery swapping for years, and I had good reasons to be. Tesla demoed a 90-second pack swap in 2013, opened a single pilot station at Harris Ranch in California, and quietly let it fade after owners showed little interest. Better Place raised about $850 million and still went bankrupt in 2013. And every year, chargers got faster, which shrank the one real advantage swapping had. My main argument was standardization. Swapping only works as infrastructure if lots of automakers share packs, and automakers don’t want to share the most expensive part of the car. NIO proved swapping can work for one brand. But one brand’s network is a perk, not infrastructure. CATL is the one company that can fix that problem, and it’s actually doing it. It supplies roughly 40% of the world’s EV battery cells, so when it shows up with a standard pack, automakers listen. 2,520 stations in under two years isn’t a pilot. Top comment by Mrvc I can see battery swapping and battery leases being big in the developing world. Possibly Europe. For the five eyes countries is probably a no. Getting people to buy a vehicle and lease a battery hasn't gone over well. The original smart evs were like that. I think the b class was too. But if someone had a lot of cash to burn building stations though out the us. Then offered a dirt cheap ev with lifetime price battery lease then maybe. Especially as there is a pretty irrational fear of battery replacement. Leased battery you change all the time takes that fear out of the equation. The vehicle would have to be sub $15k possibly under $10k. And battery lease would have to be under $80 a month probably with a cheaper under $50 tier. Even then could be a while to gain traction. Could be part of the solution to urban changing is the best solution for packs sized for real actual use. And Huawei brings autonomy. A car that drives itself into a station and leaves 99 seconds later doesn’t need anyone to plug it in. For robotaxis and commercial fleets, that solves a real problem. I still don’t think swapping replaces charging. Most EV owners charge at home, and the fastest chargers in China are now getting close to gas station times. So it’s a complement. But I’m surprised to be writing this: in China, battery swapping is starting to look like a permanent part of the EV mix rather than a gimmick. Will anyone build something like this outside of China? If you’re driving an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, no swap station needed. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. artigo.texto: “There are no more birds in the area,” Sterling, Virginia, resident Greg Pirio said at a public meeting of the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors in early July. “The sound has driven them away.” Pirio has lived in Sterling for more than a decade. Then, in 2025, Pirio and his neighbors began experiencing an “intolerable noise” stemming from the data centers that have swarmed their suburban community. Pirio said he and his neighbors, including children, suffer from headaches and sleep deprivation. Many have resorted to using mattresses and special plexiglass to keep the noise out, but this is only the beginning of the public health crisis they’re up against. “There’s a family up the street from me with four kids,” Pirio tells The Progressive. “All four children have come down with respiratory illnesses, and one had to be hospitalized.” Other residents of Pirio’s Northern Virginia suburb suffer from sinusitis and ringing in the ears as well as trouble breathing. Pirio himself says he has had to take sleeping pills to get rest amidst the noise and suffers from severely dry eyes due to the poor air quality. “I had to go to the emergency room twice in recent months,” he notes. “I have to keep my eyes lubricated all the time so I use eye drops every couple of hours along with a gel before bed.” As data centers transform the world through artificial intelligence (AI) connectivity, they are also transforming Black, brown, and working-class neighborhoods through strained infrastructure and depleted natural resources. These facilities are not hidden away in the middle of nowhere. More than half of all data centers in the United States are within a mile of a school, from Arizona and Texas to Georgia and Virginia. These data centers and the gas turbines that power them are not only looming over student playgrounds, they are also near parks, airports, office buildings, shopping malls, and even cemeteries. The epicenter of this global transformation, Northern Virginia, has been dubbed “Data Center Alley.” Three counties—Loudoun, Fairfax, and Prince William—are home to nearly 300 data centers and counting. Data centers in the region currently cover more than thirty million square feet, and more projects are proposed each year. A third of the world’s hyperscale data centers now sit in the backyard of our nation’s capital. Located near Dulles Airport, and with the greatest density of data centers on the planet, these Washington, D.C., suburbs have cashed in big time at 450,000 residents’ expense. “This issue felt distant initially,” says Bria Singleton, a Fairfax County resident who commutes into the capital five days a week for work. But the first time she heard that Northern Virginia had a data center problem, she was learning about towns like Ashburn and Sterling. “The metro line I take begins in Ashburn,” Singleton notes. Then, her Virginia town introduced a proposal to sell commercial property for a data center build-out. “As a health care consultant and Black woman, I knew what was coming and never supported data centers. There are no pros. Only cons,” she says. Now residents like her are demanding moratoriums and restitution, showing that the impacts of these centers are not tomorrow’s problem but today’s. When data centers first began popping up in the 1990s, residents were fairly out of the loop. Many of the initial data centers were no bigger than an average office building and seemed harmless enough while boasting of jobs and revenue that would benefit local residents. Data center developers often coordinate directly with local elected officials and invoke nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in the name of “competitive interests.” By the time community members find out about a new data center, it’s because they’re seeing construction vehicles show up. After a series of tax incentives rolled out in the early 2000s, one approved data center proposal turned into two, which turned into ten, which quickly became more than 200 data centers statewide. The latest data centers are no longer mid-sized operations. They are what the industry calls “hyperscale”—meaning they are far bigger than earlier versions and create sprawling industrial parks. “In the NAACP’s People’s Report,” says Abre’ Conner, the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice, “we surveyed Virginians who expressed strong opposition to some existing infrastructure and new build-outs in the wake of a high concentration of data centers within the state.” Maryland’s Prince George’s County is the focus of the NAACP report, which found that residents of that county are “susceptible to air pollution from Data Center Alley located in Loudon [sic] County, Virginia” due to close proximity, cross-state wind patterns, and the sheer size of these facilities. With construction of the first beginning in 2018, the firm Vantage Data Centers built two data center campuses in the Ashburn-Sterling area. Within a few years, residents complained of incessant noise and fumes in the air. The first of the campuses was a massive fifty-two-acre compound with six data centers covering over 1.7 million square feet. The second sits on eighteen acres with three data centers, eight natural gas turbines, and fifty-one diesel generators. Gas turbines emit at least 188 different types of pollutants that increase the risk of asthma, pneumonia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and stroke—and they do so loudly. Pirio lives 150 yards away from the second campus. “I feel it in my throat and lungs when they run the backup generators,” he says. “This data center has been a curse on our life here,” another homeowner told a 7News reporter. Hugh Kenny/The Piedmont Environmental Council A recreational trail takes pedestrians and bicyclists past a data center in Loudoun County, Virginia. artigo.texto: I’m the Mayor of Lochbuie, Colorado, and my residents are worried about our water supply. So we passed a five-year moratorium on AI data centers. Your town can, too. Like many other parts of the country, our state is facing a serious water-supply problem. Colorado’s water supply depends heavily on mountain snowpack, and our Colorado River system has been overburdened for years. This problem is exacerbated by reduced reservoir levels, population growth, and irrigation-intensive agriculture. At the same time, climate change has led to record heat and droughts. A single large-scale data center, depending on location and available resources, can use as much water as our entire town uses. Meanwhile data center energy use makes climate change worse, further endangering our shared future. Data center emissions are projected to skyrocket by 2035. Water is a finite resource and can’t always replenish fast enough to meet growing demand. We don’t want hyperscale data centers coming into our town and overburdening our already stressed water resources — and polluting our air and groundwater while they’re at it. Big data centers claim they bring jobs to communities. A closer look shows how flimsy these claims are. In reality, data centers create very few permanent jobs. Most data center jobs are temporary construction jobs, and most of those don’t go to local community members. “I do want to see businesses in our community that create jobs, but I don’t see how a data center does that when it takes up so much land and produces so few jobs,” Shannon Donnelly, one of my constituents, told me. “We need a clear, evidence-based understanding of the costs and benefits before we make such big decisions that impact people’s lives.” Shannon is not alone. I heard many comments like these at our town board meetings about water use, noise, and other pollution from data centers. So I wrote up a proposal for a moratorium on AI data centers in Lochbuie. The ensuing public meeting drew more attendees than I had ever seen. They overwhelmingly supported a moratorium, and it passed easily. What happened next reflects another troubling reality about how data centers are encroaching on unwilling communities: Brighton, which borders Lochbuie, announced a proposal for a data center there. A town boundary would not protect our water, air, animals, or residents. “We’ll see the lights and hear the noise,” constituent Desirae Zima told me. “We’ll have to live with the traffic, the infrastructure demands, the industrial equipment, and the potential impacts to water and electricity resources. We will be the neighbors dealing with the impacts to our quality of life.” Fortunately, opposition from Brighton residents was strong enough that the developer withdrew its application for the proposed data center and the city council voted to advance a one-year moratorium on any such construction. It awaits final approval. Our small town reflects communities across the country. According to a recent Gallup poll, over 70 percent of Americans oppose data centers in their local areas. Nearly 500 cities, towns, and counties nationwide have enacted or are considering moratoria on data centers. Congress and the federal government have so far refused to meaningfully regulate the data centers cropping up across the country. So for now, state and local measures like these represent the best tool to protect our communities. Artificial Intelligence has not yet surpassed good old-fashioned human common sense.

artigo.texto: Energy storage manufacturer HiTHIUM has announced that its cumulative energy storage product shipments have surpassed 200 GWh. Having begun shipments in late 2021, the company reached the 100 GWh milestone in August 2025 and added another 100 GWh in just over a year. HiTHIUM said it ranked among the world's top 2 suppliers by energy storage battery shipments in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Looking ahead, the company said it would remain focused on energy storage, with long-duration energy storage (LDES) as a strategic priority. Recall that HiTHIUM started mass production at its integrated LDES industrial park in Heze, Shandong Province, in August (see China Solar PV News Snippets). It aims to promote large-scale global deployment of its first integrated long-duration energy storage solution, featuring 1,000 Ah-class cells, and to develop integrated solutions that cover the value chain from battery cells to the grid. In its earnings forecast, Chinese inverter and energy storage equipment manufacturer Deye expects a net profit of RMB 4.22 billion to RMB 4.32 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 79.81% to 84.07% year-over-year (YoY). Net profit excluding non-recurring items is projected to be RMB 3.95 billion to RMB 4.06 billion, up 73.33% to 78.16% YoY. The company attributed the expected earnings growth primarily to rising overseas demand for energy storage. Supported by energy security policies and tighter electricity supply-demand conditions in several countries, sales revenue from its residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage products increased significantly YoY. Deye also cited its global sales network and supply-chain cost management as contributing factors. Deye released its earnings results for H1 2026, reporting that its revenue rose over 92% during the period (see China Solar PV News Snippets). Power equipment manufacturers CEEG and SINEXCEL have jointly developed a 13,800 kVA transformer for energy storage applications. The oil-immersed, self-cooled, dual-split transformer is designed for a 40-foot high-cube containerized AC/DC integrated energy storage system (ESS), enabling a rated continuous output of 13.8 MW per container. According to CEEG, the transformer achieves 99.66% efficiency, exceeding the EU Tier 2 benchmark of 99.645%. Its design reduces overall weight by ~10% and is intended to be maintenance-free. The product series now covers single-unit power ratings from 6 MW to 13.8 MW, with grid-side voltage options of 13.8 kV, 22 kV, and 33 kV. The products target GW-scale energy storage and renewable energy projects with integrated storage. Guangdong's provincial development and reform commission and energy administration have issued pricing rules for local renewable energy consumption projects, including direct green power supply, integrated source-grid-load-storage projects, and zero-carbon industrial parks. Under the policy, annual self-consumed renewable generation must account for at least 60% of total available generation and at least 30% of total electricity consumption. The minimum share of electricity consumption supplied by self-consumed renewable generation will rise to 35% for new projects from 2030. Projects connected to the public grid must pay capacity- or demand-based transmission and distribution charges. Electricity imported from the grid will no longer incur separate system reserve charges or energy-based transmission and distribution fees. Other applicable charges, including system operation fees, government funds, and surcharges, will continue to apply under the relevant rules. China's renewable energy price settlement mechanism will not cover electricity exported by these projects. Renewable energy projects already covered by the mechanism price that switch to local consumption arrangements will be deemed to have voluntarily withdrawn from the mechanism. Guangdong recently launched a mechanism price auction for 2026 renewable energy projects, with a volume of 7.934 billion kWh for distributed PV (see China Solar PV News Snippets).

artigo.texto: In a recent interview with the Journal-News, Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy was asked about his personal and financial ties to companies involved in the data center industry. According to a financial disclosure statement filed with the Ohio Ethics Commission in April 2026 covering fiscal year 2025, Ramaswamy reported holdings in Prologis, the company developing a data center project in Trenton, along with Apple, Microsoft and NVIDIA. The size of the investments was not disclosed beyond the reporting threshold requiring assets to be listed if valued at more than $1,000. The filing reported $1,137.12 in dividends from Apple stock and $20,230 in dividends from Microsoft stock. A May 2026 report from Innovation Ohio argued those investments could create a conflict of interest. The report stated Ramaswamy holds investments across multiple sectors connected to data center development, including semiconductor manufacturers, technology companies that operate data centers, real estate firms that develop industrial properties and infrastructure funds that finance data center construction. "Ramaswamy holds financial positions in every link in that chain, creating a scenario where, as governor, he would be regulating an industry in which he is also a primary shareholder," the report stated. Asked about the investments, Ramaswamy said he was unaware of the specific holdings. "Someone's gonna have to tell me what those are because I'm not aware what they are," he said. He suggested the investments may be held through index funds. "If they're part of generalized index funds, this is a non-issue for me," he said. "I have no interest in having financial interests." When asked specifically about Prologis, Ramaswamy said he did not know he owned stock in the company. "I didn't know I owned that. Thank you for telling me," he said. He later added that he had "never heard" of Prologis. "It might be a speck of dust in a portfolio of biotech and other holdings," he said. "It's sort of an inane proposition if you're in my shoes to think that that would matter." Ramaswamy said an independent manager oversees his investment portfolio and argued that his financial independence would allow him to govern without influence from special interests. "What that allows me to do is to be independent of a lot of special interests," he said. Asked whether he would keep investments in those companies if elected governor, Ramaswamy said he would not. "No. I don't think it would make sense for me to do that," he said. "We're going to follow exactly what the rules say." Ramaswamy said the wealth he accumulated came from biotechnology ventures, not data center-related investments. "If you think about it from a common-sense perspective, my wealth and the way I generated it has nothing to do with data centers; it's been in biotech," he said. "It would be a boneheaded thing to go into this position to pursue wealth. I'm spending immense amounts of my wealth on this campaign, not to make money from it." He also defended what he described as a stringent approach to regulating data centers. "I think it's going to be one of the most demanding sets of requirements anywhere," he said. Ramaswamy pointed to proposals that would require data centers to be built on abandoned industrial sites rather than farmland or near residential neighborhoods, eliminate tax abatements, strengthen environmental standards, prohibit nondisclosure agreements and require tree buffers around campuses. Acton campaign responds Ramaswamy's opponent, Amy Acton, also disclosed investments in companies connected to the data center industry in her 2025 financial filing. Those holdings included Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Iron Mountain and several semiconductor companies whose products are commonly used in servers, artificial intelligence systems and data center equipment. Virginia Schaus, a spokesperson for Acton's campaign, said Acton sold all of her individual stocks in April 2026 to avoid questions about potential conflicts of interest. According to the campaign, Acton also moved her individual retirement account investments into exchange-traded funds and other diversified funds. "She does not currently own any individual stocks, and as governor, she pledges to not invest in or possess individual stocks," Schaus said. Schaus said Acton has argued that Ramaswamy's holdings create a potential conflict of interest in a recent op-ed published by The Columbus Dispatch. On July 27, Acton announced support for a conditional moratorium on new data center development unless projects meet several requirements, including: - Paying 100% of utility-related costs - Using union labor - Operating without nondisclosure agreements - Supporting local community needs - Complying with Ohio environmental standards - Building on brownfield or industrial sites "If companies cannot meet these rigorous standards, they have no business working in Ohio," Schaus said. The Acton campaign also argues Ohio's long-term tax incentives for data center projects should be scaled back.

artigo.texto: Dan Cox blasts data centers near Adamstown school, vows permanent ban if elected Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox criticized data centers and Democratic incumbent Gov. Wes Moore during a campaign stop at a park near Carroll Manor Elementary School in Adamstown, where construction noise from nearby data centers was as loud as the children at recess. Cox said he has a plan to address data centers if elected, which includes banning them permanently, enacting a temporary freeze while working toward the ban, requiring independent environmental testing, and mandating compensation for property and environmental damage. | MARYLAND VOTER'S GUIDE: 2026 Maryland gubernatorial election "We need immediate statutory relief at a minimum, and as governor, I will issue an executive order and pursue that immediately," Cox said. Cox accused Moore and his administration of fast-tracking permits for data centers and failing to respond to public concerns. He reiterated similar criticisms made during their recent debate, where Moore defended his stance and actions. "It is important that we step in, and it's why I signed amongst the most stringent EOs, executive orders in the country, saying that data centers need to bring their own energy and their power," Moore said during the debate. "They need to make sure they are not polluting our air or our water. Data centers do not get to write the rules. We do." Cox described data centers as a nonpartisan issue and expressed confidence that his position could attract voters across party lines in November. Maryland's early in-person voting period begins Thursday, with voting by mail continuing. Election Day is set for Nov. 3.

artigo.texto: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, instead opting for a shorter-term ban In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI. Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days. Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi. Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution. SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid. Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary. The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations. The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development. Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations. The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting. Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country. Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact. "It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said. Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month. A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

artigo.texto: China continues to dominate global clean-tech manufacturing in 2026, while the United States, Europe and India are investing billions of dollars in solar panels, electric vehicle (EV) batteries, energy-storage systems and wind equipment. Major manufacturing projects by CATL, BYD, First Solar, Qcells, Toyota, Volkswagen, Reliance Industries and Tata Group demonstrate the growing competition for industrial leadership. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the global market for key clean-energy technologies reached nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025. However, annual manufacturing investment declined from nearly $220 billion in 2023 to below $200 billion in 2024. The competition is increasingly determined by factory output, manufacturing costs, supply-chain integration, technology and exports rather than investment announcements alone. China Leads Global EV Battery and Solar Manufacturing China remains the world’s largest clean-tech manufacturing hub, supported by integrated supply chains, extensive production capacity and competitive manufacturing costs. According to the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026, China manufactured approximately 16 million electric cars in 2025, representing nearly 75 percent of global production. Chinese electric-car exports exceeded 2.5 million vehicles. China also accounted for more than 80 percent of global battery-cell production, approximately 85 percent of cathode active-material production and more than 90 percent of anode active-material production. Major Chinese clean-tech manufacturing projects CATL – Lithium-ion battery manufacturing CATL operates major battery manufacturing facilities in Ningde, Yibin and other Chinese industrial locations. Its manufacturing network supplies batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and stationary energy storage. CATL’s extensive production capacity and investment in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology strengthen China’s position in global battery supply chains. BYD – Integrated EV and battery manufacturing BYD manufactures electric vehicles, Blade batteries, power electronics and other automotive components. Its vertically integrated operations reduce dependence on external suppliers and support manufacturing efficiency. LONGi Green Energy – Solar manufacturing LONGi produces solar wafers, cells and modules, including high-efficiency photovoltaic technologies. Its integrated manufacturing capabilities support China’s domestic solar market and international exports. JinkoSolar – Solar cells and modules JinkoSolar operates large-scale solar manufacturing facilities in China and international markets, producing photovoltaic wafers, cells and modules. China’s main challenge is overcapacity, particularly in solar manufacturing, where aggressive pricing has weakened margins despite strong global demand.
