artigo.texto: A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they're uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state's hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he's impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California's electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible' test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi's system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. The electricity demand locally can exceed the available supply, so the utility National Grid supported the endeavor, Williams added. Peace Bridge is considered affordable housing because renters earn no more than 80% of the area's median income, Good Carbon said. It said energy storage will be an important part of future multifamily housing projects. Viridi has been manufacturing in Buffalo since 2018. A medical research building in the city is using its battery system, too. Viridi's plant could build enough battery packs in a year to supply energy for about 14,000 average U.S. homes for 24 hours, Williams said. Harris, at NYSERDA, said the state needs more options like this for maintaining a reliable grid and managing costs. Gov. Kathy Hochul has made that a priority. “If we don’t need to build generation, we can utilize the grid that we have more effectively, that’s extremely valuable to us,” she said. artigo.texto: Emporia voters to decide on data center ban in November EMPORIA, Kan. (WIBW) - Emporia residents will decide whether the city should ban high-impact data centers. The question is on their November ballots. Even if voters reject a ban in the November 3rd vote, city leaders say data center developers won’t go un-checked. It’s an issue driving Emporia voters like Ilea Diaz to the polls. “Me and my wife went out and voted today and checked that, voted yes to ban the data center,” Diaz said. Diaz was among residents speaking against data centers at Wednesday’s Emporia City Commission meeting. “We want jobs, yes, we absolutely want jobs,” Diaz said. “But bring the right jobs, sacrificing too much. Part of the tracks are really close to an elementary school.” City leaders say they are thinking about those issues. The City Commission released 10 pages of development guidelines it would require from any high-impact data center. The guidelines say data centers can still be built, but with major restrictions like companies having to pay their own power and water costs so bills don’t go up for residential customers. “We put together our first draft of guidelines with a legal team to make sure that we were doing things correctly and trying to shore in a lot of the information,” Emporia Mayor Becky Smith said. “And these are just the start of our guidelines but it also talks about noise and making people pay their way.” Mayor Smith said commissioners wanted to draft the guidelines before the vote so people would have a better idea about how development would happen. “There’s a lot of misinformation and a lot of correct information and a lot of rumors,” she said. “So you really need to dog in and trust your sources who you’re hearing from to make sure you’re getting correct information and not just rumors on the internet.” Resident Kathy Lamb isn’t convinced. “This is rural America,” Lamb said. “We live here because we like rural America. And to have it overrun by concrete and pollution and data centers, it’s just not what we want in our town.” One thing they agree on is making your voice heard at the polls. “Go out and vote,” Diaz said. “Go out and vote and be informed when you’re voting,” Lamb said. “You should go to vote,” Mayor Smith said. “Not just about this, you should vote about our governor, and our state representatives and any local issues that you have. This is your time to make your voice known at the poll.” You can see the guidelines HERE. Emporia voters also will decide a separate question to ban battery storage facilities. Copyright 2026 WIBW. artigo.texto: - The partnership will focus on vehicles using Huawei Qiankun solutions, aiming to deliver seamless energy replenishment for the autonomous driving era. - CATL has built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, with a long-term goal of expanding the network to 30,000 stations. Huawei's intelligent automotive business unit, Yinwang, or Newcool, has partnered with CATL (HKEX: 3750) on battery swapping, joining the battery maker's Choco ecosystem to further connect smart driving with energy replenishment services. Newcool, CATL and Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) have signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement to jointly develop a smart battery swap ecosystem, according to a statement released by CATL on Monday. CAES operates CATL's battery swap business. The partnership will focus on vehicles using Huawei Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions, making them compatible with the Choco network and strengthening cooperation on swappable batteries and station networks. The 3 parties plan to integrate data and services across vehicles, swap stations and the cloud, using real-time battery status and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively schedule battery swaps. Under the proposed system, vehicles would independently determine when they need energy, locate and enter a station, align themselves for a fully automated 99-second battery swap, and drive away afterward. The partnership aims to extend assisted driving capabilities to battery swapping, creating a "seamless energy replenishment experience" for the autonomous driving era. However, the announcement did not identify specific vehicle models, a service launch date or initial coverage areas. This is similar to functionality Nio Inc (NYSE: NIO) already offers at some battery swap stations, where vehicles can automatically enter a station and complete a battery swap while using navigation-assisted driving. CATL chairman and CEO Robin Zeng, Huawei senior vice president and Newcool CEO Jin Yuzhi, and Yang Jun, co-president of CATL's marketing system, attended and witnessed the signing. For CATL, Newcool's participation provides a new avenue to expand vehicle partnerships for the Choco network as its station footprint extends from cities to highways. As of September 29, CATL had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, according to the statement. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. Previously announced plans also call for building 1,000 highway battery swap stations in 2026 and 2027, creating a nationwide network spanning 11 north-south and 9 east-west highway corridors. Newcool grew out of Huawei's intelligent automotive solution business Unit, known as the car BU. It was formally established as a separate company in January 2024, initially wholly owned by Huawei. Huawei currently holds an 80% stake in Newcool, while Seres (HKEX: 9927) and Avatr, the EV unit of Changan Automobile (SZSE: 000625), each hold 10%. In April this year, Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group Corp (JAC) announced plans to invest in Newcool without disclosing the proposed investment amount. Completion of the transaction has yet to be announced.

artigo.texto: Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy sat down with journalists from the Dayton Daily News, Springfield News Sun, and Journal-News earlier this month for an unscripted interview about some of the issues at play in this November’s gubernatorial race. We asked the billionaire biotech businessman and former presidential candidate about his plans for public education, taxes, job creation, data centers and more, along with his views on his would-be status as the country’s third richest elected official, according to Forbes. This outlet extended a similar invitation to the Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton, the state’s former health director whom Ramaswamy has roundly criticized for what he sees as shirking opportunities to present her vision for Ohio or debate her ideas. Acton’s campaign agreed this week to schedule an interview with this news outlet; a story will follow. Public education Ramaswamy, who attended Ohio public schools before attending a private Cincinnati-area high school, has campaigned on the premise that Ohio should do more to reward its best teachers. We asked him about this plan. “What I think is we just need greater discretion for principals and superintendents of school districts to be able to pay people who work in their schools, when they do a great job, to give them the opportunity to be rewarded for it,” Ramaswamy said, before turning his attention to the matter of teachers’ starting salaries in Ohio. “More broadly, I’ve also said the starting salary of teachers should be higher than what it is today. By some measures, (it’s) $38,000 a year for entry-level first-year teacher salary. I don’t think that’s enough to attract the best of the next generation into the profession,” he said. When asked about how much he’d like to raise teachers’ starting salary, Ramaswamy said his administration would look into it. He said, “I think it’s got to be something that’s relatively meaningful to make this a more compelling profession for young people to want to go into.” Ramaswamy added that he believes too much of public school funding goes toward aspects of the education system outside of the classroom, and said he wants to prioritize in-classroom instruction. Voters will decide who will represent them in the Ohio Statehouse and in other races. Plus, several tax measures on the ballot will decide how much you pay in taxes and the future of area schools and other local governments. Here are information and tools to help you cast an informed ballot. He went on to say that he believes teachers are “heroes, not magicians,” and said he believes that parents should be asked to take more accountability for their children’s education. “If the kid doesn’t show up at school and they’re chronically absent, there has to be some matter of accountability for the parent,” he said. “I think our public schools can also do a better job of setting standards and expectations for the family and for the parent, which I think will make it easier to set up our teachers for success in the classroom.” This outlet asked Ramaswamy about his stance on teacher unions, which he said he wanted to eliminate throughout his 2024 presidential campaign. He responded: “I’ve never, in this particular race, I’ve not proposed any of those changes, but what I do intend to look at is on a holistic basis, how are we going to improve education?” His wealth Forbes recently reported that, if elected, Ramaswamy would become the third richest public official in the country. His current net worth of $2.3 billion has more than doubled since March 2025, and it ranks only behind President Donald Trump and Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker among current elected officials. This fact has been used against Ramaswamy on the campaign trail, with Acton quick to say his status makes him inherently disconnected from the average Ohioan. When this outlet asked him if he was sympathetic about a voter being uncomfortable voting for a billionaire, here’s what Ramaswamy said: “I think what I am deeply sympathetic to is that families are struggling to get ahead and costs have risen faster than wages, and families are struggling to make ends meet when, in fact, they should be doing more than make ends meet, they should be getting ahead.” He said he had that experience growing up in what he described as a middle class family. “Having had that upbringing, I have seen the full arc of the American dream,” Ramaswamy said. “That’s the place I come from to say, the more we celebrate success and upward economic mobility, the more of it we will get. The more we villainize upward economic mobility, the less we will get for Ohioans.” Beyond that, Ramaswamy considers the line of attack hypocritical, given Acton’s decision to run alongside David Pepper. Pepper, who would become lieutenant governor if Acton is elected, inherited significant wealth from his father John Pepper, the former CEO of Procter & Gamble, Signal Ohio reports. “I would say shame on my opponent for resorting to this kind of identity politics — and it is a kind of identity politics, it’s co-mingled with other forms of identity politics,” he said. “Shame on her for leaning into that while actually being a person who picked a lieutenant governor as her first hire who was a trust fund multimillionaire who did not earn his wealth but inherited it. artigo.texto: BEIJING, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold, CATL's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns. CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models: Battery Asset Service Partners and Energy Replenishment Service Partners. These models allow partners to participate in battery asset services and energy replenishment, extending their role beyond one-off vehicle sales to ongoing operations. Through this integrated ecosystem, QIJI aims to turn the costs of the low-carbon transition into new growth opportunities, enabling stakehol

artigo.texto: The debate over data centers in Mason County has taken on a new wrinkle thanks to a report last week estimating the county’s schools could bring in $90 million a year — but only if residents renew a levy on the ballot in two weeks. That estimate — part of a report put out last week by Treasurer Larry Pack’s office — is based on projected property tax revenue from two new controversial data centers, the Monarch Compute Campus, currently under construction, and the proposed Project Tamarack data center. Last year, Mason County Schools brought in $10 million from the excess levy, according to data from the state Tax Division, meaning that the schools would get a 9-fold jump in levy revenue if the estimates are correct. However, Mason County Schools will only get the money if voters approve a renewal of the school excess levy on Nov. 3. Pack and some county officials are worried that may not happen. “We were hearing people say that Mason County is going to get all this tax money from the data center, so they don't need to pass this excess levy,” said Pack. “That’s not how the bill works, and that's not the impact.” Pack said he believes opposition stems from a misunderstanding about how the data centers are taxed. Under House Bill 2014, the controversial 2025 law that established state-wide regulations for high impact data centers, county boards of education do not immediately get access to data center property tax revenue. The money is contingent on voters passing the levy renewal. “If a county school board has no excess levy, they get zero money from the construction and operation of data centers in their county,” Pack said. Mason County officials have been trying to get the message out: The vote isn’t for or against the two data centers, which will stay either way. But if the levy fails, the data centers will, in effect, get a $90 million tax break and Mason County Schools will lose out on the extra tax revenue. “We’re talking not only academics, but band trips, athletic trips on busses. We're talking about helping out the extracurricular activities in the county as well as the academics,” said Rick Handley, president of the Mason County Commission. He said he supports the levy and is encouraging others to vote for it as well. Elaine Matheny is an advocate with Mason United, a group that has been fighting against the two data center developments. While she plans to vote for the levy, she said it hasn’t changed her opposition to the projects, and she’s skeptical about promises of how much money they will bring in. “Look at all the other extract industries that we've had in this state,” she said. “Look at the promises for the lottery and all the funds that were going to take care of the school system. Has that happened? No. We still have lots of problems funding our schools.” The levy question comes as Mason County — and West Virginia more broadly — debates how to handle the data center development. Proponents, including Gov. Patrick Morrisey and many Republicans in the Legislature, have argued that data centers will be an important economic boon for the state that will bring in money and growth. Opponents, however, have raised concerns about issues like water usage and pollution from the power plants needed to generate the enormous amounts of electricity the data centers require. Residents also worry about rising electricity prices and noise pollution created by the thousands of servers these centers house. In the background of it all is HB 2014. The law prevents local county zoning officials from blocking data center development and allows the developers to keep information about their projects from the public. It also spells out how the tax revenue from data centers will be split, with the state getting 50% while the local county keeps 30%. Regardless of how the vote shakes out, Pack expects lawmakers to reevaluate the law next year, especially when it comes to how revenue is split. “I do think that generally local folks know better how to spend the money than Charleston does,” he said. “So I think we'll have a spirited discussion about these allocations next session.” Election Day is Nov. 3. artigo.texto: Tianneng revela portfólio de baterias multiquímicas e impulsiona ecossistema de novas energias localizadas AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 20 de outubro de 2026 HUZHOU, China, 20 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — O Tianneng Holding Group revelou seu portfólio de baterias multiquímicas em sua Global Alliance Partner Conference 2026 (Conferência Global de Parceiros da Aliança 2026) em Huzhou, Zhejiang, sob o tema “Liderando o Benefício Ecológico”, reunindo aproximadamente 300 parceiros de todo o mundo. O portfólio abrange quatro vertentes de tecnologia de baterias — chumbo-ácido, íons-lítio, íons-sódio e estado sólido — para aplicações que incluem veículos elétricos de duas e três rodas, veículos de baixa velocidade, força motriz industrial e armazenamento de energia para residências, data centers voltados a IA, usuários comerciais e industriais, além de projetos em escala de concessionária. Parceiros da Argélia, Indonésia, Nigéria, Camboja e Brasil participaram de uma mesa redonda sobre produção local, eletrificação de veículos de duas rodas, armazenamento de energia e transformação da distribuição, concordando que as raízes locais e a sinergia do ecossistema são essenciais. Mi Yue, secretária-geral da New Energy Industry Association for Asia and the Pacific (NEIAAP, Associação da Indústria de Novas Energias para a Ásia e o Pacífico), incentivou a inovação, o reconhecimento mútuo de normas e a colaboração transfronteiriça na cadeia de suprimentos. Guo Kuilong, secretário-geral da Câmara de Comércio da China para Importação e Exportação de Máquinas e Produtos Eletrônicos (CCCME), afirmou que a câmara utilizará sua plataforma para ajudar empresas de novas energias em sua expansão global e promover a cooperação na cadeia industrial para um crescimento mutuamente benéfico. “A incerteza torna os pilares da certeza ainda mais vitais”, disse Zhang Tianren, presidente do Tianneng Holding Group. “O Tianneng Group se concentrará em baterias melhores e soluções de sistema mais abrangentes, impulsionando a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento, a fabricação local e o fortalecimento da marca para construir uma cadeia de suprimentos verde, resiliente e localizada, com parceiros globais.” Sobre o Tianneng Group Fundado em 1986, o Tianneng Group é líder global em soluções de energia verde, impulsionando a inovação em energia para mobilidade elétrica, sistemas de armazenamento de energia e economia circular. Com 21 bases de produção inteligentes, a empresa oferece valor sustentável a mais de 100 países e regiões. artigo.texto: Schneider Electric’s third quarter organic revenue jumped 17% to €11.5 billion euros ($12.9 billion US) — a record high for any quarter — the French multinational energy technology company said in an Oct. 16 earnings release. The company’s business associated with data centers “continues to be exceptionally strong with another quarter of triple digit demand growth in Q3, further improving our visibility into 2027 and 2028,” said Schneider’s CFO, Nathan Fast, during an earnings call. Schneider Electric has seen triple digit demand growth in orders associated with data centers for “three out of the last four quarters,” Fast said during the call. Morgan Stanley analyst Max Yates asked how much exposure the company has to neocloud businesses like CoreWeave. Fast said, “We do not break down exactly the impact or the split of hyperscaler, colo, neocloud, et cetera.” Schneider CEO Olivier Blum added, “We are extremely careful to select those companies that will be there in the long term.” Schneider Electric’s Energy Management segment made its most revenue in North America in the third quarter, but saw a higher organic growth rate of 32.4% in China and East Asia, compared to 20.3% That continues a trend in 2026, where North America led overall revenue volume but Asia saw a higher organic revenue growth rate. The sales growth in China was “led by everything to do with investment in AI infrastructure, driving growth in the data center and [semiconductor] segments, in particular,” said Fast during the call. “In our geographic trends, we add China alongside the U.S. and India in the countries we expect to drive growth. This is based on the strength of what we have seen over the recent quarters and which we believe is set to continue.” North American demand continues to grow, driven by momentum in data centers, “where we saw sustained high demand for prefabricated solutions and cooling,” Fast said. Blum said the company has also been bolstered in the European market by the “massive acceleration” of electric car adoption, as well as heat pumps. “We see very fast growth,” Blum said. “This fast growth is not only the growth of the EV charger, but every time you install an EV charger, you have to extend your electrical panel, so that creates a great opportunity, great synergy in a place where, for instance, in Europe, we have a very strong market share.”

artigo.texto: A U.K. homeowner planning a battery and solar installation asked if they could sign up for Octopus Go's cheap overnight rate without owning an electric vehicle. The replies pointed to a reassuring answer for standard Go users — but also a painful catch for anyone hoping to switch between tariffs to maximize savings. Here's what to know The uncertainty started in a Reddit thread on r/OctopusEnergy, where the poster said Octopus had not given a consistent answer as they got ready for a battery-and-solar upgrade. The poster wrote, "I'm about to get a 32kwh battery installed plus solar, but don't currently have an EV." Users replying to the thread said they had not seen much enforcement around EV ownership on standard Octopus Go. One commenter wrote, "I've been on and off Go for 5 years and not had any issues. No EV, just as house battery," and another claimed, "You be fine, no one checks for Octopus Go." A separate reply noted that even if regular Go works without an EV, leaving later may be expensive because of a newer fee: "If you do get away with it you are locked into Go for 12 months as it has an exit fee now." For homeowners thinking about battery storage to unlock cheaper off-peak rates, EnergySage can help compare home battery storage options, including competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has teamed up with electrification brand Qmerit to help homeowners get the best price on home battery storage solutions. More background Adding battery storage is one of the best ways to protect your home during outages, save money on energy, and gain more energy independence. Pairing a battery with rooftop solar also gives homeowners more control over when they buy power from the grid and when they use or export their own electricity. The thread also drew a line between the standard Go plan and Intelligent Octopus Go. One person said they had received an email about disabled smart charging and added that the Loyal version of IOG would need a linked car or charger within seven days. Another commenter clarified the distinction, writing, "That's IOG. The OP is on about regular Go." What can be done? Anyone using a battery to lower electric bills may want to check switching rules and exit fees before choosing a tariff. As one commenter put it, "Ideally you want to be on Flux during the Spring/Summer to make the most of the export rate and Go in Winter." People in the discussion also pointed to software as a way to squeeze more value from battery storage. The original poster said, "I'll probably look at Agile Outgoing and combine it with Axle events, then let PredBat handle it all," while another commenter mentioned Wonder Watt's "Wonder Batt" beta for people who are not comfortable with Home Assistant. For households that want backup power without committing to a full-house system, Pila is another company offering strong battery backup options. Pila's plug-and-play batteries are priced at a fraction of what a whole-home backup system would cost. artigo.texto: Invinity Energy Systems (LSE:IES) has announced plans to raise at least £20 million through a combination of institutional investment and a retail share offer, with proceeds intended to support product development, manufacturing expansion and working capital requirements. The vanadium flow battery manufacturer is proposing a fundraising at 10 pence per share, comprising a cornerstone subscription from the National Wealth Fund, an institutional placing and a separate offer to retail investors. The National Wealth Fund, an existing major shareholder, has committed to invest at least £10 million, with the potential to increase its participation to £12.5 million. The fund may also match retail investor subscriptions on a pound-for-pound basis, subject to the proposed arrangements. The total fundraising is capped at £25 million. Invinity intends to allocate approximately £10 million of the proceeds to accelerate product development and reduce manufacturing costs. A further £8 million is earmarked for working capital, while £2 million is expected to support additional manufacturing capacity in the UK and US. The planned investment forms part of the company's efforts to increase production efficiency and support the delivery of its existing commercial commitments. Management said the fundraising would strengthen Invinity's ability to execute its revenue plans for 2026 and 2027, which it considers well supported by existing commercial activity. The company also reported a commercial pipeline exceeding 12.5 gigawatt-hours (GWh), although this figure represents potential business opportunities rather than confirmed revenue. Invinity is working towards introducing an investment-grade insurance arrangement intended to improve the financial acceptability of its battery systems for prospective project customers and financing partners. The company is also progressing projects including FlexBase's Technology Centre Laufenburg, while implementing measures to reduce corporate overheads. Invinity develops and manufactures vanadium flow batteries designed for long-duration energy storage applications, including electricity grid infrastructure and renewable energy integration. For investors, the proposed fundraising represents a significant financing development, providing additional capital for operations and expansion if completed. However, the issuance of new shares at 10 pence would increase the company's share count and dilute the percentage ownership of existing shareholders who do not participate.

artigo.texto: Overview: - Van Buren Township Planning Commission approved final site plans for Google's 1-gigawatt data center and accompanying utility substation on 282 acres north of I-94. - The facility will use 2-3.6 million gallons of water daily and employ 50-200 people. - Read details on the projected noise, water usage, and power demands from the hyperscale data center. The site plans for a 1-gigawatt Google data center and an accompanying electrical substation received final approval last week from the Van Buren Township Planning Commission. 🗳️ Civic Action Toolbox — see how you can get involved Why it matters The Van Buren Township data center could affect nearby residents' quality of life through noise, dust, and climate impacts. Who's making public decisions The Van Buren Township Planning Commission granted the site plan approval. The Michigan Public Service Commission oversees DTE's contracts and proposed gas plants, and EGLE regulates wetland and stream impacts. Upcoming Meetings Contact Your Representatives Civic Actions: What You Can Do What to watch for next Watch whether Van Buren Township adopts stricter data center zoning rules, and how regulators rule on DTE's proposed natural gas plants in Milan and Handy townships ahead of the planned December 2027 startup. Are you taking action? Let us know. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox Residents have said the “Project Cannoli” data center proposed by developer Panattoni could bring noise to the nearby Haggerty subdivision, harm water resources, and impact energy reliability and affordability. Project backers say it represents a boon for jobs and investment that will bring significant tax dollars to the area. The commission is compelled to approve the project because it’s a principal permitted use under the township’s zoning rules, Van Buren Township Planning Commissioner Jeffrey Jahr said Wednesday, Oct. 14. “I feel that the applicant has met all of the objective specific requirements for us to grant the request,” he said. Saline Township, in neighboring Washtenaw County, was sued by a data center developer that alleged exclusionary zoning in September 2025 after the township board denied the rezoning needed for Oracle and OpenAI’s 1.4 GW data center. Whether Van Buren Township places more restrictions on data centers will need to be evaluated, Jahr said, adding that he is leaning toward doing so. Residents say they’re already dealing with noise, dust Township residents said Wednesday they are already dealing with noise and dust from the project. Several people played recorded dump truck noise on their phones. Over 2,700 people have signed an online petition opposing the data center. Van Buren Township resident Tracy Osborne, who lives next to the data center site, said he’s concerned about the impact constant data center noise could have on his daughter with special needs. “My concern is not simply whether this facility meets a number on a noise report,” he said. “It is whether neighboring families will be able to enjoy their homes without continuous disruptive equipment noise.” A Panattoni spokesperson told Planet Detroit in a statement that the company takes resident concerns seriously, including noise and dust, and is committed to minimizing impacts. Multiple parties are working in the area, including utility providers, and not all work is associated with the project, the spokesperson said. Representatives for Panattoni said Wednesday that the I-94 Service Drive will be used for site access during construction — not Haggerty Road — to minimize resident impacts. Here’s how the data center could impact residents. How big will the project be? The project is set to occupy 282 acres north of I-94, east of Haggerty Road, west of Hannan Road, and south of Wayne County Community College. The project will permanently impact 13.55 acres of wetlands, require six culverts in regulated streams, and fill and abandon 573 linear feet of a stream, John Jones, an environmental quality analyst with Michigan’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), said in June. Developers will offset wetland and stream impacts by purchasing wetland mitigation bank credits in the Huron River watershed and creating 1,174 feet of new stream channel on the property itself, Jones said. Forty-five percent of the acreage at the site will remain undeveloped under a conservation easement, Josh Capps, Panattoni’s director of data center delivery, said Wednesday. The data center will use roughly 1 GW of electricity, according to the township’s frequently asked questions document. One gigawatt is roughly equivalent to the power used by 800,000 homes. What are the economic impacts? The project represents a “generational investment from one of the best companies in the world,” Adam Kramer, president of data centers for Panattoni, said Wednesday. The data center will require 9.8 million labor hours for its construction and employ 50-200 employees on site, he said. Developers have already awarded $2 billion in contracts to Wayne County businesses, he said. The data center is projected to be the largest taxpayer in Van Buren Township and one of the top five taxpayers in Wayne County, Kramer said in February. How much noise will the project produce? Modeling shows the data center will comply with Van Buren Township’s noise limit of 67 dBA, Paul Kammer, an engineer with the consulting firm Fishbeck, said Wednesday. dBA is a weighted decibel scale for judging loudness, with 67 falling between the volume of a normal conversation and a vacuum cleaner, according to a Yale University decibel chart. Panattoni’s Capps said sound from the facility would largely fall below the area’s ambient nighttime noise. The loudest noise will be to the south and east of the facility, with anticipated dBA readings of 62.1 and 59.7, respectively, he said. artigo.texto: Leilão de baterias Aneel: transmissoras podem ficar de fora A área técnica da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas. O entendimento consta de Ofício Conjunto enviado à diretoria da agência. A medida, se confirmada, pode impactar diretamente a competitividade das empresas do setor elétrico. Reversão de receitas para modicidade tarifária O ofício conjunto vincula a participação das empresas à destinação de parte ou total da receita dos projetos à redução das tarifas de transmissão. O documento cita: “Além disso, mantém-se a necessidade do benefício à modicidade tarifária, mediante reversão total ou parcial das receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE para a concessão, em favor dos usuários do SIN [Sistema Interligado Nacional]”. Ainda segundo o ofício, os contratos firmados exigem autorização prévia para atividades estranhas ao objeto da concessão e estabelecem que parte ou toda a receita desses negócios contribua para a modicidade das tarifas de transmissão. No entanto, o ofício não define percentual, base de cálculo ou metodologia para a reversão. O texto usa a expressão “receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE”, sem individualizar a receita fixa do CRCap (Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade para Potência). Essa lacuna gera insegurança jurídica para as transmissoras interessadas no leilão. Manifestação técnica, não deliberação da diretoria Vale destacar que a manifestação é das áreas técnicas; o documento não registra uma deliberação da diretoria colegiada da agência sobre os editais ou sobre a legitimidade dessa captura. Ou seja, o posicionamento ainda pode ser revisto ou ajustado pela instância superior da Aneel. A diretoria colegiada é responsável pelas decisões finais sobre regras de leilões e regulação do setor elétrico. Fontes ouvidas pela reportagem dizem que se o entendimento for mantido, as empresas transmissoras podem ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. A incerteza regulatória pode afastar players importantes e reduzir a competitividade do certame, com reflexos no preço final da energia para consumidores e empresas. Taesa contesta reversão da receita fixa “A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão”, sustenta a Taesa em um dos tópicos da contribuição enviada à Aneel. A transmissora argumenta que a receita fixa do contrato de reserva de capacidade tem natureza distinta e não deveria ser capturada para reduzir tarifas de transmissão. A empresa defende que a reversão comprometeria a viabilidade econômica dos projetos de armazenamento. Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes com as mesmas obrigações contratuais. Isso criaria uma desvantagem competitiva clara para as transmissoras, que poderiam optar por não participar do leilão. Impacto no setor elétrico e na economia O leilão de baterias é visto como estratégico para ampliar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico e integrar fontes renováveis intermitentes. A eventual exclusão das transmissoras pode reduzir o número de proponentes e elevar os custos dos projetos vencedores. Para o comércio e a indústria do interior paulista, como Araçatuba e região, tarifas de energia mais altas pressionam os custos operacionais e a competitividade das empresas locais. A definição sobre a reversão de receitas deve ocorrer antes da publicação do edital definitivo do leilão. Empresários e associações setoriais acompanham o tema de perto, pois a energia elétrica é um insumo essencial para a produção e os serviços. A fonte não detalhou se haverá nova rodada de contribuições ou audiência pública sobre o assunto. Perguntas Frequentes O que a área técnica da Aneel defende sobre a participação de transmissoras no leilão de baterias? A área técnica da Aneel defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas, conforme consta em Ofício Conjunto. Como a reversão de receitas das transmissoras no leilão de baterias afetaria a competitividade? Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes, podendo ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. A Receita Fixa do CRCap está sujeita à reversão para modicidade tarifária da transmissão, segundo a Taesa? Não, a Taesa sustenta que ‘A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão’, conforme um dos tópicos de sua contribuição.

artigo.texto: The Accidental Activists of Data Center Alley These would-be rebels in Northern Virginia joined the fight against data centers mostly to stop the encroachment on their homes and exclusive private communities. I am hiking on a nature park that cuts through 45 miles of Northern Virginia, crisscrossing grassy terrain, wetlands, wooden bridges, and goldenrod, and then a dozen promontories offering the most unnatural of sights—windowless, hulking block-long data centers and their attendant transmission lines and substations. I heard “the hum” of the centers before I saw them; their sound resembled a horde of cicadas on meth. I felt nervous, and somewhat overwhelmed, as I counted roughly 20 of them in just the two miles I walked on the Washington and Old Dominion Railroad Trail in Loudoun County. Here is the country’s thickest concentration of data centers—233 centers in all, over 3 percent of the county’s overall land mass. Data Center Alley, as it’s called, is a harbinger of what is to come in this country if tech hyperscaling continues unchecked. But Loudoun County is not only an example of tech infrastructure running amuck. It’s also an example of a semi-successful battle to press pause. The week I visited in September, local activists had just secured a significant victory when the county’s Board of Supervisors voted 7–1 to impose a 12-month pause on board action for data centers and electrical substations. It was one win for the broader opposition, who were cross-partisan, unlikely dissidents in their 50s and 60s, who joined the fight mostly to protect their own homes and exclusive private communities. Some of them even refused to say a bad word about AI, claiming the fear of data centers in popular imagination was “overblown,” even though they themselves had been organizing against them as they encroached on their homes. One of these accidental activists is Jessica Medeiros, 55. I met her in front of her home, in the Oak Trail Square development in Sterling. She works with juvenile offenders by day, as a pretrial officer in nearby Prince William County. In her off hours, she is just another empty nester of two grown children, hanging with her boyfriend, enjoying frequent outdoor runs in the area and five-times-a-day walks with her dog. Well, that was before the gargantuan blue Vantage VA2 data center at the end of her street, four city blocks long and wide, rose up. That Vantage VA2 center happens to be one of the worst ones out there. For one thing, it isn’t connected to the electrical grid, meaning its energy comes from on-site or nearby power plants. These plants are primarily powered by natural gas; the VA2 center uses gas turbines and backup emergency diesel generators. This reliance means that such hubs risk being louder than normal, filthier than normal, and ultimately worse for the environment than normal. As a case in point, on the morning we met, Medeiros pointed out where the soot from the day usually falls. More and more developers have sought power plant equipment like turbines and generators to elide regional power grids, which are now stressed under the data center’s electricity requirements. To me, these data centers are a physical embodiment of both the decline of the rule of law and the rise of the tech oligarchs. They are, of course, part the national conversation around AI and have become a center of the activism against it. In the first half of 2026, the Data Center Watch project by AI security company 10a Labs found that at least 75 data center projects worth $130 billion were disrupted by local groups in the first quarter and at least 45 projects worth $68 billion in the second. The Data Center Opposition Report found that 640,000 people are in anti-data center Facebook groups in the United States. Gen Zers have joined groups like New Jersey’s Climate Revolution Action Network, or CRAN. “To me, this center…is just indicative of what is happening in our country, because the money and the power are taking over the lives of citizens,” says Medeiros, a petite blonde who describes herself as having the energy of a puppy, with the swift gait of a runner, despite a recent foot injury. She was rapidly walking around the perimeter of a building that looks like a post-lobotomy IKEA. It has got the same cheerful cobalt exterior but no furniture, customers, or meatballs inside, only racks and heat. “Last week, Trump eliminated the, what was it? Oh yeah, the emissions level requirements for these power plant. For people like us, that basically screws us. We don’t have those protections anymore.” (The Trump EPA had recently exempted data centers from publicly disclosing their emissions.) Medeiros and her neighbor Greg Pirio, 75, a government contractor who specializes in foreign aid, are two of a number of neighbors who have thrown themselves into protesting the Vantage plant, attending community meetings and town halls, doing press, creating systems for monitoring noise and air quality, and petitioning their local representatives. But the center has also taken its toll, they say, on their bodies. Both have gone to doctors and Pirio twice to the ER, with extremely dry eyes that they believe were caused by the plant. (After an hour, my own eyes were throbbing, and I was blinking for tears to relieve the irritation.) For more vulnerable people in the area, the effects have been even worse. According to Medeiros and other neighbors, one family’s four children have all developed respiratory problems as a result. Medeiros’ voice is a rasp, now, as well, which she attributes to the centers. They aren’t just imagining things. A recent report, “Health-Informed Computing: Estimating and Addressing the Public Health Impact of Data Centers,” modeled emissions from data center electricity and on-site generator usage, projecting health risks and costs particularly in host communities. artigo.texto: Chicago-area households are about to get a clearer picture of where energy-hungry data centers are connecting to the grid — but they will not get the added protection PJM had sought during power emergencies. Here's what to know According to Fox News, on Oct. 12, PJM Interconnection planned to activate a new "Large Load Registry." The grid operator, which oversees Chicago and a large swath of the Midwest and East Coast, will require utilities to identify single-site customers with exceptionally high electricity use, including factories and data centers. With those reports, PJM hopes to spot major new sources of demand earlier instead of being surprised after the system is already under strain. The operator has said a surge in electricity-hungry data centers is a key reason the region could run into a supply crunch beginning in 2027. The registry was only part of PJM's original proposal. It also sought tougher requirements for major new power users, including a rule that would have forced them to line up additional electricity or face being among the first customers curtailed during emergencies. FERC rejected the most disputed parts of that broader plan, saying PJM had overreached by trying to shape how states and local utilities prioritize shutoffs and how rates would apply to those customers. More background For Illinois households, the outcome is mixed: PJM will gain better insight into where very large new electric loads are being added, but residents lose a proposed protection that could have put data centers ahead of homes in line during emergency shutoffs. For homeowners concerned about utility bills as grid strain increases, upgrading heating and cooling equipment is one of the clearest ways to cut costs and guard against rising energy prices. Palmetto can help homeowners understand their HVAC options and reduce their energy bills with newer, more efficient HVAC systems and heat pumps, while its Comfort Plan network can help connect you with vetted installers and efficient heating and cooling solutions for your home. If supplies tighten, PJM still cannot cut power to data centers and other major new users before homes, hospitals, or schools. The power to make that decision remains with state officials and local utilities. In comments to Utility Dive, FERC Commissioner David Rosner said noncritical data centers should be shut off before ordinary customers during an emergency, Fox News reported. At the same time, he said state regulators should write those rules, underscoring a wider debate over who should be protected first as electricity demand climbs quickly. What can be done? The clearest change that is still happening is the registry itself. PJM should get earlier notice about new factories or data centers that could add stress before the 2027 crunch it has warned about. Households can also focus on the part of the energy equation they control most directly: home efficiency. In the second half of this transition, many residents will be looking for ways to lower their own bills, and the Palmetto Comfort Plan includes $0-down options that can lower heating and cooling costs by up to 50%. Palmetto Comfort Plans also include 12 years of free maintenance, which can make an efficient HVAC or heat pump upgrade easier to manage over time. artigo.texto: 3D printing could improve large-scale renewable energy storage October 21, 2026 By University of Waterloo Media Relations University of Waterloo researchers develop a new electrode design that could make redox flow batteries more effective for storing wind and solar energy Talking Points Researchers at the University of Waterloo have developed a 3D-printed electrode that enhances the efficiency and safety of redox flow batteries (RFBs), which are crucial for storing renewable energy from sources like wind and solar. Led by Dr. Maxime van der Heijden, the team utilized natural structures to redesign a key battery component, improving liquid movement and chemical reactions. - The new electrode design increases performance by 52% using triply periodic minimal surface geometries. - RFBs use water-based electrolytes, making them safer than traditional lithium-ion batteries. - This innovation supports large-scale energy storage, addressing the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources. This advancement is significant as it could lead to more efficient energy storage solutions, essential for integrating renewable energy into the electrical grid and ensuring a stable power supply for communities. Researchers have created a 3D-printed electrode that could help make it easier and safer to store large amounts of renewable energy generated by wind and solar farms. Led by University of Waterloo professor Dr. Maxime van der Heijden, the research team drew inspiration from natural structures to redesign a key component of redox flow batteries (RFBs), a technology that can store electricity for later use. The new design helps battery liquid move more efficiently, allowing the chemical reactions that store and release energy to occur more effectively. Redox flow batteries work differently from the lithium-ion batteries commonly found in phones, electric vehicles and many energy-storage systems. These batteries use water-based electrolytes rather than the flammable materials found in lithium-ion batteries, making them a potentially safer alternative for large-scale energy storage. Redox flow batteries are a complementary technology to lithium-ion batteries for large -scale energy storage applications. Their water-based electrolytes make them a safer option for storing renewable energy at the scale needed to supply, for example, communities and the electrical grid with continuous renewable energy. “Instead of storing energy in solid materials, they store energy in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks,” said van der Heijden, a chemical engineering professor at Waterloo. “The amount of stored energy can be increased simply by using larger tanks, making them well-suited for large-scale renewable energy storage and grid applications.” That flexibility could become increasingly important as more electricity comes from renewable sources. Wind and solar power are intermittent, as they do not always produce electricity when it is needed, creating a need for technologies that can store excess energy and return it to the grid later. Researchers used 3D printing to create porous RFB electrodes, enabling precise control over their structure and fluid flow. “With 3D printing, we can design the internal structure of an electrode in ways that are difficult to achieve using conventional manufacturing,” said van der Heijden. “That gives us much greater control over how the liquid moves through the battery and reaches the surfaces where the energy-storing reactions take place.” A key innovation was the use of triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) geometries, complex, repeating three-dimensional shapes that can resemble structures found in nature. The researchers tested several TPMS designs and found that one known as the “diamond” geometry worked best, increasing performance by 52 per cent. They then used a digital light-processing 3D printer to produce the porous structures, which were heat-treated to form conductive carbon electrodes capable of carrying electricity. The team successfully tested the electrodes in laboratory flow cell experiments and in a working vanadium redox flow battery, demonstrating that the 3D-printed designs can function in an operating battery. The proof of concept could help pave the way for more efficient redox flow batteries designed for large-scale energy storage. Future research will focus on increasing the electrodes’ surface area, improving manufacturing methods and exploring advanced design tools to create even more effective electrode structures. —————————– The study, Enhancing Mass Transport in Redox Flow Batteries with 3D-Printed Triply Periodic Minimal Surface Electrode Structures, appears in the Journal of Energy Storage.

artigo.texto: Nvidia weighs $4.5bn AI data-center push in Indonesia A proposed investment in Batam could expand Indonesia's AI capacity, but analysts warn of the strain data centers place on water and power JAKARTA, Indonesia (MNTV) – Nvidia is exploring a $4.5 billion investment to build data-center infrastructure in Batam, Indonesia, and expand the country’s artificial intelligence capacity, the Indonesia Business Post reported. Coordinating Economic Affairs Minister Airlangga Hartarto said the government was prioritizing the digital economy to help reach a 6% growth target in 2027. Indonesia currently has 600-700 megawatts of operational data-center capacity, with a further 1.3 gigawatts in the pipeline, representing an estimated $15-20 billion in potential investment. Such projects, he said, require ample land, reliable electricity and adequate water. Those requirements have drawn scrutiny. Timothy Wong, head of research at DBS Group, said Indonesia needed to rethink its approach given how much electricity and water the facilities consume. “Data centers are very intensive users of electricity and water, and the Indonesian government actually needs these resources for its population,” he said. A DBS colleague, Amit Sinha, said AI projects must plan for power, cooling, water and community impact, pointing to options such as renewable energy, closed-loop liquid cooling and recycled water.

artigo.texto: - The launch comes as Li Auto shifts its batteries from CATL to in-house developed ones produced by its joint venture with Sunwoda. - The Lianshan system covers batteries, electric drive units and the charging network. Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI) has launched its in-house developed electric powertrain technology system named Lianshan, covering batteries, electric drive units and charging network. The company pledged two lifetime guarantees — against battery self-ignition and against fire after collisions — as it seeks to ease consumer safety concerns while expanding the use of its in-house batteries. The Chinese automaker announced the system at its Power Day electric technology event on Tuesday. It said the Lianshan battery, Lianshan electric drive and charging network are all developed in-house, and that it will take care of "everything about electricity." Under the Lianshan battery guarantee program, if a vehicle self-ignites due to quality problems with the original battery and meets scrapping criteria, Li Auto will compensate the owner with a new vehicle of the same configuration. If a battery catches fire following a collision or chassis scraping and the vehicle is scrapped, the company will cover the gap between the vehicle damage insurance coverage amount and the actual insurance payout. The program is subject to eligibility conditions. The launch comes as Li Auto accelerates the switch of its models' batteries from CATL (HKEX: 3750) to in-house developed batteries, which are produced by a 50-50 joint venture it established with Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207) in 2025. Li Auto also disclosed on September 4 that it plans to invest 2.65 billion yuan ($394 million) in Sunwoda's power battery subsidiary, Sunwoda Electric Vehicle Battery Co Ltd (Sunwoda EVB), and will directly hold an 8.79% stake after the deal closes, becoming its second-largest shareholder. CATL is the world's largest power battery maker, and its batteries are generally seen by Chinese consumers as safer and more premium. Persuading potential customers to accept batteries made by Sunwoda will not be easy for Li Auto, and the raft of safety commitments unveiled on Tuesday appears to be aimed at that concern. When CATL signed a 5-year strategic cooperation agreement with Li Auto in September 2025, the battery maker said more than 1 million Li Auto vehicles equipped with its batteries had been delivered, with no thermal runaway incidents caused by the batteries themselves. In January, Li Auto delayed some Li i6 deliveries due to insufficient battery supply and encouraged order holders to switch to versions equipped with Sunwoda batteries, offering an additional 2-year or 40,000-kilometer battery warranty extension. Sunwoda EVB was sued in December 2025 by Vremt, a Geely-affiliated company, which sought 2.31 billion yuan in damages, alleging quality problems with the battery cells it had delivered. At Tuesday's event, Li Auto said the Lianshan battery uses a high-stability cathode, a low-lithium-consumption anode and a dual-formula electrolyte for long life, supporting continuous dynamic repair. Batteries across all models will retain at least 75% health within 8 years or 160,000 kilometers, it said. The company said cell-level material improvements, highly integrated battery packs and vehicle-level energy management have increased range across all models. Under the CLTC standard, the new Li L8 offers 430 kilometers of pure electric range and the 2026 Li i6 offers 780 kilometers, an overall improvement of more than 8% over the 2025 versions. On safety, Li Auto said the underside of the Lianshan battery can withstand a 500-joule impact without catching fire or exploding, remain watertight after 48 hours submerged in 1 meter of water, and that the full pack will not catch fire for 24 hours after a single cell goes into thermal runaway at 50 degrees Celsius. The company said its new-generation 5C ternary lithium cells run 12 degrees Celsius cooler during supercharging than ordinary 2C ternary lithium cells. For lithium iron phosphate batteries, its adaptive algorithms keep state-of-charge estimation error within 3% and increase peak power output at low charge in winter by more than 40%. The Lianshan electric drive uses a proprietary patented CAR119 cast aluminum rotor material, adding more than 15 kilometers of pure electric range in urban driving and more than 8 kilometers on highways. Li Auto also restructured the power module so that current flows directly to the chip, adding another 30 kilometers of range and freeing up 24 millimeters of headroom. The company said 4 million of its in-house developed silicon carbide power chips have gone into production vehicles over the past year with zero failures. The next-generation electric drive system will deliver more power and range without increasing in size, it said. On the charging network, Li Auto's supercharging stations now exceed 4,200, covering cities, highways and scenic areas, and span the "12 vertical and 13 horizontal" expressway corridors, with an average of one station every 100 kilometers to be achieved within the year. The company said equipment availability stands at 99.9 percent, and all highway supercharging stations are equipped with 5C superchargers. Li Auto founder, chairman and CEO Li Xiang said on Monday that the company decided in 2020 to develop its own batteries, and that its existing battery suppliers remain partners to this day. On September 28, he said the company would not define its in-house development strategy as "de-anyone," and thanked CATL for its support in the joint development of batteries for the Li One and Li Mega. Li had previously mentioned that the company uses a in-house developed Lianshan quality monitoring system to connect data from upstream materials, cell manufacturing, pack production and vehicle use. The system unveiled on Tuesday shows the name has been extended to the entire electric powertrain technology suite. Li Auto said on September 7

artigo.texto: Pittsylvania County’s Berry Hill megasite will eventually have 21 data center buildings, built in phases over 15 years, according to permits filed by Stack Infrastructure. The project, an AI data center campus, “represents the largest private single-investment commitment” on record with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, according to permit information. When formally approved, the project will also be the largest economic development deal in Southside Virginia’s history. It’s expected to create up to $100 billion in investment and more than 2,500 jobs with salaries of more than $80,000 over a 20-year period. At full build-out, the campus — called Project Crossroads — will require about 3,000 megawatts of capacity power, mostly generated on-site, said the permit application. The application requests construction and environmental permitting from multiple agencies at once. It lays out project details, like power infrastructure, wetlands impact mitigation and community engagement for Project Crossroads. The project was first made public in March through a land sale between data center developer Stack Infrastructure and the Danville-Pittsylvania County Regional Industrial Facility Authority. Many of the details in the joint permit application were not available until now. Through the land sale and a local performance agreement, Stack claimed nearly 3,000 acres at the 3,528-acre megasite in Pittsylvania. According to the joint permit application, 1,715 acres of that land are developable. The 21-building data center campus, along with its on-site power and other infrastructure, would encompass those 1,715 acres, with a total of 1,733 acres disturbed during construction. The application also included expected property tax revenue for Pittsylvania County: up to $48 million per year at full buildout. That’s about $16.5 million in taxes per year on the first 1,000 acres and an additional $16,250 per acre for every developed acre after that. The county will also receive tax revenue on data center equipment at a rate of $1.62 per $100 of assessed value. This would almost certainly make the project the county’s largest taxpayer. The biggest chunk — about 42% — of the county’s revenue for fiscal year 2027 comes from real estate taxes. The project is not receiving any local discretionary monetary incentives. Though no formal announcement about the project has been made, Project Crossroads is expected to be the second tenant at the megasite, after lithium-ion battery separator manufacturer Microporous announced that it would build a facility on about 200 acres in 2024. The Berry Hill megasite was purchased jointly by Danville and Pittsylvania in 2008. Since then, over $217 million in public and private funds have been invested in grading, infrastructure and other preparations to ready the site for development. The megasite is now “shovel-ready,” meaning it has all the resources necessary for development. In January, the planning commission and board of supervisors in Pittsylvania County unanimously approved a fast-tracked zoning change to allow “special heavy industrial” developments, including data centers and power generation, at the megasite. On-site power generation Project Crossroads is expected to use on-site power generation for its massive energy needs, according to the application. A large part of the energy will likely be supplied by natural gas, via existing transmission pipelines to the megasite. Stack also plans to build a 150-megawatt substation at the megasite, which is expected to be operational by 2028, the application says. “The utilization of onsite power generation will reduce constraints on existing grid infrastructure, while providing reliability for operations,” the joint permit application says. “The project will also require backup and emergency power capabilities to maintain operational continuity during utility interruptions.” Specifics on the type, capacity and configuration of these systems will be determined later, based on requirements of future tenants, but they may include diesel generators, natural gas-fired generators, battery energy storage systems or a combination of these. The March performance agreement includes a condition on power use. It says that there will be a minimum load capacity of 299 megawatts for the project, provided by Appalachian Power by the end of 2028. There will be no restrictions on a load capacity higher than 299 megawatts, it says. The total projected capacity for on-site power at Project Crossroads is 3,000 megawatts. By comparison, a conventional nuclear power plant can deliver more than 700 megawatts, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency. For instance, Dominion Energy’s North Anna nuclear station’s two reactors supply, together, 1,890 megawatts. The joint permit application identifies two “energy generation campuses” as part of the facility — the 80-acre Southwest Energy Generation Campus and the 125-acre Northeast Energy Generation Campus. The combined 205 acres are the minimum acreage necessary to meet the project’s planned energy needs, the application says. The company is making efforts to minimize the on-site power’s environmental impact to streams and wetlands, according to the application. Where feasible, the energy generation facilities and infrastructure were consolidated to reduce environmental impacts, according to the document. Also released with the joint permit application were thousands of other pages of permitting information, submitted to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and other agencies. In an April community outreach meeting, Pittsylvania County Economic Development Director Matt Rowe said it’s a misconception that the project will raise electric bills for ratepayers.
