artigo.texto: Yankton County is going to take its time to study the economic and environmental effects of electrical energy storage facilities. During its regular meeting on Tuesday, the Yankton County Commission approved temporary Zoning Ordinance No. 23, which imposes a 12-month moratorium on these types of facilities in the county and directs the “Planning Commission, zoning staff, emergency management officials, fire departments, highway officials, and other appropriate advisors to study such facilities, conduct public proceedings and recommend permanent zoning regulations.” According to this ordinance, “Upon the effective date of this temporary zoning ordinance, no application for a building permit, use permit, zoning or rezoning permit shall be accepted by Yankton County, or its offices, specifically for electrical energy storage facilities exceeding a capacity of 1 (megawatt hour), nor shall any permit be issued for the same.” Energy storage systems for electricity generation use electricity — or some other energy source, such as solar-thermal energy — to charge an energy storage system or device, which is discharged to supply, or generate, electricity when needed at desired levels and quality, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. According to Yankton County’s temporary ordinance regarding these systems, commercial- and utility-scale electrical energy storage facilities are an emerging land use not presently addressed with sufficiently specific siting, fire protection, emergency response, environmental protection, road use, financial assurance and decommissioning standards in the county’s zoning regulations. Batteries (electro-chemical) are one of the five types of energy storage systems for electricity generation in commercial use within the United States. “The reason I brought this to the commission is that we do have a company that is interested in putting in an electrical energy storage facility — a battery storage facility,” Yankton County Commissioner Ryan Heine said. “It’s not really well covered in our zoning. There’s been some toss-around of exactly where and how this should be permitted under our zoning. None of the places really work out good. Rather than trying to let this muddle through, we’re just going to put a clear hold on it.” He said this “hold” imposed by the temporary ordinance on electrical energy storage facilities will allow the Yankton County Planning Commission to work on a permanent ordinance on this topic. “We just want to put this in so that we have our zoning code done right and clear,” Heine said. “That’s to the benefit to our community. That’s also to the benefit to any businesses that are going to be putting in a facility like this. They know exactly what the ordinances are, and we can hopefully make a good, clean ordinance that addresses real problems and that also tries to open our county up for real opportunity.” About the temporary ordinance, Yankton County Commissioner Wanda Howey-Fox added that, “just for clarification, we need to do it as an emergency,” addressing meeting attendees and online viewers. Heine said the “emergency part is simply because we do have a business that’s looking at” potentially installing an electrical energy storage facility in Yankton County. “We do have lots of questions around it,” he said. “I like these emergency ordinances only if they’re kind of specific, so that’s why I’m trying to be very specific. I don’t want to be inadvertently affecting other things. … We don’t want to inadvertently make problems for other things … that we shouldn’t be concerned about. “The emergency part of this is simply because we do have questions and we do have a business interested in this, and we want to get it cleared up so that we have a clear field for them to start on,” he said. “An ordinance like this also definitely puts some fire for our zoning committee to get it done.” While he acknowledged that the temporary ordinance says 12 months, Heine said he hopes a permanent and “proper zoning ordinance” can be prepared by the Yankton County Planning Commission much sooner than that, adding that the permanent ordinance will eventually replace the temporary one. “I really hope it’s something fast,” Heine said. “Two to three months would be great. They could do it in two to three months.” He said electrical energy storage facilities present “a few new safety things” that Yankton County has not considered before in its zoning. “We also want to make sure that we are also in a good alignment with the (South Dakota Public Utilities Commission),” Heine said. “There’s a size of things where we don’t want to intrude on things. We don’t want to create an issue for, say, someone who has battery storage for their solar farm or their solar panels on their farm or something like that of personal use. There are sizes to make sure that we are in a good place for that. “There’s also making sure that we’re … making a good law that does not inadvertently have negative effects,” he said. “I like to make sure that we make good laws like that. As I’ve always (said) a lot to the Planning Commission and in general is to not rely entirely on setbacks because setbacks are a poor way of regulating a real problem. If there’s a real problem, let’s make a real regulation to address it, but only address real problems.” Tom Glanzer, NorthWestern Energy’s community relations manager for South Dakota and Nebraska, spoke to the Yankton County Commission about the county’s temporary ordinance on electrical energy storage facilities. “I appreciate your comments, Commissioner (Heine), on doing this sensibly,” Glanzer said. “What we’re here to do is just to explain a little bit where we’re at with it and why we’re interested in battery storage.” He said NorthWestern Energy respects Yankton County’s responsibility to protect public safety, landowners and the community through responsible zoning and permitting standards. “However, even a temporary 12-month blanket m

artigo.texto: Amazon is reversing its plan to expand its data center footprint in Virginia—forgoing its $427 million plan to build data centers on George Washington University’s Virginia campus it had signed an application for in February. The company will donate roughly 25 acres of the property to Loudoun County for community facilities instead. The agreement, dubbed “Project Potomac Promise” by Loudoun County Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall, calls for Amazon to withdraw its data center site plan, abandon legal action to pursue development on the property, and work with the county to rezone the remaining land for mixed-use development—with housing as the predominant use. Amazon will also contribute $5 million to the county’s affordable housing efforts through the Loudoun County Affordable Housing Trust Fund. “My goal was to disallow data centers or infrastructure that could support data centers on this property,” Randall said in a press conference alongside Amazon Web Services data center delivery vice president Joshua Weissman. “Through our collaborative, respectful conversations, Amazon has agreed to forego its proposed application for data centers, and of note, forego any legal action to realize data center development on this site.” Weissman told Fortune in a statement “Loudoun will be a focus for Amazon’s Built Together commitment we announced a few weeks ago, which includes tuition assistance for community colleges and local project funding.” Amazon has a long history in Virginia’s “data center alley,” where the highest concentration of data centers in the world is located. The company launched its Northern Virginia cloud region in 2006, and according to Weissman, invested more than $63 billion with more than 3,400 Amazon employees in Loudoun County itself since 2011. Amazon had announced in 2023 it intended to invest an additional $35 billion in data center campuses across the state by 2040. Loudoun County also reported there were approximately 233 existing data center buildings, representing about 56.5 million square feet of space in the county. Data centers generated approximately $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, or 39% of the county’s overall budget. A land donation worth $65 million Under the agreement, Amazon is dedicating approximately 25 acres along Route 7 to Loudon County, with a stated fair market value of about $65 million. The land is intended to accommodate a community arts center and an indoor sports and recreation facility. Randall said the county would organize public meetings to solicit residents’ input on the redevelopment. She said she expects the rezoning process to take about a year—even under a “fast-track” schedule. “What we’ll probably do is focus first on the indoor sports arena,” she said, “and focus more on the community arts center first as the rezoning process is going through.” How Amazon’s plan unraveled In February, GW president Ellen Granberg announced the university had sold the campus, but did not initially identify the buyer or disclose the purchase price. The university said the transaction would help support its “long-term financial health.” A significant portion of the proceeds were marked for an endowment supporting the university. In March, the university’s student newspaper, The GW Hatchet identified Amazon Data Services as the buyer, who purchased it for $427 million. “It just came as a sudden announcement one day that they had sold the property, and that they couldn’t disclose the buyer because there was some kind of a confidentiality agreement,” former GW professor Ellen Scully-Russ previously told Fortune. “But of course, a student newspaper did their due diligence, and by the end of the day, they knew who it was, and they knew the price, and they communicated that to the community.” In late July, Amazon filed a site plan for a proposed data center development. Named “Bridgefield Tech Center,” the proposal called for four two-story data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet. However, in April, Algonkian district supervisor Juli Briskman called for county staff to examine the potential effects of the proposed development. Briskman said the purchase price of $427 million—roughly four times the assessed property’s value—and the property’s zoning status made it reasonable to expect Amazon to pursue data center construction. But by July, Briskman challenged the prospect of adding another large data center. “Replacing the George Washington University campus with four massive data center buildings would be a profound loss for our community,” Briskman said in a press release. “The site offers a generational opportunity for education, research, housing, and other forms of economic development that could directly benefit Loudoun residents. I strongly oppose this proposal and will fight it every step of the way.” Amazon eventually decided to pursue a deal with Loudoun County and abandon its data center investment. “There was not a moment where it was decided that this was a bad idea,” Weissman said. “We just heard from the community. We partnered with Loudoun, and we just decided this was just the right thing to do.”

artigo.texto: O Google quer construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, cidade de cerca de 4 mil habitantes a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis, e aposta que o projeto pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O modelo, apresentado pela empresa como a forma correta de atender à demanda da inteligência artificial, é tema de reportagem da CNBC, que ouviu especialistas e moradores céticos. O acordo proposto com a Xcel Energy prevê que o Google financie a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da concessionária. O volume supera a capacidade do próprio data center porque eólica e solar não geram eletricidade o tempo todo. Segundo a Xcel, a nova energia atenderá todos os clientes da região, não apenas o Google, e ajudará a avançar no fornecimento local de energia livre de carbono. O contrato depende de aprovação da comissão de serviços públicos do Minnesota. O desenho inclui proteções para a concessionária: o Google pagará por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada mesmo se consumir menos e, em caso de rescisão antecipada, deverá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas de demanda. “Ninguém quer fazer uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia”, disse Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel, à CNBC. O projeto também mira a meta do Google de operar com energia livre de carbono 24 horas por dia até 2030. A empresa diz que a área de nuvem, que sustenta seu modelo Gemini, teve receita de quase US$ 25 bilhões no segundo trimestre, alta de 82% em um ano. A corrida da tecnologia por capacidade computacional é o que vem impulsionando a demanda por eletricidade. Resistência dos moradores Pesquisa do Gallup feita em março mostrou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à instalação de um data center em sua vizinhança, com o consumo de energia no topo das preocupações. Levantamento do Pew Research Center de julho e agosto indicou que metade dos entrevistados avalia que os data centers serão majoritariamente ruins para o meio ambiente e para as contas de luz das famílias. Rede envelhecida e críticas A North American Electric Reliability Corporation, entidade sem fins lucrativos que atua como reguladora do setor, afirma que os novos data centers responderão pela maior parte do aumento projetado da demanda por eletricidade na próxima década. O Departamento de Energia, sob o governo de Joe Biden, informou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e transformadores dos EUA têm pelo menos 25 anos. Para Amanda Peterson Corio, chefe global de energia do Google, o momento é ideal para usar capital privado na correção da infraestrutura envelhecida, segundo a CNBC. Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, disse à CNBC que os operadores poderiam erguer instalações menores em locais onde a rede já tem capacidade ociosa, o que reduziria a necessidade de construir nova geração e transmissão. David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, afirmou que as concessionárias têm retornos em torno de 10% sobre novos investimentos — e por isso têm pouco incentivo para acomodar data centers na rede existente.

artigo.texto: TORONTO, ON / ACCESS Newswire / October 20, 2026 / Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. (TSX:PIF) ("Polaris" or the "Company") is pleased to announce that it has awarded and executed a contract with Trina Energy Storage Solutions (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. ("Trina Storage") for the supply of battery energy storage systems ("BESS") for the Company's Punta Lima project in Puerto Rico. Trina Storage is a global utility-scale energy storage provider with 30 GWh of BESS projects commissioned and under execution worldwide, including more than 6 GWh across Latin America and the Caribbean. The Punta Lima BESS project is being advanced under Puerto Rico's Accelerated Storage Addition Program ("ASAP"), a strategic initiative designed to strengthen grid reliability through the deployment of utility-scale battery energy storage systems co-located with existing generation facilities. As background, on June 5, 2026, Polaris Power US, Inc. ("PPUS") fully executed the BESS Standard Offer Agreement (the "SO1 Agreement") with the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority, establishing the framework for its participation in ASAP. The award and execution of the supply contract with Trina Storage represents the next key milestone in advancing the Punta Lima BESS project. The Punta Lima BESS will consist of a single 35.7 MW system with an 8-hour duration. Under the SO1 Agreement, the Storage Capability of 71.4 MW will be served by the BESS through two four-hour energy delivery blocks. Total estimated gross capital expenditures for the ASAP project, including the BESS, medium-voltage transformer, tariffs and balance of plant, are expected to range from US$55 million to US$60 million and will be funded with cash on hand. Once constructed and fully operational, the project is expected to contribute approximately US$12.5 million of EBITDA in the first year of operation. PPUS, as Resource Provider, will be entitled to receive monthly fixed and performance-based payments from the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority in exchange for providing energy storage services, including capacity and grid support. The agreement with Trina calls for deliveries of the BESS containers to take place March/April 2027. Accordingly, commercial operation of the project is currently expected in the third quarter of 2027, and the agreement will run for a 20-year term from the commercial operation date. Marc Murnaghan, CEO of Polaris, commented: "The execution of the supply contract with Trina Storage is a significant milestone in advancing our investment in Punta Lima, moving the project from its contractual framework into equipment procurement and implementation. This investment reflects our confidence in Puerto Rico's long-term energy transition and our commitment to delivering critical storage capacity that will enhance grid reliability and resilience. We look forward to working with Trina Storage and our partners to advance the project toward construction and commercial operation." Polaris remains committed to delivering long-term, sustainable energy solutions across Latin America and the Caribbean and looks forward to working with Trina Storage and other stakeholders through the implementation of the Punta Lima BESS project. About Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. Polaris Renewable Energy Inc. is a Canadian publicly traded company engaged in the acquisition, development, and operation of renewable energy projects in Latin America and the Caribbean. We are a high-performing and financially sound contributor to the energy transition. The Company's portfolio includes a geothermal plant (~82 MW), four run-of river hydroelectric plants (~39 MW), three solar (photovoltaic) projects (~35 MW) and an onshore wind park (~26 MW).The Company's development portfolio also includes three projects in Mexico comprising approximately 250 MWdc of solar generation capacity and 61.6 MW / 192.0 MWh of battery energy storage, currently in the planning stage and progressing toward financial close. artigo.texto: Shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast, citing power supply delays at its Melbourne facility amid local community and stakeholder opposition. The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million. The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC. Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation. Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades. As Australia grapples with growing concerns over the impact of data center developments on local communities, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was working to establish national standards for investment. Chalmers told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Wednesday that the government welcomes investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, provided it aligns with the country's national interest, adding that the government was finalizing national investment standards to address concerns surrounding AI deployment. Australia is not alone in facing opposition to data center projects, there has been growing push back against data center developments worldwide, amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment. NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.

artigo.texto: - Plans to showcase the Xos Power Hub™ line, rapidly deployable energy storage available from 210 kWh to 3.1 MWh per unit - Displays the AC Power Hub, a towable unit that arrives, connects, and moves with the job - Invites data center, utility, and industrial teams to Booth W15500 at the Las Vegas Convention Center LOS ANGELES, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Xos, Inc. (NASDAQ: XOS) (“Xos” or the “Company”), a leading energy storage and fleet electrification solutions provider, today announced its participation in RE+ 2026, North America's largest clean energy event. Xos will share Booth W15500 with Pioneer eMobility at the Las Vegas Convention Center from November 16 to 19, 2026. At the show, Xos will present the Power Hub line and display the AC Power Hub on the booth floor. Visitors will see how Power Hub storage arrives fully integrated, connects to any source, and powers a site in days instead of the years a new grid connection can take. Xos Highlights at RE+ 2026: - Power on your terms. The Power Hub bridges data centers and industrial sites through multi-year grid delays and powers site growth ahead of utility upgrades. It also runs standalone microgrids where EV fleets can power the site, delivers grid-independent power to remote mining and agriculture operations, supports construction, events, disaster relief, and mission-critical sites, and combines into multi-megawatt utility-scale plants. - Built to scale. The Xos Power Hub™ comes in four configurations, 210 kWh, 420 kWh, 630 kWh, and 3.1 MWh of storage per unit, with up to 1.5 MW of power output per unit. Up to 32 units connect in parallel for multi-megawatt sites, and more than 250 MWh is already deployed across North America. - Any source, any site. Power Hub units arrive fully integrated on a trailer, skid, or 20-foot container: connect and power on. They pair with the grid, generators, or solar arrays, and the 210, 420, and 630 kWh units can also recharge from a DC fast charger. Grid-forming controls let a site run with the grid or on its own, switching between the two without interruption, with real-time remote monitoring, diagnostics, and control from anywhere. - On display: the AC Power Hub. Attendees at Booth W15500 will see the AC Power Hub, a towable, battery-buffered mobile generator with 210, 420, or 630 kWh of LFP storage. Dual bi-directional AC channels each deliver up to 150 kW with independent voltage and frequency control. It needs no permits, excavation, or permanent installation, and carries UL1973, UL9540A, and UL1741 certifications. - Built in America. Power Hub systems are designed in California, manufactured in Tennessee, Buy American compliant, and backed by domestic service. Public agencies can purchase the AC Power Hub through Sourcewell, OMNIA Partners, NPPGov, GSA, and California CORE. “Energy infrastructure has traditionally been a permanent, multi-year bet. The Power Hub turns it into a flexible asset: customers deploy it where they need power, scale it as demand grows, and move it when the project ends, with no stranded capital. Designed in California and manufactured in Tennessee, it also means fewer shipping delays, faster domestic service, and eligibility for public projects with Buy American requirements. Speed, flexibility, and American manufacturing are what Xos is building its energy storage business around,” said Dakota Semler, Chief Executive Officer of Xos. Demand for new power is outpacing the grid’s ability to connect it. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s 2026 “Queued Up” report, 2,061 GW of generation and storage capacity is waiting to connect to the U.S. grid, and projects can take more than five years to reach commercial operation. For data centers, industrial sites, and utilities that need power sooner, that wait is a direct barrier to growth. The Xos Power Hub’s rapidly deployable, factory-integrated approach is built to help close that gap. Attendees can see the AC Power Hub in person at Booth W15500 during Expo Hall hours. To schedule a meeting with the Xos team in advance, email marketing@xostrucks.com or visit www.xostrucks.com. About Xos Xos, Inc. (NASDAQ: XOS) is a leading energy and fleet electrification company, specializing in mobile energy storage infrastructure and battery-electric fleet solutions. The Company’s mobile and stationary energy storage systems are purpose-built for the demanding requirements of commercial, industrial, and municipal operations. They deliver reliable, cost-effective power and charging without costly utility upgrades or grid improvements, supported by proprietary fleet management software and fully electric commercial vehicles for seamless operations. artigo.texto: Australia-based battery energy storage system (BESS) company Akaysha Energy has established an AUD 1.75 billion portfolio financing platform. It will refinance the company’s four BESS projects in Australia: Brendale, Orana, Ulinda Park and Elaine. The financing is backed by 11 banks, including ANZ, BNP Paribas, Bank of China, CIBC, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Deutsche Bank, DNB, ING, Mizuho, MUFG, and Rabobank. The financing will support the company’s development pipeline of approximately 6 GW/25 GWh of large-scale battery storage projects across Australia’s National Electricity Market (NEM). Akaysha Energy owns and operates the 850 MW/1.68 GWh Waratah Super Battery in New South Wales that’s touted to be one of the world’s most powerful BESS projects (see Australia Powers Up 850 MW Waratah Super Battery Project). Blackstone has closed its fifth energy transition fund, Blackstone Energy Transition Partners V, with $8.7 billion in capital commitments. This is more than 50% higher than its predecessor fund. Blackstone says this fund has already invested in power generation, electric transmission, energy efficiency, and infrastructure businesses, including three platform companies focused on power generation and transmission development. Blackstone said it has committed more than $11 billion in new equity investments across the energy transition sector since January 2025. UK-based renewable energy company Low Carbon has launched the Dengie Peninsula Energy Park Project in Essex, UK. It is planned to have a potential capacity of 1 GW, combining solar power and battery energy storage to export clean electricity to the grid. Low Carbon says the project is intended to support the UK’s clean energy transition, with public consultation planned for early 2027. It qualifies as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) since it will have a generation capacity exceeding 100 MW. Low Carbon plans to submit a Development Consent Order (DCO) application to the Planning Inspectorate. Earlier this year, in July 2026, the UK government announced planning reforms aimed at reducing up to 12 months from the approval process for major infrastructure projects in Britain, including solar farms (see Britain Cuts NSIP Planning Process By Up To 12 Months). Shandong Electric Power Construction Corporation, a subsidiary of POWERCHINA, has secured a contract for a 500 MW/2,000 MWh standalone BESS project in Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Group 1-KSB independent energy storage power station project is part of the country's initial battery storage program, with Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) as the offtaker. Once operational, it is expected to support grid flexibility, improve power supply resilience, and facilitate the integration of renewable energy. India’s ACME Solar has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) for a 300 MW/1,200 MWh assured peak supply project under the FDRE-IX tranche at a tariff of INR 6/kWh. The project will combine solar power and battery energy storage to supply electricity for four hours daily during non-solar hours, with a minimum monthly availability of 90%. Following the agreement, ACME Solar says its signed PPAs for projects under construction reached 4.31 GW, out of a total contracted capacity of 5.38 GW under construction. Fortis Green Renewables Investment Management and Zeitinger Invest have invested in GRIPS Energy Group to support the expansion of commercial and industrial (C&I) solar and battery energy storage projects across Sub-Saharan Africa. The investment will finance the acquisition of operational renewable energy assets in Senegal, Botswana, Zambia, and Uganda, while providing growth capital for new projects. GRIPS aims to build a portfolio of more than 100 MW of solar and storage assets by 2030.

artigo.texto: Memphians react to failed data center moratorium MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - The Memphis City Council passed a new data center ordinance Tuesday night, but it is not the legislation activists and environmentalists fought for and supported. New security rules instituted after the chaotic Oct. 6 council meeting kept disruptions at a minimum, but not the disappointment. The council passed an ordinance that calls for a 135-day pause on the permitting process for data centers, far less than the 12 to 18 months the activists endorsed. The meeting lasted more than five hours, filled with emotion. Citizens expressed doubt in the council’s decision-making. “History will find us on the right side of this issue,” one man told the council. “Data centers don’t belong in neighborhoods and communities,” said another woman. “And we can’t accept an ordinance, Councilman Warren, drafted by ChatGPT and rubber stamped by SpaceXAI,” another speaker said. Councilman Jeff Warren and Councilwoman Rhonda Logan sponsored the legislation OK’d by council, which was updated at the last minute. And while Councilwoman Jerri Green said council needed more time to understand the changes, Logan disputed that. “My ordinance has not changed. Everything you talked about tonight is not under our purview. The only thing we can address is land use,” said Logan. City Council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington told Action News 5, “This item is still going to have a pause in it and it’s going to have some guardrails. It’s more of what they need and what they requested.” KeShaun Pearson, founder of Community Against Pollution, said what is needed is more community input and further study of the impact of data centers on Memphis’ air, water and electricity. What council passed, he said, doesn’t come close to addressing that. “It’s not good enough because it’s not what the people wanted,” he told Action News 5, “It’s not good enough because it was presented to the people 45 minutes before it was voted on.” His brother, State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, who successfully challenged the council’s ban on his and five others’ attendance at the meeting in federal court, said the next step in the fight against data centers will be taken at the polls. “It is apparent that the Chamber of Commerce and Elon Musk have significant sway over some of these city council members,” Pearson said, “and it’s the responsibility of the people of this city to see them for who they are and to vote them out next year.” The council has requested a data centers study. Mayor Young issued an executive order earlier this month asking for a review of policy to determine the appropriate guardrails for the facilities. Data center critics said it’s too little, too late and the ordinance passed lacks the teeth to protect the people. “It was a big missed opportunity for the City of Memphis to be a leader in the region,” said Sarah Houston, Executive Director of Protect Our Aquifer, “We could be talking with our neighbors in DeSoto County and in Millington, where they just passed a moratorium and have a collaborative approach to data center regulation so it’s more uniform. It’s a missed opportunity.” The five council members who voted no against the ordinance were: Easter-Thomas, Green, Smiley, Walker and Swearengen-Washington. Councilwoman Cooper-Sutton was not in attendance. Action News 5 was told she’s handling a family emergency in Mississippi. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: Due to the quick turnaround of press time, The Weekly focused on one key item from last night’s Santa Clara City Council meeting. We offer more in-depth coverage of other items discussed at the city council meeting in the coming days. The Santa Clara City Council kicked the can down the road again on whether to prohibit the construction of new data centers in the city. At its most recent meeting on Oct. 20, the council opted to simply note and file a report detailing the pros and cons of a moratorium on new data centers. Council Member Karen Hardy, who is also running for mayor in the upcoming election, proposed the action at a previous meeting, but the item was deferred because of overly full agendas. The council previously discussed a related matter, proposed by Council Member Suds Jain, regarding the water use of data centers. City Manager Jovan Grogan said the city is unable to provide power to new data centers and has ostensibly halted data center approvals since 2023. The proposal stirred the pot on the council. “What are we afraid of, we’re afraid of having a discussion? That worries me,” Hardy said. Council Member Kelly Cox said she believes data centers are not for every community. She called discourse around data centers “our century’s Cold War,” adding that there is “mass propaganda” surrounding the discourse around them. She opposed halting construction on new data centers, calling it “irresponsible governance.” Council Member Kevin Park said the city uses its low rates as justification for continued expansion of the city’s utility, Silicon Valley Power. “Residential rates keep going up, and it is not the residents that need the power,” he said. Public commenters amounted to union leaders advocating for the jobs that data centers provide. Mayor Lisa Gillmor called data centers the “jewel of the city,” saying Santa Clara is the “gold standard.” Other cities, she said, are “light years” behind Santa Clara. “We do it right. I am really proud of what we do,” she said. “Stop poking at our success, because we have a lot of it … we have done the right thing. We are making sure our residents’ rates are low. We supply good-paying jobs. We are still business-friendly, and that the business centers will also give back to the community.” Hardy also proposed examining how the city deals with non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) regarding data centers. “The public needs to know that we aren’t making back-room deals,” said Park. Gillmor accused her colleagues of hypocrisy, saying several of them agreed to an NDA for the FIFA World Cup and the Super Bowl held at Levi’s Stadium earlier this year. Gillmor and Cox worried that singling out data centers for NDA disclosure sent the wrong message to the public. Gillmor said the city’s “reputation was on the line.” “How can you not put this on for further action right away, otherwise you are hiding stuff,” said Byron Fleck, a public commenter and a volunteer with Hardy’s campaign for mayor. Park amended the motion to broaden the scope of NDAs from data centers to all city dealings. Grogan said he was “increasingly concerned” with the amount of work the council was delegating to the city employees, adding that the council already has 150 items on its list of priority initiatives. A motion to discuss the city’s NDAs passed unanimously. It will return to the council at the same time as when the city discusses data centers and their water usage. Santa Clara City Council Consent Calendar Spending The council approved the following spending in one motion via the consent calendar: - Two $250,000 increases to purchase orders with Reed & Graham and Granite Rock to cover up to four one-year extensions for backfill and asphalt. The total purchase order is now $1.75 million. - A $627,430 increase to a purchase order with Vintage Contractors, Inc. for additional recreational court repair and resurfacing. - $5.83 million agreement with First Shield Security & Patrol, Inc. for city security through the end of October 2029. - A three-year, $2.72 million agreement with ACE Parking for parking control and event parking operations at the Santa Clara Convention Center. - A one-year, $611,903 extension to an agreement with Performance Mechanical, Inc. for boilermaker and pipefitter services. The total is now $2.61 million. The next regularly scheduled meeting is 7 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10 in the Council Chambers at City Hall, 1500 Warburton Ave. in Santa Clara. Members of the public can participate in the city council meetings on Zoom at https://santaclaraca.zoom.us/j/99706759306; Meeting ID: 997-0675-9306 or call 1 (669) 900-6833, via the City’s eComment (available during the meeting) or by email to PublicComment@santaclaraca.gov Contact David Alexander at d.todd.alexander@gmail.com Previous Santa Clara City Council Meetings: Data Centers Take Center Stage at Santa Clara City Council New Housing Complex Set to Come to Santa Clara — Despite Lack of Retail Stadium Finances Spark Discussion About Future of Levi’s Stadium Santa Clara Handwaves VTA Civil Grand Jury Report

artigo.texto: Data center air pollution permit under public review MASON COUNTY, W.Va. (WSAZ) - An air permit application for the Monarch Cloud Campus outlines plans for the site and its’ proposed power system that would operate independently of the traditional electric grid. The plans call for more than 800 primary engines, along with six natural gas heaters, 12 emergency generators and six diesel-powered firewater pump engines. During a public meeting, the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection explained how the state evaluates whether a project like this meets air quality standards. “They want to install a power generation facility that would power their data center campus. And so they’ve applied for an air quality permit for that power-generating equipment. We’ve conducted a technical review of that application,” Terry Fletcher with WVDEP said. The application also calls for testing, emissions monitoring and record-keeping to demonstrate compliance. The permit falls under the state’s major-source permitting program, known as Prevention of Significant Deterioration. The process is intended to allow industrial development while limiting how much air quality can deteriorate. That includes modeling how emissions could affect surrounding areas, including nearby residents, farmland and the river. The review does not require a full environmental impact statement or consider broader issues such as traffic, property values or the project’s economic costs and benefits. Instead, the focus is on whether the facility meets applicable air quality requirements. “The purpose of air permitting is to ensure that a facility is in compliance with the federal and state air quality standards,” Fletcher said. “And so, this puts limits on their operating hours and how much emissions they can emit during their operation. Make sure that there are proper controls in place to make sure that they have all the emission control requirements and things like that in place to ensure that we don’t impact the air quality negatively in the air.” The state received Monarch’s application in April and revised it in May. The public comment period is now underway, with comments due Oct. 30. A virtual public meeting is scheduled for Oct. 29. Copyright 2026 WSAZ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: - The system pairs a swappable main battery with a 77-kWh range-extension battery to improve battery utilization and lower fleet operating costs. - CATL plans to have 900 heavy-duty truck battery swap stations operating by the end of 2026 and expand to 2,000 by 2027. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has unveiled a dual-electric range extension battery for heavy-duty trucks, pairing a swappable main battery with an independent on-board battery as it expands its push in freight electrification. The world's largest EV battery maker introduced the system in Beijing on Tuesday, alongside upgrades to its Qiji battery-swapping system aimed at reducing fleets' energy replenishment and battery costs. The system consists of 2 independent battery systems: a standardized, chassis-mounted swappable main battery and a 77-kWh range-extension battery behind the cab. The latter supports 3C charging and provides backup power. Drivers of conventional battery-swapping trucks typically return to swap stations with about 30% charge remaining to avoid running out of power en route, leaving part of their leased battery capacity unused, CATL said. With the backup battery, the system can increase the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from about 70% to more than 95%, allowing trucks to return to a swap station with less than 5% charge remaining in the main battery. The system can switch power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining uninterrupted power and providing redundancy under demanding operating conditions, the company said. It uses what CATL calls a "1+X" architecture. The main battery remains standardized for compatibility with the Qiji swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be tailored to requirements such as low-temperature performance, high energy density or high power. The 2 battery systems can be upgraded independently. The range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an on-board asset, while the main battery can be leased flexibly according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental expenses during idle periods. Alongside the new system, Qiji introduced the 260# and 300# standardized swappable batteries, with capacities of 432 kWh and 513 kWh, respectively, complementing its existing 75# battery. The new-generation Qiji station can complete a battery swap in 5 minutes and reduces construction costs by 10%, CATL said. It requires no excavation pit and can be deployed in as little as 5 days. The company also changed the billing method for its battery-as-a-service (BaaS) offering, charging customers for net energy charged rather than energy discharged, allowing them to retain the benefits of regenerative braking. The change can reduce per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%, further improving the economics of operating electric heavy-duty trucks, according to CATL. The company plans to have 900 heavy-duty truck battery-swap stations operating by the end of 2026 and expand to 2,000 by 2027. Its long-term goal is to deploy 10,000 stations across China with partners. Agreements covering 13,000 vehicles were signed at the event, with orders for battery-swapping products from major logistics companies including SF Holding and China Postal Express & Logistics. The launch comes amid a rapid increase in new energy vehicle (NEV) penetration in China's heavy-duty truck market. New energy heavy-duty trucks accounted for 50% of the segment in September, up from 29% a year earlier, according to China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) analysis of compulsory traffic insurance data. CATL launched its Qiji Energy heavy-duty truck battery-swapping solution in June 2023 and introduced the 75# standardized swappable truck battery in May 2025, expanding its presence in logistics. On June 30 this year, the company signed a strategic cooperation agreement with J&T Express to provide swappable batteries, swap-station equipment, and operation and maintenance services for more than 5,000 heavy-duty trucks. Beyond the dual-electric range extension system, CATL also unveiled truck batteries for different transport applications, including ultra-light and ultra-thin packs mounted behind the cab, as well as chassis-mounted batteries for short-haul and long-haul operations.

artigo.texto: 3.75 MWh fail-safe system provides energy resilience and grid support at Buffalo's 105-unit affordable housing apartment building while helping lower energy costs for residents BUFFALO, N.Y., Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Viridi, the industry leader in fail-safe distributed energy storage systems, and Good Carbon Co., today announced the deployment of a 3.75MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) at Peace Bridge Place, a 105-unit affordable housing apartment building in Buffalo, New York. The project is one of the largest indoor lithium-ion battery systems in an occupied residential building in the United States. At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi's RPSLinkIN indoor BESS is part of a broader clean energy strategy that includes geothermal heating & cooling, domestic hot water, and high efficient building envelope upgrades. The 3.75 MWh system is designed to provide extended backup power for the fully electrified building during outages, while also helping reduce demand on the local grid during peak periods. Good Carbon Co., which focuses on revitalizing multifamily properties in communities throughout Western New York, selected the system to strengthen energy resilience for residents and enable the property to enable flexible, grid-responsive energy management. "Energy is one of the biggest operating costs in multifamily housing, and how you manage it directly affects the long-term performance of a property," said Adam Serbert, CEO of Good Carbon Co. "At Peace Bridge Place, Viridi's battery and energy management technology will help us reduce peak demand, avoid higher-cost periods and participate in demand response programs. That means lower operating costs, new revenue opportunities and a stronger economic foundation for keeping the property affordable and well maintained. For us, this is not just about one building — it is about creating a model we can apply across future multifamily projects." Viridi's intelligent Energy Management System automatically stores and discharges electricity based on the needs of the fully electrified property and the local grid. It allows Peace Bridge Place to reduce electricity demand during peak periods and respond to utility signals when additional grid flexibility is needed, while providing greater energy resilience for residents. By reducing peak demand and participating in demand response programs, the system can help lower the property's energy costs while creating new revenue opportunities. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency (NYSERDA) is providing support to Good Carbon Co. for the Peace Bridge Place project through its Future Grid Challenge. The Peace Bridge Place project is a National Grid pilot focused on integrating flexible, grid-responsive technologies into its distribution network. Viridi's energy storage and energy management technology will work in coordination with EnergyHub's Edge Distributed Energy Resource Management System (DERMS), enabling the property to respond to National Grid signals during periods of peak electricity demand. "Peace Bridge Place demonstrates how forward-thinking energy storage solutions can ensure New York's multifamily buildings are meeting the energy needs of its residents while creating a more reliable and resilient electric grid," said Doreen M. Harris, President and CEO, NYSERDA. "Projects like this embody NYSERDA's mission to spur innovation that drives New York toward a clean energy future." Distributed across seven battery rooms, the 3.75MWh system is integrated with Viridi's proprietary Energy Management System (EMS), which optimizes the property's electricity use while enabling it to respond to changing conditions on the local grid in two key ways: - Peak Shaving: As the building's grid energy draw approaches a monthly peak, the battery automatically discharges to keep demand below a target threshold, reducing peak demand and associated $/kW demand charges. - Seasonal Demand Response: During peak events, National Grid dispatch signals are delivered through EnergyHub's platform to Viridi's energy management system, which then coordinates the response across the building's battery and other energy systems. For participating residents, smart thermostat setpoints can be adjusted to "pre-cool" or "pre-heat" apartments before the event, enabling reduced HVAC consumption during the event while the battery discharges. Residents can opt out of individual events at any time. Together, these actions allow the property to reduce its net electricity demand while the local grid is under the greatest strain. Deploying lithium-ion battery storage indoors at this scale requires rigorous safety standards. The risk of thermal runaway — and its potential to propagate from cell to cell — has historically constrained where lithium-ion systems can be installed. The RPSLinkIN system is designed to address that challenge through Viridi's proprietary Fail-Safe Anti-Propagation architecture, a passive safety layer designed to prevent thermal runaway from spreading between cells. That safety architecture has undergone industry-standard testing designed to evaluate how battery systems behave during a thermal runaway event. During UL 9540A testing, a cell was intentionally driven into thermal failure to determine whether the event would spread to surrounding cells. Viridi's technology prevented cell-to-cell propagation, with no detectable release of heat, sparks, smoke, gas or flames. RPSLinkIN has also earned UL 9540 Listing from TÜV Rheinland, providing third-party certification of the complete energy storage system. "This project demonstrates what becomes possible when energy storage is designed to serve the building and the grid at the same time," said Jon M. Williams, CEO of Viridi. artigo.texto: Maily Kocinski grew up in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, a rural town 70 miles northwest of Milwaukee. She still lives there on a small farm — complete with a creek — with her husband, Robert, along with “two horses, barn cats, a dog, and four peacocks.” Kocinski is worried about her new neighbors. Meta Platforms Inc., the technology giant that owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is building a hyperscale data center in Beaver Dam. The facility, currently under construction with a $1 billion price tag on a 520-acre site of former Wisconsin farmland, is part of an estimated 3,000 new technology developments proposed or underway across the U.S. to serve as the backbone of the artificial intelligence and machine learning wave. Kocinski is concerned about the Meta project’s impact on water flows and quality on her farm, house and neighboring properties. She contends the water problems began after construction started last year. “It was bone dry. It smelled like fertilizer,” Kocinski said of the creek the first time she noticed the issues. “We have had a couple of neighbors whose wells have gone dry.” Soon after, the water returned with a gush — bringing new concerns, including erosion that might require rebuilding a small bridge over the creek. Kocinski said these fits and starts in water flow have occurred approximately 30 times since she first noticed the issue in May 2025. She also said that the water supply to her farm and home has turned murky. “It was cloudy, too,” Kocinski said. She has reached out to government agencies, Meta and other companies involved in building the new data center. “Every time I called, I was told to talk to a different department,” she said. “This is a big old mess.” Kocinski eventually commissioned her own water study, which showed higher-than-acceptable levels of strontium — an alkaline earth metal that can cause cardiovascular or kidney issues in high doses. A new water filtration system for her farm to lower those levels could cost as much as $40,000, she said. She worries the spike in strontium stems from the construction site less than two miles away, questioning whether blasting caused the shift and whether ample environmental due diligence was conducted before work began. In a response provided to Adams MultiMedia, Meta stated that a review of geographic information systems (GIS) data and a third-party analysis indicate the creek originates at a quarry near Kocinski’s property and does not extend into the data center parcel. Meta added that construction is occurring on the portions of the property farthest from her farm. Roberta “Bobbi” Marck, mayor of the city of Beaver Dam, said she has met with the Kocinskis twice, including once alongside Meta and its water engineering consultant. Meta — which currently operates 28 data centers in the U.S. — emphasizes that it uses more efficient, closed-loop cooling systems that recycle and reflow water used to cool servers and equipment. Facebook’s parent company also stated it will invest in operational water efficiencies at its facilities and fund local water restoration projects. ‘A LOCAL STORY’ The Kocinski family’s concerns represent a single snapshot of a much wider national debate over how the surge of AI infrastructure will affect local water systems. Data centers are undeniably thirsty. Water-fueled cooling systems are essential to keep rows of servers and computing equipment from overheating. Larger facilities can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute (EESI). Globally, water use by data centers could double to 2.46 trillion gallons by 2030, according to a United Nations report. By 2030, AI data centers are projected to use “enough water to meet the needs of all 1.3 billion people in sub-Saharan Africa for an entire year,” according to UN Secretary General António Guterres. AI and data centers are national and global waves with machines learning programs poised to change the nature of work, creativity and innovation. AI could also potentially displace workers from their livelihoods. “But water is really a local story,” said Rich “Raz” Razgaitis, a clean water and sustainability expert and CEO of FloWater, a Denver-based purification company. Razgaitis said that a data center’s impact varies widely depending on local water supplies and infrastructure. “That’s why small towns really need to be at the table,” he said, stressing the need for transparency. “We’re in uncharted territory.” He added that water systems across the nation have historically been underfunded compared to other utility infrastructure. FARMERS’ FEARS Tim Negris, executive vice president with MOCA Systems Inc., a Boston tech firm working with contractors, architects, and engineers, said that community resistance is often driven by local farmers and agriculture advocates worried about lost land and a potential strain on water supplies. “The fear around water is being driven by agriculture,” Negris said, pointing to similar tensions playing out in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Maryland and Iowa. In Dubuque County, Iowa, County Supervisor Harley Pothoff said local concerns about water, energy and farmland helped drive a local data center moratorium approved in May. He said a one-year pause gives the community time to evaluate the impacts of a proposed data center on a 400-acre parcel — including on a nearby local airport. “I have some concerns,” Pothoff said. “It just seems awfully big.” Opponents of the Iowa project claim it could consume up to 3 million gallons of water daily. artigo.texto: Group holds Lexington walkout against AI and data centers LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - A small but vocal group of Lexington residents is working to shape the rules before more data centers move in. The group, No AI in KY, welcomed speakers and singers Tuesday to show unity against artificial intelligence. Members describe reasons for walkout Reva Russell English, a member of No AI in KY, said singing was included because of a long history of using song as resistance in the United States and around the world. No AI in KY is not just an organization, but words members live by as artificial intelligence use grows daily. The group gathered outside the Lexington government center Tuesday, joining a nationally organized walkout against AI. English said the National Walkout to Freeze AI was organized by Irreplaceable. “We don’t have like a set location to walk out from so a lot of people did leave their jobs early or called out sick today,” English said. Moratorium approved, zoning changes ahead English said Lexington city leaders are listening. In early October, the council approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers. English said the fight is only beginning. During that time, leaders will strengthen the zoning ordinance text amendment, or ZOTA, to decide where and how centers can be built. “We’re going to be around the whole time when they build that new ZOTA and they build that new zone we’re going to make sure that they keep data centers in a way isn’t going to harm this place and its people,” English said. Students raise concerns about AI and creativity “I can only imagine what that will do to the next generation of artists and creatives and how their creative ability will be impacted and the thing is that we don’t know because it’s not been around long enough for us to know,” Mehta said. Mehta said AI does not just impair creativity — it plagiarizes it, using human work to mimic human creativity. He said that is why he is fighting against AI and data centers. English said the group wants more people to join its effort. “It’s a fight for the future, it’s a fight for our lives and we would like more people to be a part of it with us,” English said. The Urban County Council will hear public comments on data centers at its 6 p.m. council meeting Thursday. Copyright 2026 WKYT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: STL (Sterlite Technologies) has expanded its Neuralis Data Center portfolio with pre-terminated fiber trunk assemblies supporting fiber counts from 48 to 6,912. The new high-density cabling solutions are designed to help hyperscale and enterprise data centers accommodate growing bandwidth demands from AI, cloud computing and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The launch addresses a key challenge for data center operators: increasing network capacity while reducing installation time and making better use of limited cable routing space. For European data center operators and infrastructure designers, the assemblies offer an approach to scaling optical connectivity without significantly expanding existing pathways, trays and conduits. High-density fiber for space-constrained data centers The portfolio includes two product families covering indoor data hall connectivity and larger-scale indoor/outdoor installations. STL’s indoor pre-terminated fiber trunk assemblies support 48 to 576 fibers, with cable diameters ranging from 5.8 mm to 12.2 mm. Designed for high-density MMC, MPO and LC terminations, the assemblies meet ANSI/ICEA S-83-596 requirements and are available with UL OFNP plenum or OFNR riser-rated cables. For campus, inter-building and inter-row connections, STL offers indoor/outdoor assemblies supporting 144 to 6,912 fibers. The highest-density version accommodates 6,912 fibers in a single cable with an outer diameter of 32 mm. These assemblies feature OFNR/LSZH jacketing and UL 1651-rated sunlight resistance, making them suitable for installations requiring outdoor exposure. Factory termination targets faster deployment Both product families are factory-terminated and 100% tested before delivery, reducing the need for on-site connector installation and helping operators accelerate network deployment. Connector options include MMC, MTP/MPO and LC, with Base-8, Base-12, Base-16 and Base-24 configurations to support different switch and patch-panel architectures. The assemblies are available with bend-insensitive ITU-T G.657.A2 single-mode fiber in 200 µm or 250 µm formats. Indoor versions also support OM4 multimode fiber for shorter-distance connections. STL has integrated its patented IBR rollable ribbon technology into both product families. The color-coded bonded ribbon design is intended to simplify fiber identification and improve splicing efficiency in high-fiber-count installations. Ultra Low Loss connector performance options are also available for applications with demanding optical loss budgets. Supporting AI infrastructure expansion The new assemblies reflect the growing importance of cable density and installation efficiency as data center operators expand optical infrastructure to support AI workloads. “Every data center customer we work with is trying to solve the same equation – more capacity, less time. That’s exactly what this extension of Neuralis portfolio is built around. Our Pre-Terminated Trunk Assemblies are designed for dense networks, they are pre-tested, ready to connect on arrival, and flexible. This is connectivity built for how data centers are actually being constructed today; high density, tight timelines, zero room for error”, said Dr Badri Gomatam, CTO, STL. The expanded portfolio gives operators additional options for increasing fiber capacity within existing physical infrastructure while limiting field termination work.

artigo.texto: Gelion PLC (AIM:GELN, OTC:GELNF, FRA:X0S) told investors it expects to generate its first commercial revenues from its sulfur battery technology in the current financial year, backed by a strengthened cash position and development agreements with major industrial and automotive partners. The company reported pro forma cash of £9.6 million at 30 June 2026, up from £4.1 million a year earlier, following an oversubscribed £9.9 million net fundraising. Its adjusted EBITDA loss widened to £4.4 million from £4.1 million, although this was 10.4% better than analyst expectations. Total income slipped to £2.5 million from £2.7 million but exceeded consensus forecasts by 17.1%, with government grants and R&D incentives covering 63.2% of research expenditure. Customer revenue fell to £49,000 from £912,000 following the completion of a legacy energy storage project. Gelion has since secured a £2 million funded development agreement with Japan's Mitsui Kinzoku and a co-funded proof-of-concept programme with a top-five global automotive manufacturer. Both are expected to contribute modest commercial revenue in FY27 as the company advances its Nano-Encapsulated Sulfur technology towards customer qualification and manufacturing scale-up. Chief executive Matt Wood said the company was moving "from technology validation towards customer programmes, qualification and scale-up", with a focus on converting technical progress into commercial adoption. "2026 has been an important transition year for Gelion, marked by continued advancements in our sulfur battery technology and growing commercial validation of our NES™ cathode platform through partnerships with leading global industrial and battery sector participants," Wood said. He added: "Supported by a strengthened balance sheet, strong partner engagement and a clear focus on commercial execution, we are confident in our strategy and the opportunity ahead. "As we move from technology validation towards customer programmes, qualification and scale-up, our focus remains on converting our technological leadership into commercial adoption and long-term shareholder value." Gelion also noted on Wednesday that it is winding down its Integration Solutions business and pursuing the sale of its Battery Minerals subsidiary to focus investment on sulfur cathode materials designed for use in existing battery manufacturing infrastructure.

North Lebanon Township supervisors unanimously agreed to advertise an ordinance regulating data centers at their monthly meeting Oct. 19. The ordinance, which places the use in the industrial zoning district, will be up for adoption at the board’s Nov. 16 meeting. Solicitor Amy Leonard explained that the 34-page ordinance was modeled after multiple other municipalities’ data center ordinances and was revised based on comment from the township planning commission. The township’s existing code of ordinances does not address data centers specifically, meaning a developer could make a case to construct a data center in any zoning district. If passed, this ordinance would limit data centers to industrial land and subject them to aesthetic, dimensional, landscaping, screening, and noise/vibration requirements. In addition to the ordinance’s requirements, Leonard said, data centers would also need to follow general requirements for the industrial zoning district. Requirements for data centers laid out by the ordinance include a water feasibility study, a drought response plan, minimum 20-acre lot size, maximum height of 45 feet plus up to 15 feet of roof-mounted equipment, 100 or more feet of landscape buffer, and a sound and vibration study. However, this list is not all-inclusive. This comes alongside increased demand for data centers both locally and nationwide. Residents have voiced concerns about utility impacts, noise and vibration, and pollutants, including in the case of a proposed data center in South Annville Township that was ultimately scrapped. Throughout the county, multiple municipalities have recently implemented ordinances governing data centers. artigo.texto: Long County weighs temporary moratorium on data center development Long County leaders are considering a temporary moratorium on future data center development. The discussion comes as data centers draw increasing scrutiny nationwide and neighboring Liberty County recently paused new data center applications in unincorporated areas for 120 days. Although no project is currently proposed in the county, Long County’s Planning and Zoning Commission discussed Monday night whether to recommend a temporary moratorium to county commissioners, who have the final say. “My concern is that Long County has not touched on this subject at all, and it’s becoming a hot button item,” said Lisa Ruise, with Long County Planning and Zoning. Ruise also expressed concern about the potential community response to a proposed data center. “I don’t think our community can withstand the drama and the anger and outrage that a possible data center would bring,” she said. However, some planning and zoning commissioners were not on board. One commission member said they were not ready to support a moratorium without first exploring whether data center development could provide additional revenue for the county. “I’m not saying yes or no, but I’m not willing to just go and put that stop light on this right now without looking into it,” the commissioner said. Questions about the county’s ability to support a large-scale facility also have emerged. “I personally do not believe we have the infrastructure, power, water or ground to be able to hold such possibilities,” said Long County resident Ramsey Sleevar, who attended the meeting Monday. “I don’t think it needs to be dead in the water, but it definitely needs to be in place where people can be more educated." The Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing and vote on a proposed data center moratorium at its next meeting, Nov. 16. If the measure advances, it will go to county commissioners for final approval.

artigo.texto: Gelion PLC (AIM:GELN, OTC:GELNF, FRA:X0S) shares rose over 12% to 18p on Wednesday morning after the sulfur battery technology company reported that its £9.6 million pro forma cash balance and new partnerships with global automotive manufacturers strengthened its position to commercialise its battery technology. Gelion reported total income of £2.5 million for the year to 30 June 2026, down from £2.7 million a year earlier but 17.1% above analyst consensus, mainly reflecting government grants and research and development tax incentives. The adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation loss widened to £4.4 million from £4.1 million in the previous financial year, although it was 10.4% better than analyst consensus as the company continued investing in technology development, partnerships and commercialisation. Pro forma cash and cash equivalents stood at £9.6 million, with no debt, and were 21.1% above analyst consensus, providing funding for the next phase of development. Operational progress included expanded collaborations with TDK Corporation, QinetiQ UK, Nissan Technical Centre Europe and the University of Oxford, alongside development work on its nano-encapsulated sulfur technology, designed as a lower-cost alternative to critical minerals used in lithium-ion battery cathodes. After the financial year ended, Gelion signed a £2 million funded development and scale-up agreement with Mitsui Kinzoku and agreements with two major global automotive manufacturers to test its sulfur cathode technology for electric vehicle batteries. The company also reported that independent testing by the National Laboratory of the Rockies showed cells retained 92% of reference capacity at a 20-fold higher cycling rate, supporting further evaluation for defence, aerospace and drone applications. Chief executive Matt Wood said the company was moving from technology validation towards customer programmes, qualification and scale-up, with a focus on converting its technology into commercial adoption. Gelion said it had strengthened its intellectual property portfolio with six new patent grants across the US, Europe and Asia, and will hold an investor presentation on Thursday, 22 October.

artigo.texto: A U.K. homeowner shopping for battery storage got sticker shock after receiving a quote where the installation cost was about as much as the hardware. The homeowner wanted to add a Fogstar 32-kWh battery paired with a 6-kW inverter package, and they got a quote for £6,999. After finding what appeared to be the same hardware online for £3,995, the shopper turned to Reddit to ask whether the roughly £3,000 installation charge was standard. Here's what to know On Reddit, the homeowner said the plan was for a battery-only setup at a three-bedroom semi. They were aiming for a larger battery because a heat pump was expected to be installed. "I can see on the fogstar website that this combo is available for £3995 so a 3 grand installation cost feels steep?" the original poster wrote. One commenter joked, "Must be nice to make £3k for one days work." Battery storage can be one of the most effective ways to improve energy independence and keep a home better protected during outages. A system sized with a future heat pump in mind can also help cut energy costs by storing power for use when it is needed most. Anyone comparing quotes for battery storage can explore EnergySage to learn about home battery storage options, including competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has teamed up with electrification brand Qmerit to help homeowners get the best price on home battery storage solutions. A reply agreed the price looked elevated and focused on the system layout, saying, "It does seem a little bit high." More background Another Redditor offered a price comparison, writing, "I'm getting 2x16kwh fogstar with 6kw inverter for £4900." While that example does not represent an exact match, it gave the original poster a much lower installed price for roughly the same total storage capacity and inverter size. That led the OP to note that Equivolt also worked in their area, suggesting they should get another quote. Adding battery storage to a house is a major investment, and comparing options can have a meaningful impact on the experience. In this case, the homeowner went to Reddit and got a good lay of the land, but that is likely not enough in itself. What can be done? Getting multiple quotes from competing companies and understanding all the charges is important. Also, separating hardware costs from installation costs can make a quote easier to understand and compare. In this case, the homeowner was able to compare a £3,995 online bundle with a £6,999 installed quote, making the labor and other installation-related charges easier to examine. One clear takeaway is to gather more than one estimate. The original poster had initially been looking for a "sense check," and the shared quotes that commenters provided gave them a concrete baseline to pursue. For shoppers who want backup power but are not ready for a whole-home setup, Pila offers strong battery backup options. Pila's plug-and-play batteries are priced at a fraction of what a whole-home backup system would cost. Much of the discussion centered on sharing quotes and suggesting that the poster get more than one quote. It is hard to judge a deal from just one quote, and this battery shopper has some calling to do. Where can I learn more? There is plenty to consider when trying to make your home cheaper and cleaner to run. • SunPower and Palmetto are offering home backup batteries without upfront costs to homeowners. • GM wants EV owners to power homes in blackouts, though install costs remain a sticking point. • In New Orleans, officials launched $10,000 upfront incentives for residents adding battery backups. • Jackery unveiled a home battery system with automatic fire suppression and 100 safeguards. artigo.texto: Pitt County to hold public hearing on data center moratorium GREENVILLE, N.C. (WITN) - Pitt County commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to schedule a public hearing on a proposed temporary moratorium on data centers. The hearing is set for Nov. 16. The vote followed a presentation by Pitt County Planning and Development Director Jonas Hill. Hill said a moratorium would give the county time to study the impact of data centers. He highlighted regulatory gaps including a lack of standards for electrical load infrastructure, low-frequency noise compliance and air quality from generators. “They use and consume a tremendous amount of water. There’s no standards for water usage in our current ordinance at all,” Hill said. Hill said current ordinances regarding data centers do not distinguish between small or hyperscale facilities. Hill said 24 counties in North Carolina currently have moratoriums on data centers, including Greene County and Wake County. Several residents spoke in favor of a data center moratorium at the meeting, saying it is important for county leaders to have enough time to make an informed decision. “Often it’s in community of color or working class communities because the billionaires impact these monstrous things. I think they can do that and get away with it because people might not know their rights,” Pitt County resident Don Cavellini said. Another resident, Zoey Dixon, said data centers pose environmental, social and employment threats. “I had nearly 10 years of tech experience. I am somebody who will not use AI, for example, and this has already cost me multiple job opportunities,” Dixon said. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved.

The battery swap partnership between Huawei's automotive business and CATL (HKEX: 3750) reportedly plans to introduce its first model in 2027 under Epicland, a brand jointly developed by Dongfeng and Huawei. Cailian reported the plan on Tuesday, without identifying the model. A day earlier, Huawei's intelligent automotive business, Yinwang, or Newcool, signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement with CATL and its battery swap operator. The report provides an initial product timeline for the collaboration between Huawei's intelligent automotive technology business and CATL's battery swap network. The previously announced agreement did not specify any models or a service launch date. Under the cooperation announced on October 19, Newcool formally joined CATL's Choco swap ecosystem. Newcool will work with strategic partners to make vehicles using Huawei Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions compatible with the Choco swap network and connect them to it, expanding access to battery swap services. The partnership also includes Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES), CATL's battery swap operator. The 3 parties plan to connect vehicle, battery swap station and cloud systems, using real-time battery status and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively arrange battery swaps. Under the plan outlined in the earlier statement, vehicles would autonomously locate a station, enter it and align themselves, then drive away after completing a fully automated battery swap in 99 seconds. These capabilities are part of the cooperation roadmap. Epicland launched its first model, the X9, on September 24 and began nationwide deliveries at Huawei's Songshan Lake campus on October 18. The X9 is a large, 3-row, 6-seat extended-range electric SUV, with Huawei Qiankun ADS 5 driver assistance fitted as standard across the lineup, along with the HarmonySpace 6 cockpit. The report did not identify the X9 as the battery swap model planned for 2027. Epicland is among the brands developed by Huawei's Qiankun business in partnership with domestic automakers. It is not part of the Huawei-led HIMA (Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance) business.

artigo.texto: Oct 21 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that companies building data centers should pay a "dividend" to the communities where they are sited if they want to make the developments popular. "I have watched the process closely, and data centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck," Trump said in a Truth Social post. Data centers fueling the rise of AI have become a political flashpoint in communities across the country given the high quantities of water and power they require, with opposition uniting voters across ideological lines. The Trump administration, which has prioritized rapid AI development to compete with China, has also noted the shifting voter sentiment. "New and large, in some cases gigantic, Data (centers) are mandated by me to make their own electricity, and give or sell any excess back to the local community, or grid," Trump said in his post. Trump said in February that major technology companies must build their own power plants for their data centers in order to protect consumers from rising bills. AI giant Anthropic and Elon Musk have laid out blueprints in recent days for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom. The creator of Claude models said over the weekend it is committing 5% of its shares to a new fund for the "public good", while Musk pledged on Monday to give one SpaceX share to "every kid in America", arguing for such direct distributions as the burgeoning sector faces public scrutiny. (Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru; Editing by Tom Hogue and Jan Harvey)
