artigo.texto: CATL expands battery-swapping footprint with Huawei Huawei‘s intelligent automotive component subsidiary, Yinwang (or Newcool), has entered into a strategic partnership with CATL and its battery-swapping service arm, Chocolate Swap. The agreement, signed on October 19, 2026, aims to integrate Huawei’s intelligent driving solutions with CATL’s “Chocolate” battery-swapping ecosystem. According to CATL and Yinwang, the collaboration focuses on creating a seamless, automated energy replenishment experience. By connecting vehicle, station, and cloud data, EVs equipped with Huawei’s intelligent driving systems will be able to autonomously locate, enter, and align with battery-swapping stations. The process is designed to be highly efficient, enabling a full battery swap in just 99 seconds before the vehicle autonomously departs. Roadmap for 2027 According to industry reports, the partnership is already accelerating the development of its first wave of vehicles. A total of five battery-swapping models are planned for launch in 2027. The inaugural model will be a product under the Epicland brand, a collaborative brand between Dongfeng and Huawei. Additionally, GAC and Huawei’s collaborative brand, Aistaland, has also incorporated battery-swapping models into its future product planning. While CATL has established a robust network of 2,520 “Chocolate” battery-swapping stations across 200 cities as of September 29, 2026, the adoption of its battery-swapping technology in consumer-facing passenger vehicles has remained limited. By integrating with Huawei’s intelligent driving ecosystem, CATL gains a powerful gateway to reach a broader range of mainstream passenger vehicles. For Huawei, the partnership completes its intelligent service ecosystem by adding a vital energy replenishment scenario, further enhancing the convenience of its intelligent driving solutions. Market Context and Challenges The move comes as CATL faces increasing pressure in the power battery market, with third-quarter net profit growth slowing and gross margins tightening. By shifting from a simple battery supplier to a provider of full-lifecycle energy services, CATL aims to deepen its ties with automakers and secure long-term revenue streams beyond initial battery sales. So far, all of China’s major traditional state-owned car manufacturers (FAW, Dongfeng, Changan, SAIC, GAC, BAIC) have launched battery-swap models based on CATL’s Chocolate technology. GAC and Dongfeng, mentioned above, already had their own battery-swapping models even before this latest CATL-Huawei partnership. GAC’s model has already gone on sale, while Dongfeng’s has appeared in the regulatory filings. CATL has so far built 2,520 battery-swapping stations and aims to have built 3,000 by 2026. This week, it also announced plans to build 900 Qiji battery-swapping stations for heavy goods vehicles by the end of the year. With its ever-expanding battery-swapping network, CATL is gradually becoming an energy supplier.

artigo.texto: O RN não pode perder a corrida dos data centers No próximo dia 23, a FIERN sediará a Data Center Conference 2026, reunindo investidores, empresas de tecnologia, especialistas e autoridades em torno de um dos setores mais disputados da economia global. O momento não poderia ser mais oportuno para o Rio Grande do Norte. Enquanto a inteligência artificial amplia a demanda por processamento e armazenamento de dados em escala sem precedentes, estados brasileiros começam a definir suas estratégias para atrair um mercado que movimentará bilhões de reais nos próximos anos. Levantamento da consultoria Innova Assuntos Públicos identificou 20 projetos de lei relacionados a data centers em 11 assembleias legislativas entre 2025 e outubro de 2026. Dos projetos mapeados, nove possuem caráter restritivo, sete são favoráveis aos empreendimentos, dois combinam incentivos e exigências e dois são neutros. O que antes era visto quase exclusivamente como um tema restrito a uma parcela pequena da sociedade ganha impulso e chega aos legislativos com visões de mundo diferentes e mostra o quanto a temática ganha centralidade nas decisões dos governos daqui para a frente. Ceará e Goiás, os únicos a transformar propostas em legislação, optaram por oferecer previsibilidade regulatória. O Ceará criou um modelo de licenciamento escalonado de acordo com o porte e o potencial poluidor dos empreendimentos. Goiás combinou incentivos, zonas prioritárias e procedimentos simplificados. Em ambos os casos, a mensagem que deixam é que investimentos dessa magnitude procuram regras estáveis e segurança jurídica. O Rio Grande do Norte ainda não possui uma política ampla para atração de data centers, mas deu um passo importante ao aprovar, por meio do Conema, uma regulamentação específica para o licenciamento ambiental do setor. Ao estabelecer critérios conforme a potência instalada e diferenciar exigências de acordo com o sistema de refrigeração utilizado, o Estado sinaliza que compreende o momento, mas ainda precisa que o tema se consolide com uma legislação específica que dê a segurança jurídica para quem pretende investir. Essa discussão ganha importância adicional diante da reforma tributária. Durante décadas, a disputa por investimentos esteve associada aos incentivos de ICMS. Esse instrumento perderá relevância nos próximos anos. A vantagem competitiva passará a depender de fatores mais duradouros, como rapidez no licenciamento, segurança energética, disponibilidade hídrica e qualidade da infraestrutura. Em outras palavras, os estados deixarão de competir por benefícios fiscais e a previsibilidade do licenciamento e regras relacionadas à água e à energia terão mais relevância. Às empresas também cabe entrarem cedo nesses debates, com dados e diálogo com as comunidades locais para a construção de regras mais favoráveis, mostrando a importância desses investimentos para o desenvolvimento do Estado. A liderança na geração eólica, o crescimento da energia solar, os projetos de hidrogênio verde e a posição estratégica na agenda da transição energética colocam o RN em uma situação privilegiada. A Data Center Conference será uma excelente oportunidade para fazer esse debate de forma madura. O RN precisa definir a estratégia. Porque, na economia digital, os investimentos tendem a chegar primeiro aos lugares que sabem exatamente o que querem. Os que se planejam costumam colher os resultados antes dos demais. Quem hesitar correrá o risco de assistir ao futuro passar pela janela.

artigo.texto: The world’s largest battery maker, CATL, has combined swappable battery packs with an onboard range-extender system to solve range anxiety in heavy-duty electric trucks. Drivers on long-haul routes often pull into stations while their packs still hold substantial power. The new dual-battery design runs two independent energy systems inside a single vehicle. This allows haulers to use virtually all stored power without the risk of stopping short of a charger. “The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and QIJI battery swapping offers the best solution for electrifying heavy-duty trucks,” said Jesse Yang, CEO of QIJI Energy. The core technology uses a setup called a “1+X” architecture. Instead of relying on a conventional fuel-burning combustion generator for range extension, the powertrain splits work between two entirely electric battery packs. The main battery rests in the truck chassis and is built to be swapped out quickly at robotic stations. Behind the driver cabin sits a secondary 77 kWh battery capable of 3C fast-charging, which acts as a permanent onboard reserve. Steady flow of torque Having two separate power systems fundamentally changes how the vehicle manages electricity. In conventional operations, drivers rarely use the bottom 30 percent of their battery capacity. With a secondary pack always on board to act as an energy cushion, the main battery can safely be drained much deeper. More from Transportation See All Drivers can run the primary chassis pack down until less than 5 percent of its charge remains. This lifts the total depth of discharge from roughly 70 percent to more than 95 percent, squeezing far more work out of every charge cycle. When the main chassis battery finally runs dry, onboard switching electronics reroute power to the cabin-mounted backup within milliseconds. Because this transfer occurs almost instantly, the electric drive motors maintain a steady flow of torque without any drop in vehicle momentum. Engineers can also modify each battery system independently because the two circuits operate separately. The swappable chassis unit stays standard to match charging docks, but the backup pack can be tailored to specific driving conditions. To handle diverse logistics duties For instance, operators working in sub-zero regions can install cells with cold-resistant chemistry. Other trucks can carry alternative backup variants focused on ultra-high energy density or extra power delivery for difficult routes. Physical swapping equipment has also been expanded to handle diverse logistics duties. Alongside the existing 75# unit, the system introduces two higher-capacity standardized blocks: a 432 kWh pack known as the 260# and a 513 kWh pack known as the 300#. Automated bays complete the physical swapping process in five minutes, maintaining a mechanical success rate of 99.99 percent on the first attempt. The dual-pack setup extends into asset accounting as well. The backup unit remains with the truck as a permanent vehicle asset. “Aside from the dual-electric solution, CATL also introduced a new lineup of heavy-duty truck batteries tailored to different vehicle configurations and operating requirements at the event,” concluded the Chinese giant in a press release. “The lineup includes rear-mounted ultra-light and ultra-thin batteries for weight- and space-sensitive applications, as well as chassis-mounted solutions for short-haul and long-haul operations.”

artigo.texto: Snyder outlines plans for 7th term, addresses data center ad Incumbent discusses school funding and data center regulations ahead of Nov. 3 election WAUSAU, Wis. (WSAW) -Representative Pat Snyder says he has a plan in mind if he is reelected to a seventh term representing the 85th District, which covers Wausau and Weston. School funding Snyder has previously worked in the Assembly to get more funding for special education departments at public schools. That effort did not pass. Snyder said he is confident it will pass if he can bring it back to the state Assembly if reelected. Snyder and his opponent, John Kroll, agree there should be more funding for public schools. Snyder said there needs to be a plan in place and that the policy should not be generalized. “When they say fully funded, they don’t ever have a number of what fully, because I asked the three when we had our executive session, what is fully funded? Well, just enough to make sure everything’s covered. We got to have a number because the taxpayers would like to know,” Snyder said. Data centers Snyder’s view on data centers differs from Kroll’s. While Kroll does not want data centers, Snyder said they are an inevitability given how much media is consumed. Snyder said that does not mean he is against regulations and protecting Wisconsin’s nature. He said local governments have been doing the right thing by making data centers follow their set rules. “If you do come in, get the local control taken care of, it has to be enclosed water and it has to be your own generation. You bring your power and you can’t put the excess or taxpayers to be anywhere troubled by that,” Snyder said. Response to political ad One political ad running against Snyder says he gave $2 million to a data center near Milwaukee. Snyder said that is not true. He said when utility rates go up, the Public Service Commission sets and approves the rate increases, not legislators. “When they say that I gave $2 million for Microsoft down in Southeast Wisconsin, that was the 2023 budget that Governor Evers signed and passed. He could have vetoed that,” Snyder said. Snyder helped propose a bill that would put restrictions on data centers in 2025. He originally voted no. Amendments included an AI review council, which earned his yes vote. Snyder said technology growth should be possible in Wisconsin, but done in a responsible and controlled way. artigo.texto: Wisconsin regulators will conduct a full statewide review of the environmental impacts of data center development under a legal deal reached among environmental groups, a data center developer and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. The settlement reached Friday stems from a lawsuit filed in July by Midwest Environmental Advocates, or MEA, on behalf of Sierra Club against the DNR in Ozaukee County Circuit Court. The DNR, Sierra Club and Denver-based Vantage Data Centers signed off on the deal. The groups sued over the agency’s decision to issue permits for the $15 billion Lighthouse data center campus in Port Washington without conducting an environmental impact statement. The project is being developed by Vantage Data Centers and tech companies Oracle and OpenAI to expand capacity for artificial intelligence, or AI. Under the deal, the DNR will conduct a strategic analysis of the anticipated build-out of AI data centers and associated infrastructure to power them under current plans and projections. The review will analyze the direct, indirect and cumulative effects of the buildout on the state’s agriculture, air and water quality, climate, energy, economy, cultural resources and more. MEA attorney Michael Greif said the DNR approached environmental groups about settling the lawsuit by either agreeing to an environmental impact statement for the Port Washington project or a broader statewide review of data centers. “That second option was really exciting to Sierra Club because it would provide a holistic, comprehensive look at the environmental impacts and the financial impacts of these AI data centers on the state and on communities, and that’s something that very few states have done across the country,” Greif said. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul enacted the nation’s first statewide moratorium on data centers while the state reviews their effects on the environment and energy use. The deal reached Friday among the DNR, groups and Vantage does not pause permitting of data center projects while the state completes its review. “That’s something that the next governor certainly could put in place, and I think that’s something that would be the right approach for the state,” Greif added. Crowley supports ‘pause’ in development during yearlong review Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley said in a statement that he would support halting new data center projects while the environmental analysis is taking place. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “David Crowley has been clear that he doesn’t believe we should move forward with any new projects until firm guardrails are in place. As governor, he will work with the legislature to pause development until the review is complete and the new guardrails are in place,” a Crowley campaign spokesperson said. Both Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany have called for new standards or guardrails before any new data centers move forward. A spokesperson for Tiffany’s campaign said Tiffany has consistently said there should be no new data centers without five standards that include ending subsidies for data centers and barring non-disclosure agreements. “Under my administration, the DNR will hold every proposed project to Wisconsin’s environmental standards before a permit is issued, ensuring our water, land, and natural resources are protected. If a project doesn’t meet these standards or the local community doesn’t support it, it will not move forward,” Tiffany said on his website. Tiffany’s spokesperson did not address the new statewide environmental analysis announced in the legal settlement. Vantage will pay all costs tied to the strategic statewide analysis A Vantage spokesperson said it supports a thoughtful, fact-based discussion about responsible data center development and has agreed to fund all costs tied to the strategic statewide analysis led by the DNR. “The analysis will examine the environmental and economic considerations associated with data center development, providing policymakers and communities with additional information as the state considers the industry’s continued growth,” said Mark Freeman, Vantage’s vice president of global marketing. The DNR will retain sole control over the review, and the agency will have full authority to determine whether any future application or project complies with state laws. The DNR must complete its strategic analysis by Jan. 31, 2028, according to the deal. A DNR spokesperson said late Monday that the statewide analysis will be an important tool to understand impacts and inform future policy decisions. “We are also pleased that, under a negotiated settlement agreement with Sierra Club and Vantage, the DNR will be able to conduct the independent strategic analysis at no additional cost to Wisconsin taxpayers,” the agency said. The DNR must seek public comment and hold one or more public hearings on the analysis, and it will include summaries of the effects of data center development on energy bills. Under the settlement, permits for the Lighthouse data center campus will remain valid, and further environmental review of those approvals is not required. Ward said the deal is an opportunity to ensure the state understands the impacts of projects, including future phases of the Port Washington campus. The first phase would use 1.3 gigawatts of energy, but it could require up to 3.5 gigawatts of electricity. Sierra Club will withdraw its petition for a contested case hearing on the agency’s decision, but the DNR will provide records requested by environmental groups. artigo.texto: October 21, 2026 Introduction Critics often argue that data centers bring large buildings and heavy power demand but few jobs, and on its face the argument is easy to accept.[i] A finished hyperscale campus can run with a relatively small permanent staff.[ii] Yet a count of the people working inside a finished facility captures only a fraction of the sector’s economic footprint. Before a campus opens, electricians, ironworkers, and engineers spend years building it, and specialized manufacturers supply the power and cooling equipment that runs it.[iii] Once it opens, operators buy electricity, maintenance, and security from Iowa businesses and replace servers and other hardware every few years.[iv] That activity matters more in Iowa than in most states. Iowa ranks among the Midwest’s leaders in data center capacity, both in facilities already operating and in projects still in development.[v] National research finds that counties with data centers see “positive effects on total employment, construction employment, establishments, payroll, tax returns, adjusted gross income, and wages.”[vi] This report estimates how much Iowa employment, income, and output these data center lifecycles support. It first documents the size, location, and development of Iowa’s data center sector. It then estimates the direct investment owners and operators have made to date and have announced for the coming years. Common Sense Institute then uses the Regional Economic Models, Inc. (REMI) Tax-PI+ model to simulate the direct, indirect, and induced effects of two phases of spending—construction and initial equipment, and ongoing operations and equipment replacement. Finally, the report opens the door to future CSI research on the sector’s tax impacts, community investments, and resource demands. Key Findings - Data center owners and operators have invested or announced at least $53 billion in Iowa buildings and equipment through 2031 (table 1). - Investments in Iowa data centers to date total an estimated $15.1 billion, or about $4,700 for every Iowan. - Announced investments from 2027 through 2031 would add an additional $38.0 billion. At an average of $7.6 billion per year, these direct investments represent roughly 2.8% of Iowa’s current annual GDP. - Ongoing operating and replacement spending totaled an estimated $4.4 billion in 2026, and announced projects would add about $10.6 billion a year by 2031. - Announced construction and initial equipment purchases would support about 12,775 jobs by 2031, counting direct, indirect, and induced effects. - From 2027 through 2031, they would add about $10.4 billion to GDP and $6.3 billion to personal income (table 3). - The ongoing operations of Iowa’s data centers produce more sustained jobs and more economic activity than their initial construction. - Operations at existing data centers support an estimated 12,647 Iowa jobs in 2026, or nearly three jobs for every direct job (tables 4 and 6). - Once operating, announced projects would support about 29,597 jobs in 2031. From 2027 through 2031, they would add about $18.5 billion to GDP and $9.0 billion to personal income (table 4). - Job gains reach well beyond technology, to electricians, construction workers, retail workers, teachers, and motor vehicle operators (table 5). - Data centers pay more than other employers for the same job titles, from 12% more for security officers to almost 100% more for electrical engineers (figure 4). - Average annual pay in the industry that includes data centers reached $125,759 in 2025, nearly double the $63,469 average for all Iowa workers. - Relative to its population, Iowa is the Midwest’s data center leader, with more operating capacity per resident than any other state in the region (figure 1). - Iowa’s data centers have 71.8 megawatts (MW) of operating capacity per 100,000 residents. Megawatts measure how much electricity a facility can draw at once, which is the most reliable gauge of a data center’s size. - Iowa ranks second in the Midwest in total operating capacity (2,324 MW), behind only Ohio. Including planned projects, it ranks fourth in total capacity and second per capita, behind only Indiana. - Iowa’s data center sector is on track to more than triple in size by 2031 (table 1). - Announced projects would add 5,257 MW to today’s 2,324 MW of operating capacity in about five years. Building what exists today took more than two decades (figure 3). Iowa’s Data Center Landscape This section describes Iowa’s data center sector and what its jobs pay. It begins with the size, location, and development of the state’s data center facilities and compares Iowa with the rest of the Midwest. It then compares pay at data centers with pay at other employers. Cleanview provides the data.[vii] Planned capacity figures for all states are a snapshot. artigo.texto: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage The Wiikwemkoong First Nation in Canada is using a data center to help preserve its heritage The Wiikwemkoong First Nation in Canada is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. The data center on the Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario stores digital files, including Anishinaabe language videos. Chief Tim Ominika emphasizes the importance of protecting the community's language and data. The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers. WIIKWEMKOONG UNCEDED TERRITORY, Ontario (AP) — For thousands of years, Indigenous peoples have passed down their traditions and culture through oral storytelling. Now, a Canadian Indigenous community is using a data center to help preserve its heritage. The Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory in rural Ontario installed a small data center as it modernized its recordkeeping systems. Among the digital files it holds are video recordings of Anishinaabe speaking their native language. “Our language is one of the biggest things that most First Nations across the country are losing,” said Wiikwemkoong Chief Tim Ominika. “We will have our knowledge keepers, our language speakers who may be moving on to the spirit world, but their legacy is still going to be protected for many years to come by having our own data systems in place and protecting that.” The idea of digital sovereignty has gained momentum in places like Europe, where leaders are wary of the widespread influence of American Big Tech. For the Wiikwemkoong First Nation and other Indigenous communities, it is also about asserting authority over their own information after historically being excluded from its collection and use by colonizers. About the size of a single-car garage, the data center installed last year also stores the community's corporate documents, health data for residents, and security camera footage. “The purpose of all of this is having the ownership, access, control and possession of our information,” Ominika said. It’s about preventing anyone else from “having authority or setting their guidelines on what they could do with our data.” The First Nation has been transferring all its information from a Microsoft data center in Toronto, about 190 miles (305 kilometers) south, said Michael McCormick, the community’s chief technical officer. Other Indigenous communities have been taking an interest Wiikwemkoong is on the eastern end of Manitoulin Island in Lake Huron, an area that attracts visitors with its rugged wilderness, extensive waterways and Anishinaabe cultural offerings. The reserve prides itself on being Canada’s only “unceded territory,” because it never signed a treaty surrendering its land. The data center, which underpins a modernization of Wiikwemkoong’s administrative services, also has paved the way for new public safety infrastructure, including a drone fleet and a network of surveillance cameras. A backup data center on the mainland and public Wi-Fi transmitters are also planned for the community of about 4,000 people. The chief declined to disclose how much is being spent on the projects. Improvements to data storage gained urgency after a flood in 2022 resulted in the loss of some of its digital records, which had been scattered in various offices. “That information is very important to us. And in order to protect it, keep it safe, we said ’Why can’t we not look at developing and creating and implementing our own data sovereignty program?'” Ominika said. Wiikwemkoong’s upgrade program is among the first for Indigenous communities in Canada that include First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Delegations from other Indigenous communities in Ontario and neighboring Manitoba have come to check out the project, McCormick said. The chief said he has to explain to visitors that their data center is not like the giant ones relied on by artificial intelligence companies that require vast amounts of land and water. Wiikwemkoong's data center sits in a secure bunker next to the administrative office, accessed by a facial recognition scanner. Its four racks of computer servers are cooled by a pair of fans — not water — and it has “a relatively small carbon footprint,” McCormick said. In the U.S., a few Native American tribes like the Navajo Nation have for years been operating their own data centers for local infrastructure services. Wiikwemkoong's data center is believed to be the only one on Indigenous territory in Canada, but McCormick said other Indigenous leaders are increasingly savvy about control of their data. The Chiefs of Ontario, which represents 133 First Nations in the province, held a data sovereignty conference earlier this year that included a panel on AI and data centers. For generations, Indigenous communities worldwide have had no say in how information on them has been collected, interpreted and held by governments, researchers and institutions, said Carmen Jones, director of research and data management for the Chiefs of Ontario. “As more information is collected and stored, it is critical that First Nations determine how that data is accessed, managed, and used,” she said. The technology has addressed some issues — and raised new ones Amid the island's natural splendor, the community faces its share of problems that community leaders hope the technology can help address. Since installing the data center, McCormick’s team has added 700 surveillance cameras around the community, and a dozen drone docking stations on the administrative office’s rooftop housing a fleet of DJI drones. artigo.texto: French battery maker Saft has opened new battery production lines in Bordeaux to advance solid-state technology for electric aircraft and space applications. The TotalEnergies subsidiary inaugurated the lines on October 19, turning years of research into manufacturing capacity. The company said solid-state batteries can offer up to 50 percent higher energy density than conventional lithium-ion batteries, alongside improved safety. Those potential gains are particularly valuable in aviation, where battery weight and performance are central considerations for electrification. The facility gives Saft the capacity to develop and produce batteries using both sulfide and polymer electrolytes at room temperature. According to the company, it is the first French manufacturer with this combination of capabilities. Solid electrolytes offer safety and density gains Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material. The electrolyte allows ions to move between the battery’s electrodes during charging and discharging. Replacing the liquid component offers a route to safer, more compact batteries. Saft identifies increased energy density as another major advantage, citing potential improvements of up to 50 percent over classic lithium-ion technology. The Bordeaux production lines span polymer semi-solid and sulfide solid-state technologies. Their inauguration follows more than a decade of research, innovation, and industrial development, according to the company. More from Energy See All “Solid-state batteries are among the most promising innovations for meeting tomorrow’s electrification needs,” said Cedric Duclos, Saft’s chief executive officer. “These new production lines mark an important milestone for Saft, as we turn several years of research into real industrial capacity, a statement of our ambition to establish France and Europe as leading players in this strategic technology,” he added. The dry electrode process The manufacturing approach also addresses emissions associated with making battery electrodes. Saft said its batteries use a dry electrode process that cuts carbon dioxide emissions from that production stage by up to 40 percent. That figure applies specifically to the electrode production stage, rather than the battery’s entire manufacturing process or lifetime emissions. The new lines represent a step toward industrializing the technology. Saft’s announcement focuses on building the capability to develop and produce these batteries, with aviation and space as target sectors. Both industries want improvements in safety, performance, and energy density. Saft says solid-state technology has attracted significant interest from the space industry and is also seen as important to aviation electrification. Aircraft battery cells enter evaluation Saft has already delivered semi-solid-state cells to Safran for the evaluation of future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. The delivery builds on a partnership announced at the Paris Air Show in June 2025 to develop high-voltage battery systems for aviation. Most of the cells are destined for Safran’s System Test Center in Niort, France. The facility handles much of the validation and integration work needed to develop battery systems for electric and hybrid-electric propulsion. Evaluation of solid-state cells and batteries is expected to begin next year. For now, the delivered semi-solid-state cells provide an earlier milestone as the partners assess battery technologies for future aircraft.

artigo.texto: BYD’s new Seagull EV is now its cheapest electric car in China with 5-minute Flash Charging, and starts at under $10,000. BYD’s second-generation Seagull EV price and range The all-electric hatchback is BYD’s smallest, most affordable EV in China. Sold as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini in Europe, the UK, and other global markets, the Seagull is among the world’s top-selling EVs. For its second generation, BYD upgraded it with more interior space, its new Blade Battery 2.0 and 5-minute Flash Charging technology, and a few added premium extras. The new Seagull EV is now on sale in China, starting at just 62,900 yuan, or about $9,500. That’s with BYD’s “Super Trade-in” promotion. Regular prices start at 65,900 yuan ($9,900), which is still less than its predecessor. The first-gen Seagull EV normally cost 69,900 yuan ($10,500) without incentives. BYD’s new Seagull EV is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000), without a trade-in. The second-generation Seagull is 425 mm longer and has a 150 mm longer wheelbase than its predecessor. It now measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. It also gains another seat thanks to the added space, with room for five passengers. Unlike the current model, which is front-wheel-drive, the new Seagull switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) that its predecessor offered. To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system. Inside, BYD overhauled the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a two-spoke steering wheel, a redesigned center console with smart storage, and added physical buttons. All variants include the DiLink 150 smart cockpit and BYD’s 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system. Buyers can upgrade to the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance. The upgraded system uses a roof-mounted LiDAR to offer ADAS features, including City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking. The front seats now include heating, ventilation, and massage functions. BYD added a few other premium extras, including ambient lighting, a 50W wireless phone charger, and smart storage. Top comment by CMG30 Small battery plus extremely fast charge equals a surprisingly useable cheap car. With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the new battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. A full recharge, or 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%. The new Seagull EV is available with two BYD Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh, providing CLTC ranges of 320 km (199 miles) and 420 km (261 miles), respectively. After launching in China, BYD is expected to introduce the larger, upgraded version overseas, likely as the second-generation Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

artigo.texto: CATL bets on battery swapping for heavy trucks with Tianxing II CATL unveils its Tianxing II heavy-truck range and argues for battery swapping on long-haul routes, while the Qiji station network remains to be built. CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited), listed in Shenzhen and Hong Kong and described as the world's largest maker of batteries for electric vehicles, unveiled its Tianxing II (å¤©è¡II) heavy-truck range on October 20, 2026. The group used the occasion to defend battery swapping as the preferred route to electrifying long-distance freight. The principle is simple: rather than recharging the battery while the truck sits idle, the haulier replaces it at a station with a full one in a few minutes. The battery sector is also driving projects in Europe, such as the construction of battery parks in Bydgoszcz by Tavion. A range tailored to different markets The range also carries an international name, Tectrans II, and varies by market. The version for the global market emphasizes very high-power charging, while the Chinese presentation, led by Gao Huan, chief technology officer of CATL's passenger car and commercial vehicle division for China, puts swapping first. CATL's heavy-truck swapping offer is called Qiji (éªéª¥) and covers swap blocks, stations and a cloud platform. The Chinese range includes batteries mounted behind the cab, suited to converting diesel trucks, and batteries placed under the chassis, including a very large-capacity version aimed at long-distance haulage. It also features a new two-battery configuration. In this setup, a large swappable battery, leased rather than purchased, provides most of the traction, while a small fixed battery, permanently installed on the truck, takes over when the large battery is nearly empty. According to information relayed after the event, leasing of the large battery would be billed on energy charged, with no unit price published to date. CATL says this configuration is already in production and that commitments covering a significant number of vehicles have been signed. Arguments put forward by the company CATL justifies its choice on physical grounds: faster charging requires higher currents, which generate more heat, so swapping would be the only route to maximum refueling efficiency. This is the company's position; it also sells a global version based on very high-power charging, and it does not reflect an industry consensus. In support of swapping, CATL cites a total cost of ownership, meaning the combined purchase and operating costs of a vehicle, lower than diesel's, as well as operating savings. These estimates rest on mileage assumptions specific to CATL, and the savings announced have changed from one presentation to another, on different bases. Deployment requires building a network of stations. Yang Jun, head of CATL's swapping business and CEO of Qiji Energy (æ¶ä»£éªéª¥), the group's heavy-truck swapping subsidiary, oversees this activity. Qiji's technology relies on "under-chassis" swapping, while Qiyuan Green Power (å¯æºè¯å¨å), an operator of swapping networks, favors "rear-mounted" swapping, with the battery behind the cab. CATL is becoming the top shareholder of Qiyuan Green Power, whose seller is China Power International Development, a subsidiary of the state-owned group State Power Investment Corporation.

artigo.texto: O Google e sua parceira Xcel Energy afirmam que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts em Minnesota ajudará a modernizar a rede elétrica com fontes de energia mais limpas, sem transferir o ônus dos custos de infraestrutura para os clientes existentes. No entanto, especialistas dizem que grande parte dessa expansão poderia ser evitada e alertam que as empresas de energia têm um incentivo financeiro para construir continuamente mais infraestrutura. A corrida para fornecer energia a centros de dados com inteligência artificial está remodelando a rede elétrica dos EUA. Se há algo em que a maioria dos americanos concorda, é que eles não querem um centro de dados perto de onde moram. Uma pesquisa da Gallup realizada em março de 2026 revelou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à construção de data centers em suas localidades. A principal preocupação era o consumo de energia. Enquanto isso, de acordo com uma pesquisa do Pew Research Center realizada entre julho e agosto, metade dos entrevistados acreditava que os data centers teriam um impacto negativo no meio ambiente e nos custos de energia das famílias. Atualmente, o Google aposta que um centro de dados de IA em grande escala pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O acordo que está propondo com a Xcel Energy inclui a adição de capacidade proveniente de sistemas de energia eólica, solar e de armazenamento em baterias — totalizando mais energia do que o centro de dados deverá consumir. Nos termos deste acordo, o Google subsidiará o custo dessa energia adicional e continuará pagando mesmo que não utilize toda a eletricidade fornecida. Pine Island, uma pequena cidade com cerca de 4.000 habitantes, localizada a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis, é onde o Google espera que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts receba apoio da comunidade local. Ao mesmo tempo, este projeto também aproxima o Google de sua meta de operar inteiramente com zero emissões de carbono, 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, até 2030. O Google, cujo negócio de serviços em nuvem dá suporte direto ao seu próprio modelo de IA Gemini, viu sua receita no segundo trimestre atingir quase US$ 25 bilhões (um aumento de 82% em relação ao ano anterior), afirmando ter encontrado o modelo certo para isso. O Google planeja financiar a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de energia solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da Xcel. A capacidade total dessas fontes adicionais supera em muito as necessidades do próprio data center; segundo o Google, isso ocorre porque a energia eólica e solar não conseguem gerar eletricidade continuamente. A Xcel Energy afirmou que essa nova fonte de energia atenderá a todos os clientes da região, não apenas ao Google. A Xcel também afirmou que essas melhorias contribuirão para aumentar o fornecimento de energia livre de carbono para a rede elétrica local. O acordo proposto entre o Google e a Xcel inclui cláusulas relativas a taxas mínimas de demanda e multas por rescisão. O Google afirma que esses termos garantem que a empresa continue responsável pelo pagamento da infraestrutura construída especificamente para ela, mesmo com a diminuição do interesse em inteligência artificial. O Google se compromete a pagar por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada, independentemente do consumo real; além disso, caso rescinda o contrato unilateralmente antes do prazo, deverá pagar uma multa equivalente à taxa mínima de demanda por até oito anos. Segundo Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva e chefe de relações com o cliente da Xcel Energy, ninguém quer investir em grandes obras de construção para depois se deparar com a falta de mercado para a eletricidade gerada e de quem a pagar. É exatamente por isso que essas medidas de segurança são necessárias. O acordo entre o Google e a Xcel Energy aguarda atualmente a aprovação da Comissão de Serviços Públicos do Estado de Minnesota. Os centros de dados estão impulsionando uma expansão sem precedentes da infraestrutura energética. De acordo com as previsões da North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), os novos centros de dados serão responsáveis pela maior parte do aumento projetado na demanda de eletricidade na próxima década. Sob a gestão do ex-presidente Joe Biden, o Departamento de Energia declarou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e transformadores nos EUA estão em operação há pelo menos 25 anos. O departamento também observou que, para atender à demanda futura com o custo mais otimizado, o sistema nacional de transmissão de energia precisa dobrar de tamanho até 2050. No entanto, os operadores de centros de dados de grande escala argumentam que podem fornecer o financiamento necessário para modernizar a rede elétrica, tornando-a também mais limpa e confiável. Amanda Peterson Corio, diretora global de energia e eletricidade do Google, acredita que o momento desta revolução industrial é particularmente oportuno, já que a empresa precisa de capital para modernizar sua infraestrutura obsoleta nos Estados Unidos. Será que os centros de dados podem utilizar a rede elétrica existente sem modificações? Jigar Shah, sócio da Multiplier, uma consultoria que auxilia startups de energia limpa em suas ofertas públicas iniciais (IPOs), sugere que os operadores de centros de dados poderiam construir instalações menores em locais onde a rede elétrica existente possui capacidade excedente. Essa abordagem minimizaria a necessidade de novas construções e os custos de investimento em novos equipamentos de geração ou transmissão de energia. Shah argumentou que a integração da crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados na rede elétrica existente reduziria significativamente os custos de eletricidade para todos os outros usuários. Ele citou a colaboração entre o Google e a Xcel em Minnesota como um excelente exemplo de como os centros de dados podem servir de catalisadores para novas tecnologias mais ecológicas. artigo.texto: Is battery storage the quick fix for apparel’s energy crisis? Battery energy storage systems could offer Bangladesh’s apparel industry a rapid path to energy security. However, the government must ensure affordable financing for factory installations If you ask anyone in Bangladesh's apparel industry what the sector needs most to survive and thrive in the years ahead, you will hear the same answer, almost without exception: energy security. The urgency is not hypothetical. A recent survey of 134 knitwear factories found that 55% had seen buyers cancel or cut orders because of gas and power shortages since late August. Across the sector, energy shortfalls are cutting output by as much as 25–30%, and the diesel needed to keep backup generators running now comes at a heavy premium. Let me be fair to those in charge. The government has been doing its best through careful rationing and prioritisation of available energy to keep the apparel industry, and industry at large, running without interruption. Entrepreneurs, for their part, are managing somehow. But managing somehow is not the same as operating smoothly. Flawless operations, the kind global buyers expect when they place their orders, require a steady supply of energy that is simply not available at the moment. So, what is the solution? The permanent answer is, of course, a long-term one. According to media reports, there has been little meaningful effort to explore domestic gas reserves over the past 17 years. Even if exploration began today, it would take a minimum of 10 to 20 years for that gas to reach our factories. We cannot ask the country's largest formal employer to wait two decades. Nor are we alone. The energy crisis is a global one, driven by turmoil in the Middle East, and the world's more forward-thinking economies are not waiting either. One quick solution they are turning to is the battery energy storage system, or BESS. What remains missing is access to finance. Few manufacturers, battered by falling orders and rising costs, can commit nearly a million dollars upfront. If the government were to extend financing directly to manufacturers — interest-free or at a low rate — installation could be completed within two to three months. No other measure on the table offers relief this quickly. The case for BESS has never been stronger. An all-inclusive turnkey system now costs around $135–165 per kWh globally, down from more than $380 per kWh as recently as 2022. A typical 5 MWh industrial system, suitable for a large apparel factory in Bangladesh, costs roughly $900,000, all-inclusive. The technology has matured, too. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry now dominates industrial storage, valued for its safety and long cycle life. A system typically lasts 10–15 years, or 6,000 to more than 9,000 cycles. With periodic augmentation, it can continue delivering power for 15–20 years. I do not speak merely as an observer. At 4A Yarn Dyeing, we have never relied on a single energy source, and our rooftop solar and backup systems have helped us absorb rising costs. Even so, more expensive diesel has increased 4A's production costs by 2–3%. If a factory with multiple backup systems feels the squeeze, one can only imagine the strain on those without them. Here, the government deserves credit for a far-sighted move. The FY2026-27 budget has removed import duties, VAT and other taxes on BESS and solar equipment until 2031 and set the corporate tax rate at 0% for solar power generation until 2035. With diesel costly and outages frequent, these incentives have made the payback period shorter and the post-tax returns on BESS more attractive than they were even a year ago. What remains missing is access to finance. Few manufacturers, battered by falling orders and rising costs, can commit nearly a million dollars upfront. If the government were to offer financing directly to manufacturers, interest-free or at a low rate, installation could be completed within two to three months. No other measure on the table offers relief this quickly. We are well aware that the economy is currently facing a cash crunch. Nevertheless, since assuming office, the government has shown a clear willingness to support industry, and rightly so, because the only way to strengthen the economy is to help its industries grow. For example, Bangladesh Bank has rolled out a Tk60,000 crore stimulus package specifically aimed at reviving closed, sick and underutilised industrial and service-sector enterprises. It is a well-intentioned initiative. If even a portion of that fund were made available for BESS installation at existing, operational factories, the impact would be immediate. Reviving closed factories carries considerable risk, and the benefits will take time to materialise. By contrast, existing factories struggling to survive today could not only stay afloat by overcoming the energy crisis but also double or even triple their capacity in the years ahead. This is not an argument against long-term energy planning. Domestic exploration must begin in earnest, and renewable energy capacity must continue to grow. But the long term will mean little if our factories cannot survive the short term. Bangladesh's apparel industry has weathered far greater storms over four decades, and each time, it has come back stronger. With the right financial support at the right moment, it can do so again and, in doing so, give the wider economy the strength it needs to grow. Abdullah Hil Nakib is the Deputy Managing Director of Team Group. artigo.texto: Flatiron Energy wins two battery storage contracts in the Bronx NYSERDA selected Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage among eight lithium-ion projects totaling about 950 MW in New York State's first bulk energy storage solicitation. Flatiron Energy says the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) has awarded contracts to two of its large-scale battery storage projects, Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage. Both projects, located in the Bronx, were selected in New York State's first solicitation dedicated to bulk energy storage. They are among eight lithium-ion projects chosen through a process the company describes as highly competitive. Elsewhere in the state, smaller storage installations are also emerging, such as the one in Buffalo, while in Germany an 840 MWh project at Bertikow has entered construction. Eight projects totaling about 950 MW According to the announcement, the eight selected projects would add about 950 MW of energy storage capacity to the state's electric grid once fully operational. Flatiron says it sited Blue Spruce Storage and Palladium Storage to support the reliability of New York City's grid. The company adds that the projects are meant to help ensure power is available during periods of high demand and reduce reliance on fossil-fueled peaking units. Doreen M. Harris, president and CEO of NYSERDA, congratulated Flatiron Energy. She highlighted the role the two projects will play in providing capacity to New York City's electricity network during peak periods. In her view, the projects are critical to improving grid reliability, reducing costs for ratepayers and deploying clean energy to meet the state's growing power needs. A 6 GW storage target by 2030 The awards fit into New York State's plan to deploy 6 GW of energy storage by 2030. Across the eight selected projects, NYSERDA estimates the inaugural solicitation will generate more than $1.6 billion in private investment. The agency also estimates the creation of more than 500 short- and long-term jobs. Juliana Mandell, Chief Commercial Officer at Flatiron, said the company was proud to have two projects selected in the first solicitation. She describes the awards as an important milestone for the company, which plans to develop the projects alongside NYSERDA and local partners. All NYSERDA-supported storage projects will be held to New York's fire safety standards, covering first-responder training, safe siting and comprehensive emergency response plans. Flatiron plans for both projects to be operational before the end of 2030, subject to required permits, local approvals and safety requirements. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: Cincinnati residents voice data center concerns as city leaders provide zoning update City leaders are studying new zoning rules for data centers as residents raise concerns about their potential effects on local communities, utility costs and the environment. Dozens of people attended a public forum Monday in Walnut Hills to discuss how Cincinnati should regulate future development. While no large-scale facility has been proposed, officials said they want rules in place before an application is submitted. “Is that what Ohio wants to be known for? Is that what Cincinnati wants to be known for?” Over-the-Rhine resident Cayley Baker asked. Residents questioned where data centers could be built and how their heavy water and electricity use might affect ratepayers. Robert McCracken of Cincinnati’s Office of Environment and Sustainability anticipated increases costs but called for protections to keep costs down. “How can the state and Public Utilities Commission look at rules that pass on the costs to the end user, the data center, and not to us?” said Ohio ranks among the top states for data center facilities. About 28 are operating in the Greater Cincinnati area, including smaller-scale sites such as CyrusOne. Cincinnati has imposed a moratorium preventing data center construction within city limits until February 2027 while officials consider zoning regulations. Baker called the process an important first step but said residents must hold city leaders accountable. “Time will tell if the city will help developers feet to the fire," she said. "I think city members do a lot of talk but when it comes down to holding people accountable and making real changes, words are cheap."

artigo.texto: Sepco wins Saudi 500MW/2,000MWh BESS project contract The project is being developed by a consortium of French energy major Engie and Saudi group Haji Abdullah Alireza & Co The Saudi Arabia Group 1-KSB Independent Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project has been secured by Shandong Electric Power Construction Corporation (Sepco). The project is said to form part of the Kingdom’s first wave of large-scale battery energy storage projects. The Al Khushaybi Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project has a planned capacity of 500MW/2,000MWh. It supports Saudi Arabia’s energy transition ambitions under Vision 2030, particularly the development of energy storage infrastructure to complement its expanding renewable energy capacity. The project is being developed by a consortium of French energy major Engie and Saudi group Haji Abdullah Alireza & Co. The Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) is the offtaker for the project, which is mainly aimed at strengthening grid flexibility and supporting the integration of renewable energy into Saudi Arabia’s power system, said a report. Upon completion and commissioning, the BESS facility will help balance electricity supply and demand by storing energy during periods of lower demand and discharging it when demand increases, it added. The project is expected to improve grid stability, enhance the resilience of electricity supply, and support the integration of solar and wind power into the national grid.

artigo.texto: CATL apresenta bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla para acelerar a adoção de caminhões pesados elétricos AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 21 de outubro de 2026 PEQUIM, 21 de outubro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A CATL apresentou hoje a inovadora bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla e a mais recente geração de solução de troca de baterias para serviço pesado, visando acelerar a eletrificação do transporte rodoviário de cargas. A competição no setor de caminhões elétricos pesados está indo além das especificações técnicas, focando-se no valor ao longo de todo o ciclo de vida do veículo. Embora a troca de baterias tenha tornado o reabastecimento de energia mais rápido e previsível, as preocupações com a utilização da bateria, os custos operacionais e o valor residual do veículo continuam afetando a economia das frotas. Para lidar com esses desafios, a CATL combina sua bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla com a estratégia da QIJI de padronização, nova infraestrutura e um ecossistema comercial completo, reunindo a troca de baterias e a colaboração em toda a indústria para acelerar a eletrificação de caminhões pesados. Uma abordagem de dupla eletrificação para a extensão da autonomia A bateria de extensão de autonomia elétrica dupla da CATL combina dois sistemas de baterias independentes, porém complementares. A bateria principal utiliza o sistema padronizado de baterias intercambiáveis montadas no chassi da QIJI para maximizar a eficiência. Um sistema de extensão de autonomia instalado atrás da cabine, atualmente equipado com uma bateria de 77 kWh capaz de carregamento 3C, fornece energia de reserva. Em conjunto, os sistemas mantêm o fornecimento ininterrupto de energia e oferecem redundância para condições operacionais exigentes. - Redundância de energia de sistema duplo Em caminhões convencionais de troca de baterias, os motoristas frequentemente retornam para uma troca com capacidade não utilizada porque relutam em deixar a bateria descarregar completamente. A energia de reserva da bateria de extensão de autonomia aaumenta a profundidade de descarga (DOD, depth of discharge) da bateria principal de aproximadamente 70% para mais de 95%, permitindo que ela seja devolvida com menos de 5% de estado de carga (SOC, state of charge). Nesse ponto, a tecnologia de comutação contínua da CATL transfere o fornecimento de energia para a bateria de extensão de autonomia aem milissegundos, mantendo uma fonte de alimentação contínua e estável. - Arquitetura “1+X” e atualizações independentes O sistema usa uma arquitetura “1+X”. Uma bateria principal padronizada mantém a compatibilidade com a rede de troca de baterias QIJI, enquanto a bateria de extensão de autonomia pode ser personalizada para condições específicas, com opções que incluem densidade de energia ultra-alta, resistência a baixas temperaturas para climas frios ou potência ultra-alta. Os dois sistemas de baterias podem ser desenvolvidos e atualizados independentemente para atender aos seus respectivos requisitos técnicos e operacionais. - Leasing flexível e gestão de ativos de baterias A bateria de extensão de autonomia de bordo, de propriedade independente, permanece com o veículo como um ativo durante toda a sua vida útil, reduzindo a dependência do acesso imediato a uma estação de troca. A bateria principal pode ser alugada de acordo com a demanda sazonal de frete, ajudando as frotas a reduzir os custos de aluguel durante os períodos de menor movimento e a gerenciar os ativos de bateria com mais flexibilidade. Essa arquitetura combina os benefícios da padronização com configurações flexíveis dos veículos, tornando os caminhões elétricos pesados mais práticos e economicamente viáveis em uma gama mais ampla de aplicações. QIJI constrói um ecossistema compartilhado de troca de baterias A QIJI complementa essas melhorias com uma estratégia de três pilares de padronização, nova infraestrutura e um ecossistema comercial completo. O objetivo é acelerar a eletrificação de caminhões pesados com um ecossistema de cadeia de valor cocriado por todas as partes interessadas, onde os benefícios são compartilhados coletivamente. - A padronização apoia uma adoção mais ampla Para acomodar uma gama mais ampla de modelos de caminhões e condições operacionais, a QIJI introduziu os blocos de troca de bateria padronizados de 260# (432 kWh) e 300# (513 kWh) juntamente com o bloco existente de 75#. O sistema permite a troca de baterias em apenas cinco minutos, com uma taxa de sucesso de 99,99% na primeira tentativa, ajudando as frotas a minimizar o tempo de inatividade e a manter a eficiência operacional. A QIJI também foi pioneira em um modelo de bateria como serviço (BaaS), no qual os clientes pagam pela energia líquida carregada, em vez da energia descarregada. Isso permite que os clientes retenham o valor da energia recuperada por meio da frenagem regenerativa, reduzindo em até 20% os custos de aluguel de baterias por kWh para usuários de planos básicos. As opções flexíveis de leasing de baterias permitem que os clientes adaptem os períodos de aluguel às suas necessidades, desde a troca de veículos usados até a demanda sazonal. Isso minimizará os custos de ociosidade e oferecerá opções mais flexíveis para períodos de inatividade fora de temporada, ajudando ainda mais as frotas a gerenciar os custos operacionais. - A nova infraestrutura melhora a eficiência dos recursos A QIJI visa fazer melhor uso de quatro recursos críticos no transporte de carga de longa distância: tempo, terreno, capacidade de carga útil e eletricidade da rede. A troca rápida de baterias reduz os tempos de espera, enquanto o layout eficiente das estações atende a mais veículos na mesma área. A capacidade da bateria é dimensionada de acordo com as necessidades de transporte, e o carregamento centralizado e coordenado permite um melhor aproveitamento da eletricidade da rede. artigo.texto: Lithium ions in battery electrolytes do not always remain isolated. Research from Columbia University shows they often form clusters without anions. It revealed a structural feature that challenges long-held assumptions about lithium-ion battery chemistry. The study combines machine learning simulations with experimental validation to examine the atomic-scale structure of these electrolytes. Its findings could guide electrolyte designs for higher-capacity, faster-charging, and longer-lasting batteries. The research was co-led by Richard Friesner of Columbia’s Department of Chemistry and Alexander Urban, Lauren Marbella, and Daniel Steingart of Columbia Engineering. Lithium ions form unexpected clusters Electrolytes are crucial to battery performance and help drive the formation of the solid electrolyte interphase, a protective film on the battery anode. This film influences battery lifespan and safety, but understanding how electrolyte structure affects its formation has remained difficult. To investigate that structure, the researchers used machine-learning force-field technology from Schrödinger, Inc., with additional support from the New York Structural Biology Center. The approach let them simulate battery electrolytes more accurately and at a larger scale. The simulations revealed that up to 40% of lithium ions in standard battery electrolytes form multi-ion clusters. Clustering became more prevalent at higher salt concentrations, challenging the assumption that lithium ions remain predominantly isolated in solution. More from Energy See All “We discovered lithium ions in batteries actually group together into clusters in the absence of anions, and that these clusters are what drive the creation of the protective film on the battery’s surface,” said Friesner, William P. Schweitzer Professor of Chemistry. Experiments support the simulations The team compared its simulations with a wide range of condensed-phase experimental data. Strong agreement between the two supported the physical reality of the predicted lithium clusters. Theoretical analysis came from the Columbia and Schrödinger teams, while Columbia Engineering contributed the experimental work. “While the most novel aspect of the paper is the theoretical simulations, the experimental work confirming the results was essential and extremely difficult to execute,” added Professor Friesner. Friesner, who is also a co-founder and member of Schrödinger’s board of directors, emphasized the importance of combining computational predictions with experimental confirmation. “Predicting this unexpected chemistry computationally and confirming it experimentally demonstrates that we can accurately model the hidden atomic details of batteries,” he said. Clues to protective film formation Quantum chemical calculations indicated that the multi-lithium clusters have particularly favorable reduction potentials. These results suggest that the clusters are key intermediates in forming the solid electrolyte interphase. That connection gives researchers a clearer basis for investigating how electrolyte chemistry influences the protective film and, in turn, battery performance. The findings provide a foundation for designing next-generation electrolytes with improved performance, stability, and charging rates. Those improvements remain potential applications of the research, rather than demonstrated battery gains reported in the supplied material. “It’s a reminder – and an exemplary example – of how advances in AI-driven simulation need to be coupled closely to experiments,” Friesner said. “Ultimately, that will allow us to accelerate our progress in solving problems in biology and materials science, including making better, longer-lasting batteries,” he added. Gates Ventures provided funding for the research. The study was published in the Nature journal.

artigo.texto: Almost everyone agrees that data centers should pay their fair share — even data center developers. The newest proposal out of Congress poses the question: What’s fair? Congress has put forward its most aggressive proposal yet to protect electricity prices from massive new data center developments. The bipartisan permitting reform bill would allow utilities to charge data centers more than other customers for using the grid and would let states charge data centers more on top of that. “I think policymakers are seeing an opportunity for a good deal to take place here between extremely wealthy technology companies and regular everyday consumers, where the technology companies put many tens of billions of dollars into the power system to pay for the upgrade and keep the costs off of everybody else,” said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies, a firm that focuses on integrating clean energy into the power grid. The bill errs on the side of “over-collection,” Gramlich said, meaning data centers could pay more than their impact on the system and effectively subsidize other customers. Trending So far, major data center developers seem to be on board — though as negotiations continue things could change. “There are many devils in the details,” Gramlich said. “Regulators at the state and federal levels will have a lot of work to do.” The data center provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would change a longstanding federal policy that allows utilities to charge customers only one of two costs: the general “embedded” costs of operating on the energy grid or the “incremental” cost of any grid upgrades necessary to serve a new project. Utilities usually only charge customers the embedded cost of operating on the grid, Gramlich said. Incremental costs are difficult to calculate and can vary widely based on the kinds of grid upgrades that are needed at the time a new customer is coming onboard. Data centers, cryptocurrency miners and other “high-density computing facilities” would be subject to both of those costs together under the bill. Awhite paper created for utility company Exelon Corporation earlier this year found that data centers could still shift costs onto other customers if they were only charged the “incremental” costs without the continued embedded cost charges. The bill would also require data centers and similar facilities to provide financial guarantees before the grid is upgraded and to continue paying grid costs even if they abandon projects early. The bill also notes that states could charge data center customers extra, beyond the incremental and embedded grid costs, using the proceeds as rebates for others on the grid. It also tells states they could choose which projects can connect to the grid first based on how much extra money they’re willing to spend to subsidize other customers. The idea of data center developers paying for the cost of upgrading the grid for their projects has been widely embraced; several of the data center provisions in the permitting bill seem directly related to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. But past attempts to avoid shifting data center costs onto the general public have included only voluntary commitments. The permitting bill would turn that directive into law. Despite the new potential costs, the data center and AI industries have been quiet and moderately supportive of the permitting reform bill, highlighting the support for energy and infrastructure projects from the bill as a whole. Staci Pies, senior vice president of government affairs and policy at Incompas, an AI infrastructure association, said data center companies have “been very clear” that they will bear appropriate costs. “They’ll contribute their fair share of whatever kind of incremental infrastructure costs are necessary in order to increase and upgrade the grid,” she said. But, she added, the costs and analysis “needs to be transparent” — particularly if states decide to charge data centers above the embedded and incremental costs. “In some instances data centers are going to say ‘we’re willing to live by this additional charge so long as it’s transparent and we understand the implications.’ And in other instances, they may not,” she said. OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta didn’t respond to requests for comment on whether they supported the bill’s data center provisions. Lobbying disclosures show the Data Center Coalition spent $480,000 on lobbying between July and September, including on the permitting reform bill. Michele Nellenbach, vice president of federal affairs at the Data Center Coalition, said the organization was still reviewing details of the bill and noted members were “investing hundreds of billions of dollars in the U.S. annually to build America’s digital infrastructure.” Some progressives have aired concerns that the bill as a whole would amount to a giveaway for data centers because of the easing of environmental laws and the provisions to limit legal challenges to projects. At the same time, there’s been concern that the proposed changes amount to overcharging data centers for grid connection. Travis Fisher, director of energy and environmental policy studies at the libertarian Cato Institute, wrote the bill’s data center provisions risk “shifting costs in the opposite direction,” which, he says, might be necessary to counter the opposition to AI infrastructure developments. Over the course of the last year, data center development has faced an incredible rise in political pushback. Communities across the country have rallied against the centers being built in their backyards out of fear of higher utility costs, pollution and other concerns. artigo.texto: ABDC pede corte de 90% no ICMS e cobra regulamentação do Redata Entidade relata projetos represados à espera das regras federais e defende ampliar os pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos. A Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC) defende uma redução de 90% do ICMS sobre equipamentos de TI sem fabricação nacional e cobra a regulamentação do Redata para destravar investimentos. Segundo o presidente da entidade, Renan Alves, há operações com infraestrutura pronta que aguardam as regras do regime para importar hardware e ocupar a capacidade disponível. Em entrevista à TV Síntese, gravada durante o Futurecom, em 8 de outubro, Alves afirmou que a associação mantém conversas com governos estaduais sobre o benefício tributário. A proposta envolve uma deliberação no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e a identificação dos equipamentos contemplados por meio da Nomenclatura Comum do Mercosul (NCM). “A ideia é você ter 90 por cento de redução do ICMS, nesses ativos de TI”, declarou. O dirigente ressaltou que o pleito se concentra no hardware que o país não produz. Segundo ele, a proposta não abrange todos os investimentos e despesas de um data center: construção, consumo de energia e outras atividades da cadeia continuariam sujeitos à tributação correspondente. Alves relatou receptividade de parte dos estados, mas também resistências. Lista de equipamentos condiciona decisão dos estados Na avaliação do presidente da ABDC, a definição dos produtos contemplados pelo Redata é necessária também para que os estados dimensionem o alcance de uma eventual redução do ICMS. O dirigente afirmou compreender a posição dos governos que aguardam a regulamentação federal antes de decidir sobre o benefício estadual. Sem a lista de NCMs, argumentou, faltam elementos para quantificar e qualificar os efeitos da medida. “Ninguém vai tomar uma decisão de olhos fechados”, afirmou. Além dos equipamentos elegíveis, Alves cobrou a definição dos critérios de habilitação das empresas, dos procedimentos de apresentação dos projetos e das eventuais exigências de auditoria. Estruturas prontas aguardam hardware A demanda imediata, segundo o executivo, inclui empresas que já operam no Brasil e precisam instalar equipamentos para ampliar seus negócios. Ele distinguiu esses investimentos dos projetos de novos entrantes, cuja implantação exige mais tempo. “O benefício é de quem já está com a estrutura pronta e você está fazendo só um crescimento orgânico”, explicou. Alves afirmou que existem projetos represados à espera do regime. Sobre a data limite para que as empresas conseguissem importar equipamentos ainda em 2026, diz que isso depende da complexidade das regras e da velocidade de aprovação dos pedidos. “O tempo que a gente perdeu, até agora ele não volta mais”, resumiu. Na avaliação do dirigente, o mercado brasileiro continuará crescendo para atender à demanda doméstica. A função do Redata seria ampliar a competitividade do país na disputa por investimentos que poderiam ser destinados a outras localidades, especialmente operações voltadas ao atendimento de clientes no exterior. Cabos submarinos para ampliar destinos dos investimentos Além da questão tributária, a ABDC defende ampliar os pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos para permitir que mais regiões disputem esses projetos. Alves argumentou que a conectividade internacional precisa integrar as políticas de infraestrutura, ao lado de estradas e linhas de transmissão. “Se você quiser que o data center venha, você precisa também fazer investimento em fibra”, afirmou. O executivo reconheceu que os empreendimentos dependem de operadores e de viabilidade econômica, mas defendeu participação do poder público na criação das condições para sua implantação.
