But now, some of the key data centers at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks during the 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair. Ukraine this month hit three main data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country’s equivalent to Facebook. Widespread interruptions to cloud services have been reported. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services all have suffered lasting disruptions. Russia prides itself on its digital advances — from an extensive e-commerce services sector to ambitious plans for developing artificial intelligence. But now, some of the key data centers at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair. Ukraine this month hit three main data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country's equivalent to Facebook. While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex’s virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions. The fallout even spread to Russia’s judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access. Most experts predict repairing the damage could take months, if not years. Some warn that Moscow’s aspirations to become a leader in AI development could be significantly set back. “This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race,” said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Data centers have been hit by both sides in the war Data centers are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other’s vital infrastructure. Russian missiles and drones have pummeled Ukraine’s power grid and other key sites, part of Kremlin efforts to weaken morale and resistance. Moscow stepped up those attacks as winter approaches, taking advantage of a shortage of U.S.-supplied Patriot interceptors, whose stockpiles have been drained by Washington's war with Iran. Ukraine retaliated with waves of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, triggering a massive fuel crisis and bringing the war home to millions of civilians. U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed the attacks for higher global oil prices, which have escalated largely due to the U.S. war in Iran. Earlier this month, Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import diesel oil, shocking Ukraine and its allies. Ukraine also hit huge warehouses for Russia's top online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centers closely followed Moscow’s recent strikes on data centers in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers. A data center in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11. The data center and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data center in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. Data centers are vulnerable While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centers are even softer targets — massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives. The vulnerability of data centers was exposed by Iran, whose drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centers in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain. AWS said last month it was unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted at two of them. Yandex has run drills for an accident that could incapacitate one of its six data centers, but it was caught unprepared when its three key facilities were hit over four days. It wasn’t immediately clear why air defenses near the sites had failed. “The problem in Russia is that they’ve got to cover a big country with air defense and they don’t have enough,” said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group. Russia’s efforts to build a ‘sovereign internet’ backfire Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow’s strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. “Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it’s relatively easier to take down,” Reiners said. Klimarev predicted the data center attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimize the damage. “Paradoxically, the strikes on data centers have saved the Russian internet from isolation, as they will now have to move computing assets, most likely, to Europe,” Klimarev said. “It’s quite likely that many Russian businesses are now roaming the European market to rent computing assets.” Russians are vexed by service disruptions Yandex dominates digital life in Russia and many former Soviet nations. artigo.texto: What India’s Forest Rights Act Can Teach Us About Data Centers Vaishnavi Patil / Oct 22, 2026 In 2025, the Andhra Pradesh government allotted 480 acres to support a $15 billion project to build a 1GW Google-Adani data center campus near Visakhapatnam. That allotment has since grown to 601.4 acres across three sites — Tarluvada (266.6 acres), Adavivaram (160) and Rambilli (174.8). The capacity appears to have grown as well, with clearance papers showing approval for 2.51GW. Despite encroaching upon the eco-sensitive zone of the Kambalakonda sanctuary and being in proximity to the Mudasarlova reservoir, the project was granted environmental clearance in just nine days. Since then, protests against this project have intensified. Vizag is not alone. Across India, as in the world at large, planned data center projects are drawing increasing dissent from local communities, who bear the real socio-ecological costs and do not foresee the promised gains of an AI future trickling down to them. States have begun to deploy policy instruments to address public concerns. However, solutions that only consider better engineering or cleaner impact metrics miss the point. This is not just a technical problem, it is also a problem of governance. A data center is a claim on land and its resources, and therefore a claim on people. Its policy, thus, must be anchored primarily in the politics of place, because scratch the surface and you will find data centers to be fundamentally a land rights issue. And India has a rich and unique history of articulating and fighting for land rights. No legal instrument represents this history better than the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, better known as the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006. It recognizes land and resource rights of forest-dependent communities, defined in its preamble as those “who have been residing in such forests for generations but whose rights could not be recorded.” In this age of data colonialism, critical resources are being extracted from communities to power a global digital system that directs the flow of value elsewhere. The FRA legacy provides us with the working grammar to confront this new form of colonialism and reaffirm pre-existing rights of communities. The grammar can be unpacked in three important rights articulated in the FRA — the right to land, right to resources, and right to development. Right to land (individual and collective rights) In the Vizag campus, two hundred of the 480 acres of the project belong to around 50 Dalit farmers of Tarluvada village. The land was given to landless Dalit farmers in the 1970s through a special program. This program is another example of the Indian state’s attempts to correct historical injustices, especially considering that a 2012 state survey revealed that 68% of Dalit households in Visakhapatnam district still do not own land. And yet, the Dalit community states that they were not consulted when the decision was made. They say that the Open Category (OCs) and Other Backward Classes (OBCs) negotiated the surrender of their land, with evidence of land-pooling and acquisition processes being used to put further pressure on them. They believe that the dominant castes withheld details from them and targeted Dalit lands specifically. It is exactly these types of power asymmetries in land and livelihoods that the FRA combats. By allowing land-dependent communities to collectively claim rights, the FRA sets an important precedent. It expands not just the definition of customary land rights but also the process for making claims. Under Section 3(1)(a), people can claim individual or collective forest rights for land they occupy and cultivate. Claims begin in the gram sabha, not the revenue department, and oral testimony and customary knowledge are permissible evidence. The Act restricts itself to forest land. However, its methodology of making individual and collective claims can be adopted more broadly. If applied to data centers, it would translate into allotment of land only after land claims are formally recorded so that structured negotiations happen with actual right-holders. Public consultation should also be mandated for data centers above a defined threshold. But how do you define that threshold? In Vizag’s case, due to the lack of categorization of data centers in the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) notification of 2006, clearances were processed for each site separately under Category B2 instead of assessing the whole project under Category A. As the Notification does not mandate public consultation for B2 projects, no hearing was conducted. Such obfuscation can be avoided if data center policies mandate cumulative assessments of projects and the EIA notification is amended. But more importantly, public consultation around data centers should draw on the FRA’s model of deliberation through local institutions. As rights under the FRA are place-based, claims and grievance redressal processes are triggered at the village level. If communities could lodge individual and collective claims to the land and resources on which they directly depend, and utilize them to demand accountability, consultation would follow regardless of the project category. If the state continues to insist on opening its land to tech conglomerates, granting rights to land-dependent marginal groups will allow them to protect their livelihoods more effectively. They are also resource-intensive, requiring an uninterrupted supply of power to run servers and freshwater to cool them. This naturally makes urban areas like Vizag attractive for data center clustering. artigo.texto: Fox ESS has introduced Power Cube, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining an inverter and batteries in a compact, stackable design. Announced in Melbourne on 20 October 2026, the system is designed to simplify installation and allow households to expand their storage capacity as their energy needs change. The launch follows a SunWiz announcement which, according to Fox ESS, ranked the company first in Australia for installed energy storage capacity in the first half of 2026. Power Cube integrates key components into one system, with the aim of reducing installation time and associated costs. Its modular EQ5500 batteries offer storage capacities from 10.92 kWh to 49.14 kWh across two to nine modules. “Power Cube has been designed with the Australian market in mind,” said Brooks Richard, Managing Director of APAC & Middle East at Fox ESS. Richard said the system’s capacity options were designed to suit a range of Australian household energy needs, while its integrated design aimed to simplify installation. System features According to Fox ESS, Power Cube includes: - Power options: CEC-approved single-phase models from 5–12 kW, with three-phase models from 5–15 kW planned for release. Both ranges support up to 200% PV oversizing. - Installation options: A compact, integrated design with an IP66 rating for indoor and outdoor installation. - Backup capability: An integrated gateway with 63A on-grid full-home backup support. - Battery protection: Inter-cell insulation and an aerosol unit in each battery module, providing protection at cell and pack level. - Integrated heating: Designed to help maintain battery performance in colder conditions. - Monitoring and connectivity: Fox Cloud 2.0 with AI functionality, real-time monitoring and remote configuration, alongside Wi-Fi, LAN and Bluetooth connectivity. Power Cube comes with a 10-year product warranty. Its modular design allows households to select an initial storage capacity and expand it as their requirements change. Ends. artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING , Oct. 20, 2026 /CNW/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold,CATL 's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models:Battery Asset Service Partners andEnergy Replenishment Service Partners . artigo.texto: The AI industry has a problem with bragging. Companies are announcing enormous new data centers to power the AI boom. Some promise facilities bigger than anything the industry has built before. There's just one problem: Most of these projects may never happen. Bernstein Research analyzed thousands of planned US data centers and concluded that only about 35% of the announced capacity is likely to get built. That's roughly 170 gigawatts of data center capacity out of a total of almost 500 gigawatts. The rest? A significant chunk of it belongs to a category the industry has a wonderfully dismissive name for: "Bragawatts." These are ambitious announcements, often from newcomers with little experience building data centers, that have a slim chance of becoming reality. "Press releases are cheap…concrete is not," Bernstein analysts wrote in a research note. Bernstein began its analysis with more than 7,000 data center projects across North America, drawing on information from Aterio, a company that tracks construction through satellite imagery, permits, and other records. The analysts narrowed that to more than 5,000 projects (partly by excluding those already canceled). Then they assessed the chances of these remaining projects being completed. The analysts considered factors such as whether construction had started, whether electricity was available, and whether the companies involved had successfully built data centers before. The results revealed a striking divide. The 'bragawatt brigade' Experienced operators including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta landed at the top. Bernstein gave these companies perfect scores of 5 out of 5 for their development credentials. Other data center specialists, such as Digital Realty, Equinix, and CoreSite, got top marks, too. O'Leary Digital, associated with celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary, ended up at the bottom, with a credibility score of 0.35 out of 5, according to Bernstein. His company has announced 15 gigawatts of data center projects, and Bernstein estimates that only 489 megawatts, or about 3%, will actually materialize. "Sorry, Kevin," the analysts wrote. Although the term "bragawatts" has been doing the rounds in the data center industry lately, it's unclear who coined it, Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei told me. "I wish I could take credit for that," she said. "I believe I originally heard it from an Equinix executive, but I don't think he owned it either." She said that while some ambitious newcomers could succeed, they haven't yet demonstrated they can deliver. "It's not that all of these guys are sort of terrible and not going to deliver, but we just have lower confidence because we don't know them," Rezaei said. O'Leary Digital responds O'Leary Digital disputed Bernstein's assessment, saying the research doesn't account for substantial work that occurs before construction begins. While acknowledging that O'Leary Digital is a young company, CEO Paul Palandjian said the team has decades of experience building major infrastructure projects and that its proposed 15 gigawatts of capacity would be built in stages over several years. The company said it has secured binding agreements covering about 11,000 acres in Utah and 13,000 acres in Alberta, obtained a 30-year development agreement in Utah, and made progress on planning, engineering, and permits at both sites. It also said the projects would generate their own electricity. The company said its early development work is funded, additional capital is committed to reaching key milestones, and experienced engineering and construction partners are involved. "We would rather be judged on milestones than on a model," Palandjian said. 'An announcement in search of a project' Other low scorers in the "bragawatt" brigade included Vermaland and Joule Capital Partners, according to Bernstein analysis based on Aterio data. Joule has announced 50 data center projects with a combined capacity of 11.7 gigawatts. Bernstein estimates that only about 11% of that capacity will actually get built. Almost all of Joule's planned capacity remains at the announcement stage, with little evidence of construction progress or of major customers committing to use the facilities, Bernstein wrote in a July note to investors. The analysts gave Joule a credibility score of 2.05 out of 5, placing it among the lowest-ranked developers in its database. "An announcement in search of a project," the analysts wrote. Vermaland has announced plans for a massive data center project in Arizona. Bernstein estimates that only 4% of its proposed 2.2 gigawatts of capacity will get built. The company is primarily a landowner, not a data center developer. Its proposed $33 billion La Osa project near Eloy had already been sharply scaled back amid local opposition and without construction approval. In late August, regulators formally rejected the project. Even before that, the analysts gave Vermaland a credibility score of 0.75 out of 5. Joule and Vermaland didn't respond to emails seeking comment this week. A yawning gap for data centers Sergio Toro, CEO of Aterio, sees similar patterns in his firm's voluminous, detailed data. Aterio's tracking shows that roughly 30 to 40 gigawatts of new data center capacity get announced each month. Yet only about 7 gigawatts begin construction each month, while 2 to 3 gigawatts actually start operating. This leaves a yawning gap. Many announced projects get withdrawn before construction begins — and before real money has been spent. "They just make the announcement, but they didn't get their approvals. Or they make multiple filings in multiple locations to see which one gets selected," Toro told me. "That's why we track with satellite if there's real movement on the ground or not." Indeed, Bernstein analysts wrote recently that the amount of "stranded" data center capacity has surged. These are projects that are either canceled, delayed, or not approved. artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, the copper foil business investment company of SKC for secondary batteries, said on the 20th that it has succeeded in developing "high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil," cited as a key material for next-generation batteries. The technology SK Nexilis developed this time is characterized by coating special carbon on the surface of copper foil to increase adhesion with the anode material. It suppresses "delamination," which can occur due to the volume expansion of silicon anode materials, enhances the structural stability of electrodes, and can help improve battery life and safety. This technology was developed in response to the recent trend in the battery industry of increasing the silicon content in anode materials to boost energy density. In particular, it focused on strengthening the adhesion between the anode material and copper foil, which becomes more important as silicon content rises. The copper foil developed in this way can also be applied to the dry-electrode process, known as a next-generation battery manufacturing process. The dry process is drawing attention as a manufacturing method that can reduce battery manufacturing expense and energy use. Because the dry process also requires stably securing adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil, the technology developed by SK Nexilis is expected to have high applicability. For mass production, SK Nexilis will build a pilot production system for high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil. It is currently verifying process stability and plans to secure technology for mass production and pursue commercialization in the second half of 2027. An SK Nexilis official said, "This development of high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil is a result to respond to technological changes in the next-generation battery market, such as expanding high-content silicon anode materials and introducing the dry-electrode process," adding, "We will proceed with optimization for commercialization without a hitch and strengthen our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technology development."

artigo.texto: Data center anxiety plays out in Senate campaign debates Democrats seek to capitalize on public sentiment over local impacts In debates and advertisements ahead of the midterm elections, Democratic candidates for Senate are consistently pressing their opponents on artificial intelligence data center policy, often as a proxy for voter fears about the economy and local impacts. In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is fond of calling Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers.” Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., tied the vote by opponent Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., for the Republican “One Big Beautiful Bill” health and tax cuts measure last year to data centers. And James Talarico is accusing his opponent in the race for the Senate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, of “selling off Texas” to data center firms. In addition to attacking each other’s policy positions on tech, candidates of both parties are attacking each other’s campaign donations from Big Tech groups and investments in data center companies. Both pro-AI and regulation-focused groups are spending millions on Republican and Democratic candidates. As Democrats have sought to put Republicans on the back foot by tying data centers to rising energy costs and the larger issue of affordability, polling data appears to support the choice. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in July and August found that 50 percent of U.S. adults think data centers are “mostly bad” for home energy costs, compared with 38 percent in January. Those polled have also gotten more pessimistic about data centers’ effects on the environment, jobs, tax revenue and quality of life for those living nearby. Dan Cassino, a professor of government and politics at Fairleigh Dickinson University, said because voters believe data centers are the cause of their higher electricity bills, the construction projects are part of affordability concerns. “President [Donald] Trump campaigned for office in 2024 saying he was going to make things more affordable, was going to break down inflation, and he hasn’t delivered on that,” Cassino said. “And that means it’s a real point of vulnerability for Republicans.” As a result, Cassino said, Democrats are “hitting Republicans really hard” on the need to regulate data centers. Pocketbook issues In a Georgia Senate debate earlier this month, Ossoff used last year’s budget reconciliation bill, which included tax breaks that Ossoff said are being used by data center companies, to criticize Collins. “Just think about this, when you are paying more for your health insurance, when a hospital in your community is closing down,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers.” Collins, in turn, said he favored “local control” over data center decisions. Data center attacks may work differently, however, against sitting members of Congress. Cassino posited that candidates like Collins who have already been on Capitol Hill may have an easier time on this issue than their counterparts coming from state and local government. “They might have been doing something indirectly, but they weren’t on zoning boards,” he said. Talarico’s race with Paxton highlights the local nature of the data center backlash, with ads tying data centers both to the cost of living and to accusations of corruption against Paxton. “The data centers bankrolled Paxton, they get tax breaks and you get stuck with the bill,” Talarico said in one ad. In another, he promised that if elected he would “take on the data centers raising our costs.” Husted, as well, is being challenged for actions during his time in state government. He served as lieutenant governor before his appointment to the Senate early last year when fellow Republican JD Vance became vice president. In an ad, Brown pointed to tax breaks his state agreed to for tech companies building data centers. Husted “gave away two and a half billion dollars to these out-of-state corporations and billionaires,” Brown said in the advertisement. “He gave up Ohio’s money, our tax money, to Meta, a company worth $2 trillion, to make sure they come to Ohio.” Other Brown ads connect data centers to rising residential electricity costs. He also pledged to “require the data centers pay the full cost of their electricity, not you.” While Husted’s own ads don’t seem to mention data centers, his work in the Senate has. He sponsored the Senate version of a bill, dubbed the “Ratepayer Protection Act,” that would encourage states to adopt standards to make data centers take on the cost of electrical grid upgrades needed to meet their new energy demand. The House-passed version stalled on a procedural vote last month on the Senate floor after Democrats said it wasn’t strong enough. In a debate last week between Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, Collins responded to Jackson’s data center attacks by pointing to her support for the Husted bill. She also said that “guardrails” on energy use are particularly important because of Maine’s high energy prices, which she blamed on Jackson, who previously served as state Senate president. Jackson agreed on the need for “real guardrails” to ensure that data centers don’t cause higher electricity costs for other consumers or hurt local water quality. Democrats’ data center arguments, while not the central issue of most campaigns, seem to be part of a successful strategy. Inside Elections rates Georgia as Lean Democrat, while Maine, Ohio and Texas, all seats currently held by Republicans, are rated as Toss-up. Effectiveness As sitting senators talk about the Ratepayer Protection Act bill, Cassino cautioned that voters may not care about Capitol Hill procedural votes. “Anything incumbents say about, ‘oh, this is what I’m doing to protect you,’ is going to ring hollow because everyone sees their electricity prices going up,” Cassino said. artigo.texto: American Battery Technology is pursuing a U.S.-based battery-materials supply chain centered on lithium-ion battery recycling and its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, targeting lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese production. The company's Reno recycling facility can process 20,000 metric tons annually, while a proposed southeastern facility would expand capacity to 100,000 tons with a $150 million Department of Energy grant and an estimated $375 million total cost. Tonopah Flats is projected to have a 45-year mine life, $2.6 billion net present value and 21.8% after-tax internal rate of return. American Battery Technology reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $21.7 million, held $49.5 million in cash and had no debt. 3 Stocks to Benefit From China's Rare Earth Export Ban on U.S. American Battery Technology (NASDAQ:ABAT) is advancing a U.S.-based battery-materials strategy built around lithium-ion battery recycling and the development of its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project in Nevada, Chief Financial Officer Alex Flores said during a company presentation. Flores said the company is seeking to build a domestic, lower-cost and environmentally responsible supply chain for battery metals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese. He cited supply-security concerns, logistics costs and environmental risks associated with overseas sourcing as major challenges for the U.S. battery industry. "Our approach is to first close the loop and then fill the loop," Flores said, referring to the company's recycling operations and its planned lithium mining and refining operations. Recycling Operations and Expansion Plans American Battery Technology operates a 138,000-square-foot lithium-ion battery recycling facility outside Reno, Nevada, with annual intake capacity of 20,000 metric tons. Operations at the site began in October 2023, according to Flores. The company's recycling process first dismantles battery packs into modules, cells and sub-cell components. It separates materials including copper, aluminum and steel, while producing a lithium-bearing intermediate known as black mass. In a subsequent refining phase, the company said the material can be processed into battery-grade nickel sulfate, manganese sulfate, cobalt sulfate and lithium hydroxide. Flores said the company currently sees stronger economics in selling black mass than in further refining it into lithium products. He said a federal directive issued on Aug. 27 banned black-mass exports, but American Battery Technology received a license allowing it to export up to $100 million of the material. The company is not selling black mass to China, Flores said, adding that its customers are primarily in South Korea and other OECD countries. American Battery Technology also plans to build a second recycling facility in the southeastern U.S. The proposed site would have annual intake capacity of 100,000 metric tons, representing a five-fold increase from the Reno facility's capacity. Flores said the project has received a Department of Energy grant equivalent to $150 million and is expected to require total capital expenditures of $375 million. The funding is a grant rather than a loan and carries performance milestones, he said. Tonopah Lithium Project On the mining side, the company is developing its Tonopah Flats Lithium Project near Tonopah, Nevada. Flores said the project encompasses 631 unpatented lode mining claims covering more than 13,000 acres and is based on a claystone lithium resource rather than conventional ore. According to Flores, the project contains 21.3 million tons of accessible lithium hydroxide monohydrate and has a projected 45-year mine life. The company expects the operation to employ more than 200 full-time workers and reach a peak mining rate near 30,000 tons per day. Flores cited the company's pre-feasibility study, published about a year ago, which estimated an after-tax internal rate of return of 21.8%, net present value of $2.6 billion and production costs of slightly more than $4,300 per metric ton of lithium hydroxide monohydrate. Planned infrastructure includes a surface mine, commercial refinery and a behind-the-meter solar field with battery energy storage. The project has received a $900 million letter of interest from the Export-Import Bank, Flores said. It has also been designated a priority project under the FAST-41 permitting framework. The company has initiated a definitive feasibility study, completed required National Environmental Policy Act baseline studies and submitted results to the Bureau of Land Management. Flores said the Bureau of Land Management approved the company's mining and refining plan of operations, which American Battery Technology had been developing since November 2022. The company was awaiting a notice of intent from the agency before moving into the environmental impact statement process. Under its expectations for the FAST-41 process, Flores said the company could break ground by the middle of the following year. Financial Results and Domestic Supply Focus Flores said American Battery Technology reported record fiscal 2026 revenue of $21.7 million, up 407% year over year. Cost of goods sold increased 67%, which he attributed to operational efficiencies at the Nevada recycling facility. The company reported cash-basis gross profit of $1.7 million, a non-GAAP figure excluding non-cash items such as depreciation and stock compensation. The company ended the fiscal year with $49.5 million in cash and no debt, Flores said. He also said American Battery Technology has operated a multi-ton-per-year integrated pilot facility that produced battery-grade lithium from Nevada claystone. The company is now pursuing strategic partners and long-term commercial offtake agreements as it seeks to expand its role in the North American battery-materials supply chain. artigo.texto: À medida que empresas de inteligência artificial (IA) com infraestrutura de hiperescala e incorporadoras aceleram a construção de data centers, elas estão deixando de depender da rede elétrica e passando a construir, cada vez mais, sistemas privados de energia atrás do medidor (behind-the-meter, ou BTM, na sigla em inglês), que operam de forma independente das conexões com a rede pública. Isso ocorre porque as filas de espera para conexão à rede se transformaram em um gargalo estrutural. Desde 2017, o prazo entre a entrada na fila e o início da operação comercial aumentou aproximadamente 60%. Atualmente, esse período supera, em média, 2.100 dias para projetos que tinham como meta começar a receber energia em 2025. Esse é um dos fatores que fazem da geração de energia no próprio local uma solução que deixou de ser apenas temporária e vem se consolidando como uma alternativa amplamente adotada. A Bloom Energy estima que, até 2030, 38% das instalações de data centers utilizarão algum tipo de geração própria como fonte primária de energia. O percentual representa um aumento de 13% em relação ao ano anterior. A mesma fonte prevê que, dentro de quatro anos, aproximadamente 27% dessas instalações serão abastecidas integralmente por energia gerada no próprio local. No entanto, ao contornar as filas de espera de vários anos para garantir acesso à rede elétrica e resolver um problema, essas empresas se depararam com outras dificuldades que não haviam previsto. Um exemplo é o fato de que as cadeias de suprimentos de equipamentos não acompanharam o ritmo de expansão dos data centers. Os prazos de entrega de transformadores e turbinas a gás estão muito acima das estimativas iniciais, que variavam de 24 a 48 meses. Na prática, a Wood Mackenzie, empresa de pesquisa, análise e consultoria sediada em Edimburgo, na Escócia, informou que os prazos de entrega de turbinas a gás atualmente chegam a seis anos. Isso levou a consultoria a observar que o atraso “mudou fundamentalmente o mercado, que deixou de tomar decisões orientadas pela economia dos combustíveis e passou a priorizar estratégias de aquisição e a viabilidade dos produtos”. Cronogramas diferentes Há também outros problemas. A complexidade dessas instalações não tem precedentes, já que muitos projetos combinam diferentes tipos de tecnologia em uma única microrrede integrada. Ao mesmo tempo, as empresas responsáveis pela operação e manutenção precisam estruturar e operar as instalações conforme os equipamentos chegam, seguindo cronogramas escalonados. A disponibilidade inédita de equipamentos e a complexidade operacional resultante impuseram uma pressão inesperada sobre os responsáveis pela operação das usinas de energia. “Os incorporadores não estão mais esperando pela rede elétrica; eles não podem se dar a esse luxo”, afirma Doug Machon, vice-presidente de desenvolvimento de negócios da Kyuden Energy Partners, empresa de operação e manutenção de usinas de energia sediada em Aliso Viejo, na Califórnia. “A fila de espera para conexão à rede é um gargalo significativo, mas não é o único. O problema se ampliou e passou a abranger a cadeia de suprimentos da infraestrutura energética, desde turbinas e transformadores até sistemas de controle e equipamentos auxiliares das usinas. Como resultado, somos cada vez mais solicitados a estruturar uma capacidade operacional antes mesmo de todos os ativos físicos previstos para a instalação definitiva terem sido entregues e a colocar em operação sistemas integrados compostos por diferentes tecnologias, cujos equipamentos chegam em cronogramas distintos. Trata-se de um trabalho fundamentalmente diferente da operação de uma usina convencional.” A Kyuden Energy Partners, assim como empresas como Consolidated Asset Management Services (CAMS) e Ethos Energy, está entre os diversos fornecedores de serviços de operação e manutenção que ajudam os participantes do setor a superar esse desafio. Desafios de execução Embora cada projeto atendido por esses fornecedores tenha características próprias, determinadas complexidades se repetem. Entre elas estão a integração de diferentes tecnologias de geração em uma microrrede; o uso de fontes temporárias ou provisórias de energia até que a infraestrutura permanente esteja disponível; a contratação, integração e capacitação de grandes equipes técnicas e de manutenção para garantir operações presenciais ininterruptas; e a coordenação do comissionamento e da entrada em operação de diferentes fases do projeto, que ocorrem de forma escalonada. Em comparação com projetos tradicionais de geração de energia em grande escala, a Kyuden constatou que cada um desses obstáculos representa um desafio de execução. A CAMS, fornecedora de serviços de operação e manutenção (O&M) e gestão de ativos sediada em Houston, nos Estados Unidos, tem experiência em projetos que somam 70 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade de geração. A empresa oferece um programa que combina processos simplificados de licenciamento e gestão comercial com serviços diários de operação e manutenção. Sua resposta à demanda energética decorrente das cargas de trabalho de IA e da computação em nuvem está inicialmente concentrada na geração a gás natural e em fontes renováveis. Com experiência na gestão de mais de 100 instalações e de mais de 40 GW de capacidade de geração de energia em todo o mundo, a Ethos Energy desenvolveu seu Centro de Desempenho 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana (24-7 Performance Center), para oferecer um modelo de operação remota voltado aos desafios dos sistemas BTM. Com o uso de monitoramento assistido por inteligência artificial, uma única equipe monitora, opera e gerencia remotamente várias usinas ao mesmo tempo. artigo.texto: Microsoft abandona projeto de centro de dados no Reino Unido A Microsoft desistiu de um centro de dados no Reino Unido que estava a ser construído pela Nscale, depois de atrasos no acesso à eletricidade terem impedido a entrada em funcionamento das instalações. Neste artigo encontras: A decisão representa um revés para a Nscale e surge numa altura delicada para a empresa, que prepara uma oferta pública de ações este mês. A saída da Microsoft poderá aumentar as preocupações dos investidores sobre a capacidade da empresa para executar os seus projetos. Microsoft deixa projeto da Nscale devido a atrasos Segundo um porta-voz da Nscale, a Microsoft abandonou o plano para utilizar o centro de dados. O principal obstáculo terá sido a dificuldade em garantir a ligação à rede elétrica necessária para colocar o local a funcionar. O acesso à energia tornou-se um dos maiores desafios para os operadores de centros de dados. A expansão dos serviços de computação na nuvem e da inteligência artificial está a aumentar rapidamente a procura de eletricidade e de novas infraestruturas. Porque este projeto era importante Os centros de dados são fundamentais para alojar serviços cloud, aplicações empresariais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Sem energia suficiente, mesmo uma instalação concluída pode ficar impossibilitada de operar à capacidade prevista. Para a Nscale, perder um cliente de grande dimensão como a Microsoft pode afetar a perceção sobre o projeto e levantar dúvidas quanto aos prazos de outros empreendimentos. Não foram divulgados detalhes sobre o valor do contrato nem sobre os próximos passos para o local. Possível impacto na oferta pública da Nscale A notícia surge pouco antes da oferta pública planeada pela Nscale. Embora o impacto final dependa das condições do mercado e dos restantes ativos da empresa, os atrasos e a saída da Microsoft poderão pesar na avaliação atribuída pelos investidores. O caso também mostra como a falta de capacidade energética pode travar a expansão da indústria tecnológica. A procura por centros de dados continua a crescer, mas os projetos enfrentam cada vez mais limitações relacionadas com licenças, redes elétricas e disponibilidade de energia. O que acontece agora Ainda não foram reveladas novas datas para a entrada em funcionamento do centro de dados nem foi indicado se a Nscale procura outro cliente para as instalações. A Microsoft, através da Azure, que também enfrenta pressão para cortar custos, não apresentou até ao momento detalhes públicos adicionais sobre a decisão. - A Microsoft deixou o projeto de centro de dados da Nscale no Reino Unido. - Os atrasos no acesso à eletricidade terão estado na origem da decisão. - A saída poderá afetar a oferta pública planeada pela Nscale. - O episódio reforça os desafios energéticos associados à expansão da inteligência artificial. Fonte: theinformation.com

artigo.texto: - The initial models are under development, with launches planned for next year. - The first model will reportedly come from Dongfeng and Huawei's Epicland brand, expanding vehicle coverage for the Choco swap network. Huawei's automotive technology company Yinwang, or Newcool, and CATL (HKEX: 3750) have tentatively set an initial lineup of 5 battery swap models for launch in 2027, according to a media report. Newcool, CATL and the battery maker's battery swap operator are developing the vehicles, LatePost reported on Tuesday, offering further details on the initial scope of their partnership. Newcool reiterated the core provisions of the 3 parties' strategic cooperation agreement to the outlet but declined to comment on the model count or launch plans. Those details have yet to be officially confirmed. Cailian reported earlier today that the first model would come from Epicland, a brand jointly developed by Dongfeng and Huawei, with a launch planned for 2027. The specific model has not been disclosed. The 2 reports add details on the product lineup and timeline to the newly announced battery swap partnership. The strategic cooperation framework agreement announced on October 19 did not identify specific models or launch dates. Under the agreement, Newcool is joining CATL's Choco swap ecosystem to help adapt partner models using Huawei's Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions for compatibility with the battery swap network. The partnership also includes Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES), CATL's battery swap operator. The 3 parties plan to integrate data and services across vehicles, battery swap stations and cloud systems, using real-time battery conditions and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively arrange battery swaps. Under the plan outlined in the earlier statement, vehicles would autonomously locate and enter stations, position themselves for a fully automated 99-second battery swap, and then drive away. Additional partner models would help CATL expand the user base for its battery swap network. The business can generate recurring revenue from battery rentals and energy replenishment services, but requires sufficient vehicle volume to support investment in stations, battery inventories and operations. CATL had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, according to information it previously released. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. The company also plans to build 1,000 highway battery swap stations between 2026 and 2027, extending the network beyond cities to support long-distance travel. Newcool took over Huawei's former intelligent automotive solution business and supplies automakers with systems for smart driving, smart cockpits and vehicle control.

artigo.texto: The University of Illinois Springfield is hosting a presentation on Wednesday, Oct. 21, focused on the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence and data center development. The talk is free and open to the public. Mary Willis, assistant professor of epidemiology at the Boston University School of Public Health, “will investigate the local effects of data centers built in the United States and propose policy solutions to help mitigate environmental impacts and protect local communities,” according to a promotional annoucement. The event, at 6 p.m. in Brookens Auditorium, is a part the UIS Engaged Citizen Common Experience speaker series. Earlier this year, Willis, who previously studied fracking, told Illinois Times research on animals could reveal more information about the effects of hyperscale data centers on surrounding residents, animals and land. “The first study that really linked tracking to adverse health outcomes was on horse or cattle,” she said. “That’s how we kind of figured out that there was even something going on here, and so I would be 0% surprised if local animal studies are what help us actually figure out the effects of data centers faster than we will in humans.” The most immediate concern regarding the CyrusOne data center project planned for rural Sangamon County, according to Willis, is likely going to be the 420 backup emergency generators. While they will only need to run for 15 hours per year for maintenance, they would run for longer if the data center needed emergency power. “This fine, particulate matter can very quickly become a regional problem,” Willis said, though she noted it’s more of a concern for those near the site. “If you live near a coal-fired power plant, that’s probably a far more important source to consider than the data center if that’s not right near you – but this is likely contributing overall to regional air pollution.” Almost half of all Americans are living in areas with heavily polluted air, according to the American Lung Association. Sangamon County and the surrounding counties, according to the American Lung Association, rank middle of the road in particle pollution when compared to more than 200 more metropolitan areas. Polluted air is “associated with increased risks of mortality, asthma and preterm birth,” Willis said. She said she was surprised that CyrusOne plans to install that number of diesel-powered backup generators, a sentiment echoed by another researcher. In March, Max Zhang, a professor at Cornell University who researches air pollutants produced by diesel-powered generators, told Illinois Times that was the largest number of backup generators he’d ever heard of for a data center. Rising land temperatures Researchers at The University of Cambridge published a study in March that used remote sensors to observe temperature increases around active data centers. Data centers located in non-urban environments resulted in “heat islands,” where surface temperatures can rise as far as six miles away. Illinois Times asked CyrusOne about the study’s conclusions in July and whether the company had previously sampled land surface temperature around its data centers. “At CyrusOne, our facilities are designed, developed, and operated in accordance with applicable health, safety, environmental, and land-use requirements, while following established industry practices for site design, cooling, energy efficiency, and environmental performance,” wrote Blair Felter, vice president of communications. “We do not have surface-temperature data to share.” It’s unclear how nearby farmland might be impacted by the CyrusOne data center and the heat it gives off from running continuously; farmland is assessed by soil quality, which then affects the sale price and, ultimately, the tax assessment. Byron Deaner, the county’s chief assessment officer, told IT in July even if that study bears out in Illinois, farmland values wouldn’t change much until parcels of land are actually sold and the market potentially adjusts. “You really wouldn’t see any impact to those values until you started to see some farmland with those different productivity indexes sell at different rates,” he said. “Maybe that would force the Illinois Department of Revenue to revisit the values associated with those soils, if they could contribute the environmental impact of the heat to those particular soil types within the particular distance.”

artigo.texto: Brasil e China buscam ampliar a cooperação na construção de mercados de carbono, com foco no intercâmbio de experiências, na medição das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e no desenvolvimento de mecanismos capazes de contribuir para a transição econômica de baixo carbono. A possibilidade de aprofundar essa parceria foi destacada por Cristina Reis, secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, após sua participação na Conferência de Mercado de Carbono da China 2026, realizada em setembro, na cidade de Wuhan. O evento reuniu representantes de 27 países, regiões e organizações internacionais para compartilhar experiências sobre a criação e o funcionamento de mercados de carbono e discutir caminhos para a cooperação climática. Segundo Reis, a experiência chinesa oferece referências relevantes para o Brasil, especialmente na implementação gradual de mecanismos de precificação de emissões e na estruturação de sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação de gases de efeito estufa. A aproximação ocorre enquanto os dois países desenvolvem seus próprios instrumentos de política climática e participam de uma iniciativa internacional voltada à convergência entre mercados regulados de carbono. A cooperação pode contribuir para aprimorar metodologias, aumentar a transparência na contabilização das emissões e criar condições para uma maior compatibilidade entre os sistemas nacionais. Experiência chinesa pode orientar a estruturação do mercado brasileiro A China lançou seu mercado nacional regulado de comércio de emissões em julho de 2021. Desde então, o sistema passou por uma expansão gradual, com o objetivo de utilizar mecanismos econômicos para estimular a redução de gases de efeito estufa. Até o fim de agosto de 2026, o mercado regulado chinês havia acumulado negociações equivalentes a 961 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente, com movimentação financeira de 65,7 bilhões de yuans, aproximadamente US$ 9,71 bilhões, segundo os dados divulgados pela Xinhua. O país também desenvolve um mercado voluntário de redução de emissões. Até o mesmo período, 41 projetos haviam sido registrados nesse sistema, com volume acumulado de negociações de 21,71 milhões de toneladas e valor total de 1,74 bilhão de yuans. Os mercados regulados e voluntários têm características diferentes. No primeiro caso, o governo estabelece regras e obrigações para os participantes abrangidos pelo sistema. No segundo, projetos podem gerar créditos de carbono segundo metodologias específicas, que são adquiridos voluntariamente por organizações interessadas em compensar emissões ou apoiar iniciativas de redução e remoção de gases de efeito estufa. A secretária brasileira destacou a experiência da China na implantação progressiva desses mecanismos, começando por projetos-piloto, avançando para o mercado regulado e, posteriormente, fortalecendo o mercado voluntário. A troca de experiências, entretanto, não significa que o Brasil precise reproduzir o modelo chinês. As características econômicas, a estrutura produtiva e as prioridades ambientais de cada país exigem soluções próprias. O objetivo da cooperação é identificar práticas e metodologias que possam contribuir para o desenvolvimento dos respectivos sistemas, respeitando suas particularidades. Brasil implementa seu sistema regulado de carbono No Brasil, a estruturação do mercado regulado ganhou base legal com a Lei nº 15.042, sancionada em dezembro de 2024, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE). O sistema prevê a criação de regras para monitorar emissões, estabelecer obrigações para os agentes regulados e organizar a negociação de ativos relacionados às emissões e às reduções verificadas de gases de efeito estufa. Sua implementação está prevista em etapas. O processo envolve a regulamentação da lei, a preparação dos instrumentos de monitoramento e a definição de mecanismos para alocação e negociação de ativos de carbono. Em julho de 2026, o Ministério da Fazenda abriu uma consulta pública sobre uma proposta de cronograma para a implementação das obrigações de monitoramento, relato e verificação. A medida integra a preparação da infraestrutura necessária ao funcionamento do sistema. Esse processo torna a cooperação internacional particularmente relevante. A elaboração de metodologias confiáveis para contabilizar emissões é um dos requisitos para que os mercados funcionem com transparência e para que os resultados ambientais possam ser comparados de maneira consistente. Segundo Cristina Reis, Brasil e China podem aprofundar a colaboração justamente nessa área, compartilhando experiências sobre os sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação, conhecidos pela sigla MRV. Esses procedimentos permitem determinar a quantidade de gases emitidos por atividades econômicas, registrar as informações e verificar se os dados apresentados seguem critérios técnicos definidos. A confiabilidade dessas informações é fundamental para evitar a contabilização incorreta de emissões e preservar a credibilidade dos créditos de carbono. Coalizão internacional reúne Brasil, China e União Europeia A aproximação bilateral também está ligada à Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono, iniciativa lançada durante a COP30, realizada em Belém, em novembro de 2025, sob liderança brasileira. O mecanismo busca promover o diálogo entre países que adotam sistemas de precificação de carbono, com o objetivo de aproximar metodologias de contabilização, regras para créditos e procedimentos de verificação das emissões. Brasil, China e União Europeia ocupam posições de liderança na iniciativa. O Brasil exerce a presidência até 2027, enquanto China e União Europeia atuam como copresidentes. Em setembro de 2026, durante uma reunião de alto nível realizada em Wuhan, os participantes aprovaram um plano de trabalho até 2030 e definiram uma estrutura provisória para o secretariado da coalizão. artigo.texto: Data centers are the latest trail sign on a path of madness I keep cracking up at these so-called leaders and tech executives that keep trying to sell the rest of us on data centers and AI. They just do not get it at all. There are two primary factors that they, and business leaders all throughout recent history have failed to course correct on. First on the data centers, I can default to the famous line, “It is the economy, stupid.” More specifically the wealth and resource gap that has become such a drain on our economic growth and prosperity. We are getting close to ancient Roman secession of the plebs territory with how bad things have gotten. Over the last 50 or so years we have regressed from needing a reasonably well-paying fulltime job to achieve financial stability to a decade or so ago needing the same fulltime job plus a side hustle to achieve the same results. Now, not only do you need your fulltime job and side hustle but also must learn the ins and outs of day trading in order to achieve basic financial stability in modern times. All because we have this backwards idea that investors who simply throw money at a company should be treated anywhere near as well as the workers who are actually making that company run. And data centers are just the latest trail sign on that path of madness. As for AI, it is the extreme lack of guardrails businesses and governments have put on technology in the last few decades. My favorite comparison I have come up with is this: The harnessing and weaponization of atomic energy has killed less people than the creation and evolution of the cellphone. One is far deadlier than the other on paper, but there are few guardrails for cellphone use. Anthony Smith, Loveland Lest we forget, the UN remains our best hope Oct. 24 is United Nation Day, the date in 1945 when 51 nations, hoping for world peace and international cooperation after six years of war, founded our international organization. Alas, after 81 years and now with 193 members, those hopes almost seem irrelevant. The Security Council is crippled by the big powers veto threat, the General Assembly continues as a sounding board for the world’s conflicts, the World Court’s decisions can be ignored, but the specialized agencies, amid tensions, keep on with their vital work regarding health, agriculture, weather, labor, air and maritime traffic, education, finance, postal matters and other areas which encourage a functioning world. In spite of its weaknesses in 2026, the United Nations remains our best hope. Lest we forget. Richard Rush, Loveland

artigo.texto: Can larger batteries safely power residential buildings? A project in New York aims to show how A battery system that stores excess energy when it’s plentiful will power an apartment building in Buffalo, New York, when the grid is strained and electricity is costly A battery system that stores excess energy when it’s plentiful will power an apartment building in Buffalo, New York, when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. Buffalo-based battery storage manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. say the lithium-ion battery system is connected to the electric grid for Peace Bridge Place. Viridi says the 3.75 megawatt-hour system can power the building for several days. It's among the largest of these systems in a U.S. residential building. A battery system installed in a Buffalo, New York, apartment building will store excess energy when it’s plentiful and power the building when the grid is strained and electricity is costly. The manufacturer and state officials hope it will show that larger batteries can safely operate where people live and work. The 3.75 megawatt-hour lithium-ion battery system, which can power the Peace Bridge Place affordable housing complex for several days, is among the largest battery systems in a U.S. residential building, manufacturer Viridi and developer Good Carbon Co. said Tuesday. “We want our electric power to be resilient, affordable and available. Distributed battery storage accomplishes all three,” Viridi CEO Jon M. Williams said. “The only thing that has been holding up installations at scale is safety; a lot of the products on the market over the last 10 years have burned things down.” Deploying large batteries that can safely power apartment buildings is an important step toward replacing fossil fuels with renewables, experts say, but they’re uncommon because of the cost and concerns about fire risks. Already, larger batteries are paired with solar and wind projects, and homeowners are using smaller batteries to store excess energy from rooftop solar and for backup power. How batteries help keep electricity flow steady Batteries help maintain a steady flow of power when sources such as solar and wind are not producing. They charge when the sun is shining or when wind is blowing. That energy can then be used when demand is high. Batteries can also store excess electricity from hydropower, and New York is one of the top hydropower-producing states. Buffalo is close to Niagara Falls, where most of the state’s hydropower is produced. When electricity demand is high, Peace Bridge will use the battery. It will get paid by the utility for not drawing from the grid and for sending power back if needed. This helps lower the complex’s overall electricity costs, which benefits residents. The building can use the system during outages, too. The New York State Energy Research and Development Agency helped fund the Peace Bridge Place project, as part of its focus on including disadvantaged communities in the clean energy transition. “It goes a long way toward demonstrating the safety and viability of these types of projects,” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen Harris. Viridi has manufacturing facilities in Buffalo and Richmond, California, where a state grant assisted with renovations. California Energy Commission Chair David Hochschild said he’s impressed with the company. More than two-thirds of California’s electricity comes from clean energy and batteries get a lot of credit for that, Hochschild said. As electricity demand grows, batteries help ensure the grid is reliable, reduce pollution and contain costs, he added. “I believe the battery industry is the single most important energy industry for the next several decades,” said Hochschild, who co-founded the Electric Innovation Initiative to use electricity instead of fossil fuels more broadly throughout the U.S. economy. Viridi’s system passed a ‘near impossible’ test As large battery fires have garnered attention, some communities have opposed further development. However, the failure rate for batteries has decreased as more are installed, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Viridi spent six years and $10 million figuring out how to make a fireproof container for batteries. Half the cost was for batteries Viridi destroyed during testing. Viridi uses plates, pouches and spacing to isolate each battery cell. If one fails, the energy dissipates instead of spreading to the next battery, so that no gas, smoke, heat or fire escapes the container, Williams said. Jigar Shah, an expert in clean energy financing and deployment, said the Peace Bridge Place system is a milestone in overcoming safety concerns. To ensure nothing would catch fire when used inside a residence, Viridi’s system had to pass a test where the battery was forced to fail while a cheesecloth covered the container. The cheesecloth did not char or ignite, according to the test report record. Viridi announced in April it met stringent Underwriters Laboratories safety standards so its system could be installed indoors without adding additional fire suppression to a building. Shah, who led the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office during the Biden administration, said Viridi is the only company to consistently pass this “near impossible” test. Shah thinks far more U.S. homes will use batteries for backup power by 2030. The U.S. can meet much more electricity demand and avoid costly upgrades to the grid if batteries are strategically deployed, he added. New York and California officials want forward-thinking energy solutions Viridi and Good Carbon Co. chose the Peace Bridge apartments because the all-electric building uses a geothermal system for heating and cooling rather than natural gas and needed additional, resilient power. artigo.texto: China's CATL third-quarter profit growth slowest in nearly two years as competition intensifies Synopsis CATL reports slower third-quarter profit growth as intense competition in China’s EV battery market weighs on earnings. Net profit rises 14.5% to 21.2 billion yuan, below estimates, while revenue grows 58.6%. CATL also unveils new heavy-duty truck batteries and plans to expand its battery-swapping network. The third-quarter net profit growth, which follows a 36.5% rise in the second quarter, is the slowest in nearly two years Revenue climbed 58.6% year-on-year to 165.2 billion yuan, undershooting forecasts for a 60.2% increase, after growing 56.9% in the previous quarter. The EV battery specialist on Tuesday unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy-duty trucks and announced plans to expand its battery-swapping network CATL, which broadened supplies to overseas automakers, accounted for 39.4% of global EV battery usage in the first eight months of the year, up from 37.7% a year earlier, while second-ranked BYD's share slipped to 15.1% from 17.1%, industry data showed CATL's share of China's power battery installation market fell to 40.9% in September from 49.8% in January, while BYD increased its share to 21.1% from 17.4%, according to industry data. While China's domestic auto market extended a 12-month downturn in September, exports continued to support industry growth as manufacturers expanded abroad. CATL expects energy storage to contribute half of its global revenue by 2030, up from about a quarter currently, Reuters reported in June. (You can now subscribe to our ETMarkets WhatsApp channel)

artigo.texto: Siga o Portas no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga o Portas no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Veja o resumo da notícia - O avanço da inteligência artificial impulsiona a demanda por data centers, que se tornam uma nova frente para fundos imobiliários. - Fundos podem investir em data centers por meio de compra, sale and leaseback, built to suit, CRIs ou desenvolvimento de projetos. - Contratos longos e atípicos aumentam a previsibilidade da receita, mas não eliminam riscos de crédito e obsolescência tecnológica. - A qualidade do ativo é definida por fatores como preço de aquisição, disponibilidade de energia e flexibilidade para usos futuros. O avanço da inteligência artificial aumenta a necessidade de capacidade computacional, mas essa expansão depende de uma base imobiliária intensiva em energia, conectividade e sistemas de resfriamento. Nesse cenário, os data centers em fundos imobiliários ganham espaço como uma nova frente de investimento, ao lado de outros ativos alternativos como os FIIs de logística. A renda vem do aluguel do imóvel, não dos serviços de tecnologia. Data centers em fundos imobiliários: diferentes estruturas de entrada A exposição pode ocorrer pela compra de um data center estabilizado, por operações de sale and leaseback, por contratos built to suit, pelo financiamento de obras com certificados de recebíveis imobiliários (CRIs) ou pelo desenvolvimento de novos projetos. Os fundos também podem adquirir infraestrutura associada, como subestações elétricas. Cada estrutura combina de forma diferente risco de construção, energização, ocupação, crédito e necessidade de capital. Contratos longos aumentam a previsibilidade Como os ativos são altamente especializados e muitas vezes desenhados para um único ocupante, contratos atípicos e de longo prazo ajudam a alinhar o investimento ao período necessário para recuperar o capital. Reajustes por inflação e multas de saída podem proteger a receita. Ainda assim, um contrato extenso não elimina o risco do inquilino nem garante que o prédio continuará competitivo diante da evolução tecnológica. Energia e flexibilidade definem a qualidade do ativo O preço de aquisição, a disponibilidade de energia, a conexão à rede, a eficiência do resfriamento e a capacidade financeira do operador são variáveis centrais. A especialização que torna um data center valioso para determinado cliente também pode restringir usos alternativos e elevar gastos futuros de modernização. Por isso, o crescimento da IA favorece a demanda, mas não substitui a análise imobiliária, contratual e de crédito de cada operação. Veja também outras frentes de investimento em fundos imobiliários para 2026. *Com informações de InfoMoney

artigo.texto: Falling battery prices highlight Africa’s energy storage investment gap Battery prices are falling, but investment in energy storage across Africa is struggling to keep pace. The latest ESI Africa Industry Insights: Energy&Storage Volume 5 (2026) (https://apo-opa.co/3UANmwN) examines the gap between increasingly affordable technologies and the financing, regulation and infrastructure planning needed to support deployment. According to BloombergNEF, stationary battery pack prices fell to around US$70/kWh in 2025, a 45% year-on-year decline. Yet of the US$13.84 billion in energy transition investment Africa attracted in 2025, tracked by Electron Intelligence, just US$666 million, less than 5%, went towards storage and flexibility. For Nicolette Pombo-van Zyl, Editor-in-Chief of ESI Africa, storage has become essential to energy development. “It is now the part that decides whether a project gets financed, whether a grid stays stable after sunset and whether the clean energy already being generated is actually used. The industry's challenge is that capital, regulation and data have not yet caught up with that reality,” says Pombo-van Zyl. Understanding storage economics and infrastructure needs The publication examines battery storage economics, including South African modelling that places lithium iron phosphate ahead of competing chemistries for stationary applications. It also considers how deployment scale, degradation in hot climates, financing costs, import tariffs and freight affect project viability. Emerging battery technologies and their potential implications for Africa’s mineral value chains feature alongside cybersecurity risks and long-duration storage solutions. The volume also examines Africa’s expanding distributed solar market. According to Ember, approximately 26GW of solar was installed across Africa between 2023 and 2025, with only a quarter accounted for in utility-scale and off-grid figures. Improved registration and data could help planners understand this growth and its impact on electricity networks. Connecting investment with delivery The African Infrastructure Elites section highlights the growing role of storage in renewable energy financing, featuring developments including Scatec’s Obelisk project in Egypt and Mulilo’s Hartebeesfontein battery storage project. “Battery prices have done their part. What happens next depends on decisions that sit with regulators, utilities and financiers around how storage is valued for the services it provides, how it is protected as connected infrastructure, and how quickly projects are prepared to the point where capital can move. Those are solvable problems, and the sector already has the tools to solve them,” says Pombo-van Zyl. Published in partnership with Envusa Energy, NOA Group and Lyra Energy, the Energy&Storage Volume is available for free download to subscribers and non-subscribers. Download the volume (https://apo-opa.co/3UANmwN) These challenges will also inform discussions at VUKA Group’s C&I Energy + Storage Summit Johannesburg, taking place on 28–29 October 2026 at The Maslow Hotel, Sandton. The Summit brings together commercial and industrial energy users, developers and financiers to explore storage investment, energy procurement and cost certainty.
