artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Entrelinhas de Mercado: Energia vira gargalo para data centers e limita avanço da IA, diz Márcio Aguiar, diretor da Nvidia para a América Latina Publicado 20/10/2026 • 21:43 | Atualizado há 9 horas KEY POINTS A disponibilidade de energia se tornou um dos principais obstáculos para ampliar data centers e a capacidade de processamento de inteligência artificial, afirmou Márcio Aguiar, diretor-executivo da divisão Enterprise da Nvidia para a América Latina, em entrevista ao programa Entrelinhas de Mercado, do Times Brasil – Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC. “O grande gargalo da expansão de um data center, da expansão de um poder computacional é: tem energia suficiente para isso?”, disse Aguiar ao apresentador Júnior Gornelli. Segundo ele, as limitações do setor mudam conforme a tecnologia avança e já envolveram a oferta de GPUs e de memória. Para enfrentar a demanda crescente, a companhia busca otimizar o software e aumentar a eficiência dos servidores, reduzindo consumo de energia e espaço físico. O executivo explicou que a Nvidia também desenvolve CPUs, DPUs e tecnologias de conexão entre equipamentos, além das placas gráficas pelas quais é mais conhecida. “O foco tem sido sempre ao máximo otimizar o uso do software, no sentido da atualização do software para que ele consuma menos energia e traga mais poder de processamento ao cliente final”, afirmou. Aguiar citou a evolução da infraestrutura: a Nvidia já oferece um rack com 72 GPUs e anunciou outro que, segundo ele, deverá reunir 544 GPUs no mesmo espaço físico em cerca de dois anos. A concentração de capacidade exige soluções de refrigeração e aproxima a empresa de fornecedores especializados. Leia também: Nvidia vira termômetro da IA e sustenta aposta do mercado; entenda “A gente começa a atrair também mais próximos de nós empresas que têm especialização na parte de refrigeração”, explicou o executivo, ao descrever o crescimento do ecossistema ligado aos data centers. Na adoção de inteligência artificial, a recomendação de Aguiar é não investir automaticamente na GPU mais avançada. Ele defende que as companhias avaliem seus softwares, suas necessidades de processamento e a infraestrutura já disponível antes de definir novos investimentos. “Comecem pequeno, pensem grande, comecem pequeno”, aconselhou. Segundo ele, o primeiro passo é reunir uma equipe para conduzir a transformação e testar aplicações que possam demonstrar o retorno do investimento. O executivo afirmou que cerca de 80% do trabalho da Nvidia com seu ecossistema envolve educação e orientação. A companhia procura mostrar que a inteligência artificial não se restringe às grandes empresas e que projetos podem começar com equipamentos de gerações anteriores. Leia também: EXCLUSIVO: IA entra na era dos milhares de agentes autônomos, diz diretor da Nvidia para América Latina “Faz o teu benchmark, porque quem define a arquitetura de hardware são os softwares”, destacou Aguiar. Ele acrescentou que GPUs adquiridas há cinco ou seis anos continuam sendo oferecidas por empresas que comercializam capacidade de processamento na nuvem. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC Sobre robôs humanoides e veículos autônomos, Aguiar afirmou que a Nvidia pretende fornecer a capacidade computacional dessas máquinas, em vez de se tornar uma fabricante de robôs próprios. Para ele, a expansão da inteligência artificial ainda está em estágio inicial. “A gente vai ser sempre o cérebro de tudo isso”, disse o diretor, ao explicar o papel da empresa no desenvolvimento da chamada IA física. Leia também: Nvidia quer ensinar robôs a entender o mundo real; veja como Aguiar mencionou aplicações que vão além da robótica, como previsões meteorológicas, planejamento urbano, produção e distribuição de alimentos. Na avaliação dele, o processamento de grandes volumes de dados amplia as possibilidades de pesquisa e de tomada de decisões. “O intuito não é você simplesmente sair comprando só o que há de melhor”, ressaltou. Para o executivo, o objetivo é combinar ferramentas diferentes que efetivamente agreguem valor às operações das empresas. Aguiar relembrou que a Nvidia identificou novas possibilidades para suas GPUs em 2012, quando pesquisadores utilizaram plataformas originalmente voltadas a games em uma competição de classificação de imagens. A partir dali, a companhia intensificou o desenvolvimento de hardware e software para aplicações de inteligência artificial. Leia também: EXCLUSIVO CNBC: CEO da Gecko Robotics destaca parceria com Nvidia para ampliar segurança de robôs com IA “O hardware por si só […] não adianta”, explicou o executivo, ao destacar que os programas precisam estar preparados para aproveitar o processamento das placas. Após 16 anos na Nvidia, Aguiar afirmou que não imaginava a dimensão atual da transformação tecnológica. Segundo ele, a orientação da empresa é desenvolver soluções a partir das necessidades dos clientes e continuar abrindo mercados. Leia também: Nvidia supera projeções e segue à frente da concorrência na corrida pela inteligência artificial “O foco sempre foi abrir novos mercados e nunca focado em disputar mercado”, afirmou. artigo.texto: CATL Unveils Dual-Electric Range Extension Battery to Accelerate Electric Heavy-Duty Truck Adoption BEIJING , Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CATL today unveiled the innovative dual-electric range extension battery and the latest generation of heavy-duty battery-swapping solution to accelerate the electrification of road freight transportation. Competition in electric heavy-duty trucking is moving beyond technical specifications toward full-lifecycle value. While battery swapping has made energy replenishment faster and more predictable, concerns about battery utilization, operating costs and residual vehicle value continue to affect fleet economics. To address these challenges, CATL combines its dual-electric range extension battery with QIJI's strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem, bringing battery swapping and industry-wide collaboration together to accelerate heavy-duty truck electrification. A Dual-Electric Approach to Range Extension CATL's dual-electric range extension battery combines two independent yet complementary battery systems. The main battery uses QIJI's standardized chassis-mounted swappable battery to maximize efficiency. A behind-the-cab range-extension power system, currently equipped with a 77kWh battery capable of 3C charging, provides backup power. Together, the systems maintain uninterrupted power delivery and provide redundancy for demanding operating conditions. - Dual-System Power Redundancy In conventional battery-swapping trucks, drivers often return for a swap with unused capacity because they are reluctant to run the battery low. Backup power from the range-extension battery increases the main battery's depth of discharge (DOD) from approximately 70% to over 95%, allowing it to be returned at less than 5% state of charge (SOC). At this threshold,CATL 's seamless switching technology transfers power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, maintaining a continuous and stable power supply. - "1+X" Architecture and Independent Upgrades The system uses a "1+X" architecture. One standardized main battery maintains compatibility with the QIJI battery-swapping network, while the range-extension battery can be customized for specific conditions with options including ultra-high energy density, low-temperature resistance for cold climates, or ultra-high power. The two battery systems can be developed and upgraded independently to meet their respective technical and operational requirements. - Flexible Leasing and Battery Asset Management The independently owned on-board range-extension battery stays with the vehicle as an asset throughout its service life, reducing reliance on immediate access to a swapping station. The main battery can be leased according to seasonal freight demand, helping fleets reduce rental costs during quieter periods and manage battery assets more flexibly. This architecture combines the benefits of standardization with flexible vehicle configurations, making electric heavy-duty trucks more practical and economically viable across a wider range of applications. QIJI Builds a Shared Battery Swapping Ecosystem QIJI complements these improvements with a three-pillar strategy of standardization, new infrastructure and a full commercial ecosystem. It seeks to speed heavy-duty truck electrification with a value-chain ecosystem co-created by all stakeholders, where benefits are shared collectively. - Standardization Supports Wider Adoption To accommodate a wider range of truck models and operating conditions, QIJI has introduced the 260# (432 kWh) and 300# (513 kWh) standardized battery-swapping blocks alongside the existing 75# block. The system enables battery swaps in just five minutes, with a 99.99% first-time success rate, helping fleets minimize downtime and maintain operational efficiency. QIJI has also pioneered a battery-as-a-service (BaaS) model in which customers pay for the net energy charged rather than the energy discharged. This allows customers to retain the value of energy recovered through regenerative braking, reducing per-kWh battery rental costs for users on basic plans by up to 20%. Flexible battery leasing options allow customers to tailor rental periods to their needs, from second-hand vehicle transitions to seasonal demand. This will minimize idle costs and offer more flexible options for off-season downtime, further helping fleets manage operating costs. - New Infrastructure Improves Resource Efficiency QIJI aims to make better use of four critical resources in long-haul freight: time, land, payload capacity and grid electricity. Rapid battery swapping reduces waiting times, while efficient station layouts serve more vehicles within the same footprint. Battery capacity is matched to transport needs, and centralized, coordinated charging makes better use of grid electricity. These measures aim to improve both resource efficiency and operational returns.CATL plans to deploy 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations nationwide in collaboration with its partners. By connecting major freight corridors through a coordinated swapping network, QIJI aims to improve the efficiency and commercial viability of electric heavy-duty trucking. - A Commercial Ecosystem Supports the Full Vehicle Lifecycle QIJI connects truck manufacturers, financial institutions, insurers, channel partners and aftermarket service providers across the vehicle lifecycle, from purchase and operation to maintenance and resale, working together to build a comprehensive ecosystem of integrated products and services. QIJI has introduced two partnership models:Battery Asset Service Partners andEnergy Replenishment Service Partners . artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Declares Monthly Cash Dividend of $0.2708333 per Share of 13.00% Series D Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock Hyperscale Data Also Declares Monthly Cash Dividend of $0.20833 per Share of 10.00% Series E Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock LAS VEGAS , Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that its Board of Directors (the "Board") has declared a monthly cash dividend of $0.2708333 per share of the Company's outstanding 13.00% Series D Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock. Link to NYSE quote for the Company's 13.00% Series D Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock: https://www.nyse.com/quote/XASE:GPUSpD The Company also announced today that the Board has declared a monthly cash dividend of $0.20833 per share of the Company's outstanding 10.00% Series E Cumulative Redeemable Perpetual Preferred Stock. The record date for both dividends is October 31, 2026, and the payment date is Tuesday, November 10, 2026. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors, and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. The battery energy storage systems, more commonly known as BESS, are designed to stabilize electrical grids by providing steady power from renewable sources, which can sometimes be inconsistent. Many of the facilities also use lithium-ion batteries, which can create fire risks. Advertisement Lake Placid is the latest of several towns across the country to put the brakes on development, at least for now. The one-year moratorium will pause any potential construction until the village is prepared to pass stronger safety regulations. Ticonderoga, Ellenburg and Chestertown have also imposed short-term bans.

artigo.texto: The abandoned San Francisco Centre mall could find new life as a massive data center and artificial intelligence lab under a newly revealed proposal, though the idea faces immediate hurdles from city leadership and community members. The multistory shopping mall has been closed and boarded up since late January. According to a proposal confirmed by Jared Kreiger, CEO of the Maryland-based property development firm KG Growth Partners, a confidential client is exploring purchasing the entire property to convert the upper floors into a data center and AI lab. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are The plan would include public space on the ground level and water for a rooftop community garden that could be donated to nonprofits focusing on food insecurity. However, Kreiger declined to reveal the identity of the prospective buyer. The proposal comes at a complicated time for downtown San Francisco. Last week, Mayor Daniel Lurie approved a 45-day moratorium on City Hall approving any permits to build new data centers in the city. Addressing the proposal, Mayor Lurie said he was unaware of the plan and emphasized that the building remains on the market. "I am not aware of that proposal," Lurie said. "The building is still up for sale. There is not a buyer yet. I'm hopeful that we get someone in there that will bring a lot of people downtown." Communities across the country have increasingly raised concerns over data center developments, pointing to issues such as heavy water usage, environmental impacts, round-the-clock noise, and vibrations. Local reactions to the downtown San Francisco concept were mixed. Local "I've heard bad things about data centers," said San Francisco resident Paul Bodner. "By default I would not support it," added Guillaume Le Ster, also of San Francisco. Nicholas McNely, who lives a couple of blocks from the shuttered mall, questioned the motives behind such a project. "They're more trying to extract from whatever community they're trying to extract the resources from to enrich themselves so, I don't really see the reason for a data center here," McNely said. Conversely, some visitors saw potential upside. Janet Li of Burlingame noted, "If it's an AI center here, more people would work here so, I think it's good for the street." The proposal was first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and confirmed to NBC Bay Area by development consultants.

artigo.texto: Battery technology is emerging as a critical driver of India’s electric vehicle (EV) market. Due to the increasing popularity of EVs, technological developments in battery science and production costs have become more important in relation to vehicle affordability and performance, and creation of domestic EV supply chain. Over the past few years, an increasing trend of registration of EVs in India has taken place starting from 0.456 million units in FY22 to 2.536 million units in FY26.The focus is now extending beyond EV sales to the development of a broader battery ecosystem. Investments in cell manufacturing, alternative battery chemistries, critical mineral processing and battery recycling are strengthening different parts of the value chain. In addition to government schemes like the ACC Production Linked Incentive, efforts to build domestic manufacturing capabilities have been strengthened. Hence, batteries are becoming increasingly important not just for the development of India’s EV industry, but also for the country's clean mobility and energy storage ambitions in general. Source: Vahan Dashboard, Note: * - Till August 2026 Batteries form a considerable part of the total cost associated with electric vehicles, implying that battery costs and innovations are fundamental factors determining the cost and adoption of EVs. Global lithium-ion battery pack prices fell to an all-time low of Rs. 9,413.28 per kWh (US$ 108 per kWh) in 2025, reflecting an 8% decline compared to 2024, according to reports published by BloombergNEF. This fall in the cost of lithium-ion batteries is because of overproduction, increasing competition, and the use of cheaper battery technologies like LFP batteries. The Indian EV battery market is also forecasted to witness significant growth, increasing from Rs. 23,707.52 crore (US$ 2.72 billion) in 2025 to Rs. 1.50 lakh crore (US$ 15.90 billion) by 2034, which translates into a compound annual growth rate of 21.70%. It becomes vital for India to build its own domestic capability along the battery value chain to facilitate its burgeoning EV market. There is growing focus on developing a domestic battery ecosystem through investments in cell manufacturing, battery components, and battery recycling. The PLI scheme for batteries, through the ACC, has helped develop domestic manufacturing of batteries, with at least 10 manufacturers planning their battery manufacturing capacity to about 178 GWh in the next five years. A layered set of policies is trying to pull India's battery ecosystem in the same direction: cheaper cells, more of them made domestically, and a system for recovering critical minerals once batteries reach the end of their life. Apart from the aggregated production capacity of the battery manufacturers, what is more pertinent for India is the battery chemistry and technology options that are trending, and the reasons behind the selection of these technologies being different from the rest of the world. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries have started gaining popularity all over the world due to cost savings and safety benefits of such technology. It was also stated that in the year 2025, the usage of LFP batteries in global EV batteries constitutes 55% of all the batteries. In addition, LFP batteries are 40% less expensive than NMC batteries. This makes the use of LFP batteries even more pertinent considering the fact that affordability of the batteries is very important in making the EVs affordable. India is developing its battery cells manufacturing capacity as a part of the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cells (ACC). As of February 2026, at least 10 manufacturers have announced their production capacities of 178 GWh in the subsequent five years' period, helping to create the Indian battery industry. India is exploring the opportunities of sodium-ion battery technology as a part of its energy storage and battery innovation ecosystem. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has conducted the assessment of the global sodium-ion battery market and its potential for applications in India in the framework of the India-UK ASPIRE programme. The use cases for sodium-ion technology include stationary battery storage and selected mobility applications. The ACC PLI Scheme, budgeted at Rs. 18,100 crore (US$ 2.43 billion) aims to create 50 GWh ACC manufacturing capacity in India. Battery recycling becomes an important element of the ecosystem of critical minerals and clean energy in India. Within the framework of the National Critical Mineral Mission, the Government of India has approved a Rs. 1,500 crore (US$ 158.93 million) scheme to support recycling of critical minerals recovered from sources such as lithium-ion batteries. As of April 2026, 58 companies have become eligible for the scheme, taking the pledged recycling capacity to 850 KTPA and investments to around Rs. 5,000 crore (US$ 529.77 million). India's battery ecosystem is expected to gain further momentum, supported by the continued growth of EV adoption and expanding domestic manufacturing capacity. EV registrations reached 25.36 lakh units in FY26, while the ACC PLI Scheme is supporting the development of 50 GWh of domestic Advanced Chemistry Cell manufacturing capacity. Initiatives from the government such as PM E-DRIVE, investment in critical minerals and recycling of batteries have helped strengthen various sections of the battery value chain. Investments in cell production along with advances in new technologies like sodium-ion batteries and development of a recycling ecosystem are helping create an integrated industry in the field of batteries and energy storage in India. India's EV registrations increased from 4.56 lakh units in FY22 to 25.36 lakh units in FY26, reflecting the rapid expansion of electric mobility in the country. artigo.texto: Itália desponta como importante polo de data centers no sul da Europa A Itália vem se consolidando como um mercado de data centers de destaque na Europa, à medida que cresce a demanda por superinteligência, computação em nuvem e infraestrutura digital, segundo informações de inteligência de mercado da Administração de Comércio Internacional dos Estados Unidos. O país se apoia em sua localização, que liga a Europa, o Norte da África e a Ásia, além de conexões submarinas de cabos em expansão, imóveis industriais acessíveis e necessidades crescentes de computação em SI, observou o órgão. O mercado italiano tinha um valor de aproximadamente €7,5 bilhões em 2025 e deve crescer de forma substancial. O Observatório de Data Centers do Politecnico di Milano estima o investimento em cerca de €25 bilhões no período de 2026–2029, enquanto a Associação Italiana de Data Centers prevê que a capacidade nacional possa superar 1 GW até 2028 e chegar a 2 GW até 2031, ante cerca de 287 MW em 2024. Milão lidera a capacidade, enquanto Roma desempenha um papel complementar Milão continua sendo o principal polo, representando cerca de 68% da capacidade instalada de data centers na Itália. A Lombardia oferece infraestrutura de fibra existente, proximidade de grandes clientes corporativos, terrenos industriais, um ecossistema tecnológico maduro e conexões com redes europeias. Essa concentração, porém, também pressiona a infraestrutura elétrica, o uso do solo e os processos de licenciamento. Roma atua como um mercado complementar, dada sua proximidade com instituições governamentais e com a infraestrutura digital do setor público, com o Polo Estratégico Nacional e programas mais amplos de transformação digital gerando demanda por infraestrutura de computação segura e hospedada no país. Governo passa da estratégia à implementação Os data centers têm sido tratados pelo governo italiano como infraestrutura estratégica. A estratégia nacional de data centers do MIMIT busca atrair investimento estrangeiro, simplificar os procedimentos de autorização e posicionar a Itália como um polo digital europeu e mediterrâneo. Ao longo de 2026, o governo passou da estratégia à implementação, por meio de reformas no licenciamento, medidas para o sistema elétrico e a designação de grandes projetos como de relevância estratégica nacional. A disponibilidade de energia continua sendo a maior restrição estrutural do mercado. Em 2026, o governo adotou legislação para tratar dos custos de eletricidade, da competitividade industrial e da integração dos data centers ao sistema elétrico, reconhecendo que o desenvolvimento de data centers é indissociável do planejamento nacional de energia e da rede elétrica. Oportunidades para investidores dos EUA Para os investidores dos EUA, a Itália oferece a oportunidade de participar da próxima fase da infraestrutura europeia de SI e nuvem, ao mesmo tempo que ganham exposição ao corredor digital do Mediterrâneo. As oportunidades mais fortes devem surgir em campi de hiperescala preparados para SI, empreendimentos com energia garantida, reurbanização industrial de áreas já ocupadas, infraestrutura de conectividade e nos sistemas de energia que dão suporte aos data centers, segundo o órgão de comércio.

People at the session shared concerns mainly about the environment and the potential for rapid development. “I’ve always said from day one I’m not afraid of having a conversation some of you all don’t want me to have a conversation, that’s where we disagree and it’s OK to disagree but let’s do it with honor, dignity and respect,” Henderson said. artigo.texto: AI data centers boost Arizona construction jobs: Here’s why BuildStrong Academy offers free training as demand for skilled labor grows PHOENIX (AZFamily) — Artificial intelligence is affecting industries from healthcare to education to commerce, and now attention is turning to construction and skilled labor in Arizona. Signing up for a skilled labor class is getting harder as demand for workers continues to climb. Jordan Gil, 39, is one of many aspiring carpenters and electricians looking for a new career path. “I’ve been waiting to find something to work with my hands and develop a career and learn some skills and I found info online and seen a couple videos,” Gil said. “There’s a lot of work out here — everything from new construction and remodels,” Gil said. Demand for workers remains strong The need for construction workers is out there, according to Becca Haro, operations manager at the BuildStrong Academy in Phoenix. Haro said the construction industry in Arizona remains strong, with job openings for skilled laborers. She said that is encouraging amid fears about AI eliminating jobs across the labor market. “Everybody is scared that robots and computers are going to take over — but from my perspective and from what I see in the industry, I think this is actually creating a great opportunity — especially for us in Arizona,” Haro said. Data centers drive need for labor Haro said as AI continues to grow, more data centers will be needed across the state, and building them requires a strong skilled labor workforce. “I think people forget — there’s only so much you can automate or use AI for but when it comes to swinging hammers and using drills and wiring buildings, it still takes a human body to do,” Haro said. The BuildStrong Academy offers nine-week classes for free. The classes are paid for by companies and businesses that need skilled workers. For more details, visit https://homebuilding.academy. As a result, execution on these data center deals carries extra weight for the long-term story. - Next, the focus will be on how Bloom Energy's AI data center partnerships reshape the existing investment narrative around resilient on-site power. Scan a curated shortlist of AI power enablers by comparing Bloom Energy with 55 AI infrastructure stocks, both riding the same data center buildout theme. Bloom Energy Investment Narrative Recap To own Bloom Energy, you need to believe that demand for resilient on site power at data centers and other critical facilities can support a long runway of orders and profitable deployment. The business is already generating positive free cash flow and higher returns on capital, so the key near term swing factor is continued conversion of its strong backlog into on time, on budget projects. The biggest risk right now sits in execution and financing on very large AI focused builds, especially with Bloom trading on a rich P/E and a volatile share price. Recent share price moves around Q3 2026 earnings expectations do not appear to change that core equation; they mostly magnify how the stock reacts to any delivery hiccups. The Oracle Project Jupiter update is the announcement that really matters for this phase of the Bloom Energy story. Oracle plans up to 2.45 gigawatts of Bloom fuel cell capacity for an AI data center in New Mexico, with the technology replacing traditional gas turbines and diesel backup. That is an enormous reference site for on site, always on power. For you as an investor, Project Jupiter now acts as both proof point and stress test. Successful installation and operation would support Bloom's pitch that fuel cells solve grid constraints for hyperscalers. Any material delays, cost overruns, or performance issues would feed directly into worries about excess manufacturing capacity, premium valuation, and competition from batteries and renewables. What The Current Analyst Narrative Implies For Bloom Energy Bloom Energy's current analyst storyline is built around a big set of numbers. Consensus forecasts point to revenues of US$10.9b and earnings of US$2.7b by 2029. That view sits on top of projected revenue growth of 51.6% per year and an earnings move of roughly US$2.5b from US$244.9m today.

artigo.texto: Report: Iowa data center boom carries billions in economic impact Cedar Rapids and Palo will account for about a third of state’s capacity CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (KCRG) - Iowa is emerging as a national heavyweight in data centers. A new report says the state is on track to triple its data center operations by 2031. The Common Sense Institute study finds companies have already invested about $15 billion dollars into the state’s economy building and equipping data centers across Iowa, and have announced another $38 billion through 2031. A big share of that activity is clustered within Linn County, with QTS and Google data centers in development in Cedar Rapids, and another Google data center proposed in Palo. Linn County on its own accounts for roughly a third of Iowa’s total capacity. Des Moines and Council Bluffs are the other major data center locations statewide. Compared to the Midwest, Iowa currently ranks second for data center capacity, behind Indiana. Data center jobs Statewide, those projects are expected to more than triple total data‑center capacity by 2031 and support nearly 13,000 jobs from construction and initial equipment purchases. Existing data centers already support an estimated 12,600 Iowa jobs. Announced sites would push that to about 29,600 by 2031. The report says many of those jobs are outside tech — construction, electricians, truck drivers, retail workers and more. RELATED: Cedar Rapids businesses see boost from data centers Average pay in the industry that includes data centers reached about $126,000 in 2025, nearly double the statewide average. Energy demands Analysts warn the growth comes with big resource needs. At typical usage, the combination of existing and planned data centers in the state would take up nearly half of the electricity capacity the state averaged in 2024. Utilities are planning new natural‑gas plants and battery storage to keep up. READ MORE: Surging electricity demand from AI data centers puts Iowa at an energy crossroads Copyright 2026 KCRG. artigo.texto: HiTHIUM launches 8-hour batteries and a sodium-ion solution in Canada The stationary storage manufacturer announces its entry into the Canadian market with 4-hour and 8-hour lithium-ion systems and a 4 MWh sodium-ion unit designed for very cold climates. HiTHIUM, an energy storage solutions provider, has announced its entry into the Canadian market. The manufacturer says it ranks among the top two players globally for energy storage components. It reports having surpassed 200 GWh in cumulative delivered capacity and focusing exclusively on stationary energy storage technologies. A local presence in Canada According to Mizhi Zhang, HiTHIUM's President of Global Business, Toronto will serve as the main hub for Canadian operations. The company has subsidiary offices in British Columbia and Alberta, as well as operating sites in Quebec, Yellowknife and Fort Smith. Battery storage is drawing other players internationally, as with Viridi and Good Carbon installing a 3.75 MWh storage system in Buffalo, Trina Storage supplying 196 MWh to the AEJ Nozu project in Japan, or Leader Energy breaking ground on a 100 MW storage project in Malaysia. HiTHIUM says installed storage capacity in Canada is expected to double between 2025 and 2027. The country's total wind, solar and storage capacity would be on track to reach 50 GW by 2035. The company offers 4-hour and 8-hour solutions for utility-scale projects. It also unveils a 4 MWh sodium-ion solution that supports durations of 2 to 8 hours and targets very cold climates, such as Northern Canada. Two lithium-ion storage durations The 4-hour solution relies on the "âPower" 6.25 MWh container, built on HiTHIUM's own 1175 Ah cell. According to the company, most Canadian projects are currently designed around this 4-hour unit. It allows wind, solar and baseload output to be shifted to later peak times. The 20-foot container can be placed back-to-back and side-to-side, which would reduce projects' overall footprint. HiTHIUM also presents what it describes as the first native 8-hour solution based on lithium-ion technology. This 6.9 MWh BESS (battery energy storage system) uses 1300 Ah cells and has a 25-year lifespan, according to the manufacturer. It targets issues such as curtailments and industrial segments requiring zero downtime, such as AI data centers. A fire test conducted with UL Solutions HiTHIUM worked with UL Solutions at the start of 2026 on an independently conducted, extreme fire test of its 6.25 MWh block's intrinsic safety systems. A container was subjected to 24 hours of extreme combustion conditions, with its doors opened for maximum thermal spread, while neighboring containers were placed 15 cm away. Only the passive safety systems were enabled. According to HiTHIUM, the tested container remained structurally intact, with no thermal propagation across containers. The temperatures of cells in adjacent containers stayed below safety thresholds. Jordan Hebbert, HiTHIUM Senior Manager of Canada, says operational data from North American and European projects shows systems outperforming the company's guarantees, without detailing that data. artigo.texto: CATL has launched a dual battery system for electric heavy trucks that pairs a swappable main pack with a fixed range extender, so fleets can use far more of each battery before swapping. Agreements covering 13,000 units were signed at the launch. The main battery uses Qiji Energy’s standardised swappable packs mounted on the chassis, and a 77kWh extender capable of 3C charging sits behind the cab. With that backup on board, drivers can raise the main pack’s depth of discharge from around 70% to more than 95% and arrive at swap stations below 5% charge. CATL says power switches to the extender within milliseconds. The extender can be tailored for higher energy density, cold weather or high power, and it stays with the truck while the main pack can be leased to match seasonal demand. Qiji has also added standardised 432kWh and 513kWh blocks, and it says a swap takes five minutes. “The combination of the dual-electric range extension battery and Qiji’s battery swapping system offers the best solution for heavy truck electrification,” said Jesse Yang, Chief Executive of Qiji Energy. CATL plans 900 truck swap stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 across China. The design depends on that network, though. In Europe, truckmakers are focusing on megawatt charging instead, so the model may not travel easily. Why this matters: - CATL moves beyond cells. Battery leasing, swap stations and pay-per-net-energy pricing turn CATL into an energy service operator, earning recurring revenue while easing the residual value concerns that deter fleets from electric trucks. - Standard blocks set the interface. Swap packs standardised across multiple truckmakers could make CATL’s format the de facto standard for China’s heavy trucks, deepening truckmakers’ reliance on its ecosystem. - Regional infrastructure models diverge. China’s build-out of swap corridors contrasts with Europe, where truckmakers have backed megawatt charging, suggesting heavy truck electrification could follow different infrastructure paths by region.

artigo.texto: A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI. Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains New research out of Texas shows how data centers are driving up pollution. New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim. Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality. “There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.” In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025. That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite. NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be. “There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these [emissions] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA A EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) publicou a metodologia que será utilizada para calcular o custo marginal de referência, que servirá de base para a definição do preço-teto do leilão de baterias, marcado para dezembro. A nota técnica disponibilizada na segunda-feira (19) não apresenta os preços, uma vez que o dado é considerado estratégico para o certame, mas detalha como será feito o cálculo para os projetos. A metodologia utiliza um modelo de fluxo de caixa descontado, que avalia os investimentos, os custos e as receitas esperadas ao longo do empreendimento. A EPE calculará uma TEQ (Tarifa de Equilíbrio), isto é, a receita necessária para que o projeto cubra seus custos e remunere o capital, considerando os riscos e as condições financeiras adotadas. A EPE destaca que o preço-teto não será baseado apenas no custo inicial das baterias, mas também considerará os valores necessários para manter os sistemas de armazenamento aptos a operar conforme o contrato. Assim, o cálculo do custo marginal de referência considerará, além do investimento, as despesas com operação e manutenção, degradação das baterias, augmentation (reposição de componentes), tarifas de uso da rede, financiamento, seguros e tributos. Nacional x importado Quanto à divisão do leilão em dois, um para produto nacional e o outro que permite equipamentos importados, a nota técnica da EPE destaca que não se deve presumir que equipamentos nacionais serão mais caros ou mais baratos que os importados, uma vez que vários componentes entrarão na conta. “O efeito final decorrerá da avaliação conjunta dos custos, das condições de financiamento, dos prazos e dos riscos associados à cadeia de fornecimento”, diz o documento, que cita por exemplo que projetos nacionais podem ter condições diferenciadas de financiamento. Com a publicação da metodologia, a EPE agora deve avançar nos cálculos do custo marginal de referência, com as recomendações de preços-tetos. Isso será feito a partir informações dos projetos cadastrados, diligências técnicas, estudos nacionais e internacionais, referências de mercado e informações de fabricantes e bancos. A decisão final sobre o preço-teto caberá ao MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia).

Local publications are the lifeblood of small towns. In the past decade, more than 2,000 communities across the country lost an essential institution when their newspapers closed. artigo.texto: Georgia candidates up and down the ballot are campaigning on an issue that has struck a nerve across the political spectrum: data centers. A wave of data center projects across Georgia has been met with outrage in many communities in the last year or so, causing state lawmakers from both parties to push a flurry of legislative solutions during the 2026 legislative session. But in the end, none of the bills passed. Since then, Georgia has become the leading state for data centers. Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who is term-limited and leaving office after this year, has welcomed the facilities, saying at a data center-related event in Washington this summer that "we cannot let China win this race, and that's what some people want," referencing the race between the U.S. and China to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models. The November election will decide to what extent Georgia embraces the energy-hungry facilities in the future, with voters choosing a new governor, the lawmakers who shape the state's policies on data centers and other state leaders who play a role in carrying out those policies. At the top of the ballot, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, has criticized Republican nominee Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, for his investment in a data center in Texas through a company Jackson was the head of until recently. Though his campaign has tried to distance itself from that development, in his campaign financial disclosure, Jackson is listed as the CEO and president of Datahub Developers, the company that is advancing the data center in Texas that the local community is fighting. Bottoms and Jackson had a fiery exchange at a recent debate where they swapped accusations of being involved in advancing data centers. "There is a community asking him to not build a data center, a massive data center in their community, and he is moving forward. So, if he is an investor in data centers, if he builds data centers, he cannot be trusted on this," Bottoms said in the debate organized by Atlanta News First and Gray Media. Jackson fired back, accusing Bottoms of approving three data centers during her time as mayor of Atlanta, but Bottoms said that she was "not sure what data centers he's referencing," saying there was only one at Georgia Tech that wasn't one of the hyperscale data centers that cause concerns today. Attorney general candidate says family has 'moved on' from data center project once planned for their farmland At least one other candidate, Georgia state Sen. Brian Strickland, a McDonough Republican running for state attorney general, held a personal financial stake in a proposed data center as recently as the summer of 2025. But the proposal has since been shelved, according to public records and interviews. The Georgia Recorder examined financial disclosure documents for all candidates running for statewide office in November. The Recorder also reviewed other public records and reached out to all of the candidates and their campaigns to ask whether the candidate has a direct financial stake in a data center. In phone calls, text messages and emails with candidates and their campaign staff, all except those described in the story reported having no financial interest in data center projects. Public records show that Strickland, a lawyer who represents a suburban district southeast of Atlanta, was involved in advancing a $1.2 billion data center on his family's farmland in Henry County. On May 15, 2024, he authorized a real estate development firm focused on technology to pursue rezoning for the project. Strickland's personal financial disclosure statement shows that the state senator holds a greater-than-5% stake in Strickland Road Farms, which was a co-applicant in the rezoning application for the proposed 1.25 million-square-feet data center. The project came close to being finalized mid-2025 – about the same time Strickland launched his bid for higher office – but Strickland told reporters last week that his family backed out over concerns about the noise that would come from the data center and now says the project is "dead." A public hearing before the Henry County Board of Commissioners was scheduled to consider rezoning part of the farmland on June 17, 2025, but Carlotta Harrell, the commission's chair, said at the top of the meeting that the agenda item, along with other rezoning public hearings, "have all been removed at the request of the applicant and we will hear these items at a later time." County and local development officials confirmed the project is now inactive. The Democratic nominee for attorney general, state Rep. Tanya Miller, pressed Strickland on the project at last week's Atlanta Press Club debate. "It wasn't until days – and mind you, we're talking days – after he announced his run for attorney general, did he remove the agenda item from the public hearing. He didn't remove the data center application. He's playing with words. He's shape shifting," Miller said to reporters after the debate. Opponents of the data center project, like Connie Snow, a member of Conserve Henry County, a local advocacy group focused on zoning issues, say they're worried the project will be revived after the November election. "They've all told us that he's withdrawn and all this other stuff, but I don't think that it's going to go away," Snow said in an interview. "You have to also remember that all this happened coincidentally enough as it was getting close to election time." Snow also participated in a press call organized by the Democratic Party of Georgia. But Strickland said the decision to halt the project was not related to his decision to run for office and says the family now plans to add to an existing residence on the property and that his "parents decided to keep the entire farm intact." artigo.texto: City commission candidates split on data center restrictions at forum Incumbents and challengers divide over moratorium ahead of election What This Story Is About - City commission candidates at a forum discussed their positions on data center restrictions and a proposed moratorium. Why It Matters - The city’s handling of data center regulations has become a key dividing line between incumbents and challengers ahead of the election. For Context - Two city commission candidates, Don Langley and Sue Parrigan, did not attend the forum, though Parrigan provided a written statement defending the city’s existing data center ordinance. BOWLING GREEN, Ky. (WBKO) - Voters packed State Street Baptist Church Monday, Oct.19 for a candidate forum focused on city commission and contested magistrate races. Doors opened at 5:30 p.m. for a meet and greet. The forum started at 6:30 p.m., giving voters a chance to hear directly from candidates seeking to represent them on city issues and in county government. City commission candidates address data centers A central topic heading into the election is the ongoing debate over data centers. Candidates at the forum responded to questions on the issue. Incumbent Melinda Hill, who is running for re-election, voted against a proposed moratorium in June. She said restrictions already in place protect the community. “City commission voted five to zero with the strictest restrictions for data centers,” Hill said. “We’ve already put those in place. So yes, I know you’re mad there wasn’t a moratorium, or some of you are. But be thankful we put very strict restrictions for our community regarding data centers.” Fellow incumbent Carlos Bailey voted for the moratorium. He said he wanted a pause so outside experts could be brought in. “The reason why we wanted to have that is because we wanted to bring in the experts, because none of us on here were experts, to see how it is doing in other communities,” Bailey said. “We wanted to bring in people who actually are living with data centers, like Memphis and Gallatin, Tennessee. They could tell us how it affects their everyday life.” Thomas Morris said the data center debate is the main reason he is running. He said he supported a moratorium. “I went to Gallatin, Tennessee, talked to a city commissioner there,” Morris said. “I asked him what piece of advice do you have. He said, ‘take your time.’ In my opinion, we did not take our time. We rushed it through, and this is an issue that could come back to bite us.” Incumbent Dana Beasley Brown said she backed a moratorium because of transparency and unanswered questions about impact. “We haven’t done the research, like Commissioner Bailey said, about our unique karst topography and what a data center of that size, the impact it could have on it,” Beasley Brown said. “The fact that we have had a real long drought this summer, and thinking about our water usage, how we make sure we have enough for our kids and grandkids. It’s these concerns I have in mind, and the need to stop and make sure our whole community gets to give input about whether we want a data center in our future or not.” Two candidates absent from forum Two city commission candidates were not at the forum: Don Langley and Sue Parrigan. WBKO reached out to Langley for comment but has not yet heard back. Parrigan responded with a statement: “A pause does not stop a data center. A rule does! The city commission proactively voted unanimously to approve an ordinance to set rules to keep data centers off your street.” Voters react after forum Michael Trapasso was among those in attendance. He said data centers were his top concern heading into the forum. “My main issue was the data centers, of which I’m very much against,” Trapasso said. “I enjoyed hearing what people had to say, getting an idea about who these people are and how they feel about various issues. I thought it was quite enlightening.” Resident Sheila Downs said the forum was helpful for meeting the candidates, but it was difficult to draw lines between each candidate’s views. “I thought the forum was very nice. It was very informative,” Downs said. “One of the things that I noticed, and a couple of people did stand out to me, but they seemed to collaborate with each other and not a lot of them took the initiative to say, ‘this is what I’m going to do.’ So, I wasn’t able to differentiate between who was going to do what.” Both Downs and Trapasso say they’ll be heading to the polls Nov. 3. artigo.texto: In China, new-energy heavy truck sales have overtaken diesel truck sales. Just three years ago, new-energy heavy trucks accounted for only around 5% of sales, but electrification is spreading on the back of Chinese government support and lower transport costs. That contrasts with the United States and Europe, where heavy truck electrification remains in the single digits. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL; 宁德时代), the world's largest battery maker, unveiled a new battery system aimed at long-haul heavy electric trucks as it moves to tap the long-distance transport market. On the 21st, according to China First Commercial Vehicle Network, about 65,800 heavy trucks were newly registered for insurance in China's domestic market in September, of which about 33,100 were new-energy vehicles. That was 50.3% of the total, a majority. While total heavy truck registrations fell 21% from a year earlier, registrations of new-energy vehicles rose 37%. Electrification of China's heavy truck market has accelerated rapidly in recent years. According to China First Commercial Vehicle Network, the sales share of new-energy heavy trucks surged from the 5% range in 2022–2023 to 13.6% in 2024 and 28.9% in 2025, then reached 38.1% in January–September this year. New energy includes not only pure electric vehicles but also Hydrogen Fuel Cell vehicles. CATL said, "In the heavy truck electrification market, the competition between internal combustion and electric vehicles is already over; from now on, the competition will be between EV technologies and business models." Compared with major global markets, China's pace of electrification stands out even more. According to the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), in the first half of this year, zero-emission vehicles accounted for only 2.3% of new registrations of heavy trucks over 12 tons in the European Union (EU). In the United States, the figure was 0.34% last year. However, collection standards and periods differ by country. ◇ Chinese government to provide support in the 4 trillion won range for replacing old cargo trucks China's rapid electrification appears to reflect a combination of government support and improved economics. According to CATL, the Chinese government is building more than 3,000 heavy truck-dedicated charging and battery exchange facilities, centered on major metropolitan areas and expressways, to reach a 40% electrification rate for heavy trucks. It is also pushing plans to create a "carbon zero (0)" road transport network spanning a total of 30,000 kilometers. In particular, it allocated 22 billion yuan (about 4.3688 trillion won) from ultra-long-term special government bonds to support scrapping and replacing old commercial cargo trucks, and in some regions, the combined central and local government subsidies reportedly reach up to 220,000 yuan (about 43.68 million won). Electric trucks cost more upfront than diesel trucks, but their maintenance expense is relatively lower, so the longer the driving distance and the higher the utilization rate, the greater the potential cost savings. Adoption is said to be especially fast on short-haul, fixed routes such as mines, ports, steel mills, and construction sites. That is because fixed routes make it easier to secure charging infrastructure, and repeated vehicle operation can yield fuel cost savings. ◇ CATL unveils new "battery swap + auxiliary battery" system Against this backdrop, CATL has introduced a battery solution to improve long-haul efficiency for heavy electric trucks. On the 20th (local time), CATL held a product launch at the Shoudu International Exhibition and Convention Center in Shunyi District, Beijing, unveiling four new rechargeable batteries for heavy electric trucks and a new battery swap system. The new system combines a fixed auxiliary battery with the existing battery swap system. First, a main battery with up to 513 kWh capacity is mounted under the truck, and it can be replaced at a swap station in about five minutes without lengthy charging. CATL is operating battery swap systems on five major transport corridors: Guangdong–Shanghai, Chengdu–Wuhan, Changzhou–Yulin, Ningde–Xiamen, and the Hainan Island ring road. The fixed auxiliary battery is mounted behind the driver's seat. With a capacity of 77 kWh, it assists vehicle operation when the main battery's power is low. Because electric truck drivers, concerned about running out of charge, typically left about 30% remaining and then exchanged the battery, an auxiliary battery was added separately to improve this. CATL said this would allow the main battery to be used down to under 5% remaining, improving efficiency. artigo.texto: Gentari and BYD Malaysia have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to explore the deployment of BYD’s Flash Charging technology in Malaysia. The collaboration aims to expand ultra-fast EV charging infrastructure beyond showrooms, including along major intercity routes connecting key population centres. BYD’s Flash Charging technology is capable of delivering up to 1.5MW which would provide approximately 400km of driving range in just five minutes for compatible EVs under optimal conditions. The MoU was signed in Shenzhen, China, on 21 October 2026, between Gentari Group CEO Sushil Purohit and BYD Malaysia Managing Director Jacob Ma. The ceremony was witnessed by BYD Chairman Wang Chuanfu and BYD Vice President Liu Xueliang. Gentari and BYD to explore Flash Charging along major highways Under the agreement, Gentari and BYD Malaysia will jointly identify suitable locations for BYD Flash Charging stations, especially along key intercity corridors. Both companies will also assess power infrastructure requirements, battery energy storage systems (BESS), technical and commercial feasibility and potential operating models to support future deployment. The collaboration combines Gentari’s experience in developing and operating EV charging networks with BYD’s battery and high-power charging technology. Gentari Group CEO Sushil Purohit said, “Malaysia’s EV market is growing, but the next phase of adoption will depend on the quality, convenience and reliability of the charging experience.” He added, “Speed is one part of that equation. Drivers also need chargers in the right places, backed by reliable power and dependable operations. BYD’s leadership in EV, battery and high-power charging technology, combined with Gentari’s experience in developing and operating EV charging networks, gives us a strong foundation to strengthen Malaysia’s EV charging ecosystem and support wider adoption.” Gentari currently operates more than 600 EV charging points in Malaysia. Through its Gentari Go Roaming Hub, it also provides access to approximately 18,000 charging points across Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and India. BYD Vice President and General Manager of BYD Asia Pacific Auto Sales Division Liu Xueliang said, “Malaysia is an important market for BYD, and we are pleased to bring BYD Flash Charging here as part of our continued efforts to support the country’s growing EV adoption. Through our collaboration with Gentari, we look forward to exploring how this technology can contribute to a faster, more convenient and more connected charging experience for Malaysian EV users.” Meanwhile, BYD Malaysia Managing Director Jacob Ma said, “We are very excited to see this collaboration come together. As an EV leader, we believe our responsibility goes beyond delivering great vehicles. We want to give our customers the confidence to make the switch to electric and enjoy a truly seamless EV ownership experience. This is an important step for BYD in Malaysia, and we are proud to be part of the journey to build a stronger and more complete EV ecosystem for Malaysians.” Besides EV charging infrastructure, Gentari and BYD will also explore collaboration in renewable energy generation and energy storage. BYD Flash Charging stations already spotted in Malaysia As reported previously, BYD Malaysia had confirmed plans to introduce its Flash Charging technology in Malaysia, starting with Denza showrooms before expanding to other locations. The Flash Charging stations can deliver up to 1,500kW (1.5MW) of DC charging output. When paired with compatible EVs equipped with BYD’s second-generation Blade Battery technology, it can charge the battery from 10% to 70% in five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in just nine minutes. The chargers are also supported by BESS to manage the massive power demands without requiring the same level of power directly from the grid. Earlier this week, we spotted what appears to be BYD Flash Charging BESS equipment at Denza Glenmarie in Shah Alam. This was followed by another sighting at Denza Balakong, where the distinctive T-shaped overhead Flash charging structure and battery storage cabinets have already been installed. While the Flash Charging technology supports a maximum DC output of 1,500kW, compatible vehicles are required to achieve the highest charging speeds. The Denza Z9 GT is currently the only model available in Malaysia that supports BYD’s full Flash Charging capability. As shared by BYD Malaysia earlier, the Flash Charger will also be open to other BYD models and non-BYD EVs, up to their respective supported DC charging rates. BYD Malaysia has yet to reveal the official opening dates for the Flash Charging stations in Malaysia.

artigo.texto: Global Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery Market Projected to Reach US$111 Million by 2032, at 18.0% CAGR 1.1 Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery Market Summary Silicon-carbon anode materials for solid state batteries are high-capacity anode materials developed for solid-state and semi-solid lithium battery systems. They are typically based on nano-silicon, silicon oxide, graphite, and porous carbon, and are improved through composite structure design, surface coating, and interface stabilization. The materials are mainly used in automotive power batteries, high-end consumer electronics batteries, and next-generation high-safety energy storage batteries. The market is still in an early commercialization stage as solid state batteries move from sample validation and pilot projects toward small-scale production. Demand for silicon-carbon anode materials is increasing as automakers, battery manufacturers, and material companies accelerate joint development programs. Compared with conventional graphite anodes, silicon-carbon systems offer much higher theoretical capacity, but they also face challenges such as volume expansion, interfacial side reactions, initial efficiency loss, and batch-to-batch consistency. According to the new market research report "Global Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery Market Growth 2026-2032", published by LP Information, the global Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery market size is projected to reach US$111 million by 2032, at a CAGR of 18.0% during the forecast period. According to LP Information, the global key manufacturers of Silicon-carbon Anode Materials for Solid State Battery include Group14 Technologies, Sila Nanotechnologies, Amprius, etc. In 2025, the global top three players had a share of approximately 31.65% in terms of revenue. To read the full report or request a free sample report, please use the link: https://www.lpinformationdata.com/reports/1866822/silicon---carbon-anode-materials-for-solid-state-battery 1.2 Industrial Chain The upstream segment mainly includes metallurgical-grade silicon, silane, graphite, and porous carbon, with representative suppliers such as Elkem, Hemlock, and East Hope Group. Raw material purity, particle size distribution, carbon structure, and supply stability directly affect capacity performance, swelling control, cycle life, and batch consistency, while also forming the basis for cost control and mass production. The midstream segment focuses on silicon-carbon composite structure engineering, interface stabilization, swelling suppression, surface coating modification, and particle morphology optimization. The main challenge is to balance high capacity with long cycle life while controlling initial efficiency, tap density, and processing compatibility. Stable mixing, heat treatment, coating, and classification processes directly affect yield, customer qualification time, and unit manufacturing cost. Downstream demand mainly comes from automotive power batteries and consumer electronics lithium batteries. Power battery customers focus on longer driving range, fast charging capability, safety, and long-term cycling performance, while consumer electronics customers emphasize volumetric energy density and thinner product design. Silicon-carbon anodes help battery makers improve energy density and create differentiated performance for solid state batteries, premium vehicles, and high-end devices. 1.3 Influencing Factors Drivers: The core growth driver is rising demand for high-energy-density batteries. Longer-range electric vehicles, fast-charging platforms, and thinner high-end consumer electronics are pushing anode materials from conventional graphite toward silicon-carbon systems. As solid state battery development and demonstration projects accelerate, battery makers are increasing validation demand for high-capacity, low-swelling, and long-life anode materials, supporting order growth and market expansion. Challenges: The main barrier is process stability and cost pressure. Silicon materials tend to expand and trigger interfacial side reactions during charge and discharge, which raises requirements for coating, structure design, and battery system matching. If batch consistency, initial efficiency, and cycle life cannot meet customer requirements steadily, qualification cycles will be extended and production expansion and profitability will be constrained. Trend: Future development will focus on higher capacity, lower swelling, and better adaptation to solid state battery systems. Material suppliers will use nano-structure design, porous carbon frameworks, elastic coating layers, and interface modification to improve cycling stability, while developing customized products for different solid electrolytes and cell processes. artigo.texto: Nigeria’s carbon market is gaining traction following the Federal Government’s first approvals for international carbon credit sales, a Nigerian carbon project developer, 9JA Carbon Trade, has said. The company said the approvals demonstrated that Nigeria’s carbon market framework was operational, as African governments, investors and project developers were urged to move beyond developing regulations to delivering projects and securing investment. The position was made known after 9JA Carbon Trade participated in the Carbon Markets Africa Summit (CMAS) 2026, held in Kigali, Rwanda, from October 14 to 15. The summit attracted about 600 delegates from 52 countries, representing more than 150 organisations, including over 50 investors and buyers. Speaking at the event, Timothy Solomon, Co-Technical Manager of 9JA Carbon Trade, said Africa’s carbon market was increasingly being judged by its ability to deliver credible carbon credits, attract investment and ensure that host communities benefited from projects. “Kigali changed the question Africa is asked. It is no longer whether the continent can supply carbon credits, but whether it can deliver them with integrity, at fair prices and with benefits host communities can see,” Solomon said. “ Nigeria now has the framework and its first approvals. Our part is to bring forward projects worth approving,” he added. At a session on country readiness on October 14, Ibrahim Shelleng, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Climate Finance and Stakeholder Engagement, disclosed that Nigeria issued six letters of authorisation in March 2026 and two additional letters by September. A letter of authorisation is a formal government approval allowing carbon credits to be used internationally. Under the arrangement, the host country agrees not to count the authorised emission reductions towards its own climate targets. Reacting to the development, Ekene Okpara, also a Co-Technical Manager at 9JA Carbon Trade, said Nigeria’s progress in issuing authorisations gave developers confidence in the country’s approval process. Okpara, however, sought clarification on whether the Federal Government planned to enter into a bilateral carbon agreement with another country. He also asked what guidance was available for developers whose projects were still awaiting approval from the National Council on Climate Change, the body responsible for approving carbon projects in Nigeria. On October 15, the company participated in a round-table discussion at the summit’s solution lab, which examined ways to reduce risks for private investors, including political risks, insurance, financing and access to carbon credit buyers. The discussions formed part of broader efforts to strengthen Africa’s capacity to attract private capital into carbon markets and translate climate commitments into viable projects. At the close of the summit, the Acting Permanent Secretary of Rwanda’s Ministry of Environment, speaking on behalf of the Minister of Environment, outlined six areas of agreement among participants. The priorities included strengthening market integrity, building trust, ensuring that host communities benefited from carbon projects, increasing Africa’s share of the value generated by the market, improving regulatory implementation and securing long-term investment. Governments were urged to complete and implement their carbon market regulations and publish information on authorisations and credit transfers to improve transparency. Buyers and investors were also encouraged to move beyond expressing interest in African carbon credits and sign multi-year purchase agreements at fair prices. Development partners and financial institutions were called upon to support project preparation, identified at the summit as a major obstacle preventing viable projects from reaching the market. Opening the summit on October 14, Rwanda’s Minister of Environment, Dr Bernadette Arakwiye, said developing regulations alone was insufficient without effective implementation. “Writing rules is one thing, and running them is another,” she said. Arakwiye noted that improved cookstoves accounted for approximately 87 per cent of Rwanda’s issued carbon credits, while agriculture had generated barely one per cent of voluntary carbon market credits over two decades. The summit also examined emerging international demand for carbon credits and the growing importance of quality standards in determining their market value. The International Air Transport Association told delegates that the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA), a United Nations-backed scheme for international aviation, would become mandatory for airlines in 2027. Credits used under the scheme must carry a government letter of authorisation. Lukas Visek of the European Commission said a Commission proposal envisaged European Union purchases of carbon credits covering up to 260 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2036 and 2040. Participants were also told that higher-quality credits were attracting better prices. Lorna Ritchie of the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market said credits bearing its Core Carbon Principles label sold for about 25 per cent more on average than unlabelled credits. Meanwhile, carbon ratings agency BeZero Carbon said reforestation credits ranged from $5 to more than $40, depending on their ratings. The summit also highlighted gaps in Africa’s carbon market infrastructure, particularly the continent’s dependence on external verification services. The African Union Development Agency-New Partnership for Africa’s Development (AUDA-NEPAD) told participants that more than 90 per cent of carbon project verification work in Africa was still handled by organisations based outside the continent, contributing to delays affecting projects. artigo.texto: Effingham County hires firm to oversee Project Camellia data center Commissioners vote to bring in outside oversight for OpenAI campus EFFINGHAM COUNTY, Ga. (WTOC) - Effingham County commissioners voted to hire an outside firm to represent the county’s interests and oversee Project Camellia, the plan allowing OpenAI to build a 1,400-acre data center campus in the county. Residents say they want their voices heard as county leaders move forward with the project. County hires Charles Abbott Associates Effingham County voted to hire Charles Abbott Associates. The firm previously helped with the Hyundai site in Bryan County and the children’s hospital in Atlanta. County leaders said the firm will be their point of contact to address issues at the site, such as truck traffic or construction noise. The firm said it plans to have 12 people providing oversight, inspections and reviews of phase one of the project. “We currently provide building inspection and plan review services across the nation to over 100 communities. We’ve dealt with roughly two dozen data centers across the country as well, large distribution centers,” said Will Hart. Firm’s experience and meeting format The firm said it only works with local governments and has 40 years of experience with large industrial projects. Firm representatives only took questions from county leaders. There was no public comment for this portion of the meeting. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Partners with Muehlbauer Group for Production Equipment SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced a planned 100 megawatt-hour (MWh) capacity cell production line to meet demand for solid-state batteries from markets including AI data centers, aerospace and defense. To develop this line, QS has partnered with Muehlbauer Group, a leading German automation and manufacturing technology company, as an ecosystem provider of cell assembly equipment. QS is currently demonstrating scalable production of solid-state batteries using its highly automated Eagle Line pilot facility in San Jose. Muehlbauer evaluated the Eagle Line processes and developed design enhancements to bring the technology to mass production; engineering work on higher-throughput processes and equipment for the new line is underway. Start of cell production is targeted for 2028. "We are excited to welcome Muehlbauer to the QS ecosystem," said Dr. Siva Sivaram, president and CEO of QS. "Muehlbauer is an experienced and respected global player in manufacturing automation and battery equipment, and they've shown top-tier system integration capability, impressive engineering depth, and the scalability mindset necessary to bring our groundbreaking technology to the gigawatt-hour scale. They join a world-class ecosystem of technology partners as we bring solid-state batteries into mass production." "The Eagle Line proved to us that QuantumScape's solid-state technology is ready to scale to the next level," said Josef Markus Mühlbauer, CEO of Muehlbauer Group. "We have been working on-site with QS in San Jose to develop a scale-up plan built on the foundation of the Eagle Line. With decades of experience in turning innovative technologies into scalable production processes, we are proud to be a preferred partner within QuantumScape's ecosystem and to contribute our expertise to the mission of revolutionizing energy storage and enabling a more sustainable future." About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future.
