artigo.texto: Spokane County Commission extends halt on data centers through June, passes regulation baton to state A monthslong public pressure campaign led Spokane County officials this week to extend the existing pause on permitting for load data centers. The Spokane County Commission voted unanimously Tuesday on a resolution that halts the acceptance and processing of data center permits until June 1, 2027, or until the county establishes rules for the tech behemoths, whichever comes first. The measure replaces a pause put in place by the county commissioners in August that would’ve expired in December. The Spokane County Planning Commission was expected to have code updates and zoning amendments to present to the board for approval by the commission’s last meeting of the year if the board did not vote to extend the pause. Tuesday’s action included a work plan for how those updates will continue to move forward. The new timeline introduced by the commissioners could mean state lawmakers will now weigh in on the data center discussion. The matter is anticipated to come before the Legislature in the next session, which means Gov. Bob Ferguson could be weighing laws pertaining to data centers that will supersede any action by the county before the pause is up. Commissioner Al French, who faced heavy criticism, accusations and threats following the revelation through public records requests he participated in several meetings with industry members, called the ordeal a “political nightmare,” instead of what could have been a step forward for the county. He does not know if any company would be interested in moving forward locally in the current climate, he said. He took the offensive with members of the crowd who’ve been vocal in their distaste of French, often in less than socially acceptable ways. “This has certainly been an interesting 120 days,” French said. “Many of you have revealed the lengths you’re willing to go to to ensure that you get your way. You have lied to the public, you have engaged in character assassinations, you created and spread conspiracy theories, and quite frankly, just embarrassed yourself.” Spencer Lambdin, an outspoken member of the crowd as of late, screamed an expletive at French and stormed out of the meeting. “I think to myself as I listen to your accusations, ‘How proud your parents must be,’” French said, raising his hand in the direction of Lambdin. “He makes my case for me.” French took the time ahead of the vote to “clarify” the record and dispel rumors, accusations and “slanderous” comments lobbed by local residents lately, he said. He had Chief Civil Prosecutor Matthew Folsom corroborate the legal definition of public record regarding those aforementioned meetings to address the accusation they were held in secret. He did not discuss the ordinance with anyone at Avista, with a proposed data center developer or related industry members ahead of the vote, he said. He also has not entered into any nondisclosure agreements with anyone, or receive any compensation for “recruiting” companies or business leaders to Spokane – something he’s done throughout the Pacific Northwest for years, he said. “My reward in attracting a company or helping an existing company expand is helping someone get a job that might not have one, or get a better paying job than they already have,” French said. “… When I worked with Amazon to bring them to Spokane, my reward was seeing over a thousand people, residents in Hillyard, getting a good paying job with benefits working at the Amazon fulfillment center.” Planning Director Scott Chesney said the work plan directs the commission to consider the updates as part of the comprehensive plan update required by state law. The commission will continue their work, but state law may be updated prior to that point under the new pause timeline. Commissioners across party lines conveyed willingness to implement an extension early on, but it did little to quell concerns in what’s become a contentious issue locally and nationally. Over the past few months, constituents packed the county governing board’s weekly meetings, repeatedly calling for an extension on the pause, or moratorium, as soon as it took effect. A similar saga played out in public testimony Tuesday. Spokane resident Brittany Anderson, a stay-at-home mom who’s gained a local following in advocating against data centers, was one of many who told the commission she was not in support of the extension because it still left “significant loopholes,” like the possibility of breaking up a center between smaller parcels, she said. Anderson, and several who testified, referenced existing drafts of updates considered by the planning commission and included in part in the work plan moving forward. “I do not endorse this weak approach to safety and sustainability,” Anderson said. “Our residents deserve meaningful protection and transparency.” Anderson announced on social media this week that she’s running as a write-in candidate for Washington’s 5th Congressional district, in opposition to Democrat Carmela Conroy and Republican Rep. Michael Baumgartner. Her entrance to the race comes as some voters are already casting ballots. She said voters deserve more choice in the race. She did not share much on campaign points, only that she cares “about clean water, protecting our environment and farmland, affordable living, human rights, peace, and a government that answers to the people rather than wealthy donors and powerful interests.” “These aren’t issues I suddenly discovered during an election year,” the statement reads. “They’re issues I’ve already been speaking about, researching, and fighting for.” Folsom assured there were no workarounds for a developer to receive permits under the approved resolution. artigo.texto: O recuo na infraestrutura da Nscale em Loughton deve-se a atrasos na ligação à rede elétrica britânica. A Microsoft confirmou o cancelamento do acordo celebrado com a startup britânica Nscale para o aluguer de capacidade de computação num novo centro de dados dedicado à inteligência artificial (IA) em Loughton, a nordeste de Londres. A decisão assenta em constrangimentos infraestruturais na rede elétrica do Reino Unido. Segundo a imprensa britânica, a distribuidora UK Power Networks informou a Nscale de que o complexo de Loughton não teria acesso à energia elétrica necessária antes da década de 2030. Em declarações oficiais, um porta-voz da multinacional norte-americana esclareceu que a “decisão dizia respeito a um único local” e sublinhou que a empresa “continua empenhada na sua parceria com a Nscale”. Por seu turno, a Nscale confirmou que está a procurar fontes alternativas de energia elétrica para o local e que o percalço não afeta os restantes contratos da empresa. Impacto nas Ambições Britânicas e no Mercado de IA O projeto de Loughton tinha sido classificado pelo ex-primeiro-ministro britânico Keir Starmer como “o maior centro de dados de IA soberano do Reino Unido”. O anúncio do cancelamento surge numa altura em que a Nscale prepara a sua Oferta Pública Inicial (IPO) em Nova Iorque, com uma valorização estimada em 35 mil milhões de dólares. A desistência da Microsoft junta-se a outro recuo recente no mercado britânico de supercomputação: no início do ano, a OpenAI retirou-se de uma parceria com a Nscale e a Nvidia que visava implementar uma versão britânica do projeto de infraestruturas Stargate.

artigo.texto: Proposal to pause new data centers in Michigan City sparks protests over Google exemption MICHIGAN CITY, Ind. (WSBT) — Michigan City's Common Council took the first step toward pressing pause on future data center developments. But one major project would be exempt. Protesters outside Tuesday's meeting said the proposed moratorium does not go far enough because Google's data center project is already under construction and would not be affected. A proposal to pause new data center developments is back before the Michigan City Common Council, but opponents say the ordinance leaves out a major piece — Google's data center project that is already underway. They want the council to remove that exemption before moving forward. Protesters gathered outside City Hall before Tuesday's council meeting, chanting and holding signs. They say they are concerned about future data center projects and the rules governing the Google project that is already underway. "It totally exempts Google and all of its future phases and build out for a moratorium and effectively pause on data center development here," said protester Ashley Williams. The ordinance would pause future data center development, but it would not apply to current projects like Google's, which has already broken ground. Councilman Bryant Dabney (D), one of the ordinance's sponsors, says the city has no plans to stop the project. "Some people want us to stop what's going on now, but we have millions of dollars that have already been given to Michigan City with permitting fees, building fees that are happening over there," said Dabney. Tuesday was only a first reading of the ordinance. The council will be able to make amendments during its second reading at their next meeting on November 4.

artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – The Philippines will develop a national carbon market policy framework to regulate carbon credit projects and transactions, as the government seeks to attract climate investment and strengthen implementation of its emissions-reduction commitments under the Paris Agreement. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. ordered the development of the framework through Executive Order No. 127, signed on Oct. 13, directing the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to establish rules for the country’s participation in domestic and international carbon markets. The order, announced by the Presidential Communications Office on Saturday (Oct. 17), designates the DENR as the Philippines’ national authority for carbon markets and establishes an Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets to coordinate government policy and oversee implementation. The proposed Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework will set requirements for carbon credit projects, project approvals, transaction monitoring and benefit-sharing arrangements. It will also establish safeguards to ensure that carbon market activities comply with national policies and international standards. The government aims to use carbon markets to expand access to climate finance, technology and investment while supporting projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs,” the executive order states. The Philippines’ nationally determined contribution (NDC) sets out its climate commitments under the Paris Agreement. Carbon markets can help finance emissions-reduction activities by allowing eligible projects to generate credits that can be traded, subject to applicable rules and safeguards. Under the order, the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets will be chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair. Other members include the DENR, Department of Energy, Department of Agriculture, Department of Transportation, Department of Trade and Industry, and Securities and Exchange Commission. The committee will coordinate policies across government agencies, review implementation of the framework and approve reasonable processing fees for carbon market applications and certifications. The DENR will also establish and maintain the Philippine National Carbon Registry, a digital system intended to track carbon credits and related transactions. The agency is required to submit the proposed framework to the inter-agency committee for review and approval within 30 days of the executive order taking effect. The order will take effect upon publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. The framework is expected to provide a coordinated basis for the Philippines’ participation in carbon markets, including mechanisms for international cooperation under the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets. Its detailed rules, however, remain to be developed. ***

artigo.texto: Envision commissions a 125 MWh battery storage system for OCP in Morocco Envision Energy announces the commissioning of a 25 MW / 125 MWh LFP battery system at OCP Green Energy's Benguerir site, backed by $20 million in financing. Envision Energy has announced the commissioning of Morocco's first large-scale lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery energy storage system. Installed at OCP Green Energy's mining site in Benguerir, the system offers 25 MW of power and 125 MWh of capacity. According to the company, it is currently undergoing testing ahead of commercial operation. Battery storage is expanding across several markets, as shown by the installation of a 3.75 MWh storage system in Buffalo by Viridi and Good Carbon, the energization of three 24.6 MWh storage sites in Japan by GRITZ and the start of construction of 840 MWh of storage at Bertikow by Enlight and ENERTRAG. In Morocco, the contract with Envision Energy was signed in late 2025. A tool for managing peak hours Envision Energy says it supplied the entire system and led the commissioning work. The group integrated the batteries with the site's solar generation, grid conditions and industrial load profile. The system is designed to shift excess solar electricity produced during the day to peak consumption hours. According to the company, this shift would cut the site's electricity bill by about 25% during those peak hours. With five hours of storage, the system functions more as an industrial energy management tool than as a short-term grid asset. It is designed for a 25-year lifespan with daily charge and discharge cycles. Financing and national targets The project benefits from $20 million in financing from the Clean Technology Fund, managed by the African Development Bank Group. For OCP, the focus is on reducing peak-hour costs over the system's lifetime rather than on the battery's capacity itself, according to the project's description. John Lee, Envision Energy's managing director for the Middle East and Africa, called the project a historic step for Morocco's energy transition. Omar Kadir, CEO of OCP Green Energy, said storage extends the group's energy strategy and could help integrate renewables into the national grid. The project supports the country's target of drawing 52% of its installed electricity capacity from renewable sources by 2030, according to the release. artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, durante evento político nos Estados Unidos. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP) Estagiária de jornalismo Publicado em 21 de outubro de 2026 às 11h44. O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta quarta-feira, 21, que data centers no país devem produzir sua própria energia elétrica e firmar acordos financeiros com as populações dos locais onde eles se instalam. As declarações ocorrem em meio a tensões entre moradores do interior do país e o setor tecnológico, que avança pelo território com data centers para atender à alta demanda da inteligência artificial. "Determino que novos data centers de grande porte — em alguns casos, gigantescos — produzam sua própria energia elétrica e forneçam ou vendam qualquer excedente para a comunidade local ou para a rede elétrica; assim, não haverá aumento nos preços da eletricidade. Na verdade, pode até ocorrer uma redução substancial.", afirmou o republicano em publicação na rede social Truth. "O mesmo vale para outros aspectos! Se as empresas quiserem que seus data centers sejam bem aceitos, que paguem à comunidade — e/ou aos indivíduos que a compõem — uma espécie de 'dividendo'." Ele afirmou também que tem "observado esse processo atentamente", em que data centers "que eram muito malvistos em determinadas regiões tornaram-se extremamente bem aceitos após a formalização de um acordo financeiro". A expansão acelerada de datacenters de IA pelo interior da América do Norte está gerando conflitos entre moradores e grandes empresas de tecnologia. De acordo com dados da plataforma Data Center Map, existem 4287 estruturas nos Estados Unidos, sendo 1500 deles em construção. Essa nova onda de investimentos tem uma diferença essencial daquilo que já existe no país. Ao passo que 87% dos datacenters em operação estão em áreas urbanas, 67% dos novos estão sendo construídos em áreas rurais. Nessa frente de expansão, porém, as empresas de tecnologia têm encontrado resistência da população. Centenas de organizações em 42 estados dos EUA já se mobilizaram contra projetos em suas comunidades, segundo levantamento da Data Center Watch divulgado pela Wired. Os casos se multiplicam. Nos estados de Montana e Utah, comunidades com poucos recursos políticos e jurídicos tentam frear obras bilionárias. Um estudo de 2023 estimou que gerar entre dez e cinquenta respostas de tamanho médio em chatbots de IA consome meio litro de água. A Agência Internacional de Energia calculou que datacenters usaram 140 bilhões de litros de água globalmente só para resfriamento em 2023, segundo a CBC. Do lado das empresas e governos, o argumento é de segurança nacional e competitividade econômica. "O potencial do que estamos criando é muito importante para a defesa e para a economia", disse o investidor Kevin O'Leary, que apoia a construção de um datacenter de 4 mil acres em Utah, à CNN. O governador do estado, Spencer Cox, foi na mesma direção: "Cada estado tem uma obrigação de permitir que esses datacenters sejam construídos." Do lado dos moradores, a demanda é mais transparência, estudos independentes e tempo para avaliar o impacto antes que as obras comecem. Caroline Gleich, ativista ambiental de Utah, disse à emissora: "Vamos fazer um estudo de impacto ambiental e publicá-lo. Vamos colocar algumas coisas por escrito e dar à comunidade tempo para revisá-las."

artigo.texto: Facing pushback on data centers, tech giants are promising hosts more money and fewer secrets With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America’s technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses. The promises come as anti-data center sentiment has become a potent issue in the midterm election with control of Congress and 36 governors’ offices on the line. In addition to ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build. With host communities across the U.S. turning against their gargantuan data centers, America's technology giants are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts, keep fewer secrets or shower more money onto the communities willing to allow the server warehouses. The new raft of promises from the world's richest companies comes as anti-data center sentiment has become a potent issue in the midterm elections, with control of Congress and 36 governors' offices on the line. Despite backing from President Donald Trump, the data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom have become politically toxic. Community opposition that blocks municipal permits has become a bottleneck, and tech giants could face even more challenges if voters next month elect more public officials who are skeptical of data centers. The tech industry says it has gotten the message. In addition to ramping up financial incentives, officials with Google and Meta said in interviews with The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent with communities where they would like to build. Companies are also making pledges to reduce their impact on the environment and offering assurances that data centers will boost local property values — all while maintaining AI is a positive force for the American economy, despite its skeptics. Tech giants pledge more transparency Devi Thomas, Google’s global head of community development and engagement, told AP that she wouldn’t call resistance to data centers a “backlash,” but that “there are often community questions to be addressed.” “Early public consultation is increasingly a very important part of the process. We have done as much as we can to make sure communities are involved early on,” Thomas said. Earlier this month, Amazon rolled out its “Amazon Data Center Commitment," including pledges to improve the environmental rating of its backup diesel generators and disclose more about its data centers' energy and water use. It also said — as have Microsoft and Google — that it had stopped requiring government officials to sign non-disclosure agreements. The use of non-disclosure agreements has meant people in host communities may know little or nothing about a project until it shows up on a municipal board’s voting agenda. Besides that, tech companies often have hidden their involvement in a project behind a code name and developers who do the legwork with local governments, critics and other developers say. That practice “raises people’s suspicion as to what’s truly happening,” said Anita Verma-Lallian, a developer with data center projects in Arizona. Meta is always evaluating how well it shares information with communities, said Lindsay Elin, Meta’s vice president of public policy and external affairs. “As part of that work, we are reviewing our use of non-disclosure agreements,” she said in a statement to the AP. In a report this month that sharply criticized data center giants including Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft, several Senate Democrats said companies have used non-disclosure agreements to freeze out the public. The report also said the companies aggressively seek state and local tax breaks and do not cover the entire cost of the electric-grid buildout needed for energy-hungry data centers. Spending ramps up in host communities, along with skepticism The dominant players in the industry — Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft — project they’ll spend more than $600 billion this year combined on capital projects, primarily data center construction in the U.S. Even as the companies prepare to spend more to entice communities — payments that some critics call “bribes” — Trump urged them in a social media post Wednesday to pay people and communities a “dividend” if they “want to make their Data Centers popular.” “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.,” Trump wrote. Meta and Amazon said recently they will each spend $1 billion on financial incentives to host communities in the coming years, on top of millions they already spend to support schools, charities and job training. Google says its investments in local programs in data center communities will reach $1 billion by the end of 2027. Microsoft has pointed to a couple local tax breaks that it will forego. And Google recently said for all of its new data center campuses, the company will pay full real property taxes on the buildings and land. The companies have known since last fall that community opposition was becoming a serious problem. Data center demand began driving up electric bills last year across a 13-state electricity grid stretching from Illinois to New Jersey and Maryland, angering ratepayers. The outcry led to promises from the tech giants to pay the cost of the power infrastructure to feed their data centers, while Microsoft rolled out its five-point “Community-First AI Infrastructure” plan. artigo.texto: India’s Downstream Battery Storage Manufacturing Capacity Reaches 86 GWh Only 21.6% of India's battery manufacturing capacity is operational October 22, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights India’s operational battery energy storage manufacturing capacity is heavily concentrated in downstream manufacturing, which accounts for 92% of the total, while cell manufacturing represents just 8%, according to Mercom India’s recently released Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report. India’s downstream battery storage manufacturing capacity, including battery packs, containers, and integrated energy storage systems, stands at approximately 86 GWh. The gap between cell and downstream manufacturing capacity highlights the country’s dependence on imported battery cells, materials, and specialized equipment. Only 21.6% of India’s combined operational and planned battery storage manufacturing capacity is operational. The remaining capacity comprises projects under construction or announced. Most identified cell manufacturing capacity has yet to become operational. “India’s battery manufacturing industry is expanding rapidly, but domestic cell production is still at an early stage. While downstream manufacturing has grown much faster, enabling companies to assemble battery systems domestically, the industry continues to rely on imported cells and materials. A large amount of cell capacity is under construction or announced, but the real challenge will be converting that capacity into stable commercial production,” commented Raj Prabhu, CEO at Mercom Capital Group. Manufacturing Capacity and Pipeline India’s existing cell and downstream manufacturers accounted for 47% of identified capacity across operational and planned facilities, while new entrants accounted for 53%. Lithium-based chemistries dominated manufacturing capacity across both cell and downstream manufacturing segments. Converting planned capacity into commercial production remains a challenge, particularly for cell manufacturing. Geographic Distribution Gujarat accounted for 51% of India’s battery storage manufacturing capacity under construction, followed by Maharashtra. Together, Gujarat and Maharashtra accounted for 71% of battery storage manufacturing capacity under construction. Competitive domestic manufacturing will require consistent production quality, competitive costs, and sufficient capacity utilization. “Manufacturers will need to achieve competitive costs, consistent quality, strong yields, and sufficient utilization, and that will be much easier with a clear demand trajectory and better visibility on how quickly storage deployment will scale. India has a significant opportunity to build a competitive battery manufacturing ecosystem, but demand and supply need to develop in parallel,” Prabhu said. Battery Costs and Import Dependence Battery systems accounted for more than half of utility-scale energy storage project capital expenditure in the second quarter of 2026, with cells representing a substantial share of battery system costs. Cell pricing and sourcing remain important to project economics and domestic manufacturers’ competitiveness. Despite the expansion of downstream manufacturing, India continues to depend on imported cells, materials, and specialized equipment. The gap between operational cell and downstream capacity highlights the need for an integrated domestic battery supply chain. Government Support Government programs support the development of domestic battery cell manufacturing capacity. The production-linked incentive program for advanced chemistry cell manufacturing has allocated ₹181 billion (~$1.91 billion) to support 50 GWh of manufacturing capacity, plus an additional 5 GWh for niche technologies. Among projects receiving active support under the program, 6.4 GWh of manufacturing capacity is operational, while another 28.6 GWh is under construction. The government’s viability gap funding program also mandates a 20% local-content requirement for supported projects. Eligible downstream components and services can satisfy this requirement without the use of domestically manufactured battery cells, limiting its direct effect on demand for domestic cell production. Manufacturing Outlook Further expansion will depend on storage deployment and the conversion of planned manufacturing capacity into commercial production. Manufacturers need visibility into project awards, storage deployment, and equipment demand to support long-term investment in cell manufacturing. Competitive costs, consistent quality, higher manufacturing yields, and adequate capacity utilization will remain important as new facilities begin operating. “For domestic manufacturing to continue expanding, manufacturers need clear long-term visibility on storage deployment, project awards, and equipment demand before committing large amounts of capital to new cell plants. That visibility is critical to supporting capacity expansion, maintain utilization, and improve cost competitiveness. Domestic manufacturers will ultimately need to compete on cost, quality, reliability, and supply availability as more capacity comes online,” said Prabhu. Mercom India’s Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report assesses India’s stationary battery storage manufacturing sector, from materials and cells to packs, containers, power electronics, and integrated battery energy storage systems. The report covers operational and planned capacity, technology trends, supply-chain dependencies, demand, government policies, localization opportunities, and manufacturing challenges. It also provides an outlook through 2030. For the complete report, visit: Energy Storage Manufacturing Ecosystem Report.

artigo.texto: Spartanburg County weighs new rules for data center development Officials discuss changes to zoning ordinance as residents push back on Pine Street project SPARTANBURG COUNTY, S.C. (FOX Carolina) - Spartanburg County officials are considering new standards for data center development as they work to establish rules for future projects. The county’s Land Use Committee discussed potential amendments to the Performance Zoning Ordinance, known as the PZO, during a meeting Tuesday at Cleveland Park’s event space. The discussion followed months of research and visits to other parts of the country to examine how other jurisdictions regulate data centers. The county’s planning and development director led a discussion comparing data center regulations in nearby counties and other states. Potential new standards Proposed changes could address the size and type of data centers, their equipment and their proximity to existing homes. Other potential standards include setbacks and buffers, noise mitigation, and measures to manage the effects of electricity and water use. Land Use Committee Chair Grant DeShields said regulating data centers requires balancing competing interests. “The complication of trying to regulate data centers in a proper way that we don’t alienate new data centers from coming here, but at the same time protect our legacy landowners that live here and the people and the citizens that we already have that enjoy peaceful neighborhoods,” DeShields said. DeShields said the county’s current moratorium on data center development is temporary and that establishing permanent regulations is a priority. “There are not data center specific regulations at all. That was the reason for the moratorium to begin with,” DeShields said. County staff also are considering whether to restrict where larger data centers can be built. One option is an overlay district that would designate specific areas for the facilities. The PZO governs development in the county’s Southwest Planning Area, an unincorporated area near Duncan, Lyman, Reidville, Greer and Woodruff. The rest of the county, including the Pine Street corridor, is governed by a separate ordinance, the Unified Land Management Ordinance, or ULMO. DeShields said any changes to the PZO would apply to the entire county, including areas governed by the ULMO. The Valara data center site along South Pine Street falls under the ULMO. The project has faced legal challenges over its classification as a “minor development.” DeShields said the county is working to address potential environmental impacts at the Valara site through a community development agreement. He said the agreement includes environmental studies and monitoring requirements, separate from the broader zoning changes under consideration. Resident reaction Spartanburg County resident Lisa Weir attended Tuesday’s meeting and said she was encouraged by the discussion. “I feel like they are understanding the necessity to put guardrails around or fences around what’s happening with the data centers,” Weir said. Weir said she appreciated hearing about standards used in other areas, including a jurisdiction in Pennsylvania that she said requires buffers of 500 to 1,000 feet between data centers and other properties. She described the county’s current land-use ordinance as “very complicated” compared with those in other communities. But she questioned why the discussion had not happened sooner. “This meeting could have taken place about a year ago,” Weir said. Weir cited the Pine Street site’s proximity to schools, including E.P. Todd, Pine Street School and the South Carolina School for the Deaf and the Blind, as a primary concern. She urged more residents to join opposition to data center development without additional regulations. “I would appreciate if many more people of Spartanburg would mobilize and get involved in it. Because it is imperative that we do this,” Weir said. “It won’t be an immediate thing that we see. But it will have long-term health effects down the line. For everyone.” What’s next Tuesday’s discussion was not a final vote on new data center regulations. County staff must continue developing the proposed amendments before they can proceed through the formal review and approval process. City staff said they plan to discuss recommendations to the planning commission sometime in November. Feel more informed, prepared, and connected with FOX Carolina. artigo.texto: CPQD integra projeto de R$ 68,6 milhões para fabricar células de baterias Iniciativa liderada pelo SENAI prevê planta semiindustrial de baterias de íons de lítio para mobilidade elétrica e armazenamento de energia. O CPQD participa de um projeto de R$ 68,6 milhões voltado à produção nacional de células de baterias de íons de lítio, utilizadas em veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Conduzida pelo Instituto SENAI de Inovação em Eletroquímica (ISI-Eletroquímica), a iniciativa prevê a implantação de uma planta semiindustrial para fabricação de componentes, testes de processos produtivos e desenvolvimento tecnológico em parceria com a indústria. O CPQD atuará na avaliação do desempenho e do comportamento das células produzidas, utilizando sua experiência em ensaios laboratoriais para verificar requisitos técnicos de qualidade, segurança e confiabilidade. Planta semiindustrial terá produção de células de íons de lítio A infraestrutura será instalada no ISI-Eletroquímica e contemplará diferentes etapas do processo produtivo, desde a preparação dos materiais utilizados nos eletrodos até a fabricação de componentes, montagem das células e formação eletroquímica. A unidade permitirá produzir os primeiros lotes em escala pré-industrial e validar procedimentos de fabricação. Também será utilizada para desenvolver tecnologias em colaboração com as empresas participantes, considerando as necessidades de aplicação dos componentes. CPQD fará avaliação técnica das baterias A atuação do CPQD no projeto está relacionada à experiência acumulada pela instituição em pesquisas sobre baterias e sistemas de energia. O centro de pesquisa desenvolveu infraestrutura laboratorial para avaliação desses dispositivos ainda no período de expansão da telefonia celular no Brasil. Ao longo dos anos, participou de projetos envolvendo tecnologias de armazenamento de energia com empresas como Embraer, Marelli, CETEP, CPFL e PHB Eletrônica. Essa experiência será aplicada à análise técnica das células fabricadas na nova planta, fornecendo informações para o aperfeiçoamento das soluções desenvolvidas. “O desafio é criar condições para que o Brasil avance em uma cadeia industrial estratégica, com capacidade para produzir, testar e aperfeiçoar tecnologias utilizadas em diferentes setores da economia”, afirma Gustavo Sinzato, gerente de Soluções em Energias Renováveis do CPQD. Projeto reúne empresas de energia e indústria automotiva A iniciativa conta com a participação de empresas de diferentes segmentos industriais, entre elas Petrobras, WEG, Stellantis, Volkswagen, Marcopolo, Arkema, CBA e Grupo Moura. A colaboração envolve instituições de pesquisa e representantes da indústria interessados no desenvolvimento de tecnologias para mobilidade elétrica e armazenamento de energia. Entre os objetivos estão a ampliação da capacidade brasileira de fabricação de componentes e o desenvolvimento de processos que possam ser utilizados na cadeia produtiva de baterias de íons de lítio. artigo.texto: Over the course of a sometimes contentious, sometimes awkward hour, the two candidates for Wisconsin governor sparred over taxes, data centers and abortion in the only debate of their general election campaign Wednesday night. Both Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democrat, and U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican, declined on several occasions to attach specific numbers to their policy proposals, instead offering broad assurances that taxes would be cut while priorities would remain well funded. From their opening remarks onwards, both repeatedly criticized one another’s records, as each sought to appeal to voters in what is expected to be a close race largely defined by concerns over the economy and rising costs. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. “Taxes have went up every single year that David Crowley has been county executive. You know what he’s going to do as governor,” Tiffany said in his opening remarks, when asked about his strong support for the policies of President Donald Trump. Asked about rising taxes in Milwaukee County, Crowley said he was proud of his bipartisan achievements — including one deal that increased the county sales tax — and accused Tiffany of selling out Wisconsin. “This is about having a governor who’s going to work for you, someone who’s going to invest in your future, or someone who’s going to work for the billionaires that are bankrolling their campaign or doing exactly what Donald Trump wants them to do,” he said. Crowley, a moderate Milwaukee Democrat running as a pragmatic dealmaker, and Tiffany, a staunch conservative from the Northwoods running as a common-sense everyman, both said they’d restructure taxes but offered few specifics. Tiffany said he would return the state’s projected $3 billion surplus to voters directly, and eventually said it would be through a combination of income tax and property tax reductions, and a 10 percent tax cut for families earning less than $150,000. “I would prefer not to do it as a one-time check because people don’t plan their futures based on one-time checks,” he said, referring to a failed deal out of the Legislature that included rebate checks. “So I want to see long-term tax reductions that … people are going to benefit from not just next year, but in the future, also.” He did not offer specifics when asked how he would make up for lost tax revenue, but said it would derive from a growing economy. “There is enough money in Madison to be able to backfill those things that we need to,” he said. Crowley was even more vague on his plans for restructuring taxes. Asked whether he would create a new tax bracket for Wisconsin’s highest earners, Crowley first pointed to Tiffany’s vote for Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included tax cuts for America’s highest earners. Then he called for a holistic change to the state tax system, including changing how the state distributes money to local communities. “Do you have a number and a percentage?” asked Matt Smith, a reporter with WISN-TV and one of the debate moderators. “What I have is … that we have to make sure that we’re working with the state Legislature to make sure that we’re creating a fair and taxable system that works for all income earners,” Crowley responded. Some overlap among contentious policy differences Unsurprisingly, Crowley and Tiffany disagreed on many issues. Tiffany said he would mandate that local, county and state law enforcement coordinate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, while Crowley said that local law enforcement should not enter into detainer agreements, and that ICE should be banned from wearing masks. Tiffany said he would support researching medicinal marijuana, while Crowley has called for full legalization of both medicinal and recreational cannabis, which he argued could bring in revenue to cover healthcare costs. There were some areas of overlap. Both said that they would not end the private school voucher system, and Tiffany said he would consider raising the income cap for which students can participate. Crowley said that the voucher system, which was developed in Milwaukee, should not be expanded, and that more money should go toward public schools. “But I don’t think that you can just abruptly shut down this program,” he said. “As of this moment, we are not in a position to push all of these children towards any of our public schools.” They sparred over data center development, although they agreed on the broad strokes of putting restrictions on developments. Tiffany said he would require any proposals to follow certain conditions, including ensuring that utilities don’t go up, not converting farmland and offering local communities control. He accused Crowley of flip-flopping on the issue of repealing tax incentives for tech companies to site their developments in Wisconsin. “I have been consistent over the last year, that we are not going to pay those subsidies to these companies. He just came around in the last week when he figured out that’s where the public is,” Tiffany said. “I will not put my finger to the wind when making decisions like this.” Crowley responded that he has long been “open to reforming the sales tax incentives that these data centers have been getting,” and that he would sign a bill to repeal those incentives, which were written into the 2023 state budget by the GOP-held Legislature and signed by Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley also said that he supports pausing existing developments while a statewide environmental review is conducted. artigo.texto: FracTracker e Public Citizen identificaram 35 ações de permissão tomadas pelos reguladores no Texas nas semanas após o governador Greg Abbott ordenar uma moratória. Os reguladores do Texas não pararam de processar licenças para projetos de data centers quando o governador Greg Abbott ordenou uma pausa no mês passado, de acordo com uma análise de registros públicos divulgada na segunda-feira pelo grupo de vigilância de petróleo e gás FracTracker. Em meio a uma onda de oposição pública à crescente construção de infraestrutura digital no Texas, a Abbott instruiu a Comissão de Qualidade Ambiental do Texas, em uma carta de 21 de setembro, “para suspender todas as licenças solicitadas pelos data centers”. Mas o FracTracker, em colaboração com o Public Citizen, identificou 35 ações de autorização tomadas pelo TCEQ para projetos de data centers nas semanas subsequentes. “A TCEQ continuou analisando os pedidos e emitindo aprovações que permitem o prosseguimento do desenvolvimento do data center”, disseram os grupos em um comunicado à imprensa na segunda-feira. “Essas ações não sinalizam uma agência tentando fazer uma pausa.” O escritório da Abbott e o TCEQ não responderam imediatamente a um pedido de comentário. Abbott descreveu a sua moratória sobre projectos de centros de dados como uma oportunidade para as agências estatais avaliarem o impacto das instalações nos recursos hídricos e na estabilidade da rede. “Nenhuma outra agência estadual deverá avançar com aprovações regulatórias relacionadas a data centers até que esta informação seja adquirida”, escreveu Abbott em sua carta de 21 de setembro ao diretor executivo da TCEQ, Kelly Keel. Desde essa carta, o TCEQ acelerou ou designou engenheiros para 14 licenças, aprovou a cobertura de águas pluviais para 11, certificou estimativas de emissões para sete e emitiu edital público para três, de acordo com documentos de licenciamento coletados pela FracTracker e Public Citizen. As licenças referem-se à construção de instalações de geração de energia a gás para instalações que necessitam de muita energia. Todos os maiores projetos de energia a gás atualmente propostos no Texas destinam-se especificamente a servir centros de dados, que são planejados principalmente para operar inteligência artificial. Os projectos libertariam dezenas de milhares de toneladas de poluentes regulamentados, de acordo com documentos de licenciamento, bem como mais de 100 milhões de toneladas por ano de gases com efeito de estufa – uma quantidade enorme, aproximadamente igual às emissões anuais de um país industrializado de média dimensão. No dia seguinte à pausa da Abbott nas licenças de data center, em 22 de setembro, FracTracker e Public Citizen descobriram que a TCEQ enviou avisos de aprovação preliminar para três grandes projetos: NRG Prairie Energy Center, a usina de energia ABI-1 da VoltaGrid e o data center autoalimentado da Nexus em Hubbard. A agência abriu períodos de comentários públicos sobre dois desses projetos nos dias seguintes. FracTracker e Public Citizen encontraram aprovações de licenças de gerenciamento de águas pluviais para construção de data centers emitidas após 21 de setembro, inclusive para o Caldwell Valley Technology Park no condado de Caldwell, campus Abilene de Crusoe e campus Cedar Creek da EdgeConneX. O relatório identificou vários outros projetos que continuam a avançar através de licenciamento. Por exemplo, os registros mostram que o TCEQ recebeu um pedido de licença para geradores na Edged Energy em Dallas em 6 de outubro, e um engenheiro concluiu uma revisão inicial em 9 de outubro. “Nossa pesquisa descobriu inconsistências gritantes entre as ações regulatórias e as diretrizes do Governador Abbott”, disse Sam Law, gerente de comunicações da FracTracker Alliance e autor do relatório. “Precisamos de uma pausa real para estudar as ameaças que representam à terra, à água e aos meios de subsistência dos texanos.” Sobre esta história Talvez você tenha notado: esta história, como todas as notícias que publicamos, é de leitura gratuita. artigo.texto: Over half of Indiana counties now restrict data centers The number of Indiana communities pausing or outright banning data center development has grown. About thirty communities had enacted some form of ban in July. Now, that number has increased to at least 50 counties — or over half — across the state. That’s according to the Indiana University Environmental Resilience Institute, which tracks the local regulations. The collected data shows 32 counties have passed moratoriums, 14 regulatory ordinances, and in four communities data centers are not permitted. At least one county — Marshall — has made that ban permanent. Read More: Madison County commissioners extend data center moratorium for full year “What we’re seeing that’s new but not really surprising since July is an increased number of moratoria, and also several of those moratoria becoming permanent decisions, whether that is a ban on data center development or an ordinance like an updated zoning code or other local policy,” said Therese Dorau, Assistant Director for Climate Policy and Implementation at the Institute. Some counties approved a limited time for temporary bans. Data centers are large facilities that house the computer servers behind cloud computing, streaming services and artificial intelligence. Because those servers run constantly and generate significant heat, the facilities can draw enormous amounts of electricity and water. Indiana lawmakers created policies to lure large data center developers to the state, including laws that enable tax breaks and other incentives. That has attracted large technology companies like Google, Amazon and Meta. These developments have drawn opposition in communities around Indiana and across the U.S. due to concerns about electricity, water and land. Critics have also questioned environmental impacts like noise and air pollution, as well as whether the economic benefits such as long-term jobs will actually benefit local communities. Some data projects are making moves to connect to the electrical grid. Earlier this month, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission approved a $737.3 million plan by Central Indiana utility AES Indiana to power a 390-megawatt Google data center project in Monrovia. The companies said Google will cover 100% of the costs, but critics are concerned that $74 million in transmission upgrades will be passed to customers. The IU institute created an updated resource with information about what science and research says about some of these topics. “In my opinion, a responsible use of a moratorium is to take a pause. It’s not to make a permanent decision, but really, it’s a way to say we’re going to put a timeframe on which our government is going to do more in-depth research about what is right for our community,” Dorau said. Contact WFYI data journalist Zak Cassel at zcassel@wfyi.org

artigo.texto: There are now 170 megapacks in place alongside the onshore converter station for Ørsted’s Hornsea 3 Offshore Wind Farm, near Norwich, Norfolk. Each is the length of a classic Routemaster London bus but weighs the same as five buses. The system, known as Iceni after the Norfolk-based warrior tribe of the Roman era, will have a capacity of 600 MWh (and a 300 MW power rating). This is equivalent to the daily power consumption of 80,000 UK homes. The Iceni team comprises specialists from Ørsted, Hitachi Energy, Knights Brown & Tesla working together on this first-of-its-kind project. What makes this BESS unique is the split layout of the site with the two areas, separated by the Hornsea 3 Onshore Converter station, linked by 18 x 33 kV cables, each over 600 meters in length. In addition, the shared grid connection point with Hornsea 3 has added additional technical complexity over a stand-alone connection point to the National Grid. The project is now in the final stages of the mechanical and electrical installation, with the 33 kV cross-site cables currently being installed and terminated. The first stage of commissioning and testing is well underway, and preparations are being made for energization of the BESS Transformer. When completed, the battery energy storage system will be one of the largest in Europe. Beatrice d’Eufemia, Project Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said: “It’s a milestone moment for Ørsted that construction is now complete on our first large-scale battery energy storage system in the UK. “The system will make the best use of renewable energy produced in the UK as when electricity generation exceeds demand, the excess can be stored and then used when demand is greater, helping balance the grid, and lower electricity costs for everyone.” Richard Swann, Construction Manager for Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said: “It’s a real testament to the hard work, dedication and cooperation of the team from many different organizations that the construction has been completed successfully.” David Shillabeer, Head of Transmission & Distribution, at Knights Brown, said: “Reaching this milestone is a significant achievement for everyone involved in the Iceni project. Delivering a battery energy storage system of this scale has required close collaboration between Ørsted, Knights Brown and the many other organizations that have contributed to its success. “Beyond the engineering, the scheme has enabled us to invest in local people, develop skills and create opportunities across Norfolk and the wider region. We are proud to have played our part in an important project that will support the UK’s transition to a more resilient, low-carbon energy system, while leaving a positive legacy for the communities in which we work.”

artigo.texto: Partners with Muehlbauer Group for Production Equipment SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced a planned 100 megawatt-hour (MWh) capacity cell production line to meet demand for solid-state batteries from markets including AI data centers, aerospace and defense. To develop this line, QS has partnered with Muehlbauer Group, a leading German automation and manufacturing technology company, as an ecosystem provider of cell assembly equipment. QS is currently demonstrating scalable production of solid-state batteries using its highly automated Eagle Line pilot facility in San Jose. Muehlbauer evaluated the Eagle Line processes and developed design enhancements to bring the technology to mass production; engineering work on higher-throughput processes and equipment for the new line is underway. Start of cell production is targeted for 2028. "We are excited to welcome Muehlbauer to the QS ecosystem,” said Dr. Siva Sivaram, president and CEO of QS. "Muehlbauer is an experienced and respected global player in manufacturing automation and battery equipment, and they’ve shown top-tier system integration capability, impressive engineering depth, and the scalability mindset necessary to bring our groundbreaking technology to the gigawatt-hour scale. They join a world-class ecosystem of technology partners as we bring solid-state batteries into mass production.” "The Eagle Line proved to us that QuantumScape’s solid-state technology is ready to scale to the next level,” said Josef Markus Mühlbauer, CEO of Muehlbauer Group. "We have been working on-site with QS in San Jose to develop a scale-up plan built on the foundation of the Eagle Line. With decades of experience in turning innovative technologies into scalable production processes, we are proud to be a preferred partner within QuantumScape’s ecosystem and to contribute our expertise to the mission of revolutionizing energy storage and enabling a more sustainable future.” About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future. The company’s next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. For more information, visit www.quantumscape.com. About Muehlbauer Group With around 4,500 employees at 40 locations worldwide and 45 years of experience, the Muehlbauer Group has developed into one of the most advanced suppliers of complete production solutions. The company has achieved a leading position in the semiconductor industry with its unique die sorting technology and serves 90% of worldwide demand for RFID. More than 90,000 machines and systems have already been installed worldwide, and the Group specialises in high-precision, high-speed assembly systems, even in cleanroom environments. For more information, visit www.muehlbauer.de. artigo.texto: Algeria, Tunisia and Egypt are stepping up investment in renewable energy and battery storage, with new wind and solar tenders alongside plans to expand local energy storage manufacturing across North Africa. Algeria’s state-owned electricity utility Sonelgaz has issued a tender for the development of two wind farms with a combined capacity of 200 MW. The projects will be located in the provinces of Laghouat and Djelfa, with each facility expected to contribute 100 MW of wind power. The contract covers engineering, civil construction, equipment procurement, installation and commissioning. The scope offers opportunities for renewable energy developers and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies capable of delivering large-scale wind infrastructure, including the electrical systems required to connect the projects to the national grid. In Tunisia, the state-owned electricity and gas company STEG has launched a procurement process for a 50 MW solar power plant in the Tataouine Governorate. The facility will be equipped with a battery energy storage system (BESS) rated at 10 MW/20 MWh, enabling electricity generated during periods of strong sunlight to be stored for later use. The project is supported by financing from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). READ: Uganda targets commercial oil production by June 2027 Energy flexibility The inclusion of battery storage is expected to improve the management of intermittent solar generation and provide greater flexibility in electricity supply. The tender could attract companies specialising in photovoltaic technology, energy storage equipment and integrated power management systems. Egypt is pursuing a different approach by developing domestic capacity to assemble battery storage systems. Rosatom’s energy storage division has entered into a partnership with Telecom and Technology to establish an assembly facility with an annual production capacity of 500 MWh. The facility will target industrial and telecommunications customers, sectors that require dependable electricity supplies and backup power solutions. In Israel, Doral Group is expanding its Hadarey Shean project with an additional 150 MW of solar generation capacity and 800 MWh of battery storage. The expansion is valued at approximately US $260.89M, according to the reported investment figure. The projects demonstrate the region’s growing focus on combining renewable electricity generation with storage technologies to improve power system reliability. Algeria’s wind tender and Tunisia’s solar-plus-storage development are creating procurement opportunities, while Egypt’s planned assembly facility could strengthen the regional supply chain for battery systems. For international developers and EPC contractors, the latest initiatives provide potential opportunities across project design, construction, equipment supply and storage integration. Companies seeking contracts in the region will need to assess technical specifications, grid connection requirements, financing conditions and local procurement rules. As renewable energy deployment expands across North Africa and neighbouring markets, the ability to deliver projects that combine generation capacity with effective storage solutions is likely to become increasingly important for developers seeking to compete in the region.

artigo.texto: VW ID. Cross ganha versão com bateria menor por R$ 158 mil na Europa Com bateria menor de 37 kWh e autonomia de até 324 km, nova opção de entrada do SUV elétrico busca atrair motoristas urbanos e trabalhadores que dependem do deslocamento diário A Volkswagen deu início à pré-venda de uma nova opção de entrada para o ID. Cross, menor SUV 100% elétrico da alemã. A novidade adota um pacote de baterias menor, de 37 kWh, mirando consumidores que buscam menor preço de aquisição para trajetos urbanos ou de deslocamento diário. Na Alemanha, a versão parte de 27.995 euros (cerca de R$ 158 mil), valor que torna o utilitário esportivo o elétrico de entrada da marca. A nova configuração expande o portfólio apresentado globalmente em meados de julho, que estreou com a versão topo de linha Style por 36,5 mil euros (cerca de R$ 222 mil). Baterias, autonomia e recarga A nova bateria de 37 kWh de capacidade líquida oferece autonomia de até 324 km (WLTP). Ela pode ser combinada a dois níveis de potência: 85 kW (116 cv) e 99 kW (135 cv), ambas atingindo velocidade máxima de 160 km/h. Para os motoristas que buscam maior alcance, a gama do ID. Cross contempla ainda o conjunto com bateria de 52 kWh e motor de 155 kW (211 cv), capaz de rodar até 427 km com uma única carga. Em estações de carregamento rápido em corrente contínua (DC) de até 105 kW, as baterias recuperam de 10% a 80% da carga em cerca de 24 minutos. Versões, espaço e tecnologia a bordo O ID. Cross com bateria de 37 kWh é oferecido nas linhas de acabamento Trend, Life e Style. Mesmo na opção de entrada Trend, o SUV compacto inclui itens de série como assistente de estacionamento dianteiro e traseiro (Park Distance Control) e integração com smartphones sem fio (App Connect). Construído sobre a nova plataforma MEB+, o modelo tem dimensões externas similares às do T-Cross convencional que conhecemos aqui pelo mercado brasileiro (4,15 metros de comprimento), mas aproveita a arquitetura elétrica para ampliar o espaço interno: - Porta-malas principal: 475 litros (20 litros a mais que o T-Cross a combustão), além de um compartimento sob o piso. - Porta-malas dianteiro (frunk): 25 litros sob o capô, ideal para acomodar os cabos de recarga. - Cabine digital e nostálgica: traz tela central de 12,9 polegadas e painel digital de 10,25 polegadas, que conta com um modo clássico capaz de reproduzir o layout analógico dos mostradores do Golf de primeira geração. - Assistências avançadas: opcionais e versões superiores contam com o sistema Connected Travel Assist (que reconhece semáforos e para o carro automaticamente no sinal vermelho), função Vehicle-to-Load (V2L, para alimentar eletrônicos externos de até 3,6 kW), som Harman Kardon e bancos elétricos com massagem. Mira no mercado brasileiro Embora a chegada do ID. Cross ao Brasil ainda não tenha sido confirmada oficialmente pela matriz, o SUV compacto é considerado um dos fortes candidatos da ofensiva elétrica no país. Por compartilhar o apelo de nome e porte do T-Cross, um dos maiores acertos da marca e líder de vendas no mercado nacional, a novidade surge como o produto de volume ideal para acelerar a estratégia de eletrificação da fabricante alemã na América Latina.

artigo.texto: Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. O Brasil acaba de transformar em lei uma política de incentivos para ampliar a instalação de data centers no país. O Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata) chega em um momento de forte crescimento da demanda por capacidade computacional, impulsionada pela inteligência artificial, e encontra um país com atributos importantes para disputar esses investimentos, entre eles uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável com possibilidade de expansão a custos competitivos. A oportunidade é evidente, mas empreendimentos que concentram centenas de megawatts de demanda contínua também exigem pensar em como o sistema elétrico brasileiro será capaz de absorver essa nova carga sem comprometer a expansão do sistema nem implicar custos aos demais consumidores. Um dos pontos de atenção do Redata está na exigência de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão. A regulamentação dirá o que cabe nessa segunda categoria, mas a possibilidade de incluir o gás natural traz uma contradição importante. O gás natural entra nessa discussão por uma questão de operação. Data centers funcionam 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, com uma carga praticamente constante e exigências elevadas de continuidade do fornecimento. Ao mesmo tempo, a expansão do parque elétrico instalado no país tem se dado principalmente por meio de fontes variáveis, como solar e eólica. Essa combinação de demanda firme e oferta variável aumenta a necessidade de flexibilidade do sistema elétrico, hoje atendida em parte justamente pela geração térmica despachável a gás. O processo depende ainda da expansão das redes de transmissão. Tais reforços podem levar de cinco a dez anos, enquanto um data center pode ser implantado em prazo muito menor, da ordem de um ano e meio. A discussão sobre flexibilidade, portanto, não pode ser separada das condições da rede e do planejamento de sua expansão. O estudo do Instituto E+ Metodologia Integrada para Transição Energética e Desenvolvimento Industrial no Brasil, prestes a ser concluído, simula a entrada de data centers, projetos de aço de baixa emissão e processamento de terras raras no sistema elétrico entre 2029 e 2039. O estudo mostra que a capacidade da rede é determinante para a localização e a escala desses investimentos. Além de geração disponível, é preciso que a infraestrutura elétrica tenha capacidade para atender a nova carga no ponto em que ela será conectada. Nas simulações, Campinas apresenta melhores condições para grandes data centers em conexões à rede de 500 kV, enquanto, em Fortaleza, a estrutura de 230 kV oferece as condições mais favoráveis analisadas. Em níveis inferiores de tensão, a capacidade para receber grandes cargas diminui. No Pecém, a concentração de projetos eletrointensivos pode levar diferentes empreendimentos a disputar capacidade de conexão antes da entrada em operação das obras de expansão previstas para a rede. A expansão da transmissão, por sua vez, pode demorar muito além do prazo de implantação de um data center, o que torna a capacidade de conexão uma variável cada vez mais relevante para a localização e o cronograma desses investimentos. A contratação de energia deve assegurar adicionalidade, contribuindo para ampliar a oferta de energia limpa e competitiva necessária ao atendimento da nova demanda. A entrada da dessas cargas requer expansão da oferta de baixa emissão e dos recursos de flexibilidade, sem que os custos sistêmicos associados a esses empreendimentos recaiam sobre os demais consumidores. Por fim, o Redata acerta ao associar incentivos à instalação de data centers no país a contrapartidas em pesquisa e desenvolvimento, capacidade computacional para o mercado brasileiro e eficiência no uso de recursos. Mas a escala do consumo elétrico exige que a política pública olhe também para a produtividade energética. Afinal, a atração de data centers precisa caminhar junto com o planejamento elétrico de uma maneira favorável à sociedade brasileira como um todo. Os incentivos devem contribuir para ampliar a oferta de energia limpa e competitiva, assegurar capacidade de rede e gerar valor para o país, preservando as vantagens energéticas que tornam o Brasil atraente para esses investimentos. Clauber Leite é diretor de Energia Sustentável e Bioeconomia do Instituto E+ Transição Energética.

artigo.texto: Saft inaugurates its first solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux TotalEnergies' subsidiary opens lines in Bordeaux combining sulfide and polymer electrolytes. It targets aerospace and space, with energy densities stated to be up to 50% higher than lithium-ion. Saft, a subsidiary of TotalEnergies, is inaugurating new production lines for solid-electrolyte batteries, known as "all-solid-state" or "Solid-State" batteries, at its Bordeaux site. According to the company, it becomes the first French manufacturer with development and production capabilities combining sulfide and polymer technologies at room temperature. The announcement comes in a market where manufacturers are stepping up investment, such as the 12 GWh joint venture formalised by Premier Energies and RCT Nexor. Separately, according to Wood Mackenzie, four-hour storage beats gas peaking on cost. A solid electrolyte replacing the liquid one All-solid-state batteries replace the traditional liquid electrolyte with a solid one. Saft says this architecture provides a higher level of safety. It would also allow energy densities of up to 50% higher than those of conventional lithium-ion batteries, according to the group. The manufacturer also highlights more environmentally responsible manufacturing processes. Dry electrode production would cut the CO2 emissions associated with that step by up to 40%, according to Saft. The company specifies that the solid electrolyte combines sulfide and polymer technologies at room temperature, which, it says, offers a wide range of applications. Aerospace and space in focus Saft is targeting the electrification and decarbonisation of aeronautics and space, two sectors where gains in safety, performance and energy density are particularly strategic, according to the company. In aviation, it says it has already delivered semi-solid cells to assess future electric and hybrid aircraft architectures. The group identifies all-solid-state batteries as a key technology for the gradual electrification of aviation. It also points to strong interest from the space sector in these cells. Cedric Duclos, Chief Executive Officer of Saft, states that the new line turns several years of research into concrete industrial capabilities and confirms the ambition to make France and Europe leading players in this technology. Saft, which claims more than 100 years of experience in high-performance batteries, is 100% owned by TotalEnergies. The company did not disclose, in this announcement, a production capacity or an investment amount for the new lines. artigo.texto: Boone City Council approves guidelines for potential data center The Boone City Council approved a Memorandum of Understanding with Lightedge on Monday, moving the city one step closer to potentially hosting a data center. The agreement includes stipulations such as capping the data center's monthly water use at 75,000 gallons, which is roughly equal to the usage of five five-person households. Lightedge would not qualify for city property tax incentives and would be required to pay for any necessary utility upgrades. Mayor Dave Casotti said the city is carefully considering the potential impact of the project. "We would not do something for Boone that would harm the economy, the infrastructure, the environment," he said. Not everyone supported the council's decision. Nearly 50 people attended Monday's meeting, but approximately a dozen left after learning public comments on the data center would not be heard. Some attendees stayed and expressed their concerns. "You're elected officials listening to your constituents — they overwhelmingly don't want a data center. You are failing your constituents," one said. Ultimately, no final decision has been made, and Boone is just one of several locations being considered for the project. If the data center does come to Boone, Casotti said the council has taken steps to ensure the process is well-prepared. "We didn't do this by the seat of our pants," Casotti said.

artigo.texto: Almost nobody wakes up thinking about a data center. But by the time you’ve checked the weather, paid a bill and answered a few emails, you’ve probably used several. Your bank runs on them, your hospital, your streaming account, every AI tool you’ve tried, and increasingly, more of the public services you rely on. You just never see them. That’s becoming a problem for my industry. In August, supervisors in Pinal County, Arizona, voted down a large data center campus after so many residents turned up to object that the county opened five overflow rooms across three buildings. Some said they hadn’t even heard about the project until several meetings in. Developers have lost similar votes this year in Florida, Virginia and North Carolina. I work on the power systems inside these buildings, in Britain and increasingly in the US. A lot of the backlash is aimed at the wrong target. Some of it is our own fault, and we should own that. Start with water, because that’s what most people worry about. Agriculture accounts for around 72% of the world’s freshwater withdrawals, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. Data centers barely show up in that picture. That’s no comfort if you live next to a new campus in a dry county, and I get that. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates US data centers used about 17 billion gallons of water for cooling in 2023, and that could double or even quadruple by 2028. The water used to generate their electricity is roughly 12 times that again, and companies rarely report it. In Britain the picture looks very different. Research for England’s water market operator puts data centers at about 0.2% of non-household water use, a figure the government quoted in Parliament last month. A cooler climate helps, and so do cooling systems that barely use water for most of the year. So national figures don’t tell you much either way. What matters is the specific site, where it is, and how it’s cooled. Why the anger, then? Part of it is simple. The benefits of cloud services and AI are spread across millions of people. The costs, real or imagined, land on one town. Residents see the construction trucks, the new power lines and the backup generators. They don’t see the hospital or the bank that relies on what’s inside. These are also big, windowless, heavily secured buildings. When people can’t easily find out how much water and power a site will use, or who actually benefits, politicians fill the gap with rhetoric. And a data center is an easy stand-in for bigger fears about AI, climate change, jobs and big tech. A planning meeting turns into a vote on the future. I don’t blame people for that. Using AI or watching Netflix doesn’t mean you give up the right to ask how it’s made. So, here’s what I think my industry needs to do. Publish the numbers. Water and energy use, how they’re measured, and how they’ll change as a site grows. That should include the water behind the electricity, not just what goes through the cooling system. Build for the place. A cooling design that works in a cool, wet climate can be the wrong choice in the desert. Water, grid capacity and what the community actually wants should decide where and how we build. Take power seriously. In my experience it’s often a harder problem than water. A large campus can draw as much electricity as a small city. When the grid connection isn’t ready, the fallback is usually on-site gas or diesel generators, and “temporary” tends to last a lot longer than anyone said. Communities are right to ask for a proper connection plan and firm limits on how long those generators run. Treat residents as partners. Tell them early and give them a real say. If we promise jobs, tax revenue or better infrastructure, put numbers on it, not just headlines. The good news is the technology is moving the right way. Newer sites increasingly use air cooling or sealed liquid loops that keep reusing the same water instead of evaporating it. That isn’t universal yet, which is why planning standards matter. Efficiency is also just good business. Power and water drive our costs, our resilience and our ability to grow, so we have every reason to use less of both. But we should prove it with measured results, not targets and press releases. The quickest way to win back trust is site-by-site public reporting, so communities can check what was promised against what was delivered: water, energy, cooling method, backup generation. That lets planners do their jobs properly. They can steer projects away from water-stressed areas, test whether grid plans are realistic, and hear local concerns while designs can still change, instead of telling the community after everything’s been decided. Judge data centers on how well they’re designed, powered, sited and run. Scrutiny on those terms is fair, and we should welcome it. Blanket opposition isn’t. It ignores the services everyone depends on and the improvements that are already here. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – In August, several San Antonio councilmembers, including District 6’s Ric Galvan, proposed a possible moratorium on the city accepting applications for new data centers. “My council colleagues do not fully support that,” Galvan said. “We had a couple of folks who did, and it was four or five of us that supported it fully, but not enough to move forward.” He said 19 of the city’s 28 data centers are in his district alone and more applications to build new ones have been filed. Galvan said the district’s appeal, combined with an outdated city land use code, allows data centers to be built near housing developments and hospitals. “As the energy [production infrastructures] are built, the fiber optic cables are built, as well as the land is available, right, it’s been easy for a lot of data centers to come in and say, well, we’ll set up here,” Galvan said. Among the proposed regulation items is updating the land use code, restricting new data centers to areas already zoned for industrial or heavy commercial use and requiring city council approval before a data center can be built. Galvan laid out, “We’re asking for specific use authorization. A very technical term, but just means that any kind of development in this category needs a specific form of authorization from the City Council. We do this for bars. We do for amusement parks. We do it for carnivals. We do all kinds of different developments in our city every two weeks of city council.” The councilman said this type of authorization is something the city can utilize when it comes to developments including data centers. Galvan said the public comment portion of the meeting is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. at the Cliff Morton Development and Business Services Center (One Stop) located at 1901 S. Alamo Street. (WSET) — The proposed STACK data center project in Berry Hill is drawing opposition from Danville and Pittsylvania County residents concerned about its potential impact on the community. A protest in Danville on Monday highlighted concerns about the development’s projected energy use, water consumption and possible noise. The project is expected to include 21 buildings and use up to 3,000 megawatts of power. Plans call for the development to span approximately 3,000 acres at the megasite off Berry Hill Road. Residents have questioned how the project could affect utility bills and the environment. SEE ALSO: Data centers become midterm minefield as candidates scramble to answer voter backlash Vic Ingram, chairman of the Regional Facility Authority, pushed back against some of those concerns, saying residents should not expect higher utility bills because of the development. When asked about concerns over water use and the environment, Ingram criticized the information circulating among opponents. “What’s propaganda? You know, I think it was like seven folks. I didn’t see anybody that I knew that lived in this area,” Ingram said. “The propaganda by those protests, as well as what you read on social media, is in part generated by people that just really don’t know.” Meanwhile, Pittsylvania County’s director of economic development says the project is now expected to generate $48 million in revenue, with that figure projected to increase. The project’s first building is expected to be fully operational by 2028.
