artigo.texto: On Monday, the Pittsburg City Council agreed to a future agenda item request to discuss a 45-day moratorium on data centers. The item was approved in a 4-0 vote with mayor Dionne Adams recusing herself. The moratorium will return either later this week or at the earliest date possible. According to other cities (such as the City of Oakley), and the law, a city can only impose a moratorium for 45-days. However, this is the first step of a 2-year moratorium as long as the city is working on policy. Including two 1-year extensions. Councilmember Juan Antonio Banales laid out a 45-day plan for a moratorium. Banales explained that phase 1 of the project has already been entitled and approved. That decision has been made and they would honor their legal obligations, but any future data center developments in Pittsburg have not decided. He said that is where the community staff has an opportunity to influence future developments. He provided a plan for which the community can participate over the next 45-days and beyond: A formal pause: proposing this week during a special meeting that the council consider a 45-day moratorium on future data center development in the city of Pittsburg. (Covering phase 2 & 3 and other future developments, but does not impact Phase 1) “The moratorium does two things, first it gives our community clarity. There is a lot of confusion out there about what is the status of data center projects and developments,” explained Banales. “This makes it clear. Second, it allows our advisory committee on data centers to finish its work.” He also said Pittsburg Power and AVAIO are currently negotiating the power agreement for Phase 1. If a deal is reached, it will come before the council for approval. Next Steps: Advisory Committee Recommendations. Banales said he expected the recommendations to come back to the city council. Policy Framework: once recommendations are in, council will give clear policy framework for data centers in Pittsburg. “That means, where should data centers not be allowed. Where are they appropriate and what standards should they have to meet before it can be considered – including design, noise, water and energy use,” said Banales. “The goal is future decisions are made under rules set in advance rather than one project at a time.” He again proposed the 45-day pause for a formal moratorium, consider power agreements, let committee finish its work and set a policy. “Many of you have engaged on this issue with passion, research and with real care for this city and this is what exactly what civic participation should look like and it has made the process better. Disagreement is welcome here, strong opinions are welcome here,” said Banales. “But some of what we have seen in recent weeks has crossed a line. Personal attacks, threats, behavior meant to intimidate rather than persuade are not acceptable.” A five-minute recess was called due to audience interference, however, Banales wanted to continue. “Pittsburg is better than that, Pittsburg has always been a city Councilmember Jelani Killings confirmed this moratorium would not impact Phase 1 and there are now responsibilities they cannot renege on. He noted a lot of the information provided by the public has not been factual and the city wants to put out information that is pertinent to project adopted. He also said they have worked to improve community engagement and to share factual information. “The process is still unfolding and the engagement is still happening,” said Killings who added he supported the 45-day moratorium and allow the advisory committee to finish their work. Baneles then made the motion for a 45-day moratorium to be discussed at a special council meeting later this week or earliest date possible. It was approved in a 4-0 vote with Mayor Dionne Adams recusing herself. Back in June 2018, the council began the process for a 100-acre Technology Park and by December 2024, AvAIO partnerd with the city of Pittsburg. The 300,000 square-foot data center is set to be located on the old Delta View Golf Course site which has been labeled a “technology center” after the golf course closed in 2018. artigo.texto: New certification program supports flexible system configurations and helps reduce complexity when modular installations undergo certification and code authority review. - The certification addresses modular DC energy storage systems that connect evaluated subsystems, including power conversion systems. - Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database for verification by code authorities. - Evaluations address electrical safety, communication and interoperability between the system and identified subsystems. NORTHBROOK, Ill., October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, today announced a new certification pathway designed to help manufacturers of modular direct current (DC) energy storage systems, used for backup power for critical infrastructure and grid-scale energy storage, bring systems to market with greater flexibility and clearer documentation for installation reviews. An energy storage system captures energy so it can be stored for later use and provides electricity to the grid or to a building's wiring system. A battery energy storage system can help save energy by reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from one form to another, including conversion between alternating current (AC) and DC. It can also simplify the connection to solar panels, backup generators and other equipment. Many of these systems use a modular design, allowing manufacturers to combine different components for a project. However, confirming that those components work safely together can make certification and installation reviews more complex. The new certification program offers manufacturers an alternative to seeking a full matched-assembly system listing at the outset. When a compatible subsystem is identified, the resulting certification documentation can provide manufacturers, developers and code authorities with information about the evaluated configuration. "Modular energy storage designs require a clear way to demonstrate how the system and its critical subsystems work together," said Wesley Kwok, vice president and general manager of the Energy and Industrial Automation group at UL Solutions. "This certification program gives manufacturers, developers and code authorities documented information about evaluated system combinations while supporting a more flexible approach to DC energy storage system design." Through the new certification program, UL Solutions evaluates the DC energy storage system with each identified subsystem to applicable requirements of UL 9540, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. The evaluation addresses electrical, communication and interoperability between the system and its evaluated subsystems. Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database under the DC energy storage system certification category, allowing code authorities to verify evaluated combinations.

artigo.texto: The Hayward City Council is scheduled to vote Tuesday on a temporary moratorium on consideration and approval of new data centers in the City. The moratorium is being recommended to give City staff time to thoroughly evaluate the economic, environmental, public health, cost-of-living and other effects of data center development in Hayward. Data centers are buildings designed and equipped for high-density computing and require dedicated uninterrupted power supplies and cooling systems. The advent and expansion of artificial intelligence is driving development of larger-scale and hyperscale data centers with ever increasing energy demands. In Hayward, there are four existing and approved data centers near Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s Eastern Substation in the southwestern portion of Hayward’s industrial crescent on the City of Hayward’s westside: - A 24-megawatt (MW) facility called SF09 operating on a 10.9-acre site along Corporate Avenue. - A 35-MW facility called SF11 operating on a 4.24-acre site also on Corporate Avenue. - A 49-MW facility called Hayward Exchange @92 operating on 6.57 acres of a larger industrial campus along Clawiter Road near Breakwater Court. - A 76.6-MW facility called Stack Data Center (SVY03A) under construction on an 11.3-acre site on Eden Landing Road. Additionally, the City has been approached by a developer planning to submit applications for two new data centers that would operate at 99 megawatts each within a half mile of Hayward’s existing data centers in the vicinity of Arden Road and Corporate Avenue. The moratorium, if adopted, could remain in place for up to two years. Effectively, it is intended to call a time-out and provide time to monitor and analyze the cumulative impacts of current and potential future data center development on energy and water supplies, air quality, industrial noise levels, City emergency response capacity and City economic development priorities. For more information, you can read the staff report to the City Council and related materials on the City of Hayward’s legislative website and a Frequently Asked Questions page on data center development in Hayward on the City of Hayward’s main informational website, www.hayward-ca.gov.

artigo.texto: Trending LORDSTOWN – In a unanimous opinion, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that Lordstown officials were within their rights to stop processing the site-plan review requested by a Bristolville 25 developer, which was the first step toward obtaining a permit to construct four three-story data centers and ancillary structures in an area of the Trumbull County village zoned for industrial use. Last year, village officials imposed a moratorium after Bristolville 25 had issued a permit request with the village planning/ zoning office. Mayor Jackie Woodward said she learned of the court’s decision Tuesday. “This is a pretty significant victory not only for Lordstown but all the municipalities in Ohio who want to maintain the ability to decide and do what is best for their local communities. This sets a precedent for other communities dealing with the same situation with data centers. It allows each community to decide what they want and what is best for their local area.” The court’s decision indicates that Lordstown does not have to complete a site-plan review for a proposed data center that was submitted days before the village imposed a moratorium on data centers. In November 2025, Lordstown passed an ordinance banning data centers within the corporate boundaries. In January 2026, the village repealed the total ban and replaced it with a six-month moratorium on data center construction, which was set to expire July 4. Before its expiration, the council extended the moratorium through the remainder of 2026. Bristolville 25 initiated the first step in October 2025 under Lordstown's codified ordinances to construct the data centers and was notified the next day by the village planning and zoning administrator that a ban on data centers was pending before the village council. Two weeks later, the village council adopted the ban, which it later converted to a moratorium on data centers. Bristolville sought a writ of mandamus from the Supreme Court to compel the village to follow its site plan review process and act upon it under the village's pre-moratorium ordinances. The company argued the village must follow the zoning law in effect on the day the company submitted its plan, which at that time did not prohibit data centers. The court ruling stated that Bristolville's arguments may have prompted a duty for the village to act on the request had the company completed all the steps required to apply for a zoning permit. Because the company had not completed the required preliminary steps to apply for a permit, the village was under no obligation to consider its proposal. Bristolville purchased land from BHGH Properties in February 2025 to construct the data center complex. Under village law, an applicant for a zoning permit for new construction must undergo a site plan review overseen by the village zoning and planning office. Village officials submit a final site plan review for approval by the village's planning and zoning commission. If the commission approves the site plan, then a developer can file for a zoning permit. No construction can begin until a zoning permit is issued. Bristolville delivered its draft site plan to begin the permitting process in October 2025. The village planning and zoning administrator responded, notifying Bristolville about the pending ban, and stated the office could not begin the site plan review until the village council decided on the ban. Bristolville responded by asking the planning and zoning office to proceed because, at that time, data centers were still permitted under village law. Village Solicitor Matt Ries, who reviewed the draft site plan, notified Bristolville that the village officials were proceeding with the site plan, but indicated that, based on the newly enacted ban, the proposal would likely be prohibited. Once the ban was transformed into a moratorium, the village suspended any further review of Bristolville's plan. While the moratorium was in effect, the village's obligations to conduct site-plan reviews or to act on any application for a permit for data-center construction were suspended. Bristolville said the company then asked the Supreme Court to order the village to move forward with the review. Because it submitted its site plan for review before the moratorium, Bristolville argued that the village had a legal duty to proceed with the review. The court stated that Lordstown does not have a duty to act on the request, "unless the moratorium is unenforceable as to Bristolville's submission." Late last year, village council pulled back on its ban on data centers and in January approved temporary moratorium instead. Solicitor Matt Ries has said the originally ban was scheduled to take place in December 2025 but the 180-day moratorium was approved in January, which would give the village or any municipality an opportunity to study the environmental pollution concerns. Ries has said under a Lordstown ordinance, a company has to operate within the permit with what was approved as a site plan review. He said courts favor moratoriums over bans because they are temporary. Village residents have expressed concerns that any large-scale data center would strain Lordstown's energy and water systems, drive up utility bills and bring other complications. At the time company officials said the proposed facility by Bristolville 25 Developers LLC was to be built on 133 acres in both Trumbull and Mahoning counties, employing 120 full-time employees with an average wage of over $84 an hour. artigo.texto: ‘Not off the table’: East Lansing weighs data center rules amid AI discussion Michigan State University hosts discussion on responsible AI use and data centers EAST LANSING, Mich. (News 10) - Michigan State University brought students face to face with two topics on artificial intelligence Monday during a public discussion on how to use AI responsibly and how East Lansing is preparing to accommodate the data centers that power it. The discussion was part of East Lansing’s “Data Week,” a series of talks on AI and data centers leading up to a community forum on a proposed data center ordinance later this week. Professor compares AI to a tool Teagan Dixon, a professor at the Broad College of Business, compared AI to a tool in a workshop. “It’s not just something that’s a corporate thing anymore. It’s on our phones. It’s in our smart apps. It’s in our smart devices,” Dixon said. “A hammer can be used very irresponsibly in a multitude of ways... but you give a woodworker a hammer and they’re going to build something... I think that there’s so much fear about it that the bad things are what’s talked about more than the good things,” Dixon said. City says data center not off the table The discussion also touched on the issue of bringing a data center to East Lansing. Principal Planner Landon Bartley said it’s not off the table. “We don’t have any current applications, but we’ve received a lot of interest,” Bartley said. That’s part of why the city has a moratorium in place until March 2027, giving planners time to write an ordinance addressing noise and other environmental concerns. “Can it be on-site or off-site, renewable or not? Water, can it be evaporative cooling or something else that won’t use as much water?” Bartley said. Bartley said it’s important for residents to weigh in before any ordinance is final. “I think the big concern that I’ve heard from people is not those small ones. It’s the big ones, the hyperscale ones that we’ve seen elsewhere in the country... if they have specific concerns, show up to a meeting and air those concerns,” Bartley said. Bartley said the city of East Lansing has some smaller scale data centers in the area already, and there is not enough land available for a hyperscale data center like the ones that have drawn concerns in other communities. Community forum set for Thursday Residents will have a chance to weigh in later this week. The city’s planning and zoning staff will hold a community forum on a data center ordinance to guide future proposals. The forum will begin at 6:30 p.m. Thursday at the Hannah Community Center. artigo.texto: - Bridge Michigan held its inaugural Issues Summit on Wednesday at Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit - Panels drew from the newsroom’s yearlong reporting initiative, Bridge Listens, and were moderated by Bridge reporters - Topics included health, education, the environment, the economy and affordability Bridge Michigan held its inaugural Issues Summit on Wednesday afternoon, bringing together civic leaders, policymakers and subject-matter experts to discuss some of the most pressing issues in the state. Held on the campus of Marygrove Conservancy in Detroit, the event was also livestreamed for an online audience that included a watch party at Alpena Community College. Bridge journalists moderated panels about education, healthcare and data centers. More than 375 people attended the event either in person or virtually. The summit grew out of Bridge Michigan’s yearlong Bridge Listens initiative, which asked readers what issues matter most to them in this election year. “For 15 years, Bridge Michigan has been working to make Michigan better through our high-quality, nonpartisan journalism and public engagement,” Katy Locker, CEO of Center for Michigan, said to kick off the summit. Related: “We believe good information matters, listening matters and Michigan needs more spaces like this one, where people with different perspectives can come together for thoughtful, respectful conversations about the issues shaping our future.” With Election Day two weeks out, the summit included panels and discussions about the political races, policies and candidates that will help shape the future of Michigan and the country. Senior Capitol Reporter Lauren Gibbons, who has covered the US Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, gave her insight on the race of national significance that has set campaign fundraising records. “I keep telling people, everyone is asking, and this is most likely going to be a toss-up race,” she told Stephen Henderson, founder and executive advisor of BridgeDetroit and host of “Michigan: We Need to Talk.” Capitol Reporter Simon Schuster spoke on stage with Henderson about the race between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican US Rep. John James to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Senior Health Reporter Robin Erb moderated a panel focused on why healthcare costs are climbing and how consolidation and drug prices are affecting coverage. “We all remember the game of tug-of-war as a kid,” said Dr. Deidre Hurse, a public health researcher and medical educator. “And we have families that are just trying to be healthy. They’re trying to get their kids to school. They’re trying to go to work, and opposing them is a complicated health system that isn’t giving them the grace to be healthy.” Capitol Reporter Jordyn Hermani moderated a panel on how affordability challenges shape Michigan’s economic outlook, from housing costs to wages to the ways the state can start addressing the issues. Senior Environment Reporter Kelly House facilitated a discussion about one of the most controversial topics that will play a factor in races up and down the ballot: Data centers. And Education Reporter Isabel Lohman moderated a panel about how Michigan can build a 21st-century workforce when its K-12 foundation is struggling. Venessa Keesler, president and CEO of Launch Michigan, said the state is capable of fixing its education system. “But we have to be really honest about the fact that Michigan starts and stops and starts and stops and starts and stops and we let politics come in. We make policy competitive and not collaborative. And who pays for that is our kids.” Matt Mencarini is a Report for America corps member who covers data and accountability for Bridge Michigan.

artigo.texto: Battery banks are (rightfully) getting a bit of a reputation on planes these days, so safer, more stable options are needed. Enter the LASER ChargeCore Powerbank range using new semi-solid state battery tech, offering enhanced battery safety and stability. LASER has been at the forefront of powerbanks, even introducing the newer LiFePO4 batteries to their battery banks last year, and are now introducing semi-solid state batteries with a focus on safety and peace of mind. Chris Lau, Managing Director of LASER said “We’ve been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options. Simply put, I believe that Semi Solid State chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today. We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks.” The new ChargeCore PowerBanks come in three capacities, 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh and 27,000mAh offering a USB Type-C and two USB-A ports giving you versatile charging for your phones, tablets and more. The 10k and 20kmAh PowerBanks are able to deliver 20W of power across the three ports, while the 27,000mAh option can charge devices at up to 35W. All three models include an easy-to-read digital battery display showing how much is left, as well as including integrated protection against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating. The new ChargeCore PowerBanks are available now in Black, with LASER also announcing Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry colour options are coming soon for their 10K and 20K ChargeCore PowerBanks. While the ChargeCore range is arriving now, LASER is also looking ahead, with Magnetic Charging and Waterproof options also using the semi-solid state battery tech coming soon. You can find the new ChargeCore Everyday Semi Solid State Series at Harvey Norman and Laser Online. The 10,000mAh with 20W USB-C PDis priced at $49.95, while the 20,000mAh with 20W USB-C PD is priced at $69.95. Lastly, the 27,000mAh ChargeCore PowerBank with 35W USB-C PD charging is priced at $99.95. artigo.texto: Graco Announces Technology Partnership with ABB to Bring High Torque ETM Technology to Data Center Cooling This license agreement positions ABB and ETM to address a fast-growing, mission-critical cooling market where efficiency, reliability, and energy consumption are increasingly important to data center economics MINNEAPOLIS--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 21, 2026-- Electric Torque Machines (ETM), a wholly owned subsidiary of Graco Inc. (NYSE: GGG) and owner of patented Transverse Flux Motor (TFM) technology, today announced that ABB has signed a license agreement covering the use of ETM’s technology in data center cooling towers and heat rejection systems. The agreement builds on a successful collaboration between ABB and ETM in industrial applications to capitalize on one of the fastest-growing areas of global infrastructure. As artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and high-density data centers accelerate demand for thermal management, cooling performance is becoming increasingly important to energy use, operating cost, reliability, and the ability to support higher-density computing. ETM’s TFM architecture is built for applications that need high torque, low speed, and efficient direct drive. By reducing mechanical complexity, TFM-based systems can help customers create cooling solutions that are simpler, use fewer drivetrain components, and are better suited to the reliability demands of modern data centers. The agreement creates a path to participate in a multi-year infrastructure buildout where differentiated motor performance can become a competitive advantage. “This is an exciting opportunity to bring a differentiated motor technology from Graco’s ETM business into one of the most important infrastructure markets in the world,” said Mark Sheahan, Chief Executive Officer of Graco Inc. “ABB’s decision to expand its relationship with ETM reflects confidence in the technology, the team, and the commercial opportunity ahead. Together, we can help customers simplify cooling systems, improve reliability, and convert thermal management from a cost challenge into a strategic advantage for the next wave of data center growth.” “ABB continually evaluates technologies that can deliver meaningful value to customers through improved efficiency, reliability, and ease of operation,” said Jesse Henson, President, NEMA Motors, ABB. “Our work with ETM has shown the potential of direct-drive motor systems, and we are pleased to expand that work into cooling applications where performance and uptime matter.” “Data center cooling is one of the most dynamic opportunities in the electric motor industry,” said Justin McMahon, Global Business Line Leader, ABB. “Combining ABB’s market reach with ETM’s TFM technology gives us the opportunity to develop next-generation motor solutions for mission-critical cooling and thermal management systems while helping customers improve resiliency, simplify maintenance, and support the efficient expansion of large-scale cooling capacity.” “The best validation of a technology platform is when a partner expands the relationship after working with it firsthand,” said Jeffrey Weiss, President of Electric Torque Machines. “ABB has worked closely with ETM to leverage TFM technology in industrial applications, and this agreement moves that work into a high-growth market where direct-drive performance can make a real economic difference. We believe TFM can help redefine what customers expect from motor systems in cooling towers and other critical infrastructure.” Under the license agreement, ABB and ETM will develop TFM-based products for data center cooling towers, heat rejection, and related thermal management applications, with the companies targeting the first installations in data center environments by the end of 2029. ABB and ETM will continue collaborating on product development, application engineering, customer qualification, and market development. The opportunity brings together complementary strengths: ABB’s scale, channel access, and customer relationships, and ETM’s motor technology, in a market where performance, reliability, and energy efficiency are increasingly central to data center operating economics. About GRACO Graco Inc. supplies technology and expertise for the management of fluids and coatings in both industrial and commercial applications. It designs, manufactures and markets systems and equipment to move, measure, control, dispense and spray fluid and powder materials. A recognized leader in its specialties, Minneapolis-based Graco serves customers around the world in the manufacturing, processing, construction, and maintenance industries. For additional information about Graco Inc., please visit us at www.graco.com. About ABB ABB is a global technology leader in electrification and automation, enabling a more sustainable and resource-efficient future. By connecting engineering expertise and software, ABB helps industries optimize, electrify, and automate their operations, improving performance while reducing environmental impact. artigo.texto: The Northern Virginia locality with the most data centers in the commonwealth is set to consider a plan to pause new data center and substation applications for one year. At its meeting Tuesday, Loudoun County’s Board of Supervisors is scheduled to vote on a resolution being referred to as a “Legislative Pause on Data Center and Substation Applications.” The proposal would prevent the Board of Supervisors from acting on any legislative application that proposes or would allow for a data center or substation, retroactively effective Sept. 15, 2026. It includes exceptions for projects aimed at improving grid reliability. The step comes after elected officials approved a plan directing county staff to draft a resolution for the pause during a meeting last month. The idea isn’t considered a moratorium, which Loudoun’s lawyers said wouldn’t be legal. Instead, it’s a push to slow data center growth in the suburb with over 200 of them. “If it brings them to the table to renegotiate some of what’s going on, then that’s fine,” Loudoun resident Edward Facundo told WTOP. “It’s not that we don’t want data centers. I think that needs to be done in a way that makes sense for the county and makes sense for the people that live here.” Supporters of the data center industry argue the tech hubs bring jobs and generate tax revenue for communities. Loudoun’s elected officials said the pause is necessary so the county can finish creating rules overseeing the industry and ensuring surrounding neighborhoods are protected. “Just driving through Ashburn and some of these places, they’re an eyesore,” Loudoun resident Stephanie Fulbright said in Sterling on Monday afternoon. “They add no beauty or anything to our community, and fortunately, I don’t have to live with it in my backyard. But a lot of people do.” Related stories - Fauquier County restricts future data center development with new zoning rules - Close to home or across the state, Marylanders don’t want data centers, poll finds - ‘The people are fed up’: Md. governor signs executive order targeting data centers The proposal would pause consideration of an application for a year from the time it’s filed. There are currently 33 active legislative applications for data centers or substations, according to county documents. One is solely a grid-reliability substation. Under the draft plan, projects considered “grid reliability” substations can still advance through the process. Those are defined in the resolution as electrical substations that meet a specific set of criteria. Kathy Kadane, who said she’s lived in Loudoun since 1990, said she supports the yearlong pause, because “if the federal government right now is too dysfunctional to regulate Big Tech in all its various forms, then I think the counties and states have to step up.” Jareer Elass, meanwhile, said the pause is necessary because data centers are “taking up valuable land. It’s a drain on our resources, and it’s AI, and I’m anti-AI.” Get breaking news and daily headlines delivered to your email inbox by signing up here. © 2026 WTOP. All Rights Reserved. artigo.texto: UL Solutions Introduces Certification Pathway for DC Energy Storage Systems, Simplifying Reviews of Modular Installations New certification program supports flexible system configurations and helps reduce complexity when modular installations undergo certification and code authority review. - The certification addresses modular DC energy storage systems that connect evaluated subsystems, including power conversion systems. - Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database for verification by code authorities. - Evaluations address electrical safety, communication and interoperability between the system and identified subsystems. NORTHBROOK, Ill.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 20, 2026-- UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS), a global leader in applied safety science, today announced a new certification pathway designed to help manufacturers of modular direct current (DC) energy storage systems, used for backup power for critical infrastructure and grid-scale energy storage, bring systems to market with greater flexibility and clearer documentation for installation reviews. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261020793648/en/ Modular DC battery energy storage systems can be configured with different components to meet project needs. The new UL Solutions certification pathway evaluates identified system combinations for electrical safety, communication and interoperability. An energy storage system captures energy so it can be stored for later use and provides electricity to the grid or to a building’s wiring system. A battery energy storage system can help save energy by reducing the number of times electricity must be converted from one form to another, including conversion between alternating current (AC) and DC. It can also simplify the connection to solar panels, backup generators and other equipment. Many of these systems use a modular design, allowing manufacturers to combine different components for a project. However, confirming that those components work safely together can make certification and installation reviews more complex. The new certification program offers manufacturers an alternative to seeking a full matched-assembly system listing at the outset. When a compatible subsystem is identified, the resulting certification documentation can provide manufacturers, developers and code authorities with information about the evaluated configuration. “Modular energy storage designs require a clear way to demonstrate how the system and its critical subsystems work together,” said Wesley Kwok, vice president and general manager of the Energy and Industrial Automation group at UL Solutions. “This certification program gives manufacturers, developers and code authorities documented information about evaluated system combinations while supporting a more flexible approach to DC energy storage system design.” Through the new certification program, UL Solutions evaluates the DC energy storage system with each identified subsystem to applicable requirements of UL 9540, the Standard for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment. The evaluation addresses electrical, communication and interoperability between the system and its evaluated subsystems. Compatible subsystem models are documented in the UL Product iQ® certification database under the DC energy storage system certification category, allowing code authorities to verify evaluated combinations. UL 9540 testing covers electrical, electrochemical, mechanical and other types of energy storage technologies used in systems intended to supply electrical energy. Its evaluation framework includes charging and discharging, protection, controls, communication between devices and other system-level considerations. artigo.texto: Tesla Gigafactories for cells & packs A new lithium battery energy storage system manufacturer opened a site in the United States in September and intends to serve the commercial, industrial and utility-scale markets, according to Solar Power World. NeoVolta Power, a joint venture between the lithium brands NeoVolta and PotisEdge, unveiled a 4-GWh manufacturing facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, located roughly an hour northeast of Atlanta. The site is designed to support solutions that are compliant with foreign entity of concern rules and eligible for domestic content treatment for U.S. project developers. NeoVolta CEO Ardes Johnson spoke with the publication after the factory opening about the outlook for domestic battery storage manufacturing. Johnson said NeoVolta began in 2018 as a residential battery storage company founded by Brent Willson in La Jolla, California, shipped its first system in 2019 and listed on Nasdaq in 2022. For several years, he said, the business focused on selling home battery systems such as the NV14 through certified solar installers. That changed when the residential storage market contracted sharply after federal incentive changes, he said. The pullback made clear that a broader footprint was needed across residential, commercial, industrial and utility-scale segments, and that the company needed to move from selling equipment to manufacturing it domestically. Johnson described NeoVolta today as a U.S. energy storage manufacturing platform, with the path from a garage-built residential unit to a gigawatt-hour-scale line in Georgia as the central story of its growth. The Pendergrass facility is about 210,000 square feet on the I-85 corridor in northeast Georgia and is operated through NeoVolta Power, the joint venture with PotisEdge, a LONGi Green Energy company. The first production line has a 4-GWh capacity at full run rate, with a second line intended to move toward 8 GWh as orders warrant. Johnson said manufacturing at the site goes beyond final assembly. NeoVolta Power has its own battery management system, storage energy management system and intelligent cell contact system, a combination he described as the real differentiator rather than mechanical integration alone. The intelligent cell contact system sits directly on the battery pack with voltage and temperature sensors on every cell, which Johnson said can detect a failing cell minutes before a safety event, confirm a thermal event within about a minute to trigger suppression and identify degradation trends months in advance. He described the design as more automatable and lower cost than the wire-harness approach still common in the industry. The battery management system draws on electric-vehicle-grade heritage and handles cell- and pack-level monitoring, active balancing and full protection, according to Johnson. The energy management system is the layer that allows the systems to participate in grid services such as frequency regulation and arbitrage rather than only storing energy passively. When cells arrive in Pendergrass, he said, the work performed there is the engineering value-add: integrating cells with proprietary hardware and software into a finished, grid-ready pack and container, built and tested on NeoVolta's own equipment. Johnson said the company faced many challenges that required careful thought and solutions. NeoVolta had no prior large-scale manufacturing experience, having focused entirely on residential storage, which is why the Pendergrass venture was structured as a partnership rather than a solo build. PotisEdge brought equipment installation, commissioning and ramp-up expertise that NeoVolta lacked in-house, he said. While the plant is highly automated, the company is staffing up engineering, facilities, operations and supporting talent to scale efficiently. The policy environment around foreign entity of concern rules has also been complex, Johnson said, given that NeoVolta Power's manufacturing partner has ties to a Chinese parent company. The joint venture had to be structured carefully, with NeoVolta holding the controlling interest including all board seats, to stay compliant, and he noted that the rules are still being finalized by the IRS, which complicates planning. The domestic cell supply chain is not yet mature, Johnson said. U.S.-made cells are not abundantly available at the volume or price point needed, so Chinese-sourced cells have bridged the gap in the near term even as non-foreign-entity-of-concern content requirements rise each year toward 2030. He also cited the operational and financial lift of a first-of-its-kind ramp: commissioning a new line, hiring and training a production workforce, converting pipeline into signed binding contracts and financing through a mix of equity, debt and project-level financing, all while the legacy residential business was contracting. Johnson said the U.S. is in the early stages of a real onshoring shift that is likely to happen in stages rather than overnight. Most U.S. manufacturers, NeoVolta included, still rely on imported cells, first from China and moving toward Southeast Asia and eventually toward domestic cell production as capacity comes online, he said. He pointed to the SK On agreement as an illustration: 9 GWh of U.S.-manufactured LFP cells from 2027 to 2031, under a framework that could scale to 18 GWh. Cells are only one part of the value chain, according to Johnson, and other components also matter for differentiation. He said many manufacturers still treat the DC block as little more than a container of batteries with cells and a basic battery management system, while NeoVolta engineers its battery management, energy management and intelligent cell contact systems directly into the DC block. Products such as NVAPEx therefore carry power electronics and controls, including cell-level safety monitoring, active management and grid-facing intelligence, rather than functioning as a passive box of cells.

artigo.texto: Data centers need water to stay cool and functional, and lots of it: The larger facilities can consume as much water a day as a town of 50,000 people, and because much of the cooling involves evaporation, freshwater is often preferred. That raises serious questions about the environmental impact of the cloud compute we use to run AI queries, host photos and videos, stream music, and all the rest. Researchers are trying to get a handle on what the impacts on water usage actually are. In a new study published in Environmental Science & Technology, researchers led by a team from the Carnegie Institution for Science in the US mapped the location of the 9,347 currently identified data centers worldwide. When the local water conditions of all these sites were analyzed, the team found that around 25 percent of data centers are in areas where there's a water gap during at least one month of the year – that's when water demand outstrips supply. Based on climate models and 3 °C (5.4 °F) of average global temperature rise from 1900 levels, the number of water-stressed data center locations would rise to 33 percent within as little as 10 years, the researchers found. "These facilities are not landing in empty landscapes," says environmental scientist Lorenzo Rosa, from the Carnegie Institution for Science. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms." While electricity can be spread across long distances through a power grid, the same can't be said for water. It typically needs to be sourced locally, which means the local conditions at sites chosen for data centers really do matter. Water typically gets pulled from lakes, rivers, and aquifers – which can all vary seasonally in terms of the water they supply. "The energy footprint of data centers has been quantified in detail because electricity is metered and reported," says Rosa. "Water scarcity is measured locally, inconsistently, and often not at all." "So, we built the map because it did not exist." The map showed that 41 percent of global data centers are competing directly with cities and municipalities for their water, while for another 28 percent of sites the primary water use is for agriculture. For 523 facilities – that's a little over 5 percent of the total – there are already water gaps for at least 9 months of the year. There were differences in terms of climate change impact too. Most data centers pushed beyond the water gap threshold by temperature rises would be in the US, the modeling showed, while in countries such as the UK and Germany there wouldn't be much change. "Data centers typically have the financial capacity and institutional priority to secure water supplies whenever water is available," write the researchers in their published paper. "As a result, the primary risk may not be to data center operations themselves but to other water users within the same basins." The researchers note that information on data center water usage remains limited – the giant tech companies involved are reticent to share the exact level of demand these facilities are putting on our natural resources. More accountable reporting would definitely help, which might require intervention from regulators and governments. There is some positivity from the researchers at the end of their paper, though, pointing to efforts to use wastewater and treated seawater in place of freshwater, as well as improvements in data center heat management. What's clear is that changes are needed before the data center water drain gets worse. "The extent to which water-stress exposure translates into operational impacts for data centers themselves or into measurable consequences for other water users remains an open question to address," write the researchers. "Ensuring data center long-term viability will require siting and governance choices that account for local hydrological limits." The research has been published in Environmental Science & Technology. This article was fact-checked by Rachel Garner and edited by Fiona MacDonald. While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know.

artigo.texto: BMX launched the SolidSafe Duo on Oct. 19 for the iPhone Duo, pairing a custom 5,000mAh semi-solid-state cell with a 360-degree rotating stand and integrated USB-C lanyard. BMX launched the SolidSafe Duo on Oct. 19 for the iPhone Duo. The new phone shape demands accessories that match its proportions, and this pack avoids overhang by using a custom 5,000mAh semi-solid-state cell instead of a standard lithium-ion design. A conventional cell would force the battery past the edges or cut capacity. The semi-solid-state format gives BMX the flexibility to shape the pack around the iPhone Duo's dimensions. The cell contains less liquid electrolyte than standard lithium-ion batteries. Less liquid means less flammable material inside the cell, which lowers fire risk from heat, physical damage, or internal short circuits. Battery recalls have made that trade-off visible. The integrated rotating ring stand handles portrait reading, landscape video, and partially folded hands-free calls. It rotates 360 degrees and stays attached when you shift position, so you never remove the pack to change angles. Charging reaches up to 15 watts through MagSafe or 20 watts via the attached USB-C lanyard cable. The cable stays with the battery, eliminating a separate cord to pack or lose. The same cable accepts up to 15 watts to recharge the pack. A full-color LCD shows remaining capacity and live charging wattage at the same time, so you can track both how much power you have left and how fast it is charging. The SolidSafe Duo costs more than generic MagSafe packs. For iPhone Duo owners, the tailored fit and semi-solid-state safety profile justify the premium. Less expensive options will likely arrive in coming months, but this is a solid launch option. This is part of the MagSafe Monday series, which examines the latest MagSafe and wireless charging gear for Apple devices. Source:9to5mac.com

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Central Georgia Electric Membership Corp. will deploy up to 50 MW of small-scale, customer-sited energy storage in partnership with Base Power, the organizations said last week. - Set to begin in 2027, the deployment marks Base Power’s first utility partnership outside its home state of Texas, Base and CGEMC said. CGEMC will charge the batteries when wholesale power prices and members’ energy demand are low and discharge during periods of peak demand, helping to stabilize the grid across its 14-county territory southeast of Atlanta. - The batteries will add capacity to a CGEMC system that could see substantial large-load growth in the coming years. Multiple data center projects are proposed or under development in its territory, including a 240-MW Equinix campus near Hampton. Dive Insight: Base Power operates as a retail energy choice provider in Texas and the Illinois zone of the PJM Interconnection, and as a direct partner for public power entities in parts of Texas. The company says its fleet has more than 750 MWh of capacity spread over 30,000-plus homes. Base is one of several companies that provide deeply discounted home battery subscriptions via energy choice retail frameworks in restructured markets or utility partnerships in regulated markets. In both scenarios, Base installs and maintains relatively large residential backup batteries at little or no direct cost to the homeowner. When the grid is up and running, Base or its utility partners charge and discharge the batteries to shave demand peaks, mitigate price spikes and tap energy arbitrage value. During outages, Base says each 39.2-kWh battery can provide up to 36 hours of backup power. Base’s partnership with CGEMC marks its first outside Texas and one of its first in a regulated utility market. Base is also partnering with El Paso Electric, a vertically integrated utility serving parts of far west Texas outside the deregulated Electric Reliability Council of Texas market, on a resilience-focused pilot program. While that means the company and its utility partners target different value streams, the core business proposition — using distributed batteries to reduce power supply costs — remains the same, company spokesperson Gabriel Federman said in an email. “In Texas, that means addressing transmission and energy costs through peak-shaving and arbitrage. In Georgia, the main value is in transmission and reducing capacity obligations,” Federman said. “However, the core principles and the value of distributed storage [are] consistent across markets.” Both transmission-scale energy storage and customer-sited distributed batteries deliver benefits at the wholesale level, according to an analysis published in September by the consultancy ICF. Distributed BESS offers additional value in alleviating distribution grid congestion, boosting local resilience and allowing utilities to defer grid upgrades, ICF said. Unlike vertically integrated utilities that earn a regulated rate of return on infrastructure spending, member-owned rural electric cooperatives like CGEMC and not-for-profit municipal power utilities like Base Power partner Austin Energy have strong incentives to minimize wholesale power costs and avoid expensive system investments. Regardless of local market structure, they’re tapping distribution-connected energy storage for help — from networked residential batteries to multi-megawatt installations at substations or industrial sites. George Weaver, CGEMC president and CEO, framed the utility’s partnership with Base Power as a win for members themselves and the grid they pay to support. The 50-MW deployment will “add flexible local capacity to support our electric system while giving participating members greater peace of mind through dependable backup battery power,” Weaver said in a statement.

artigo.texto: Littleton and Brighton are joining a growing number of communities seeking to halt data center development to give staff time to develop zoning regulations and catch up with the rapidly growing technology. Littleton and Brighton both unanimously advanced moratoriums on data center applications Tuesday following a growing number of community concerns about the developments and their potential impacts. Recommended Stories Littleton unanimously approved a six-month moratorium on first reading, and Brighton gave final approval to a one-year moratorium. A number of residents in both communities spoke against data centers, citing concerns including water usage, noise, heat, energy consumption, environmental impacts and quality of life. In both meetings, staff said the moratoriums would allow time to study the impacts of data centers and integrate regulations into zoning codes that do not specifically address data centers in a comprehensive manner. “The purpose of the moratorium is to analyze the various land uses related to data centers,” Littleton City Attorney Reid Betzing said. “To find out if they are appropriate and, if they are, where they are appropriate.” Brighton’s moratorium comes as a proposed data center project that faced considerable public backlash was withdrawn. The proposal called for a 2.5 million-square-foot data center campus in northeast Brighton composed of eight two-story buildings. According to 9News, the application was withdrawn shortly before the council approved the moratorium on first reading Oct. 6. Brighton’s moratorium suspends the acceptance, processing and approval of applications while the City Council determines what regulations may be appropriate to mitigate impacts on the community. Littleton Councilmember Pam Grove said much of the concern is centered on hyperscale data centers, which use significantly more energy than smaller facilities. Grove said she is aware of six state bills that may be introduced on the topic of data centers, ranging from outright bans to environmental protection regulations. Littleton and Brighton join communities including Denver, Larimer County and Broomfield that have passed moratoriums for similar reasons. Aurora is also considering a moratorium following public backlash over a proposed data center development. 9News contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: As emissões de gases de efeito estufa do Brasil recuaram 6% em 2025, atingindo o menor patamar em oito anos, segundo dados do Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões e Remoções de Gases de Efeito Estufa (Seeg), do Observatório do Clima. O resultado foi impulsionado pela queda do desmatamento em todos os biomas, especialmente na Amazônia e no Cerrado. Esta é a terceira redução anual seguida (-12,7% em 2024 e -7,5% em 2023), que somadas resultam em queda de 26% nas emissões brutas no período, revertendo o ciclo anterior — entre 2019 e 2022 o país registrou uma alta expressiva do desmatamento. “Os últimos três anos reverteram uma tendência de mais de uma década de crescimento de emissões”, disse David Tsai, coordenador do Seeg e gerente no Instituto de Energia e Meio Ambiente (Iema), em coletiva de imprensa realizada nesta quarta-feira (21). As emissões brutas somaram 2,06 bilhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente no ano passado. A maior parcela vem da mudança do uso do solo (39%), que é a conversão da vegetação nativa em outros usos, como agropecuária e urbanização — ou seja, desmatamento. A agropecuária foi o segundo maior emissor (30%), seguida de energia (21%, inclui transportes), resíduos (5%) e processos industriais e uso de produtos (5%). O Seeg também calcula a quantidade total de remoção de carbono, que foi de 650 milhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente em 2025. Assim, as emissões líquidas do país (emissões brutas descontadas as remoções) totalizaram 1,41 bilhão de toneladas no ano. As remoções ocorreram no setor de mudança de uso da terra e florestas, que abrange duas atividades: crescimento de vegetação secundária e remoção de carbono por áreas protegidas (vegetação mantida em terras indígenas e unidades de conservação). De onde veio a queda A redução nas emissões brutas foi puxada pela forte desaceleração do desmatamento, observado em todos os estados e biomas brasileiros, principalmente na Amazônia e no Cerrado. Enquanto o setor de uso da terra reduziu significativamente suas emissões, os demais setores apresentaram estabilidade ou alta. Resíduos tiveram o maior crescimento proporcional, com alta de 3,6%, associado ao crescimento populacional e ao descarte em aterros e lixões e no tratamento de efluentes. Já energia registrou alta de 1,2% nas emissões, impulsionada pelo setor de transportes (com maior consumo de diesel e gasolina) e pela geração de eletricidade, cujas emissões subiram 6% devido ao acionamento de termelétricas a gás. As emissões da agropecuária permaneceram praticamente estáveis, com queda de 0,1% — o aumento de 6,45% da agricultura foi compensado pela redução nas emissões da pecuária. O segmento de processos industriais e uso de produtos também ficou estável, com leve variação positiva de 0,2%. “É um resultado bem positivo em nível nacional, em função da redução das emissões de uso da terra, e mostra a importância e a efetividade não só de continuar controlando o desmatamento, mas iniciar, de fato, medidas contundentes nos outros setores”, disse Tsai. O Brasil está em processo de regulamentação do seu mercado de carbono, que vai estabelecer um limite para as emissões de setores poluentes da economia. No Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), cada empresa recebe cotas (os CBEs). Quem emite menos que sua cota vende o excedente, e quem emite mais compra cotas ou créditos (os CRVEs). Estamos no rumo das metas? Segundo análise da equipe do Seeg, o ciclo de quedas recente permitiu ao Brasil recuperar o atraso causado pela disparada de emissões de anos anteriores. O país ficou, assim, mais próximo de cumprir as metas estabelecidas em sua contribuição nacionalmente determinada (NDC, na sigla em inglês) no âmbito do Acordo de Paris. O limite de emissões líquidas para 2025 era de 1,32 bilhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente, correspondente a uma redução de 48,4% em relação a 2005. O Brasil não conseguiu cumprir a meta do ano. O resultado de 1,41 bilhão de toneladas de emissão líquida ficou 6% distante do objetivo. Para 2026, a estimativa do Seeg é que as emissões líquidas do país somem 1,22 bilhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente. O cálculo considera os dados mais recentes de desmatamento do Prodes (Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros por Satélite) e uma projeção linear das emissões dos demais setores, baseada na tendência dos últimos cinco anos. “Isso nos coloca na zona onde deveríamos estar para cumprir a meta de 2030”, disse o coordenador do Seeg. A meta brasileira para 2030 é de limite de 1,2 bilhão de toneladas. O Observatório do Clima avalia, no entanto, que essa trajetória será ameaçada em uma eventual mudança de governo.

artigo.texto: WETEX 2026 showcases battery breakthroughs and water technologies in Dubai DUBAI — The 28th edition of the Water, Energy, Technology and Environment Exhibition (WETEX) opens on Tuesday at Dubai World Trade Centre, bringing together international companies and industry specialists to showcase technologies aimed at addressing energy, water management and sustainability challenges. Running from October 20 to 22, the exhibition is organised by Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) and serves as a platform for businesses, investors and decision-makers to explore emerging technologies, partnerships and commercial opportunities across regional and global markets. Battery technology takes centre stage German company ALGATEC is presenting a new battery technology that it says can achieve an energy density of up to 1,000 watt-hours per kilogram. The company describes the technology as a cost-effective alternative to conventional systems, manufactured without lithium or rare earth elements. ALGATEC says the technology is designed to address challenges including volatile supply chains and rising raw material costs. The company has also outlined plans for a dedicated gigafactory to support large-scale industrial production. The performance and commercial viability of the technology will be important considerations as it moves towards potential wider deployment. Packaging business unveils new UAE brand The exhibition is also providing a platform for the Abdul Wahid Al Rostamani Group to introduce VerraPak, the new brand replacing its Sinyou packaging business in the UAE. The company says VerraPak will combine local manufacturing, technical expertise, advanced printing and customisation capabilities to develop packaging tailored to customers’ products and operational requirements. Its approach also emphasises responsible practices and closer collaboration with clients. Huda Al Rostamani, chief commercial projects officer at the group, said the launch reflected growth opportunities in the packaging business, supported by demand from the UAE’s food, hospitality and consumer goods sectors for quality, consistent and environmentally responsible solutions. Water treatment technologies target efficiency Japanese company Toray is showcasing technologies including reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration and membrane bioreactors, with a focus on reliable and efficient water treatment and resource management. Takashi Kurai, president of Toray Membrane Middle East, said the exhibition provides an opportunity to engage with utilities, municipalities, government entities, consultants, contractors and property developers. The company expects these discussions to support potential partnerships and expansion across regional markets. Chinese manufacturers are also presenting filtration and purification systems for residential, commercial and industrial applications. Anhui Chero Technology is highlighting sediment and activated-carbon filter cartridges, reverse-osmosis membrane housings and customised filtration solutions designed to improve water quality and system performance. Fumatech Technology is showcasing membrane technologies for sustainable water treatment, including reverse osmosis, nanofiltration and ultrafiltration, alongside desalination, ultrapure water production and systems designed to minimise liquid waste through water recycling. Regional demand drives commercial opportunities WETEX brings together technologies across water, energy, environmental sustainability, digital transformation and green development. DEWA reported that the 2025 edition attracted more than 50,000 visitors and 3,100 exhibitors, highlighting the event’s role in connecting international suppliers with regional buyers and public-sector organisations.

artigo.texto: Taunton City Council unanimously approves data center ban TAUNTON, Mass. (WJAR) — The Taunton City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to ban data centers amid discussion of a proposed facility at an industrial park in the city. City Hall was packed as opponents turned out for the vote, with residents raising concerns about potential environmental impacts and strain on the local power grid. “I found out, like most people via Facebook, because I wasn’t given a letter,” said Taunton resident Willembert VanBruniswaardt. He also accused data center companies of misconduct. “We’ve seen these data center companies perform all kinds of, frankly, criminal actions. I’m not going to sugarcoat it,” he said. In a letter to Mayor Shaunna O’Connell, property owner VMD Industrial requested an exception to the ban. Asked about the property owner’s warning that the decision could cost it a multimillion-dollar deal, O’Connell said business development must be balanced with residents’ needs. “We always support business, but it has to be done the right way,” she told NBC 10 News. “I know the priority of the council and my priority is to protect the resources that our residents rely on every single day.” The Planning Board said Tuesday night that the John Hancock Road property did not qualify for an exception because no permit application was pending. City leaders said the proposed facility could not be grandfathered in without an existing application. “I’m glad people were here tonight to hear the actual facts, because when people believe the gossip and, you know, crap that’s on Facebook or whatever social media, it starts problems,” O’Connell said. Officials said the ban has no expiration date and would remain in place unless changed through another zoning hearing. - ALSO READ: One year after near-fatal stabbing, Former Fall River Mayor William Flanagan eyes 2027 run The council also approved a moratorium, which officials said would provide additional legal protection if the ban is challenged. Despite the unanimous vote, VanBruniswaardt remained cautious. “I would not describe this as a win. I would describe this as we scored a goal. But there’s still an hour left in the match,” he said. “If someone really wants a data center here, they are going to pour everything they have into it.”

artigo.texto: Trending When a city plans something big, it should not check driver’s licenses at the door. That is what happened Monday night in Woodward. The City Council cancelled its regular meeting and instead held what it called a "community conversation” in the Woodward-Granger High School auditorium. The notice required attendees to show a photo ID with a Woodward address or a piece of mail with their name and Woodward address before they could enter. Security officers and police were there to oversee the screening of IDs. I was there as president of the Iowa Freedom of Information Council and was turned away. So was a rural Dallas County resident interested in data centers. A KCCI reporter saw at least two others who were refused entry. Inside, Mayor Todd Folkerts and three Microsoft officials announced that the company had closed on the purchase of about 600 acres in the Woodward Eco Business Park, on the city’s south side, for a data center campus. About 200 residents listened for 90 minutes. Folkerts said the council would need to approve a development agreement and a site plan before the project could proceed. Fewer than a majority of the five council members attended, so the gathering likely falls outside Iowa’s open meetings law. Legal or not, the residency screening was a mistake. It treated a regional decision as a private family matter. Consider what a data center brings. Microsoft’s representatives told the crowd a closed-loop cooling system would spare the city’s water supply and buying electricity from a wholesaler would protect residential rates. Those are promises about water and electricity, and neither resource stops at a city limit. New power lines would cross farm fields. Construction trucks would use county roads. Storm water runs downhill without regard to annexation maps or city boundaries. A farm family just outside town will live with the data center's lights, noise and traffic as surely as any resident of Main Street. That farm family pays property taxes, too -- just not to the City of Woodward. Iowa law already recognizes that a city’s choices reach past its borders. Section 354.9 of the Iowa Code allows a city to review subdivision plats as far as two miles beyond its city limits, giving the city a voice over how its rural neighbors’ land is developed. On October 12, Woodward denied those same neighbors a seat in the auditorium. The venue underscored that point. Woodward-Granger High School belongs to the Woodward-Granger Community School District, which has its central offices in Granger and reaches into Dallas, Boone and Polk counties. Taxpayers in Granger and the surrounding countryside helped pay for that auditorium. The city used the school district's building and then told people without a Woodward address to stay outside. Iowa’s local governments cooperate all the time. Chapter 28E of the Iowa Code allows cities, counties and other public bodies to share services and work together for mutual advantage. The Legislature has directed the courts to interpret that law liberally. Twelve central Iowa cities, utilities and water districts, including the Xenia Rural Water District, formed Central Iowa Water Works under a 28E agreement to plan the region’s drinking water together. Metro Waste Authority grew out of a 28E agreement among Des Moines-area governments dating to 1969. Polk County and its cities fund emergency management jointly through another 28E agreement. None of these partnerships asks a neighbor for proof of address before letting the person listen to a discussion of matters of mutual concern. A residents-only rule divides communities. It turns the city limit into a wall, as if the people on the far side have no stake in what happens on the near side. This also invites the same treatment in return. If Granger, Madrid or Dallas County someday puts a landfill on Woodward’s doorstep, Woodward residents will want to attend meetings where such a development is discussed. They should get in. Everyone else should, too. Monday’s rule was also unneighborly. Picture a farmer who plans a hog confinement on his fence line and invites only his own household to hear the details. The people downwind would not call that a community conversation. They would call it a snub. I told KCCI the requirement that only Woodward residents could attend Monday's information session “erodes the trust and confidence” in Woodward city government. And the damage spreads beyond Woodward. Woodward still has time to fix this. The development agreement and site plan still need council approval. The council will have to take these up at regular, properly noticed meetings that are open to anyone who wants to attend. Woodward officials should invite the Dallas County Board of Supervisors, the Woodward-Granger school board and nearby townships to hear the plan. It should publish what Microsoft has said about water, power and traffic. Woodward’s neighbors will live with this data center. They deserve to hear about it, ask about it and argue about it in the same room as everyone else. A project this large deserves the widest audience -- not the narrowest. Randy Evans is the executive director of the Iowa Freedom of Information Council. He can be reached at DMREvans2810@gmail.com.

artigo.texto: We have spotted what appears to be a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) for the BYD Flash Charger at Denza Glenmarie in Shah Alam. If our observation is accurate, Denza Glenmarie, which is operated by Sisma Auto, could very well be the location of the first BYD Flash Charger in Malaysia. Why are the BESS units a dead giveaway? Even though the charger’s signature T-shaped structure that houses the charging connectors has not yet been installed at the site, the hardware that we spotted at Denza Glenmarie visually aligns with the BYD Flash Charge energy storage enclosures that we have seen in China. Back in May, Managing Director of BYD Malaysia, Jacob Ma, revealed that Denza showrooms would be among the very first locations to receive BYD Flash Charge stations. He has also confirmed that the BYD Flash Charger will be open to EVs from all brands, rather than being exclusive to BYD and Denza vehicles. BYD Flash Charge can deliver up to 1.5MW, supported by BESS Introduced globally earlier this year, BYD Flash Charge stations are capable of hitting a peak DC charging rate of up to 1.5MW (1,500kW). With supported vehicles, here’s how the charging duration would be: - 10-70% in 5 minutes - 10-97% in 9 minutes - Add 3 more minutes if the temperature is cold Hence, BYD has come up with a tagline for the Flash Charging technology to represent the speed: “Ready in 5, Full in 9, Cold Add 3,”. In order to support the ultra-high power demand and overcome grid limitations, BYD has integrated BESS into the Flash Charge station. These battery banks are being charged from the local grid during idle periods and unleash massive power bursts when a compatible EV plugs in. The battery in each cabinet has a capacity of 185kWh, so you are looking at a 370kWh total battery capacity for each Flash Charger. When required, the BESS draw energy from the grid at speed of between 100kW to 560kW, depending on the infrastructure capability. Meanwhile, Flash Charge’s T-shaped pillar doubles as a “Zero Gravity” cable management system. The charging cables are suspended from the top to ensure that the cables remain clean and off the ground at all times. Not to forget, they can also slide from left to right to accommodate EVs with either left- or right-mounted charging ports. Which BYD models in Malaysia can support Flash Charging? To hit a DC charging speed of 1,500kW, the EV must support BYD’s 1,000V platform and be equipped with the 2nd generation BYD Blade battery. Currently, the only BYD model in Malaysia that can fully support Flash Charge is the Denza Z9 GT, which was launched here back in July. However, non-BYD EVs or older 400V/800V BYD models can still plug in and charge at their maximum supported DC intake rate. As Jacob Ma previously explained, an 800V EV capable of taking 220kW DC will draw 220kW at a BYD Flash Charger. If an 800V vehicle supports up to 600kW, the Flash Charger will supply the full 600kW without issue.

artigo.texto: Data Centers Can Delay, Not Dodge, the Power Crunch Efficiency gains and flexible workloads may create near-term capacity for AI, but utilities will need proof that those reductions can be delivered when the grid needs them. Data center operators facing power constraints can accommodate more AI computing by improving efficiency and shifting flexible workloads, but those measures are unlikely to remove the need for new electricity infrastructure. That is the central conclusion of a new Infosys analysis of AI energy demand through 2030. The report argues demand-side measures can deliver usable capacity sooner than new generation, transmission, and grid upgrades. However, it also points to a harder question for developers, utilities, and customers alike: how much of that flexibility is actually available when the grid needs it most? Mit Majumdar, executive vice president and global head of services, utilities, resources, and energy at Infosys, told Data Center Knowledge that AI-driven energy management, advanced cooling, and peak-load optimization can create meaningful near-term headroom. He did not provide a numerical estimate of additional AI capacity those measures could support. “However, [these measures] are more likely to delay rather than eliminate the need for new infrastructure,” Majumdar said. “The best path forward is a dual-track strategy: maximize existing capacity while accelerating investment in generation, transmission, and grid modernization.” Match Power Flexibility to the Right Workloads The Infosys analysis identifies a mismatch between AI adoption cycles measured in months and energy infrastructure development measured in years. Operators can respond in part by changing when computing occurs, but the amount of flexibility depends on the workload. “Flexible workloads such as model training, retraining, and batch processing can often be scheduled around grid conditions, while real-time inference and customer-facing applications generally cannot,” Majumdar said. A facility serving both categories, therefore, cannot assume that its entire AI load is available for curtailment. Operators need to distinguish between work that can wait and applications whose customers require an immediate response. Customer agreements must also reflect that distinction. Majumdar said broader flexibility will require service-level agreements (SLAs) that match workload requirements, along with demand-response incentives and pricing structures that reward customers for shifting non-urgent computing. “Greater flexibility will require new commercial models, including workload-aware SLAs, demand-response incentives, and pricing structures that reward customers for shifting non-urgent compute,” he said. The commercial question extends beyond whether a task can technically run later. Operators need customer commitments that make scheduling changes available when grid conditions require them. Phase Capacity Around Changing Demand Efficiency improvements also create uncertainty for developers deciding how much infrastructure to build. AI adoption is increasing computing demand, even as advances in models, chips, and cooling continue to change the power required to deliver that compute. The report recommends choosing models suited to the task and applying techniques such as quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation to reduce computational requirements. It also calls for measuring energy use and carbon emissions at the workload level. Majumdar said developers should respond with staged construction rather than locking in every phase of a project to current assumptions. “A modular approach allows capacity to scale as demand evolves while preserving flexibility to benefit from advances in AI models, chips, and cooling technologies,” he explained. That approach gives developers opportunities to adjust later phases as customer requirements and equipment capabilities become clearer. It also keeps efficiency gains in the planning process rather than treating demand growth as the only variable. “The goal is to avoid both overbuilding and underestimating long-term demand,” Majumdar said. Prove Load Reductions Before Relying on Them For utilities considering demand-side savings as support for new data center connections, projections alone are not enough. They need to determine whether operators can deliver reductions under the conditions that matter to grid reliability. “Utilities should require measurable and verifiable proof, including historical performance, real-time monitoring, and contractual commitments to reduce load when needed,” Majumdar said. Historical performance can support a claim, while real-time monitoring and enforceable commitments establish how that claim will be tested in operation. Operators and utilities also need to agree in advance on responsibility if the promised flexibility fails to materialize. Majumdar argued neither party should bear the entire burden. “Risk should be shared: operators should stand behind performance claims through guarantees, while utilities should establish clear qualification and verification standards to ensure reliability,” he said.
