artigo.texto: Expansão de Data Centers no Brasil Vai Além de São Paulo, mas a Rede Elétrica Decide o Que Será Construído A expansão dos data centers no Brasil foi além de São Paulo, embora esse mercado ainda concentre 76% da capacidade operacional do país. Desenvolvedores agora buscam projetos em escala de gigawatts no Rio de Janeiro, Ceará e Rio Grande do Sul. A mudança promete mais capacidade regional, mas também expõe uma restrição difícil. Energia anunciada não é o mesmo que energia conectada. A história imediata não é a perda do status de São Paulo como capital computacional do Brasil. Seus clientes, densidade de rede, infraestrutura de nuvem e operadores estabelecidos continuam difíceis de igualar. A mudança é que a infraestrutura de IA exige mais eletricidade e terreno do que o cluster tradicional pode fornecer com facilidade. Rio AI City, o mercado de Fortaleza conectado por cabos e a Scala AI City no Sul do Brasil oferecem alternativas diferentes. Juntos, eles desafiam a suposição de que quase toda grande implantação precisa permanecer próxima de São Paulo. Ainda assim, suas enormes metas de capacidade descrevem sobretudo futuros campi, não servidores que já processam cargas de trabalho. Essa distinção define a próxima fase do crescimento dos data centers no Brasil. Incentivos fiscais podem reduzir custos de equipamentos, enquanto a energia renovável pode fortalecer a tese de investimento. Nenhuma dessas vantagens elimina a construção de linhas de transmissão, análises ambientais ou a necessidade de fibra confiável e clientes. A Expansão dos Data Centers no Brasil Está se Tornando uma História Nacional O mercado deixou de ser uma exploração regional e passou a uma disputa entre diversos polos de infraestrutura distintos. São Paulo continua sendo o centro de gravidade. Segundo a análise de mercado original, o mercado metropolitano responde por 76% da capacidade operacional de data centers do Brasil. Ele combina a maior base de clientes do país com fibra densa, pontos de acesso à nuvem e campi de colocation consolidados. Essas vantagens se reforçam mutuamente. Empresas colocam cargas de trabalho perto de regiões de nuvem e pontos de troca de tráfego. Em seguida, operadores expandem onde já há demanda e opções de interconexão. Novos clientes recebem uma escolha maior de provedores, o que atrai ainda mais infraestrutura. Esse ciclo explica por que os data centers de São Paulo dominaram por tanto tempo. Também explica por que os mercados regionais não substituirão a cidade simplesmente oferecendo terrenos mais baratos. Um novo local precisa fornecer eletricidade, telecomunicações resilientes, trabalhadores qualificados e um caminho convincente para a demanda dos clientes. No entanto, as exigências da computação de IA estão mudando a seleção de locais. Clusters de alta densidade podem exigir compromissos de energia muito maiores do que implantações empresariais convencionais. Por isso, os desenvolvedores precisam de locais onde terreno e eletricidade possam sustentar campi em fases, medidos em centenas de megawatts. O Rio de Janeiro está se apresentando como um polo de IA e nuvem, e não como uma cópia menor de São Paulo. A Rio AI City combina uma instalação existente da Elea com um campus proposto ao redor do Parque Olímpico. O plano prevê 1,5 gigawatt inicialmente e 3 gigawatts até 2032. Um anúncio de junho de 2026 vinculou esse plano a um investimento de US$ 550 milhões na plataforma mais ampla de infraestrutura da Elea. Autoridades municipais disseram que o financiamento poderia iniciar um ciclo mais longo de expansão, chegando a US$ 10 bilhões. Esses números abrangem ambições e capacidade de financiamento, não salas de data center concluídas. Fortaleza oferece uma proposta diferente. A cidade está próxima de um grupo incomumente denso de pontos de aterragem de cabos submarinos que conectam o Brasil à América do Norte, Europa, África e outros mercados latino-americanos. Essa posição pode reduzir a dependência de rotas que passam pelo Sudeste brasileiro. A conectividade internacional dá a Fortaleza um papel crível em serviços de nuvem, distribuição de conteúdo e processamento de dados para exportação. Também torna o Ceará relevante para operadores que buscam energia renovável perto de uma grande porta de entrada de cabos. Essa combinação atraiu novos campi e expansões de instalações existentes. No Rio Grande do Sul, o argumento se concentra em terrenos disponíveis, energia renovável e acesso ao Cone Sul. O estado faz fronteira com Argentina e Uruguai, enquanto o Paraguai pode ser alcançado por redes regionais. Porto Alegre já sustenta um mercado menor de colocation que pode ancorar um desenvolvimento mais amplo. A Scala AI City ilustra a escala dessa ambição. O projeto em Eldorado do Sul começa com 54 megawatts planejados de capacidade de TI e tem potencial declarado de expansão para 4,75 gigawatts. A meta total abrange um horizonte de desenvolvimento longo, portanto não deve ser confundida com oferta operacional. Cada região busca um papel diferente. O Rio quer um grande campus de IA próximo a uma importante economia urbana. Fortaleza combina energia com cabos internacionais. O Rio Grande do Sul oferece uma plataforma no Sul com espaço para desenvolvimento em múltiplas etapas. É por isso que a expansão dos data centers no Brasil está se tornando uma história de infraestrutura nacional. Os locais emergentes não são intercambiáveis e não competem apenas por terreno. Cada um precisa transformar uma vantagem regional em capacidade computacional confiável. A Liderança de São Paulo É Tanto uma Vantagem Quanto uma Restrição A infraestrutura madura de São Paulo mantém sua predominância, mas essa mesma concentração agora dificulta a expansão. O ecossistema existente da cidade oferece uma certeza que os mercados emergentes não conseguem reproduzir imediatamente. Clientes podem escolher entre operadores estabelecidos, conectar-se a diversas redes e acessar grandes plataformas de nuvem. Desenvolvedores tamb

artigo.texto: Nscale Loses Microsoft Deal as Power Delays Threaten AI The cancellation highlights the financial risks developers face when grid connections fall behind project schedules and customers cannot wait for capacity. Microsoft has terminated its contract for Nscale’s planned AI data center in Loughton, England, after delays to the site’s expected power connection. The cancellation highlights a growing challenge for data center developers: customer demand and financing commitments do not guarantee that electricity will be supplied in time to meet commercial schedules. For developers, delayed power can leave construction and financing costs running while revenue remains out of reach. For cloud operators, it can mean scrambling for replacement capacity when a planned facility misses its delivery schedule. The risk can be especially acute for neocloud providers, which often depend on a small number of large customers and finance GPU deployments against specific contracts. Nscale announced the Loughton project in 2025 as a 50 MW campus that could scale to 90 MW, with plans to deploy 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs for Microsoft Azure. A company spokesperson confirmed that Microsoft terminated the contract. Nscale remains committed to the site and is exploring alternative power sources as well as other UK expansion opportunities, according to the spokesperson. The company also said the issue does not affect its other contracts with Microsoft and that the broader relationship between the companies remains strong. The Guardian reported that UK Power Networks told Nscale it could not supply enough electricity for the site until the early to mid-2030s, well after the project’s planned opening. The companies have not disclosed any financial consequences tied to the termination. “Capacity that isn’t energized generates no revenue, but the costs keep running,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group. Power Timing Remains a Core Risk AI infrastructure projects depend on three elements aligning at the same time: a creditworthy customer, financing supported by that customer commitment, and available electricity, Cordovil said. Developers generally have more control over winning customers and arranging financing than they do over the timing of utility power delivery. Grid operators can revise connection commitments by six months or a year, and in some cases longer, Cordovil said. Permitting processes that depend on third parties can also push projects off schedule. “The problem isn’t necessarily that AI demand disappears,” said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group. “It’s that capital can become committed long before the physical and financial assumptions supporting its recovery are proven.” How severe those consequences become depends on the underlying contracts, including missed-milestone provisions, termination rights, and equipment commitments. Nscale has not publicly detailed how much it spent on the Loughton project, whether any termination payments apply, or what contractual protections were in place. Neocloud May Be More Exposed Than Hyperscalers A delayed site can create a larger financial shock for neoclouds than for hyperscalers, Cordovil said. Neoclouds often operate with more concentrated customer bases, higher capital costs, and GPU financing tied to specific deployments. “A hyperscaler can absorb one delayed site across a large, diversified fleet and balance sheet,” Cordovil said. “A neocloud typically has more concentrated customers and a higher cost of capital.” If an anchor customer walks away, the provider can be left with equipment and financing structures built around a deployment that no longer has a buyer. A replacement customer may recover part of the investment, but not necessarily the original economics. “The issue with neoclouds is that the debt and financing is colossal, and the demand they’re betting on is not assured,” said Owen Rogers, senior research director of cloud computing at Uptime Institute Intelligence. Nscale’s September IPO filing reported $103.4 billion in active and contracted total contract value as of Aug. 31, 2026, compared with $2.6 billion in active contract value. The filing said Microsoft’s agreements with the company provided for payments of up to $43.8 billion through December 2033, subject to delivery and service-availability requirements. Separate agreements with Anthropic provided for up to $44.6 billion. Nscale also said in the filing that, as of the prospectus date, it had not secured binding financing commitments for the GPU equipment and infrastructure needed to fulfill the Anthropic agreements. The filing does not specify how much financing or equipment spending, if any, was tied specifically to Loughton. Contracted Capacity Is Not the Same as Operating Capacity For analysts tracking AI infrastructure build-outs, the Loughton cancellation is a reminder that announced capacity, contracted capacity, and operating capacity are not interchangeable. “Contracted capacity is meaningless until it’s energized capacity,” Cordovil said. “Backlog only turns into cash if the neocloud can actually build and power the capacity on time,” Rogers said. He added that customer commitments must remain in place long enough for providers to recover their investments. Power Delays Can Reshape GPU Economics Power delays can also compress the window developers have to earn returns on expensive accelerators before newer hardware generations change the economics. “Nvidia is now releasing new generations roughly every year, so today’s best GPU won’t be top-end for long,” Rogers said. Older hardware can still be used for inference and less demanding workloads, he added. Osnato said providers can lose money even when their GPUs remain commercially useful. artigo.texto: Micro-resfriamento xMEMS Entra em Produção em Massa para Dispositivos de IA e Componentes de Data Centers A xMEMS anunciou em 20 de outubro a produção em massa de dois chips de micro-resfriamento, levando fluxo de ar ativo a dispositivos nos quais ventiladores convencionais têm dificuldade para caber. O anúncio de micro-resfriamento da xMEMS abrange óculos de IA, smartphones e determinados componentes de data centers. Sua importância está no posicionamento do resfriamento: mais próximo de pequenas fontes de calor, dentro de produtos com pouco espaço para hardware rotativo. O marco de produção precisa de algum contexto. A xMEMS já havia informado que seu menor XMC-2400 estava sendo enviado em julho. O anúncio de outubro abrange esse dispositivo junto ao maior XMC-4800 e amplia a mensagem comercial da empresa. Ele não estabelece que algum dos chips tenha aparecido em um produto de varejo publicamente identificado. A disputa subjacente é entre o resfriamento ativo direcionado e projetos que dependem principalmente da dissipação de calor por meio de um gabinete fino. A Frore Systems, cuja tecnologia AirJet já aparece em um mini PC ZOTAC, oferece uma referência comercial. Para fabricantes de dispositivos, a decisão envolve desempenho sustentado, consumo de bateria, espaço físico e conforto. Um componente de resfriamento precisa melhorar todo esse equilíbrio. O que muda com o anúncio de produção do micro-resfriamento xMEMS O anúncio disponibiliza dois componentes de resfriamento para integração comercial, enquanto a adoção em produtos finalizados permanece em grande parte não divulgada. Segundo o anúncio de produção em massa da empresa, o XMC-2400 é voltado a dispositivos compactos, incluindo óculos e armazenamento pessoal. O XMC-4800 é destinado a smartphones e subsistemas de data centers de menor consumo. Os primeiros produtos comerciais com o XMC-2400 são esperados para o início de 2027. Essas categorias descrevem diferentes problemas de integração. Os óculos precisam de resfriamento dentro de uma armação vestível. Os celulares precisam de controle térmico sem ceder espaço interno excessivo. O hardware de armazenamento precisa operar de forma consistente dentro de um gabinete ou sistema que restringe o fluxo de ar. Uma arquitetura de componente comum não torna esses requisitos de engenharia intercambiáveis. Para os fabricantes, o status de produção importa porque muda a conversa de planejamento. Um protótipo pode demonstrar que uma ideia merece investigação. Um componente em produção oferece a uma equipe de projeto algo mais concreto para avaliar em fornecimento, montagem, qualificação e suporte. Essas etapas ainda exigem evidências além do anúncio de um fornecedor. A cronologia também limita como o evento deve ser enquadrado. Em seu anúncio de produto de julho, a xMEMS disse que o XMC-2400 já estava sendo enviado e apoiava suas primeiras vitórias de projeto em óculos. Uma vitória de projeto significa a seleção para um projeto de cliente; ela não estabelece necessariamente disponibilidade no varejo. Portanto, outubro não deve ser descrito como a primeira divulgação de que o XMC-2400 havia chegado à produção. O desenvolvimento mais claro é o anúncio que abrange ambos os modelos em produção e seus mercados pretendidos. Essa distinção preserva o marco sem transformar uma declaração comercial atualizada em uma estreia técnica inteiramente nova. A mesma cautela se aplica à palavra “comercial”. Envios de componentes, qualificação de clientes, anúncios de dispositivos e disponibilidade para consumidores são eventos separados. Um fornecedor pode alcançar a produção enquanto seus clientes continuam refinando os produtos. Os leitores devem evitar tratar essas etapas como evidência da mesma coisa. Para potenciais compradores, a consequência imediata é uma relevância maior durante a avaliação de produtos, e não uma recomendação de compra imediata. Não há no anúncio um par de óculos ou smartphone identificado pelo nome para avaliar. A alegação de produção se torna mais útil quando vinculada a um dispositivo finalizado, uma carga de trabalho identificada e um resultado mensurável. É por isso que a próxima etapa importa para mais do que engenheiros térmicos. Gerentes de produto que decidem quais recursos permanecem locais precisam entender os limites operacionais do hardware. As equipes de software precisam saber se um dispositivo mantém seu comportamento depois de aquecer. Um componente de resfriamento em produção introduz outra opção de projeto nessas decisões. Dispositivos finos de IA colocam o desempenho sustentado à frente de breves demonstrações A aplicação mais forte é um dispositivo cujo tempo útil de operação é limitado pelo calor, e não pela capacidade de processamento anunciada. IA de borda significa executar inteligência artificial em um dispositivo local em vez de depender inteiramente de servidores remotos. Seus requisitos térmicos dependem da carga de trabalho real. Uma interação curta e uma tarefa prolongada baseada em câmera criam condições operacionais diferentes, mesmo quando usam o mesmo processador. Considere óculos que capturam vídeo continuamente enquanto realizam análise local. A experiência relevante inclui duração da gravação, temperatura da superfície, capacidade de resposta e uso da bateria. Um dispositivo que lida confortavelmente com uma demonstração breve pode se comportar de forma diferente durante uma sessão prolongada. O resfriamento merece atenção quando essas diferenças limitam o recurso pretendido. Isso pressiona os fabricantes de dispositivos, em vez de atingir diretamente uma empresa específica de processadores. As equipes de hardware precisam escolher quanto trabalho manter dentro do gabinete disponível. Suas respostas podem incluir reduzir a atividade de processamento, alterar o projeto físico, mover o trabalho para outro lugar ou adicionar capacidade térmica. artigo.texto: Candidates challenging Rep. Higgins weigh in on SpaceX, carbon capture, data centers Meet the candidates for Louisiana’s 3rd Congressional District LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC) - Meet the five people challenging Rep. Clay Higgins for his seat in the U.S. House, representing parts of Southwest Louisiana and Acadiana. NOV. 3 ELECTION: - Early voting locations and what’s on your ballot - Key races to watch in Louisiana and across the country in the 2026 election This year’s Congressional races have been a rollercoaster for voters across the state. Voters in Louisiana’s 3rd Congressional District were originally supposed to choose their next representative through separate party primaries back in May. That changed in April, when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Louisiana’s congressional map. The ruling didn’t target District 3 directly, but Governor Jeff Landry suspended primary elections for all six of Louisiana’s U.S. House seats while the state redrew its map. Because of the compressed timeline that followed, Louisiana reverted to its older “jungle primary” system for Congress this cycle, meaning candidates from every party run against each other on the same ballot, rather than in separate party primaries. That’s why Republican incumbent Clay Higgins, Republican challenger Kate Cotten, Democratic nominee John Day, Priscilla Gonzalez and Caleb Walker, and Tia LeBrun are all on the same Nov. 3 ballot. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the vote on Nov. 3, the top two finishers will meet in a runoff on Dec. 12. We requested an interview with Rep. Higgins for this story. His office did not make him available. Here’s where the five participating candidates stand on four issues shaping the district right now: - The $100 billion SpaceX Starbase Louisiana spaceport planned for Vermilion Parish - Proposed carbon capture projects and the related fight over eminent domain - The rapid growth of data centers statewide, and - The use of non-disclosure agreements by Louisiana elected officials. Kate Cotten (R) Background Cotten runs Cotten’s Downtown, a family hamburger restaurant in Lake Charles. She first worked at Cotten’s at 12 years old, when she started helping her father. She says she’s been a registered Republican her entire life. Cotten entered the race later than most of the field; she says she decided to run specifically because of how the primary rules changed. “The decision was made to put all the qualifying Democrats on the November ballot against Clay Higgins, an incumbent Republican in a red state,” Cotten said. “With the people only voting party lines, I saw that as an opportunity for him to perhaps win outright because their vote would be split so much... I think it’s important that if Republicans win, that it’s a fair race.” SpaceX Cotten says she doesn’t have enough information yet to take a firm position on the incentive package Louisiana offered SpaceX, but she’s skeptical of the promised benefits. “I would really need to see more research that proves that development like that results in positive impacts for our coast and our community,” Cotten said. “I’ve yet to see anything that showed that. Promises, yes, but hard evidence that shows we...” She added: “Any time that these projects are launched, there is a cost to the environment and we need to just be upfront and honest about it.” Asked what she saw as the district’s biggest opportunity among the issues discussed, Cotten pointed to SpaceX. “I would imagine SpaceX would be the biggest opportunity as it’s one of the newer things, and when a product is new, there are opportunities, chances to get in on the ground floor,” she said. “But again, due diligence must be done and how it’s going to affect us.” Carbon capture and eminent domain Cotten said she isn’t familiar enough with carbon capture specifically to take a position. On the broader question of whether companies should be able to use eminent domain to acquire land for CO2 pipelines, she’s the only candidate in the field who stopped short of supporting a ban. “Anytime that you take a right away from an American, I have a lot of hesitation,” Cotten said. “I think it’s something that should be decided on a case-by-case basis. And any sort of a widespread ban I’m hesitant to support.” Data centers Cotten said she opposes shifting the cost of new power infrastructure onto ratepayers, if that’s how the billing structure actually works. “What I’ve heard is that a customer’s rate is based on the usage in that area and that these data centers were going to result in higher bills for the customers,” she said. “If that’s how it works exactly, I absolutely don’t support that.” She declined to answer what conditions she’d want attached to a data center project in the district. NDAs Cotten opposes the use of non-disclosure agreements for most government economic development deals, with one caveat. “I don’t support it outside of maybe proprietary information for their line of business,” she explained, referring to NDA’s commonly used in private business deals. “But when it has to do with pricing transparency and maybe tax breaks, things of that nature, I don’t support NDAs... It’s imperative that we be transparent about these deals.” She named NDAs as the field’s biggest risk: “If it’s not technology related to their line of business, why shouldn’t the public know what sort of a tax break someone got?” John Day (D) Background John Day, a Lake Charles Democrat, has spent roughly 30 years working in healthcare, insurance and the private sector. He says that background shaped his decision to run. Day was endorsed by the Louisiana Democratic Party, but since there was no primary, he is one of several Democrats vying for the seat. “I started running because I thought I could do a better job than Clay Higgins,” Day said. “I was disgusted and embarrassed.” But asked why voters should choose him, Day pointed to his career expertise in insurance and healthcare as some of the many reasons he’s qua

artigo.texto: ARC Capital compra data center em sua estreia na Europa Transação de 100 milhões de francos em Genebra deve ser seguida por outras quatro aquisições A brasileira ARC Capital fez na Suíça a primeira operação de sua plataforma europeia. Acaba de comprar um data center de 9,7 megawatts, com licenças para chegar a 20 MW, ao lado do aeroporto de Genebra e próximo à Organização Europeia para a Investigação Nuclear (CERN). Trata-se de um negócio de 100 milhões de francos suíços (cerca de R$ 609 milhões). A gestora já desembolsou 65 milhões francos, sendo 10 milhões em equity e 55 milhões em dívida. Os 35 milhões restantes virão também de dívida e a ARC deve ficar com cerca de 40% do cheque final após reunir coinvestidores na transação. “Seguimos o modelo de atuação do Brasil, com capital proprietário e chamando coinvestidores, e também como financiadores”, diz Vinícius Senger, o sócio da ARC responsável pela operação na Europa. O data center adquirido foi operado no passado pela IBM e vendido a uma família suíça, que contratou a CBRE para a manutenção. “Não tinha nem poeira”, diz Senger, que está fechando o contrato com o novo ocupante. A operação nasceu de uma parceria firmada no início do ano com a Gira Power, plataforma de Wissam Anastas, ex-head de infraestrutura do Deutsche Bank. Ele é minoritário no equity e atua na prospecção de ativos e captação clientes. Outros quatro data centers estão em negociação avançada e vão ficar sob a mesma holding. Ainda este ano, a ARC deve fechar a aquisição de um ativo na Alemanha e os outros três, que ficam na Noruega, França e Suécia, no primeiro trimestre de 2027. Senger se mudou para Londres há quase dois anos e desde então analisou com o time local, composto por sete pessoas, mais de 450 negócios em 20 países do continente. São quatro teses principais de investimentos por ali. A primeira é a de data centers de médio e grande porte e a segunda é o NAV finance, em que a ARC dá crédito a outras gestoras com garantia nos ativos de seus fundos. A terceira é a de defesa, que financia empresas com contratos com governos de rating AAA e dificuldade de acesso a capital de giro, num momento de alta nos gastos do setor. Um banco italiano, por exemplo, não financia empresa fora da Itália, e a ARC entra com invoice finance. A quarta, batizada de sniper shot, seriam operações com prazo curto e com gatilho de eventos específicos, que não se enquadram no perfil das outras teses mas no perfil de estruturação da casa. Para o executivo, a ARC tem competitividade nas transações pela flexibilidade de cheque - enquanto os grandes grupos de operações estruturados focam apenas operações bilionárias - e agilidade na concessão. “Não falta capital na Europa, mas falta flexibilidade. A gente consegue fazer um desembolso em quatro ou cinco dias”, diz. Até meados do ano que vem, a ARC deve investir cerca de 500 milhões de euros (R$ 2,8 bilhões), considerando as tratativas mais avançadas no momento. Desse montante, cerca de 150 milhões de euros devem ir para a tese de defesa, com o restante entre NAV finance e data centers.

artigo.texto: Portland, Westbrook look to tighten regulations on potential data centers The two Cumberland County cities held meetings on Monday where the city councils voted to advance restrictions on data center construction. Portland, Westbrook look to tighten regulations on potential data centers The two Cumberland County cities held meetings on Monday where the city councils voted to advance restrictions on data center construction. On Monday, Portland and Westbrook held separate city council meetings to discuss restrictions on data centers. Right now, no data centers have been proposed, but each council took actions to change land use codes. PORTLAND: The city council voted to ask Planning and Urban Development to develop recommendations to present to the city council. Those recommendations will center around land use as it relates to data center noise, placement and environmental concerns. The city council is also worried about the placement of potential data centers and the proximity to neighboring buildings in Maine's largest city. This was not a ban or moratorium on data centers in Portland. WESTBROOK: In June, the city council proposed a moratorium on data centers, with an exception for "server rooms" as part of businesses. Under it, no data centers can be built on land in the city. Monday's comments also focused on land near Rock Row where the city does not want data center construction. No proposals have been submitted, according to Mayor David Morse. The city council is expected to vote to finalize that moratorium at its next meeting after public comment. "Westbrook welcomes thoughtful investment, always. Part of thoughtful planning includes determining which uses are appropriate for our community and ensuring development serves the people who live here. The prospect of investment must be weighed against the use of our resources and the effects on residents' quality of life," Morse said. Back in April, Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a moratorium on data centers in Maine.

artigo.texto: Franklin County panel addresses data centers, but residents question transparency FRANKLIN COUNTY, Va. (WDBJ) - The Franklin County Board of Supervisors held a panel discussion on data centers this week. No vote was taken and no project is currently on the table. The board described the session as an opportunity for people to learn more about what is and is not true about the experience of having a data center in the county. Panelists who work with data centers regularly were brought in to speak to supervisors. Afterward, some residents said the real story is whether anything discussed will change how the board moves forward, and whether the board will be transparent about its decisions. What other localities learned The panel walked supervisors through what other localities have learned from hosting data centers, including water limits and tax deals. Mecklenburg County, which has had a Microsoft data center for 20 years, said it should have asked for more. “Today, the environment is much more favorable to put much more leverage on the locality against the data center,” said Alex Gottschalk, Mecklenburg County administrator. “Our tax rate would be much higher.” Water supply concerns raised The Western Virginia Water Authority said the water source is key, and groundwater will not get the job done, at least not at the scale that would make a deal worthwhile for the county. “Groundwater is just not a reliable source in this part of Virginia for large scale industrial activity,” said Michael McEvoy, executive director of the Western Virginia Water Authority. “We can supply about a million gallons a day. It wouldn’t be a really big data center.” Resident says comparison is unbalanced Franklin County resident Christine Sizemore said the panel was not balanced. She said Mecklenburg County’s experience would not be Franklin County’s experience, based on where Summit View Park is located. “Their data centers are in an industrial park that is away from communities, away from residential areas, which is not the case here,” Sizemore said. Common ground on transparency Gottschalk and Sizemore agreed that more transparency would be beneficial. “I would strongly suggest that the priorities be set out in that community and all the needs be articulated and then the potential funding sources for those needs be identified,” Gottschalk said. “A data center may be among them. It may not be among them. I think that’s a choice that should be reserved for each locality to make on their own.” Copyright 2026 WDBJ. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Cincinnati launches zoning study to guide data center growth, seeks public input CINCINNATI (WKRC) - Cincinnati is taking steps to get ahead of the growing demand for data centers, and it held a public meeting about its zoning study aimed at understanding their potential impacts and how the city should regulate them. The city began its data center zoning study in February at the direction of the city manager. City research presented at Monday's meeting said there are 240 data centers in Ohio, giving the state the sixth-most data centers in the country. Cincinnati officials also said the city currently has eight data centers. Sophia Ferries-Rowe, a city planner with the Department of City Planning and Engagement, said the study is intended to give the city time to determine long-term rules for data centers. “The purpose of the IDC [Interim Development Control Overlay #89 "Data Centers" and Zoning Study] is to give us, as a city, time to study data centers and figure out how we want to regulate them permanently in our zoning code,” Ferries-Rowe said. A primary goal of the study is to define what a “data center” is for zoning and regulatory purposes. The study is also examining what regulations other cities across the country are putting in place. During the meeting, the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati and Greater Cincinnati Water Works discussed how data centers use water and addressed common concerns. Scott Bessler, superintendent of the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati, said the city has a lot of high-water-use customers, and generally, data centers are under the same regulations as other high-use customers. “Our primary concern is protecting our treatment plant performance and public infrastructure,” Bessler said. "So, construction and start-up activities of data centers have been known to create wastewater containing chemicals, metals, or other elevated nutrient levels." The meeting also included information about the energy data centers use. One slide in the presentation compared the energy a certain size of data center uses with a city that uses the same amount of energy. It showed that a medium-sized data center uses between 43.8 and 438 gigawatts annually, which is equivalent to a city with a population between 3,500 and 34,000. The slide used Mason as an example of a city, residences and businesses, that would use the same amount of power a medium-sized data center uses. "It requires a lot of energy," Rob McCracken from the city's Office of Environment & Sustainability said. "Electric utilities are allowed to recoup their investment. So, any investment in infrastructure they make, all the ratepayers pay." That is one concern Manny Addo had, who attended the meeting. "If we can find a way where we could shave that cost and let it go where it belongs, it would be a great idea," said Addo. Attendees were able to ask questions. One attendee raised concerns that data centers vary widely, particularly those used for artificial intelligence, and asked whether zoning should consider not only size but also reusability, citing a lack of plans for reuse for some facilities. Addo said he found the presentations helpful, and is happy the city is trying to get ahead of things. “The rapid growth of data centers may pose a challenge, because we may not be able to grapple with the growth and to anticipate or cover all the disadvantages that it might come with,” Addo said. The team working on the study hopes to have zoning recommendations by February, though the study could be extended if necessary. City officials said Cincinnati currently has no building permit applications for data centers. If an application is submitted before zoning code changes are adopted, it would have to be approved by the Planning Commission.

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump is calling for data centers to pay for their own power and pay dividends to local communities — a stark change for the president less than two weeks before the election and as opposition to data centers is growing. In Memphis, Tenn., where the City Council was weighing a temporary moratorium on data centers on Tuesday, ultimately voting against the move, attendees used fiery language to describe their feelings. “Lives are at stake and blood is on your hands,” council meeting attendee Tikeila Rucker said. "Supporting a pause on data centers is a vote for reaffirming your dedication to the people of Memphis, not the billionaire class," said attendee Amber Sherman. It’s a scene playing out across the country as Americans raise concerns that data centers, which provide the computing power for artificial intelligence, will drive up electric bills and consume massive amounts of water. Now the president is pitching a new solution. He wrote early Wednesday morning that new data centers are “mandated by me to make their own electricity and give or sell any excess back to the local community.” He added: “If companies want to make their data centers popular, they should pay a ‘dividend’ to the community.” It was not immediately clear how the president’s demand could be implemented. Trump’s social media post marks a shift in tone for the president, who previously criticized data center opponents as wanting to “end up being backwards and poor,” as he said at a rally earlier this month in Ohio. “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio,” he said. “You can’t just turn it off. They’ll go to China.” Todd Eisenstadt, research director at American University Center for Environmental Policy, said data centers are an easy target. He said there’s been a growing uneasiness with data centers tied with a more existential fear over the development of artificial intelligence. A new Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll found 66% of Americans oppose construction of new data centers and also disapprove of the president’s handling of AI. “Perhaps the wind has shifted and this is a defining issue of the election,” Eisenstadt told Spectrum News. “And he’s on the wrong side of it. So, he’s trying to swim the other way here at the last minute.” The number of data centers has exploded. Estimates show there are at least 3,000 nationwide.

artigo.texto: CATL shares drop 11% as new battery tax bites, full-quarter hit still to come CATL (SZSE: 300750, HKEX: 3750) closed down 11.41% at HK$364.80 (c. $46.48) in Hong Kong on October 21, 2026, after the battery maker's third-quarter profit slipped from the quarter before. Net profit attributable to shareholders was 21.25 billion CNY (c. $3.16 billion) for the three months to September 30, up 14.54% from a year earlier but down 5.77% from the second quarter. Sales kept growing much faster than profit. Revenue rose 58.58% to 165.22 billion CNY (c. $24.59 billion), yet gross margin fell to 20.69%, from 23.15% in the second quarter and 25.80% a year earlier. That is CATL's lowest quarterly margin since the fourth quarter of 2022. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more Part of the squeeze is a new tax. China resumed a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and four other battery types on September 1, 2026, and the rate doubles to 4% on September 1, 2027. CATL's taxes and surcharges line reached 3.54 billion CNY (c. $526.7 million) in the first nine months, up from 1.84 billion CNY a year earlier. Almost all of that rise landed in one quarter. Third-quarter taxes and surcharges were 2.21 billion CNY (c. $329.5 million), against 597 million CNY (c. $88.8 million) a year earlier, after a first half of 1.33 billion CNY. The third quarter carried only one month of the new tax, so the fourth quarter will be the first to bear it in full. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more On the earnings call on October 20, CFO Zheng Shu said the tax is built into the product price, so CATL cannot pass it on to carmakers until prices are renegotiated. Those talks are still under way, and management said the outcome differs by customer and by timing. Asked how much of the cost CATL would carry itself, the company said it was too early to say. Export rebates are the second hit. The VAT rebate on exported batteries was cut from 9% to 6% on April 1 and will be scrapped on January 1, 2027. CATL said the cut barely showed in second-quarter results because revenue is booked some time after shipment, so it came through more fully in the third quarter. Akin Li, executive president of CATL's overseas business, at the TECTRANS II truck battery launch in Hannover, September 14, 2026 (CATL) Management put most of the margin drop on product mix rather than tax. CATL said it delivered some low value-added projects in the quarter, which raised the share of simpler products in its sales. Its power and energy storage batteries together sold more than 260 GWh in the first nine months, and inventories rose 53.15% to 144.77 billion CNY (c. $21.55 billion) from the end of 2025. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more Raw materials added pressure. Lithium carbonate climbed from under 60,000 CNY a tonne (c. $8,930) in mid-2025 to more than 210,000 CNY (c. $31,254) in June 2026, before easing to 130,000 to 160,000 CNY in September, and battery prices have lagged that rise. CATL's revenue growth of 56.19% for the nine months roughly matched the 57.6% rise in China's power and storage battery sales, to 1,681.7 GWh. The result came in below forecasts. Bernstein had expected quarterly net profit of 22.9 billion CNY (c. $3.41 billion), Goldman Sachs 24 billion CNY (c. $3.57 billion) and CLSA 25 billion to 26 billion CNY. Before the results, JPMorgan cut CATL's Hong Kong shares to neutral from overweight and lowered its target price to HK$500 from HK$725, while keeping an overweight rating on the Shenzhen shares. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more JPMorgan argued that carmakers facing the consumption tax, lower export rebates and trade barriers will push part of those costs back up the supply chain. It called this a redistribution of profit along the chain rather than an ordinary price war, with CATL hit first and smaller battery makers hit harder. The Hong Kong shares had already fallen 6.58% to HK$411.80 on October 20, so the two sessions took about 17% off the price. In Shenzhen, the A shares fell more than 12% on October 21 and now sit more than 50% below their record high of May 7, 2026. Battery equipment maker Lead Intelligent (HKEX: 470) fell 9.58% in Hong Kong, and rival cell maker CALB (HKEX: 3931) lost 3.57%. Cash is tighter too. Operating cash flow for the nine months fell 23.60% to 61.63 billion CNY (c. $9.17 billion), while prepayments to suppliers rose 85.26%. An executive said CATL began shortening payment terms and paying some suppliers in advance in the third quarter, and that this could weigh on cash flow for a while. Advertisement – Continue scrolling for more CATL is still locking in its biggest customers. On October 10 it signed a long-term agreement with SERES (HKEX: 9927), whose AITO models have all used CATL batteries, to expand their plant-in-plant battery project at the SERES Super Factory to more than 20 GWh a year. The announcement did not mention the new tax. The SERES Super Factory, where Phase 2 of the plant-in-plant project is planned at 10 to 12 GWh a year (CATL) Management still expects demand to hold up. CATL said growth of 20% to 30% in global power and energy storage battery demand is achievable in 2027, citing commercial vehicles, Europe and overseas storage, and it expects its Choco-Swap passenger car network to pass 3,000 stations this year. That network added Huawei's Yinwang as a partner on October 19. Storage is the bright spot CATL keeps pointing to. Mesa Grande Band Tribe completes first public clean energy installation Solar and batteries power three tribal facilities Systems cut costs and ride out grid outages Stock video by Los Muertos Crew via Pexels Oct 20, 2026 Mesa Grande Band Completes First Public Clean Energy Installation on Reservation The Mesa Grande Band of Diegueno Mission Indians, working with the Solar Electric Light Fund, has finished installing solar and battery storage systems at three Tribal facilities on the Mesa Grande Reservation in San Diego County, California, according to the Tribe. The project represents the first public clean energy installation on the reservation and advances the Tribe's long-term effort to strengthen energy sovereignty. Solar panels and batteries now serve the Tekamuk, Hallyeyaaw and Golden Eagle administration buildings. The three structures function as civic and community hubs, supporting Tribal government, housing services, cultural and educational programming, food distribution and emergency response. The solar systems are sized to cover the three facilities' present electricity needs while leaving room for future growth. Combined, they are expected to produce roughly 60 MWh of solar electricity each year and to reduce the Tribe's electricity costs by at least $16,780 annually. The battery storage allows the administration buildings to keep running independently of the electric grid during outages, which the Tribe describes as common in the rural community. Curtis La Chusa, chairman of the Mesa Grande Tribal Council, commented that electricity is often taken for granted and tends to go unnoticed until service is lost, while noting that power interruptions are a regular reality at Mesa Grande. He said outages there can last for days at a time, disrupting the services the Tribe provides to its members. The installation builds on more than two decades of Tribal efforts to expand access to reliable, affordable clean energy. Grid electricity did not reach the reservation until the 1950s, and some homes remain off the grid today, relying on small generators for basic household needs. Over the years Mesa Grande has pursued residential solar, renewable energy planning and workforce development. Four Tribal members with prior solar installation training were employed on the project. Bob Freling, executive director of the Solar Electric Light Fund, the nonprofit that facilitated the project, said reliable and affordable energy gives communities room to invest in future priorities. He indicated that lower energy costs and stronger resilience can free up resources while providing a sustainable foundation for growth, and that the organization looks forward to seeing how clean energy helps Mesa Grande meet its goals. The clean energy work coincides with the Tribe's start on a long-term plan for new housing and community infrastructure. The plan calls for 1,500 new homes to address housing affordability and supply shortages that have historically limited how many members can live on Tribal land. The development would include the first new housing built on the reservation since 2005. La Chusa said Mesa Grande has a bright future ahead, describing the effort as beginning with enabling Tribal members to return home and providing the spaces and services needed for them to thrive. Funding for the project came from the William, Jeff and Jennifer Gross Family Foundation and others, according to the Tribe. Interactive table based on the Store Companies dataset for this report. 1. artigo.texto: Denton City Council members unanimously voted Oct. 13 to adopt development code amendments related to data center zoning restrictions, their proximity to homes and required environmental protections. The details The Denton Development Code updates are intended to prevent facilities from impacting neighboring homes and businesses, keep land use standards up to date with current data center trends, protect water supplies and prevent surface water and groundwater contamination, Assistant Planning Director Angie Glass said at the meeting. They also act as a stopgap while the city considers a moratorium, a temporary pause on accepting and processing new applications. “[These amendments protect] us more while we're going through the moratorium phase,” Councilmember George Ferrie said. Updates to the code for data centers include: - Restricting data centers from being constructed anywhere in Denton to zoning districts labeled as light industrial, heavy industrial and public facility, all three of which require a special use permit - Restricting water cooling methods to closed-loop or free-air systems - Requiring water and wastewater demand studies with their initial application - Expanding the minimum setback from residential zones from 100 feet to 300 feet - Prohibiting any light spillover into residential property lines - Requiring approvals from the Texas Public Utility Commission and Electric Reliability Council of Texas prior to placement on a City Council agenda for consideration The amendments apply to the two previously permitted data centers in Denton if they expand or modify their sites in the future, along with new data center developments within city limits. The city rejected a new data center application in early October because it did not meet all of the city’s initial submission requirements, Glass said. City Attorney Mack Reinwand said parts of that application could potentially be reviewed under the prior standards. What’s next The council will hold the second public hearing and the first reading of the proposed data center moratorium Oct. 27. The first public hearing was held Sept. 22. City Council is required to hold two public hearings before it can vote on passing the moratorium. The earliest council members can vote on implementing a moratorium is at their Dec. 1 meeting. If the resolution passes, all new development and permitting for data centers in Denton city limits will be halted effective immediately, according to previous reporting.

artigo.texto: (KNSI) — The St. Cloud City Council voted 5-0 Monday night to set a November 16th public hearing on proposed data center rules. Council Member Tami Calhoun pulled the item from the consent agenda for discussion, mainly to thank city staff for their work preparing the proposal. “I was so appreciative that [Community Development] Director [Matt] Glaesman had given us all this background information because that’s what we need. We need the information going forward.” No developer has brought a specific project to the city. Calhoun told KNSI data centers are relatively new and the city’s planning rules haven’t caught up. “So we need to be sure, be proactive, and be sure that we get exactly what we want in there before we’re ever approached to ask if we want a data center.” Calhoun says energy use, noise and what happens to a building if a data center operator leaves are among the concerns she’ll be weighing before the hearing. In a memo to the council and Planning Commission, Glaesman says adopting standards ahead of a site-specific proposal is the best practice. The city’s code currently has no data center category and allows a broad “communication facility” use by right in the I3 planned industrial district, with no design standards. The proposal has two parts. A comprehensive plan amendment would call data centers a valuable part of the city’s economy and tax base, while saying the city must limit effects on residential areas and address noise, public resources and the environment. A land development code amendment would create two categories. Smaller enterprise data centers, with 2,000 servers or fewer, 10,000 square feet or less of building area and 50 megawatts or less of peak electrical use, would be allowed by right in the C3 Central Business and C5 Highway Commercial districts. Larger hyperscale facilities would need a conditional use permit in the I3 district and would have to stay a quarter mile from residential zoning. All data centers would have to submit studies on noise, environmental impacts, community impact, backup power, sustainability and decommissioning. Projects of 450,000 square feet or more also require a state environmental review, and the memo says findings from that review could be grounds to deny a permit. The Planning Commission recommended approval of both items on a 4-2 vote October 13th. In a September 8th letter to the city, Pipefitters Local 539 voiced support for responsible data center development and asked for clear, objective standards with no arbitrary geographic restrictions. ___ Copyright © 2026 Leighton Media. artigo.texto: Offshore Data Center e Kalypso miram gás encalhado para computação offshore A Offshore Data Center LLC firmou uma parceria com a Kalypso Offshore Energy com o objetivo de ajudar proprietários de gás offshore a monetizar reservas encalhadas, subutilizadas e subvalorizadas por meio da geração de energia para computação de IA no mar, segundo o World Oil. As duas empresas avaliarão instalações recém-construídas, bem como a reutilização de infraestrutura offshore existente, incluindo estruturas ociosas selecionadas, para computação modular de borda e de inferência. Art Schroeder, fundador e diretor-presidente da Offshore Data Center, observou que muitas plataformas no Golfo da América estão programadas para descomissionamento, embora algumas possam ainda manter vida estrutural útil. Ele afirmou que as empresas pretendem colaborar com operadores e reguladores, junto com a Kalypso, para explorar a instalação de data centers modulares em ativos existentes adequados, gerando nova receita a partir de recursos offshore e potencialmente adiando determinados gastos com a Obrigação de Aposentadoria de Ativos. A instalação da geração de energia e da computação próximas aos recursos de gás offshore tem como objetivo encurtar a cadeia tradicional, na qual o gás é convertido em energia e depois enviado a um data center em terra. A Offshore Data Center está reunindo parceiros como a Horton do Brasil, cujos projetos de casco semissubmersível, segundo as empresas, poderiam ser até 50% mais leves, com estabilidade aprimorada. De acordo com as empresas, isso permitiria que a construção na costa do Golfo dos Estados Unidos competisse com estaleiros na Coreia, na China e em Singapura. Parceiros da Offshore Data Center também fornecem sistemas de resfriamento em circuito fechado destinados a reduzir substancialmente as cargas de resfriamento dos data centers. A Kalypso liderará o trabalho de cabos submarinos que ligam as instalações à rede elétrica, às redes de comunicação e à costa. Isso abrange o desenvolvimento de rotas, a engenharia, a instalação e a conexão de cabos de fibra óptica, de energia e umbilicais, além de suporte de reparo, operações e manutenção. Owen Rataj, diretor da Kalypso Offshore Energy, afirmou que um data center offshore é tão bom quanto os cabos que o conectam, e que fibra de baixa latência até a costa, conexões de energia confiáveis e capacidade de reparo e manutenção próximas aos ativos são o que transformam uma plataforma offshore em capacidade de computação utilizável.

O Piauí avançou na implantação da política estadual de crédito de carbono com a realização da primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor do REDD+, nesta terça-feira (20), no Centro de Educação Ambiental (CEA), em Teresina. A iniciativa busca reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa provocadas pelo desmatamento e pela degradação florestal, além de criar mecanismos para beneficiar comunidades que contribuem para a preservação ambiental. O encontro foi aberto pelo secretário de Estado do Meio Ambiente e Recursos Hídricos, Feliphe Araújo. O conselho reúne representantes do poder público, da sociedade civil, da academia, dos povos indígenas, das comunidades quilombolas e tradicionais, da agricultura familiar e do setor produtivo. A proposta é garantir participação social, transparência e segurança na construção da política, que poderá gerar recursos para a conservação das florestas e beneficiar populações envolvidas na proteção dos biomas piauienses. Política prevê benefícios para comunidades Feliphe Araújo destacou que a implantação do projeto é uma das prioridades da gestão estadual. Segundo o secretário, a política precisa ser construída com regulamentação, diálogo e participação dos diferentes setores da sociedade. “Queremos proteger nossas florestas e, ao mesmo tempo, gerar recursos para beneficiar as pessoas que ajudam a preservar o meio ambiente. Por isso, é fundamental que esse processo seja construído com diálogo, transparência e participação de todos os setores”, afirmou. De acordo com o secretário, o Estado já avançou na elaboração de normas, na regulamentação da iniciativa e na busca por parceiros para viabilizar o projeto. A experiência de outros estados, como o Tocantins, também é utilizada como referência para orientar as próximas etapas. REDD+ busca reduzir emissões e preservar florestas O REDD+ é um mecanismo voltado à redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa associadas ao desmatamento e à degradação florestal. A iniciativa também pode viabilizar pagamentos por serviços ambientais, com benefícios para povos indígenas, comunidades quilombolas, populações tradicionais e agricultores familiares. Além da política de crédito de carbono, o secretário ressaltou a importância de associar a preservação ambiental ao desenvolvimento econômico. Entre as ações complementares citadas estão a recuperação de áreas degradadas, a educação ambiental, a fiscalização e a prevenção e o combate aos incêndios florestais. A primeira reunião do Conselho Gestor representa uma etapa na organização da governança do projeto. A estrutura busca assegurar que as decisões sejam debatidas coletivamente e que a política estadual seja desenvolvida com responsabilidade ambiental e participação social.

artigo.texto: Chery pairs 12C liquid battery cells with 400 Wh/kg solid-state technology Chery outlined its Rhinoceros Battery roadmap at the 2026 Chery Global Innovation Conference on October 20, including a dedicated Rhinoceros S solid-state battery pilot line scheduled to enter operation in 2027, reports IT-Home. The schedule adds a manufacturing milestone to Chery’s existing development plan. The company previously targeted solid-state battery applications in vehicles as early as 2026, while chairman Yin Tongyue said in September that vehicle-level testing would begin in 2027. Pilot-line operation and vehicle validation are separate stages, and neither establishes a date for customer deliveries. The manufacturing timeline also needs context. Chery completed construction of a 0.5 GWh pilot line for 60 Ah-class solid-state cells in February 2026 and issued equipment procurement tenders in early October. Chery has not clarified whether the line scheduled to enter operation in 2027 is that facility, a separate installation, or a further stage of commissioning. Rhinoceros S specifications and development challenges Chery lists the Rhinoceros S solid-state battery at 400 Wh/kg, with an operating temperature range of -40°C to 100°C. The company also reported an internal thermal-box test at 200°C. Still, it did not disclose the test duration, state of charge, or sample configuration needed to compare the result with standardised battery-safety tests. The 400 Wh/kg figure is not new in itself. Chery previously presented solid-state technology targeting 600 Wh/kg. Its development programs use different electrolyte and cathode formulations: earlier reporting identifies a sulfide-based electrolyte and high-nickel ternary cathode for the 400 Wh/kg cell, compared with an in-situ polymerised electrolyte and lithium-rich manganese cathode for the 600 Wh/kg route. The figures therefore describe different technical approaches and should not be treated as directly comparable versions of the same cell. Chery identified material-interface contact, battery-pack integration, and its proprietary Dedicated Management System (DMS) as engineering priorities. In solid-state cells, maintaining stable contact between the solid electrolyte and electrodes during repeated charging and discharging remains a key technical challenge. The timing places Chery among several Chinese automakers and battery manufacturers targeting solid-state battery trial production or vehicle validation around 2027. CATL and BYD have both targeted small-scale solid-state battery production for that year. Their plans are at different development stages and do not indicate that any of the companies will reach mass production in 2027. Liquid cells, sodium-ion storage and ammonia-fueled SOFC The Rhinoceros portfolio also covers liquid-electrolyte cells and sodium-ion batteries for energy storage. Chery lists a peak charging rate of 12C and a sustained average above 8C for its liquid cells; these figures do not apply to the Rhinoceros S solid-state battery. Its sodium-ion storage cells are rated for up to 15,000 cycles in commercial, industrial, and residential applications. For vehicles, Chery has outlined a long-term solid-state battery range target of up to 1,500 km. This remains a development target, not a confirmed range for a production vehicle. Chery also presented an ammonia-fueled solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) system for stationary power generation. The conference slides identify ammonia as the fuel and describe green ammonia produced using wind and solar power. They list electrical efficiency of 60%, combined heat and power (CHP) efficiency of 90%, adjustable output from 30% to 100%, and a 90-day deployment window. Ammonia can serve as a hydrogen carrier for fuel-cell systems, but fuel processing and ammonia production affect overall efficiency and emissions. Using renewable electricity to produce ammonia does not, by itself, establish zero lifecycle emissions. An independent assessment of the stated efficiency figures would require more operating details. Proposed applications include decentralised power generation and remote charging infrastructure. Their viability would depend on fuel supply and transport, installation requirements, electricity demand, and operating costs.

artigo.texto: Warrick County weighs new data center rules as Alcoa ‘Project Alloy’ draws closer WARRICK CO., Ind. (WFIE) - A massive data center could be coming to Warrick County, and the company behind it isn’t an outsider — it’s Alcoa, a business that has operated in the county for decades. The project, known as “Project Alloy,” is a proposed data center eyed for roughly 700 acres of Alcoa-owned land near the company’s power plant. Warrick County Commissioners, county legal counsel and representatives of Warrick County Economic Development met with the development team on October 16 in a closed executive session — a meeting allowed under Indiana’s Open Door Law for interviews and negotiations with an industrial or commercial prospect. County officials say the discussion was preliminary and informational. No vote was taken, no nondisclosure agreement was signed, and no commitment was made. “I find it kind of exciting that it’s not somebody coming from outside here. It is here. They are Warrick County. They live and work here. They have a vested interest in the success of the county, not just the success of the data center, but the success of the people that live here,” said Warrick County Commissioner Sarah Seaton. What We Know About Project Alloy Based solely on information the development team provided to the county, officials say Project Alloy includes a letter of intent to develop roughly 700 acres of Alcoa-owned land, with only a fraction of that acreage expected to be built out and the rest left undeveloped as separation from surrounding properties. The development team says it has an existing relationship with a prospective end user and told the county there will not be any adverse effects on existing Alcoa or Kaiser operations. The project remains in the due-diligence stage. According to the county, Alcoa’s evaluation will address environmental conditions, water supply and cooling, electrical demand and grid impacts, threatened and endangered species, geological and mine-subsidence risk, drainage and floodplain conditions, traffic, noise, lighting, air emissions, and fire protection needs. More fully developed plans aren’t expected for county review until sometime in the first half of 2027, according to the development team. The county is not paying for those studies, and officials say they have not been told who will conduct them or what methods will be used. The county says it will ask the development team to share completed studies with the public if it moves forward with permits. Commissioners emphasize that none of this information has been independently verified. The county has not determined whether existing water, electric, road or public-safety capacity is sufficient, whether taxpayers or utility customers would bear additional costs, or whether the project would deliver the tax revenue, jobs or other economic benefits the development team has described. A New Rulebook, Regardless of Project Alloy’s Outcome Separately — and for months before Project Alloy became public — the Warrick County Commissioners and Area Plan Commission have been developing a permanent data center ordinance. Officials say the ordinance isn’t written around any single project; it’s meant to establish standards for any data center that might propose to locate in the county, including, but not limited to, Project Alloy. Earlier this year, the Area Plan Commission formed a committee to study data center development, drawing on input from residents, county officials and other stakeholders, and reviewing ordinances adopted in other jurisdictions. The draft ordinance would create a new “Data Center Overlay” (DC-O) zoning district. Under the proposal, a data center could only be built on property zoned both general industrial (M-2) and DC-O — and getting that DC-O designation would require a site-specific rezoning approved by elected county commissioners, not an administrative board. The ordinance also specifies that a data center cannot be approved through a special exception or similar process that bypasses that legislative vote. The draft includes specific numerical standards, including: - Noise: Operational sound from a project could not exceed 55 decibels (dBA) at a neighboring home or residential zoning boundary — roughly comparable to normal conversation — with stricter limits for tonal noise. - Lighting: Exterior lighting would be capped at 0.5 foot-candle at a neighboring residential boundary and limited to “warmer” bulb temperatures to reduce glare and light pollution. - Setbacks and buffers: Data center buildings would need to sit at least 300 feet from homes or residential zoning, with intensive outdoor equipment — generators, transformers, battery storage — set back at least 500 feet. A landscaped buffer of at least 100 feet would be required near residential property. - Water use: The ordinance would ban “once-through” cooling systems for routine operations, require water-efficient cooling technology, and require developers to disclose and cap peak-day water demand. - Decommissioning: Developers would be required to maintain a decommissioning and restoration plan, reviewed at least every five years, along with financial assurance to cover removal and restoration costs if a project shuts down or is abandoned. If a project fails to move forward, the ordinance is designed to return the property to its prior zoning. “Is it a good fit not just for the county, but for their specific site? Is it a good fit for the neighbors in the area? What is it going to do to local roads, traffic and things like that? And it gives us the ability to say, no, this probably isn’t going to work well for us, or we think we have found one that might,” Seaton said. How Residents Can Weigh In The ordinance remains a draft, and officials stress no final decision has been made. The public will get two formal chances to respond: - Area Plan Commission public hearing: November 2, 2026, 6 p.m., Friedman Park Event Center - Commissioners

artigo.texto: Demanda de data centers impulsiona vendas da WEG no exterior no 3º tri Mercado externo respondeu por 62,5% da receita da companhia, que produz geradores de energia e motores para sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração A demanda por equipamentos destinados a data centers contribuiu para o crescimento dos negócios da WEG no exterior no 3º trimestre de 2026. Segundo balanço divulgado nesta 4ª feira (21.out.2026), a fabricante brasileira registrou aumento nas vendas de geradores de energia e equipamentos industriais, principalmente na América do Norte. O mercado externo respondeu por 62,5% da receita da companhia, a maior participação de sua história. Eis a íntegra do relatório (PDF – 306 kB). A WEG registrou lucro líquido de R$ 1,67 bilhão no período, alta de 0,9% em relação ao mesmo trimestre de 2025. A receita operacional líquida somou R$ 10,86 bilhões, crescimento de 5,7% na comparação anual. Desse total, R$ 6,79 bilhões vieram do mercado externo, avanço de 8,3% em relação ao ano anterior. A demanda por data centers beneficia duas áreas de atuação da companhia. A divisão de geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia fornece geradores utilizados como fonte de eletricidade de reserva para essas instalações. Já a área de equipamentos eletroeletrônicos industriais atende à demanda por motores e sistemas de automação, que são utilizados em ventilação e refrigeração, necessários para controlar a temperatura dos equipamentos de processamento de dados. No segmento de geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia, a receita no mercado externo atingiu R$ 2,49 bilhões, alta de 24,1% em relação ao 3º trimestre de 2025. A WEG destacou o desempenho dos geradores Marathon, nos Estados Unidos, destinados principalmente ao fornecimento de energia de reserva para data centers. Esses equipamentos são produzidos por uma divisão da empresa norte-americana Regal Rexnord, adquirida pela WEG em 2024. As vendas de transformadores para reforço da infraestrutura elétrica dos Estados Unidos também contribuíram para o resultado da companhia no exterior. A divisão de equipamentos eletroeletrônicos industriais registrou receita externa de R$ 3,75 bilhões, crescimento de 1,1% na comparação anual. Segundo a companhia, houve continuidade da demanda por motores elétricos de baixa tensão e produtos de automação, com destaque para sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração para data centers, além dos setores de óleo e gás e mineração.

artigo.texto: SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- A BYD Energy Storage desenvolveu uma rede abrangente de serviços pós-venda em uma estrutura de vários níveis: operação e manutenção de estações, centros de projetos, centros regionais e sede global. A BYD Energy Storage opera nove centros de O&M de 2.500 metros quadrados em todo o mundo. Ela conta com uma rede de serviços de pós-venda em diversos países como China, Chile, África do Sul, Reino Unido, Estados Unidos, Austrália, Japão, Polônia e Oriente Médio. Novos centros de serviços serão inaugurados na África do Sul e na Bulgária em 2027 para expandir ainda mais sua presença global de serviços. Os centros desempenham funções essenciais, como armazenamento e gestão de peças de reposição, reparo e manutenção de baterias, alocação regional de peças de reposição, reciclagem de baterias e treinamento de engenheiros contratados localmente. Os centros regionais da BYD Energy Storage estão em total conformidade com os requisitos regulamentares locais, oferecem treinamento estruturado para a força de trabalho e viabilizam uma resposta local rápida. A equipe de serviços profissionais é composta por mais de 200 engenheiros de campo e mais de 100 especialistas em P&D. A empresa aplica SLAs de serviço padronizados: resposta em até 24 horas, chegada ao local em até 48 horas e solução de problemas em até 7 dias. A rede global de serviços da empresa alcança uma ampla cobertura. Ela forma uma rede de suprimentos multiponto que garante a entrega rápida de peças de reposição em todo o mundo. Além disso, com suas linhas de produção locais, as equipes de operação e manutenção integram recursos regionais para oferecer serviços locais de reparo de baterias, fornecendo aos clientes globais um suporte pós-venda rápido, conveniente e localizado. "Nossa presença global de serviços é adaptada às nossas implementações de BESS em rápido crescimento. "O suporte pós-venda confiável sustenta a operação estável de longo prazo dos ativos de armazenamento de energia", comentou He Dehong, Chefe de Serviço Pós-Venda Global da BYD Energy Storage. Guiado por sua visão de capacitar o setor global de armazenamento de energia com serviços digitais e inteligentes, o sistema global maduro de O&M da BYD Energy Storage apoia fortemente sua crescente presença no armazenamento de energia em baterias. A empresa liderou as remessas globais de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), superando 60 GWh em 2025, e entregou, ao todo, mais de 650 projetos de armazenamento de energia, contando com serviços pós-venda padronizados e localizados que garantem a operação confiável dos ativos. artigo.texto: Martin city leaders discuss regulations to get ahead of any potential data centers MARTIN, Tenn. (WBBJ) - The city of martin is getting ahead of a possible data center. City leaders held a meeting to set regulations before any project involving the construction of a data center is even proposed. They recommended capping noise at 60 decibels day and night, requiring 30 foot setbacks for small data centers, and 75 to 100 feet for hyperscale centers, keeping buildings mostly hidden from view, and limiting driveway access. The ordinance passed unanimously. “The regulations I’ve been working on for communities would define what a data center is and then would set up additional requirements, additional buffer from the nearest residential structure,” explained Donny Bunton, Martin city planner. If no regulation was put in before the proposal, it falls under general industrial use requirements, which are not as restrictive and do not include a buffer for the nearest residential structures. artigo.texto: Trending WHEELING - A preliminary draft of proposed amendments to the city of Wheeling’s Planning and Zoning code to include rules and regulations specifically for data centers was reviewed by city leaders on Tuesday night. Members of the Rules Committee of Wheeling City Council met at length prior to Tuesday night’s regular council meeting to discuss the proposed draft. Officials stressed the comprehensive document, currently 15 pages in length, is still a work in progress. However, several language tweaks and suggestions for changes were offered during Tuesday night’s session, and city leaders proposed the latest version of the draft be posted on the city’s website today in order to give the public the opportunity to review it and provide input to council members as the proposed amendment moves forward. "Put it out to the public with the understanding that this is a working draft," Councilman Dave Palmer noted. "That way, we can be contacted with suggestions from the public, listen more to ideas that are out there, and see if we thought we missed anything. It’s going to change. But I think we do have to get it out there to the public." The discussion comes in the wake of concerns by city leaders and the public over the past several months about the looming development of a new data center in the Wheeling neighborhood of Warwood. The former Centre Foundry & Machine Company property was acquired last year by the Silicon Foundation, an energy and artificial intelligence compute infrastructure company with international roots which plans to develop a new data center and energy technology campus at the Warwood location. Mayor Denny Magruder and other city leaders thanked Wheeling City Solicitor Rosemary Humway-Warmuth for working to put together the proposed zoning amendments, along with help from Building and Planning Director Brenda J. Delbert, City Clerk Jessica Holloway and others. This included research stemming from within the city’s own existing codes to municipalities around the country that have addressed similar situations. "I know some folks thought that we weren’t working on this, but those folks who have been working on it I think have been doing so for more than three months," Magruder said. "I think it’s a good move in the right direction." The city has already developed a memorandum of understanding with Silicon Foundation in which the company agrees not to apply with the state to expand and become what is considered a high-impact data center. Vice Mayor Jerry Skavounakis, chairman of the Rules Committee, said there was no previous example in the state of West Virginia on which legislation specific to municipal planning and zoning for data centers could be based. "There’s not a template that she was able to use," the vice mayor said. "There isn’t one. This is something she had to do from scratch. "I know you put a lot of time and effort into this, and I appreciate it," he told the city solicitor. The planning and zoning amendments to include language pertaining to data centers would first require a permitting process. A special use permit application would have to be submitted and approved, and the application process alone would involve a considerable list of requirements. Permitting requirements address a checklist of issues related to the site plan, a utility impact review, anticipated electrical demand and expected peak demands, adequate electrical service without unreasonable burden to city services and public utilities, daily maximum water demands and consumption, wastewater discharges, description of proposed cooling and water conservation measures, location and specifications of backup generators, anticipated air emissions, anticipated noise-producing equipment, proposed storm water management, noise levels and other issues. "There’s a list of things that they have to provide the city," Councilman Ty Thorngate said. "I think that is, to me, the most important thing in this." The application fee alone is currently set at $5,000, according to the proposed language. A surety bond must be provided by the applicant, as well. Currently, the surety bond is set at $75,000, but Humway-Warmuth noted this can be increased. "This is in case that applicant does not fulfill what they are required to fulfill," she said. "We’re not wed to that amount. It may be something you may want to modify - that’s at your discretion." The applicant must also cover the cost for industry experts the city will hire as consultants to review their application to make sure the company is meeting the requirements, to make any recommendations and to assure that industry standards are being met. "This allows us to use experts within this field, rely upon them, and then pass the cost off to the application - which would be the proposed data center, not the citizens," Sklavounakis said. Proposed language also includes potential fines for violations, but city officials noted that financial punishment would not likely have much of an impact on a company involved in data center development. "The big issue isn’t just the fines, we want to make sure that if they are doing stuff that they’re not supposed to be doing, we can revoke their permit in addition to the fines," Sklavounakis said. "If this data center wants to come here, the first thing they’re going to have to do is they have to get a permit. They’re not going to be able to operate without a permit." Humway-Warmuth noted the basic framework of the draft was based in part by language developed more than two decades ago when wireless communication boomed across the country and cell phone towers and infrastructure came to the city. The city created wireless telecommunication-specific ordinances to address issues related to these developments and several tweaks have been implemented in the city over the years, as well.
