artigo.texto: More than 30 community members took to Virginia Beach Town Center Tuesday night to call on lawmakers to enact a statewide data center moratorium. Chesapeake Climate Action Network partnered with several organizations to march as part of a two-week tour across the commonwealth. Tuesday’s event was the only stop in Hampton Roads. The demonstrations call for pausing all data center development across the state to allow time to establish protections for public health, environmental and economic protections. Data center development has exploded in recent years, with advocates arguing the growth is in response to people consuming an equally growing amount of data due to technological advancements. Northern Virginia alone has become a global hub for the facilities to the tune of roughly two-thirds of the world’s data centers. That growth has downsides, though. Hyperscale data centers can require roughly 100 megawatts of power and consume up to 530 million gallons of water per year to operate. Facilities of various sizes can also have effects on neighboring communities’ air quality, groundwater and noise pollution. According to Catherine Setaro, Hampton Roads field manager with Virginia League of Conservation Voters, those downsides are unacceptable for Virginia residents, and developers who profit off the facilities’ unchecked growth need to be leashed. “Big tech has had a free pass in Virginia for too long, which is why we’re dealing with more of these industrial facilities than anywhere else in the country,” Setaro said during the rally. “Virginians are fed up. They are tired of a system where big tech can do whatever they want without consequence, cashing in while Virginians bear the cost.” While data center growth has thus far been limited in Hampton Roads, smaller facilities that consume fewer resources still exist in places like Virginia Beach. The Chesapeake City Council blocked a developer’s proposal to build 350,000-square-foot data center last year after outcry from residents. Several localities are now researching what regulating data centers could look like. This summer, Chesapeake enacted an 8-month moratorium and restricted where they can be placed and Virginia Beach enacted a 1-year moratorium. At the state level, Gov. Abigail Spanberger issued an executive order in September shedding by-right approval of large data center projects and instead requiring local approval. For Chesapeake resident Linda Tindell, that doesn’t mean the threat of Hampton Roads residents seeing a data center in their community has gone away completely. As she stood in Fountain Plaza wearing an elephant costume alongside her pet donkey named Darla, Tindell said she’s one of many Chesapeake residents concerned about future development at the former Frank T. Williams farm in southern Chesapeake. The 4,000-acre property was recently sold to a private investment firm called Praetorian Fund with no disclosed purchase details and some residents are wary it could become a future site for data center development. Tindell, a Republican, said reining in data centers in something that crosses party lines. She said she wants to protect her community from facilities that could impact nearby ecosystems and farms that are home to animals like Darla. “People are showing up. It’s a nonpartisan issue,” said Tindell, adding that Darla is an independent and has yet to cast her ballot. “Environmentally, it’s too aggressive. It’s too much too fast.” Michael Jamieson is another concerned Chesapeake resident. He loves hiking and spending outdoors in places like the Great Dismal Swamp. However, if data centers are allowed to continue their expansion, he said those ecological gems will be tainted by the time his daughter grows up. He said he wants to do something about it so his daughter’s future hikes in Chesapeake remain protected. “It comes down to the natural environment that’s going to be harder to experience,” Jamieson said. “For me, it was important that my daughter see her dad come out and talk and actually do the things he talks about at home, not just yell at the TV.” Devlin Epding, 757-510-4037, devlin.epding@virginiamedia.com

artigo.texto: North Elba's town board voted unanimously Tuesday to approve a one-year moratorium on battery energy storage systems, freezing construction, installation and even review of any such project anywhere in town while officials scramble to close gaps in local zoning rules. The vote lands squarely in the middle of two pending Ray Brook solar-farm applications that would pair roughly 25 megawatts of power generation with battery units, leaving their fate uncertain just as developers push forward with permitting. Town officials say they hit pause after realizing their zoning had gaps when it comes to energy projects, according to WCAX. North Elba Town Supervisor Rick Preston told the station he doesn't believe the town will consider individual battery applications going forward, adding plainly: “We don't see a battery energy storage system being suited for North Elba or the village of Lake Placid. We just don't have the acreage for it.” The newly enacted local law prohibits the construction, establishment, installation, review or approval of any battery energy storage system while it remains in effect, according to a public notice posted by the town of North Elba. Two Ray Brook Proposals Now in Question The moratorium arrives as North Elba weighs two separate solar-plus-storage applications in Ray Brook. One proposal, pitched by ClearPath Energy, would place a solar farm and battery storage system on roughly 50 acres of private property off Pendergast Road, according to the Daily Gazette. Citizen Portal described this same ClearPath proposal as two adjacent community solar-plus-storage arrays beside FCI Ray Brook, totaling about 24,000 panels and approximately 40 megawatt-hours of battery capacity. The other proposed Ray Brook solar farm, which Preston said is unlikely to advance, sits too close to a municipal water-supply tank for comfort, per the same Daily Gazette account. It remains unclear whether the ClearPath project could be exempt from the moratorium given its current stage in the permitting process, the newspaper's report notes — a question town officials have not resolved. Part of a Wider Adirondack Pattern North Elba's move follows similar moratoriums already adopted in the Adirondack towns of Champlain and Ticonderoga, per WCAX's reporting. But the trend reaches far beyond the Lake Placid area. According to the Adirondack Explorer, roughly one-fifth of the Adirondack Park's 101 towns and villages have passed battery-storage moratoriums this year alone, with 21 municipalities filing local laws since January 1 that delay construction for periods ranging from six months to a full year. Town boards across the region have repeatedly framed these pauses as necessary to gather more information on the public and environmental safety of the technology, the Adirondack Explorer reports. The scale of the slowdown is significant: testimony from William Acker cited by the outlet put the number of municipalities with active moratoriums above 100, delaying more than one gigawatt of battery storage projects statewide. New York has set a goal of bringing 6 gigawatts of energy storage online by 2030, a target that becomes harder to hit as local governments hit pause one by one. Towns Split Between Bans and Narrow Carve-Outs Some Adirondack municipalities have gone further than a temporary freeze. Fort Ann, Gloversville and Forestport have banned battery energy storage systems outright, according to the Adirondack Explorer. Accounts of neighboring St. Armand's action differ: the Adirondack Explorer reported in one piece that the town passed a one-year moratorium on building battery systems following a public hearing in Bloomingdale, while a separate Adirondack Explorer report states St. Armand is repeating its process after failing to evaluate the local law under the State Environmental Quality Review Act. The Daily Gazette, meanwhile, described St. Armand's June action as a moratorium covering batteries over 600 kilowatt-hours. Not every Adirondack town has slammed the door. The Adirondack Park Agency has already permitted a 10-megawatt, four-hour battery storage system in Northampton — described by the Adirondack Explorer as the park's first large-scale project, consisting of two five-megawatt AC systems with six lithium-ion batteries each. That approval came even as more than 160 people packed a local firehouse before Northampton's own town board separately passed a one-year moratorium on further projects. Ticonderoga's six-month moratorium, passed in March, was nearing its end as officials considered another six-month extension, and Hadley's moratorium was also on the cusp of expiring with a renewal in the works, per the same outlet. Local Capacity to Vet Complex Projects a Recurring Concern Part of the hesitation reflects a broader resource gap. Local Authorities Having Jurisdiction often lack the resources or expertise to evaluate critical battery storage permitting documents, which contain technical data that drives important siting requirements, according to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority. NYSERDA guidance also discusses peer review and fire-code requirements for these systems. For North Elba, the moratorium buys time rather than settling the matter. Preston has said the pause gives the board a year to study impacts and revise its code, and town officials have stressed it is not intended as a permanent solution. Whether the Ray Brook proposals ultimately move forward, get rejected, or wait out the year in limbo remains an open question the town has yet to answer.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- Huawei-affiliated Chinese smart vehicle company Yinwang Intelligent Technology, CATL and Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology Ltd. ("CAES") signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement on October 19 to develop an intelligent battery-swapping ecosystem for autonomous vehicles. Image source: CATL Key Takeaways ·The partners plan to connect vehicle, battery-swap station and cloud systems, allowing charging needs to be forecast and services dispatched using real-time battery data and users' travel patterns. ·The proposed system would enable vehicles to identify when energy replenishment is needed, find and enter a station, align automatically, complete a battery swap in 99 seconds and leave without driver intervention. ·Yinwang has joined CATL's Choco-Swap ecosystem and will work with partners to adapt participating vehicle models for access to the battery-swap network. ·CATL's Choco-Swap network had 2,520 stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29. The company plans to expand the network to 30,000 stations and connect its urban and highway coverage. Image source: CATL Partnership scope The three companies will also cooperate on swappable batteries and network development. The partnership is intended to expand Yinwang's "10-minute Qiankun intelligent-driving service radius" and provide battery-swapping services for vehicles using Huawei Qiankun Intelligent Automotive Solutions.

artigo.texto: Publicidade A Nscale, empresa de computação em nuvem voltada para inteligência artificial, está em negociações para vender capacidade computacional à Anthropic em um acordo que pode alcançar cerca de US$ 45 bilhões, segundo pessoas familiarizadas com as conversas. A desenvolvedora de data centers apoiada pela Nvidia busca fechar um segundo grande contrato com a empresa responsável pelo chatbot Claude para uma nova instalação em seu complexo de data centers Monarch, na Virgínia Ocidental, disseram as fontes. A Anthropic já possui acordos com a Nscale para infraestrutura que somam até cerca de US$ 44,6 bilhões, de acordo com documentos regulatórios relacionados à planejada oferta pública inicial (IPO) da Nscale. O segundo edifício do complexo Monarch teria capacidade para entregar 460 megawatts de poder computacional, utilizando os avançados chips de IA Vera Rubin, da Nvidia, afirmaram algumas das pessoas. A Anthropic também teria direito de preferência sobre um terceiro prédio previsto para o campus. O acordo pode ser finalizado nos próximos dias, segundo as fontes, que pediram anonimato porque as negociações são privadas. As discussões continuam em andamento, os detalhes ainda podem mudar e nenhuma decisão definitiva foi tomada. Representantes da Anthropic e da Nscale não comentaram o assunto. Um novo contrato bilionário de computação fortaleceria as perspectivas da Nscale para seu IPO, no qual a companhia busca atingir uma avaliação de aproximadamente US$ 30 bilhões. Um grupo de investidores tem pressionado a empresa a reduzir essa meta de valuation, segundo reportagem anterior da Bloomberg. Nasdaq sobe mais de 1% com recuperação de parte das perdas por temores com IA Semana ainda contará com a divulgação de importantes balanços de big techs, que deverão sugerir perspectivas para os investimentos e receitas Fed vê IA pressionar inflação, mas outros podem ter que arcar com o remédio Fed vê boom da IA agravando dor de cabeça da inflação, mas outros podem ter que arcar com o remédio A Anthropic, uma das maiores clientes da Nscale, tornou-se um dos principais motores da demanda global por data centers voltados à IA. Entre os acordos já assinados pela empresa estão um contrato de US$ 50 bilhões com a Fluidstack, outro de US$ 10 bilhões com a startup de infraestrutura Volta e um acordo de US$ 45 bilhões com a SpaceX, de Elon Musk. Continua depois da publicidade Documentos do IPO mostram que o complexo Monarch, na Virgínia Ocidental, poderá ser expandido para mais de 8 gigawatts de capacidade elétrica bruta quando estiver totalmente concluído. Parte do campus Monarch seria inicialmente alugada pela Microsoft, que havia anunciado em março a assinatura de uma carta de intenções para o projeto. No entanto, a Microsoft desistiu da instalação durante o verão do hemisfério norte, abrindo espaço para que a Anthropic assumisse a operação, informou a Bloomberg News. A Anthropic, avaliada em US$ 965 bilhões em maio, também é candidata a realizar seu próprio IPO nos próximos meses, potencialmente um dos maiores da história recente do setor. Ao mesmo tempo, a empresa continua buscando mais poder computacional para sustentar seu crescimento. Continua depois da publicidade Investidores têm demonstrado crescente preocupação com os volumes de dívida utilizados para financiar a explosão de investimentos em data centers de inteligência artificial, o que tem afetado desde ações de fabricantes de chips até títulos de dívida de empresas de computação em nuvem. A Nscale entrou com pedido público para listagem nos Estados Unidos em setembro, mas ainda não iniciou formalmente o processo de divulgação da oferta, apesar de o prazo regulatório de espera já ter expirado. A companhia está respondendo a questionamentos da Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos EUA (SEC) e pretende dar início ao roadshow assim que essas questões forem resolvidas. No mês passado, a empresa levantou US$ 3,36 bilhões em uma rodada pré-IPO liderada pela Third Point, de Dan Loeb, com participação de investidores como Nvidia, Apollo Global Management, Citadel, Hudson Bay Capital e Abu Dhabi Investment Council. artigo.texto: What Effingham County can expect if AI data center comes to town: Lessons from Abilene, Texas ABILENE, Texas (WTOC) - Effingham County could soon be home to one of the largest AI data centers in the country. To show what having an AI data center next door actually looks and sounds like, WTOC traveled to Abilene, Texas — the town already living with one. What sits eight miles outside Abilene is Stargate — an 875-acre campus and the first campus of OpenAI’s broader AI infrastructure effort, developed by Crusoe with cloud capacity from Oracle. It is already operating. Project Camellia is different — it is a future campus OpenAI itself is designing for Effingham County, with power delivery planned in phases between 2028 and 2032. PREVIOUS COVERAGE In two days in Abilene, two themes emerged: thousands of workers to build it, and the strain they put on housing, roads, water and power. Housing and workers To build Stargate, between 5,000 and 9,000 temporary workers poured into the area, residents and city officials said. The city didn’t have enough housing — or roads built for the extra traffic. Residents and city officials say the influx caused rental rates and cost of living to double, even triple. Many homes were turned into rental properties to house the workforce. The shortage led to dozens of RV parks in and around Abilene to house workers. “They were coming into town and filling up everything available and really pretty quick,” said Scott Senter, of Better Homes and Gardens Realtors. “We kept hearing, oh they’re going to have to build more and we need to build more. That meant more people. It’s impossible to get ready for that kind of influx of people in your community.” Abilene Mayor Weldon Hurt acknowledged the pinch, but said it is temporary. “As the construction nears and the count of our temporary workers goes down, the housing bubble will adjust itself and the pricing will adjust back down,” Hurt said. “But it is a pinch right now, we’re not denying that.” Traffic and deadly crashes Residents say between 4 and 5 p.m. around the site and on the highways is the worst time to drive. During a recent city council meeting, one city leader noted traffic crash fatalities have increased — something many residents blame on the wave of workers. “About 30% in Taylor County and that’s due to the increase of traffic, I mean the traffic has increased tremendously,” Hurt said. “It is so packed on the roads typically. It’s like Dallas — if you’ve ever been there, Dallas traffic is... awful,” said Abilene resident Gretchen Spoon. Hurt said he understands the frustration over traffic and construction, but calls it the price of progress — pointing to a surge in tax revenue he says will benefit the city long term. Water and power Water and power are the two biggest questions in Effingham County. In Abilene, the mayor says water fears haven’t played out — and OpenAI says the Effingham design is meant to follow the same model. Both campuses use the same idea — closed-loop cooling that recirculates water instead of losing it to evaporation. WTOC previously reported Camellia would use about 30,000 gallons a day from treated surface water. In Abilene, the mayor says once the system is charged, use drops to just a few thousand gallons a year. “So they’re not water hogs. They require a lot of power, but they are on the grid,” Hurt said. “If there’s a demand for power from ERCOT, they have to reduce their intake too. So, they’re on the grid just like we all are.” Hurt added many new data centers have on-site power, noting: “We have an abundance of gas in this region. And so they’re going to take advantage of that gas to generate power with gas power generators.” On power, both campuses plug into the grid — in Abilene it is ERCOT, where Stargate must cut back when demand spikes. In Effingham, WTOC previously reported Camellia would draw up to 3,210 megawatts at peak from Georgia Power. OpenAI says Camellia is designed for offsite power generation, with no diesel backup generators after completion, plus vegetative buffers and noise monitoring. Be sure to tune into Steven Glover’s full investigative WTOC+ special on Monday, where he dives into what exactly Southeast Georgia can expect. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Petição contra data center da Anthropic no Canadá já tem 12 mil assinaturas Petição contra data center da Anthropic na Nova Escócia já ultrapassa 11.800 assinaturas. Moradores criticam impacto ambiental e na rede elétrica. Entenda a polêmica. A Anthropic, empresa por trás do assistente de IA Claude, decidiu alugar um data center na Nova Escócia, no Canadá, mas a população local não está muito animada com a ideia. Uma petição no Change.org já ultrapassou 11.800 assinaturas e pede a suspensão do projeto. O data center, que será construído pela EverWind Fuels perto de Port Hawkesbury, em Cape Breton, deve entrar em operação em duas fases: a primeira até o fim de 2027 e a segunda em 2028. Resumo - Petição contra data center da Anthropic no Canadá ultrapassou 11.800 assinaturas. - Moradores temem impacto ambiental e consumo de energia do data center. - Empresa prometeu pagar por melhorias na rede elétrica local. - Brasil ainda não tem movimento organizado contra data centers. O morador Kevin Fifield, que criou a petição, afirma que a decisão “impacta significativamente o meio ambiente, a rede elétrica e a comunidade como um todo”. Segundo ele, o projeto beneficia “apenas alguns poucos” enquanto os custos são divididos de forma desproporcional entre os cidadãos da província. A CBC News informou que o empreendimento será tocado pela EverWind Fuels, que já levantou US$ 8 bilhões (cerca de R$ 40,5 bilhões) em capital privado, e que tanto ela quanto a Anthropic prometeram arcar com eventuais upgrades na rede elétrica local. O que levou a população a se levantar? Não é só na Nova Escócia que a instalação de data centers de IA enfrenta resistência. Em junho, a cidade de Hamilton (Ontário) considerou uma proibição temporária para novos centros de dados, e Vancouver também pediu uma pausa nas aprovações. Em ambos os casos, houve protestos. Na Nova Escócia, manifestantes foram às ruas em Halifax e contaram com a presença do diretor de políticas da Anthropic no Canadá, Jacob Glick. Ele disse à Global News que “os canadenses estão usando Claude em números crescentes, e queremos que nossa infraestrutura fique perto das pessoas que dependem dela”. 12 mil assinaturas da petição contra o data center O problema é que os moradores não querem justamente essa proximidade. A preocupação principal é o consumo de energia: data centers de IA precisam de muita eletricidade, e a Nova Escócia ainda depende de fontes fósseis. Além disso, há receios sobre impacto ambiental e valorização imobiliária. Recorte Brasil: onde entra o país nessa história? Por enquanto, o Brasil não tem um movimento organizado contra data centers no mesmo nível, mas o debate sobre consumo energético e pegada ambiental da IA também está começando a pipocar por aqui. Grandes empresas como Google e Meta já instalaram centros de dados no país, mas a discussão pública sobre licenciamento e impactos locais ainda é tímida. O caso canadense serve de alerta: se a demanda por IA continuar crescendo, a pressão sobre infraestrutura e opinião pública tende a aumentar também em terras tupiniquins. O que diz a Anthropic e o que ainda está em aberto A empresa alega que o projeto trará empregos e desenvolvimento para a região, e que já se comprometeu a pagar por melhorias na rede elétrica. Mas a petição segue ganhando força – com mais de 12 mil compartilhamentos e comentários abertos. A questão que fica é até que ponto a opinião pública vai pesar na decisão final, que depende de aprovações ambientais e municipais. Enquanto isso, a Anthropic enfrenta outros desafios no Canadá: editoras locais a processam por violação de direitos autorais – mais uma frente de batalha para a empresa de IA. Valores em reais convertidos pela cotação de fechamento do Banco Central de 19/10/2026 (US$ 1 = R$ 5,06). Conversão direta, sem impostos nem taxas de importação. 📲 Essa história ainda tem desdobramentos pela frente. artigo.texto: Redata amplia incentivo a data centers, mas capacidade local não elimina risco operacional Novo regime tributário busca atrair infraestrutura de nuvem e inteligência artificial para o Brasil, enquanto empresas reforçam importância de redundância, segurança e continuidade 20.10.2026 A criação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, o Redata, abre uma nova etapa para a expansão da infraestrutura digital brasileira. Instituído pela Lei nº 15.504/2026, sancionada em 15 de setembro, o regime estabelece incentivos tributários para instalação, modernização e ampliação de centros de processamento de dados voltados a serviços como computação em nuvem, processamento de alto desempenho e inteligência artificial. Serviços e Informações do Brasil A medida surge em um cenário de forte dependência de infraestrutura localizada fora do país. Segundo diagnóstico do Ministério da Fazenda, cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras são atualmente atendidas por serviços prestados no exterior. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Regime exige contrapartidas O Redata não prevê apenas incentivos fiscais. As empresas que aderirem ao programa deverão cumprir compromissos relacionados ao mercado interno, pesquisa, desenvolvimento e sustentabilidade. Entre as exigências está a disponibilização mínima de 10% da capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados beneficiada pelo programa para o mercado brasileiro. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Também estão previstos investimentos em pesquisa e desenvolvimento no país e critérios relacionados ao uso de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão. Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, o regime contempla ainda requisitos de eficiência hídrica e compromissos específicos para o suprimento energético das operações. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Mais infraestrutura pode ampliar opções para empresas Para companhias que contratam serviços de nuvem, a expansão da capacidade instalada no Brasil pode aumentar as alternativas de fornecedores e permitir maior diversificação da infraestrutura. Isso, porém, não significa automaticamente redução de custos ou aumento de disponibilidade. Na avaliação da ITGLOBAL.COM, empresas precisam observar não apenas onde os dados estão hospedados, mas também como o ambiente foi estruturado. Entre os critérios estão governança dos dados, redundância, segurança, disponibilidade contratada e capacidade de recuperação diante de falhas. Resiliência depende de arquitetura A presença de mais data centers no país não elimina a necessidade de planejamento de continuidade. Estratégias de Disaster Recovery, definição de objetivos de recuperação e distribuição de cargas entre ambientes diferentes continuam relevantes, especialmente para aplicações críticas. “A ampliação da capacidade de data centers no Brasil é um avanço importante para o mercado, mas a disponibilidade de infraestrutura não garante, por si só, a continuidade das operações”, afirma Peter Jilinski, diretor regional da ITGLOBAL.COM. Segundo ele, a confiabilidade depende da forma como os ambientes são estruturados e dos mecanismos de recuperação previstos. Escalabilidade e previsibilidade também entram na decisão Outro ponto de atenção para gestores de TI é a capacidade de ampliar recursos conforme a demanda. Escalabilidade, previsibilidade de custos, suporte, segurança e conformidade devem ser analisados em conjunto no momento de escolha de um provedor. Com isso, o Redata pode ampliar a oferta de infraestrutura local, mas a decisão empresarial continuará dependendo de fatores que vão além da localização física dos servidores. Brasil tenta reduzir dependência externa O governo federal apresenta o regime como parte de uma estratégia de atração de investimentos em infraestrutura digital e fortalecimento das cadeias tecnológicas ligadas à indústria 4.0. A legislação também busca estimular atividades relacionadas a computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e outros serviços intensivos em processamento de dados. Serviços e Informações do Brasil Para o mercado corporativo, o avanço da capacidade nacional pode significar mais opções. A resiliência, porém, continuará dependendo da qualidade da arquitetura, da governança e do planejamento de continuidade de cada operação. INBOX Aprenda algo novo todos os dias. artigo.texto: VOLUSIA COUNTY, Fla. — The Volusia County Council voted 6-0 Tuesday to stop large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas because of concerns about water resources, infrastructure capacity and local environmental impacts. According to the county’s agenda, large-scale data centers are defined as facilities with an anticipated monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more. Under the decision, the county cannot accept, process, review, approve or issue applications or development approvals for projects above that threshold. “We beat this horse pretty good. I think it’s time to put it to rest,” said David Santiago, District 5 representative on the Volusia County Council. The facilities do not fit the county’s environment, Volusia County Chair Jeff Brower said. “They just don’t work in Volusia County because of the way our aquifer is structured,” Brower said. “We believe it endangers the aquifer. It uses a lot of water.” Developers can still apply for projects under 50 megawatts, but Brower said they would go through a rigorous review process. He said county staff would review a project first, followed by a zoning and regulation committee, before the council votes on it. “I was concerned with 20 megawatts and above, but I think we have that protection written into this ordinance,” Brower said. Suzanne Scheiber, founder and president of Dream Green Volusia, said she supports the ban on large-scale data centers and remains focused on their potential impacts. “Imagine that amount of industrial waste. Where are you going to put that?” Scheiber said. “It’s going to turnover, and then you also have the noise level that’s caused. Even if they used reclaimed water, for example, there is a turnover of that as well.” The ban applies only to unincorporated areas of Volusia County. Cities and towns within the county will decide how to handle data center proposals within their limits.

artigo.texto: If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard. A Gallup survey conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed the construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage. Half of Americans surveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs. Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal with Xcel Energy would add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use. Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power. Google's bet that AI can finance a cleaner grid Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis. Google hopes that its new 780-megawatt data center plan will build goodwill with the Pine Island community and keep the company on track to meet its goal of operating on carbon-free energy, 24 hours a day, seven days a week by 2030. Google — whose cloud business powers its own Gemini AI and brought in nearly $25 billion in second-quarter revenue, an 82% increase from a year earlier — says it has found a model for doing this the right way. The company plans to finance the addition of 1,400 megawatts of wind, 200 megawatts of solar and 300 megawatts of battery storage to Xcel's grid. Those additions amount to more than the capacity of the data center itself, which Google said is because wind and solar do not generate energy at all times. Xcel Energy said the new power will serve all customers in the local area, not just Google. Xcel also said the upgrades will help advance the local grid's carbon-free energy supply. The proposed agreement between Google and Xcel includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, which Google says will keep the company on the hook for the infrastructure being built on its behalf, even if the AI boom cools. Google will pay for at least 75% of its contracted capacity, even if it uses less, and would owe up to eight years' worth of those minimum demand charges if it terminates the agreement early. "Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power," said Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy. "That's where these protections come in." The agreement between Google and Xcel Energy is pending approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission. Data centers are driving a historic power buildout New data centers will account for "most" of the projected increase in electricity demand over the next decade, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit regulator. The Department of Energy under President Joe Biden reported that more than 70% of U.S. transmission lines and power transformers were at least 25 years old and found that the cheapest ways of meeting future demand would require the nation's transmission system to more than double in size by 2050. But hyperscalers argue that they can finance badly needed grid upgrades while also making the grid cleaner and more reliable. "The timing of this industrial revolution couldn't be more perfect," said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of energy and power. "It's right at the time when we needed capital to fix aging infrastructure in the United States." Could data centers use the grid as is? Jigar Shah, a partner at Multiplier, a consulting firm that helps clean energy startups go public, said data center operators could be constructing smaller facilities in places where the grid already has unused capacity. That would minimize the need to build — and pay for — new generation or transmission equipment. "If you fit the load growth that the data centers want into the existing grid, everybody's rates go down by a lot," said Shah. That's because the existing grid has enormous fixed costs from the infrastructure already in place: power plants, transmission lines, substations. If one new customer comes onto the grid and pays a large slice of that, everyone else's bills go down. "And so the question really is, why are people not doing these 25-megawatt data centers? Why are they doing 1,000-megawatt data centers? And it turns out people are just lazy," Shah said. "They're like, well, it's easier for me to contract one data center that's one gigawatt in size than figuring out how to do something on the order of 40 data centers that are 25 megawatts each." Industry watchdogs also warn of another reason that utilities often prefer to build new infrastructure, rather than make more use out of their existing grid. "When [utilities] build something new, they fund part of that investment with dollars from their investors on Wall Street, and they enjoy incredibly high, exorbitant returns on those investments, typically around 10%," said David Pomerantz, executive director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog agency. Building a data center that fits neatly into an existing grid provides little opportunity for a utility to make new money. What if a hyperscaler offers to pay for those grid investments? "One way to leverage data centers to lower people's bills is for data centers to provide that capital at much cheaper rates than the utility," said Pomerantz. "But that's a big problem for the utility. And this fight is actually already emerging." Still, Shah said, the Google/Xcel project in Minnesota is a good example of a data center project acting as a catalyst for newer, greener technology. "Google came in and said, well, here's a new way of doing things, using new technologies. How about we do it that way? And then that helps ratepayers. artigo.texto: Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL) has issued an advisory introducing updated requirements for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and co-located Renewable Energy Generating Stations (REGS) used for charging. The guidelines specify minimum energy storage discharge durations, connectivity conditions, and commissioning timelines to improve the efficient utilisation of the Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) grid. Under the revised framework, connectivity applications are classified into different categories based on their eligibility and application timelines. Projects falling under the Right of First Refusal (RoFR) category will be subject to a minimum BESS discharge duration of two hours. This requirement applies to existing connectivity grantees and eligible applicants who submitted applications under Regulation 5.2 or Regulation 5.11(a) up to February 21, 2026. Applicants under the RoFR category must also comply with the applicable conditions for co-located renewable energy generation and inverter capacity. Depending on the option selected, developers may be required to apply for co-located REGS under Regulation 5.2 or ensure that the total connected rated inverter capacity remains within their granted connectivity limits at all times. These provisions are intended to maintain compliance with approved transmission connectivity arrangements. For applications outside the RoFR category, CTUIL has prescribed a minimum BESS discharge duration of four hours. The same requirement applies to standalone BESS projects located at renewable energy pooling stations. The higher storage duration is intended to support better utilisation of available transmission infrastructure and improve the operational efficiency of energy storage installations. Although applying for co-located REGS may not be mandatory for every non-RoFR applicant under Clause 1(1) of Annexure IV of the General Network Access (GNA) Regulations, CTUIL has encouraged developers to install matching renewable energy generation capacity equivalent to the BESS energy storage rating in megawatt-hours (MWh). For standalone BESS projects at pooling stations, however, applications for co-located REGS under Regulation 5.2 remain mandatory. Developers must also ensure that inverter output stays within the permitted connectivity limits. CTUIL has further advised that the capacity of co-located renewable energy generating stations used for charging should match the BESS storage capacity. These charging facilities must be commissioned either from the start date of BESS connectivity or within 36 months from the date of the in-principle grant or firm start date, whichever is later. Developers may also draw electricity from the national grid to charge their storage systems, subject to the availability of transmission margins. The advisory also provides a transition mechanism for pending applications that do not currently meet the four-hour storage requirement. Applicants with under-process standalone BESS or non-RoFR projects may seek an increase in energy storage capacity in MWh without changing the overall installed power capacity in MW. Such requests can be raised during Connectivity and Medium-Term Open Access System (CMETS) meeting discussions. Developers choosing to upgrade their projects must submit the required eligibility documents under Regulation 5.2(h) within two months of the advisory’s publication or the relevant approving CMETS meeting, whichever is later. The upgraded projects must also comply with applicable land requirements, financial conditions and scheduled commercial operation date (SCOD) regulations. Through these measures, CTUIL aims to establish clearer storage requirements for different connectivity categories while supporting efficient transmission planning and the integration of renewable energy and battery storage projects into India’s power grid. artigo.texto: A company behind Wyoming’s artificial intelligence data-center boom has launched a $105 million fund for Yellowstone National Park. In a Monday announcement, officials touted the donation as the largest private gift in National Park Service history. But the contribution is also raising questions about the role of private philanthropy as data-center development transforms the rural West. Funneled through the official nonprofit partner of the park, Yellowstone Forever, the donation from energy giant Tallgrass, a Blackstone Inc. portfolio company, is intended to fund research and conservation; develop a new visitor education center at Norris Geyser Basin; and expand opportunities for students and families to experience and learn about Yellowstone, according to Yellowstone Forever CEO and President Lisa Diekmann. As U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posed for pictures at Yellowstone’s Old Faithful Inn on Monday alongside Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon and representatives of Tallgrass and Blackstone, officials didn’t discuss the environmental impact of AI data centers. Instead, they touted what the donation would do for the park. “More than 120 years ago, President Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone of Yellowstone’s iconic gateway, enshrining the promise that our National Parks exist for the benefit and enjoyment of the American people,” Burgum said in a press release. “This historic $105 million investment honors that legacy, bringing together the best of American enterprise and conservation to expand access to Yellowstone and inspire the next generation to experience America’s great outdoors.” But across the country, only about 11 percent of Americans support the construction of an AI data center in their communities, according to recent polling from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. Brian Childers lives about three-and-a-half miles from a Microsoft AI data center south of Cheyenne — near the separate Tallgrass facility that’s under construction. He’s hard of hearing, he says, but he still can’t escape a constant, overwhelming hum. Birds have left his property, he said, and at night the sky never quite gets dark. He said the gift to Yellowstone feels like the companies are trying to buy goodwill from politicians and the public. “I’m glad (the park) got the money, but if these things are going to impact the people around southeast Wyoming, (the corporations) need to be paying a premium on the electricity they use so that the people don’t have to pay extra,” Childers told Mountain Journal in an interview. Colorado-based Tallgrass manages more than 10,000 miles of pipelines and, with Google as a partner, is developing a 2.7 gigawatt AI data center near Cheyenne, Wyoming. Matt Sheehy, brother of Montana Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy, led the company from 2019 until earlier this year. Tallgrass is also a subsidiary of Blackstone, the largest financier of data centers in the world and major financial backer of Tim Sheehy’s former company Bridger Aerospace. The National Parks Conservation Association, Park County Environmental Council, Wild Montana and the Greater Yellowstone Coalition all declined to comment on the donation. On social media, however, an uproar ensued. “Putting the wolves in charge of the sheep,” one person commented on Yellowstone’s Instagram post, joining a slew of detractors. Tax dollars only cover the basics of Yellowstone National Park’s operations, according to Yellowstone Forever’s Diekmann, who said she hopes the gift will inspire further donations. America’s first national park still has a large need, she added: Yellowstone has a $1.2 billion backlog of maintenance that this donation will not address. In an interview, Mountain Journal asked Diekmann about how closely Yellowstone Forever examined the public pushback to data centers and their ecological consequences elsewhere in Wyoming and across the country in their decision to move forward with the donation. “We are focused on mission-aligned programs,” she said. “I think that the business of Blackstone and Tallgrass and their commitment to the communities in which they work is very important. And this is reflected in this donation.” Tallgrass officials declined an interview. But in an emailed statement, the company touted its contributions to the Wyoming economy, including some of the nation’s largest carbon sequestration technology. “We’ve always believed that energy from Wyoming should create opportunities for Wyoming, and that means more than the jobs we provide and the taxes we pay,” the company said. “It means being a force for good across the entire state, not just in the specific communities where we operate. Our investment in Yellowstone is one way we’re acting on that belief.” Blackstone also declined to comment. In the Yellowstone press release, however, the company lauded its donation. “This historic gift reflects our belief that infrastructure investment can and should be a force for good, helping us invest in Yellowstone’s future and the growth of the communities that surround it,” Sean Klimczak, global head of infrastructure for Blackstone, said in the statement. Experts say there might be more at play. “This falls right into that category of philanthropy designed to win over stakeholders who might be unhappy with you,” Thomas Lyon, a professor of business and sustainability at the University of Michigan who focuses on greenwashing, told Mountain Journal. Donations from data centers across the country are increasingly common, according to reporting from Spotlight PA. They often run in the millions of dollars. In one instance, locals pushed back on a proposal to give every household in Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, $10,000 if officials approve an Amazon data center. Some called it a bribe. Southeast Wyoming, like Phoenix and Northern Virginia, is rapidly becoming a hub of data-center development. artigo.texto: Resumo - Nscale negocia vender capacidade à Anthropic em acordo de até US$ 45 bilhões - Seria o segundo grande contrato entre as duas empresas no complexo Monarch - Novo prédio teria 460 MW e usaria chips Vera Rubin, da Nvidia - Acordos já firmados entre as empresas somam até US$ 44,6 bilhões A Anthropic, responsável pelo chatbot Claude, negocia com a Nscale um contrato de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) que pode alcançar US$ 45 bilhões. A informação é de pessoas próximas às negociações. A Nscale, empresa de computação em nuvem apoiada pela Nvidia, pretende fechar um novo acordo para ampliar sua operação nos Estados Unidos. Dessa vez, o contrato envolve uma segunda instalação no complexo de data centers Monarch, na Virgínia Ocidental. As duas companhias já mantêm contratos de infraestrutura que somam aproximadamente US$ 44,6 bilhões. Os valores aparecem em documentos regulatórios relacionados à oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO) da Nscale. Novo prédio terá chips Vera Rubin da Nvidia O novo edifício do complexo Monarch poderá oferecer 460 megawatts de capacidade computacional. Para sustentar a operação, a Nscale pretende utilizar chips de inteligência artificial Vera Rubin, desenvolvidos pela Nvidia. Além disso, a Anthropic poderá obter preferência na contratação de um terceiro prédio que a Nscale planeja construir no mesmo campus. Segundo fontes ouvidas sob anonimato, as empresas podem concluir o acordo nos próximos dias. No entanto, as negociações continuam e ainda podem sofrer alterações. Procuradas, Anthropic e Nscale não comentaram o assunto. Quando estiver totalmente concluído, o complexo Monarch poderá ultrapassar 8 gigawatts de capacidade elétrica bruta, conforme os documentos do IPO. Inicialmente, a Microsoft ocuparia parte das instalações. Em março, a companhia chegou a anunciar uma carta de intenções para participar do projeto. Entretanto, segundo a Bloomberg News, a Microsoft desistiu da instalação durante o verão do hemisfério norte. Com a decisão, a Anthropic ganhou espaço para ampliar sua presença no complexo. IPO da Nscale e a corrida por data centers O possível contrato de US$ 45 bilhões surge em um momento estratégico para a Nscale. A companhia prepara sua estreia na Bolsa e busca alcançar uma avaliação de mercado próxima de US$ 30 bilhões. Nesse cenário, um novo acordo bilionário poderia fortalecer o interesse dos investidores na oferta. Apesar disso, parte do mercado pressiona a empresa a reduzir sua expectativa de valuation, segundo informações anteriores da Bloomberg. Enquanto isso, a Anthropic amplia seus investimentos em infraestrutura para acompanhar o crescimento da demanda por inteligência artificial. A companhia já firmou outros contratos bilionários para garantir capacidade computacional. Entre eles, estão acordos de US$ 50 bilhões com a Fluidstack e US$ 10 bilhões com a startup Volta. Além disso, a empresa fechou um compromisso de US$ 45 bilhões com a SpaceX, de Elon Musk. Com esses investimentos, a Anthropic se tornou uma das principais responsáveis pelo avanço da demanda global por data centers voltados à IA. Em maio, o mercado avaliava a companhia em aproximadamente US$ 965 bilhões. Agora, a empresa também aparece entre as possíveis candidatas a realizar um IPO nos próximos meses. Caso avance com a abertura de capital, a operação poderá figurar entre as maiores ofertas recentes do setor de tecnologia. Ao mesmo tempo, a expansão acelerada da infraestrutura de IA aumenta a preocupação dos investidores com o endividamento das empresas. Afinal, a construção de data centers exige investimentos elevados, muitas vezes financiados por meio de empréstimos e emissão de títulos de dívida. Essa preocupação já afetou diferentes segmentos do mercado, desde ações de fabricantes de chips até títulos emitidos por empresas de computação em nuvem. Apesar desse cenário, a Nscale mantém seus planos de abertura de capital nos Estados Unidos. A companhia apresentou o pedido de listagem em setembro, mas ainda não iniciou a divulgação formal da oferta. Atualmente, a empresa busca responder aos questionamentos da Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC). Após concluir essa etapa, pretende iniciar o roadshow, período de apresentações aos potenciais investidores. Antes disso, em agosto, a Nscale levantou US$ 3,36 bilhões em uma rodada de investimentos pré-IPO. A operação teve a liderança da Third Point, gestora de Dan Loeb. A rodada também contou com aportes de Nvidia, Apollo Global Management, Citadel, Hudson Bay Capital e Abu Dhabi Investment Council.

artigo.texto: MILWAUKEE – Milwaukee County Executive and Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany made their last-ditch appeal to voters in their first and only televised debate, less than two weeks before the Nov.3 midterm election. The two candidates running to be Wisconsin’s next governor sparred over policies including affordability, data centers and education in the highly anticipated debate at Marquette University Oct. 21. The race generated national attention when Crowley upset frontrunner democratic socialist Rep. Francesca Hong in the Aug. 11 partisan primary. Both major parties and individual donors have poured millions into a race that will determine who gets to lead one of the most closely contested states in the country for the next four years. The two candidates for governor wasted no time attacking one another in the debate hosted by WISN-12 News. Tiffany, of Minocqua, tried to distance himself from President Donald Trump while hammering Crowley on raising taxes. Crowley, from Milwaukee, appealed to Wisconsin over why he is the right choice for the state, drawing on his past record passing bipartisan legislation in Milwaukee County. In the latest Marquette Law School Poll on Sept. 30, Crowley holds a three-point lead over Tiffany among likely voters, but the race remains a toss-up with a 4.8% margin of error. Ben Wikler, former chair of the Democratic Party of Wisconsin, stood in for Crowley at the press conference following the event. Affordability Both candidates cited affordability as a top priority and laid out their plans to lower costs for Wisconsinites. Tiffany said he would end Gov. Tony Evers’ 400-year-veto for school funding increases, which can raise property taxes if not offset by state funding. He also said he wants to eliminate taxes on tips and overtime and reduce taxes on middle-income families who make $150,000 or less by 10%. Tiffany was quick to criticize Crowley over his role in the passage of Act 12, a bipartisan bill that increased the state’s shared revenue program and eliminated a property tax via a 2% sales tax hike. “[Crowley] said that he believed higher taxes are not a burden when he nearly doubled the sales tax,” Tiffany said. “That was the one year property taxes went down. He raised the sales tax instead. Taxes went up every single year. You know what he’s going to do as governor.” Crowley, who led the passage of Act 12, has used this as an example for how he will work across the aisle as governor. Crowley did not directly answer a question over whether he would create a new tax bracket for Wisconsin’s highest earners. Instead, he pointed to Tiffany's support of President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and ending the war in Iran, which he said “raised record” gas prices. Regular gas prices in Wisconsin are nearly $2 more per gallon than one year ago, and diesel is up by nearly $3. “Tiffany had the ability to lower costs for families just at the gas pump. He voted to protect the war in Iran and we’ve seen our diesel and gas prices skyrocket,” Crowley said. Tiffany voted against five House resolutions directing Trump to end the war in Iran, the last one on March 5. He was not present for the Sept. 15 roll call vote that prompted Trump to remove hostilities and U.S. armed forces. The two candidates answered questions over what they would do with the state’s $3 billion budget surplus. Tiffany said the state should return “all of that to the taxpayers” through long-term tax relief. Crowley provided a more extensive answer, saying he would funnel the money to education, childcare and healthcare for working families. Crowley’s campaign released a policy plan for Wisconsin renters in early October along with a student renters’ Bill of Rights, calling for a cap on rent increases and longer notice before evictions for all Wisconsin residents. Tiffany claimed rent increases frequently result from utility rate hikes. He said as governor, he would halt utility rate increases. “I think we need to build a growing economy here in Wisconsin where we don't have to worry about that, where we make sure people get good jobs,” Tiffany told The Daily Cardinal. “[Renters] may not realize [increases are] a result of their utility bill… the landlord oftentimes has it included.” Trump and election integrity Tiffany, while he had typically aligned with President Donald Trump in Congress, has recently tried to distance himself from the president, particularly on the war in Iran and certifying the 2020 presidential election. He previously voted against ending the war and certifying former President Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential win, but has since gone back on both. Meanwhile, Crowley’s campaign has tried to highlight that connection. “We’ve always had free and fair elections,” Crowley said. “It is very clear that he is working for Donald Trump.” When asked why he voted to overturn the 2020 election, Tiffany pointed to private election donors like Mark Zuckerberg. He added that a Dane County Clerk allowed people to declare themself indefinitely confined, which was another reason he voted to overturn the election. Tiffany said Crowley is too focused on what he is against rather than what he is for. “While my opponent, you can see early on in the debate, is consistently focused on being against Donald Trump, I’m for Wisconsin,” Tiffany said. Both Tiffany and Crowley said they would certify the 2028 election as governor, no matter the winner. Tiffany declined to answer whether he would eliminate the Wisconsin Elections Commission, saying they need to first explore viable alternatives to the commission. “We may have to keep the Wisconsin Elections Commission,” Tiffany said, adding it depends on a willing legislature. artigo.texto: Data-center companies are ponying up to find out which communities will resist them the least. Startup Hamlet has parsed tens of thousands of city council meetings by scraping local governmentsâ video recordings, tagging comments as friendly or hostile to a potential project. CEO Sunil Rajaraman told Semafor that a large fund that finances data centers and a data-center developer are among its paying customers, looking for whiffs of a moratorium. âWhere there might be more favorable political viewsâ may well determine where future projects get built, Rajaraman said. Investors backing these projects are also obvious customers for a real-time feed into Americansâ growing antipathy toward data centers. The appetite for such data shows the lengths to which the tech industry is going to find where projects are most likely to go through, in the face of a national groundswell of anti-data center activism that has turned community sentiment into a financial risk. Other Hamlet customers include real estate developers, political action committees, and retailers, Rajaraman said. The company on Tuesday launched new rankings for where cities and counties stand on a host of hot-button issues (ranging from zoning laws to pickleball), and a portal for people to look up what their elected officials have said. (Among large local governments, Corpus Christi, Texas ranked No. 1 in speakersâ opposition to data centers.) âThis is public sphere data,â Rajaraman said. âThe data needs to be out there so America can make better decisions.â

artigo.texto: President Donald Trump is calling for data centers to pay for their own power and pay dividends to local communities — a stark change for the president less than two weeks before the election and as opposition to data centers is growing. In Memphis, Tenn., where the City Council was weighing a temporary moratorium on data centers on Tuesday, ultimately voting against the move, attendees used fiery language to describe their feelings. “Lives are at stake and blood is on your hands,” council meeting attendee Tikeila Rucker said. "Supporting a pause on data centers is a vote for reaffirming your dedication to the people of Memphis, not the billionaire class," said attendee Amber Sherman. It’s a scene playing out across the country as Americans raise concerns that data centers, which provide the computing power for artificial intelligence, will drive up electric bills and consume massive amounts of water. Now the president is pitching a new solution. He wrote early Wednesday morning that new data centers are “mandated by me to make their own electricity and give or sell any excess back to the local community.” He added: “If companies want to make their data centers popular, they should pay a ‘dividend’ to the community.” It was not immediately clear how the president’s demand could be implemented. Trump’s social media post marks a shift in tone for the president, who previously criticized data center opponents as wanting to “end up being backwards and poor,” as he said at a rally earlier this month in Ohio. “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio,” he said. “You can’t just turn it off. They’ll go to China.” Todd Eisenstadt, research director at American University Center for Environmental Policy, said data centers are an easy target. He said there’s been a growing uneasiness with data centers tied with a more existential fear over the development of artificial intelligence. A new Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll found 66% of Americans oppose construction of new data centers and also disapprove of the president’s handling of AI. “Perhaps the wind has shifted and this is a defining issue of the election,” Eisenstadt told Spectrum News. “And he’s on the wrong side of it. So, he’s trying to swim the other way here at the last minute.” The number of data centers has exploded. Estimates show there are at least 3,000 nationwide.

artigo.texto: SUFFOLK, Va. — Suffolk City Council voted unanimously, 8-0, to approve an ordinance temporarily prohibiting data centers in the city as leaders consider how to manage future development. Mayor Michael Duman said the city will not accept data center applications during the moratorium. “At this particular time, we will not be accepting any applications for data centers whatsoever,” Duman said. The ordinance also establishes a definition of a data center, describing facilities that house computer servers and equipment used to process and store data. Timothy Wheels, a Suffolk resident who owns a technology company specializing in artificial intelligence and website development, was the only person to speak before the council vote. Wheels said the fast-changing technology industry presents challenges for local governments trying to establish rules for data center development. “It's not much type of governance because all this is new,” Wheels said. He said he supports the moratorium because it gives the city time to prepare for the growing use of artificial intelligence. “I'm in favor because it buys us time to come up with a plan, to come up with a strategy to prepare ourselves on how we use AI,” Wheels said. The decision comes as communities across Hampton Roads weigh the potential benefits and impacts of data center development. Earlier this week, residents from across the region gathered in Virginia Beach to call for a statewide pause on data centers. Chesapeake and Virginia Beach city councils also halted data center expansion earlier this year. Supporters of data center development say the facilities can bring investment, tax revenue and construction jobs to local communities. In Suffolk, city leaders have not specified how long the moratorium will remain in effect. For now, the ordinance puts data center applications on hold as the city considers its approach to future development. Click here to see how we use AI at WTKR News 3.

artigo.texto: Michigan gubernatorial candidates John James and Jocelyn Benson were asked in a debate about their stance on data centers. In the 2026 Michigan gubernatorial debate hosted by WDIV and moderated by morning co-anchor and Flashpoint host Jason Colthorp, the candidates answered questions on topics Michiganders care most about, particularly data centers. James’ campaign has gotten more than $100,000 in donations from data center developers, and the congressman has some investments in data center companies. Benson’s husband is a senior vice president at the company trying to build a massive data center in Saline Township and lobbied for it before the township board. Both candidates have talked about a one-year moratorium on data centers, but they were asked why voters should trust either of them to make decisions in their best interests rather than the companies’ interests. In the debate, Benson said her family has not profited from data centers, and she disclosed her finances. She also said she supports a moratorium to pause new data center development until guardrails are in place. Benson claimed James voted four times to deny local residents a choice about whether data centers could come to their area. “I have a plan to ensure that your voices are protected and heard,” Benson said. “He’s voted against that right that you should have.” James accused Benson of gaining $370,000 in profit and omitting the information in 2025. “[Benson] and her husband bulldozed the will of the people of Saline to carpet over the productive green farmland against her commitment,” James said. “Of course, she’s gonna come up with a moratorium after they’ve already made out with $370,000 on these deals with back rooms.” James said his five-part moratorium aims to stop new data centers until there’s a plan to protect the communities. You can listen to the candidate’s full statements from the Oct. 15 debate on data centers in Michigan by watching the video at the top of this article.

artigo.texto: Dow Launches VOLTRICELL Platform to Advance Battery Innovation Dow Inc. DOW recently launched VOLTRICELL, a new battery cell materials platform designed to optimize battery manufacturing and improve performance. The platform expands Dow’s battery solutions portfolio and strengthens its presence in the industry. Dow, which is among the leading companies in the chemical space, along with DuPont de Nemours, Inc. DD, Eastman Chemical Company EMN and Air Products and Chemicals, Inc. APD, aims to bring together materials for electrodes, separators, coatings and battery cell packaging, including binders, dispersants, rheology modifiers, surfactants and specialty additives, through VOLTRICELL. These materials are designed to support higher energy density, longer cycle life, faster charging and scalable manufacturing. The platform integrates emerging technologies such as sodium-ion, silicon-anode and solid-state batteries. The new launch will be complemented by VORAFORCE TP1415 polyurethane resin for lightweight, flame-retardant composites, DOWSIL EF-6559 silicone foam for thermal management and electrical insulation, and DOWSIL FC-2024 coating for protecting battery housings and enclosures during thermal events. The introduction of VOLTRICELL supports growth by addressing manufacturers’ demand for materials that improve battery performance, safety and production scalability across the battery value chain. It builds on its deep materials science expertise and application development capabilities to foster innovation. For the second half of 2026, management plans to focus on growth and innovation in attractive end markets, investments to strengthen the portfolio and balanced capital allocation. Dow expects the growth and productivity benefits from Transform to Outperform to accelerate through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027. Dow expects approximately $200 million in additional benefits from Transform to Outperform during 2026. This raises the company’s expected total in-year benefits from self-help initiatives to more than $1.3 billion. Another industry leader, DuPont, raised the midpoint of its full-year 2026 operating EBITDA and adjusted earnings guidance. The company now expects net sales in the range of $7.16-$7.19 billion, operating EBITDA between $1.75 billion and $1.77 billion and adjusted earnings of $7.17-$7.32 per share. The outlook reflects continued strength across healthcare, industrial water and aerospace end markets. Management expects mid-single-digit organic sales growth in the second half and remains focused on productivity, profitable growth and shareholder value creation. Eastman, on its second-quarter call, said that it expects earnings to improve significantly from 2025. The company remains on track to deliver cost reductions of $125 million to $150 million, net of inflation. For the third quarter, adjusted earnings are projected to approach the second-quarter level of $1.97 per share. Advanced Materials EBIT is expected to increase on improved price-cost and asset utilization, while Fibers earnings should benefit from higher acetate tow purchases. Additives & Functional Products earnings are expected to decline modestly due to seasonal agriculture weakness, while Chemical Intermediates earnings are projected to ease as supply-chain disruptions lessen. Air Products, for fiscal 2026, raised its adjusted earnings guidance to $13.39-$13.49 per share from the prior range of $13-$13.25. For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, Air Products expects adjusted earnings of $3.55-$3.65 per share. The company now anticipates fiscal 2026 capital expenditures of approximately $3.5 billion, below its earlier projection of about $4 billion. Management expects new asset contributions, pricing actions and productivity initiatives to support performance, while remaining cautious because of macroeconomic uncertainty. artigo.texto: Siga Startups no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. Siga Startups no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. A falta de infraestrutura para energia elétrica está colocando obstáculos à expansão da inteligência artificial até mesmo em projetos que contam com grandes empresas de tecnologia. A Microsoft desistiu de um contrato para ser a principal cliente de um data center da Nscale em Loughton, no Reino Unido, depois que atrasos na conexão à rede elétrica empurraram a previsão de fornecimento de energia para 2030. O problema está na capacidade da infraestrutura elétrica de acompanhar o ritmo de expansão dos data centers. No Reino Unido, os pedidos de conexão à rede de transmissão para consumo de energia cresceram 460% nos seis meses até junho de 2025, segundo o governo britânico. Como resultado, alguns empreendimentos enfrentam esperas de até 15 anos para conseguir uma conexão à rede elétrica. O empreendimento estava previsto para entrar em operação no início de 2027. O plano era instalar 23.040 unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs) GB300, da Nvidia, com capacidade computacional de 50 megawatts para apoiar os serviços de nuvem Azure da Microsoft no país. A decisão, porém, não significa o fim da parceria entre as duas empresas. Em comunicado à Reuters, a Microsoft afirmou que continua comprometida com a Nscale e com o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura digital. Segundo a companhia, a saída diz respeito exclusivamente ao local de Loughton. A Nscale também declarou que mantém uma relação de longo prazo com a Microsoft e que o problema não afeta seus outros contratos. A empresa afirmou que segue comprometida com o projeto e com o mercado britânico, enquanto avalia fontes alternativas de energia para viabilizar a operação. Infraestrutura computacional Fundada em Londres para fornecer infraestrutura voltada à inteligência artificial, a Nscale oferece capacidade computacional, data centers, energia e software para treinar e executar modelos de IA. A empresa, inclusive, entrou com um pedido de IPO nos Estados Unidos em setembro de 2026, com planos de listagem na New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) sob o ticker NSCL. A Nscale disputa esse mercado com empresas como CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe e Lambda Labs, que também fornecem infraestrutura computacional para aplicações de inteligência artificial. O episódio reforça que a expansão da IA depende não apenas da disponibilidade de chips e investimentos, mas também de condições físicas para operar os sistemas. Sem energia e conexões à rede elétrica no prazo necessário, projetos de grande porte podem sofrer atrasos ou perder contratos antes mesmo de entrar em funcionamento. Apesar do revés em Loughton, a Nscale segue atraindo investidores. Em 25 de setembro, a empresa anunciou a captação de US$ 3,36 bilhões por meio de notas conversíveis, que são empréstimos que podem virar ações da companhia no futuro. A rodada foi liderada pela Third Point e contou com a participação da Nvidia, que ainda se comprometeu a aportar mais US$ 1 bilhão em novembro. Segundo a Nscale, o dinheiro será usado para ampliar sua plataforma, que inclui desde usinas de energia próprias, instaladas junto ao local de consumo, até data centers e grandes clusters de GPUs. A Nscale também já deu o primeiro passo para abrir capital. A empresa protocolou recentemente seu pedido de IPO, com listagem prevista na Bolsa de Nova York (NYSE). O número de ações e a faixa de preço ainda não foram definidos. Siga Startups no Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. artigo.texto: Data center stocks are being squeezed on Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave. Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity. The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities before some names clambered back into the green. CoreWeave shares are up 1.6% after dropping 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 1% while Iren was down about 4% in late morning trading. HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away. "Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside. Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters. Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses. Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out. Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates. Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note. Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030. "Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said. Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC. "At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."

artigo.texto: Data Center Conference reúne especialistas e setor de energia na Casa da Indústria, em Natal A estrutura necessária para abrigar centros de processamento e armazenamento de dados estará em pauta na Data Center Conference, marcada para 23 de outubro, na sede da Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte (FIERN), em Natal. Realizado pelo Grupo FRG, o encontro reúne representantes dos setores de tecnologia, energia, infraestrutura, meio ambiente e engenharia. O presidente da FIERN, Roberto Serquiz, participará da abertura do evento. “Quando falamos de data centers, falamos da estrutura que sustenta serviços que usamos todos os dias, das operações das empresas às plataformas digitais. Para receber esses empreendimentos, é preciso reunir energia, conectividade, engenharia e planejamento ambiental. Queremos colocar esses setores na mesma mesa para discutir o que o Rio Grande do Norte pode oferecer e quais desafios precisam ser enfrentados para transformar esse potencial em investimentos”, ressalta Tiago Fraga, CEO do Grupo FRG e presidente do Conselho da World Carbon Association (WCA). Os data centers abrigam equipamentos que processam e armazenam informações utilizadas por empresas, serviços públicos e plataformas digitais. Seu funcionamento depende de uma estrutura que envolve fornecimento de energia, conectividade, refrigeração e segurança, conectando diferentes áreas de conhecimento e atividade econômica. Entre os palestrantes confirmados estão o vice-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC), Luis Tossi, e o especialista em infraestrutura de data centers Júlio Lima. Também participam André Martins, presidente executivo do IBTD; Lucas Themata, presidente da APCA e representante do Grupo Thêmata; e Ricardo Salles, presidente do Instituto BR+. O setor energético estará representado por Fabíola Almeida, diretora-presidente da Neoenergia Cosern, e Dennis Falcon, diretor técnico e comercial da Potigás. A programação também contará com Roberto Wagner Costa, presidente do Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia do Rio Grande do Norte (Crea-RN), e Larissa Dantas, diretora institucional da entidade. A lista de convidados inclui ainda Hugo Fonseca, diretor administrativo e financeiro da Codern; Olavo Bueno, diretor-presidente do PAX RN; Ângela Paiva, presidente do Conselho do PAX; Mayara Leal, do Idema; e Kepler Brito, representante da OAB/RN no Conema. O evento tem apoio da FIERN, WCA, ABDC, Crea-RN, Potigás, Neoenergia Cosern e Banco do Nordeste. As inscrições podem ser feitas pelo site www.conferenciadatacenter.com.br.
