artigo.texto: UPDATE: Hermantown Planning Commission recommends council approve data center permit 11:45 PM UPDATE - The Planning and Zoning Commission voted 6 to 1 recommending Hermantown City Council to approve the Special Use Permit. HERMANTOWN, Minn. (Northern News Now) - Hermantown’s Planning and Zoning Commission took up the Special Use Permit needed to begin data center construction on Tuesday night. The meeting included multiple hours of presentations and public comment. As of 11:00 pm Tuesday, they have not made their recommendation on the SUP. Hermantown city documents define a Special Use Permit as a permit that clears buildings for uses that they consider desirable, but that may pose potential hazards that would need to be mitigated. The planning and zoning commission held a public hearing on the Special Use Permit for Google’s proposed data center before making its recommendation to council. The meeting brought in both sides of the data center debate. Site Setup Before public comment, the commission went over nearly every aspect of the proposed data center building, from traffic impacts to the utilities setup and architecture of the site. The 8-building campus would include three 375 thousand square foot data center buildings, each of which would have a 150 thousand square foot mechanical building and an equipment yard beside it. “The buildings are designed to house the IT infrastructure required to store, process, and transmit the data utilized in everyday digital services for users worldwide,” said Hermantown Community Development Director Eric Johnson. Stormwater System A big topic of discussion among the commission was stormwater management. The City’s engineer said that out of the 234-acre site, 191 acres will be disturbed. He said that once water is collected and treated by the on-site stormwater system, that runoff will go into the Midway River. But the setup raised questions from commissioners. “We get snow runoff extraordinaire with the ground still solidly frozen,” said Planning and Zoning Commissioner Beth Wentzlaff. “These things, according to what I’m seeing, are not going to work very well.” Hermantown City Engineer David Bolf responded to her concern. “I have designed basins for 30 years, and I have never experienced a problem with frost,” he said. City leaders say the meeting will go late into the night if it needs to. After the presentation, the commission will hear from the public, where over 20 residents are signed up to speak. After the commission makes its recommendation, that’ll be taken to the City Council, which will be voting on the Special Use Permit on Monday. If that vote goes through, the city says Google will be cleared to use that land to build its 1.6 million-square-foot data center. Pending Litigation There are currently two lawsuits against the city from Stop the Hermantown Data Center. RELATED: Stop the Hermantown Data Center announces new lawsuit against city City leaders say despite the pending litigation, their legal counsel says they are cleared to proceed with the Special Use Permit and final plat decisions. Google representatives said if the SUP goes through, they will need to get other permits from other government agencies. “Our development timeline is subject to ongoing permitting and regulatory approvals that will trail the City’s SUP process,” said a Google Spokesperson. “Our earliest construction start is during the 2027 construction season; this is subject to the ongoing permitting processes, business demand, market conditions, and other associated factors.” Click here to download the Northern News Now app or our Northern News Now First Alert weather app. Copyright 2026 Northern News Now. Ghada El Ehwany, Managing Partner of Baker McKenzie Cairo, commented: “We are delighted to have supported CATL on this strategic project, which brings advanced battery technology and manufacturing capabilities to Egypt. The transaction reflects growing investment in the country’s industrial and clean technology sectors and demonstrates Egypt’s increasing role as a regional hub for advanced manufacturing and innovation.” Additionally, Zeinab Shohdy, M&A Counsel, commented: “This transaction called for a carefully tailored approach that balanced the parties’ commercial objectives while rigorously protecting CATL’s proprietary technology assets. We are proud to have helped establish a robust framework that enables CATL’s cutting-edge expertise and innovation to be deployed in Egypt while fully supporting its strategic business objectives.” Baker McKenzie acted as local counsel to CATL and advised on the structuring and implementation of the comprehensive contractual framework governing the parties’ technology cooperation, encompassing the commercialization of CATL’s advanced technology in Egypt while safeguarding its intellectual property rights and proprietary know-how. The scope of work included advising on the structuring and negotiation of the project agreements, navigating regulatory considerations across the transaction, and developing bespoke contractual protections designed to safeguard CATL’s long-term commercial interests. The Baker McKenzie Cairo team was led by the office’s Managing Partner Ghada El Ehwany, M&A Partner Hani Nassef, and Counsel Zeinab Shohdy, and further included Mohamed Elfar, Heba Samy, Omar Zaki and Mohamed El Baroudy. artigo.texto: Compromise on emissions allowances reached. EU backs away from tougher proposal Brussels, 21 October (CTK correspondent) - EU member states and the European Parliament have reached a provisional agreement on changes to the European Commission's proposal from April concerning the ETS 1 emissions trading system. The EU Council announced the agreement. The Commission proposed amending the so-called Market Stability Reserve (MSR), which regulates the supply of allowances on the market. It originally wanted to halt the mechanism that permanently invalidates allowances when there is a surplus in the reserve. The agreement, however, provides for the mechanism to be retained, while the threshold for invalidation will rise from 400 million to 700 million allowances. "The new rules will strengthen the Market Stability Reserve's ability to intervene in the market through the potential future release of allowances, which is intended to protect European industry from extreme price fluctuations. At the same time, they are intended to send a clear signal to the market and maintain safeguards against an excessive surplus of allowances," the EU Council said. The provisional agreement still needs to be formally approved by both the European Parliament and EU member states. The Market Stability Reserve helps regulate the number of allowances on the market. It reduces supply in the event of a surplus and releases allowances when there is a shortage, helping to stabilise prices. The Commission has previously said its aim is to increase stability and predictability. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš is among those calling for changes to the emissions trading system. "Since the invalidation mechanism began operating in 2023, more than three billion emissions allowances have been invalidated and withdrawn from the market. This restored the balance between supply and demand and addressed the historical surplus of allowances that had built up in the ETS," the EU member states said in a statement. "While the Commission's proposal provides for the permanent suspension of the allowance invalidation mechanism, the co-legislators have provisionally agreed on a compromise: the invalidation mechanism will remain in place, but the threshold for invalidation will rise from the current 400 million to 700 million allowances," the text adds. In addition to its April proposal concerning the Market Stability Reserve, the European Commission presented a comprehensive review of the ETS 1 emissions trading system in July. It says, for example, that it wants to maintain the free allocation of allowances beyond 2030, but to link it more closely to investment in decarbonisation. Companies will therefore have to submit and implement emissions reduction plans to continue receiving support. Discussions on these proposals have only just begun in the European Parliament. The ETS emissions trading system is intended to encourage companies to reduce emissions. Companies have to buy allowances for every tonne of CO2 they emit. The more they emit, the higher their costs, making investment in cleaner technologies worthwhile. ETS 1 is Europe's main emissions trading market and covers energy, heavy industry and aviation in the EU. ETS 2 is due to come into operation in 2028, following a one-year delay, and is expected to cover road transport and building heating. The ETS is the EU's main tool for tackling climate change and is not the main cause of the current rise in energy prices in Europe, Reuters noted. The agreed changes, however, respond to demands from some governments, including those of Poland, Italy and Czechia, which want to mitigate the impact of the ETS on electricity prices. According to EU data, ETS costs account for an average of about 11 percent of electricity bills in Europe. The figure varies from one of the 27 member states to another; in Poland, for example, it is 24 percent, reflecting the dominant role of coal-fired power plants in the country's energy mix. In Czechia, it is 20 percent, a similarly high share to Italy's. Translation disclaimer This article is a machine translation of the Czech original and has not yet been fully reviewed. artigo.texto: O paranaense e administrador de empresas Lúcio Lopez, fundador e CEO da Greenline, empresa brasileira de tecnologia para o mercado de carbono, projeta faturamento de R$ 250 milhões e quer ampliar a escala de sua operação, que monitora 1,5 milhão de hectares de florestas em propriedades privadas no Brasil. Segundo estimativas divulgadas por ele, os projetos acompanhados registram sequestro médio anual de cerca de 25 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. Depois de investir mais de R$ 35 milhões de recursos próprios no desenvolvimento de sua tecnologia, a empresa prepara uma nova frente de negócios: créditos de carbono protegidos por seguro contra riscos fundiários, cibernéticos e políticos. Em setembro, anunciou uma parceria com a RCGI-USP Carbon Registry para fornecer evidências digitais que poderão ser consideradas no registro de projetos. A aposta combina escala, monitoramento por satélite e mecanismos de rastreabilidade para tornar o mercado mais confiável e, na visão de Lopez, mais acessível. “Até hoje, em oito anos, todo o investimento foi feito por mim e pela minha própria família. Se somar tudo, já são mais de 35 milhões de reais”, afirma o empresário. A trajetória que levou à criação da Greenline começou em 2018, quando Lopez acompanhava dos Estados Unidos notícias sobre desmatamento e incêndios florestais no Brasil. Com passagens pela indústria moveleira, pelo comércio exterior e pelo mercado financeiro, passou a estudar como incentivos econômicos poderiam tornar a preservação florestal uma alternativa mais rentável para os proprietários de terras. De acordo com dados da Embrapa Territorial, 66,3% do território brasileiro (cerca de 564 milhões de hectares) é coberto por vegetação nativa, sendo que 25,6% (218,2 milhões de hectares) estão preservados dentro de propriedades rurais privadas pelos próprios produtores. Esta é uma grande oportunidade para a Greenline poder conectar, o produtor que preserva e sequestra carbono com empresas que querem mitigar sua pegada de carbono, como as aéreas Gol, Latam, e Azul; bancos, como Banco do Brasil e Bradesco; indústrias como CSN, Gerdau e Vale; e a até petroquímicas como Petrobras e Braskem. Lopez se reuniu com todas. “Em cada setor, fomos buscar opiniões sobre se seria interessante ter um novo standard de crédito de carbono utilizando dados espaciais”, diz Lopez. Em termos de potencial, o agronegócio brasileiro poderá gerar até 314,3 milhões de créditos de carbono entre 2025 e 2035, com potencial de movimentar até R$ 3,5 bilhões no mercado internacional. A estimativa faz parte do estudo O Agronegócio Brasileiro no Mercado Internacional de Carbono – Oportunidades Econômicas, Elegibilidade e Impactos na NDC, divulgado pela Associação Brasileira do Agronegócio (ABAG). Uma nova camada de evidências para os créditos A Greenline desenvolveu uma plataforma de monitoramento, relato e verificação digital, conhecida como dMRV, que combina dados de satélites, sensoriamento remoto, inteligência artificial e informações geoespaciais. A tecnologia utiliza dados de agências como a Agência Espacial Americana (NASA) e a Agência Espacial Europeia (ESA), além de um índice próprio, o GLVCI (Greenline Vegetation Carbon Index), que, segundo Lopez, analisa 16 domínios e aplica mais de 100 índices de vegetação. A proposta é acompanhar as mudanças nas áreas monitoradas com atualizações frequentes e recuperar informações históricas para estimar alterações na vegetação e no estoque de carbono. Na prática, a tecnologia pode reduzir a dependência de levantamentos exclusivamente presenciais e gerar registros digitais que ajudam a documentar a situação de cada área ao longo do tempo. É essa capacidade de produzir evidências sistemáticas que levou à aproximação com a RCGI-USP Carbon Registry, registradora vinculada ao Centro de Pesquisa e Inovação em Gases de Efeito Estufa da Universidade de São Paulo. A colaboração, firmada em setembro deste ano, prevê que informações produzidas pela plataforma da Greenline possam ser consideradas na avaliação de projetos, desde que atendam às metodologias e aos critérios estabelecidos pela registradora. “O mercado de carbono depende da confiança nas informações apresentadas pelos projetos. Essa parceria fortalece justamente esse aspecto. A tecnologia da Greenline acrescenta uma camada adicional de evidências, oferecendo mais segurança de que os dados apresentados refletem efetivamente a realidade observada em campo”, afirma Ruy Rêde, gerente de Transferência de Tecnologia e Inovação do RCGI-USP. O executivo ressalta, porém, que a tecnologia não substitui o papel institucional da registradora. “Nosso papel continua sendo avaliar as evidências produzidas ao longo do processo, mas contar com uma tecnologia reconhecida de verificação digital aumenta a robustez e a credibilidade das informações que chegam à registradora.” A separação de responsabilidades é central para a credibilidade do sistema: a Greenline fornece dados técnicos, enquanto a registradora avalia as evidências segundo suas próprias regras. A parceria não representa aprovação automática dos projetos nem elimina a necessidade de auditorias e verificações independentes. Metodologias adaptadas aos biomas brasileiros Para Odair Carrel, diretor executivo da RCGI-USP Carbon Registry, a inovação não está apenas no uso de satélites, mas na combinação entre tecnologia e metodologias capazes de refletir melhor as características dos ecossistemas brasileiros e de outros países do Hemisfério Sul. “O que estamos fazendo é uma inovação no mercado de carbono mundial. Nós estamos trazendo as metodologias embasadas no IPCC e na UNFCCC, que são as bases metodológicas de captura e mensuração de carbono, para a realidade do mercado brasileiro e do Hemisfério Sul”, afirma Carrel. O executivo argumenta que muitas metodologias tradicionais foram concebidas considerando as condições do Hemisfério Norte. artigo.texto: 💻 A Anthropic, desenvolvedora do assistente de inteligência artificial Claude, está perto de ampliar ainda mais sua estrutura de computação. A Nscale, empresa de nuvem voltada à IA e apoiada pela Nvidia (NVDA), negocia a venda de capacidade computacional para a Anthropic em um acordo que pode chegar a cerca de US$ 45 bilhões, de acordo com pessoas a par das conversas. Acompanhe todas as notícias pelo celular! Baixe o app Se confirmado, este será o segundo grande contrato entre as duas empresas. Segundo documentos regulatórios ligados à oferta pública inicial planejada pela Nscale, a Anthropic já possui acordos de infraestrutura com a companhia que somam até aproximadamente US$ 44,6 bilhões. O negócio pode ser concluído nos próximos dias, segundo as fontes, que falaram sob condição de anonimato por se tratar de negociações privadas. As conversas seguem em andamento, os termos ainda podem mudar e nenhuma decisão definitiva foi tomada. Anthropic e Nscale não comentaram o assunto. Novo prédio terá 460 megawatts e chips Vera Rubin O novo contrato envolve uma instalação no complexo de data centers Monarch, que a Nscale desenvolve na Virgínia Ocidental, nos Estados Unidos. O segundo edifício do campus terá capacidade para entregar 460 megawatts de poder computacional e utilizará os chips de IA Vera Rubin, da Nvidia, a geração mais avançada da fabricante, segundo parte das fontes. Pelo desenho em discussão, a Anthropic também teria direito de preferência sobre um terceiro prédio previsto para o mesmo complexo. A dimensão do projeto ajuda a entender o interesse da empresa. De acordo com os documentos do IPO da Nscale, o campus Monarch poderá ultrapassar 8 gigawatts de capacidade elétrica bruta quando estiver totalmente concluído. Espaço foi aberto depois da desistência da Microsoft A entrada da Anthropic no complexo tem um antecedente curioso. Parte do campus Monarch seria inicialmente alugada pela Microsoft (MSFT), que em março havia anunciado a assinatura de uma carta de intenções para o projeto. No meio do ano, porém, a gigante de tecnologia desistiu da instalação, o que abriu espaço para que a Anthropic assumisse a operação. A Anthropic, uma das maiores clientes da Nscale, se transformou em um dos principais impulsionadores da demanda mundial por data centers dedicados à inteligência artificial. A empresa vem fechando uma série de acordos de grande porte para garantir capacidade computacional. Entre eles estão um contrato de US$ 50 bilhões com a Fluidstack, outro de US$ 10 bilhões com a startup de infraestrutura Volta e um acordo de US$ 45 bilhões com a SpaceX (SPCX), de Elon Musk. A busca por mais poder computacional acompanha o crescimento acelerado da companhia. Em julho, a Anthropic ultrapassou US$ 65 bilhões em receita anualizada, e em maio a empresa foi avaliada em US$ 965 bilhões. A desenvolvedora do Claude também é candidata a realizar sua própria abertura de capital nos próximos meses, em uma operação que pode estar entre as maiores da história recente do setor de tecnologia. Acordo pode reforçar o IPO da Nscale, avaliado em US$ 30 bi Do lado da Nscale, um novo contrato bilionário chega em um momento estratégico. A empresa busca uma avaliação de aproximadamente US$ 30 bilhões em seu IPO nos Estados Unidos, mas um grupo de investidores vem pressionando para que a companhia reduza essa meta de valuation. Um acordo dessa magnitude com um cliente como a Anthropic tende a fortalecer os argumentos da empresa diante do mercado. A Nscale protocolou o pedido público de listagem em setembro, mas ainda não iniciou formalmente a divulgação da oferta, embora o prazo regulatório de espera já tenha terminado. A empresa responde a questionamentos da SEC, órgão regulador do mercado de capitais americano, e pretende começar o roadshow com investidores assim que essas questões forem resolvidas. No mês passado, a companhia levantou US$ 3,36 bilhões em uma rodada pré-IPO liderada pela Third Point, de Dan Loeb, com participação de investidores como Nvidia, Apollo Global Management, Citadel, Hudson Bay Capital e Abu Dhabi Investment Council. 💰 O avanço dos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA, porém, vem acompanhado de cautela no mercado. Investidores têm demonstrado preocupação crescente com o volume de dívidas usado para financiar a expansão acelerada dos data centers, tema que tem pesado sobre ações de fabricantes de chips e sobre os títulos de dívida de empresas de computação em nuvem.

artigo.texto: Avery Dennison Introduces Adhesive Tapes for Battery Energy Storage Systems PAINESVILLE, Ohio — Avery Dennison has introduced a portfolio of pressure-sensitive adhesive tapes designed to improve assembly efficiency and provide thermal and electrical protection in battery energy storage systems. Battery energy storage systems typically use lithium iron phosphate cells grouped into modules, packs and containerized units. Within those assemblies, pressure-sensitive adhesives can be used to bond and insulate cells, thermal barriers and electrical connections. The new portfolio includes tapes designed for thermal runaway protection, high-voltage insulation and no-cure assembly. Battery energy storage systems face the critical challenge of thermal runaway propagation between cells, which can cascade through entire modules in seconds. Thermal barriers, mica sheets, aerogel pads and ceramic paper are one solution, but these materials are fragile, shed fibers or crumble during handling and assembly. Acrylic- and rubber-based adhesives like those made by Avery Dennison with Flame Tough™ flame-retardant adhesive properties allow multilayer solutions and an ability to manufacture these materials into packs. For electrical protection, the company's Volt Tough dielectric tapes are designed to insulate cells, busbars, cooling plates and module housings in systems that routinely exceed 1,000 volts DC. The materials are tested for breakdown voltage and dielectric strength using GB/T 1408.1-2016 and ASTM D3755 test methods. The pressure-sensitive tapes also provide instant bonding without the mixing, dispensing equipment or cure time required by liquid adhesives. They can be incorporated into automated assembly lines, while precision die-cutting provides dimensional accuracy for tight tolerances and colored variants can aid detection by machine vision systems. artigo.texto: Por Kleber Karpov O Distrito Federal ocupa a segunda colocação nacional no volume proporcional de buscas na internet por Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês), ficando atrás apenas de Santa Catarina. O levantamento, produzido pela empresa de transição energética Descarbonize Soluções a partir de dados consolidados de ferramentas de busca do Google, apontou que o interesse geral dos brasileiros por soluções voltadas a estocar eletricidade cresceu 48% nos últimos 12 meses, somando mais de 50 mil pesquisas diretas. A aceleração dos termos técnicos ligados ao modelo BESS foi o grande destaque do período, ultrapassando 104 mil consultas digitais — salto de 120% no intervalo anual. Já no recorte de volume total por equipamento, as baterias estacionárias convencionais preservam o topo das procuras populares, acumulando 248 mil pesquisas (+22%). Expressões complementares como “bateria para energia solar” (69 mil pesquisas, +22%), “kit energia solar” (61 mil, +22%) e “kit energia solar off-grid” (27 mil, +53%) também registraram expansão contínua. Custos em queda e leilões federais A movimentação de mercado reflete mudanças de custos e marcos regulatórios. De acordo com a BloombergNEF, os valores para instalação de estruturas de armazenamento de grande porte utilitário recuaram mais de 50% desde 2022, apresentando retração de 27% apenas no último ano e tornando a tecnologia mais barata que a implantação de termelétricas a gás natural. No setor público, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) colocou em consulta pública os primeiros certames exclusivos para contratação de capacidade de armazenamento no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), cujos leilões estão programados para dezembro de 2026. “O método de geração de energia por meio da luz solar está cada vez mais acessível e popular. Existe uma forte relação entre o interesse crescente por BESS e a consolidação das baterias estacionárias, visto que são soluções complementares para assegurar estabilidade e autossuficiência ao sistema”, explicou o CEO da Descarbonize Soluções , Patrick von Schaaffhausen. Ranking estadual A lista dos estados mais engajados na busca por soluções BESS reúne os seguintes entes da federação: O primeiro lugar catarinense acompanha a formação de polos industriais na Região Sul, onde o Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) financiou R$ 280 milhões para a edificação de uma fábrica do setor em Itajaí (SC). Já no Distrito Federal, o alto volume decorre da centralização dos debates regulatórios, jurídicos e governamentais sobre a matriz energética nacional. Em regiões como Amapá e Roraima, o interesse reflete o histórico de vulnerabilidades nos sistemas isolados e o processo recente de conexão à rede do SIN. artigo.texto: GGGI Launches New Guidance to Put National Development Priorities at the Heart of Article 6 Strategies October 22, 2026 Category GGGI’s new policy-design framework helps governments shape carbon market participation to mobilize finance, support economic transformation, retain domestic value and advance development and climate goals. SEOUL, 22 October 2026 — The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) has launched new guidance to help governments turn international carbon market participation into a deliberate instrument of national development and economic transformation. Launched today at the Global Article 6 Forum in Seoul, Making Article 6 Work for Host Countries: A Comprehensive Policy-Design Framework for National Article 6 Strategy links countries’ climate and development priorities to the decisions that shape carbon market activity: which investments to encourage, which mitigation outcomes to transfer internationally, what value to retain domestically and what conditions to apply. (“Host countries” are the countries where mitigation activities take place and from which emission reductions may be transferred abroad.) These choices have consequences across the economy. They can influence technology deployment, investment in priority sectors, public revenues and benefits for communities. They also affect a country’s own climate commitments, since mitigation outcomes transferred abroad can no longer be counted toward its own targets. The guidance connects four levels of policy design: national climate and development priorities; specific Article 6 objectives; the policy tools available to pursue them; and the detailed settings that determine how those tools operate. This gives governments a practical route from ambition to implementation. A government seeking to accelerate deployment of a priority technology, for example, can assess how different eligibility rules, authorization conditions and financial measures could support their objective. The framework also helps governments assess how their policy choices interact. For example, a levy may generate public revenue while weakening investment incentives; a transfer limit may protect national climate commitments while reducing potential carbon revenues. Examining these choices together helps governments design a coherent policy package that can deliver their priorities. “Greater strategic clarity from governments can shape where investment flows and how carbon markets develop. When countries make their priorities explicit and translate them into coherent, predictable policies, developers and buyers can better identify opportunities, assess risks and structure investments around those priorities. This guidance helps governments provide that direction, creating stronger conditions for carbon finance to deliver lasting development and climate benefits,” said Fenella Aouane, Head of Carbon Finance at GGGI. The guidance was prepared under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF). It was led by Wesley Ramnauth, with contributions from Mark Hopkins and Evans Bedu-Prah, and reviewed by experts from GGGI, the OECD, the World Bank and Carbon Limits. Governments can use the framework to develop a national Article 6 strategy, refine an existing approach or assess a specific policy decision. Its emphasis on explicit objectives, coherent policy choices and periodic review supports adaptation as national priorities and market conditions evolve. Download the full guide: https://gggi.org/report/making-article-6-work-for-host-countries/ About the Global Green Growth Institute The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) was founded as a treaty-based international, inter-governmental organization in 2012 at the United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development. GGGI supports its Member States in transitioning their economies toward a green growth model that simultaneously achieves poverty reduction, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and economic growth. With 55 Member States and 30 Partner countries and regional integration organizations in the process of accession, GGGI delivers programs and projects in over 57 countries. These initiatives encompass developing innovative green growth solutions, technical support, capacity building, policy planning & implementation, and assistance in building a pipeline of bankable green investment projects, project financing, investments, and knowledge sharing. GGGI’s work contributes to its Member States’ efforts to fulfill the Sustainable Development Goals and the Nationally Determined Contributions to the Paris Agreement. About the Carbon Transaction Facility The Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) is a GGGI country-driven mechanism that supports governments and the private sector in developing countries and emerging economies to participate in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. By combining readiness support with transaction facilitation, the CTF helps turn climate ambition into action through transparent, high-integrity carbon transactions aligned with the Paris Agreement. For media inquiries, please contact: Diba Safitri Associate, Carbon Finance Communications, GGGI diba.safitri@gggi.org Thematic Areas

artigo.texto: Mercado global de conectores de sinal: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do mercado de conectores de sinal até 2035: demanda por largura de banda em data centers impulsiona o crescimento Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Conectores de Sinal, o mercado inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compras mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de suprimentos regionalmente mais diversificada. O mercado global de conectores de sinal entra em uma fase de crescimento estrutural, à medida que a infraestrutura digital, a eletrificação veicular e a automação industrial intensificam a demanda por interconexões rápidas e confiáveis. Na base de referência de 2026, o mercado é reconhecido como viabilizador essencial da integridade de sinal em telecomunicações, data centers, eletrônica automotiva, sistemas industriais e dispositivos de consumo. Diferentemente dos conectores de potência, os conectores de sinal são definidos por largura de banda, miniaturização e densidade de contatos, e sua demanda acompanha os ciclos de inovação da eletrônica a jusante, e não simplesmente os volumes unitários. O horizonte de previsão 2026-2035 abrange um período em que os investimentos em data centers, a implantação de 5G/6G, os sistemas avançados de assistência ao motorista e a digitalização das fábricas vão remodelar o mix de produtos em direção a conectores de RF de alta frequência, fibra óptica e placas de passo fino. As cadeias de suprimentos continuam concentradas nos polos industriais da Ásia-Pacífico, mas a demanda se globaliza, com América do Norte e Europa investindo em capacidade regional para componentes críticos de conectividade. A intensidade competitiva é elevada, com multinacionais aproveitando portfólios amplos e empresas especializadas mirando aplicações de nicho de alto desempenho. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados sobre tamanho de mercado, segmentação, comércio, preços e dinâmica competitiva, fornecendo a fabricantes, distribuidores e investidores um arcabouço analítico transparente para decisões estratégicas até 2035. O cenário-base para o mercado mundial de conectores de sinal pressupõe a expansão contínua da infraestrutura digital e do conteúdo eletrônico por dispositivo, sustentando uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) moderada de um dígito até 2035. Espera-se que a demanda seja liderada pela modernização da largura de banda em data centers, onde taxas de sinalização mais altas exigem conectores avançados de RF, fibra óptica e placas de alta densidade, e pela eletrônica automotiva, à medida que as arquiteturas veiculares migram para controladores zonais e de domínio. A automação industrial e os dispositivos médicos acrescentam uma demanda resiliente, orientada por especificações. O cenário-base incorpora a normalização das cadeias de suprimentos, adições graduais de capacidade na Ásia-Pacífico e a regionalização contínua da produção de componentes críticos. Espera-se que os preços permaneçam competitivos nas categorias de conectores de uso geral, enquanto os conectores premium de alta frequência e para ambientes severos sustentam as margens. Entre os riscos estão pausas cíclicas nos investimentos de telecomunicações e data centers, a volatilidade das matérias-primas e atritos na política comercial, mas não se assume que esses fatores descarrilhem a trajetória de longo prazo. Projeta-se que o índice de mercado suba de 100 em 2025 para aproximadamente 168 em 2035, o que corresponde a uma CAGR de cerca de 5,3%. Essa perspectiva implica crescimento em volume nos segmentos maduros e crescimento em valor concentrado nas famílias de conectores de alta velocidade, miniaturizados e específicos para aplicações. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Expansão da largura de banda em data centers e investimentos em hiperescala impulsionando a demanda por conectores de RF de alta velocidade, fibra óptica e placas de passo fino - Migração da arquitetura eletrônica automotiva para ADAS, controladores zonais e eletrificação, elevando o conteúdo de conectores por veículo - Implantação de 5G e acesso fixo sem fio exigindo conectores de RF e modulares aprimorados na infraestrutura de telecomunicações - Automação industrial e adoção da Indústria 4.0 sustentando a demanda por conectores circulares e retangulares robustos - Miniaturização da eletrônica de consumo e dos dispositivos vestíveis impulsionando os volumes de conectores placa a placa de passo fino e modulares - Digitalização de dispositivos médicos e demanda de equipamentos de teste por conectores de sinal de alta confiabilidade Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Pausas cíclicas nos gastos de telecomunicações e data centers podem causar volatilidade de demanda no curto prazo - A volatilidade dos preços de cobre, ouro e plásticos de engenharia pressiona as margens - Atritos na política comercial e controles de exportação perturbam as cadeias transfronteiriças de conectores - A complexidade de projeto e os ciclos de qualificação prolongam o tempo de lançamento de conectores de alto desempenho Estrutura da Demanda por Indústria de Uso Final Telecomunicações e Data Centers (participação estimada: 28%) Telecomunicações e data centers representam o maior e mais dinâmico conjunto de demanda por conectores de sinal. A demanda atual está ancorada em equipamentos de rádio e transporte 5G, implantações de fibra até o ponto final e construções de data centers em hiperescala, onde taxas de sinalização mais altas exigem conectores de RF de baixa perda, conectores de fibra óptica de alta densidade e conectores de placa de passo fino. artigo.texto: EU ETS Revision 2026: Industrial Transformation Requires the Right Framework Conditions The European Commission has presented a draft for the further development of the EU ETS 1 beyond 2030, thereby providing an impetus for the future design of the European emissions trading system. The draft forms the basis for the upcoming discussions on a central instrument of European climate policy. With its proposal of 17 July 2026 to revise the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS1), the European Commission has proposed extensive changes to the existing system for the period after 2030. At the heart of the proposal are adjustments to the emissions reduction pathway (LRF), the introduction of conditionalities for free allocation, the integration of permanent CO₂ removals, the use of international carbon credits, and modifications to the Market Stability Reserve. In addition, free allocation for sectors covered by the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) would be phased out more slowly than currently envisaged. Furthermore, the Commission proposes a partial extension of the ETS to aviation and maritime transport, as well as the inclusion of waste incineration, thereby broadening the scope of the system in several areas. The BDI welcomes the Commission’s intention to maintain the ETS as the central market-based instrument for achieving climate objectives beyond 2030. At the same time, we see several shortcomings in the Commission’s proposal. The success of the ETS as a driver of industrial decarbonisation depends critically on whether the conditions needed for industrial transformation are actually in place. These include, in particular, a robust hydrogen and CO₂ infrastructure, renewable electricity at competitive prices, and functioning markets for climate neutral products. In many ETS covered sectors, these prerequisites are not available yet. Against this background, the BDI opposes additional conditionalities for free allocation proposed by the Commission. Free allocation serves the sole purpose of protecting against carbon leakage and compensating companies for CO₂-costs that international competitors outside Europe do not face. Conditionalities can therefore not function as an investment instrument and substitute for missing economic or infrastructural framework conditions. Additional requirements would weaken carbon leakage protection without addressing the underlying causes of insufficient transformation investments. One of BDI’s key priorities is safeguarding the international competitiveness of German industry. To date, no effective solution exists for exports from the EU to third country markets. European companies are required to bear the costs of the EU ETS1 while competing internationally with producers from countries that do not face a comparable carbon price. This creates significant competitive disadvantages. BDI therefore proposes a dedicated export solution to close this regulatory gap and preserve the international competitiveness of European manufacturers. As effective carbon leakage protection continues to require a sufficient volume of freely allocated allowances, we also advocate adjusting the balance between auctioning and free allocation. Specifically, we propose lowering the minimum share of allowances that must be auctioned, thereby increasing the volume available for free allocation accordingly, including to provide allowances for an export solution. Only in this way can both a realistic benchmark design and effective carbon leakage protection be ensured. We also see potential in the use of international emissions reduction credits to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness in third countries while providing for cost-effective decarbonisation options. Without introducing additional requirements for such credits, preference should be given to emissions reduction projects implemented with European technology. The coming months will be decisive for shaping the European emissions trading system after 2030. BDI is committed to ensuring that the ETS supports both climate protection and industrial competitiveness. The decarbonisation of industry can only succeed if climate policy ambitions and economic realities are brought into alignment.

artigo.texto: A China está a intensificar os investimentos no armazenamento de energia e na conservação dos ecossistemas, procurando conciliar a transição energética com a proteção ambiental. As duas prioridades foram destacadas em iniciativas divulgadas pela agência estatal Xinhua. Durante a Conferência Mundial de Armazenamento de Energia, realizada em Ningde, foram apresentados dados que atribuem à China 56% da expansão mundial da capacidade de armazenamento em baterias em 2025. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a produção chinesa de baterias destinadas a este setor ultrapassou 420 GWh, mais 110% do que no período homólogo. Paralelamente, o Presidente Xi Jinping defendeu o reforço da conservação ecológica durante uma visita à Mongólia Interior. Na reserva natural do lago Huangqihai, destacou a importância da recuperação das zonas húmidas, da proteção da biodiversidade e do cumprimento da legislação ambiental. A estratégia inclui ainda novas inspeções ambientais e a aplicação do Código Ecológico e Ambiental, em vigor desde agosto. Apesar dos progressos anunciados, persistem desafios relacionados com os custos das tecnologias, a fiscalização e a sustentabilidade dos resultados a longo prazo.

artigo.texto: Insourcing versus Integration: Toyota, BYD, and Two Roads to the Global Market In a recent Defense.info piece, “BYD, Batteries, and the Architecture of Dependence,” I looked at BYD as the clearest automotive expression of what Kenneth Maxwell and I have called the “Architecture of Dependency.” I ended that piece by treating Toyota’s solid-state battery program as the most credible industrial counter now on the table. But there is a deeper Toyota story, and it is not about chemistry. It is about how a foreign automaker decides to enter a market that is politically hostile to it. Toyota answered that question forty years ago, and one of the people who helped shape the answer was my friend Harald Malmgren. BYD is answering the same question today, and its answer is very different. Putting the two side by side shows something that the tariff debate tends to miss. The real question is not whether a foreign carmaker builds factories in your country. It is what those factories become. The Malmgren Lesson Harald Malmgren trained as an economist in the United States and at Oxford, worked as a research assistant to Thomas Schelling, and was brought into the Kennedy administration by McGeorge Bundy as one of the “Whiz Kids.” He worked defense issues in the Pentagon through the Cuban Missile Crisis, then handled trade and foreign policy for Presidents Johnson, Nixon, and Ford, and advised the Senate in two separate stints. When he left government, he set up a consulting practice and worked with the CEOs of major global corporations. One of them was Toyota. As he told me in our 2024 interviews for Assessing Global Change: Strategic Perspectives of Dr. Harald Malmgren, he worked closely with Toyota’s chief executive and his team on “in-sourcing” the manufacture of Toyotas into the United States. Toyota went on to build cars in America at scale, as he had urged. That advice came out of a particular way of thinking. Malmgren had sat on both sides of the table, in the executive branch and in Congress, on trade and on security. He understood that trade friction is never only economic. It is political, it is about domestic constituencies, and if it is left unaddressed it hardens into policy. The Japanese auto challenge of the early 1980s was exactly that kind of problem. In April 1981, Toyota placed self-imposed limits on its U.S. passenger-car exports under the voluntary restraint arrangement, capping Japanese shipments at 1.68 million vehicles a year. Toyota’s own history records that, even with the restraints in place, criticism of Japanese cars did not subside and Congress was moving toward local-content legislation. A company could have treated that as a barrier to get around. The Malmgren insight was to treat it as a signal: if you want to be accepted in the American market for the long term, become part of the American economy. What Toyota Built What followed was not a tariff workaround. It was a long, deliberate process of turning Toyota into an American industrial company. The first step was a partnership with an American incumbent. In 1984 Toyota and General Motors formed New United Motor Manufacturing, Inc. (NUMMI) at a closed GM plant in Fremont, California. Toyota described the venture at the time as a model of U.S.–Japan industrial cooperation that would support American jobs and the parts industry. Just as important was the labor settlement. In September 1983, Toyota reached an agreement with the UAW stating that “labor and management are partners for achieving shared goals,” which Toyota itself called a revolutionary labor-management agreement for its time. The second step was going it alone. Camry production began at the wholly owned Georgetown, Kentucky plant in 1988, and Georgetown became Toyota’s largest production facility in North America. The third step, and the one that matters most for this comparison, was putting capability in place and not just assembly. Toyota opened its Technical Center in Ann Arbor in 1977 and later set up the Toyota Supplier Support Center to share Toyota Production System knowledge with American firms. The Toyota Production System was not kept as a Japanese secret. It was taught to American suppliers. It is worth being clear that Toyota did not start out fully localized. At NUMMI, Toyota initially imported engines, transmissions, and other key functional components from Japan, sourcing only items like glass, interior trim, and paint locally. What set Toyota apart was the direction it took over time: the higher-value parts of the chain moved toward the host country. The results four decades later speak for themselves: - Toyota describes its total U.S. investment as reaching nearly $60 billion since it began operating in the U.S. nearly 70 years ago, with roughly 48,000 direct U.S. employees and more than 35 million vehicles built across 11 U.S. plants. - Toyota Motor North America reports more than $50 billion a year in domestic parts purchases, with about 75 percent of a typical vehicle’s content coming from outside suppliers and more than 1,000 supplier locations in North America. - Imports accounted for only about one-fifth of Toyota’s U.S. sales, which is why the 2025 tariffs did not knock it off course. Toyota sold 2,518,071 vehicles in the U.S. in 2025, with electrified models making up 47 percent. And the battery, the part of the vehicle where BYD’s model is most concentrated, is the part Toyota is now putting on American soil. Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina, in Liberty, is Toyota’s first in-house battery plant outside Japan, a $13.9 billion facility with 30 GWh of annual capacity and 14 production lines at full build-out, with up to 5,100 jobs planned. Alongside it, Toyota committed up to $10 billion in additional U.S. investment over five years, starting with a $912 million hybrid-capacity investment across plants in West Virginia, Kentucky, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Missouri. artigo.texto: GCL Technology to acquire 81.91% of Sichuan GCL Lithium Battery Technology for CNY 2.5 billion GCL Technology Holdings has entered a non-binding memorandum of understanding to purchase approximately 81.91% of Sichuan GCL Lithium Battery Technology, an LFP cathode material manufacturer, from Golden Concord Group — the parent company controlled by GCL Technology chairman Zhu Gongshan and his family. According to a filing by the Hong Kong-listed company, the preliminary price stands at roughly CNY 2.5 billion. Cash would account for about CNY 650 million, while approximately CNY 1.85 billion would come through newly issued GCL Technology shares priced at no less than HK$1.30 apiece, or as many as about 1,671 million shares. An independent valuation will determine the final price. As the seller is controlled by the chairman's family trust, the transaction would constitute a connected transaction under Hong Kong listing rules. GCL Technology said it anticipates seeking a specific mandate from independent shareholders for the new share issuance. Due diligence is allotted 30 days, with three months of exclusivity for negotiating a formal agreement. The seller has guaranteed the target's combined adjusted net profit will reach at least CNY 620 million across 2027 and 2028. It has further pledged to develop a sixth-generation LFP cathode material achieving a compacted density above 2.8 g/cm3 by the close of 2028, with compensation payable should either commitment fall short. LFP capacity Meishan-based Sichuan GCL Lithium, located in Sichuan province, operates 120,000 tons of annual LFP production capacity at its first-phase facility, which sits on about 355 mu within a planned 1,000-mu site. A June report from GCL noted that production started in July 2023 and that the company supplies Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. (CATL) and Haichen Energy Storage. Through subsidiary Leshan Xinneng New Materials Technology, GCL Technology already produces LFP cathode material. Shipments from the first 200,000-ton phase commenced in June at an average tax-inclusive price of CNY 60,320 per ton, and the operation has been profitable since starting up, according to the company. GCL Technology said the acquisition would assist it in reducing reliance on pricing cycles for polysilicon and wafer products while improving earnings stability. The company recorded a net loss attributable to shareholders of CNY 2.08 billion in the first half of 2026, 17.2% larger than a year prior. It described the polysilicon industry as having fallen into involution once again during the first half of 2026, with prices plunging below the cash costs of most enterprises. Granular silicon averaged CNY 31.97/kg excluding tax, compared with a cash production cost of CNY 25.23/kg. In May, the company outlined plans to become a multi-product new energy materials platform centered on silicon, lithium and carbon. It referenced Chinese government data indicating the country's cumulative new-type energy storage capacity hit 153 GW/396 GWh by the end of June, an increase of about 61% year on year. The transaction follows an unsuccessful attempt to address polysilicon overcapacity via consolidation. Last year GCL Technology raised funds to back a government-supported plan under which China's six largest polysilicon makers would contribute about CNY 50 billion to acquire and idle roughly one-third of national capacity. China's antitrust regulator subsequently stopped that plan, and competitor Tongwei has since taken steps to acquire polysilicon producer Qinghai Lihao. - 1. artigo.texto: CATL launches “Dual-Electric Range Extender” to drive heavy-duty truck electrification On October 20, CATL officially unveiled its “Dual-Electric Range Extender” technology and the expanding plan for its “QiJi” heavy-duty truck battery-swapping ecosystem. The “Dual-Electric Range Extender” technology Over 430,000 electric heavy trucks already run on CATL batteries, representing over 70% of the market in the world. According to CATL, the debate between diesel and electric heavy trucks is effectively over, with the market entering an “electric-versus-electric” competitive phase. Data shows that the penetration rate of electric heavy trucks in China surged from 5.2% in 2022 to 50.28% in September 2026. The Dual-Electric Range Extender system utilises an “A+B” architecture: - A (bottom-mounted swappable battery): A swappable, high-capacity battery (432 kWh or 513 kWh) for primary driving, available via a flexible leasing model to reduce upfront costs. - B (range-extender battery): A fixed battery pack (77 kWh) that provides backup power. This system allows for deep discharge of the primary battery (down to 5% SOC) without the “range anxiety” associated with traditional electric trucks, as the system switches to the range-extender pack when needed. This approach, combined with a 5-minute battery swap capability, aims to match the operational efficiency of diesel trucks while lowering the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). CATL estimates that compared to diesel trucks, the E-E system can save users over 460,000 yuan (68,700 USD) over a three-year cycle. Scaling the “QiJi” ecosystem To support this technology, CATL is expanding its “QiJi” battery-swapping network. The company has standardised battery blocks into two sizes: the 260# (432 kWh) for 3,800 mm wheelbase vehicles and the 300# (513 kWh) for 4,200 mm wheelbase vehicles. The infrastructure rollout: - Current status: 5 major trunk lines are operational, with over 5 million km of stable operation. - Near-term goal: 900 battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026. - Long-term goal: 2,000 stations by 2027, covering the national highway network, with an ultimate target of 10,000 stations. At the launch, CATL signed agreements with 14 major partners, including SF Express, ZTO Express, and YTO Express, with an initial order volume of 13,000 units. artigo.texto: The Converter as the Control Point for AI Data Center Power With AI workloads driving unprecedented growth in data center power demand, projected by some analysts to reach as much as 70% annually through 2027, the industry's first AI power debate centered on capacity: where will the next hundreds of megawatts come from? AI factories introduce concentrated, fast-changing loads that can create steep ramps in demand and power consumption. At the same time, utilities and grid operators are scrutinizing how very large loads behave during disturbances, not simply whether enough generation exists to serve them. This creates a new design requirement. The data center must remain highly available while presenting the grid, on-site generators, and internal distribution system with a manageable load profile. The solution is a coordinated power architecture in which converters, storage, controls, protection, medium-voltage equipment, and digital systems work as one. Within that architecture, PCS has become increasingly important. As AI facilities grow in scale and complexity, they are evolving from simple power electronics components into key control layers that help coordinate how energy moves through the site. No longer just a conversion device In a conventional description, a converter does what it says: converts direct current from a battery or renewable source into alternating current for the facility or grid and reverses that flow when charging storage. In an AI data center, a modern PCS functions as a high-speed, controllable electrical interface, regulating active and reactive power, limiting current, shaping ramp rates, supporting voltage and frequency stability, and responding through grid-connected and islanded operating modes. That distinction matters because AI power problems happen on several timescales. Fast converter controls can respond to sharp electrical changes, battery energy storage systems (BESS) can buffer sustained ramps or temporary capacity limits, and Power Plant Controllers (PPC) can coordinate the PCS with generators, utility signals, switchgear, facility-management systems, and state-of-charge constraints. Together, these layers help make volatile loads more predictable. Four roles for power conversion in the AI power architecture 1. Load smoothing and generator protection AI workload changes can push on-site generation and utility connections beyond comfortable ramp-rate or power-quality envelopes. A bidirectional PCS paired with BESS can absorb excess power or inject power rapidly, reducing sudden changes seen by the rest of the system. 2. Voltage support and disturbance ride-through Converters can supply or absorb reactive power and follow a defined ride-through behavior. The objective is to prevent a short grid event from becoming a large, coordinated loss of data center load or a site-wide transfer event. 3. Grid-connected, islanded, and restoration modes With appropriate system design, controls, and protection, storage and PCS can support transitions between grid-connected and islanded operation, stabilize an islanded bus, and contribute to restoration or black-start pathways. These are system functions and must be validated at the site level. 4. Capacity shaping and flexible interconnection When a grid connection is constrained, storage can reduce peaks, manage import limits, and help the facility operate within an agreed envelope. This does not eliminate the need for interconnection studies or network upgrades, but it can create additional design options. A practical architecture For large campuses, PCS should be evaluated as part of a repeatable medium-voltage building block rather than as an isolated converter. A typical architecture can combine battery blocks, medium-voltage transformers, switchgear, power plant controllers, protection, telemetry, and supervisory controls. Modular, factory-tested blocks reduce the number of site interfaces and create a platform that can be repeated as the campus expands, reducing integration risks and streamlining deployment. The control hierarchy is equally important. Converter-level controls provide the fastest response. Plant controls coordinate multiple converters and enforce site-level active-power, reactive-power, voltage, frequency, and import or export objectives. Higher-level energy management can optimize state of charge, demand response, market participation, and on-site generation use. Clear ownership of each control loop is essential to avoid conflicting commands or unstable interactions. Model first, then prove the response AI data centers require a validation process that connects product capability to site behavior. The work should begin with the actual load profile, grid strength, fault levels, generator characteristics, protection philosophy, and intended operating modes. Steady-state studies alone are not enough for the most dynamic use cases. Electromagnetic-transient models, hardware-in-the-loop testing and staged commissioning can be used to test ramp events, voltage disturbances, current limits, control handoffs, and islanding sequences before the full site is energized. This model-to-test-to-commission approach also changes procurement. Instead of buying an inverter only against a nameplate rating, owners can define measurable performance at the point of interconnection: response time, ramp-rate control, reactive capability, recovery after a fault, operating envelopes, and telemetry. The commercial specification becomes a performance specification. From passive load to grid-interacting energy system The power challenge facing AI data centers is not solved by adding capacity alone. It is solved by coordinating capacity with controllability. As campuses combine utility connections, on-site generation, batteries, renewables, and increasingly power-dense compute, the converter becomes one of the few assets capable of acting fast enough to keep those elements working together. artigo.texto: For most of the past decade, the question about energy storage was whether it would ever be affordable. That question has been answered. Stationary battery packs fell to around $70/kWh in 2025, down 45% year on year, according to BloombergNEF. Africa installed an estimated 17GW of solar in 2026, a 45% rise on the year before, according to energy think tank Ember. And in South Africa, more than 90% of residential solar systems now sold include a battery system. Yet of the $13.84 billion in energy transition investment Africa attracted in 2025, as tracked by Electron Intelligence, just $666 million, under 5%, went to storage and flexibility. That gap, between how cheap storage has become and how slowly it is being financed, protected and integrated into grid planning, runs through the latest ESI Africa Industry Insights Volume into Energy & Storage. According to Nicolette Pombo-van Zyl, Editor-in-Chief of ESI Africa, storage has stopped being the add-on that gets bolted onto a renewable project at the end. “It is now the part that decides whether a project gets financed, whether a grid stays stable after sunset and whether the clean energy already being generated is actually used. The industry’s challenge is that capital, regulation and data have not yet caught up with that reality,” says Pombo-van Zyl. The cheapest battery is not always the cheapest system Comparative modelling in South Africa puts lithium iron phosphate (LFP) ahead of every rival chemistry for stationary storage, with a levelised cost of storage of about R4.05 to R4.25 per kilowatt-hour (kWh). Paired with solar PV, it delivers electricity at around R1.92/kWh, undercutting gas turbine peaking at R7.07/kWh. But the ESI Africa volume shows that battery chemistry is only the start of the pricing. Deployment scale, physical degradation in hot climates and the cost of capital decide whether that advantage survives a real project. Import tariffs and freight can inflate storage capital costs by 15 to 35% across emerging markets. A companion feature maps the chemistry landscape beyond LFP, from sodium-ion, which removes lithium from the equation and is now entering utility tenders in India, to LMFP, lithium manganese-rich and solid-state batteries. Its takeaway for a minerals-rich continent points to a threat that the cheapest battery chemistry may use less of the minerals Africa wants to move up the value chain. artigo.texto: Publicidade O avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) está aumentando a demanda por infraestrutura física e abrindo novas possibilidades de investimento no mercado imobiliário. Nesse cenário, mostra a XP, os data centers, instalações responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e circulação de dados, podem ganhar relevância e representar uma nova frente de atuação para os fundos imobiliários (FIIs). Embora a IA seja frequentemente associada ao desenvolvimento de software, sua operação depende de uma estrutura física robusta, que envolve semicondutores, energia elétrica, redes de transmissão, sistemas de resfriamento e data centers. Essa cadeia pode ser dividida em três grandes frentes: semicondutores, infraestrutura e otimização de negócios. Enquanto a primeira reúne os componentes necessários ao processamento de dados, a segunda abrange os recursos físicos que sustentam a tecnologia. A terceira envolve a aplicação da IA para transformar operações e modelos de negócios em diferentes setores da economia. Leia Mais: Dupla taxa, falta de transparência e emissões: as maiores dores dos cotistas de FIIs Como os FIIs podem investir em data centers Segundo a XP, os fundos imobiliários podem acessar esse mercado por meio da aquisição de data centers operacionais, do financiamento de projetos em desenvolvimento e do investimento em infraestruturas associadas, como subestações elétricas. Nesse modelo, a exposição do cotista é imobiliária. O fundo adquire o imóvel e recebe os aluguéis pagos pelo operador responsável pelo data center ou pela infraestrutura locada. Continua depois da publicidade As receitas provenientes de serviços de computação em nuvem, processamento de dados ou outras atividades tecnológicas permanecem com o operador, e não são diretamente apropriadas pelo fundo. A distinção é importante porque o crescimento da demanda por inteligência artificial não garante, por si só, retornos elevados para os FIIs expostos ao segmento. O desempenho do investimento continua condicionado ao preço de aquisição do imóvel, às condições contratuais, à qualidade técnica da estrutura, à disponibilidade de energia e à capacidade financeira do inquilino. A perspectiva de expansão dos serviços digitais pode favorecer a ocupação dos empreendimentos e a capacidade de pagamento dos locatários. Continua depois da publicidade Ainda assim, diz a XP, o resultado depende de como cada ativo foi adquirido, da estrutura de financiamento e das necessidades futuras de investimento para manter a infraestrutura competitiva. Além disso, a exposição a data centers pode oferecer aos fundos acesso a um segmento com características distintas de outros mercados imobiliários. A demanda por infraestrutura digital está ligada à expansão dos serviços tecnológicos, embora isso não elimine riscos de crédito, vacância ou obsolescência dos imóveis. Leia Mais: Data centers ganham espaço nos FIIs após Redata? Fundos miram renda de longo prazo Continua depois da publicidade Sale and leaseback, built to suit e desenvolvimento de novos projetos Os FIIs podem acessar o segmento por diferentes estruturas de investimento, com níveis variados de risco e previsibilidade de receitas. Entre as possibilidades estão a compra de ativos estabilizados, as operações de sale and leaseback (SLB), os contratos built to suit (BTS), o financiamento de obras por meio de certificados de recebíveis imobiliários (CRIs) e o desenvolvimento de novos empreendimentos. Na aquisição de um ativo estabilizado, o fundo compra um data center já construído, conectado à rede elétrica e ocupado por um inquilino. Essa estrutura reduz a exposição aos riscos de construção, energização e comercialização, embora permaneçam os riscos relacionados ao contrato, ao locatário e à necessidade de modernização do imóvel. No sale and leaseback, o operador vende o imóvel ao fundo e permanece no local como locatário, mediante um contrato de aluguel. A operação permite que a empresa libere capital anteriormente imobilizado no empreendimento para direcioná-lo à expansão das atividades, à compra de equipamentos ou ao desenvolvimento de novos projetos. Continua depois da publicidade Já no modelo built to suit, o imóvel é construído ou adaptado de acordo com as necessidades específicas do futuro ocupante. Em contrapartida, o locatário firma um contrato de longo prazo, que deve remunerar adequadamente o capital investido pelo proprietário. Contratos longos ajudam a reduzir riscos, mas não eliminam problemas Para a XP, o elevado grau de especialização dos data centers reforça a importância de contratos de locação de longo prazo, especialmente quando o imóvel foi desenvolvido para atender às necessidades de um único operador. Essas estruturas podem ampliar a previsibilidade das receitas e reduzir a exposição a renegociações frequentes. Contratos atípicos podem prever prazos extensos, reajustes periódicos pela inflação e penalidades por rescisão antecipada. Quando essas penalidades são elevadas e vinculadas ao saldo de aluguéis até o vencimento, podem desestimular a saída antecipada do inquilino e favorecer o alinhamento entre o prazo contratual e o horizonte de retorno do investimento. A infraestrutura de data centers apresenta uma particularidade para o mercado imobiliário: as características técnicas que tornam um empreendimento adequado a determinado operador também podem limitar suas alternativas de uso. A disponibilidade de energia, os sistemas de resfriamento e as especificações construtivas influenciam tanto a operação quanto o potencial de reutilização do imóvel. artigo.texto: Residents in four Madison County townships will vote in November on an advisory measure asking whether data center development should be allowed in their communities. Ballot initiatives in Chouteau, Granite City, Nameoki and Venice townships will ask voters whether they support future data center development and construction. In Illinois, townships are subdivisions of local government that operate alongside cities and villages. The township’s elected board may oversee local infrastructure, such as water and sewer services. Each of the townships included in the advisory measure overlaps with Granite City. Because the measures are nonbinding, they would not ban data centers even if residents vote against the projects. Heather Groetecke, a lifelong Granite City resident, led the effort to collect signatures for the initiatives. She first became aware of potential data center development near her home in Nameoki Township when officials held community meetings this spring about proposals for two sites in Granite City and another in nearby Pontoon Beach. Groetecke said she began organizing when officials failed to answer her questions about environmental hazards and other concerns. “I (have) never really even been involved in politics in my whole life, and I don’t really like it either,” she said. “But I don’t want a data center.” Groetecke initially wanted to put a data center moratorium on the ballot. But she said political advisers close to the signature campaign recommended a nonbinding measure because it would be easier to pass. “They can still do what they want to do,” Groetecke said. “But if we win by the majority, I think that speaks volumes.” Data center proposals in the Granite City area Data center developers are eyeing the Granite City area for projects. City officials heard public comment about a proposal involving two sites along the Route 3 industrial corridor. Officials in nearby Pontoon Beach heard a similar proposal in May, the Alton Telegraph reported. The Belleville News-Democrat reported that the Granite City project received mixed reviews in a February forum. Trade union leaders voiced support for the potential economic development and property tax revenue, while other residents said they were concerned about utility rate hikes, environmental impacts and transparency. Developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure said in a public city council meeting in Granite City last November that it doesn’t sign nondisclosure agreements with local governments. The developer also promised not to use groundwater wells to cool its data centers and suggested “enforceable” zoning requirements to limit noise and light pollution. Cloverleaf officials have said the company works with big names in tech, including Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google and OpenAI. Some residents accused Granite City Mayor Mike Parkinson and other city officials of misleading the public when they said that they knew little about data center development in public meetings. Residents said in May that officials negotiated a possible land sale for a data center project with special governing district America’s Central Port before alerting the public. Parkinson told the Belleville News-Democrat that the documents cited by residents were taken out of context and that the city never collaborated with the port authority to bring in data center projects. Months before the community meetings, Parkinson, Madison County Executive Chris Slusser and Granite City’s economic development director, Cathy Hamilton, were among several St. Louis-area leaders who toured a Google data center on a trip financed by Greater St. Louis Inc. Officials were asked to sign nondisclosure agreements before touring the facility. Granite City officials say the data center project was tabled along with similar proposals in Edwardsville and Troy, Illinois. Granite City officials did not respond to requests for comment.

artigo.texto: Three roundtable groups weighed options Saturday during the first of three public discussions about data centers being held at different Statesboro venues. But if participants decided anything, it was only for themselves. Open to everyone, the next will be held 9 a.m. Thursday, Oct. 22, in the Statesboro Home Builders Association building, 1223 Merchants Way. Then the third and final installment in this "deliberative discussion series" is scheduled for 6 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Jones-Love Cultural Center at Luetta Moore Park, 121 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive. The Institute for Vibrant and Engaged Communities, or IVEC, from Georgia Southern University is hosting the series, "Weighing the Options: Data Centers in Our Community." The first session started at 5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, in the Honey Bowen Building at Memorial Park on Fair Road. About 20 people or one or two more, including the organizers, showed up. "At the Institute for Vibrant and Engaged Communities, we believe community engagement is an important part of community governance, and so we have created these forums because this is an issue that is important to the community," said IVEC Director Candice Bodkin, Ph.D. "We're personally concerned that there's not good conversation or dialogue that's happening around concerns about data centers." As she noted, citizens speaking at formal hearings such as those of the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners or Statesboro City Council often are assigned three or five minutes each, with no back-and-forth dialogue. "So this is an opportunity for folks to sit down with their neighbors, talk about their concerns, talk through some options," Bodkin said. "It's not meant to be that we come to a conclusion, or decision, that this is what we recommend." However, the IVEC team is taking notes of participants' concerns and ideas, with the intent of delivering a report to city and county leaders. Jayce Sudweeks, Ph.D., who co-founded the institute with Bodkin four years ago but is now in a new position with the university — director of Interdisciplinary Clusters of University Excellence — helped lead the event. Four graduate students completed the IVEC team that hosted the Saturday conversation. Participants gathered around three tables for mostly separate, small-group discussions. Basic rule: 'Be kind' Sudweeks emphasized a couple of points at the outset. "Number one, the university has not taken a stance for or against data centers," he said. "So we're trying to be as neutral and unbiased as we can, and so for this report we want (to hear from) everybody. It will reflect people who are for it, people who are against it, all of those types of things." Then he asked participants "to be kind and polite to your neighbors" in the room and across the table. Guidebook's facts IVEC has produced a 26-page deliberation guide entitled "Data Centers in Our Backyard: How should our community decide?" and gave copies to participants at the check-in table. According to the introductory pages, 73 data centers were operating in Georgia as of December 2025. Around that time, Georgia Power was approved by the state Public Service Commission for approximately 10 gigawatts of new capacity, mostly for data centers. The average residential monthly power bill had increased by $43 since 2022. Meanwhile, Georgia since 2018 has exempted data center equipment from state and local sales tax, with state estimates placing the revenue loss at about $2.5 billion in fiscal year 2026. The IVEC guide lists its sources for these facts, and some local ones. One of those local facts is that about three out of four voters in Bulloch County's primary election in May, in ballot questions asked by both parties, opposed data centers locating here. Another factoid highlighted in the guide is that the maximum size allowed for a data center under Statesboro's 2026 data center ordinance is 50 acres. "The term 'data center' covers a wide range of facilities," notes one section of the guide. It mentions that a small data center, "about the size of a large room" is already located in Statesboro, reportedly helping speed internet service for businesses. But Project Camellia, the data center OpenAI announced in July it plans to build in neighboring Effingham County, would occupy a nearly 1,400-acre campus and use 3.2 gigawatts of electricity. So, 4AM Development LLC's proposed two-story, total 230,000-square-foot building on an almost 27-acre site on Burkhalter Road in the edge of Statesboro is between those extremes. With a set of high-voltage transmission lines already running parallel to one side of the triangular tract, the developers applied to Georgia Power for an up to 99-megawatt supply. Timelines of events The guidebook carries a detailed timeline for that project and the city's actions. On Aug. 18, the tract was rezoned from R-4 high-density residential to "O" for office by a 3-2 vote of City Council, including the mayor's tiebreaker. But the project also needs a special use permit, also requiring council approval, and that process is now being held up by a legal challenge filed by a group of citizens in Superior Court. A parallel timeline traces the Bulloch County Board of Commissioners' actions in regard to data center policy. This includes a moratorium on data centers in the county unincorporated area, in effect most of the year and now extended until Dec. 31. An outright ban was defeated by commissioners' 4-3 vote, including the chairman's tiebreaker, Sept. 1, and the commissioners are now naming an up to 21-citizen "working group" to study the issue. The county working group will be a completely different thing from the IVEC sessions.
