artigo.texto: Data center stocks remain under pressure after Korea IPO plunges 30% - Shares of cloud provider Elice Group dropped 30% during their market debut in South Korea. - Elice Group has been compared to CoreWeave, the U.S. neocloud at the center of last week's sell-off. - Concerns about overcapacity in computing power amid lackluster AI revenues are persisting. Data center stocks are being squeezed on Tuesday following a lackluster initial public offering overnight from a South Korean cloud company that has been compared to U.S. neocloud CoreWeave. Shares of Elice dropped 30% during their market debut overnight, as investors grow increasingly wary of artificial intelligence-dedicated computing power providers amid concerns about overcapacity. The bearish sentiment spilled into U.S. tech equities before some names clambered back into the green. CoreWeave shares are up 1.6% after dropping 4% just after market open Tuesday; Nebius shed about 1% while Iren was down about 4% in late morning trading. HSBC said in a Monday note that the troubles for the heavily levered CoreWeave are not going away. "Debt market woes and moderating LLM revenues are exacerbating structural concerns for neoclouds," HSBC analyst Abhishek Shukla wrote. Shukla has a reduce rating on CoreWeave with a price target of $39, implying 36.5% downside. Elice's IPO was small, having raised just $150 million, according to Reuters. Its market cap also equates to roughly $1.3 billion. The company provides a range of AI-related services, including cloud computing equipment, training libraries and application interfaces for businesses. Despite its size, investors are likely looking at it as a a signal of investor sentiment toward the AI build-out. Trouble for neoclouds, which some investors see as the weakest link in the emerging AI value chain, started earlier this month with less-than-stellar revenues reported by the private AI algorithm companies and pressure from higher interest rates. Frontier model Anthropic showed a deceleration in quarterly revenues, with sales dropping from 140% growth in the second quarter to 45% in the third. OpenAI also disappointed, reporting revenue that was $20 billion shy of what analysts expected, analyst Stephanie Roth at Wolfe said in a Sunday note. Profitability concerns for AI algorithm companies were the focus of a report last week from advisory firm Gartner predicting that 80% of neoclouds could cease independent operations by 2030. "Our research indicates that enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures" between 2027 and 2030, Will Sommer, senior director analyst at Gartner, said. Gartner stood by its analysis in a Monday interview with CNBC. "At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions," Gartner chief forecaster John Lovelock told CNBC. "Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly."

artigo.texto: Nove projetos de armazenamento de energia em baterias estão em licenciamento no RN Nove empreendimentos estão em licenciamento ambiental no Idema. ONS diz que tecnologia pode reduzir em até 50% os cortes de geração de energia. Excedente poderá ser usado quando houver maior demanda. O Rio Grande do Norte possui nove empreendimentos em processo de licenciamento para instalação de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias (BESS) junto ao Instituto de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e Meio Ambiente (Idema). A tecnologia é fundamental para que o setor de energias renováveis consiga enfrentar um importante gargalo: os cortes de geração de energia (curtailment), que afetam fortemente o estado. O tema ganha destaque até esta sexta-feira (22), com a 7ª edição do Energy Storage Brasil, que acontece na sede da Federação das Indústrias do Rio Grande do Norte (Fiern), em Natal. De acordo com o Idema, a maioria dos processos de licenciamento para armazenamento em baterias está atrelada a projetos de energias renováveis já existentes. O prazo para emissão das licenças depende das especificidades de cada projeto. “Depois que o processo é iniciado, o empreendedor recebe um Termo de Referência com um prazo de 120 dias para apresentar documentos e estudos ambientais necessários”, informou o órgão. Dentro desse prazo, o tempo de entrega do material depende de cada empreendedor. “Após isso, o Idema vai analisar se os estudos atendem aos requisitos exigidos ou se serão solicitadas providências”, completou. Além disso, segundo o Idema, serão cobrados resultados que, porventura, deixarem de ser apresentados no material entregue. Emília Casanova, secretária-adjunta da Secretaria de Desenvolvimento Econômico do estado (Sedec/RN), detalhou que as baterias são estruturas cujos tamanhos podem variar: algumas se assemelham a caixas eletrônicos, enquanto outras são bem maiores, com dimensões próximas às de um contêiner. “Tudo vai depender da potência dessa bateria, que varia de acordo com cada projeto. Elas servem para armazenar a geração de energia excedente que pode ser despachada em um momento de pico e até mesmo vendida como energia extra para o mercado livre”, conta. O mercado livre é a modalidade em que os consumidores habilitados podem escolher de quem comprar energia elétrica e negociar condições contratuais diretamente com fornecedores, geradores ou comercializadores, diferentemente do mercado regulado pelo Governo Federal, por meio de leilões. Segundo Emília Casanova, a busca por licenciamento no RN é resultado da Resolução 01/2026 do Conselho Estadual do Meio Ambiente (Conema), aprovada no final de abril e que estabeleceu critérios para o licenciamento ambiental de sistemas BESS. “Além do RN, apenas Rio Grande do Sul, Bahia, Ceará e Piauí possuem legislação que permite aos empreendedores solicitarem licença para esse tipo de armazenamento”, diz a secretária-adjunta. De acordo com o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), as baterias podem diminuir os cortes de energia em cerca de 40% a 50%. Os equipamentos podem ser instalados próximos às usinas de produção de energia ou perto das unidades consumidoras, conforme cada projeto. O diretor executivo da Associação Brasileira de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE), Fábio Monteiro, ressaltou que, como o armazenamento de energia em baterias vai equilibrar o sistema elétrico do país, é importante que haja uma discussão permanente sobre o tema. “O armazenamento viabiliza a retomada do crescimento das renováveis, equilibra nosso sistema elétrico, reduz custos para o consumidor e otimiza o uso da rede de transmissões”, disse ele. Idema emitiu três licenças para data centers no RN O Energy Storage Brasil segue nesta sexta-feira (23), durante a DC Conference – International Data Center Conference, com as discussões voltadas para data centers, que são centros para armazenar, processar, gerenciar e distribuir grandes volumes de dados e aplicações de forma segura e ininterrupta. “Trazer a discussão das tecnologias de armazenamento de energia para um evento como esse é algo muito produtivo”, destaca a adjunta da Sedec/RN. Segundo o Idema já foram emitidas três licenças para data centers de pequeno porte (de até 40 megawatts) no Rio Grande do Norte. Desses, um está em operação, em Currais Novos, ligado a um projeto de energia renovável. Ainda segundo o órgão ambiental, não houve pedido de licenciamento para grandes equipamentos, com capacidade acima de 40 megawatts. O evento é realizado pelo Grupo FRG Mídias e Eventos, referência na organização de fóruns, congressos e encontros estratégicos nos setores de energia e infraestrutura, juntamente com o Grupo FRG Mídias e Eventos. A escolha de Natal para o encontro tem a ver com a posição geográfica estratégica que o Rio Grande do Norte ocupa no Nordeste, próximo de estados importantes como Pernambuco, Paraíba, Ceará, e principalmente, com a importância local da produção de energias renováveis. “O poder de produção do RN abre oportunidades para diversos segmentos, dentre eles o BESS, que é o principal ator quando se fala em armazenamento de energia no setor elétrico”, diz Tiago Fraga, CEO do Grupo FRG Mídias e Eventos. “É o quarto evento que nós realizamos em Natal por conta da questão logística, mas também pelo fato de o estado estar inserido no mapa da transição energética brasileira”, afirma. O encontro conta com apoio da Fiern e do Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia (Crea-RN) e reúne especialistas, empresários, investidores, pesquisadores e representantes do setor público para discutir o avanço das tecnologias de armazenamento. artigo.texto: EU countries and the European Parliament have reached a provisional agreement to amend rules governing how carbon permits are cancelled in a stabilising tool within the EU Emissions Trading System. The deal, agreed on 20 October, changes the “invalidation” rules for allowances held in the Market Stability Reserve (MSR), a mechanism designed to absorb surplus permits from the market or release them to prevent sharp price swings, the Council of the EU said in a release on Wednesday. More than 3 billion allowances have been invalidated and removed from the market since the mechanism began in 2023. Under the provisional agreement, the invalidation mechanism will remain in place, but the threshold for when allowances in the MSR can be cancelled will rise to 700 million, from the current 400 million. The updated threshold would take effect immediately after the changes are formally adopted. Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment, stated that the outcome provides “immediate flexibility” for European industry while seeking to ensure price stability and protect the “integrity” of the EU carbon market. What happens next The provisional agreement still needs to be confirmed by both the Council and the European Parliament before it can be formally adopted, the Council said. The co-legislators also agreed that a gradual decrease of the invalidation threshold should be considered as part of a wider review of the emissions trading system now underway. The Council said the European Commission had proposed an indefinite halt to invalidation, but the two institutions instead agreed to keep the mechanism while adjusting its threshold. The Commission proposal was presented as a short-term measure linked to efforts to address high and volatile energy prices referenced by EU leaders in March.

artigo.texto: Transmission grid fees in Belgium could increase by 92% for battery energy storage systems (BESS) and by 150% for offshore wind projects by 2035, according to a study by Aurora Energy Research examining the evolution of network tariffs and their economic implications for energy projects. The report, titled Transmission Grid Fees in Belgium: Outlook & Impact Assessment, was commissioned by Adaptogen Capital, BayWa r.e., Norther, Otary and Storm, amid regulatory changes affecting the costs of accessing and using Belgium's electricity transmission infrastructure. The analysis follows the publication of the tariff methodology for the 2028–2031 regulatory period by Belgium's energy regulator, CREG, ahead of transmission system operator Elia's expected publication of updated grid tariffs in 2027. Grid fees for batteries could reach €112/kW by 2035 One of the main changes examined in the study is the planned phase-out of the 10-year grid fee exemption for battery energy storage systems, a mechanism that has helped limit network costs for eligible storage projects. According to Aurora's central scenario, the combined effect of removing this exemption and rising overall network costs could result in a 92% increase in the total grid fee burden for a typical battery, reaching €112/kW by 2035. The study estimates that, without mitigation measures, average annual margins for battery storage projects could fall to €47/kW. Björn Hofman, Senior Associate, Advisory, at Aurora Energy Research, warned that rising grid fees could place additional pressure on the economics of battery storage projects and other grid-connected assets in Belgium. He noted that discount mechanisms are available, including incentives to avoid charging during peak hours and the potential introduction of voluntary flexible connection agreements. However, these measures are unlikely to fully offset the projected increase in network costs. Offshore wind faces a potential 150% increase The second major regulatory change identified by Aurora is the introduction of a capacity-based feed-in fee for electricity injected into the grid, which would add another cost component for renewable electricity generators. According to the analysis, Belgium's projected feed-in fees could reach €11/kW, exceeding the levels expected in neighbouring markets. Germany is preparing similar charges in the range of €4–7/kW, while Belgium has yet to announce comparable protections for existing projects or developments that have already committed investment. Aurora notes that Germany has announced a 20-year exemption for assets that reach a final investment decision (FID) before the new fee enters into force. The Netherlands is also expected to introduce an equivalent exemption to maintain comparable investment conditions across European markets. Belgium, by contrast, has not yet made a similar commitment to protect projects from changes to the tariff framework after investment decisions have been taken. This regulatory difference could affect the competitiveness of Belgian renewable energy projects relative to those in neighbouring countries. Industry representatives call for protection of existing investments Mathias Verkest, CEO of Otary, warned that allocating grid costs between electricity consumers and producers could have implications for final electricity prices and the financing conditions of new projects. He explained that developers may seek to pass additional costs on to consumers. Where this is not possible, higher network charges could instead translate into increased risk premiums, potentially raising the cost of financing new developments. Verkest therefore supported the introduction of grandfathering provisions to protect existing and upcoming projects, following the approach adopted in Germany and the Netherlands. Similarly, Christophe De Schryver, Executive Manager at Norther, stressed that investment in renewable electricity generation depends on a stable and predictable regulatory framework over long periods. He warned that introducing substantial new injection charges without protecting previously committed investments could undermine investor confidence and weaken Belgium's attractiveness for future energy investment. Aurora identifies measures to limit rising network costs The study outlines several measures that could help contain the increase in transmission charges, including alternative financing arrangements for part of the required grid investment, stimulating electricity demand to expand the tariff billing base, and stricter cost controls. For the remaining costs, Aurora recommends implementing grandfathering exemptions for existing and upcoming projects, maintaining discounts for avoiding consumption during peak periods, and extending flexible connection discounts to both voluntary and imposed agreements. The consultancy warns that, without regulatory action, higher network charges could delay investment decisions in storage and renewable electricity generation while increasing costs for electricity consumers. The report therefore identifies the evolution of transmission tariffs as a factor that could influence the profitability of BESS and offshore wind projects, financing conditions and the deployment of renewable energy capacity in Belgium over the coming decade.

artigo.texto: When Cardinal News sketched which western Virginia sites might qualify under Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s new data center study, the list read like a map of the region’s industrial past: former coal lands in Buchanan, Dickenson and Wise counties, the old Radford Foundry, Roanoke County’s Smith Gap landfill, and the former Kim-Stan landfill outside Clifton Forge. The governor’s executive order asks the state to identify brownfields and previously developed sites that could spread data center investment beyond Northern Virginia while limiting the strain on energy, water and land. The study is due in March. That is a reasonable goal. But a state list does not decide where data centers go. Localities and developers do. The more important question for communities west of the Blue Ridge is what happens after their name appears on a map like this. If the pattern from the rest of Virginia holds, the answer is that developers arrive first. Land gets optioned quietly. Engineers confirm power and water. A finished application lands before the planning commission, and residents are invited to react to a deal they had no hand in shaping. Virginians have noticed. In 2023, 69% of voters told the Washington Post–Schar School poll they would be comfortable with a data center in their community. This spring, 35% said so. I read that less as a verdict on the technology than as a verdict on the process. Rural communities do not have to accept that process. Whoever owns the land can turn it around. A county, an industrial development authority, a foundation or a nonprofit that controls a developable site does not need to wait for a developer’s proposal. It can write its terms first and then invite developers to compete to meet them. If it leases the land rather than selling it, those terms stop being promises made at a public hearing. They become lease covenants, enforceable for decades. What should those terms say? Developers should pay for the grid infrastructure their projects require, so local ratepayers don’t. Projects should strengthen the local grid, for example by backing up hospitals, schools and emergency services during outages. Training should start before construction, through the community college, with hiring commitments that can be measured. Water use, wastewater, noise and on-site generation should come with firm limits and public reporting. And the process should be open, with no nondisclosure agreements. None of this is anti-developer. Serious developers know that projects with community commitments built in get approved, and get approved faster, than projects that have to defend themselves after the fact. Two cautions matter as much as the terms. First, confirm the power before anything else. Utility timelines for large new loads now stretch for years. A site that cannot be served will draw no bids, however good its terms. Brownfields also carry their own engineering and liability questions, especially landfills and cleanup sites. Second, keep the process competitive. The quickest way for a landowner to lose its leverage is to give one familiar developer a first look and never run an open solicitation. With one bidder, there is no comparison and no fallback. The state’s study gives western Virginia a few months before the calls start. Communities that use that time to decide what they need, and write it down, will not be choosing between a bad deal and no deal. They will be choosing among developers who have already agreed to their terms. Terry Lee is the founder of Garvey Labs, a Washington, D.C., firm that helps communities set the terms for data center deals so the investment builds local wealth, strengthens the local grid and protects drinking water.

artigo.texto: Expansão da inteligência artificial impulsiona investimentos em sistemas privados de energia, mas escassez de equipamentos e atrasos nas entregas desafiam o setor INFRAESTRUTURA DIGITAL Data centers apostam em energia própria e 38% devem ter geração independente até 2030 Por Redação A expansão da inteligência artificial e dos serviços de computação em nuvem está levando empresas de tecnologia a investir na produção própria de energia para abastecer seus data centers. A estratégia busca reduzir a dependência das redes elétricas convencionais e acelerar a implantação de novos empreendimentos. Segundo projeções da Bloom Energy, 38% dessas instalações deverão utilizar sistemas próprios de geração como principal fonte de energia até 2030. A mudança ocorre diante do aumento dos prazos para conexão à rede pública. Desde 2017, o intervalo entre a solicitação de acesso à energia e o início das operações comerciais cresceu aproximadamente 60%. Atualmente, a espera média supera 2.100 dias, o equivalente a quase seis anos, considerando projetos que pretendiam iniciar o fornecimento em 2025. Para contornar as limitações da infraestrutura elétrica, empresas responsáveis pela construção e operação de data centers estão adotando sistemas conhecidos como behind-the-meter (BTM), que permitem gerar energia diretamente no local de consumo, reduzindo a necessidade de conexão à rede pública. A Bloom Energy estima que aproximadamente 27% dos data centers poderão ser abastecidos integralmente por energia produzida em suas próprias instalações até 2030. A alternativa oferece maior autonomia energética e pode reduzir os riscos de atrasos na entrada em operação dos empreendimentos. Entretanto, o crescimento da demanda por esses sistemas criou novos desafios para o setor. Entrega de equipamentos pode levar seis anos A procura por turbinas a gás, transformadores e outros componentes necessários à geração de energia tem superado a capacidade de fornecimento dos fabricantes. De acordo com a consultoria Wood Mackenzie, os prazos de entrega de turbinas a gás já chegam a seis anos, ultrapassando as estimativas anteriores, que variavam entre dois e quatro anos. Com isso, a disponibilidade de equipamentos passou a influenciar diretamente o planejamento dos projetos. Além dos custos de produção, as empresas precisam considerar o tempo necessário para adquirir, instalar e colocar os sistemas em funcionamento. Outro desafio está na integração de diferentes tecnologias de geração em uma única estrutura, especialmente quando os equipamentos chegam em etapas distintas. Operação exige novas soluções tecnológicas A complexidade dos sistemas privados também está ampliando a demanda por empresas especializadas em operação e manutenção de infraestrutura energética. Entre as companhias que atuam nesse mercado estão a Kyuden Energy Partners, a Consolidated Asset Management Services (CAMS) e a Ethos Energy. A CAMS possui experiência em projetos que somam 70 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade de geração e concentra parte de sua atuação em soluções que utilizam gás natural e fontes renováveis. Já a Ethos Energy, com experiência na gestão de mais de 100 instalações e 40 GW de capacidade de geração, desenvolveu um centro de monitoramento remoto que utiliza inteligência artificial para acompanhar simultaneamente diferentes unidades produtoras de energia. A tecnologia permite identificar falhas, acompanhar o desempenho dos equipamentos e apoiar a manutenção das operações. Expansão dos data centers depende de planejamento A busca por independência energética representa uma mudança no modelo de implantação dos data centers. Em vez de aguardar exclusivamente a disponibilidade da rede pública, as empresas passam a incorporar a geração própria desde as etapas iniciais dos projetos. Essa transformação, entretanto, exige investimentos adicionais, equipes técnicas especializadas e maior coordenação entre fornecedores de equipamentos e operadores. Com o crescimento da demanda por processamento de dados e inteligência artificial, a capacidade de garantir fornecimento contínuo de energia deverá permanecer entre os principais fatores de competitividade do setor. Embora a geração própria ajude a superar as restrições de conexão elétrica, a disponibilidade de equipamentos e a complexidade operacional continuam condicionando o ritmo de expansão da infraestrutura digital.

artigo.texto: Crédito de carbono de alta qualidade sobe 75%, diz MSCI AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 7 de outubro de 2026 Os créditos de carbono classificados como de alta qualidade pela MSCI tiveram valorização de 75% em 12 meses e chegaram a US$ 14 por tonelada, enquanto os de menor qualidade são negociados abaixo de US$ 2. Os dados foram apresentados por Guy Turner, diretor-geral da área de mercados de carbono da companhia, durante a Climate Week NYC, realizada em Nova York em setembro de 2026, e indicam avanços em três frentes: ampliação dos sistemas regulados, diferenciação de preços por qualidade e mobilização de capital. Segundo a apresentação, foram registrados US$ 5,5 bilhões em investimentos em contratos futuros e projetos, distribuídos em mais de 200 transações, com um quarto dos recursos destinado a iniciativas de remoção de carbono. Os contratos de compra antecipada de créditos de restauração da natureza monitorados pela MSCI, com entrega prevista para 2035, alcançaram US$ 45 por tonelada, alta de 10% em relação ao primeiro semestre de 2025. Sistemas regulados ganham escala No período analisado, a União Europeia passou a incluir integralmente as emissões do transporte marítimo no comércio de emissões do bloco, o EU ETS. A Indonésia avançou em normas para dar clareza e amplitude às negociações de carbono, e o México se comprometeu a lançar um sistema nacional em 2027, com cobertura de 40% de suas emissões. Na Ásia, a Índia colocou em operação um portal para administrar registros e transações do período de conformidade de 2025 a 2027, que abrange 740 entidades e mais de 700 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). O Vietnã contabilizou as primeiras operações de seu sistema, referentes ao ciclo 2025 a 2026, e o Japão tornou obrigatório o GX-ETS, que cobre 40% das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa e reúne entre 300 e 400 empresas. Para Laura Albuquerque, co-CEO da Future Climate e membra do Comitê da Ambição Net Zero da Rede Brasileira do Pacto Global da ONU, durante cerca de duas décadas a defesa desses mercados se apoiou em estudos sobre seu potencial para reduzir o custo de cumprimento das metas climáticas. “A lógica econômica permanece: direcionar recursos para oportunidades de redução e remoção de emissões que permitam alcançar essas metas com maior eficiência. A diferença é que, hoje, a experiência acumulada oferece dados concretos para orientar decisões de política pública e investimento”, afirma. Demanda corporativa e integridade No segmento de créditos, os números da MSCI mostram atividade consistente. Cerca de 4 mil empresas definiram metas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), o equivalente a 4 bilhões de toneladas de emissões, e um quarto delas assumiu compromissos de emissões líquidas zero (net zero). Em 12 meses, mil novos projetos foram registrados, outros 1.150 entraram na carteira em preparação e empresas aposentaram créditos provenientes de 2.850 projetos. A projeção da MSCI indica que as aposentadorias globais de 2026 devem ficar próximas do volume de 2025, em torno de 200 milhões de toneladas. Na leitura da co-CEO, o sinal mais relevante está na distância de valor entre projetos, que torna a avaliação de qualidade parte central da decisão de alocação de recursos para compradores e investidores. A executiva observa ainda que a convergência em torno dos Core Carbon Principles, definidos pelo Conselho de Integridade para o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM, na sigla em inglês), cria uma linguagem comum sobre integridade, mas exige que preços e financiamento reconheçam os custos de desenvolvimento. Capital antes da receita Para as desenvolvedoras, o cenário evidencia a necessidade de recursos antes da geração de receita. “Projetos exigem recursos para estruturação, implantação, monitoramento, ratings para a verificação ao longo de anos. A valorização dos créditos de qualidade precisa se traduzir em condições de financiamento que permitam produzir essa oferta”, diz Laura. Segundo ela, os contratos futuros podem contribuir nesse processo ao conectar a demanda dos compradores ao ciclo de investimento dos projetos. O Brasil tem diferentes vias de demanda em construção: o mercado voluntário; o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042, de 11 de dezembro de 2024, com os Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs); os mecanismos do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris; o programa de combustível sustentável de aviação (SAF, na sigla em inglês) previsto na Lei nº 14.993; e o Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional (Corsia). Na avaliação da executiva, são caminhos com regras e escalas distintas, que precisam ser considerados na estruturação dos investimentos. Laura pondera que preços, investimentos e aposentadorias não substituem a mensuração dos resultados climáticos, embora demonstrem uma base observável de atividade econômica, demanda e alocação de capital. “Para o país, a oportunidade está em usar essa experiência para desenvolver um mercado capaz de financiar projetos de qualidade, e o próximo avanço dependerá de transformar os sinais de demanda em capital disponível para quem entrega reduções e remoções verificáveis”, conclui a executiva. artigo.texto: Trending For over an hour, Rachel Wallace, Democrat candidate for the 9th congressional seat, answered questions from the audience at a town hall held this week at Lycoming College. Although she admitted that not everyone might not agree with what she was saying, her goal was not to over promise and then not be able to deliver results on those promises. Right out of the gate, Wallace got down in the weeds about what are some of the key issues in the election where she is facing off against Republican Congressman Dan Mueser, who has been in office since 2019. Although she was critical of Mueser for not being a resident of the district he represents-which is legal in Pennsylvania-in her opening remarks, Wallace particularly criticized the fact that her opponent voted for last year's budget bill, which Republicans have called the "One Big Beautiful Bill", and how it has affected residents of the district. "Dan Meuser voted for a budget bill that is an absolute disaster for our part of Pennsylvania. It cut food assistance for more than 8,000 people in our communities here. It cut health insurance for nearly 30,000 people in our district, essentially defunding our hospitals and our nursing homes. It tried to take away local control on AI data centers, and it gave an $80 billion tax break to AI data center developers," Wallace said. Seeing his vote spurred her on to run for his seat in the House of Representatives. She continued by outlining the three things she is focusing on in her campaign. The first, she said, is lowering costs. "Will you raise your hand if you feel good about how much everything costs right now? You're not that blessed. Me neither. At the grocery store, at the gas pump, on our utility bills, at the pharmacy, looking at our healthcare premiums and deductibles going up next year, everything costs too much, and Dan Meuser has voted in support of all of those policies, from the budget bill...through the war in Iran, which has been a disaster...to tariffs that are hurting us and our farmers and our local employers. So there is a lot to be done in Congress next year to lower costs, and that needs to be at the top of priority list because people here are struggling," Wallace said. "The one thing I want to underline here is home heating oil, since last year, has gone up 75 percent, and one-third of our district heats their homes with home heating oil. So this is not an election about national politics. This is not an election about how we're feeling about the country. This is an election about how we're feeling about heating our own homes, and it is going to be a crisis. It is going to be scary here in Pennsylvania, and we're going to need to take fast, short-term action because it is not going to be pretty if we don't. So we need to lower costs," she said. Citing stories that Mueser has doubled his wealth since he got in office, Wallace stated that her second priority if elected would be to root out corruption and fraud in Washington. "Don't you think it's long past time that we ban congressional stock trading," she asked the audience who responded by applauding loudly. Her third and final priority, she said, would be to bring people to solve local problems. She highlighted the problems volunteer fire companies are having with the cost of equipment increasing. "They fight fires, they recruit other firefighters, and they sell chicken barbecues to try to raise a million dollars to buy a fire truck. And many of our fire departments do all of those things for free. It is a tremendous service. It says something about Pennsylvania and who we are that our communities do that for free," she said. She noted that the amount of funding available to help with buying firefighting equipment has not changed in the past 20 years. "Years ago, it cost 200, 300,000 to buy a truck. Now it's over a million dollars, but the pot hasn't changed. And so this is what I'm talking about when I talk about how do we solve our local problems. We've got to get that fund up so that it meets the needs of our firefighters," she said. Wallace also cited AI data centers as another huge issue, with seven of the 12 counties in the district she's seeking to represent "somewhere in the pipeline of at least one, if not more AI data centers." "I went to Muncy, (I) sat down in Lebanon, in Frackville. I've been with our farmers in central Pennsylvania who are fighting losing their land for power lines for a data center in Allenwood...We just need to take a pause here. We need a short pause so that our local and county ordinances can catch up, so that Harrisburg can catch up. They got some tax breaks they've got to repeal last time I checked, and so that Washington can catch up, and we can get everybody's house in order before we move forward here, because things are happening incredibly fast, and our communities are being asked to pay the cost. When big tech and AI developers, they're the ones who should pay the cost, not us," she said. She also feels the country needs to slow down in developing AI. "I think we are moving very fast to a world that we do not understand where we are going. We do not understand what AI is capable of. We do not understand what it means for our economy. We don't understand what these data centers are going to do to our water, to our quality of life. We need to slow down and make sure that we have answers," she said. Questions from the audience ran the gamut from the rising costs of healthcare to a critique of the administration to whether she would agree to abolishing ICE. artigo.texto: - Nigeria has commissioned a 1MW solar mini grid with 2.4MWh of battery energy storage in Tallasse, Balanga Local Government Area, Gombe State, serving 6,028 active connections. - The facility powers productive-use businesses, including electric groundnut oil processing, rice milling, flour grinding and electric tricycles, linking clean electricity directly to rural enterprise and job creation. - The project forms part of the US$750 million Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, which targets 1,350 mini grids and electricity access for 17.5 million Nigerians. The Federal Government, through the Rural Electrification Agency, has commissioned the Tallasse solar mini grid in partnership with the Gombe State Government and a private sector developer. The facility combines 1MW of solar generation with a 2.4MWh battery energy storage system to improve supply reliability for households, commercial users and productive enterprises. The project serves 6,028 connections, comprising 5,929 residential customers, 84 commercial connections and 15 dedicated productive-use nodes. Its design moves beyond household electrification by supporting agricultural processing, local logistics and small business growth in a community that had lacked a national grid connection for more than 17 years. The Tallasse installation includes electric groundnut oil processing equipment, modular rice milling machinery, flour grinding facilities and electric tricycles. These assets are intended to help farmers process produce locally, reduce operating costs, create income opportunities and strengthen rural value chains. Officials said the battery storage component is central to the economic case for the project, because reliable power is required to sustain milling, processing and transport activities. The approach reflects a wider policy shift from measuring installed capacity alone to measuring the commercial and social value created by electricity access. The Tallasse project is being delivered under the Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, a US$750 million World Bank funded initiative managed by the Rural Electrification Agency. DARES aims to provide new or improved electricity access to more than 17.5 million Nigerians through private sector led distributed renewable energy solutions. The programme targets the deployment of 1,350 mini grids, including 250 interconnected systems, alongside more than one million standalone solar home systems. It is also expected to support more than 237,000 micro, small and medium enterprises and replace more than 280,000 polluting petrol and diesel generator sets. DARES is designed to mobilise more than US$1 billion in private capital, with additional parallel financing from development partners, including US$100 million from the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet and US$200 million from the Japan International Cooperation Agency. The commissioning of the Tallasse facility coincided with the flag-off of four interconnected mini grid projects in Dukku, Bajoga, Kumo and Kaltungo, with a combined planned capacity of 16MW. The wider Gombe programme is expected to deepen off-grid electricity penetration and support commercial activity across the state. The Rural Electrification Agency said the initiative forms part of a broader national strategy to expand mini grids, embedded generation, solar home systems and dedicated clean power solutions for universities, markets and agricultural clusters. The agency is also working to unlock domestic and international financing to accelerate private sector participation in Nigeria’s distributed energy market. artigo.texto: AI’s GPU Refresh Cycle Is Becoming a Stranded-Capital Problem Key Highlights - Proactive lifecycle planning involves designing infrastructure that accommodates hardware upgrades and facilitates easy disassembly and component reuse. - Effective disposition strategies include asset traceability, secure sanitization, and compliance with international trade and data security regulations. - Market timing and operational readiness are critical; continuous assessment of asset value ensures hardware is sold or repurposed at optimal moments. - Design-for-recycling principles should be integrated into hardware architecture, emphasizing modularity and material recoverability to extend equipment lifespan. - Organizational alignment at the executive level is essential to prevent stranded capital and maximize the return on AI hardware investments. The AI infrastructure buildout is measured in gigawatts and successive generations of accelerators. But as operators bring new compute capacity online, a less visible question is gaining financial urgency: What happens to GPU systems when their first production assignment ends? For hardware that remains functional but no longer meets the performance or efficiency requirements of a leading-edge AI cluster, retirement need not mean obsolescence. Equipment may be redeployed, resold, harvested for components or processed to recover materials. The outcome depends on decisions made long before a system leaves its rack. That was the central argument advanced by Linda Li, chief strategy officer of Re-Teck and its parent company, Li Tong Group, in the latest onsite installment of the DCF Show podcast, hosted by Data Center Frontier Contributing Editor Doug Black at the DCF Trends Summit 2026 in Northern Virginia. For Li, the acceleration of GPU refresh cycles is making lifecycle management a question of capital preservation, facilities design and executive governance—not merely IT asset disposition. Plan for the Exit Before the Equipment Arrives Li draws on more than two decades of her company’s work in reverse supply chains for consumer electronics and telecommunications equipment. Both sectors have managed rapid generational shifts without assuming that every displaced device had exhausted its useful life. “We are dealing with a totally different organism,” she said, describing the combination of rapid accelerator iterations, rising rack power density and increasingly sophisticated thermal requirements. The response, in her view, has two levels. The first is physical infrastructure: facilities designed to accommodate successive generations of servers without extensive reconstruction. Scalable power distribution, adaptable raceways, modular rack systems and high-capacity air and liquid cooling can create room for hardware transitions that may arrive sooner than originally expected. The second is the network of partners and contracts around the assets. Rather than recruiting an IT asset disposition (ITAD) provider when a refresh is imminent, operators should assess processing capacity, certification, geographic reach and compliance during procurement. Li pointed to the telecom industry's transition from 3G to 4G and 5G. In that environment, she explained, the contract to supply next-generation network equipment can also obligate the supplier to take back and decommission what is being replaced. She believes AI infrastructure purchasing should incorporate similar provisions. “What kind of planning needs to be done and when it needs to be done” are inseparable questions, Li said. “You can't answer one without the other.” Finding the Next Life of a GPU The appropriate disposition pathway cannot be fixed years in advance. Li described a framework established when equipment enters service, with final decisions made at retirement as its condition, market demand and operational needs become clearer. The first consideration is remaining capability. An accelerator that is no longer economical for frontier model training may still be useful for inference, enterprise AI or academic research. For large operators with multiple sites or classes of workload, moving the equipment internally can preserve more value than selling it—and can reduce the need for additional purchases. That requires identifying suitable destinations and approving transfers in advance. Otherwise, reusable systems can become stranded in the organizational handoff. The second consideration is component-level economics. Demand for an entire previous-generation server may soften even while individual GPUs, memory modules or specialized networking cards retain strong market value. Recovering those parts requires an engineering understanding of the equipment’s design and assembly, not just the ability to transport and recycle a chassis. Harvested components can also become internal service spares. That approach may help operators maintain installed systems while reducing lead times and dependence on replacement-parts supply chains. For Li, the relevant unit of value is not always a complete server; sometimes it is the individual component that can serve another application. Her third consideration—one she said should actually rank first—is risk. Data security, access controls, regulatory obligations and environmental rules can override an otherwise attractive commercial opportunity. The fourth is material recovery: recovering and refining valuable inputs when equipment or components cannot be economically reused. Together, the four factors place resale and recycling within a broader decision process. The aim is not simply to maximize the price of decommissioned hardware, but to retain value without compromising security or compliance. The Resale Market Won’t Wait Hardware value is also time-sensitive. During the conversation, Black relayed an anecdote heard earlier at the summit about H100 accelerators attracting unusually high prices in secondary markets. Li cautioned against assuming such conditions would last.

artigo.texto: 0 a 100% na bateria do iPhone 18 Pro: a pegadinha O iPhone 18 Pro finalmente carrega rápido de verdade, mas a Apple jogou bem baixo um detalhe na hora da compra. A fonte de energia do smartphone dobrável iPhone Duo, primeiro aparelho da Apple na categoria teve novos detalhes técnicos revelados. Um deles envolve a bateria do aparelho e uma comparação inevitável com dispositivos rivais. Ao todo, o conjunto de baterias do iPhone Duo tem 4.883 mAh. Outro dobrável com o mesmo formato de tela, chamado de passaporte, é o Galaxy Z Fold 8 da Samsung — que fica apenas logo atrás, com 4.800 mAh de bateria. Nesse quesito, a Maçã vence também o iPhone 18 Pro (4.288 mAh) e o dobrável Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold (4.806 mAh), mas fica atrás do Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (5.000 mAh) e do Motorola Razr Fold (6.000 mAh). Porém, a quantidade de mAh não significa necessariamente que a bateria de um dispositivo dura mais em qualquer condição. Esse valor envolve a capacidade da fonte de bateria em armazenamento de energia (medido em mAh, ou miliamperes-hora), mas o consumo depende de outros componentes do hardware e otimização do sistema operacional. Mais detalhes do iPhone Duo A Apple não costuma detalhar todas as especificações dos seus celulares, incluindo a quantidade de RAM e o tamanho da bateria. Porém, desta vez ele acabou fazendo isso de forma acidental. Os valores foram revelados em documentos submetidos pela empresa no EPREL, um órgão regulador da União Europeia que obriga a divulgação desses dados para eletrônicos de consumo. Como aponta o Tom’s Guide ao analisar o documento, outros detalhes revelados pela submissão incluem detalhes como: - a certificação IP68 de resistência contra água e poeira; - a duração garantida de 1.000 ciclos de recarga para a bateria (ou seja, para manter ao menos 80% da capacidade total); - a durabilidade de 140 quedas em um teste de resistência até quebrar (quando fechado) e somente 35 quedas (no modo aberto); - uma resistência contra riscos na tela parecida com a do iPhone 18 Pro Max no display externo; - um grau de reparabilidade (facilidade e possibilidade de conserto) de 2.65, número inferior aos rivais da Samsung e ao iPhone 18 Pro Max. Por que o iPhone Duo só está com previsão de entrega de fevereiro de 2027 no Brasil? Entenda nesta matéria! /Com informações de Tom’s Guide.

artigo.texto: EPRI Research: Li-Ion Battery Storage Failure Risk Down 98% Since 2018 As battery storage deployment accelerates across the U.S., a new report by the Electric Power Research Institute highlights that safety performance is significantly improving in newer systems than in vintage lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) designs. According to EPRI’s “Risk Factors and Failure Statistics of Lithium-Ion BESS” white paper within its Battery Energy Storage System Failure Incident Database, annual BESS failures per deployed GWh declined 98% between 2018 and 2025. The analysis found that BESS safety risk overall is comparable to oil-filled transformers, which reportedly maintain a 0.1% annual failure rate as a long-established power grid technology. EPRI attributes these lessons learned from early failures that caused destructive fires to having been incorporated into the latest designs and best practices. The institute explained that some of its incident research dates back to 2011. Still, drawing on more than a decade of cumulative incident data, the institute urges operators to conduct safety reviews and retrofits for early-vintage systems to mitigate fire risks. These concerns are underscored by previous incidents at high-profile facilities. The fires at Moss Landing, Morris and Surprise Vistra Corp.’s battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, serves as an early example of these early-vintage risks. A major lithium-ion battery fire in January 2025 damaged over half of the site’s 300-MW system. The Moss Landing facility suffered a second fire in September 2026 due to leftover, damaged batteries that reignited during ongoing cleanup efforts. In 2021, another major fire incident took place at the Superior Battery Inc. warehouse in Morris, Illinois, which contained roughly 180,000 to 200,000 pounds of lithium batteries. While the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency conducted extensive air quality testing around the incident, investigators determined that the blaze was triggered by a water reaction from a severe roof leak. Rainwater reportedly dripped onto the batteries, sparking an initial reaction. Before those disasters, a thermal runaway event in Surprise, Arizona, severely injured eight firefighters in 2019. An internal cell defect within the utility-sized lithium batteries used on-site for storage and distribution of solar energy at the APS McMicken substation triggered the failure, according to an Arizona Public Service analysis. As these batteries fail, technical safety flaws, such as escaping gases, create intense and potentially devastating fire dangers to utility-scale BESS made up of lithium-ion chemistry. BESS advancements driving down failure rates All of these incidents occurred during the period of EPRI’s research, which highlights that while the rate of battery storage failures is becoming less frequent relative to massive-scale deployment, they can still be severe. EPRI noted that the 2019 BESS failure incident in Arizona was part of a wider BESS safety research effort, initiated to inform energy storage industry stakeholders and the public. Residential energy storage system failures were not tracked in this research. Managing these risks, however, remains a critical focus as BESS installations accelerate nationwide, driven by utilities dealing with grid constraints and the growing power demands of AI data centers. Currently in the U.S., installed capacity has passed 52 GW and has grown at an average rate of 70% per year over the last three years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Lakshmi Srinivasan, principal team lead of Energy Storage at EPRI, told EnergyTech that key aspects evaluated that weren’t known before include statistical analysis on the impact of indoor versus outdoor BESS architecture. Srinivasan noted that the data “demonstrates that modularization and spacing can limit the amount of a system that is damaged in an incident, also limiting first response needs and environmental and public health impacts.” These latest BESS advances have reportedly yielded major benefits in California, where utility-scale storage capacity grew to 13 GW by the end of 2024. According to EPRI, this has directly reduced the state's reliance on “Flex Alerts,” which are voluntary calls for residents to reduce consumption during peak demand periods, typically on hot summer days. “The number of Flex Alerts has dropped to zero (in 2023 and 2024) from 11 in 2022, due to the use of energy storage to reduce supply constraints,” said Srinivasan. Safely scaling future storage deployments EPRI aims to help power operators apply these standards to accelerate large-scale renewable integration. This guidance is particularly critical as operators navigate thermal risks for lithium-ion BESS across various project types, including behind-the-meter installations. To mitigate these risks, Srinivasan explained that conducting safety analyses of older systems can “help ensure the latest safety designs and practices are being implemented for all systems operating today.” While safety improvements are a continuous process, Srinivasan emphasized that dedicated research and development efforts are actively reducing risks in both existing and new BESS deployments. These advancements ultimately aim to deliver tangible benefits to the grid and local communities. “These benefits include supporting grid flexibility, reliability and resilience through applications such as renewable integration and peak demand reduction,” she added. Although lithium-ion remains a dominant mix for energy storage due to its high energy density and quick discharge, the industry is actively seeking alternatives to mitigate foreign supply chain risks and thermal safety concerns. artigo.texto: A China está a intensificar os investimentos no armazenamento de energia e na conservação dos ecossistemas, procurando conciliar a transição energética com a proteção ambiental. As duas prioridades foram destacadas em iniciativas divulgadas pela agência estatal Xinhua. Durante a Conferência Mundial de Armazenamento de Energia, realizada em Ningde, foram apresentados dados que atribuem à China 56% da expansão mundial da capacidade de armazenamento em baterias em 2025. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a produção chinesa de baterias destinadas a este setor ultrapassou 420 GWh, mais 110% do que no período homólogo. Paralelamente, o Presidente Xi Jinping defendeu o reforço da conservação ecológica durante uma visita à Mongólia Interior. Na reserva natural do lago Huangqihai, destacou a importância da recuperação das zonas húmidas, da proteção da biodiversidade e do cumprimento da legislação ambiental. A estratégia inclui ainda novas inspeções ambientais e a aplicação do Código Ecológico e Ambiental, em vigor desde agosto. Apesar dos progressos anunciados, persistem desafios relacionados com os custos das tecnologias, a fiscalização e a sustentabilidade dos resultados a longo prazo.

artigo.texto: Beyond Colossus: 5C Advances $575M Memphis AI Factory Expansion Key Highlights - 5C Data Centers is converting a former Fred's distribution complex in Memphis into a high-density AI computing facility, with a $575 million fourth-phase construction permit application. - 5C plans to expand available power at MEM01 from approximately 20 MW to 84 MW, using fuel cell technology to supply additional capacity rather than relying on a corresponding increase in utility power. - The project's announced AI architecture includes NVIDIA GB200 and newer GB300 NVL72 systems, liquid cooling, high-bandwidth networking and integrated storage to support large-scale AI training and inference. - Memphis is considering a data center moratorium and new zoning standards while conducting a 90-day policy review addressing electricity demand, water resources, air quality and community impacts. - 5C has secured more than $1.4 billion in financing for its North American AI infrastructure platform, supporting development in Memphis and other markets as questions remain about execution, infrastructure capacity and local economic benefits. Memphis has emerged as a major center of AI infrastructure development, driven largely by the extraordinary scale of xAI's Colossus supercomputing operations. But the city's growing AI computing market extends beyond Elon Musk's flagship project. At the former headquarters and distribution complex of discount retailer Fred's, 5C Data Centers is developing another substantial AI computing facility, combining industrial adaptive reuse with a phased expansion strategy and plans for behind-the-meter power generation. On October 6, 2026, a $575 million commercial alteration permit application was filed for the fourth phase of 5C's MEM01 data center at 4300 Getwell Road. The application covers approximately 504,000 square feet of the property's 1.1 million-square-foot building, representing the largest construction phase yet proposed at the site. MEM01 is already operating. According to September reporting from The Daily Memphian, 5C had established operations in approximately 200,000 square feet of the former Fred's property, leaving substantial additional space available for conversion. The latest permit application marks a significant escalation in the scope of the development. The expansion also introduces a major new element to 5C's power strategy. On October 11, 5C Group Chief Revenue Officer Brad Nimri told The Daily Memphian that the company plans to increase available power at MEM01 from approximately 20 MW to 84 MW over the next six months, using fuel cell technology to supply the additional capacity rather than relying on a corresponding increase in electricity from Memphis Light, Gas and Water (MLGW). Like Colossus, which began with the conversion of a former Electrolux manufacturing facility, 5C's development reflects the growing role of industrial adaptive reuse in AI infrastructure. The projects differ considerably in scale and their approaches to on-site power generation, but both illustrate the challenge of transforming existing industrial properties into high-density computing environments with substantial electrical requirements. As Memphis considers tighter oversight of data center development, 5C's expansion underscores a broader industry challenge: bringing new AI computing capacity online while navigating power constraints, regulatory scrutiny and mounting concerns over the environmental and community impacts of large-scale infrastructure. From Retail Distribution to AI Infrastructure The MEM01 development occupies a property with a long history in Memphis commerce. Fred's operated hundreds of discount retail and pharmacy locations across the southeastern United States before declaring bankruptcy in 2019. Its former headquarters and distribution complex on Getwell Road, near Memphis International Airport, served as a major logistics hub for the regional retail chain. In June 2026, 5C acquired the 1.1 million-square-foot complex and its approximately 58-acre property from Olymbec USA for $25 million, according to Shelby County property records, securing ownership of a site where data center construction and infrastructure modifications were already underway. The project's development history reflects a rapid escalation in scale. Plans submitted in late 2024 and reported in 2025 contemplated converting the property into a data center supporting an initial 15-MW IT load. An April 2025 construction permit, valued at $25 million, described a more limited initial deployment of 2.5 MW, together with infrastructure designed to support future expansion. Additional permits issued in early 2026 included $100 million for interior construction and $8 million for accessory structures. The October phase-four application, valued at $575 million, represents a substantial increase in the scope of planned construction, although permit valuations do not necessarily represent completed capital expenditures or the project's total investment. The expansion also illustrates the distinction between announced capacity and operational computing infrastructure. According to 5C's published data center portfolio, the Memphis facility's 20-MW capacity for 2026 is fully committed, with additional capacity listed for subsequent years. That commercial designation does not establish how much electrical capacity has been energized or how much IT load is currently supporting customer workloads. The company has not publicly disclosed a complete inventory of installed and operating AI accelerators at the site, leaving the precise scale of its commissioned computing infrastructure unclear. artigo.texto: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta quarta-feira (21) que novas e grandes instalações de data centers no país deverão produzir a própria eletricidade. A proposta inclui que o excedente energético seja doado ou vendido para a comunidade local ou para a rede elétrica. Segundo Trump, a medida visa evitar aumentos nos preços da energia elétrica, podendo, inclusive, gerar uma queda "substancial" nos custos para os consumidores. A declaração foi feita na rede social Truth Social. O líder norte-americano defende que outros aspectos desses empreendimentos sigam a mesma lógica de contrapartidas para as regiões que os abrigam, garantindo benefícios mútuos. Proposta de "dividendo" para comunidades Trump explicou que está monitorando de perto os data centers e chegou à conclusão de que as empresas devem "pagar a comunidade, e/ou os indivíduos da comunidade, um 'dividendo'". Ele observou que instalações impopulares tornaram-se bem aceitas após acordos financeiros. "Façam acordos e construam", escreveu o presidente dos EUA. Ele argumenta que a expansão dessa infraestrutura é "boa para os Estados Unidos", impulsionando o desenvolvimento com responsabilidade local.

artigo.texto: The European Commission has selected 77 projects to receive funding under the Innovation Fund call for proposals announced in December 2025. The total amount of funding is €3.4 billion, drawn from revenues generated by the European Union Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS). These projects come from various EU countries and span a range of sectors – from energy-intensive industries and ‘green’ energy to reducing the use of fossil fuels in aviation and shipping. This was reported by the European Commission. The spectrum of decarbonisation The winning projects span 23 countries in the European Economic Area. The list includes technologies of various types and scales. These include projects in the following sectors: - energy-intensive sectors — steel, cement and chemicals, as well as the production of advanced decarbonised fuels; - manufacturing – this refers to equipment in the clean technology sector. Specifically, this includes heat pumps and electric vehicle batteries, as well as critical raw materials; - renewable energy – the use of wind, solar and hydro power; - mobility – reducing the use of fossil fuels in aviation, road transport and maritime transport. The cumulative environmental impact of implementing all 77 projects is a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions of 290 million tonnes over the first ten years. This is equivalent to a reduction in CO₂ emissions of approximately one tonne every second for a decade. "These projects demonstrate that European innovators are turning climate ambitions into industrial leadership. By reinvesting revenue from the EU Emissions Trading System into clean technologies, the Innovation Fund is helping companies enter the market, reduce emissions and strengthen Europe’s competitiveness,” emphasised Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commissioner for Climate Action. The winners of the competition were selected across five categories: Large-scale general decarbonisation – 12 projects totalling €1.58 billion. The funding will be directed towards low-carbon fuels and emissions management in industry, particularly in the ferrous metallurgy and chemical sectors. General medium-scale decarbonisation – 17 projects totalling €458 million. This group includes projects relating to chemical products, oil refineries, the maritime sector, glass, ceramics and building materials, cement and lime, bioenergy, cast iron and steel, as well as hydrogen. General small-scale decarbonisation – 20 projects totalling €124 million. The projects presented here are from the critical raw materials processing sector, the pulp and paper industry, the construction sector, oil refining, the chemical and hydrogen industries, and so on. Clean technology manufacturing – 12 projects worth €895 million aimed at the production of solar panels, batteries for electric cars, heat pumps, electrolysers and rare-earth magnets. Pilot projects – 16 initiatives totalling €394 million. In addition, 84 projects, although they did not receive funding, did pass the evaluation process. This may therefore help them to secure funding for their implementation from other sources – whether private or public. It should be noted that Ukraine’s National Emissions Trading System has not yet been approved. There is currently one ministerial bill and three parliamentary bills, each of which proposes different options, including the use of funds generated by the NETS. A detailed comparison can be found in this article by EcoPolitic.

artigo.texto: Florence County Board approves data center moratorium, ends Flock camera use Board votes unanimously on both measures Tuesday night FLORENCE, Wis. (WLUC) — Florence County’s 20-year Comprehensive Plan came into question at Tuesday night’s county board meeting because of the potential of proposed data centers in the county. The current 20-year plan, required by Wisconsin State Statutes, establishes land use goals and policies for the unincorporated areas of the county. Moratorium resolution Florence County Board Chair Chad Hedmark says he is concerned about the long-term use of large buildings built for data centers. “Long term I’m concerned about a large building that isn’t used later on. If they were to build something and doesn’t need this one, who winds up with that, that problem and it would be a problem,” Hedmark said. Battery Energy Storage Systems, or BESS, refers to devices that charge or collect energy from the electric grid or generation facility. That energy is stored and then discharged at a later time. The Florence County Zoning Committee did not contemplate the potential impacts of data centers and BESS at the writing of the initial 20-year Comprehensive Plan, leading to the proposed moratorium resolution. In a previous zoning committee meeting, the decision was made to recommend a moratorium on land uses for the development of data centers. That resolution was put to a vote at the Florence County Board meeting. With the board’s unanimous “yes” vote, the resolution passed. The resolution will give the zoning committee up to 18 months, and potentially longer if needed, to revise the Florence County 20-year plan and allow more time to review and revise the county’s zoning regulations and land use policies regarding data center development. Flock camera discussion The board also discussed Flock cameras during the meeting. Florence County currently has two active Flock cameras. After discussion with those in attendance, the board voted on discontinuing the use of Flock cameras. With another unanimous “yes” vote, Florence County will turn the Flock cameras off, and bags will be put over them until they are removed. artigo.texto: BYD Energy Storage Expands Global After-Sales Network With Nine Operations and Maintenance Centers BYD Energy Storage operates nine operations and maintenance centers of 2,500 square meters each. The company plans two new sites in 2027 and reports contractual response times for its battery systems. BYD Energy Storage has built an after-sales service network in four tiers: station-level maintenance, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters, according to the company. The group operates nine operations and maintenance (O&M) centers worldwide, each covering 2,500 square meters. The announcement comes in a sector where several players are expanding their capacity, such as Saft, which inaugurated its first solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux, or Grenergy, which secured $457 million for 446 MW of solar and storage in Chile. A geographic footprint set to widen The after-sales network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland and the Middle East. BYD Energy Storage says new service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027. The sites perform several functions: spare parts storage and management, battery repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, battery recycling and training of locally hired engineers. According to the company, its regional centers comply with local regulatory requirements and enable rapid on-site response. The service team includes more than 200 field engineers and more than 100 research and development (R&D) specialists. BYD Energy Storage says it applies standardized service level agreements (SLAs): response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. Localized spare parts supply and repairs The company says the network forms a multi-point supply chain intended to ensure rapid delivery of spare parts worldwide. It adds that its O&M teams rely on localized production lines and integrate regional resources to carry out battery repairs locally. "Our global service footprint is tailored to our fast-growing BESS deployments. Trustworthy after-sales support underpins the long-term stable operation of energy storage assets," said Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. The company cites a vision of empowering the global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service. Shipment volumes reported by the company BYD Energy Storage says it topped global battery energy storage system (BESS) shipments in 2025, with more than 60 GWh. It reports having delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total. artigo.texto: Carlsquare advised diveo GmbH on the sale of three agri-PV and BESS co-location projects to an established German energy provider Carlsquare advised diveo GmbH (“diveo”) on the sale of three agri-PV and BESS co-location projects to an established German energy provider. The three projects are located in Southern Germany, are spread across different medium-voltage grid areas and have a grid connection capacity in the double-digit megawatt range. diveo, a spin-off of the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, is an independent developer of agri-PV and battery storage projects in Germany. The company focuses on commercially viable co-location concepts that combine long-term agricultural use with renewable power generation and flexible storage operation. Its goal is to create economically attractive solutions for landowners, farms and asset operators that last for decades. The buyer is an established German energy provider that is active in, among other areas, the development, construction and long-term operation of renewable energy assets. The projects combine agricultural use with solar power generation through single-axis tracker agri-PV systems and high-capacity battery storage. The co-location concepts enable flexible trading of the energy generated, as well as operation of the battery storage systems as hybrid or grid-charged storage that can draw power from the public grid and market it. In this way, the projects combine long-term, economically viable agricultural management with efficient use of grid connection capacity. As the share of renewable energies grows, so does the need for flexibility in the power system. Combining yield-optimized agri-PV systems with flexibly marketable battery storage opens up additional revenue potential and creates attractive investment opportunities. The transaction underlines the interest of established energy providers in integrated agri-PV and BESS projects. “The successful sale of the three projects shows that agri-PV combined with battery storage is an attractive business model for large energy providers as well. What matters is the interplay between farmers who want to unlock new economic prospects for their land, efficient project development and asset operators with a long-term focus. This creates projects from which agriculture and the energy sector benefit equally. We would also like to thank Carlsquare for their professional support throughout the transaction.” – Kai Klapdor, Managing Director, diveo GmbH Carlsquare acted as exclusive financial advisor to diveo.

artigo.texto: NORTH PORT — In some cases, two things cannot be true at once. In North Port, an outgoing city official, or five commissioners, are not telling the truth about a data center project. During an interview with The Daily Sun, a departing city staff member said all five commissioners knew about a proposed data center in North Port, previously under a non-disclosure agreement, months before public meetings about it. All five commissioners have said, and maintain, that they learned about the data center and NDA around the time residents did. Despite their denials, Ray stuck to her guns. ‘POLITICALLY INCONVENIENT’ North Port’s Development Services Director Alaina Ray is leaving the city, in November after joining in 2021, because she does not feel safe anymore. Ray said she’s received due to threats and harassment. Ray said she planned on retiring in North Port, but is instead moving out of state for her next gig. She would not say where she is going for safety reasons. Ray said she was being followed, harassed and threatened by some. The harassment started after the data center conversations began. When data centers were discussed in North Port hundreds attended the meetings. The vast majority spoke in opposition of one being built in town. Due to the threats, Ray is scared to leave her home on her own. During an interview, Ray said that every commissioner knew about a proposed data center by February. Data centers, and a moratorium on their building in North Port, was first discussed in public on July 21. She also said commissioners knew about the NDA beforehand as well. “Sorry if that’s politically inconvenient for anyone,” Ray said. BARBARA LANGDON Vice Mayor Barbara Langdon said she will miss Ray’s work behind the scenes. Ray, she said, has been effective at working with developers, getting them to do things they are not required to do for builds. “I hope this is not the first in a series of defections,” Langdon said. “I can honestly say that before Alaina’s departure, we have the strongest staff we have ever had.” Langdon condemned the treatment of Ray. “It’s unacceptable. It’s hateful,” Langdon said. “This has got to stop. It’s not who we are. It’s frightening, actually. Langdon said it is not the first time someone has felt the wrath of some residents. She cited one person who provided more “balanced” comments on data centers, at previous meetings, being attacked online. Regarding what Ray said, Langdon said she is sure whatever Ray said, she believes to be true. She does not think Ray would lie. Langdon said she knew about the data center “maybe a week, or week and a half before that (first) meeting.” “We were caught flat-footed just like tons of municipalities across the United States,” she said. “We find out about stuff, a lot of times, when the community does.” DAVID DUVAL “The whole situation is upsetting,” Commissioner David Duval said about Ray’s alleged harassment issues. He said it’s not just about the city nor Ray. “Whether I agree with the city manager, or Alaina Ray, or staff, I will speak and then I will vote. But you don’t ever hear me harassing someone. I feel bad for Alaina in that way,” Duval said. He said a number of public comments, at the meetings about data centers, said “we know where you live and we will never forget.” Duval noted how threatening that sounds. As for Ray’s accusations, however, Duval said: “I cannot speak for the other commissioners but for myself that’s just not true.” “I’m not saying she’s a liar, but I’m not sure what she’s referring to,” Duval said. Duval expressed frustration with the way the data center issue transpired. The project was under an NDA and no commissioners signed it, he said. “I felt that I, as a commissioner, was purposely held out of the loop,” Duval said. DEMETRIUS PETROW Commissioner Demetrius Petrow was frustrated with Ray’s comments. He feels as though commissioners must be involved with projects as big as the proposed data center. Steps have been taken by commissioners to scrap NDAs altogether, and to have projects of certain types come before them before approval. A new Unified Land Development Code passed in 2024 allowed projects to bypass the commission and get administrative approval as long as no rules were being broken. Even if some developments that come through cannot legally be denied, per state laws that some argue neuter home rule, commissioners recently agreed certain projects should still come their way. “I’m very upset,” Petrow said. “We’re playing games that are almost childish. This is not right...I think it’s a blatant, false accusation. I was not aware of any of this stuff. Maybe some commissioners did know about this but I did not.” Petrow said if there are commissioners who do know, Ray should name them. He said he was not one of them. “If I was lying, the city could easily provide proof (with public records.) I don’t hide anything,” Petrow said. Petrow noted commissioners had heard about the NDA in December, but they were unsure of what kind of project it was. “If she’s referring to that, then you have to be really stupid to think that was the point that we were all informed,” Petrow said. Petrow said he learned about the data center June 25, in a one-on-one meeting with City Manager Jerome Fletcher, a little over a month before the first public meeting about it July 21. Regarding Ray’s alleged harassment, Petrow said he does not think Ray was ever actually attacked, away from social media. “All the secrecy ... that’s what bothers me. And then playing victim?
