artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich-EVE Energy held a product launch and production-line ceremony at its Chengdu base on October 20, according to a post on BYD's WeChat account, unveiling its Longquan No. 3 2.0 all-solid-state battery and a sodium-ion battery solution for electric two-wheelers. Three products—the Longquan No. 3 2.0, a polyoxygen all-solid-state battery and a solid-liquid battery—also rolled off the production line. Image source: EVE Energy All-solid-state battery targets brain-computer interfaces The Longquan No. 3 2.0 all-solid-state battery is designed for brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. The technology has the potential to help patients with paralysis or speech impairments regain certain functions through brain-controlled interactions. Non-invasive BCI systems face challenges including limited signal precision, restricted functionality and reliance on external headsets, making large-scale deployment difficult. Invasive systems can deliver stronger signals with less noise, enabling deeper human-machine interaction and the restoration of visual and auditory functions. However, batteries implanted in the skull must meet stringent requirements for biocompatibility, long-term sealing, leak prevention and minimal immune rejection, while achieving high volumetric energy density in a very small space. Conventional liquid-electrolyte lithium batteries have struggled to combine high safety with high energy density, posing a barrier to clinical adoption. The battery uses an anode-free design, a customized form factor and insulation-dam technology. In a titanium-cased button cell measuring 23 mm in diameter and 4 mm thick, it achieves a volumetric energy density of 1,045 Wh/L, 40% higher than conventional liquid-electrolyte batteries, according to EVE Energy. The company says the design can accommodate more signal-collection channels within the limited space available in the skull, extend operating time and enable smaller devices that may reduce surgical trauma. Replacing liquid electrolyte with a solid electrolyte also eliminates the risks of leakage and thermal runaway associated with liquid electrolytes, according to the company. At the event, EVE Energy signed strategic cooperation agreements with Jingyu Medical and Sichuan Provincial People's Hospital. The partners plan to connect research and development, industrialization and clinical application to support the broader clinical use of implantable BCIs. Sodium-ion batteries designed for electric two-wheelers EVE Energy has also introduced a sodium-ion battery solution specifically designed for electric two-wheelers, targeting industry challenges such as short battery life, performance degradation during storage, reduced range at low temperatures and safety limitations. The company highlights four claimed advantages of the solution: Long cycle life: Cell cycle life reaches up to 10,000 cycles. Based on one charge every two days, EVE Energy estimates a service life of more than 25 years, potentially matching the lifespan of the vehicle. Wide operating temperature range: The battery supports discharge temperatures from -40°C to 60°C. At -20°C, its discharge capacity retention rate exceeds 93%. Storage stability: After being stored for one year in a fully discharged state, the battery retains a capacity recovery rate of more than 98%, according to the company. Safety: EVE Energy says the battery does not catch fire or explode under puncture, cutting or crushing tests, and does not undergo thermal runaway under overcharging or short-circuit conditions. Multiple technology routes support product development The simultaneous production-line rollout of the three products marks a milestone in EVE Energy's development of advanced battery technologies. The company is advancing several technical approaches in parallel, including its Longquan solid-state series, polyoxygen all-solid-state batteries, in-situ solidification and solid-liquid batteries. These technologies are being developed for different applications, including vehicles, consumer electronics and implantable medical devices.

artigo.texto: A backcountry community group has filed a lawsuit to block the construction of a proposed solar and battery storage project that would industrialize about 588 acres in unincorporated East County, arguing the development’s environmental review was flawed. An association of residents of the community of Boulevard and the surrounding Mountain Empire region — dubbed the Back Country Community Alliance for Responsible Development — are objecting to the San Diego County Board of Supervisors’ recent approval of the Starlight Solar Project. First proposed by the developer in 2022, the project includes a solar farm capable of generating up to 100 megawatts and a 217-megawatt battery energy storage system, constructed in two phases. The community group last week filed a petition in San Diego Superior Court, arguing the project violated the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and failed to disclose or mitigate the risks of toxic plume exposure from a battery thermal runaway event. Residents of the unincorporated town have opposed the development, citing concerns that clean energy projects continue to put their safety at risk. The development was proposed by Empire II LLC. “The lawsuit is without merit and will be addressed going forward,” Jim Whalen, a spokesperson for the developers, said in a written statement. The project will include unprecidented setbacks from homes and public roads, no use of local groundwater and adequate onsite supply of fire protection water, Whalen added. A spokesperson for the Board of Supervisors, which unanimously approved the project in September, said “we are unable to comment on litigation.” At the time of the project’s approval, county officials cited concerns that state energy regulators could green-light the project if the county denied the proposal, noting state approval likely wouldn’t include benefits for the community. In the lawsuit, the group said they do not oppose renewable energy projects, noting the backcountry region already hosts multiple wind, transmission and solar projects, but said the proposal failed to properly analyze risks from a potential lithium-battery fire — which are notorious for burning for long periods of time. Further, their petition argues that county leaders’ approval of the renewable energy development relied on a late plume study that contradicted the environmental review process. However, Whalen noted the project’s approval included the county’s first-ever battery plume analysis. The county’s recommendations did not require the developer to relocate the project’s phase-two battery storage facility from its original northern location. Residents of Boulevard have pushed to move the battery storage farther south, primarily due to fire safety and evacuation concerns. In a letter to the Board of Supervisors, county staff said “the originally proposed location of the Phase II batteries has seven residences within 2,230 feet” while the alternative Phase II location “will have approximately two residences within 2,230 feet,” the group’s petition noted. Starlight Solar was approved with some concessions for Boulevard residents, including groundwater monitoring, community benefits and additional fire safeguards. But the backcountry group urged officials to pause the project’s approval, noting the county is actively drafting its own regulations for battery storage facilities. “The reality is, no one knows the details because this is new technology and this is an extreme risk,” said Thomas Wall, a 10-year resident of Boulevard. Boulevard has experienced three wildfires in the last 130 days, which opponents said only underscores the need for further evaluation before one of the state’s largest battery storage energy systems is added to the desert town’s landscape. County documents showed conflicting figures on battery-fire toxic-plume distances, with one claiming a maximum of 366 feet with no homes at risk, while another cited up to 2,230 feet with seven homes at risk, and that contradiction should have been resolved before the project was approved, the petitioners argued. Many backcountry groups have sued to halt construction of clean energy projects in unincorporated East County in recent years. In 2024, a pair of ranchers filed a petition to halt the construction of 60 wind turbines on the Campo Indian Reservation. In 2021, a group of Jacumba residents brought an unsuccessful lawsuit against the county and developer to block a proposed 600-acre solar and battery project. This story was updated with a comment from the developer.

artigo.texto: Taunton weighs one-year data center freeze as developer warns deal is at risk TAUNTON, Mass. (WJAR) — Taunton officials are considering a one-year freeze on new data centers, but an industrial property owner warns the delay could jeopardize a multimillion-dollar development deal. The Taunton Municipal Council is scheduled to discuss the proposed 365-day moratorium Tuesday. City leaders say the pause would allow them to review zoning rules and assess the infrastructure, electrical and environmental demands of data centers. VMD Companies, which owns an industrial building at 50 John Hancock Road in the Myles Standish Industrial Park, urged Mayor Shaunna O’Connell in a letter to exempt certain existing industrial buildings. The company said a yearlong delay would derail a pending agreement with a confidential technology tenant. According to VMD’s filings with the Taunton Municipal Lighting Plant, the proposed project would require 24 megawatts of electricity across two phases: 13 megawatts for the first phase and an additional 11 megawatts for the second. While acknowledging the city’s need for caution, VMD is asking officials to exempt existing industrial buildings that are already approved, comply with building codes and generate property tax revenue. Some area residents have raised concerns about data centers’ potential effects on the environment, water resources and surrounding communities. “We need to really look at the impact,” said Peggy Hall, of Easton. “And not just let these big businesses and billionaires just roll over these small-town communities where they think that they can just come in and suck up our land and not have any repercussions.” Jackson Isenstadt, of Norton, said a pause could give officials more time to evaluate potential concerns. “All these other data center lawsuits that are happening now, other things could come out in the next year about them,” Isenstadt said. “So maybe a one year pause would be a good thing.” The council is scheduled to meet at 7 p.m. Tuesday in the Chester R. Martin Municipal Council Chambers at City Hall.

artigo.texto: Two agreements for a stand-alone BESS of 250 MW/1 GWh in the Bukhara Region of Uzbekistan have been signed by AMEA Power, a UAE-based renewable energy company. The documents, a Battery Storage Services Agreement and an Investment Agreement, were signed in Tashkent on 16 October 2026. The signing took place at the first meeting of the Energy Sector Investors' Council, where Uzenergosotish JSC and the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade signed for Uzbekistan. With 1 GWh of storage behind 250 MW of output, the system will be able to run at full power for four hours. The project will therefore support Uzbekistan, which aims to raise its energy storage capacity to 4.5 GW by 2030. In Egypt, AMEA Power has already commissioned a 600 MWh BESS at its 1 GW Benban solar PV project. AMEA Power signs two agreements for 1 GWh BESS in Uzbekistan The Bukhara Region of Uzbekistan is to get a four-hour BESS of 250 MW from AMEA Power, which has signed a services agreement and an investment agreement for it. Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. NESTA EDIÇÃO. Fundo de Inovação da UE destinará € 3,4 bilhões a 77 projetos de tecnologias de emissão líquida zero. Entre os selecionados, 27 são ligados ao transporte e receberão € 1,3 bi para combustíveis sustentáveis e eletrificação, entre outras soluções. EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: Combustíveis sustentáveis de aviação (SAF, em inglês), navegação (e-metanol e amônia), biometano e tecnologias de eletrificação serão financiados na Europa com recursos do mercado regulado de carbono, em uma estratégia que busca reduzir emissões e garantir independência energética. A Comissão Europeia divulgou nesta segunda (19/10) a seleção de 77 projetos de tecnologias de emissão líquida zero para receber apoio financeiro de € 3,4 bilhões, dos quais, 27 estão relacionados à descarbonização do setor de transportes, com € 1,3 bilhão em subvenções. A chamada do Fundo de Inovação foi lançada em dezembro de 2025, e usará as receitas do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia (EU ETS) para financiar tecnologias consideradas inovadoras, com foco na indústria de baixo carbono. A próxima rodada está prevista para dezembro de 2026, com uma categoria de € 1 bilhão para a fabricação de tecnologias limpas que reduzam riscos com cadeias de suprimentos, em linha com o RESourceEU. Dos projetos relacionados ao setor de transportes, oito dos selecionados tratam exclusivamente da produção de combustíveis sustentáveis, enquanto cinco abastecerão também outros segmentos da economia. Cinco propostas para SAF receberão € 367 milhões em subvenções. Três delas estão na França. A lista divulgada pela Comissão Europeia menciona o projeto BELair, de produção de combustíveis sintéticos (e-SAF), na Normandia, com capacidade para produzir até 13 mil toneladas por ano. Outro é o H4 Marseille Fos, que pretende construir uma cadeia de valor integrada de e-SAF na zona portuária industrial de Marselha-Fos, para produzir até 75 mil toneladas/ano de combustível sintético a partir de hidrogênio de baixo carbono, e-metanol e CO2 capturado. Já o projeto L’Ardoise prevê a construção e operação de uma planta integrada de conversão de eletricidade em combustíveis líquidos (Power-to-Liquid, PtL), em Laudun-L’Ardoise. A previsão é que a unidade produzirá 70 mil toneladas anuais de querosene sintético e 40 mil toneladas anuais de e-metanol para o transporte marítimo. Os outros dois projetos estão na Espanha e nos Países Baixos. Localizado na fábrica de cimento da Holcim em Villaluenga de la Sagra, na província de Toledo, o ECO2FLY quer estabelecer uma cadeia de valor totalmente integrada de captura, utilização e armazenamento de carbono (CCUS, em inglês) industrial para a produção de e-SAF. Enquanto no Porto de Roterdã, o projeto EFR está apostando na rota metanol-para-combustível de aviação (MtJ, na sigla em inglês). A instalação terá capacidade para produzir aproximadamente 280 mil toneladas de e-SAF por ano, utilizando e-metanol importado. No horizonte da navegação Além do SAF, dez dos projetos selecionados para desenvolver tecnologias inovadoras para o transporte, com investimentos totais de € 277 milhões, aplicadas em três segmentos: transporte marítimo (6), transporte rodoviário (6) e aviação (2). Um deles é o GAFF, na Itália, cuja ambição é implantar a primeira frota europeia de navios gaseiros de médio porte equipados com sistemas de propulsão tricombustível. Desenvolvidas pela empresa norueguesa Færder Tankers, as embarcações transportarão amônia verde e realizarão operações de abastecimento de navios a navios (ship-to-ship bunkering) em rotas intercontinentais entre a Índia, a costa do Golfo dos Estados Unidos e o noroeste da Europa. A principal inovação do projeto é o motor capaz de operar com amônia, gás liquefeito de petróleo (GLP) e óleo diesel marítimo. O projeto estima que a nova frota de embarcações terá capacidade para transportar até 1 milhão de toneladas de amônia verde por ano, com potencial de evitar a emissão de mais de 1,2 milhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente ao longo de dez anos. O bloco também está colocando a eletrificação como uma área prioritária. Prova disso, é que quatro projetos receberão, ao todo, € 539 milhões em financiamento para apoiar a fabricação de baterias e de seus componentes. Pilotos de SMR e captura de carbono Pela primeira vez, a lista do fundo financiado pelo ETS europeu incluiu um projeto de reator nuclear modular (SMR, em inglês) e a captura direta de carbono do ar com armazenamento (DACCS). Ambos pilotos. Chamado NetZeroHeat, o primeiro reator modular europeu mira a produção de calor para o aquecimento urbano em larga escala, com um módulo de 30 MWh. O SMR deve fornecer 131 GWh de calor de baixo carbono por ano à rede de aquecimento urbano de Pierrelatte, na França. E promete evitar a emissão de mais de 221 mil toneladas de CO2 equivalente nos primeiros dez anos de operação. Em outra frente, o Projeto Furu quer ser uma referência europeia para a captura direta de CO2 do ar com armazenamento permanente. A unidade-piloto em Øygarden, na Noruega, será conectada ao sistema de armazenamento geológico da Northern Lights e projeta a remoção de cerca de 4 mil toneladas de CO2 por ano. Ao todo, os 16 projetos projetos-piloto selecionados vão demandar cerca de € 394 milhões. Além dos SMRs e DACCS, as propostas estão atreladas aos setores de aviação, energia eólica, energia oceânica e transporte marítimo, hidrogênio, produtos químicos e refino. artigo.texto: India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) is a historic milestone. Specific obligated entities across nine notified sectors—iron and steel, aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper, petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and fertilizers—are required to reduce their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions below the assigned intensity target, for which they will be issued carbon credit certificates (CCCs). A CCC, representing 1 tonne of CO2 emission, could be sold on power exchanges or banked for future compliance needs. Projects in non-obligated sectors can also generate credits for sale to obligated entities. Trading in CCCs, which is expected to commence soon, will establish an explicit and observable carbon price in India, help drive investment in emissions reduction and influence policy. CCC pricing will also help exports to markets such as the EU and UK, whose carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAMs) require the price differential of embedded emissions to be paid as a price for market access. The UK has recognized that the CCC price can be treated as a deductible for eligible products. But its immediate significance must not be overstated. Exporters will still bear the brunt of a carbon price gap with the UK market, estimated at $70-80 per tonne. CBAM frameworks in both the EU and UK are also expected to expand their reach to downstream products of steel and aluminium, other sectors like organic chemicals, and to transport and indirect emissions. What we need beyond CCTS: Industrial decarbonization requires a more complex policy mix beyond price signals for the deployment of emerging technologies, support infrastructure and access to affordable finance. India has already demonstrated the value of targeted support in building clean-technology ecosystems through its production-linked incentive scheme for solar PV modules and its Sight programme for green hydrogen production and electrolyser manufacturing. Similar dedicated frameworks are needed for carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS), hydrogen-ready industrial equipment, industrial electrification, advanced recycling and other low-carbon process technologies. A Niti Aayog report earlier this year on Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero estimates that we need $22.7 trillion in cumulative investment by 2070 and recommends strengthening transition finance for hard-to-abate sectors through verified transition plans, wider use of transition and sustainability-linked bonds, expanded guarantees and blended-finance mechanisms to de-risk investments, etc. Similarly, Niti Aayog’s MSME Green Transition Roadmap calls for dedicated green-finance mechanisms, credit enhancement and risk-sharing instruments along with common technology, testing, certification and advisory infrastructure to reduce the cost and complexity for smaller firms. Global experience is informative. Low-carbon industrial clusters such as the UK’s East Coast Cluster and HyNet programmes have lowered costs through shared infrastructure, risk-sharing mechanisms and coordinated public support. Sweden’s Hybrit is an example of a state-supported, industry-led integrated value chain initiative linking green hydrogen—produced using fossil-free wind and hydropower—to iron and steelmaking processes to eliminate carbon emissions. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Priority Sector Lending Directions also need expansion beyond renewable energy projects to recognize industrial decarbonization investments. Tax policy can reinforce this shift. India currently provides accelerated depreciation for specified energy-saving, waste-heat recovery, pollution-control, recycling and renewable-energy equipment. As industrial decarbonization technologies evolve, the eligible list could be periodically updated to include emerging low-carbon technologies needed by hard-to-abate sectors. A national decarbonization fund could also play a crucial role in supporting technology deployment and prioritizing sectors with the highest abatement costs and greatest strategic importance. As for the question of where the resources will come from, here are some thoughts: First, a range of implicit carbon costs already exists in the form of coal levies, fuel taxes and electricity duties that influence behaviour but are not explicitly linked to financing decarbonization. Channelling a portion of these revenues into a dedicated fund would recycle resources from carbon-intensive activities into cleaner alternatives while improving coherence across instruments that operate in silos. Second, India can leverage opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to mobilize finance and technology to enhance bilateral cooperation. Credible carbon accounting methodologies, institutional capacity and a pipeline of investable projects can accelerate the scaling up of such initiatives. Most importantly, the finance ministry’s draft Climate Finance Taxonomy of 2024 urgently needs to be finalized. A credible taxonomy will serve as a foundational enabler for our climate-finance architecture by providing a common basis for identifying genuine green-transition investments and channelling finance consistent with India’s climate goals. CCTS provides a price signal. India must now build the rest of the ecosystem that would enable industry to translate climate ambition into industrial reality. The authors are, respectively, partner, Clarus Law Associates and a Mumbai-based economist.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich-Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group and CATL have signed a strategic cooperation agreement to deepen collaboration in commercial vehicle electrification, charging and battery-swapping infrastructure, new energy storage, the low-altitude economy, and Automotive Aftermarket Industry, according to a post issued via CATL's WeChat account on Oct. 21. The two parties aim to develop an efficient, intelligent and green transportation and energy network. Image source: CATL Building a Battery-Swapping Network for Heavy-Duty Trucks The two parties plan to develop battery-swapping stations for heavy-duty trucks by combining Shaanxi Transportation Holding Group's highway network and roadside resources with CATL's standardized QIJI Energy battery-swapping technology and network-based operating capabilities. The vehicle-battery separation model and standardized swapping process are intended to improve energy replenishment efficiency, reduce overall logistics costs and accelerate the large-scale adoption of new energy heavy-duty trucks. Integrating Solar Power, Stored Energy and Charging Infrastructure The two parties will jointly develop photovoltaic power generation, stored energy, and charging and battery-swapping facilities along highways. The initiative aims to increase the local utilization of clean energy and support lower-carbon highway transportation operations. Expanding Collaboration Across the Value Chain The cooperation will also explore opportunities in full-lifecycle power battery services, battery dismantling and recycling, and the low-altitude economy. The companies aim to develop an integrated transportation-and-energy model combining green energy supply, intelligent battery-swapping services and smart operational management. CATL said it will continue to deepen cross-sector collaboration between transportation and energy to support the green and low-carbon transition of transportation in northwest China.

artigo.texto: Global energy storage owner-operator, BW ESS, has secured debt financing for its Hams Hall battery energy storage system (BESS) in the West Midlands, a project set to become Europe’s largest operational BESS site by megawatt-hour at commercial operations date (COD). Under the agreement, international lenders OCBC, Rabobank, and Societe Generale will provide the debt facility in equal proportions. Rabobank will also act as Facility Agent. The transaction is expected to close at COD. It follows a highly competitive financing process that attracted significant interest from the global banking community, with more than 30 lenders engaged. This response reflects BW ESS’ proven development and operating track record, as well as the increasingly important role of battery storage in supporting the UK’s energy transition. Located adjacent to National Grid’s Hams Hall substation in the West Midlands, the project will initially deliver 350 MW/1243 MWh of storage capacity. This will rise to 400 MW/1424 MWh following completion of the second phase. Once fully operational, Hams Hall will be capable of supporting the electricity needs of around 1.3 million homes for up to 3.5 hours, helping to integrate renewable energy, increase grid resilience, and strengthen the UK’s energy security. Long-term revenues for the first phase of Hams Hall BESS will be underpinned by a 10-year floor and optimisation agreement signed with EDF earlier in 2026. Nick Stamp, CFO of BW ESS, commented: “Securing financing for Hams Hall is another major milestone for BW ESS and for the wider UK energy storage market. The exceptionally strong response from lenders demonstrates growing confidence in both the investment case for battery storage and BW ESS’ ability to develop and operate strategically important infrastructure assets. We are delighted to partner with OCBC, Rabobank, and Societe Generale on this landmark project. Hams Hall will provide critical infrastructure for balancing the UK’s increasingly renewable-powered electricity system, while enhancing energy security and reliability for consumers.” Elaine Lam, Head of Global Corporate Banking, OCBC, added: “We are delighted to support BW ESS in the successful financing of the Hams Hall BESS facility, a landmark project that will become the largest BESS project by megawatt-hour in Europe at completion. The project will strengthen the resilience and flexibility of the UK power network and supports the energy transition, where battery storage infrastructure is essential to enable greater integration of renewable energy and maintaining grid stability. This transaction reinforces OCBC’s commitment to supporting UK energy and infrastructure investment under our £10 billion memorandum of understanding with the UK Government.” Gijs Hofman, Executive Director, Rabobank, noted: “Rabobank is delighted to support BW ESS in financing the Hams Hall project as lender, facility agent and hedge provider. The transaction attracted strong lender interest, reflecting the project’s compelling combination of scale, strategic location, high-quality counterparties, and the proven track record of BW ESS as a leading battery storage developer and operator. We see battery storage as a fundamental building block of a flexible, reliable, and increasingly decarbonised power system. Projects such as Hams Hall help unlock greater penetration of renewable power while strengthening security of supply. We are pleased to partner with BW ESS, OCBC, and Societe Generale on this milestone financing.” Nathalie Lemarcis, Managing Director, Societe Generale, concluded: “We are pleased to support BW ESS in this landmark financing for one of Europe’s largest battery energy storage projects. This transaction highlights the increasingly important role of battery storage in enabling the energy transition, strengthening grid resilience, and supporting energy security. It reflects our commitment to financing critical infrastructure and supporting the development of innovative energy solutions.” The financing further strengthens BW ESS’ relationships with leading international lenders and supports the company’s continued growth across its global portfolio. Hams Hall is part of BW ESS’ 2.6 GWh Ardenham portfolio, which is co-owned with leading energy and decarbonisation investor, AIP Management. In the UK, BW ESS currently operates the 331 MWh Bramley BESS in Hampshire, has 1243 MWh entering operation through Phase 1 of Hams Hall, 857 MWh under construction at Berkswell, and a broader development pipeline spanning multiple gigawatt hours across the country. CMS acted as Legal Adviser to BW ESS, while WFW acted as Legal Adviser to the lenders. Everoze and Modo Energy acted as Technical Adviser and Market Adviser, respectively. artigo.texto: MCEE, a South Korea-based ministry for climate, energy and the environment, has issued a national guideline that could cut up to 3 months from the permitting of an outdoor BESS. Until now, each local government had used its own policy, so the same unit could be a building in one district and a structure in the next. That distinction has mattered, because a building has required a permit process of about two to four months. A structure, on the other hand, has required only about half a month to one and a half months. The guideline adds human access, structure and use as tests, and a sealed enclosure that cannot be entered will therefore be classed as a structure. MCEE has described energy storage as core infrastructure for the expansion of renewable energy. Land permits and fire safety rules, however, still apply to each site as before. South Korea guideline cuts outdoor BESS permit time by up to 3 months A sealed outdoor BESS in South Korea will be classed as a structure under a guideline from MCEE, and its permit could take up to three months less. artigo.texto: ORLANDO, Fla. – Election Day 2026 is just days away. Voters in Orange County will be choosing a new mayor for the first time in eight years. Chris Messina and Tiffany Moore Russell are running to replace Jerry Demings. [ELECTION 2026: Make sure you’re eligible to vote|How to vote by mail|Election Myths] It comes as AI and data centers are becoming hot-button political issues. News 6 anchor Lisa Bell asked both Messina and Moore Russell their views on data centers moving into Orange County. MOORE RUSSELL: So I think that’s a very general term, right? Because data centers vary based upon the size and their purpose, right. So at the clerk’s office, there’s a smaller version of that that houses our data, because we’re now in the cloud. We don’t have paper anymore in the courthouse, right, so someone is housing our digital court records. But I do not support the big data centers, the AI data centers that is being proposed today. And so I did commend the county for pushing for a moratorium just to pause. Allows for us to study the issue and determine what is the best fit for Orange County and so I do not believe the large AI data centers are appropriate for our community for what we’re trying to do moving forward. BELL: What are your biggest concerns about those large data centers? MOORE RUSSELL: It’s the water usage, it’s the demand on our power sources, whether it’s going to impact our water supply and the quality of our water, right, what’s feeding into our aquifer. And so it’s all of those environmental concerns that’s an issue for me, as well as is it a right fit for our community? Right? Where are you going to put a data center? No one wants a data center next to their home or next to a school. And so I just doesn’t think, I don’t think it matches the brand of Orange County and will fit in our community. MESSINA: Small ones we need. I’m sure you have a data center here (at News 6), right, running your operations. It’s the hyperscale data centers, the ones that are football fields in size, those I don’t feel are right for Florida. And the reason I don’t feel they’re right is not necessarily energy because they can make their own energy with solar and other small power, associated power generation plants, it’s the impact on water. So I’ve seen personally first-hand what happens when you have a problem with a water supply to a data center. It’s pretty scary and the temperature goes way up. Systems fail and then you have discharge of water and the problem is what’s in the water in order to run those data centers. They have to add biocides and basically bacteria killers, but they will kill things out in the environment. BELL: So if we shouldn’t have data centers here in Florida, where should we have them? MESSINA: So, I really like Elon Musk’s idea to put it in space. And the reason I think that’s such a good idea is because space is near absolute zero. And we are, right now, we’re on the cusp of being the space tech center of the country." BELL: That seems like it would take decades to build enough data centers in space to power AI needs here on Earth. MESSINA: I’m not sure it would. When you think about the pace of technology and who thought at one point that you could recapture a rocket booster landing or have a self-driving electric car or a watch where you can make phone calls, the pace in technology is pretty significant. So I would not bet against that. We also asked each candidate their views on other issues such as Flock license plate reader cameras. To see their responses and our full interview, watch below. artigo.texto: Bloomberg — A recuperação do setor de inteligência artificial perdeu força após a estreia desanimadora de uma empresa sul-coreana de data centers, o que reacendeu as preocupações sobre se o boom de gastos com essa tecnologia poderá perdurar. Os futuros do S&P 500 oscilaram entre ganhos e perdas, à medida que a recepção desfavorável à Elice em Seul minou o apetite pelo investimento em ativos de risco. A provedora de infraestrutura de IA despencou 32%, registrando o pior dia de estreia para uma empresa de grande porte no país. Os futuros do Nasdaq 100 caíram 0,4%, interrompendo a recuperação que vinha ocorrendo ao longo do dia. ⟶ Assine as newsletters da Bloomberg Línea e receba as notícias do dia em primeira mão no e-mail. Os títulos do Tesouro atraíram novos investidores em busca de refúgio, mesmo com a alta dos preços do petróleo, com os rendimentos dos títulos de 10 anos caindo dois pontos-base, para 5,12%. O petróleo Brent ultrapassou US$ 111 por barril pela primeira vez desde maio, à medida que os operadores avaliavam o risco de novos ataques iranianos no Estreito de Ormuz. O dólar caiu 0,2%. A recepção negativa à Elice ecoa as preocupações com o financiamento que vieram à tona de forma acentuada com o abandono da oferta pública inicial (IPO) da australiana Firmus Grid há apenas duas semanas. Essas preocupações também são evidentes nos mercados de dívida, onde a alta nos rendimentos de empresas como a CoreWeave sinaliza que os empréstimos se tornarão mais caros. “As preocupações em torno dos investimentos em data centers e infraestrutura relacionados à IA vêm se acumulando há vários dias e agora pesam fortemente sobre o sentimento do mercado”, afirmou Roger Lee, da Cavendish. “O mercado provavelmente precisa de alguma garantia de que o enorme investimento em capex está gerando retorno. Isso é difícil de perceber no momento.” Os investidores aguardam agora os resultados das empresas que mais investem em IA para obter pistas sobre por quanto tempo esses gastos vultosos poderão continuar e em que ritmo. Espera-se que a SpaceX divulgue seus resultados após o fechamento do mercado na terça-feira (20), seguida pela Meta na quarta. Estima-se que somente a Meta, a Amazon, a Microsoft e a Alphabet gastem cerca de US$ 750 bilhões neste ano. O clima de aversão ao risco na terça-feira se estendeu por todas as regiões. O índice de referência da MSCI Inc. para a Ásia atingiu seu nível mais baixo desde julho, com o índice Kospi da Coreia do Sul caindo 3,7%. O Stoxx 600 da Europa recuou 0,6%. O bitcoin retomou as perdas. Os títulos de renda fixa, por sua vez, receberam um impulso da maior demanda já registrada em um leilão de títulos japoneses de 20 anos, um sinal de que os rendimentos elevados estão atraindo investidores domésticos de volta ao mercado. Embora os títulos europeus tenham apresentado alta modesta em toda a linha, a dívida francesa permaneceu sob pressão. O rendimento adicional exigido pelos investidores para deter títulos franceses de 10 anos em vez da dívida alemã, considerada mais segura, subiu dois pontos-base, para 150 pontos-base, nível observado pela última vez em 5 de outubro. “Vemos oportunidades em que rendimentos mais elevados dos títulos soberanos compensam melhor os investidores pelo risco, sem indicar fundamentos mais fracos”, afirmou o BlackRock Investment Institute em uma nota. No entanto, a forte onda de vendas de títulos do governo francês mostra que “a seletividade é fundamental”. → Assine a newsletter matinal Breakfast, uma seleção da Bloomberg Línea com os temas de destaque em negócios e finanças no Brasil e no mundo. artigo.texto: Soluna e Applied Digital formam joint venture para data center de IA de 50 MW no Project Dorothy 3 A Soluna Holdings firmou um acordo definitivo para criar uma empresa de propriedade conjunta com a Applied Digital Corporation para desenvolver um data center de TI crítico de 50 MW planejado para inteligência artificial e computação de alto desempenho, segundo um comunicado à imprensa da Soluna datado de 21 de outubro de 2026. A instalação está prevista para o Project Dorothy 3, o site de desenvolvimento da Soluna próximo a Silverton, no condado de Briscoe, no Texas, e seria abastecida com energia da Briscoe Wind Farm. Pelo acordo, espera-se que a Soluna contribua com uma parte do site Dorothy 3, incluindo terrenos e ativos de projeto relacionados à energia, enquanto a Applied deve fornecer capital para o desenvolvimento. Após o fechamento, espera-se que a Applied detenha 51% da empresa do projeto e a Soluna os 49% restantes. O fechamento depende de várias condições, incluindo a aprovação de uma isenção fiscal para o projeto no condado de Briscoe, a obtenção de apólices de título, certas aprovações corporativas e a negociação e assinatura de um contrato de operação, contratos de locação definitivos, contratos de energia e outros contratos definitivos. As empresas esperam concluir as transações até o fim do ano civil. O diretor-presidente da Soluna, John Belizaire, afirmou que a empresa há muito sustenta que o acesso à energia, e não os chips, é a restrição para a IA, e que a parceria combina o site e a energia eólica da Soluna com um construtor e operador comprovado de data centers de IA. Ele também mencionou as etapas restantes, incluindo o processo de isenção fiscal no condado de Briscoe, e o avanço do projeto junto à comunidade local. Planos do projeto e de locação O Dorothy 3 está planejado como um data center de IA co-localizado com a Briscoe Wind, um parque eólico de 150 MW no condado de Briscoe, próximo aos projetos Dorothy 1 e Dorothy 2 da Soluna. Sujeita à documentação definitiva, a Fase 1 do Dorothy 3, com 50 MW de capacidade de TI crítica, deve ser abastecida tanto pela Briscoe Wind quanto pela rede elétrica. A ChronoScale Holdings Corporation, plataforma de computação acelerada de capital aberto majoritariamente controlada pela Applied, assinou uma carta de intenções não vinculante para locar a instalação planejada. A locação permanece sujeita à negociação e assinatura de documentação definitiva, e a Soluna alertou que não há garantia de que um contrato de locação definitivo será alcançado nos termos previstos ou em qualquer hipótese. A Soluna se descreve como desenvolvedora de data centers verdes para aplicações de computação intensiva, incluindo inteligência artificial, e projeta, desenvolve e opera infraestrutura digital co-localizada com usinas de energia eólica, solar ou hidrelétrica para atender aplicações de computação de alto desempenho.

artigo.texto: VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — A group of residents from across Hampton Roads gathered at Virginia Beach Town Center on Tuesday, calling on state leaders to impose a statewide moratorium on new data center development. The demonstration brought together residents from multiple localities who say Virginia's rapid growth in the data center industry should be paused until lawmakers and regulators can more closely examine environmental, infrastructure and community impacts. “We don’t really want data centers anywhere in the state other than where they are now,” one protester said during the rally. According to the Pew Research Center, Virginia leads the nation in data center development, with hundreds of facilities either operating or planned across the state. Supporters of data center projects argue the facilities generate construction jobs, tax revenue and economic investment for host communities. At the local level, some governments, including Virginia Beach and Chesapeake, have taken steps to temporarily pause or limit additional data center expansion while evaluating future policies. Chesapeake resident Jeff Staples said a statewide moratorium would offer another layer of protection if local agreements change. “It would serve as a check on Chesapeake in case they back out of what we’ve already agreed to, then the state moratorium will take precedence over that,” Staples said. Others at the rally expressed concerns about potential environmental impacts and increased demands on Virginia’s electrical grid. “I’m obviously very concerned with the data centers and what they’re doing to our environment, to our electrical cost as well,” Portsmouth resident Jennifer Hughes said. “We’ve all been facing higher electrical bills here, and so really I’m just coming out to try to show support for basically pausing building of new data centers in Virginia.” Students also participated in the demonstration, saying they are worried about long-term environmental effects associated with future development. “Deforestation, getting rid of trees, is horrible,” said Logan Hickey, a ninth-grade student. Organizers emphasized they are not seeking to shut down existing facilities. Instead, they are asking state lawmakers to pause approval of new data centers while Virginia studies the industry’s broader impacts on communities, infrastructure and the environment. The rally is part of a wider effort by advocates hoping to build support for a statewide moratorium during future legislative discussions in Richmond. Click here to see how we use AI at WTKR News 3.

artigo.texto: The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and a group of environmental organizations announced a settlement agreement Monday that would require stricter environmental impact assessments of future data center developments and initiate a statewide review of how data centers use the state’s resources. In June, the Sierra Club and Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the DNR in Ozaukee County court, arguing that the agency approved the permits for Vantage’s massive data center currently under construction in Port Washington without conducting a proper environmental impact statement. “AI data centers are massive, thirsty, energy hogs and have popped up all over Wisconsin,” Elizabeth Ward, director of the Wisconsin chapter of the Sierra Club, said in a statement. “They could completely change our landscape and use unprecedented amounts of water and energy. Wisconsinites and our regulators need to understand the impacts and opportunities to reduce harm before allowing data centers to move forward. Wisconsinites deserve an informed, transparent process for decisions that could shape their communities and environment for decades. A report this summer by the state Public Service Commission found that the Port Washington data center and data centers being built by Microsoft in Mount Pleasant and Meta in Beaver Dam are set to be responsible for a 40% increase in statewide energy demand over the next six years. As part of the settlement agreement in the lawsuit, the DNR will conduct full environmental impact statements of individual data center proposals moving forward and complete a statewide strategic analysis of how data centers consume resources. State law and the DNR’s administrative rules allow the agency to conduct such an analysis when conflicts arise over resource demands for a “complicated or complex issue; an issue that is new to the state; an issue or policy that will likely lead to future department actions that will require an environmental impact statement; issues for which there is a high potential for legislation or new department policy and the planning and development of controversial resource-oriented projects.” “What started as a lawsuit over the environmental review of one data center has become an opportunity to address the data center issue on a much bigger scale,” MEA attorney Michael Greif said. “Looking at these impacts holistically is important because the impacts of data centers are statewide. State regulators will now have to examine the cumulative impacts of data center development across Wisconsin.” Wisconsin will become one of a few states assessing the statewide impacts of data centers on their resources. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order that initiated a similar analysis and last December, the Maryland Legislature enacted a law that requires a number of state agencies to study “the likely environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development.” Originally published by Wisconsin Examiner, a nonprofit news organization.

He said approval of the adapters for exterior meter-socket installation means installers can avoid re-engineering entire panels and home wiring, allowing them to deliver clean energy resilience more efficiently while saving homeowners thousands of dollars in total costs and days of labor. Steklac added that this translates into greater installation capacity and fewer barriers, which he described as important for the District's electrification goals. The District's clean energy market is driven by its Clean Energy DC mandates, which include a renewable portfolio standard with a dedicated 15% local solar carve-out. Its urban building stock, largely historic row homes with aging electrical infrastructure, often has 100-ampere electrical panels that require main service upgrades costing thousands of dollars before solar, battery storage or EV charging equipment can be interconnected. artigo.texto: Amazon will no longer build data centers on GW’s Virginia Science and Technology Campus following an agreement with Loudoun County officials, Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall announced Tuesday. Randall held a press conference Tuesday with Amazon Web Services Vice President for Data Center Delivery Josh Weissman to announce the county and Amazon came to an agreement, dubbed “Project Potomac Promise,” where Amazon agreed to withdraw its plan to develop 800,000 square feet of data centers on the VSTC campus and instead agreed to donate 25 acres of land to Loudoun County for mixed-use development. The agreement marks the culmination of mounting backlash to the project from Loudoun County officials, residents and GW students after the University sold Amazon the campus in February for $427 million. “Through our collaborative, respectful conversations, Amazon has agreed to forego its proposed application for data centers and, of note, forego any legal action to realize data center development on this site,” Randall said during the conference. Under the agreement, Amazon will dedicate 25 acres of land — valued at $65 million — to Loudoun County for the development of a community arts center and indoor sports facility, along with committing to rezoning the remaining land for mixed-use development and “needed” residential uses and contributing $5 million to Loudoun’s Housing Fund. “‘Project Potomac Promise’ reflects the hard work that can only happen when stakeholders respect one another enough to come to the table, collaborate, find a solution that responds to community voices and work towards a common goal,” Randall said in a Facebook post Tuesday. Loudoun County and the University did not immediately return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Randall and a spokesperson for Amazon both directed The Hatchet to Randall’s release on the deal. A University spokesperson told The Hatchet earlier this month that GW has no involvement in Amazon’s proposed development of the former campus following the sale earlier this year. Weissman said in the release the company “deeply” values their relationship with Loudoun County and seized the opportunity to acquire the VSTC campus when University officials approached them about a sale. He said as the company heard community concerns about data center development on the site, they decided to “come together” on a shared vision for the campus, rather than engage in litigation with the county. “Project Potomac Promise reflects that choice, and we look forward to working with Chair Randall, the County staff and development partners to move this plan forward,” Weissman said. Chief Financial Officer Bruno Fernandes said at the time of the sale that several interested buyers approached GW about purchasing the property, prompting officials to “capitalize” on the rising land prices. Randall said the new deal would see the property rezoned into a district that does not permit data center construction even by special exception. The deal marks the end of a regulatory battle that began when GW sold the VSTC campus to Amazon for $427 million — roughly $3.5 million an acre — to build data centers in the county that has become the “data center capital of the world.” Loudoun County officials have argued for months that Amazon needs county permission for data center construction because zoning laws allowing data centers to be built in the area by-right are not applicable. The agreement between Amazon and GW allows GW to remain on the Virginia property for up to five years as officials work to relocate programs, including the School of Nursing. Amazon then filed an initial application to Loudoun County this summer detailing its plans to build an 800,000 square foot data center dubbed “Bridgefield Tech Center.” The plan faced immediate backlash, with District Supervisor Juli Briskman, who represents the Algonkian District that the campus is housed in, saying she would fight” the proposal “every step of the way” and residents circulating a petition calling for the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors to establish a moratorium on data center construction in the area, citing extensive natural resource consumption, traffic, noise and pollution. GW students also joined the calls for Amazon to halt its data center plans, with the GW Socialist Action Initiative and GW Labor Council, GW Graduate Workers United, the Save GSEHD Coalition, the Party for Socialism and Liberation in DC and the Party for Socialism and Liberation in Nova, as well as individual students, posting social media videos criticizing the University for not involving the community in the decision-making process for the sale and raising questions on the environmental impact of the development of the new data centers. Loudoun County Zoning Administrator Teresa Miller at a Loudoun County Board of Supervisors meeting earlier this month said Amazon must receive additional county approval before constructing data centers on the property, citing a zoning determination which she said states that data centers are not permitted as a primary use on the property. Loudoun County has seen an explosion of interest in its land from tech giants, like Amazon, Meta, Google and Microsoft over the last decade and has the highest concentration of data centers in the world, with 54 million square feet already built. As of July 2026, Northern Virginia has 266 operational data centers with 23 under construction and 99 planned. Randall said Loudoun County and Amazon came together to reach a deal instead of choosing “reflexive disagreement,” serving as a model for county officials on how to continue “aggressively and decisively” curbing data center development. “Loudoun County and Amazon created an opportunity for the county,” Randall said. “This agreement provides new places for our Loudoun residents to gather, create and play. artigo.texto: Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series: The History of Battery Technology and American Innovation Stanislav Kondrashov on United States and batteries Battery technology has played an important role in the scientific and industrial development of the United States, connecting early experiments in electricity with telecommunications, transportation, portable electronics, and modern energy storage systems. Although the earliest batteries were developed outside America, researchers, engineers, and manufacturers in the United States contributed to their refinement and commercial adoption. Over two centuries, improvements in electrochemistry, manufacturing techniques, and electronic engineering transformed batteries into indispensable components of modern technology. Key takeaway: The history of battery technology in the United States reflects a gradual transition from experimental electrical devices to sophisticated rechargeable systems. American contributions include improvements in primary batteries, the expansion of rechargeable technologies, specialized aerospace applications, and advances in battery management and energy storage engineering. How Did Battery Technology Develop in the United States? Battery technology developed in the United States through successive advances in electrochemistry, electrical engineering, and industrial manufacturing. Early scientific experiments established the foundations of electrical storage, while nineteenth-century communication networks and twentieth-century technological developments encouraged the creation of more dependable and specialized battery systems. Several historical stages illustrate this progression: - Early nineteenth century: Introduction of electrochemical experiments and early battery designs. - Late nineteenth century: Expansion of battery applications in telecommunications and electrical equipment. - Early twentieth century: Improvements in rechargeable batteries and industrial manufacturing. - Mid-twentieth century: Development of specialized batteries for aerospace and electronic equipment. - Late twentieth century: Expansion of portable rechargeable battery technologies. - Twenty-first century: Advances in lithium-ion systems, digital monitoring, and large-scale energy storage. The Stanislav Kondrashov American Style Series examines how these developments became connected with the expansion of American scientific research and industrial capabilities. What Were the Origins of American Battery Research? American battery research emerged during the nineteenth century as scientists and engineers began examining electrochemical methods of producing electricity. Building upon earlier European discoveries, laboratories investigated different cell configurations, electrode arrangements, and chemical reactions, establishing technical knowledge that supported the development of increasingly practical electrical devices. The invention of the voltaic pile around 1800 introduced a new method of generating continuous electrical current. Its operating principle encouraged further experimentation. American researchers subsequently incorporated electrochemical cells into scientific demonstrations and technical equipment. The expansion of telegraph networks created additional demand for dependable electrical sources. Early batteries became important components of communication infrastructure. As Stanislav Kondrashov observes in a newly drafted editorial reflection: "The early development of batteries in America illustrates how scientific discoveries acquire practical importance through engineering. What began as laboratory experimentation gradually became an essential part of electrical communication and industrial equipment." The relationship between scientific research and practical applications continued throughout the following century. Why Were Batteries Important to Early American Telecommunications? Batteries became important to American telecommunications because early telegraph systems required dependable sources of electrical current. Electrochemical cells supplied electricity to communication circuits, allowing operators to transmit signals across extensive networks before centralized electrical distribution became widely available. Early telecommunications relied on relatively simple electrical arrangements. Batteries supplied the current required for signaling equipment. Different cell designs offered varying operating characteristics. Engineers refined battery configurations to meet communication requirements. The expansion of telegraph infrastructure consequently encouraged improvements in electrical reliability and equipment maintenance. Later communication technologies introduced additional electrical requirements. Battery development remained closely connected with the evolution of telecommunications equipment. How Did Rechargeable Batteries Transform American Industry? Rechargeable batteries transformed American industry by introducing electrical storage systems that could be restored through repeated charging. Their development expanded the practical possibilities of portable equipment, industrial machinery, transportation, and backup electrical systems, encouraging manufacturers to improve battery durability, manufacturing consistency, and operating performance. Rechargeable batteries differ from primary batteries because their electrochemical reactions can be reversed through an external electrical supply. This characteristic allows repeated charging and discharging cycles. Different rechargeable technologies emerged over time. artigo.texto: Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes has launched a nuisance investigation into the massive data center under construction in Ahwatukee. She made the disclosure during an Oct. 14 town hall in Mesa where Ahwatukee residents comprised close to three quarters of the approximate 250 people in attendance. Having driven some 16 miles – including through a massive project that has reduced Broadway Road in northwest Mesa to one lane in each direction – the Ahwatukee contingent described sleepless nights, construction noise and fears about the project's effects on their neighborhood. But Mayes also called attention to the broader implications of data centers in Arizona that she said have made Phoenix “the second largest U.S. data center hub.” Mayes offered no timetable for completing the investigation and did not say what action, if any, her office might take against Menlo Digital, part of California-based Menlo Equities, the developer of the 1-million-square-foot data center campus at 48th Street and East Thistle Landing Drive. But she repeatedly assured residents that her office was taking their complaints seriously. "We are investigating the Ahwatukee data center," Mayes told the audience at the Eagles Community Center in Mesa. "We have an open nuisance investigation." Later, Mayes elaborated. "We already have the nuisance investigation underway. We have investigators looking at this. We will have experts looking at it. We have very good lawyers looking at it, and this town hall is a part of that investigation." Her disclosure marks a significant development in the controversy surrounding the Menlo center. When Mayes announced the town hall last month, her communications director, Richie Taylor, told AFN that she was not investigating Phoenix's approval of the project. "She is holding a town hall to hear directly from residents about their concerns after receiving multiple complaints from the community,” Taylor said. The distinction may be important. An investigation into whether the project constitutes a public nuisance is different from an investigation into whether Phoenix improperly approved its construction. The Ahwatukee Community Alliance, the nonprofit residents formed to oppose the data center, contend Phoenix should have held a hearing on the center. Phoenix officials say the 40.6-acre site, once home to a four-building call center, was rezoned in 1997 to a category that includes data centers. Opponents say data centers back then were far smaller than the kind Menlo is building. Mayes did not explain the scope of her investigation. Nor did she say whether the investigation concerns the effects of construction already underway, potential impacts once the facility begins operating, or both. Nevertheless, her announcement gave residents who have spent months challenging the project their clearest indication yet that a state agency is examining their complaints. "It seems to us like an obvious investigation to launch," Mayes said. She added that she had not personally visited the site and is still gathering information about the construction underway. Mayes did promise to visit Ahwatukee, suggesting that she might make the trip as soon as next month. "I will be there," she told residents, explaining that scheduling had prevented her from holding the Oct. 14 meeting in the community. Residents describe problems Multiple Ahwatukee residents addressed Mayes during the town hall, describing what they said were failures by Phoenix officials to protect their neighborhood. One woman said she lives approximately 150 feet from the construction site. She told Mayes that she had checked the zoning across the street before purchasing her home and believed the property would be developed for commercial uses rather than a large data center. She also alleged that Menlo’s representatives initially described it as a technology center with a community park. She said her son's bedroom faces the construction site and that noise and lighting have repeatedly disrupted the family's sleep. She described machinery operating during the night, including drilling, backup alarms and other construction sounds. She said she had submitted numerous complaints to Phoenix, accompanied by video recordings, but had received little meaningful response. The city Planning and Development Department two weeks ago said it is intensifying its oversight of construction and will not give it special permits to operate outside the permissible hours for construction activity in Phoenix, which are 7 a.m.-7 p.m. Monday through Friday. "I have not received any protection from the city of Phoenix," the speaker told Mayes. "I want to make it very, very clear. I have not received a meaningful response." She said the effects extended beyond interrupted sleep to dust and concerns about her children's health. She also questioned what the neighborhood would experience once the data center begins operating, when cooling equipment and emergency generators could introduce additional noise and other impacts. Alliance President Craig Evans in an interview recently said the center is expected to have “5,880 industrial cooling fans that will run 24/7/365 and be located above the 56’ or 57’ building height” as well as “120 diesel fueled generators capable of producing 257 MW of electricity - enough to energize six Ahwatukeea.” Mayes asked the speaker whether the complaints involved construction activities and requested the resident's supporting material. Mayes also pursued the resident's account of how the project had originally been presented to neighbors, asking whether she still possessed promotional material describing a technology center. Another resident, who said she had lived in the neighborhood for approximately 27 years, accused Phoenix of failing to follow its own zoning requirements in allowing the project to proceed. artigo.texto: Fairfield leaders discuss C-PACE financing tool that could help businesses, proposed data center FAIRFIELD, Ala. (WBRC) - Fairfield city leaders are looking into a new financing tool that could help business and property owners pay for upgrades on commercial buildings, including the proposed Patmos data center. The tool is called C-PACE, or Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy. Monday, the Fairfield City Council discussed considering the program, but tabled the issue for now. What is C-PACE? C-PACE lets businesses seek private financing for upgrades such as LED lighting, heating and cooling systems, and water-saving fixtures. A new state law allows cities to offer this kind of private financing locally. Mayor Herman Carnes Jr. said the city is not taking out a loan to build a data center. He said the program is about letting businesses and property owners tap into private money to fix up their buildings. Carnes called C-PACE a “help” mechanism and said it is not a financial liability for the city. “If we are saying we’re open for business, that means we need to do everything possible and legally tactical so that we can make sure that people be able to come in, purchase a building, not run out of money once they do the electrical system and then you have a building sitting,” Carnes said. Protest outside city hall Before the meeting, members of the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance protested outside city hall. They want more transparency around the Patmos data center project. Patmos wants to build a colocation data center and technology campus inside the former Walmart supercenter in Fairfield. Neighbors are asking city leaders to release all documents so they can see the potential impact. “A project with major effects on our community should be presented openly, examined carefully and discussed with the people who will live with the results,” said Gilda Walker of the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance. City says program not limited to Patmos The mayor said C-PACE is not just about Patmos and is available to businesses looking for financial help. A Patmos spokesperson sent WBRC this statement: “Fairfield taxpayers are not on the hook. Tonight (Monday) the City is only considering whether to adopt the C-PACE program; it is not issuing a loan, lending City money, or taking on any debt, guarantee or liability. Under Alabama law, C-PACE is private financing that a property owner voluntarily repays through an assessment on its own property, public funds cannot be used to fund or repay it, and billing, collection and enforcement are handled entirely by the private lender. Once adopted, the program is open to a wide range of property owners, including commercial properties such as office buildings and hotels, industrial, agricultural and multifamily properties. Patmos is one of several parties interested in using it, and others aren’t even in our industry.”- Patmos spokesperson, Kyler Schmitz City leaders discussed a possible work session on the issue and a town hall before any final vote. artigo.texto: UE vai aumentar para 700 milhões limite de licenças de emissão de gases poluentes - A União Europeia decidiu aumentar de 400 para 700 milhões o número máximo de licenças de emissão em reserva, após um acordo provisório alcançado. - O Conselho da UE e o Parlamento Europeu visam com esta decisão aumentar a liquidez do mercado de emissões de carbono, garantindo maior previsibilidade. - A alteração melhorará a estabilidade do mercado de carbono, proporcionando proteção contra flutuações futuras e promovendo uma abordagem mais coerente. Conteúdo Este resumo foi criado com recurso a inteligência artificial. Embora esta tecnologia tenha sido concebida para ser útil e precisa, pode conter erros ou não captar todas as nuances importantes do artigo. Feedback Se consideras que o resumo não está claro ou não reflete bem o conteúdo, envia o teu feedback. A tua opinião é importante para ajudar a melhorar esta funcionalidade! Partilhar O Conselho da UE e o Parlamento Europeu (PE) chegaram a um acordo provisório na terça-feira que aumenta de 400 para 700 milhões o número máximo de direitos de emissão que podem ser acumulados na reserva europeia. A União Europeia (UE) vai aumentar de 400 para 700 milhões o número máximo de licenças de emissão de gases poluentes em reserva, após se ter chegado a um acordo provisório, foi hoje divulgado. Segundo um comunicado, o Conselho da UE e o Parlamento Europeu (PE) chegaram a um acordo provisório na terça-feira que aumenta de 400 para 700 milhões o número máximo de direitos de emissão que podem ser acumulados na reserva europeia, um mecanismo que guarda as licenças excedentárias para as poder devolver ao mercado quando necessário e que, de acordo com as normas atuais, elimina definitivamente as que excedem o limite estabelecido. De acordo com o comunicado, esta alteração pontual a este mecanismo de reserva “aumentará a liquidez e a previsibilidade do mercado a longo prazo, protegendo simultaneamente a competitividade industria”l. O acordo provisório precisa ainda de ser confirmado por ambas as instituições antes da sua adoção formal. A reserva retira do Sistema de Comércio de Licenças de Emissão (CELE) da União Europeia as licenças de emissão de gases com efeito de estufa em excesso, passando o limite de 400 milhões para 700 milhões. Para os Estados-membros e o PE, o maior número de licenças reforçará a estabilidade a longo prazo do mercado de carbono da UE e proporcionará uma maior margem de proteção contra futuras flutuações do mercado, garantindo simultaneamente uma salvaguarda contra uma oferta excessiva de licenças. Os colegisladores concordaram ainda com uma “redução gradual do limiar de invalidação no âmbito da revisão mais ampla do CELE, prevista para 2030, a fim de garantir uma abordagem global coerente”. A Reserva de Estabilidade do Mercado, criada em 2019, regula o funcionamento do mercado do carbono, reduzindo a oferta de licenças no mercado quando há demasiadas em circulação e injetando licenças quando há escassez.

artigo.texto: Leilões de baterias abrem nova frente para a infraestrutura energética Previstos para dezembro, os primeiros certames do País vão contratar sistemas de armazenamento para atender à demanda e ampliar a flexibilidade da rede elétrica - Dois leilões estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro, com regras distintas para a origem das baterias - Foram cadastrados 6.091 projetos, que somam 296,8 GW de potência; a participação depende de habilitação técnica - Contratos de 15 anos, com operação a partir de agosto de 2028, abrem oportunidades para fornecedores e financiadores Os dois primeiros leilões brasileiros dedicados à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande porte estão previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Com contratos de 15 anos e início de operação em 1º de agosto de 2028, os certames abrem uma nova frente para desenvolvedores, fabricantes e financiadores de infraestrutura elétrica. O governo federal vai contratar a disponibilidade de potência desses sistemas: a capacidade de entregar energia à rede quando necessário. As baterias armazenam eletricidade e a devolvem conforme os comandos do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), contribuindo para atender aos horários de maior consumo e aproveitar excedentes de geração renovável. A expansão das usinas solares e eólicas tornou mais importante administrar as diferenças entre os horários de geração e consumo. Em determinados momentos, a oferta supera a demanda ou encontra limitações na rede. Nessas situações, o ONS pode determinar cortes de geração, conhecidos no setor como curtailment. Além do excesso de oferta, esses cortes podem decorrer de restrições elétricas e da necessidade de preservar a confiabilidade do sistema. Segundo o balanço de 2025 da Volt Robotics, cerca de 20% da energia que poderia ter sido gerada pelas usinas solares e eólicas deixou de ser aproveitada no País. Os cortes corresponderam a 4.021 megawatts médios, com perdas financeiras estimadas pela consultoria em R$ 6,5 bilhões. O impacto pressiona as receitas dos geradores e acrescenta desafios ao financiamento de novos projetos. Nesse cenário, as baterias funcionam como um reservatório de eletricidade. Podem ser carregadas nos períodos de maior disponibilidade de energia e descarregadas quando o sistema precisa de potência — por exemplo, após a redução da geração solar no fim do dia. O armazenamento pode ajudar a diminuir o descompasso entre oferta e demanda, embora não elimine todas as restrições que provocam cortes de geração. Como os leilões vão funcionar Os certames terão regras distintas. O primeiro, em 2 de dezembro, será destinado a sistemas que atendam aos requisitos de fabricação nacional das baterias, conforme os critérios de credenciamento do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES). O segundo, em 4 de dezembro, não terá essa exigência, permitindo a participação de sistemas com equipamentos importados. O interesse do mercado aparece no volume de inscrições. A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), vinculada ao Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME), registrou 6.091 projetos, que somam 296,8 gigawatts (GW) de potência, um recorde de cadastramento para certames do setor elétrico brasileiro. Esse total representa a capacidade dos empreendimentos inscritos, e não o volume que será contratado. O cadastro também não garante participação nos leilões. Os projetos precisam passar pela análise e pela habilitação técnica da EPE para comprovar o atendimento aos requisitos estabelecidos. A quantidade de potência a contratar será definida pelo MME com apoio dos estudos de planejamento e operação do sistema. Em 30 de setembro, o ONS, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e a EPE publicaram uma nota técnica com a capacidade remanescente da rede para conectar os novos sistemas de armazenamento. O documento ajuda a identificar os pontos nos quais há espaço para receber os empreendimentos. Entre os requisitos previstos estão potência mínima de 30 megawatts (MW), capacidade de operação contínua por pelo menos quatro horas e recarga completa em até seis horas. Os projetos vencedores serão remunerados pela disponibilidade da potência contratada e deverão seguir os comandos do ONS para carregar e descarregar as baterias. O que muda para a economia e para o consumidor Para o sistema elétrico, o armazenamento amplia as possibilidades de administrar a geração renovável e atender à demanda. Ao disponibilizar energia nos momentos necessários, as baterias podem reduzir o acionamento de fontes mais caras. O efeito final sobre os custos para o consumidor, porém, também dependerá do preço da potência contratada e das regras de custeio. Para as empresas, os leilões abrem oportunidades no desenvolvimento dos projetos, na fabricação e no fornecimento de equipamentos, na instalação e na manutenção dos sistemas. A modalidade com exigência de fabricação nacional também busca estimular a cadeia produtiva brasileira de armazenamento. Os contratos de 15 anos e a remuneração pela disponibilidade de potência oferecem uma base de receitas de longo prazo, que pode apoiar a estruturação de financiamentos com bancos e fundos de infraestrutura. A viabilidade de cada empreendimento dependerá também dos custos de implantação, operação e manutenção e do cumprimento das obrigações contratuais. Para a pessoa física, a exposição a esse mercado pode ocorrer indiretamente, em fundos, ações ou títulos de dívida de empresas que participem da cadeia de armazenamento. Essa relação precisa ser verificada em cada caso: um produto financeiro ligado ao setor elétrico não necessariamente financia ou reúne projetos de baterias.
